chapters.text:
Under Blue

Skies

A Collection of Love Stories

BLEX WAKABI

To have loved and lost is better than to have never loved at all.

D E D I C A T I O N

Dedicated to my family, friends and all those who love despite it all. Some of you were my muses and my inspiration.

Under Blue Skies

under the vastness of the blue, shadows dance in the corners of our dreams, we build our stories woven into the fabric of summer afternoons.

here, laughter dances on the breeze, we carve our names into fleeting clouds.

memories linger like fireflies at dusk, wildflowers dance at your bare feet, each bloom a tiny love letter to you.

the river sings a melody just for you, sunlight kisses your upturned face, time slows to a sigh.

but they gather to take away our blue skies, amidst the raging winds, we stand unbowed, we stand tall against life's storms— as we weather the tempests of uncertainty.

in its embrace, strength we realize, for every dawn follows darkest day.

we'll see the stars, illuminating moments when fate's gentle hand guided us through adversity's tangled vines, reminding us that beauty blooms in struggle.

and as seasons shift like soft whispers, hearts unburdened by shadows of yesterday, we walk forward, hand in hand, under the vastness of the blue— where hope forever lingers.

with every sunset, comes a promise, there will be a sunrise, let us gather these stories under these blue skies

chapters.title: I Will Never Hit You
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

As they sat together, weaving beautiful lies about a tomorrow filled with love and fairy-tale endings, they clung to the illusion of a perfect future. She would be his princess, radiant and cherished, and he would be her prince, steadfast and true. Between soft kisses and whispered poetry, they kept the moment alive, savoring the sweetness of youth and dreams untainted by reality, untouched by the world's harshness.

The afternoon air was cool, carrying the scent of the approaching evening as the sun prepared to surrender to the moon. The beauty of life, perhaps, lies in its fleeting innocence—the naive belief that it could unfold as effortlessly as a dream. They laughed, kissed, and held each other close, sharing warmth and comfort. She spoke of her business plans, her voice full of excitement, and he promised to support her every step of the way. He still lived with his parents, while she had her own apartment since her family had long retired to the countryside.

Time slipped away too quickly, and soon, he had to leave. Parting—such sweet sorrow. A lingering goodnight kiss on the cheek, a tight embrace, and then, he was walking home. Yet, as his shadow stretched long before him in the dimming light, an unsettling feeling crept over him. A premonition? He couldn't tell. When he arrived home, the atmosphere felt off—unnervingly still, unnaturally quiet. It was the kind of silence that hangs in the air after a storm has passed, or just before one breaks. A shiver crawled up his spine as he pushed the door open, stepping into a house that no longer felt like his own. There, in the dim light, sat two figures, rigid and facing each other like adversaries. His parents. The air between them was heavy, crackling with unspoken anger, their faces etched with tension. They weren't just sitting; they were simmering, locked in a silent battle of resentment.

He greeted them softly and retreated to his room, but the unease didn't fade. The house was too quiet. Where were his siblings? He sat on his bed, dragging out his laptop, trying to shake the feeling. His phone buzzed—it was her. Did you get home safe?

He exhaled and texted back, Yeah, safe and sound. A lie, he did not know why? Determined to focus, he turned his attention to his thesis, due Monday. But then, the silence shattered. A sharp voice. An argument. That was strange— his parents never fought.

Should he step in? He hesitated. Maybe it was just a small disagreement. Something they would resolve on their own.

Still, the unease refused to leave him.

He yelled; she defended herself. She accused; he deflected.

He swore; she shamed him.

She screamed; he dismissed her with a cold, ‘Grow up.’

The silence he once cherished was now locked in battle with the noise. And the noise was winning—spreading, swelling, consuming.

He didn't know what had sparked the argument, but he knew one thing: if his siblings walked in and saw their parents like this, they'd be terrified. He hesitated at the door, his hand on the knob. Why was he stepping in? They were adults, weren't they? Shouldn't they be able to fix this once the storm passed?

But his father's voice carried no hint of restraint. His mother's was raw—anger, sadness, betrayal woven into every syllable. How could you? The words weren't spoken, but they echoed in her tone.

His father's anger surged. His mother's voice cracked. His heart pounded. Goosebumps prickled his arms. He couldn't just stand there.

Steeling himself, he descended the stairs.

The scene was worse up close. Bitterness laced their words, their voices rising, colliding, shattering the air. His mother trembled, her tears tracing silent paths down her face. His father sat still, eyes cold, thumbs idly scrolling his phone.

She wanted remorse. She wanted him to see her, to hear her. But he was somewhere else, buried in a screen, unmoved.

A tantrum, a storm, a breaking point.

And he was standing in the middle of it.

She was upset—her tears revealed everything. He didn't care; his eyes showed it as he sat there, glued to his phone, lost in his own world. She wanted his attention. She wanted him to feel something—remorse, perhaps. But he remained indifferent, his silence an insult.

“You have no shame!” she shouted.

“Woman, I'll beat you up,” he retorted coldly, his words dripping with venom.

They hadn't noticed him, not yet. But the words hit him like a physical blow. Fear churned in his stomach as his pulse quickened.

Her voice only grew louder, prodding, pushing, until he could feel his control slipping away. His body tensed, anger boiling beneath his skin.

Then, without warning, he rose. His hand swung through the air, connecting with her face. The slap echoed in the room, sharp and brutal. She stumbled, head bowing, blood dripping onto the floor. When she lifted her face, the damage was undeniable—her nose bled freely, and a bright red mark bloomed across her pale skin.

He stood there, fists clenched, teeth gritted. The sight of her, the sound of her hurt, the weight of what he'd done—it all burned in him. But in the pit of his gut, it felt like nothing more than the inevitable end of a war he'd long stopped fighting.

That slap meant everything.

It meant he wasn't sorry.

It meant he believed he had the right.

It meant he had justified it in his mind, without regret, without apology.

She stood frozen, shaken by the act, wounded by his brutality—not just the pain on her skin, but the betrayal beneath it.

Then they saw him. The young ones stood in the doorway, their eyes wide with horror. They had seen it all. Their mother, struck down. Their father—their hero —reduced to something monstrous.

He saw them too.

For a moment, the room was silent, heavy with something that could never be undone. The sin was too great, the damage already carved into their hearts.

How would they erase this from their minds? How could they ever unsee it?

Some wounds don't heal. Some scars don't fade.

“What's happening?” she asked, her voice trembling as she looked at the scene before her. How do you explain something like this to a nine-year-old? How do you tell a child that their father, the man they've always looked up to, just hit their mother because he was upset? That an argument had spiraled out of control, turning into something dark and frightening? No one knew how long they had been standing there, frozen in terror and fear.

She rushed to them, her heart pounding, and wrapped her arms around the children, shielding them from the

chaos. Gently, she led them away, trying to find the right words to explain what had just happened. But what could she say? How could she make sense of it for them?

The two of them stood there, staring at each other— father and son. To the boy, his father had always been a golden figure, almost like a hero from the Greek myths he loved to read about. His father was an English gentleman, or so he had always believed. This was the man who had taught him to never raise a hand to a woman, to respect everyone, no matter who they were. This was the man who had always seemed so strong, so kind, so perfect.

But now, the boy couldn't understand. What had just happened? Had his father turned into someone else? Had the man he admired become a brute, a chauvinistic beast he didn't recognize? The boy's heart ached with confusion and betrayal. The image of his father, once so golden and untouchable, now felt tarnished, broken.

“Son...” The voice was strained, but he couldn't bring himself to turn around. He pushed open the door and stepped out, leaving behind a place that no longer felt like home. His mother's sobs followed him, but he couldn't bear to hear them. Outside, the cool night air wrapped around him, but it did nothing to numb the ache in his chest.

She stood in the doorway, her face swollen, her nose bloodied. “Son! Wait!” But her words were nothing more than distant echoes.

He kept walking, his footsteps quickening. He wasn't sure where he was going, but he only had one destination in mind: her place. Maybe he needed comfort, maybe just someone to listen. But the pain... the confusion... it felt too big to carry alone.

The night had fallen quickly, swallowing the world in darkness. His vision blurred with the tears that filled his eyes. What would he even say to her? How could he explain what had happened, what had broken him inside?

He reached her door, standing there for a moment, his hand hovering over the knob. Should he turn around? He wasn't sure if he was ready to face the comfort she could give. But before he could make up his mind, the door creaked open.

There she was.

“Hey,” he whispered, voice cracking.

She studied him, her eyes softening with concern. “What's wrong?” Her voice was steady, but there was a gentleness in it that made his heart ache even more.

Without thinking, he stepped into her arms, feeling the warmth of her embrace. His body trembled, his weight pressing against her as if the world had been too much to carry. She didn't say anything, just held him tighter, the cold night air forgotten as they stood there, together.

The weight of it all felt a little lighter in her arms, but he knew it wasn't over. For now, though, it was enough. Just being there with her was enough.

“He disappointed me,” she murmured, her voice trembling with the weight of unspoken pain. “I had placed him on a pedestal, saw him as something pure, untouchable. The image of gold, perfect in every way—no faults, no weaknesses. But now, all of that feels like a lie.” She paused, her fingers tracing absent patterns on his hair, trying to steady herself. “Am I punishing him too much for what he's done?”

His head rested on her lap, a soft and familiar weight. He could feel the warmth of her touch, but her eyes were distant, lost in a place where pain and trust collided. She didn't speak for a while, her silence heavier than any words could be. Finally, she whispered, almost to herself, “I guess that's the price we pay for believing too much. For seeing perfection in others and never imagining that they might

fall... or that they will fail us. It's easy to love the idea of someone, but much harder to love the reality.”

Her words lingered in the space between them, and he swallowed the knot in his throat. The thought of failing her, of being just another broken promise, unsettled him. It was a fear that clung to him like a shadow, chasing him through every moment, even when he was supposed to be at peace.

“What if I fail you?” he asked, his voice strained with the vulnerability he rarely allowed himself. “What if I disappoint you the way he disappointed me?”

Her hand paused, and for a moment, he thought she might pull away, but she didn't. Instead, she ran her fingers gently through his hair, the gesture soft, comforting, but also steady with a quiet strength he didn't quite understand. “You're just afraid,” she said with a calmness that surprised him. “Fear makes us believe that the worst will always happen. But we're in this together, remember? We always navigate through everything side by side. If you fall, I'll be there to catch you. We're not alone in this.”

The silence that followed wasn't cold, but it was heavy. It was the kind of silence that spoke volumes without uttering a single word, a silence full of unspoken truths and feelings they hadn't yet shared.

He slowly sat up, lifting his gaze to meet hers. The weight of the moment pressed on him. He could feel the vulnerability,

the gravity of what was about to happen. He didn't know if he could keep the promise he was about to make, but he knew he had to try. He needed to believe in something more than his fear.

“I promise,” he said, his voice rough with emotion, “I will never hit you.”

The words hung between them, stark and raw. A promise, a burden, a hope. He didn't know if he would live up to it, but he made it anyway. It felt like the first step toward redemption—for both of them. He could already feel the weight of those words pressing on him, as if they would haunt him forever if he ever faltered. But for now, in that moment, he held onto them with everything he had.

She didn't say anything at first. She didn't need to. The way she looked at him told him everything—soft, understanding, but with the quiet resolve of someone who had learned that words could be fragile, but actions would always speak louder.

“Promise me this,” she said, her voice barely above a whisper, “that you'll never be afraid to be human.”

What you run from stays, Slowly shaping who you are, Come as you are, free.

chapters.title: Betrayal
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

the sins of the father shall be visited upon the son

Betrayal—what is it, truly? Is it the act itself, the knife plunged in the dark, or the lingering wound it leaves behind? Perhaps we never truly understand betrayal until it happens to us, until the trust we once held shatters like glass beneath careless hands.

It is not just a moment but a shadow that lingers, a whisper that replays in the depths of our mind. Those who have never felt it may define it in words, but only those who have been betrayed can describe its weight— the hollow ache, the disbelief, the slow unraveling of certainty.

Betrayal is more than an act. It is the absence left behind. This I would understand soon enough.

“Hello, Junior. Come over, I am all alone. My grandchildren are in church. Don’t you ever miss your mother?” she complained, her voice carrying that familiar mix of guilt and authority.

Of course, she knew I had nothing to do that Sunday—I had told her myself. I couldn’t lie. Sighing, I got up and prepared to leave. She had been lonely ever since my father passed, and though we visited at least three times a month, she always found the strangest reasons to call us over.

If we visited three times, she aimed for five. If we visited five, she’d find a way to make it six. It was almost impressive, her creativity.

Once, she swore she saw a crocodile in the backyard. Not just a passing glimpse—she even sent a blurry picture as proof. Mel, the oldest among us, didn’t take any chances. She called the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS), and, much like the police in white neighborhoods, we showed up quickly.

We arrived ready to wrestle a reptile, armed with nothing but our phones and a stick from the compound. The “crocodile” turned out to be an old, sun-bleached log half- buried in the mud. She didn’t even look embarrassed. She just shrugged and said, “Well, you’re here now. Might as well stay for lunch.”

It was a weird conversation with the wildlife service. We stayed with her the whole week as the Kenya Wildlife Service swept the area, though we all knew there was no crocodile. Mom, however, played the concerned citizen role flawlessly, shaking her head and muttering, “You never know these days. Wild animals are bold.”

So, our lives shifted temporarily. The house became a lively, chaotic hub, as if we had all moved back in. Mornings were a mess—everyone waking up at different times, scrambling for the bathroom, fighting over the last bit of toothpaste, and leaving cups of half-drunk tea on every available surface.

Mel, the responsible one, insisted on keeping some order. “If we’re going to be here, we need a system,” she declared, making a detailed breakfast schedule that no one followed.

I found myself squeezing onto the tiny couch at night, my feet dangling off the edge, listening to my younger sister complain about how she couldn’t get any sleep with all the snoring and soon conversations turned into relationships. She was already married and so I listened to how Josh leaves the toilet seat up and other short stories.

Mom, on the other hand, was in her element. She had all her children under one roof again. She made our favorite meals, sat us down for endless stories, and looked far too pleased when she caught us laughing together over something silly. By midweek, we knew the crocodile incident had been a

setup, but no one said anything. We stayed anyway, because deep down, we understood. She didn’t want to be alone.

And when the KWS finally cleared the area, shaking their heads at the “crocodile sighting,” we packed up to leave.

“Ah, you’re all leaving already?” Mom said, disappointment heavy in her voice.

Mel sighed. “Mom, we’ve been here a whole week.”

She waved a hand dismissively. “You say that like it’s a long time. You used to live here for years.”

We laughed, knowing this wouldn’t be the last time she found a reason to call us back. And when that time came, we’d come running again.

The memories kept me company as I drove into the compound. The gate creaked open as the maid let me in, her face lighting up with a warm smile. “Your mother has been anxiously awaiting your arrival,” she said, her voice tinged with excitement. “She even had the whole house cleaned again—top to bottom—even after doing it in the morning.”

I chuckled. That was typical of her. If she could have polished the air itself, she would have.

She met me at the door, beaming from ear to ear, as if I had been away for years.

“Hello, son! How have you been?”

I smiled, shaking my head at her excitement. “Hello, Mother. I’m good. What about you?”

“Ah, you know me. Chess, squash—simple things for an old lady like me,” she said, waving a hand dismissively. “My grandchildren don’t like my knitting, so I decided to pick up some outdoor activities instead. The maids help me once in a while.”

I raised an eyebrow. My mother, playing squash? Now that was a sight I needed to see.

“How’s Dani?” I asked, steering the conversation elsewhere.

Danielle—Dani—was the girl she had adopted, her latest charitable project. My mother’s reasoning was that since she had successfully raised and educated all of us, she had to give back to society as a way of thanking God. So she picked Dani, a girl from church, and took her under her wing, determined to guide her through university and life itself. A noble gesture—except she also made us contribute to her education, though thankfully, only a little.

And, of course, in true Mom fashion, she had a long-term vision.

“You should get to know her,” she said, slipping into that familiar tone—the one she always used when trying to set someone up.

Ah, here we go.

“You should get to know that girl. She’s friendly, she’s sweet, she’s good-hearted—she’d make a wonderful wife for you.”

I sighed. “Mother, we’ve talked about this. It’s not time for me. Besides, Danielle is like a sister to me. You should know that.”

I barely had time to finish my sentence before a spoonful of plantain chips landed on my plate.

“You are the only one who doesn’t have a family. It’s bad,” she said, plopping another spoonful onto my plate for added effect.

I groaned inwardly. That was the phrase. The same phrase that got my sisters married. The same phrase that roped my brothers into their wives.

My life was different. Sure, I had girlfriends, but I wasn’t ready to settle down yet. But try telling that to my mother.

“You’re successful, son. You have money. You’re old enough. You’re great!” She tightened her upper arm, flexing her biceps like she was demonstrating my supposed greatness. Another spoonful of plantain chips landed on my plate. I sighed, setting down my fork. “Mother, I’m not ready. I’m too young.”

She scoffed loudly, clapping her hands once, “Wewe! Too young?” She shook her head, then turned to the maid as if looking for backup. “Ona huyu mtoto!” (See this boy!) “How old do you think you are? A teenager? Should I start buying you lollipops now?” Her voice rose, filling the room with that familiar maternal authority, as usual her heavy sarcasm I always enjoyed.

My mother shook her head, clicking her tongue. “A whole grown man saying he’s too young. In our days, by your age, we had five children and a herd of cattle! Ama ni uongo?”

She turned to the maid. The maid nodded in agreement, probably fearing for her job if she didn’t.

I stifled a laugh. “Mother, you didn’t even own a chicken when you got married.” The Maid giggled and after a stern look she excused herself.

She waved me off. “That’s not the point!” Another spoonful of plantain chips landed on my plate, she took off her Kanga and sat down next to me.

“Life doesn’t wait for you to be ready or older, mwana wangu (my child). You think your father was ready when he married me? Hata pesa alikuwa hana! (He didn’t even have money!) But look at us now. Mungu ni mwema (God is good). I also want to see my grandchildren.”

I almost choked on my food. Grandchildren? She’d gone plural. I glanced at her, unsure whether to laugh or sigh. But

she had a point. Thirty wasn’t young anymore, and I couldn’t deny that I had achieved a lot already. I graduated at twenty-four with my diploma in software development, then went on to finish my degree. By twenty-eight, I had a degree, a solid job in tech, and a reputation as a software consultant for telecoms and various industries.

In my mom’s eyes, that made me successful.

But still, her words stung.

“You just want to keep chasing girls around,” she teased, her eyes narrowing playfully. “I see you, naughty boy. What would your father think?”

She knew me too well. From a young age, I had always been more interested in hopping from one relationship to the next. The same habit followed me into adulthood.

“Mamã, it’s not like that,” I said, trying to defend myself. “You know if I want to settle down, I will.”

“Then why are you not settled, boy?” she asked, raising an eyebrow.

I froze. I had trapped myself. She leaned back in her chair, her plate untouched.

“Where’s your food?” I asked, glancing at the empty space in front of her.

“Ah! Don’t mind me, eat!” She waved it off with a smile, though her eyes were sharp.

She looked at me for a moment, then her face softened. “Your father would be so proud of the man you’ve become.”

I turned to the wall, staring at the photo of him. There he was, in his government office attire, standing tall with that signature calm confidence. A man who was always there for me—supporting, guiding, and loving me without question. His death had left a hole in our lives that nothing could fill. I could find no flaws in him, no taint in his image.

“I know,” I whispered, swallowing hard. “He’d tell me his favourite phrase: Umekazana. Keep it up.”

A heavy silence hung between us, the weight of her love and my father’s absence hanging in the air.

“He’d smack you for not bringing a wife home!”

Again with this. I let out a sigh.

I wondered if I should tell her—that I had found someone. That, for the first time in my life, I had met a woman I truly wanted to spend the rest of my life with. I knew she’d be ecstatic, but I also knew the next words out of her mouth would be, “Si Dani, sindio?” (It’s not Dani, is it?)

Still, I decided to say it.

“Mom, I have fallen for someone.”

Her face lit up instantly, her smile stretching so wide you’d think I had just handed her the secret to eternal youth.

“Tell me about her!” she said eagerly.

“What about my food?” I asked, glancing at my untouched plate.

“Forget the food, you can always eat later! Now, about this girl—who is she?”

I sighed and leaned back in my chair. Here goes.

How I Met Estella

I met Estella at a company event—a youth workshop hosted by my firm. I was a speaker, she was a guest. I looked, she looked back. Sparks. Chemistry. One of those meant-to-be moments that sound like something out of a movie.

She approached me, full of curiosity, asking about the project we were launching. I told myself, Act natural. Be smooth. This is your moment.

And just as I was about to say hello, my throat betrayed me.

I coughed.

Not a subtle, clear-your-throat cough. No. A full-on, life- flashing-before-my-eyes, choking-on-air kind of cough.

She took a step back, concerned.

“Are you okay?” she asked, her voice laced with amusement.

I nodded, eyes watering. Brilliant first impression.

When I finally regained control of my body, I gave her a smile—one of those awkward, please-forget-what-just- happened smiles.

“Hi, I’m Junior,” I said, extending my hand.

She took it, her touch soft but firm. “Estella.”

And just like that, my fate was sealed.

However, that moment of fate was interrupted.

“Let’s welcome Austin Mzae, our speaker today!”

The emcee’s enthusiastic voice cut through the room, snapping me back to reality. Estella had noticed me, but duty called. I placed my drink on the table—a subtle signal that I’d be back. Marking territory, in a way.

I walked up to the stage, delivered my speech with practiced ease, and wrapped it up in record time. Applause followed, but my focus was elsewhere. My eyes instinctively scanned the room, searching for her.

She was leaving.

Panic flickered through me. I rushed toward the exit, weaving through the crowd, but her entourage had already disappeared into the night. A strange sense of devastation washed over me. It was ridiculous—I didn’t even know why, but I felt like I had lost something important before I even had the chance to claim it.

Defeated, I turned back to my table and picked up my glass of wine.

That’s when I noticed it.

A napkin, right where my glass had been.

I frowned, picking it up. It seemed ordinary at first—until I shifted it slightly and saw what was underneath, tucked beneath the tablecloth.

A phone number.

I chuckled to myself. Smart. Creative. She wanted to be found.

One phone call was all it took.

That night turned into daily talks, endless chats, and stolen moments in between our busy schedules.

Coffee dates became dinner dates.

Laughter turned into late-night conversations.

One evening, as we sat in a quiet café, Estella tapped her fingers against her cup, her head tilted in amusement.

“So… Austin Mzae, huh?” she teased. “Yet you introduced yourself as Junior. What’s the story there?”

I smirked, stirring my coffee. “My dad was Austin Mzae before I was. A respected man. Government official. When people hear that name, they don’t think of me. They think of him. So, I go by Junior to avoid confusion. It’s simpler.”

She grinned. “Simplicity is overrated. ‘Austin Mzae’ sounds like a name for a president or a movie star. Meanwhile, ‘Junior’ makes you sound like someone who still gets sent to bed early.”

I chuckled. “And Estella? That sounds like the name of a soap opera villain.”

She gasped in mock offense. “Excuse you! My name is classy, mysterious, unforgettable.” She leaned in, lowering her voice dramatically. “Estella… the woman who stole the CEO’s heart.”

I laughed, shaking my head. “Alright, fine. If ‘Junior’ isn’t good enough, what should you call me then?”

She tapped her chin, pretending to think hard. Then her face lit up. “J-Mzae.”

I raised an eyebrow. “J-Mzae?”

“Yes. A mix of Junior and Mzae. It has flair. It says, ‘I’m a responsible man but also a little dangerous.’”

“Dangerous? Me?” I scoffed.

“Of course,” she said, grinning. “Dangerously single. But we’re fixing that, aren’t we?”

I shook my head, smirking. “Alright, fine. J-Mzae it is. But if I get a nickname, you do too.”

“Go on, impress me,” she challenged.

I studied her for a moment, then smiled. “Tella.”

She blinked. “Tella?”

“Yeah. Short for Estella, but also sounds like ‘teller’—like someone who tells stories, keeps secrets, shares wisdom. Plus, it sounds warm. Like you.”

She stared at me for a second, then shook her head with a small smile. “Okay, that was good. Unexpectedly poetic, J- Mzae. Also if you ever call me bank teller I will hang you.”

I looked at her surprised and confused, she touched my cheek and brought her face closer. “You would have thought of it eventually.”

I leaned forward and kissed her—it took her by surprise. I looked into her eyes. “Told you I was dangerous.”

She laughed, and just like that, another piece of our story fell into place.

And then, one evening, under the warm glow of city lights, she looked at me with a quiet certainty.

“I want you to be my forever. No matter the circumstances.”

At that moment, I knew—so did I.

My mother looked at me. The expression on her face was something else—an odd mix of shock and hesitation. What was she thinking?

Then, slowly, her lips trembled into a smile. “I am so happy for you! Oh my goodness. Wow. Why didn’t you tell me any of this? Finally, my Junior has a girl to bring home.”

Before I could respond, she was already talking about wedding preparations.

“We must start planning early. Eh! I need to call your aunts! You know they will complain if they’re not involved. And the bride price—aye! You must prepare, my son. Her family will not take small cows!”

I chuckled, shaking my head. “Mum, you’ve already married me off?”

“Which Uncles do you want at the negotiations? Rigathi is too mouthy na anakuanga mlevi (and he is a drunk)……”

She was happy. A tap from her brought me back to reality.

“I have waited too long for this day!” She clapped her hands excitedly. “Now, how many children are we looking at? Five? Six? You need strong boys who will carry on the family name!”

I nearly choked.

I sighed and pulled out my phone. “Mum, this is the girl I want to marry.”

She leaned in, eager, expecting to see the woman who would make her a grandmother.

Then—silence.

A dead, suffocating silence.

The joy drained from her face like water down a drain. Her lips parted slightly, her breathing turned shallow.

“Junior… nani huyu? (Who is this?)” Her voice was tight, sharp.

I frowned. “Mom, what’s wrong? You’re looking at her like she’s a ghost.”

She sucked in a shaky breath, held her forehead, and closed her eyes. Then, slowly, she opened them and whispered,

“You cannot marry her.”

The words slammed into me like a heavy slap from an elder.

The room suddenly felt smaller, the walls pressing in. “What do you mean I can’t marry her?”

Mom clutched her forehead and let out a shaky breath. Her voice dropped to a whisper. “She’s your step-sister, Junior. Your father… he had another family.

My world stopped. The air was sucked from my lungs, leaving me lightheaded. My hands felt numb, my body weightless, yet unbearably heavy.

“What?” My voice barely made it out.

She was crying now, tears rolling freely down her face. “I should have told you earlier. I didn’t know you two would ever meet, let alone—”

I barely heard the rest. The words blurred, distorted by the deafening pulse in my ears.

Step-sister.

My father had another family. My father, the man I had idolized. The man I wanted to make proud. The man who had guided me, supported me, shaped me—

Had broken me in ways I never saw coming.

I stared at the picture of my father on the wall.

His framed government portrait. His stiff, official suit. His kind but authoritative eyes.

Liar.

A hypocrite.

I felt anger. Sadness. Confusion.

And most of all—loss.

Because in that moment, I knew.

I would have to say goodbye to the only woman I had ever truly loved.

Because of a past I never even knew existed.

Betrayal.

What is betrayal?

Is it a knife in the back?

Or is it the slow realization that the people you trusted most have left you drowning in a mess they created?

I looked at my mother cry, her tears rolling down her cheeks. Why was she this strong? I reached for her, pulling her into a hug as she wept into my shoulder. But inside me, something else was breaking.

Maybe it’s the weight of a promise never kept.

The following day, I found myself standing before my father’s grave. The wind whispered through the trees, and the sun was a muted yellow, as if the world knew that something had shifted in my life. I had always come to this place to seek guidance when things felt heavy, when I was unsure of my path. Today, I needed answers.

The tombstone was still pristine, the engraving of his name bold and dignified. Austin Mzae, it read—his name etched in stone, forever. Beneath it, the simple inscription: A man of honor and integrity.

But now, as I stood here, I questioned everything about the man I had looked up to for so many years. Had he truly been a man of honor? How could he have hidden such a secret from us? How could he have betrayed my mother—betrayed me—in such a way?

I knelt beside the grave, the earth still fresh from the rains. My hands trembled as I wiped away the dirt on

the stone, searching for some comfort that would never come.

In the quiet of that moment, I recalled a verse from the Bible, one my father often quoted in his wisdom, trying to impart to me the importance of justice and personal responsibility. Ezekiel 18:20—“The soul who sins is the one who will die. The son will not share the guilt of the father, nor will the father share the guilt of the son. The righteousness of the righteous will be credited to them, and the wickedness of the wicked will be charged against them.”

But there was another saying my father had often warned me of: “The sins of the father shall be visited upon the son.”

I whispered both phrases to myself. “The soul who sins is the one who will die... The sins of the father shall be visited upon the son...” I had spent years idolizing him, thinking he was above reproach. But now, I was left to bear the consequences of his choices—the lies, the hidden family, the betrayal of everything we stood for.

My father had passed on his legacy to me—his name, his reputation, his love for his family—but it seemed that in doing so, he had also passed me his mistakes. Could I carry the weight of his sins without letting it define who

I was? Could I move forward, loving Estella, knowing that our love was bound in tragedy?

The weight of his actions pressed down on me like the weight of the world itself.

Could I ever escape the shadows of his mistakes? Was I doomed to repeat them, to live out the consequences of a life full of secrets and lies?

The grave before me seemed to mock my struggle, as if daring me to make peace with the past. I stood there for what felt like an eternity, tears slipping down my face. Was I my father’s son? Was I bound to repeat his mistakes?

My mother’s words echoed in my mind: “She’s your step-sister. Your father had a second family.” How could he have lived with such a secret? A life full of lies, cloaked in the name of honor.

Now the gods we adored have failed us, their altars crumbling, their voices hushed. Yet perhaps the fault lies not in their hands, but in ours, where the weight of blame rests. I would sooner curse the mosquito's sting,

its needle kiss, its whispered sin, than face the truth—that I left the window open, inviting the night, the bite, the storm within.

chapters.title: Ubuntu
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

I am because we are.

God did say we were all equal, didn’t He? He sent His son to die for us, a sacrifice not for one, but for all. His son preached love—love for our neighbors, love for our enemies. He came for all of us, without distinction.

Now, imagine if He didn’t. Imagine if He created a world where some of us were above others—where a man of lighter skin, or someone of a different heritage, was destined to rule over the rest. A hierarchy. Some at the top, others at the bottom, meant to serve, meant to suffer.

If this were true, then why? Why would He give us hearts capable of loving, no matter what divides us? Why would He plant in us the ability to see beyond differences, to care for each other regardless of the skin we wear or the cultures we come from? Why would He make us capable

of compassion and kindness if some were meant to be above others?

Why did He make some of us charming, caring, with hearts open to healing? Why did He make some of us blind to the cruelty of the world, yet guided by the power of love?

If He did not create us equally, then what is the true meaning of love? And what is the purpose of our hearts, if not to bridge the divides He never intended to exist?

Despite it all, I loved him.

Even when the law said I couldn’t. When it deemed our love a crime, our touch a rebellion, our existence together an impossibility.

A white boy. His Afrikaans rolled off his tongue effortlessly, his English crisp and refined.

Yes, he wanted an African girl. They all did. It didn’t matter if she was Zulu, Sotho, Xhosa, or Tswana. To them, we were objects of pleasure, forbidden fruit to be used in the dark and discarded in the daylight. No white man wanted to be seen loving an African woman. No white man dared claim her in the open.

We were captives in our own homes. Enslaved on our own soil.

What was I saying? Oh, yes—he wanted an African girl. But he didn’t want just any. He wanted me.

What was he doing when he came to me?

Let me think... They came to stand in solidarity, or so they claimed. He was there, among us, a boy with soft hands and sharp eyes, working alongside his father, a doctor. While his father diagnosed, prescribed, and vaccinated, he ran errands, fetched supplies, and listened.

Listened to the suffering. Listened to the silence between words. Listened to the unspoken truths about the diseases that plagued our people—not just the ones of the body, but the ones of the world we lived in.

My parents wanted nothing to do with his father’s medicine. To them, white charity was a death sentence in disguise. Poison wrapped in kindness.

I went anyway. Not for treatment. Not for help.

I went to watch.

I wanted to see a doctor in action.

You see, I always dreamed of being one. A doctor.

But my dream was a joke to the world. A black girl who wanted to wear a white coat? Impossible. They laughed when I said it, as if the idea itself was absurd. As if my hands were made to serve, not to heal.

A young Zulu girl wanting to be a doctor? They laughed. When have your people ever been doctors?

A segregation in that too.

I wasn’t even black to them—I was Zulu.

Mandela was Xhosa. Why should a Xhosa man ever become president?

They divided us before they ever came. What region are you from? What language do you speak? What tribe?

We were already fractured when they arrived; they simply sharpened the edges of our broken pieces.

Yet, there I stood, watching. Watching a white man do what I had been told I could never do. Watching his son move through the clinic, speaking to our people in their own language, touching them with hands unafraid of their skin.

And he watched me too.

Not like the others did.

Not like I was something to be conquered, something to be used and thrown away.

He watched me like I was real.

“Sometimes he takes them into the tent and cuts them open to see their insides,” a voice murmured behind me.

Goosebumps rose on my skin. Not from fear of the words—I knew what surgery was—but because he was too close. Too near. If someone saw…

“Interesting,” I said, stepping away, my voice cool. I wished I had Winnie’s fire. I wished I could slap him, make a scene. But I was not Winnie.

“Relax, it’s a joke.” He scoffed. “You seem interested. Want to see up close?”

Was this a trap?

He stretched out his hand. My breath caught. This was not normal. Afrikaans boys did not offer their hands to girls like me.

Still, I took it.

“Hello, Papa. She wants to see you work, so I brought her.”

His father removed his latex gloves, wiped his hands, and stretched one toward me.

A smile—warm. Gentle.

So they did smile like that?

“Well, hello! You want to learn medicine?”

I swallowed hard. Fear held my voice captive, so I only nodded—quickly, respectfully.

“You know,” he said, “there’s hope for your people. I once knew a man who had a dream.”

His voice changed, became something softer. Reverent.

“A man named Martin Luther King Jr. He dreamt of a world where men were not judged by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character. He believed in that world. And because he believed, he changed things.”

He looked at me then. “Don’t let these laws stop you.”

But why, then, did his laws stop me from loving his son? What started as curiosity became something more. He sought me out. Once, when they treated our animals. Twice, when they cleaned the township. Thrice, when he snuck out, whispering my name in the dark.

Other times, he was too obvious.

And maybe—just maybe—I didn’t mind.

A boy and a girl. Different races. Bound by love, divided by law.

“It’s just us against them,” he would say.

But what did we know? We were young.

“They laugh at me when I say it,” I whispered to him once.

“Who?” he asked, stepping closer.

“Them. All of them. Why would I, a Zulu, ever become a doctor? Why would Mandela, a Xhosa, ever be president? They divide us before we even stand a chance.”

His fingers brushed my wrist. “Then let’s stop listening.”

But how could I? I knew I had a choice, yet where I was simply did not let me make that choice. My people did not let me make that choice.

It began as a whisper.

A breeze of hushed voices slipping through doorways, weaving through the market, rustling like dry leaves beneath cautious footsteps.

“Did you hear?”

“That girl… with that boy.”

“She is lost.”

“She will bring shame to her family.”

Whispers turned to glances—quick, sharp, laced with silent judgment.

Women no longer met my gaze. Men stiffened as I passed, their mouths drawn in disapproval. The elders, the ones who used to call me mntwanami, turned their faces away.

And my mother—she no longer sang while she cooked.

She moved through the house in silence, her movements heavy, her eyes burdened by a sorrow too deep for words. My father, once so strong in his presence, now sat at the dinner table in silence, his hands clenched into fists, his jaw tight with things he could not bring himself to say.

Then came the warnings.

“You will suffer.”

“You will bleed.”

“You will pay for this.”

They spoke of it as though it were a curse. As though loving him had sealed my fate in blood. As though I had traded my future for a fleeting dream.

“He will leave you. And when he does, you will have no one.”

But what they didn’t understand was that I had already fallen.

Fallen into a love that made the laws of men feel like distant echoes.

Fallen into a love that made me feel seen in a world that had spent its years trying to erase me.

Fallen for a boy with eyes the color of the sky after a storm, with hands that trembled when he was nervous, with a voice that softened when he spoke my name.

He called me beautiful in a way that made me believe it.

Not like the others—those who saw only the exoticism of my skin, the curve of my body, the strangeness of my name on their tongues.

No.

He saw me.

The way my lips parted slightly when I was lost in thought. The way my fingers traced invisible patterns on my arms when I was anxious. The way my eyes burned with longing when I watched his father work, scribbling notes in a language I wished I could claim as my own.

And when I cried—when the weight of the world settled on my shoulders, when the warnings wrapped around my ribs like iron chains—he held my face in his hands, tilted my chin up, and wiped my tears away with the gentleness of someone who did not yet know the meaning of surrender.

“I really like the white Zulu,” he said one day, his voice filled with wonder.

We stood before a crumbling wall, the township’s heartbeat painted in bold strokes of red and gold. Johnny Clegg stared back at us, frozen in time, caught between two worlds, belonging to neither.

“His music, his dance—it’s art.”

I wanted to smile, to let his words pull me into the safety of his world, where art and music were enough to bridge the distance between us.

But I couldn’t.

Not that day.

That day, my mother’s voice still echoed in my ears, thick with grief, pleading with me to leave him be.

That day, my father’s silence weighed on my chest, heavy and suffocating.

That day, I knew the world would never let us be.

“It’s just us against them,” he whispered.

His fingers laced through mine, warm and steady.

I squeezed back.

We were young.

What did we know?

They came in the dead of night.

Boots on dirt.

A knock that splintered the quiet like thunder.

A crash as the door was torn from its hinges, splintering the fragile peace of my home.

My mother’s scream pierced the air, but my father held her back. I didn’t fight them. I couldn’t. I had known this day would come for so long that it felt almost inevitable.

They dragged me from the house, my feet scraping against the earth, the moonlight casting shadows that seemed to stretch on forever. The truck smelled like sweat and fear. The cold metal walls of the back seat pressed in, suffocating, a constant reminder that I was a

prisoner—not of the law, but of a world that would never accept us.

At the station, the interrogation was as silent as the grave. They didn’t ask questions. They didn’t need to. They knew my crime. They knew that loving him, my white Afrikaaner boy, was enough to sentence me to this fate.

They beat me.

And the bruises they left on my skin were nothing compared to the wounds they carved into my soul.

I didn’t scream. I didn’t fight. I just let the pain wash over me, let it remind me of everything I’d lost and everything I was losing.

They called me names, tried to break me into something small enough to fit inside their laws.

But I did not break.

I only bled.

When they were done, they shoved me into a cell, cold and empty. The floor felt like stone beneath me, unforgiving, but I couldn’t feel it anymore. I couldn’t feel anything.

I thought of his smile. The way his laugh made the world feel smaller, brighter. I thought of his hands—

calloused from work but gentle when they touched my face. I thought of how he made me feel beautiful in a world that tried so hard to make me invisible.

But now, those memories felt like shards of glass. They cut me from the inside out. Was it worth it? Was he worth it?

Couldn’t I have loved someone else? Someone safer? Someone who could walk beside me without this weight on our shoulders, without the constant threat of violence hanging over us?

No.

I couldn’t.

Because when you love someone with a heart like mine, you love them fully, recklessly, without hesitation.

But now, I was paying.

I closed my eyes, feeling the sting of tears I could not shed. I drifted into a dream.

Chains. Shackles. Bars that had never truly left us.

A voice called my name, soft yet firm, like a hand pulling me from the darkness.

“Wake up. You are free to go.”

A bright light flooded the room. A silhouette stood in the doorway, tall and unyielding.

I blinked, my eyes clouded with exhaustion, then my lips moved before I could stop them.

“Is that you, Madiba?” The man who stood there wasn’t real. He couldn’t be. He was a symbol. A dream. A man who had fought the same battles I fought in ways I could never imagine.

But he smiled.

“Come,” he said, “Let’s walk you to freedom.”

And I followed him, my body aching with every step, my heart heavier than it had ever been.

The streets outside the prison were quieter than I remembered, the world feeling as though it was holding its breath. He was waiting for me. Outside the station, beneath the orange glow of a dying streetlamp.

“I won’t let them take you again.”

His fingers found mine, urgent, desperate.

His eyes burned with hope.

Hope that the world was bigger than the cage they had built for us.

Hope that love could be enough.

“Let’s leave. Tonight. Let’s run away. Somewhere far, somewhere safe. Where they can’t touch us.”

And for a moment, I wanted to believe him. He was ready to defy and fight just like Johnny Clegg, but what would the price be?

I wanted to run.

I wanted to build a life where no one cared that my skin was darker than his.

Where no one whispered in anger when he held my hand.

Where love was just love.

But I hesitated.

Because I knew the truth.

“This is no way to live,” I whispered.

“This is no way to love.”

In the dance of life, we share the beat, In your heart, my soul's retreat. I am you, and you are me,

A bond unbroken, wild and free. Ubuntu, the truth we hold, In stories shared, in hands we fold. Together, we rise, together we fall, For in our unity, we are all.

chapters.title: A Story
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

In another world, love would have healed what hate left broken.

Just paint skies of where you want to be, my love, for now.

This is a story. A love story like no other. One that will fill your heart and break it all at once. The saddest you will ever read. A love that existed against the backdrop of history’s darkest moments.

This is their story—his and hers. Two lives intertwined, yet divided by forces far beyond them. Their love was greater than the storm gathering around them.

He was Hutu. She was Tutsi. A people set against each other. Yet, only you know this. He did not. Not at first. She used her Christian name, masking her lineage, while he,

with the boldness of certainty, introduced himself with both his names.

It didn’t matter to him, not then. She was simply her— sharp-witted, stubborn, and graceful in a way that made the world seem slower around her.

“Surely, pride will be the end of you!” he teased one afternoon, arms folded, eyes alight with mischief. “You are tall and elegant. Aren’t you proud?”

She smirked but said nothing. He liked to poke at her, to unsettle her with his words, but she never let them linger.

She taught him about faith—about mercy and the weight of forgiveness. He taught her history—the stories of kings and warriors, of revolutions and betrayals. The more they learned from each other, the more they realized how much they did not know.

“Have you heard of Queen Esther?” she asked one day as they sat beneath the acacia tree, the golden light of the afternoon stretching their shadows long across the ground.

He furrowed his brows, thinking. “I remember the Book of Esther vaguely. Isn’t that the one where you claim Jesus wasn’t mentioned?”

“God,” she corrected, shaking her head.

“Well, I guess Jesus was just busy with other things that week!” he grinned, leaning in to nudge her shoulder. She rolled her eyes and pushed his face away, but the warmth in her eyes never left.

Then, her voice softened. “The king ordered the killing of her people,” she said. “But Esther threw herself before him and begged for mercy. She accused a man of plotting to destroy her people, and because of her, an entire nation was saved.”

He frowned, turning the story over in his mind. “So?” he asked.

She hesitated. For a moment, it seemed like she might say something more. Instead, she exhaled slowly, looking past him as if watching something he could not see.

“I don’t know,” she finally said. “I just wanted to tell you the story.”

She looked away, her fingers tracing absent shapes in the dirt. Then, almost as an afterthought, she murmured, “Esther is my hero, by the way. Just like the prime minister. Madame Agathe.”

He didn’t understand why she said it. Not yet. But later, when the world would crack open and blood would stain the streets, he would remember.

He would remember her voice, her hesitation, and the quiet sorrow in her eyes.

“Tribalism remains Africa’s biggest problem.”

They sat under the shade of an ancient tree, a heavy history textbook spread between them. The words on the pages blurred together—stories of old wars, betrayals, massacres. A past that refused to stay buried.

“Where do you get these books?” she asked, turning a page.

“My father,” he said. “He was a professor at a university in Uganda.”

She hesitated before speaking again. The question had been haunting her for days.

“Do you hate Tutsi people?”

Silence.

A bird called out in the distance. The wind stirred the leaves. He exhaled, long and slow, his gaze never leaving the book.

“The Tutsi have trampled on the Hutu for a long time,” he said finally, his voice even, careful. “It’s not right...”

A chill ran down her spine. The history between their people had always been there, unspoken but ever-present. But to hear it aloud, from his lips, made it real.

Her throat tightened, fear coiling in her stomach.

Then, he looked at her. And something in his face softened.

“But historical injustice is not solved with hate,” he said. “Nothing in this world will be solved by hate.”

She swallowed, waiting.

“My father married a Hutu,” he continued. “They are happy. No one tramples on anyone. How hard is it for humanity to live in peace together?”

She let out a breath she hadn’t realized she was holding. Relief flooded through her, warm and overwhelming. Without thinking, she wrapped her arms around his chest, resting her head against him. His heartbeat was steady beneath her cheek—a rhythm she wanted to memorize.

He tensed, startled. Then his hand found her back, hesitant at first, then sure. His fingers traced gentle patterns on her skin.

“What’s wrong?” he asked, his voice softer now.

She closed her eyes. “Your words. They’re powerful.”

She wanted to believe in them.

She wanted to believe in him.

But belief had never been enough to stop hate.

On November 3, 1993, the prime minister, Agathe Uwilingiyimana, stood before her people and pleaded for peace. She warned them that retaliation was not the answer, that violence would only serve those who sought to destroy Rwanda’s fragile unity.

No one listened.

On April 6, 1994, the president’s plane fell from the sky in a ball of fire. And with it, the last threads of peace were burned away.

That night, the airwaves crackled with a single command:

“Cut down the tall trees.”

And the world erupted.

She ran.

The streets were no longer hers. The homes that once held laughter were now marked with blood. Doors hung open, revealing bodies instead of families.

The radio screamed orders to kill.

To kill the cockroaches.

To not spare even the children.

One day, he was gone. The conversations about history and philosophy that had once filled her days were now replaced by an oppressive silence. She spent her time reading the Bible, listening to the birds, her only company the whispers of the wind through the trees. But even the wind felt mournful now. When she heard that the president had been assassinated, a cold terror gripped her heart. The country spiraled into anarchy. She prayed for change, for the safety of her people. But deep inside, a quiet dread gnawed at her soul.

She prayed that, perhaps, she might be like Esther— called to save her people.

Days passed, and soon she was utterly alone. She sat beneath the tree where they had once shared dreams of a peaceful future, watching the grass grow, feeling the weight of solitude pressing heavily on her shoulders. Stories of butchery spread like wildfire, each retelling a fresh wound to her spirit. The news of Agathe Uwilingiyimana’s brutal assassination hit her like a spear to the heart. The Prime Minister had been a voice of reason, urging calm, pleading against violence. Yet she was silenced in the cruelest way possible. Even the peacekeepers who tried to shield her were slaughtered —some mutilated beyond recognition.

Where was the USA, the nation that claimed it would help Africa in times of trouble? Where was the world?

Her brother had left to join the guerilla fighters in Uganda. She missed him terribly, watching the grass grow as though the earth itself might offer her answers. Then came the devastating news: America would not come.

That night, the distant murmur of men marching grew louder, echoing through the darkness like the drumbeat of death. Their voices carried a chilling chant.

“Cut down the tall trees!”

Her blood turned to ice. It was the call to kill, the order that had erased entire families, entire generations.

“Where is Kagame now?” they jeered as they slashed their way through her village. Terror was no longer a distant rumor—it was alive, breathing, laughing in the men who slaughtered without mercy. The air reeked of blood and burning flesh. The wails of the dying merged into a symphony of despair.

“Tutsi dirt! We shall kill all of you!”

Had God not heard her prayers?

She wept as she saw her mother take a machete to the head, her severed hand falling beside her lifeless body.

Houses burned, the screams of children trapped inside piercing the night air. Embers floated like dying stars in the darkness, and the scent of death thickened the air like smoke.

A rough hand grabbed her, dragging her forward.

“This one is beautiful. My manhood is tired right now. Let’s give her to the half-breed!”

She saw him then. The half-breed. The way they looked at him—a slur, a reminder that he had no true place among them.

His face was hardened by war, his hands stained with blood. The machete in his grip dripped red. Was this what he had become? A killer? The hate he once swore against now consuming him?

Hadn’t his father been Tutsi?

She cried, not for herself but for him—for what he had lost, for what he had allowed himself to become.

“She’s mine!” he growled. “I remember this woman! She refused to let me in because she was a Christian! Do you think you’re Esther? I’ll teach you a lesson! You’ll beg for your life!”

He dragged her deep into the forest, away from the others. Her hands trembled, bracing for the inevitable.

Then she felt the sting of a blade—but it wasn’t cutting her. The rope around her wrists snapped.

“My Queen Esther,” he whispered, “you have gained your life—and hopefully your people’s soon. Follow the river. You’ll find the Tutsi rebels. Tell them the Chameleon has sent you and that he’ll be compromised soon. And one more thing—scream like you’re begging for your life.”

She ran. She ran as fast as her legs would carry her, the cries of the dead still echoing in her ears. She passed bodies strewn across the grass, blood seeping into the earth.

The world had forsaken them.

But perhaps, just perhaps, love had not.

Kagame eventually took control, and peace settled like a fragile veil over the land. The scars of the past remained, etched into every stone and tree. Refugees, once scattered to the far corners of the earth, began to return. But she never went back to their place—the place where they had once sat beneath the stars and dreamed of a future unmarred by hatred.

That future had been shattered.

She had changed, as had the land. What was once a sanctuary was now a graveyard of memories.

Now, she spent her days teaching children—orphans who had lost everything, their parents buried in mass graves, their homes reduced to ash. These children needed not just education but love—a love she struggled to give, knowing how fleeting and fragile the world could be.

“Jesus said, ‘Love thy neighbor. Whether they are black, white, blue, red, brown, or even have a funny face, you should love them,’” she told them. But even as she spoke, the words felt hollow in her own mouth. Was it truly possible to love in a world that had torn itself apart?

In the quiet moments, when the children had gone, her thoughts wandered back to him. Six years had passed, and not once had she returned to the place they had spoken of so lovingly. Six years, yet she could still hear his voice, his laughter, the way he had held her when the world seemed safe.

Her brother broke the silence one evening.

“We must go back and rest our mother,” he said, his voice heavy with sorrow and resolve.

The next morning, they set off. The path was long and winding, leading them back to the place they had once called home. The land had changed—the trees not as tall,

the fields not as green. It was a shadow of what it had been, yet still familiar.

As they approached a large memorial, a chill settled over her.

“Excuse me,” she called to the caretaker. “Why is this cemetery and memorial named after a certain Jean?”

The man’s eyes softened. “Because Jean built this place,” he said. “He was a Hutu moderate, one of the few who dared to stand against the hate. He helped many Tutsi escape the massacre. After they discovered what he had done, they killed him. He’s buried here, and now we bury our dead here too.”

The words struck her like a blow. Jean. Her Jean. He had died trying to save others, while she had fled. He had risked everything to protect those whom society had condemned. And now, here, his sacrifice was etched into the very earth.

Grief swept over her. In the distance, the wind carried the soft murmur of children—a reminder of why she had stayed. But here, at this memorial, she was reminded of the courage it took to face unimaginable fear.

Jean’s courage had saved lives, but it had cost him his own.

She stood there, her breath shallow, her heart torn between the past and the present. Slowly, she whispered, “I’m sorry.”

Her brother placed a hand on her shoulder. They didn’t need to say anything more.

The land was healing, and so were they. Slowly, piece by piece, they were learning that reconciliation didn’t mean forgetting. It meant remembering—with all the pain and love—and building something new from the ashes.

When the Pharisees heard of the wise reply, They gathered in whispers, hearts full of pride. A lawyer arose, testing with care, “Teacher, what is the greatest commandment to bear?” Jesus spoke with a calm, knowing grace, “Love the Lord with all your heart in this place, With all your soul, and all your mind, This is the first, the greatest you’ll find.” “The second is like it, though not apart, Love your neighbor as you love your heart. On these two commandments all laws rest, In them, the prophets have found their quest.”

chapters.title: Boy
chapters.text:
A D O G

I do not see the world in black and white. I appreciate it.

I emerged from the cardboard box, the scent of wood shavings clinging to my fur, the world a confusing blur of towering shapes and strange, compelling smells. A large, soft creature scooped me up, her voice a squeal of delight. Her hands were warm, gentle. Another, taller shape stood beside her, smelling of leather and something musky that made my tail twitch. Later I would learn these were “lady” and “man.” For now they were simply warmth, food, and puzzling noise.

The lady fussed over me with bowls of strange-smelling food. The man, always faintly of metal, took me outside, where the world ended abruptly at a tall wooden fence. Beyond it I could hear other creatures, but he always pulled me back. We ran in circles in the yard while the lady

laughed like tinkling bells, and they shouted “boy!” so often I decided that must be me.

One night, curled on their bed, the man grumbled, “He’s a dog. He should sleep by himself.” The lady called me their baby. They compromised, and I stayed — until I barked at a shadow in the dark and he groaned, “That’s it. Living room. Tomorrow.” I never understood why my protection earned annoyance instead of gratitude.

Then came the day the man hunched over the kitchen counter, a crumpled paper in his fist, smelling of burnt toast and something sour.

“Did you even try to match the curtains?” the lady snapped.

“I had a meeting,” he growled. “Curtains weren’t exactly the priority.”

“Well, someone has to care about this house!” She walked out, and I knew, somehow, that this was only the beginning.

The days that followed were a whirlwind of small battles — the milk left out, whose turn it was to do the dishes. Their barks were constant now, a background hum of irritation. They barely noticed me, their hands no longer

finding their way into my fur. I brought the man his slippers; he shoved me away. I nudged the lady’s hand; she only sighed.

One evening it broke open. He slammed out of the house. The lady sank into a chair, her shoulders shaking, and I crept close and licked her hand. “Oh, Pix,” she whispered, her voice thick. “What are we going to do?”

One morning her scent changed — something bright and sharp. She wore a green dress that swished around her legs, her braids swaying like dark rope. “Today,” she chirped, her cheer returned, “we see the world!”

She scooped me up and we went out into blinding sunlight. In the light, I noticed for the first time that her skin was a deep, rich shade I had never seen before — darker than the man’s. We climbed into a contraption on wheels, the world rushing past the window in a blur of color.

We stopped in a vast green expanse, dotted with trees that clawed at the sky. Other dogs were everywhere — small and fluffy, tall and lean. I bounded toward them, but most ignored me. One old, grizzled dog lay beneath a tree. His name, I’d learn, was Rex.

“New to the park, boy?” he rumbled.

“I... I came from a box,” I stammered. How did he know my name?

He sighed. “So your life has just begun. A dog dies and comes back as a different dog — our years are short, so we must come back again and again.”

“Do you have a name, boy?” he asked, lying down to rest. I jumped on him and started wrestling his floppy ear instead of answering.

“A dog’s life,” he said, when he’d shaken me off, “is about service. Loyalty. I’ve lived many. In my first, I was a war dog. I ran through blood-soaked dirt, past bodies torn by metal and flame. Some men clung to my fur as they died, as if I could pull them back. I stayed with them when no one else would. Then it was another war, against people who looked and smelled just like the ones I’d loved — they taught me to hate them anyway. I died at the hand of a man who trembled as he struck the blow.”

Just then the lady called, “Pix! Here, boy!” I ran to her. She held me a little tighter than usual. “I see you made a new friend,” she said, glancing at Rex.

Rex rose slowly. “She’s not happy,” he murmured. “Something’s weighing on her.” I licked her hand and tasted it too — unease, beneath the warmth and home-scent. And then I remembered: the man’s scent had clung strangely to the doorway before we left.

Back at the house, he was waiting. “I’m sorry,” he said softly. “I promise I’ll do better.”

“That’s what you said last time,” she said, her face unreadable.

“I know. But this time I mean it.”

A long silence. Then she sighed. “Okay. We can try.” She let him pull her into an embrace, and though the air still held the ghost of tension, it softened. I barked, pushing between them, and they laughed and pulled me into their warmth too.

For a little while, things were better. “Good boy, Pix,” the lady murmured, scratching behind my ears, her voice almost back to its old warmth. They were still sad, still different — but they were talking again.

Then, out of nowhere: “So that’s it? You just walk away?” the man’s voice rang through the house.

“What else am I supposed to do?” the lady shot back. “I can’t keep having this conversation over and over!”

“Because you don’t listen! You shut me out every time things get hard!”

She laughed, but there was no humor in it. “Maybe I just got tired of waiting for you to step up.”

“That’s not fair.”

“No? What’s not fair is me holding everything together while you act like it’ll just fix itself!” She slammed a cabinet shut, then exhaled sharply. “I’m exhausted. And you just keep making excuses.”

“I’m trying. I swear to God, I’m trying.”

“Trying isn’t enough.” Her voice cracked.

Silence stretched between them, heavy and uncertain. Finally, quieter now: “Do you even want me here?”

He didn’t have an answer. She picked me up, took my leash, and left — and I hoped, distantly, that she remembered I’d eaten his shoes, because there was a real chance I’d be bringing them back up soon.

I found Rex under the big oak. “They’re at it again,” I whimpered, curling beside him.

“Humans,” he muttered. “They bicker. It’s what they do.”

“But why? It’s so pointless.”

“Pointless to you. But to them, it’s like marking territory — only instead of trees, they use words. Curtains, milk, dishes — it’s all about who gets the last word.”

I thought about it. The man always picked what we watched. The lady always decided what we ate. Maybe Rex was right. But then I remembered how they used to look at each other, eyes soft, voices warm.

“What about love?” I asked. “Was that just another way of marking territory?”

Rex watched the breeze stir the fallen leaves. “Love is different,” he said at last. “It’s the one thing they can’t control. And that scares them.”

“Then why do they keep hurting each other?”

“Because love fades. And when it does, they don’t know what to do with the space it leaves behind.”

I wanted to believe he was wrong. But I remembered the night before, after the man stormed out — the lady had put on her coat and left too. I’d followed her scent to the street corner, to a car, to a man who wasn’t the man from home. Someone new.

She spoke to him in hushed tones. He took her hand. And when she got into that car, I saw it in her eyes — that same softness she used to save only for home.

“Rex,” I whispered. “What happens when love fades... and finds someone else?”

He didn’t answer right away. When he did, his voice was quiet. “Then, my friend... the real storm begins.”

I needed a distraction. “Tell me another life,” I said.

“In another,” Rex said slowly, “I watched humans hate each other over things I never understood — fur color, eye shape, the things they call race. They’re all human. I never saw the point.” His tail drooped. “The point, I think, is just to be a comfort. A paw, a lick, a warm presence in a cold world. Your humans have their own battles. Feel their sadness. Offer what you can.”

Footsteps on the gravel. A man approaching — and Rex went rigid, his tail giving one sharp, wary flick.

“There you are, old man,” the newcomer called, easy and familiar.

“Who’s that?” I asked.

“My human,” Rex said, flat.

“The lady’s new man?”

Rex’s whole body tensed. “What? No.”

Then, from behind me: “Dad! You found him!”

Everything froze. Rex’s eyes flicked from the lady to the man and back, something shifting in his face — understanding, then something like regret.

“I’m old, my memory’s slipping,” the man said, squinting at her. “Has the lady grown rounder? Did she have pups of her own?” Rex let out a booming laugh and swatted me with his paw. “Oh, Pix — you actually thought—”

“Well you didn’t seem to know each other either!” I protested.

His grin faded, something more thoughtful settling in. “I’m old, Pix. I don’t always keep track of who’s who anymore.” He looked toward the lady. “But she has changed, hasn’t she. There’s a heaviness now I didn’t used to see. She doesn’t wear it on her face, but it’s there. Sometimes I think I’ve forgotten how to help her.”

“She’s not the only one who’s changed,” I murmured.

He nodded slowly. “No. But that’s life. A river, carving new paths. Sometimes all you can do is sit with it.”

“Say, ‘Pix, you’ve grown,’” he told me, with the ghost of his old mischief.

“How?”

“For one, you don’t answer to ‘boy’ anymore.” It was true. I didn’t know my real name — Pix, baby, sometimes mutt — but boy didn’t fit anymore either. “You used to just react. Now you choose. You’ll make a fine dog someday.”

Something settled warm in my chest, like a missing piece clicking into place.

He left, wobbling after his owner, glancing back once with a glint of mischief. I didn’t know it yet, but that was the last time I’d see Rex.

We came home to the man alone on the couch, a glass of something dark and sour in his hand. The lady’s shoulders were tight, her jaw clenched, when she walked in.

“I can’t do this anymore,” she said, her voice trembling but firm. A declaration of war in a quiet house.

Their arguments went on, louder, more frequent — words I didn’t understand but felt in the vibrations of the floor. But they no longer defined me. I had my own small joys now: sunbeams, stolen socks, the scent of a squirrel just past the window. Their noise was just weather. My own heartbeat kept its own time.

Then one day he sat beside me, his hand heavy on my back, his eyes red-rimmed. “What should I do, Pix? She wants more. Maybe I’m not ready. Maybe I’m not enough.” His voice cracked. “I love her more than life itself. But what if I break her? What if she breaks me?”

I didn’t know what a man could want from a dog in a moment like that. So I did what Rex taught me — I barked once, rolled onto my back, and dropped my slobbery tennis ball at his feet. I’m here. I’m with you.

He laughed, watery and real. “You always know how to make me laugh, huh, Pix?” Something in him cracked open, just a little — a fragile hope, rekindled.

He threw the ball. I caught it mid-air, joy surging through me. Then he barged into the other room — and let me say, the day I do that, somebody calls it biting.

She sat on the bed, surrounded by a mountain of clothes. The man got down on one knee, his hand trembling in his pocket.

“Maybe I let my fear hold me back too long,” he said. “You deserve a future. If we can love a dog together, we have a shot together. We have something real.”

“You’re basing this on the fact we got a dog?” she asked, amused, eyes shining.

“No. You moving in mattered. The key mattered. Pix mattered. It all meant us. I want every first with you — because I love you. Will you marry me?”

“Yes,” she said, voice choked with tears. “A million times, yes.”

Rex arrived a week later, his whole body a wagging, panting mess, his owner beside him. I went absolutely bonkers — barking, leaping, spinning.

“Would you just shut UP already,” Rex groaned, collapsing onto the floor like a furry sack of potatoes.

“So what finally gave you the push, son?” her father was asking inside.

“I decided to embrace the canine perspective,” the man said. “Enjoy every last minute.”

“Hear that, Pix? He learned something from you! Guess the saying’s true — men are dogs.”

They went inside, leaving Rex and me to ourselves.

“Question, Rex—”

“Shut. Up.”

“But why does he have that different hair?”

“He’s Jewish,” Rex mumbled.

“Jewish?” The word joined my growing pile of mysterious human words — mortgage, commitment, kids. “What’s Jewish?”

Rex groaned like a deflating balloon. “If I tell you, will you let me sleep?”

“Promise!”

“It’s... complicated. A way of belonging. Traditions, stories, the things that tell you your place in the world.” He paused. “I don’t know what you did, Boy, but you did good.”

“You called me Boy!” I beamed.

“Give it a rest,” he grumbled, smiling anyway.

“But what are kids? And what’s a mortgage?”

“That’s it, I’m going inside,” he declared, hauling himself up. “You’re going to drive me crazy.”

“Wait! What’s commitment?” I scrambled after him, my mind buzzing with unanswered questions. The human world was vast and confusing. I was determined to understand it — one puzzling word at a time.
