chapters.title: Haven’t You Done Enough?
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

Maturing is finally realizing that the person you turned down does not owe you friendship. They are free to walk out.

Haven’t you done enough? Maturing is finally realizing that the person you turned down does not owe you friendship — they are free to walk out. Growing up is the ability to take that step away.

My best friend—the girl I grew up with, the one who shaped my childhood with laughter and shared secrets— recently came to a realization about herself. She is a lesbian. Not a phase, not an experiment, but a truth she has accepted with unwavering certainty. She says I have to accept her too.

I am not homophobic. I don’t hate her. But I do not support her decision either. And yet, here we are, at a crossroads of understanding, where affection meets

ideology, and where love—true, profound, unconditional— seeks to bridge the gap.

She tells me love is about souls, not bodies. That genitalia is a technicality, an accident of biology, but hearts recognize each other beyond those boundaries.

We have grown together, two branches of the same tree, shaped by history—not just our own, but the history of others. We watched the world shift through a screen, through books, through voices louder than ours.

When America elected its first Black president, I was jubilant, believing it to be proof that minds were opening, that change was tangible. She, ever the realist, said, “It doesn’t mean life will be better for Black people.”

Pessimism was her shield, a defense against disappointment. But I held on to hope—not just for the Black community, but for Africa, for us, for the future.

Then came the day when love itself was legislated. When a president declared that same-sex couples had the right to marry. She was ecstatic. I was silent. Who was I to drag her back to my reality, to my doubts?

She had always been an advocate for loving freely, for rejecting the idea that culture should dictate the boundaries

of the heart. “This,” she told me, “is proof that we are evolving. That we are not as rigid, not as shackled by the past as people think. It means that Africa, too, will follow. That one day, we will be free to love without fear.”

I listened but didn’t respond. I understood her conviction, but I could see the tide rising, the cultural peer pressure growing, the world shifting in ways that felt both inevitable and uncertain.

She believes the world will teach us tolerance, that love is a choice we should respect, that every person deserves dignity, that no one should suffer for who they are. And perhaps, in that belief, she is right. But for me, it is not so simple. Not because I lack love for her, but because I am still trying to understand where I stand in a world that refuses to stand still.

Yet all those thoughts I kept to myself, buried deep in the depths of my mind, never daring to whisper them to her.

I always wondered if she would be influenced. Maybe my answer came too soon. When her boyfriend shattered her heart, leaving her devastated, I was there. The end of high school marked the end of her first love—the boy she thought was forever. I held her through the storm, through her broken pieces and demons. I was her shelter, and I had hoped, foolishly, that she would see me. That she would look at me the way I looked at her. Did I ever mention that I adored her?

Then came university, a different world altogether. It was diverse, bursting with colors, languages, and beliefs. High school had never been my place, but I hoped to belong here, and more than anything, I hoped that she would finally see me. That my love, long unspoken, would be recognized.

That was when we met Mary, a Swedish student. A trio was born, but soon, I found myself the third wheel. We would talk after classes, linger in the school lobby, waiting for our next lectures or simply for time to pass. But she gravitated toward Mary, drawn to her in a way that went beyond friendship. I saw it happen—saw her eyes soften, saw the magnetic pull. And suddenly, I was on the outside looking in. A duo had formed, and I was just an orbiting satellite.

I studied international relations. I was taught about tolerance, about the power of diplomacy, about how persistence could change the tide of history. But how do you negotiate with the heart?

A friend once asked me, “Why are you always around her if she can’t return the love you give her?”

I didn’t know how to answer without sounding cliché.

“It’s not just because we grew up together,” I wanted to say. “It’s because I adore her, thorns and all. Because no matter the pain, she has always been there for me, and I want to be there for her. Because when she laughs, the world feels lighter, and when she smiles, the dullness fades away.”

But those words remained unspoken. Instead, I simply said, “I don’t know.”

It was around the time the African-American president was preparing to leave office. He had done much, but he could have done more. In his final days, he spoke of reparations, a gesture long overdue. We sat in the school lobby, watching his farewell address.

“Well, not a lot has changed,” I muttered, playing the pessimist for once.

“Depends,” she said, her voice light with certainty. “History was written. There have been changes—you just have to be positive.”

She turned then, her eyes locking onto Mary’s. A giggle, a knowing smile, and then a kiss.

My heart clenched. A new kind of pain blossomed inside me, sharp and unforgiving.

I had lost her in ways I never thought possible.

This was my new reality—she would never love me. Then I remembered her words: “You have to be positive.” For what, though?

I stood to leave, as a new era approached. The news of Uganda fighting against homosexuality was still fresh. The words of our president declaring that homosexuality bills were not a concern for our people echoed in my mind. The chains of forced tolerance were tightening around us.

“Tolerance… would they tolerate us?” I muttered bitterly. Too loudly, it seemed, as heads turned to stare at me.

“I want you to write a thesis on your beliefs about neocolonialism,” my professor said as he left the lecture hall. “Speak of what it is and what it is doing to poorer nations. This is what you think and understand.”

I sighed in exasperation. What did he know about neocolonialism? A white man from a developed nation, rich enough to create the very system that kept us in chains.

“Can we talk?” her voice startled me. I had been avoiding her since my outburst in the lobby.

“What do you want?” I asked coldly, shoving my books into my bag. I had never spoken to her like this before. It must have stung.

“I haven’t seen you in days,” she said softly. Her voice wavered, and I saw her smother a sigh.

“I’ve been busy.”

Her eyes glistened with unshed tears. “You know you can tell me anything,” she whispered, her voice cracking.

Remorse spread through me like an infection. Maybe now was the time to finally say it—to tell her how I felt.

“Why am I nothing but your friend?” My voice was quieter now, raw. “I have given you nothing but love, yet I am still nothing but your friend.”

Silence pressed against us. When I turned, I found her crying, her eyes red and swollen.

“Is that it? Or is there something more?” I asked, confused.

“What if we became more than just friends? What then? You’d get tired of me and just leave?” she sobbed.

This wasn’t just about me.

“What’s wrong?” I asked sympathetically. It always happened to me—I’d flare up one moment, only to soften the next, my hand reaching out in an attempt to comfort. But she slapped it away, resentment flashing in her eyes. There was no fixing this.

“Look, I’m sorry I wasn’t there when I was supposed to be. We can talk about it if you want,” I offered, but she

had already turned toward the door. I knew I wouldn’t get a response after that outburst.

“Everyone is growing tired of me, and it hurts.”

That was it. She walked away, fury likely burning inside her, though her tears had carried away the sharp edges of her rage. She had composed herself before stepping out.

“Is it so hard to admit that you’re a victim of a cultural influence that isn’t yours?” I shot back before she could leave. She froze at the doorway, her fingers tightening on the doorknob. The air between us crackled with unspoken words, tension coiling in the silence. “Why do you always want people feeling sad for you when you make your own choices?” I added, my voice laced with frustration. I knew what I had done, and I wasn’t taking it back.

She turned slightly, her voice tight. “I make my own choices, and if you can’t tolerate me, leave me be!”

I felt the weight of her words settle in my chest. A gray cloud of sadness loomed over me. What had I done? My best friend would never look at me the same way again.

Needing to clear my head, I walked into an empty lecture hall, hoping to vent my frustration on an unassuming chair or table. Instead, I stumbled upon a couple kissing passionately, the boy’s hands eagerly

exploring the girl’s body. Embarrassed, I muttered an apology and rushed out, only to pause at the door. I opened it again briefly, wondering—had I really just seen that? But it didn’t matter. I had other things to focus on.

Deadline. The best motivation to get work done. Mine was just eight hours away. What would I write about? Foreign debt? Conditions for receiving aid? Then it struck me.

The chains of neocolonialism will continue to dangle as long as Africa’s leaders accept scraps from the tables of world powers and hoard them for themselves. Neocolonialism is a food chain.

This pertains to the youth of the continent—the trendsetters and followers. Don’t they grow up so quickly...?

I hesitated. Pertains didn’t feel right. I searched for a better word, but my mind wandered back to what I had seen earlier. Why would she do that to her? Mary had seemed to be enjoying herself, but—was she even into women? That was a question for another time.

Foreign countries tighten their grip on growing nations, exploiting corrupt regimes that crush their own people.

I could have run to tell her about Mary, tattled like a child, but a voice whispered in my head: Haven’t you done enough?

The real question is, haven’t they done enough? From the chains of imperialism to slavery, and now...

A growl in my stomach reminded me I hadn’t eaten. I headed to the fridge for a snack when I heard a slow, hesitant knock at the door. I wasn’t expecting anyone. My status showed I was out on a drive with my roommate—a lie.

I opened the door reluctantly. There she stood, looking like a mess. Swollen eyes, evidence of tears shed long before she reached my doorstep.

“She just became distant and cold,” she said, stepping inside, coffee in hand. “Then she told me it wasn’t working—just like that. No conversation, no warning. And when I asked why, she yelled at me, told me I should have read the signs. How was I supposed to know? I thought she was just having a bad day.”

She sniffled, took another sip of her coffee. I stayed silent. After everything that had happened—the argument, my final words, the encounter with Mary—I didn’t know what to say.

“Please don’t do this to me. Your silence is just going to hurt more,” she pleaded, trying to meet my eyes. Still, I said nothing. Was it anger? Sadness? Or just the exhaustion of always offering empathy?

She sighed. “Remember when we were kids? You asked why I didn’t have a girlfriend, then said you hoped I’d find someone good enough for me one day.”

I did remember. And from the look on her face, so did she.

She stared into her coffee cup. I followed her gaze, seeing her reflection rippling in the dark liquid. What was she thinking?

I stood up and walked toward the door. Maybe the strength I had now was what our continent needed.

“If you have no other business, you can leave now.”

Her voice wavered. “I’ve always had the crippling fear that if I chose to love you differently, you’d leave.”

I turned to face her, but she was already looking away. “I’ve carried the weight of unrequited love for so long. Haven’t you done enough?”

Haven’t we had enough? I stayed hoping and I had expectations still alive Holding on too tight Head up in the clouds

chapters.title: Letters
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

May my letters to you forge a path.

The weight of grief pressed down on her, a heavy blanket muffling the vibrant colors of her grandmother’s once- lively home. The task of cleaning loomed, a mountain of memories and dust. Her own room, a sanctuary of sorts, seemed the logical starting point.

Stepping into her closet was like stepping back in time. There, nestled amongst the ghosts of her past, hung her wedding dress, a testament to a love that had spanned decades. The familiar scent of old fabric and lavender filled the air. Her fingers brushed against the smooth silk, a pang of bittersweet longing resonating within her. Nearby, her company secretary outfits whispered tales of a different life, a life of ambition and purpose. And then, her gaze fell upon the worn leather boots, companions on

countless adventures shared with her grandfather, each scuff and scratch a reminder of laughter and shared joy.

A small, red box, tucked away in the corner, caught her attention. It was an unfamiliar object, a relic from a past she hadn’t known existed. Curiosity piqued, she lifted the lid. Inside, a collection of letters, fragile and yellowed with age, lay bound together with a faded ribbon. The top letter, written in a childish scrawl, bore the name “Romano.”

Dear friend, it began. Hello there friend from wherever. I am Penelope and yes I’ve heard the jokes. I hope I can write to you forever and know what goes on in your country. Write me back.

A wave of nostalgia washed over her. She recognized the handwriting, her grandmother’s, so young and full of innocent enthusiasm. Beneath the letter was a reply, a crayon-drawn missive from Romano.

Dear friend, it read. Hello, I am Romano. I wouldn’t make fun of your name it’s beautiful. I live in Italy and I really like pasta. We will soon be in South Africa, father says he has business there, you should visit sometime. I’ll put in my new post information.

A smile touched her lips. Her grandmother, at six years old, corresponding with a pen pal from across the world. She could almost picture her, sitting at her little desk, carefully crafting her replies. Another letter, also in crayon, confirmed her suspicions.

Dear Romano, Penelope wrote. That sounds exciting, you’ll see lions and all sorts of stuff. I’ve always wanted to live in London and meet the queen. I live in Kenya, you should come visit. We have bad people called the Mau Mau causing trouble. You should visit too, I am six years old what about you.

The innocence of their exchange was heartwarming. The world, in their young eyes, was a place of endless possibilities, a place where friendships could blossom across continents. A later letter, written when Penelope was sixteen, revealed a more complex world.

Dear Penny, Romano wrote, the childish scrawl replaced by a more mature hand. Hello my lovely friend, I am sorry for staying silent for so long, I was sent to boarding school and got enlisted once I was seventeen. I got your letter after I visited my father’s house in South Africa. We have encountered a few financial issues, father is too proud to liquidate his assets. How have you been though?

A wry smile touched her lips as she read the next letter. “Seems like gentlemen existed in my grandma’s period,” she murmured, a stark contrast to the modern men who “ghost

you and expect you to be welcoming after eight months. Ten months, even,” she added with a click of her tongue.

Dear Romy, Penelope’s elegant cursive flowed across the page. Hellooooooo, I have missed you so much. When did you join the army? You have to tell me everything. I know I took a while to reply, but I also happen to be in boarding school. Father joined the independence government; he has very little time for me these days. That said, I attached a picture of our new airport in Mombasa. Please visit. Also, I added my phone number in case you feel the need to call.

Love, Penny.

“My grandmother was something else,” she chuckled. The care she took with her handwriting, the eagerness to share her life – it was a world away from the fleeting connections of the present.

The next letter, from Romy, offered a surprising proposition.

Dear Penny, it read. Hello again, I have a proposal. Why don’t we just stick to letters? This could be our new hobby. We write to each other and tell each other stories of where we are. Show the next generation how we colored each other’s world, and when we are ready, we’ll meet, be it here or there. The world is a small place. I am currently fighting the government. They are forcefully enlisting men to go fight a senseless war in Vietnam. Well, that would explain our ridiculously large military budget. Also, I’m going to

become a citizen soon. I don’t know if I told you, but I am Italian. I sent a package of a painting I did.

Love, Romy.

“These two agreed to never hear each other’s voices, then you have modern guys, already calling once they get a number from ‘a friend’,” she muttered, shaking her head. A question nagged at her: what had happened to the painting? She scanned the room, then ventured into the hallway, her search growing more frantic. It was nowhere to be found. Returning to the closet, she picked up the next letter.

Dear Romy, Penelope wrote, her tone filled with warmth. I am so touched by the painting; it is beautiful. It is almost as though you captured it with a camera. I sent you some pictures of our beautiful Uhuru Park, Masai Mara, and the Thompson Falls. I have taken up photography as a hobby. My father supports me, and so does my boyfriend. I have been waiting to tell you this. I met him in a coffee house, and we were both reading the same novel by our favorite author. It was a romance story called “By Chance”—it was ironical.

Love, Penny.

A gasp escaped her lips. “That’s not how you and guka met!” she exclaimed. The image of her grandparents, locking eyes over a shared novel in a cozy coffee shop, clashed sharply with the story she had always been told. According to family

lore, they had met at a funeral, a minister’s funeral, of all things. It was a story that had earned them the coveted family award for “Weirdest Way I Met Your Mother/ Grandmother.” The romanticized version in the letter felt like a betrayal of that quirky, slightly morbid, and utterly unique beginning. The discrepancy between the letter and the family narrative deepened the mystery. Who was telling the truth? And what other secrets were hidden within these fragile pages? The desire to uncover the truth, to reconcile the conflicting narratives, fueled her curiosity. She knew she couldn’t stop now. She had to keep reading, keep searching, keep piecing together the fragments of her grandmother’s past.

Dear Penny, Romy wrote, his tone a mix of exuberance and regret. Oh dear! I thought you’d wait for me, I thought I’d love you till we grow old. I am so happy for you, and I was joking; let the man love you day and night. Today we marched for gay rights; we shall not relent till all people have rights, and they call them human rights. I also met a young man by the name of Stephen King. I mentioned your name, and he seemed to have an idea. Well, I’ve sent you a story of his. Tell me if you love it.

Love, Romy.

“So this guy ditched war and came to march with black people, gay ones too, and those who didn’t want to fight in Vietnam. Grandma, your pen pal is scared of flying. I wish I

could have better news,” she mused, a hint of admiration in her voice.

A heavier note entered the next letter.

Dearest Penelope, Romy’s words were tinged with a hint of guilt. I haven’t received a letter from you in ages; I hope all fares well. I have a son now, my wife—who I had forgotten to mention, no, let me not lie to you, my greatest friend. I got her pregnant, and I couldn’t bear the shame of her being a single mother. So I married her. It is illegal to abort a child, but all in all, I wanted it to have a life. Please write to me as soon as you can.

Love, Romy.

“Wow, Grandma, you’re ghosting our guy in letters? Also, a wife? Weren’t you gay?” she exclaimed, a half- eaten bun in her hand. A loose photograph slipped from the envelope. It was a snapshot of a beaming Romy, a woman she assumed was his wife, and the most adorable little boy. Another photo, of a person she didn’t recognize, lay tucked behind. “Well, that means family albums never have everything,” she concluded.

Dear Romy, Penelope’s reply was filled with a profound sadness. I apologize for not writing sooner. I have been

mourning; my boyfriend died. All I’ve had was the comfort of my cat, Snuffy. I couldn’t write despite every letter you sent. You have a very beautiful family. Your son looks like you. As a soul left the earth, another came in. He shall grow up to be the sweetest little boy ever. I fell into a hole of despair; I cannot find the strength to crawl out of it. I only pray for strength.

Love, Penny.

“Well, that explains why she hasn’t ever had a break-up. I always wonder why my relationship history is more traumatic,” she reflected, unaware that she was speaking aloud.

Dear Penny, Romy wrote, his words laced with empathy. I simply lack the words to comfort you; you are in my prayers. I wish I could come to comfort you and your family; I myself have had a tragedy befall me. My father has passed on. There were problems between us, but I simply find it hard to believe he’s gone. I wish I could tell him one final time that I forgive him; those three words would lift all from my heart. We will recover. I sent you a care package from Sicily; we went for our honeymoon there since we never did get one. Your nephew is in the hands of his grandmother.

Love, Romy

The letters offered a glimpse into her grandmother’s life, a life she had never known. They were a treasure trove of memories, a connection to a past that was both familiar and foreign. As she carefully placed the letters back in the box, she felt a sense of connection to her grandmother, a deeper understanding of the woman she had loved so dearly. The cleaning could wait. For now, she would delve into the past, piece by piece, letter by letter.

“Note to self, your dream man is Italian, living around in South Africa, the USA, and taking holidays in Italy. He’s also married, so despair and die!” she declared dramatically, flopping onto her back. Her thoughts drifted back to the painting, and then to the house itself. It had been in her family for generations, a legacy passed down through time. “I came and found it,” her grandmother had often said, a sense of quiet pride in her voice. The boma was vast, encompassing acres of land, yet her grandmother’s cottage- like house had remained untouched, a testament to its special place in their history.

Dear Romy, Penelope wrote, her words brimming with news. It has been long. I know. I’m finally graduating! Oh, how I miss your jokes. I recently traveled to Nigeria, and strangely, I met someone who made my heart race again. He is also Kenyan. He makes me laugh, and he is studying so he

can work in the government. I have sent a picture of him. My photography is getting better. I found comfort and home in him. Where are you now, you globe trotter? I would like to visit you soon.

Love, Penny.

A wistful smile played on her lips. The beauty of their correspondence struck her. They painted vivid pictures of their worlds with words and shared snapshots of their lives without the aid of modern technology. They lived their stories and then shared them with each other, a tangible connection across the miles. She couldn’t quite explain the pull these letters exerted on her, a fascination with a world so different yet so intimately connected to her own.

Dear Penelope, Romy’s letter carried a note of weariness. I have finally retired to my cottage in Italy. My son is serving in the army. He told me he was gay; I’m not sure how I felt about that. Sometimes I thought that our stories would pave the way for our children or grandchildren to find true love. I have found out that I had a brother from another mother; he died. I feel like I have lost a lot. I fear my son will be rejected because of his sexual orientation, but I have hope.

Love, Romy.

The letters grew scarcer, the intervals between them stretching longer. A sense of unease settled upon her. Was this the beginning of the end of their correspondence?

Dear Romy, Penelope wrote, her hand guided by the weight of years. I write to you with my granddaughter at my side. She is so tiny and fragile. In her, I see hope and love. We named her Mumbi. It translates to ‘the creator.’ I also have built a cottage. I live in what I call a boma; soon, my sons shall build houses in the boma, and my sons-in-law too. I look at the oak tree where Mumbi shall swing with siblings, cousins, and friends. Where she will kiss her first boy, and they shall meet my wrath. I see her laughing around a bonfire with family. I have lost track of time. I’ve seen and read IT. Stephen King should have told you what he had planned.

Love, Penny.

It was a testament to the enduring power of family, the promise of future generations, and the subtle shift from youthful dreams to the realities of a life lived. The mention of Stephen King and IT brought a smile to her face. It was a small, almost insignificant detail, yet it grounded the narrative in a shared cultural moment, a connection that transcended the personal. The letters were more than just a historical record; they were a living testament to the enduring power of friendship, love, and the human spirit. And as she held the last letter in her hand, she knew that the story wasn’t over. It was just waiting to be continued, not on paper, but in the lives of those who came after. “Okay let’s keep reading,” she declared to herself.

That was the last letter. Mumbi carefully placed it back in the box, a pang of sadness mixed with a strange sense of completion. Her grandmother had kept all the letters, a treasure trove of memories she had intended to share with Mumbi one day. As Mumbi reflected on the stories within, she marveled at her grandmother’s uncanny foresight. Everything Penelope had predicted about Mumbi’s life had come to pass with astonishing accuracy.

“Well, can’t say I expected much. He is a typical guy!” she muttered, a touch of wry amusement in her voice. With a renewed sense of purpose, she began cleaning, carefully moving her grandmother’s antique furniture. Six hours later, punctuated by four twenty-minute breaks, the room was spotless. A well-deserved fast-food treat seemed like the perfect way to celebrate her accomplishment.

“Mumbi! There’s mail for shosh,” one of her cousins shouted from the hallway. “Check if they’re asking for her photos for the exhibition.”

“Why can’t you?” Mumbi grumbled, the familiar price of being the family favorite. Sighing, she took the letter from the mailman. The return address was a hospital in Nairobi. “We cleared everything, doctor,” she murmured to herself, tearing open the envelope. Her heart skipped a beat as she unfolded the letter.

Dear Penny, Romy wrote, his words a mix of urgency and warmth. In my last will and testament, I said if I was ever in

a vegetative state, I should be brought to your country to live out my last moments. I am currently in Nairobi, at the Aga Khan Hospital, under treatment. My last wish is to see the person who made my days so joyous. Not that I’m in a vegetative state; I’m just chilling with my grandson, as my grandson would say it.

Love, Romy.

Mumbi froze, the letter trembling in her hands. How could she possibly tell him that Penelope, the woman who had filled his life with joy for decades, was gone? The weight of the secret pressed down on her, a burden she felt ill-equipped to carry.

“Penelope junior,” she whispered to herself, her mind racing. “If you give this man the news through a letter, he’ll die. You’ll be as guilty as the Penelope that led him on for years and then decided to die. If you don’t write back, you’ll still kill him. If you don’t show… wait, show up? What if he’s a serial killer waiting to kill me or Grandma?”

She paced back and forth, her heart pounding in her chest. The possibilities, both real and imagined, swirled around her, creating a whirlwind of anxiety. The safest option seemed to be to ignore the letter, to let Romy

believe that Penelope was still alive. But the thought of denying him his last wish, of leaving him in a state of hopeful anticipation, gnawed at her conscience. The alternative was to tell him the truth, to shatter his world with the news of Penelope’s death. But how could she do that, especially after all they had shared? And then there was the fear, the irrational but persistent fear that Romy was not the gentle, loving man her grandmother had corresponded with for so many years, but a dangerous stranger with unknown motives.

A sudden, unexpected thought cut through the chaos. What if she went to see him? Not as Penelope, but as her granddaughter, Mumbi. She could introduce herself as Penelope’s namesake, a connection to the woman he had loved, and offer him comfort in his final days. It would be a way to honor her grandmother’s memory, to fulfill her last unspoken wish, and to finally meet the man who had been such an important part of her life. The decision was made. She would go. She would face her fears and meet Romy, not as Penelope, but as the link to the past, the bridge between two worlds.

“Look what you got me into you old…”

“Dear Mom,” Mumbi texted, her fingers flying across the screen. “I’m in a hitch.”

“Honey, you know you’re texting; you don’t have to say ‘dear Mom’,” her mother replied.

“Oh, sorry. Anyway…” Mumbi launched into a rapid-fire explanation of the situation, the letter, her fears, and her indecision. Her mother’s response was brief and to the point. “Go see the man.” A follow-up text added, “Besides, we cannot leave Russia after we got here.”

Mumbi stared at the phone, a wry smile twisting her lips. “Well, with that reply, I think I know where my abandonment issues stem from,” she muttered.

The hospital loomed before her, an imposing structure of glass and steel. She stood frozen on the sidewalk, the weight of her mission pressing down on her. She was scared, more scared than she had anticipated. What was she going to say? How was she going to explain her presence?

Suddenly, someone bumped into her, jarring her out of her thoughts. A surge of anger coursed through her, but it quickly subsided when she saw him. He was cute, undeniably cute.

“What, you scared of hospitals?” he said with a playful smirk, before walking away.

Mumbi took a deep breath and stepped inside. “Mumbi, you’ll make an excellent documentary about a dimwit killed by a serial killer in the hospital,” she chastised herself. She approached the nurses‘ station, her heart pounding in her chest.

“Hello, is there a Romano here?” she asked.

The nurses exchanged confused glances.

“Why are you looking for my uncle?” a voice said from behind her. She turned to see… Bumpy, the cute guy from the entrance. Of all the people in the hospital, she had to run into him again. Now came the difficult part, the explanation.

“Well,” she began, trying to sound casual, “he kinda used to send my granny letters. They were pen pals and stuff like that.”

The nurses seemed satisfied with her explanation.

“It would have been strange if you were her,” one of them commented. “How does someone stay so young and beautiful from the 60s?”

Mumbi felt a flicker of annoyance at the blatant charm, but it was quickly overshadowed by a wave of relief. This is how all her disastrous relationships started, she thought wryly.

“Well, my grandmother is no longer with us,” Mumbi said, her voice tinged with sadness.

“Why? What happened?” he asked, his brow furrowed with concern.

“She died, like, the life in her is gone, gone, baby!” Mumbi blurted out, then immediately cringed at her awkward phrasing.

The entire reception area seemed to fall silent. She assumed they had all overheard her clumsy explanation, and she felt a wave of embarrassment wash over her.

“But I’m fine,” she quickly added, trying to lighten the mood. “Now, how do we break this to your uncle?”

He looked at her, his expression a mix of sadness and understanding. “I’ll let you in on a secret,” he said quietly. “I wrote that last letter because it was his final wish. I need to pull the plug on him so he can rest. I want to cremate him and spread his ashes over a hillside. He also wished your grandma was here.”

The revelation hit Mumbi like a ton of bricks. He knew. He had known all along. And he had been waiting for her.

A warm, fuzzy feeling enveloped Mumbi, a comfortable sense of connection. Then, she remembered the uncle. She looked into his eyes, and he looked back, a silent acknowledgment passing between them.

“Hey, do you have a picture of the Kijabe hills?” she asked, the question seemingly coming out of nowhere. The odd thing was, her grandmother had never been one for hiking. So how did she end up on that particular hill?

“Not that I know of. Well, my uncle kept talking about a picture, but I can’t seem to find it.”

“I can’t find a bloody painting he sent over here,” Mumbi replied, a hint of frustration in her voice.

They looked at each other again and smiled, a shared sense of bewilderment connecting them. Mumbi didn’t feel quite so overwhelmed anymore, but she couldn’t explain why this strange situation suddenly felt so… right.

“Would you like to go see him?” he asked. Then what? she thought, but she nodded anyway, a strange compulsion guiding her.

As they stood by the bedside, looking at the frail figure lying in the hospital bed, he spoke. “Takes a strong bond to do what they did.”

Mumbi’s heart ached with a bittersweet mix of emotions. “It was love. Unconditional love, the kind you need every day. To know you’re held. To know you’re appreciated.” She leaned down and gently kissed his forehead.

“Hey,” he said, turning to her with a warm smile. “Would you like to get coffee sometime?”

She smiled back, a genuine smile this time. Then, the old man in the bed stirred, his eyes fluttering open. In a surprisingly strong voice, he called out a name, the name of his long-distance friend. “Penny!”

Mumbi stepped back, her heart pounding in her chest. A wave of dizziness washed over her, and she stumbled, grabbing onto the bedside table for support. She looked at the old man, his eyes now wide open and focused, a look of recognition and longing in them. Then, she looked at his grandson, who was staring at his uncle with a mixture of shock and disbelief.

“He’s awake,” she whispered, her voice trembling. “He’s actually awake.”

The old man’s gaze shifted to her, his eyes softening with a hint of warmth. “Penny?” he whispered, his voice weak but clear.

Mumbi’s mind raced. What was she supposed to do? How could she explain that she wasn’t Penny, that she was just her granddaughter? But before she could say anything, the old man closed his eyes again, a peaceful smile gracing his lips.

“He’s gone,” his grandson said softly, his voice filled with a mix of sadness and relief.

Mumbi nodded, tears welling up in her eyes. She felt a strange sense of connection to this man, this man who had loved her grandmother so deeply. She reached out and gently touched his hand, a silent farewell passing between them.

She turned, a spring in her step, the weight of the encounter settling into a bittersweet memory. “See you around,” she told his grandson, offering a small, knowing smile that held the unspoken understanding of their shared experience. She paused, considering the invitation for coffee. “Actually,” she said, changing her mind, “I think I will take you up on that coffee. But first,” she added, a mischievous glint in her eyes, “there’s something I need to show you.” She pulled out her phone and began scrolling through her photos, stopping at a picture of Kijabe hills. “It’s… um, my work. We should visit.”

Dear Romy, Penelope’s letter was filled with a sense of finality. I haven’t sent you much, ever since the painting. I have handed it down to my daughter; she will do the same for her daughter. I have decided to send you a picture of

Kijabe hills, the last place I went before he died. Something broke my fall. Doctors said I was lucky to walk again.

Love, Penny.

Dear Penny, Romy wrote, his tone tinged with a hint of playful exasperation. I don’t understand why you called to mention that these letters should be kept a secret. It broke the mystery, but I’m happy I heard you. I shall start a tradition soon. I have framed your picture. I shall have my ashes spread there.

Love, Romy.

chapters.title: When We Were Children
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

We are not born with hate. It is taught to us.

I was hanging off the jungle gym, my fingers gripping the cool metal bars as I swung back and forth. At twelve years old, I was the oldest among us.

“What do we play today?” I called out to Marie, who sat under a tree, lost in the pages of a book.

“Why bother?” she replied without looking up. “The white people are leaving the country.”

Probably our last days here. Kenya had attained self- government, then doubled up with independence. The Mau Mau had won. For years, they had fought our people— fought my people. Now the government was buying our land and urging us to leave.

“Doesn’t mean we can’t have fun!” I said, dropping from the jungle gym.

Marie sighed. “I don’t know, Andy. Ask Manny.”

Manny and his siblings stood nearby, watching me. They were the only Indians we were allowed to play with—mainly because their parents were rich and well-connected. His little brother, Bahubu, was too young to do much more than sit and blubber, while his sister, Sakshi, clutched the hem of her dress and stayed close to him.

“Let’s go on a treasure hunt!” Manny suggested, his eyes lighting up with excitement.

“The only treasure you’ll find out here is a Mau Mau ready to kill you,” Marie muttered.

I walked over to her and snatched the book from her hands. Chemistry. I rolled my eyes. “Have fun while you can! We’re going back to cold, damp, icy Britain soon. When do you think you’ll ever see this country again?”

“Never, if we have to,” she snapped. “Give me back my book!”

I smirked and tossed it a few feet away. She lunged past me, but before she could grab it, Manny scooped it up and hesitated.

“Manny!” I called out. “We’re going into the forest today!”

Marie crossed her arms. “It’s not safe.”

I ignored her, repeating the words I had heard from my father. “Marie, our ancestors tamed the forests of Britain. They explored and conquered these lands, made them ours. That’s why we’re here today.”

We walked together into the forest, stepping onto paths worn by generations of feet—some belonging to people like us, others belonging to those who wanted us gone. The towering trees cast long shadows, their branches swaying with the wind. Birds fluttered above, and the undergrowth rustled with unseen creatures. The air smelled damp, rich with the scent of earth and life.

A shiver ran down my spine. I felt watched. Eyes, unseen but present, trailed us from the darkness of the trees.

“The Home Guard won’t be happy we came here alone,” Marie muttered.

“When did you last see the Home Guard out here?” I countered.

She had no answer. Ever since the British government had surrendered control, we—the white settlers—had been told to leave. The indigenous Kenyans wanted

their land back. They had fought for it, and they had won.

A sudden rustle in the bush made me freeze. My heart pounded in my chest. I turned my head sharply, but the others hadn’t noticed. The shadows seemed to shift, the forest itself holding its breath.

I looked around, my heart hammering against my ribs. Adrenaline surged through me as my eyes darted left and right.

Where was it? Who was it?

I forced myself to take a slow, calming breath.

“What’s wrong?” Marie asked. I didn’t answer. Something held my attention. Behind a bush, a girl peeked out. Her dark complexion glowed under the sunlight. The moment she realized I had seen her, she turned and ran.

Normal people don’t chase those who tried to murder their kind. But I wasn’t normal in that moment. I took off after her, my legs pumping as I raced up the hill. “Wait!” I called out, but she kept running.

Marie and the others followed, Marie pleading for me to stop. But I wasn’t listening. This could have been a trap,

but why would they bother killing us when we were already leaving?

I chased her until we reached a boma. A thorn bush fence encircled a small, grass-thatched hut. I hesitated, then climbed over it carefully, even though the entrance was right there. My father had taught me that the Mau Mau were expert bomb makers—who knew if they had rigged the entrance?

Manny walked right through the opening. Nothing happened. He took the thrill out of it all!

We circled the hut, its mud walls cracked from the sun. I stood on my tiptoes, peering through the small window.

I imagined myself as the Home Guard. They would storm in, kicking doors open, dragging out suspected Mau Mau fighters from the reserves. I wanted to feel that power—to see what was inside.

I lifted my foot and kicked the door. It barely budged.

“Should we go back?” Marie asked, eager for any excuse to leave.

“No!” I snapped. My fingers fumbled for the latch. I twisted it one way, then another. Nothing.

Manny pulled out a thin wire, twisting it with careful precision. Where had he even gotten it?

The latch gave way with a soft click. I will never be sure how he can do some things but I liked it.

We stepped inside. The air was thick and warm, carrying the scent of earth and sweat. Darkness swallowed us, the dim light from the doorway barely illuminating the room ahead. My breath hitched.

Something was in here with us.

“Mbeberu!” A soft voice, filled with both fear and defiance, cut through the silence. The word stung. That’s what the Kenyans called us.

I turned and saw her standing there—the girl from before. She gripped a spear in her small hands.

I jumped back, my pulse racing. “Hey now!” I stammered, unsure what to say.

She could have killed us in an instant. We were no match—two white children and three Indian ones against a Kikuyu child soldier. This wasn’t a story where we fought and survived.

“We are not here to hurt you!” I said, my British accent thick on my tongue.

Either my voice disgusted her, or she had noticed something behind me, because her expression twisted in a swirl of emotions.

“Rudi kwenu,” she spat. “We’ve had enough of you people!”

At least she spoke English. My Kikuyu was barely passable.

“Do you want to play with us?” The words tumbled out of my mouth, ridiculous and childish. But I wasn’t thinking—I was only trying to reach her.

She hesitated, confused.

“Look, we can be friends. Don’t hate us just because of what the adults are doing.”

A tense silence stretched between us.

Then I realized something—Marie was gone.

Panic gripped me. My heartbeat surged. She’d die out there alone!

I turned and ran to the door, frantically searching the trees. “Help us! Please!”

The girl stared at me, deliberating. Then, with a sigh, she walked ahead, guiding us.

It didn’t take long to find Marie. She was running, shrieking, “Help! There’s a Mau Mau child soldier after us! She had my brother and my friends!”

Now they were hers? Not surprising, coming from Marie.

The girl caught up to Marie and tackled her, pinning her down. They struggled near the edge of a slope.

Marie thrashed, screaming for help.

“Will you relax?!” I shouted, praying they wouldn’t tumble down. Manny and his siblings remained silent, forbidden to speak.

The forest watched, waiting to see who would win.

“Where are we?” I asked the girl.

She turned her head, scanning the unfamiliar surroundings, just as bewildered as we were. Shadows stretched long over the thick canopy, the air heavy with the scent of damp earth and distant, unseen creatures. My heart still pounded from the panic of before, convinced we had been doomed—until she had leaped effortlessly onto a tree and started climbing.

She moved with an ease that defied hesitation, her bare feet finding steady purchase against the rough bark. Not once did she falter, not even with the boys below her, some of whom—had this been different circumstances— might have been indecent enough to sneak a glance beneath her skirt. But she was far beyond reach, her focus solely on the horizon.

Moments passed, then she sighed. A heavy, hopeless sound.

“I can’t see town,” she called down.

Then, just as swiftly as she had ascended, she began her descent, her movements controlled and instinctual. The second her feet met the ground, she turned away from us, striding off without a word.

“Wait—where are you going?” I called after her as she made her way up a ridge, her small frame disappearing into the dense undergrowth.

She didn’t stop, didn’t so much as glance back. Her voice, when it came, was devoid of warmth.

“Your people will come find you. I have no business with coloniser children.”

The words struck like a slap. Cold, firm, and absolute.

I opened my mouth, ready to protest, but she continued walking.

“We can’t survive out here alone!” I pleaded, the fear creeping into my voice despite my best efforts to sound composed. Because the truth was, we couldn’t. We had no idea how to navigate the wild, how to find food or water, or how to protect ourselves when night came.

The girl stopped then, just for a moment. Her head tilted slightly, as though she found the entire situation amusing in a dark, ironic way. When she spoke, her words were edged with something ancient, something laced with generations of pain.

“Your people came, conquered these lands, taught us a new religion, built forts, fought our people—and yet you, their offspring, cannot survive a single night in a forest.”

Her gaze met mine. “What kind of children are you?”

A slow, shameful heat crawled up my neck. I had no answer. Because she was right.

But pride is a stubborn thing. It rears its head even when it shouldn’t.

I lifted my chin, squared my shoulders, and spat the words before I could stop myself.

“Leave us, you savage African! We’ll find our way out!”

She said nothing. She only stared, something unreadable flickering across her face before she turned and disappeared into the trees.

The hours that followed were long and cruel. The sun dipped beyond the hills, shadows creeping in like silent hunters. The deeper we wandered, the more lost we became. The forest was no longer just trees and foliage —it was an abyss, swallowing us whole.

Marie’s frustration boiled over.

“Ben! Do you even know where we’re going?!” Her voice trembled on the edge of fury.

I didn’t.

I had no idea where we were.

I was leading us deeper into the unknown, into something dangerous, and worst of all—I knew it.

Manny clutched his younger brother, who hadn’t stopped crying since sunset. His sister whispered hushed comforts, but her voice was tight, brittle with

fear. Every rustling branch, every distant howl, sent shivers down my spine.

We were lost.

And I had led us here.

“If you hadn’t angered that girl, maybe she would’ve helped us!” I snapped.

Marie’s head jerked toward me, stunned. “Me?!”

“Yes, you!” I strode toward her, my voice rising. “You acted like she was something disgusting, like she was a threat! You ran from her like she was the danger here!”

She stared at me, breathing hard.

The truth settled between us, thick and suffocating.

We had needed her.

And now, because of our own arrogance, she was gone.

“If only we had stayed back at the farm! Maybe we wouldn’t be in this mess!”

Now the blame was mine? I turned to Marie, astonished. That was the card she’d play, huh?

“Maybe we shouldn’t even be playing with you!” she snapped. “You always think you’re better than all of us. I wonder why we even bother!”

I clenched my fists, swallowing the frustration rising in my throat. I had done nothing but tell the truth. Yet here we were, lost in the wilderness, tearing at each other like wild dogs instead of working together.

“Before you kill each other,” a voice cut through the trees, calm and laced with something unreadable, “I found a way for you to get back.”

We spun around.

It was her.

She had come back for us.

The breath I hadn’t realized I was holding left my chest in a rush. Nightfall had already swallowed the land whole, its darkness thick and suffocating, but relief washed over me at the sight of her. Without her, we might have wandered until exhaustion or worse found us first.

By the time we reached the edge of the forest, lanterns and flashlights flickered through the trees. Then—voices.

Our parents.

The moment we saw them, we ran.

We sprinted toward their outstretched arms, the weight of fear finally slipping from our shoulders. They pulled us close, voices shaking with relief, hands gripping our backs like they feared letting go would mean losing us all over again. No one asked where we had been. Not yet. That conversation would come later, but for now, all that mattered was that we were home.

That evening, I passed through the dimly lit hall toward my room, exhaustion weighing heavy on my limbs. But as I neared the living room, I saw him—my father.

He sat by the fireplace, staring into the flames, his face lined with something heavier than weariness.

I hesitated in the doorway.

“Father.”

His gaze lifted slowly, the firelight casting shadows over his features. He looked exhausted. No—more than that. He looked burdened.

“What is it, Benson?”

I swallowed, unsure why I suddenly felt nervous.

“When we were lost today, a young African helped us.”

His expression didn’t shift. He only sighed, long and deep, before turning back to the fire. Silence stretched between us, thick and unreadable.

I almost bid him goodnight. Almost turned away, assuming the conversation was over.

But then he spoke.

“Benson,” he murmured, voice low and firm, “let no one ever tell you that a man is lesser than you. Tables will turn.”

His words settled deep, though I didn’t fully grasp their weight at the time.

Years later, my father explained that the girl would have helped us either way—not because she had to, but because the war for independence was already over. She saw no point in harming us, not because she had forgotten, but because she had learned something.

You see, when we were children, we were taught that our enemies were inferior. But somewhere in those years of innocence, we learned something different.

That man is equal.

That our real enemy was never a people, never a nation— only our own hate and pride.

I have returned to Kenya, searching for the girl who once saved us.

I do not know where to begin.

But perhaps, the journey starts at my father’s house— where it all began.

To love is to look beyond flaws and failings, To preserve it all. For they say: Love is patient, love is kind, A humble heart, a selfless mind. It bears all things, it never fails, Through joy and sorrow, it prevails. Hate may rise, but love will mend, A faithful bond, a steadfast friend. No waters drown, no flames consume, For love endures beyond the tomb. So in all things, both great and small, Let love be done—let love be all.

chapters.title: What If We?
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

There are a million possibilities and realities. I am just happy I am getting to spend them with you.

They sat together, each absorbed in their phones, the occasional glow of the screen illuminating their faces. He stole a glance at her—she looked demure, lost in whatever she was reading. Just a normal hangout between friends. Or at least, that’s what he told himself.

Then he remembered something.

He had built an app—nothing too fancy, just a fun little project he’d been working on. The X-Verse. He was still fine- tuning the name, but it was functional enough. He sent her the link.

She looked up at him, brows raised. “What’s this for?”

“Click it,” he said, a mischievous smile playing on his lips.

A notification popped up: Let’s play a memory game. Another followed: Reminisce on how we met. A blank card appeared on her screen, ready to be filled in. She was supposed to type her memory and swipe when she was done.

She started to speak, “Not much, our school had games—”

He pressed a finger to his lips, cutting her off with a teasing look. She narrowed her eyes at him before relenting with a small smile and returning her focus to the app.

Her fingers moved across the screen, and after a moment, she swiped. He felt his phone buzz with her response.

Well, our school had games, and you were a very chill, quiet guy. I thought you were rude and maybe even dangerous. My roommate said hi, and you said hi back. We had a short conversation about names.

He chuckled, shaking his head as he read. Dangerous? That was a first. His fingers hovered over the keyboard before he began typing.

Yeah, and later that night, we went out clubbing with our friends. I got wasted trying whiskey for the first time, and you took me outside for some air. We wandered the city for hours, talking about nothing and everything. Then we went back to the club because you were worried we’d get arrested for loitering.

She laughed softly as she read it. The notification popped up again, this time with a more intriguing challenge: Now for the real test! Show us alternate realities of how you’d have met!

A tiny cartoonish black hole sucked away their previous cards, and a new prompt appeared. A floating space avatar wobbled on her screen, waiting.

She groaned, tilting her head back. “I can’t think of anything!”

He smirked, glancing away as she let out a dramatic whimper. A few seconds passed, and then his phone buzzed again.

He looked down. Her prose had earned sixteen points.

“Well, beginner’s luck for the first story!” he teased.

She grinned, holding up his screen. “Yours is a nine.”

He feigned a gasp, grabbing her phone in mock disbelief. She yanked it back before he could read more.

She had written:

We’re on a long bus ride, both heading to some unknown destination. I ask you for the window seat because I love

watching the scenery. You move without hesitation, barely looking up. We introduce ourselves, and I save my own number in your phone—just in case you forget.

He smiled, shaking his head. “You tired? Lemme see if I can beat your score.”

“You wish.”

He thought for a moment, then started typing.

We meet in math class. I’m seated beside you. The teacher walks in, and the first thing I do is whisper a joke about her wig looking like a mop. You glance at me, deadpan, and correct me—it’s not a wig, they’re locs. I stare, caught between embarrassment and amusement. That’s how it starts. We develop a bad habit of always sitting together, passing notes back and forth, laughing at the dumbest things. We make the teacher mad, but somehow, she never separates us.

He swiped and waited. A second later, she giggled.

“You got a ten,” she said, grinning.

“Just like you… wait, what?” He sat up straight, snatching her phone again, scanning the screen like it might be broken. “No way.”

She cackled, pulling it back. “Face it. I win.”

He folded his arms, feigning disappointment. But inside, he felt something shift, something small but significant. Maybe this wasn’t just a normal hangout between friends after all.

In round two, a notification told them: Describe a scenery to a first-time meeting.

Late July afternoon. A crisp breeze sneaks in every time the café door swings open, but golden rays of sunlight cut through, spilling onto the counter like melted honey. The scent of roasted coffee beans and freshly baked pastries clings to the air, wrapping around me like a warm embrace.

“The usual?” Your voice carries over the gentle hum of conversations and the faint hiss of steaming milk. You always know my order. You stand there, effortlessly at ease, your apron slightly dusted with cocoa, the little blue beanie perched on your head like a crown of familiarity. I smile and nod. I could choose something different, but why change perfection? That cup has been my favorite ever since you recommended it.

Within minutes, you craft my mocha, swirling cinnamon on top like an artist perfecting their masterpiece. The rich aroma rises, mingling with the scent of espresso and vanilla. My fingers itch to curl around the warm cup before you even set it down.

“A cup for a pretty lady!” You announce with a teasing grin, sliding it across the counter. The words are playful, but there’s something in the way your eyes linger—a flicker of something unspoken.

I step closer, fingers brushing the ceramic, the warmth seeping into my skin. “Why don’t you join me?” I ask, my voice light but hopeful.

You sigh dramatically, glancing at the clock. “My shift ends in four,” you lament, holding up four fingers as if counting down a lifetime. Your boss, ever watchful, casts a sharp glance our way, and you suppress the urge to vault over the counter.

I chuckle, shaking my head. “Guess I’ll just have to wait, then.”

And so we do—spending the fading afternoon lost in conversation, weaving stories between sips of coffee, letting the world outside blur into the background.

“Quick question, why am I the one serving the coffee?” he asked, raising an eyebrow.

“Because, my friend, you made me the best coffee in history!” She sprawled on the table before them dramatically.

“Great. If IT doesn’t work out, I’ll be a barista,” he muttered, checking her score.

She grew curious as he went silent, peering at his phone. He smirked and hid behind his screen.

She lunged for it, but he was quicker.

“Beg for the result,” he teased.

She spotted a kid passing by and signaled with her eyes. The child grinned, understanding instantly, and snatched his phone, handing it to her.

He was left dumbfounded.

“Twenty! I’m getting better at whatever this is,” she declared.

“It’s an idle game. I kinda created it to help writers, but I developed an AI to generate scenes and rank them based on a lot of things,” he explained.

“You could just say you’re a nerd and leave it at that,” she scoffed, rolling her eyes.

“Also, yours wasn’t a first-time meeting!”

“It was the first time chilling with you, though. I begin to wonder—who taught who between you and the AI?”

It was his turn. He looked around the park for inspiration.

The breeze danced through the meadow, carrying the scent of damp earth and fresh blossoms. The trees whispered in hushed rustles, their emerald leaves swaying in unison. Above, the sky stretched endlessly, a sea of sapphire dotted with drifting clouds, their shadows gliding across the grass like ghosts of forgotten dreams. The golden warmth of the sun wrapped around me, lulling me into drowsiness—until the sound of distant laughter yanked me back to the present.

The picnic sprawled across the field, a colorful array of blankets, baskets, and buzzing conversations. There would be games, stories, and an endless parade of food. I had come for the potluck, drawn by the promise of a feast. The checkered cloth beneath us was a mosaic of delights— from steaming homemade dishes to hastily grabbed store- bought snacks. You, ever predictable, had brought your favorite fish and chips. I despised it, the oily scent

clinging to my fingers—but I ate it anyway, because your laughter made the sacrifice worth it.

Then, the sky shifted. The once gentle clouds thickened into an ominous mass of slate and charcoal. A hush fell over the meadow as the first droplets kissed the earth, cold and foreboding. Thunder growled in the distance, a low warning. Chaos erupted as people scrambled to pack their things, dashing for shelter beneath the wooden gazebo.

You moved swiftly, your best friend helping you gather plates and napkins, stuffing everything into a basket. I ran toward the gazebo, only to find it overflowing with panicked guests. The rain pounded down, drenching me within seconds, my clothes clinging to my skin like a second, heavier layer. My teeth chattered as I turned, unsure where to go.

Then, you appeared. Standing just beyond the gazebo, you stretched out your hand toward me, palm open, unwavering.

The rain turned into a relentless downpour, but we stood firm, side by side. You pulled a shawl from your backpack, shaking off the droplets before wrapping it around my shoulders. It smelled like you—like warmth, like home. Your eyes crinkled at the corners as you smiled, that same

smile that turned the worst moments into something magical.

A sudden clap of thunder split the sky, making me flinch. You squeezed my arm, steadying me.

“Relax,” I murmured, my voice laced with amusement. “Worst case scenario—we die. Best case scenario—we get superpowers.”

And in that moment, soaked to the bone beneath a raging storm, you laugh.

“What were you writing? An encyclopedia?” She squinted at his screen, then at him, her expression unreadable.

He shifted under her gaze, feeling a sudden tension settle between them.

“You don’t like my fish and chips?” she asked, scowling.

“Well… the dish is very British if you ask me,” he said, attempting nonchalance.

Her eyes narrowed further. This was going downhill fast.

“I like your fish without the chips and chips without the fish,” he tried, flashing an innocent grin. “Tough crowd much?”

She pouted and turned away, her silence heavy. He could almost feel the storm of her mood rising.

He sighed. “Look, I once got food poisoning from fish and chips. Ever since then, it became my archenemy. Batman can’t feast on his sworn foe.”

Her lips twitched. He had her.

He reached out, gently hooking his index finger under her chin, lifting her head just enough to meet his gaze.

Finally, a smile broke through.

“Fourteen,” she announced.

He groaned, leaning back dramatically. She, on the other hand, was grinning ear to ear. It was her turn.

I’m seated by the pool when you emerge from the water on the other end. Droplets trail down your skin as you stride toward the bar, ordering something ice-cold. A glass of cola, its condensation trickling down the sides. The way you push your sunglasses up your nose, the way the sunlight catches in your hair—it all feels cinematic.

The heat is relentless, shimmering across the water. I dive in, the coolness swallowing me whole. I sink to the bottom, sitting there for a moment, weightless. When I glance up, I see you standing at the edge, watching. There’s a flicker of concern in your eyes.

As I rise to the surface, gasping for air, you check your watch.

“Thirty seconds,” you say with a smirk. “Bet I could last longer.”

“Prove it,” I challenge.

You jump in, yelling “Cannonball!” like an overexcited toddler, sending a wave that drenches me all over again. We laugh, then dive together, sinking into the stillness below. We sit there, staring at each other, neither of us willing to break first. You grin, and suddenly, a stream of bubbles escapes your lips, floating toward the surface. I chuckle, releasing a few bubbles of my own.

You start rising, your body moving instinctively, as if pulled by some unseen force. I reach out, catching your wrist—but the current has other plans. We both break the surface, laughing, breathless, but we don’t even know why.

“Thirty-two seconds,” you declare proudly.

“I beat you by microseconds,” I shoot back.

“What are you talking about? My head came out last!”

“At your birth, maybe,” I tease.

You fake a wince, then grin. We bicker back and forth.

He read her entry and shook his head in amusement. She had outdone herself. Again.

His eyes flicked toward his phone. The game had another prompt:

Now, describe the future.

He looked up at her, then back at the screen.

I don’t know what the future holds, but I hope we never grow out of this.

I hope you still make me cover my eyes whenever you change your t-shirt, even though we both know I’ll sneak a peek and get scolded for it. I hope you still cover mine when your hot lesbian roommate undresses in the room, despite me not even looking.

I hope you never stop treating me like a kid, teasing me like I don’t stand a chance against you, even when we both know I do.

I hope that every time I yell ‘Marco,’ you’ll still answer with ‘Polo,’ no matter where we are—whether in a crowded airport, in a new city, or even when we’re old and gray, sitting on a porch, laughing at our own ridiculousness.

I don’t need to know the future. I just need to know that you’ll be in it.

He pressed Submit, then exhaled, staring at the screen.

For the first time, this game wasn’t just a game anymore.

She smiled at the message, warmth spreading through her chest. He always did this—effortlessly pulling at her heartstrings, acting as if it were nothing. As if making her feel special was just a casual, everyday thing.

She hesitated for a moment, fingers hovering over the keyboard. Would he like what she had written? Would he understand what she meant?

Then, with a deep breath, she hit Send.

I remember the second time we met.

You greeted me with “Hey, you.” Just like that. Like I was someone worth recognizing. Worth remembering. From that moment on, it became our thing—you always greeting me the same way, and me pretending not to expect it, even though I did.

I love how you sneak up behind me, just to make me jump, just to hear me squeal. I love the way you cover my eyes, only to appear in front of me a second later, acting innocent—like you hadn’t just stolen my sight for fun.

I love the endless stream of ridiculous nicknames you text me or whisper when we hang out, each one worse than the last. I hate the one you gave this app, though. Seriously. What were you thinking?

But still, I want more. More terrible jokes. More absurd nicknames. More of you struggling to find words every time I ask, “How do I look in this dress?”—knowing full well you’re at a loss but refusing to admit it.

As for the app? Name it Alt or something. Or if you ever run out of ideas, just name it after me. That way, at least one thing in your life will have a perfect name.

He read it, his expression unreadable at first. Then, just for a second, she swore—he blushed.

She smirked.

“Yeah, I’m not calling it SpookyVerse or AltVerse,” he said, leaning back.

A notification popped up on his screen. He glanced at it.

She had given the app a five-star rating.

He looked up at her, suspicious.

She grinned mischievously.

“SpookyVerse… or I take them all back!”

As long as my story is told by you, I will rest. In whispers of dusk and songs of the west. Carried by echoes where memories roam, A voice like the wind still calling me home. As long as my praises are sung by you, I will smile, Through rivers of time, through sorrow and trial. Even when shadows stretch far and wide,

Your words are the light where I still abide. So speak of my love, my laughter, my fight, Let not my name fade into the night. For as long as your heart keeps singing me true, I will live on—in the soul of you.

chapters.title: Berritto
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

When tomorrow comes, I’ll be on my own. It’ll feel wrong.

Forgive me if I tell this story wrong. It’s something I just heard. A story of love that never saw its aspirations and dreams fulfilled.

At a time when the clans in Somalia went to war, Hargeisa chose to separate herself from her mother country. Of course, we differed, how, you may ask? Our imperial masters were different – the Italians and the British. Smallest things made us differ. Funny.

You know what is inspiring about this story? It’s how it began.

A girl in a hijab walking home from madrasa, when a boy stands in her way. A bully, she thinks!

“I’ve been trying to catch up to you for a while now!” Yes, one of those who chase you down to confess their undying love, she had finally met one. She thought she’d never get this opportunity to turn down such a handsome guy.

“Aye! I’m not interested in whatever you have to say,” she raised her hand at him and walked past him.

“Maxay? Gabadhan?” He laughed.

“Don’t call me ‘this lady’...I have a name!”

“You forgot your henna!” he said candidly, bringing a tube of henna from his pocket. She gasped, surprised.

“Aiii! If Imam saw this, I’d have died! Thanks for that!”

She grabbed the tube from him. With that, he was gone and away he went.

“Ay! Stranger, I didn’t get your name?”

“Osman!” He kept walking.

“You don’t want to know mine?”

“I’ll find it out, Berrito,” she didn’t understand why she found herself in a daze during dinner.

She hadn’t touched her food. Why did she find him so attractive? Love at first sight?

“Astur!” Her father brought her back to reality with a bark of her name.

“What is bothering you, young lady?” Her mother asked. She quickly went back to eating. How could she tell her parents this? Would they understand? Her sister had been married off in an arranged marriage. This is one of the stories where she’d elope if she fell for him.

Later that night, she heard her father listening to the radio. He looked worried. The radio, blaring in Somali, talked about the war for Somaliland independence. Many had gone to fight. They had just fought to annex Ogaden and they failed. Now they were rebelling, resisting a beast in human skin, Siad Barre. See, he had taken power from Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke, who was shot by his bodyguard two years into his leadership. Her brother was one of those fighting this junta government that didn’t belong there.

Astur’s heart pounded in her chest. The whispers of war, always a distant hum, now vibrated through the very walls of her home. She thought of Osman. Was he involved? The thought sent a shiver down her spine. She didn’t even know him, yet the possibility of him being caught in the conflict terrified her. She lay in bed, the radio’s static and her father’s worried murmurs weaving a tapestry of fear and uncertainty. Sleep eluded her. Every creak in the house

sounded like approaching soldiers. Every rustle of leaves outside her window, like gunfire. She wondered if Osman was thinking of her too, under the same moon, perhaps even closer to the fighting. The henna tube lay on her bedside table, a small, fragrant reminder of their brief encounter, a symbol of a connection that felt both innocent and impossibly fragile in the face of the looming war. The war that threatened to engulf everything, even the fragile spark of first love.

She paid no attention to the news, how would it affect her anyway. As long as her brother came home. She’d be happy. The cold night didn’t seem to bother her as she sat on the roof of her house thinking. She thought of what he said “Berrito” why that? Why wait? Her mother’s yells brought her down. Why did Somali mothers yell so much? She thought.

The next day she was early, she always was but she was specifically early to avoid interruptions if she saw him. She wandered the halls like a lost apparition, she wondered if she’d run into him and maybe give him her name. She did wonder what she was doing, would he do this? She wanted to give up and go to class, till she heard a voice.

“Salaam aleikum?” She was startled and gasped, surprised. It was Osman, right behind her. She stuttered trying to respond.

“We can do good-morning if you’ve forgotten how to greet the Islamic way,” she couldn’t hide her embarrassment. She used a side of her hijab to cover her face as she blushed. “I expected a good student who is early to be in class meditating on the word of Allah. You roam these halls like a ghost.” She couldn’t tell him she was looking for him. They stood in the hall awkwardly, he tried to look at her to at least find a reaction but she looked away.

“I never got your name by the way?” She felt a wave of joy run through her. He asked!

“Astur....” she said shyly and timidly.

“That name means to conceal, right?” she nodded, “explains why you keep hiding behind the corners of your hijab?” This guy! Why would he turn this into a joke? Her smile quickly faded as she gave him a cold stare that would send fear into anyone’s heart. “Relax! I was playing. Want to go read before the imam comes in?” She chuckled as he led her to the class.

“When I told you that you didn’t get my name you said you would find it out tomorrow, why?” she asked as they walked. “To get a reason to look for you—or the other way round.” They both laughed at that. She found it cheesy but nice of him. They sat and recited some verses together. The imam found it odd, there were no classes today. He found the two, they kept going, blissful of the world around them.

He coughed making them turn to look at him. He showed no anger, no smile to say I am proud of you. He just looked at them. “There were no classes today and it is not safe for you to roam the streets.”

“Why?” Osman asked, perplexed. “The Somali army has advanced, and they are coming here to Hargeisa.” Osman looked at the Imam in disbelief. Did that mean the Somali National Movement was failing? Was this the end of it all?

“Pray for our victory and our sovereignty,” the Imam told them as he walked them to the gate. He’d get them a taxi. “Berigeena waa qurux,” Osman kept chanting. Our tomorrow is beautiful. He’d occasionally tap on the side of the door. “What does that mean?” she asked, holding his hand. He looked out of the window and back at her.

“What our tomorrow should be. A tomorrow of beauty and peace. When my father left Mogadishu after the Ogaden war, he told me, ‘Soomaaliweyn should not be a reason to go to war. It should not be why we attack our neighbors and make their lives hell. It should be why we are closer to them.

Because they welcomed our brothers and sisters.’ As-Sūmal al-Kubra should be a tomorrow of peace. The Greater Somalia is a calling for peace! Berritto—Tomorrow.”

She looked at him, inspired and enlightened. She wanted a tomorrow where the sons of the soil did not go to war just because of some ideology.

“Tomorrow scares me. It is uncertain, unpredictable, and sometimes hopeless. It disappoints and hurts,” she told him. He just sighed and kept chanting his mantra. She thought he was upset by her pessimism.

“The holy word says: ‘No soul knows what it will reap tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die; it is God who is all-knowing and all-aware.’ Surely Allah alone has the knowledge of the Hour. We have nothing to lose if we try.”

“Can I be your Berritto?” she asked him, squeezing his hand. The uncertainty disappeared when he squeezed back and looked at her. She had arrived at her stop. She suddenly felt the uncertainty as he let her hand go. He looked at her reassuringly. She walked to the door.

That evening after their prayers, she looked at her father pace around the room, waiting for the news briefing.

“Mama. Am I going to be married off like my sister?” She asked. Her mother showed no reaction. “Why ask?”

“I love a boy. We have a vision for tomorrow. I hope it is fulfilled, inshallah,” she whispered to her. Her mother, who was busy weaving, was quiet for a moment. She looked at her husband, and she was sure he had heard. “Ilmahayga (my child), you are to love whomever you choose. Tomorrow is yours, Berri adaa leh. Take it!”

As they sat there, they heard explosions rocking the outskirts of the city. Finally, the news came on. The reporter sounded somber and saddened. He explained that they were surrounded and the army was attacking. Hargeisa had fallen.

The acrid smoke stung Astur’s eyes, a constant reminder of the inferno that had engulfed her life. The wails of her mother, echoing the collective grief of the Isaaq people, were a soundtrack to the nightmare unfolding around her. The world she knew, vibrant with the scent of frankincense and the lively chatter of the marketplace, had been replaced by a grotesque caricature—a battlefield littered with the debris of shattered homes and broken lives. Osman, his laughter still ringing in her ears, was now just a ghost, a phantom limb of a life that had been brutally amputated.

The landmine that claimed her parents also stole a piece of her own soul. Her father, refusing to abandon her mother in her final moments, became a martyr, a testament to love in the face of annihilation. The image of their intertwined hands, forever frozen in time, fueled Astur’s resolve. She clung to Osman’s words, “Berigeena waa qurux”—“Our tomorrow is beautiful”— like a lifeline in the swirling chaos. They were more than just words; they were a promise, a whispered prayer for a future that seemed increasingly impossible.

The horrors she witnessed were seared into her memory: the vacant stares of orphaned children, the desperate cries of mothers searching for their lost sons, the rivers of blood staining the once-sacred soil. The dream of a unified Somalia, a dream Osman had so passionately articulated, lay in tatters, crushed under the weight of hatred and violence. Yet, even amidst the ruins, a tiny ember of hope flickered within Astur. It was the ember Osman had ignited, the belief in “Berritto,” the possibility of a dawn after the long, dark night.

Years blurred into a tapestry of suffering. The war, a ravenous beast, devoured everything in its path, leaving behind a trail of devastation and despair. Astur, no longer a frightened girl but a hardened young woman, carried the weight of her losses like a physical burden. The pain of losing her parents, the ache of never seeing Osman again, the memories of the atrocities she had

witnessed—they were all etched into the very fabric of her being. But she also carried something else: the undying flame of Osman’s vision.

She dedicated her life to mending the broken pieces of her world. She worked tirelessly, her hands calloused and her spirit unyielding, to rebuild shattered communities, to offer solace to those who had lost everything, to give voice to the voiceless. She became a beacon of hope in the suffocating darkness, a living testament to the resilience of the human spirit.

The foundation she established, bearing the motto “Berigeena waa qurux,” became a symbol of hope for a war-torn nation. It was a promise whispered in the face of despair, a testament to the enduring power of dreams. Astur, the girl who had clung to Osman’s words like a prayer, became the woman who embodied them. She never forgot him. His laughter, his touch, his belief in a beautiful tomorrow—they were all woven into the tapestry of her life. And though she never saw him again, she knew that somewhere, amidst the ruins and the sorrow, the echo of his “Berigeena waa qurux” still resonated, a promise whispered on the wind, a seed planted in the ravaged earth, waiting for the right moment to bloom. Her tomorrow, her very existence, became a living monument to his dream, a testament to the enduring power of love, loss, and the unwavering belief in a beautiful tomorrow.

Distant tomorrow, Part of you walks by my side, Always in my heart.
