chapters.title: Your Echoes
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

Grief is the unexpressed love we didn’t get to tell.

The night pulsed with the rhythm of pursuit. Daudi’s aged muscles burned, each stride a testament to a lifetime lived and a lifetime lost. The alarms, sharp and invasive, were a cruel echo of the world he was leaving behind—a world that had caged his sons, stolen his mate, and shrunk his domain to the confines of a memory.

They were coming. He could smell them—the metallic tang of the rangers, the frantic eagerness of the dogs, their barks a chorus of judgment rather than mere sound. Mtafute! Find him! The command echoed in his mind, a brand seared into his soul. He wouldn’t be found. Not this time.

The moon, a silver coin tossed into the vast darkness, offered the only guidance he trusted. It had witnessed his triumphs and his heartbreaks, bathed his cubs in its gentle glow, and now, it illuminated his final escape. He ran until his lungs screamed for air, until his paws bled, until the memories threatened to drown him. He ran until he reached the whispering acacias, the place where his life had truly begun.

He collapsed beneath the ancient tree, its gnarled branches reaching out like welcoming arms. Exhaustion claimed him, but not before a familiar scent drifted on the wind—the scent of rain on dry earth, of sun- warmed fur, of Wahu.

He awoke to a touch, softer than the whisper of the wind. Wahu. Age had painted silver streaks through her golden coat, but her eyes, those luminous pools of love and understanding, held the same fire he remembered.

“You came,” she breathed, her voice a melody he had carried in his heart for decades.

He tried to rise, a surge of joy and grief warring within him, but she pressed a gentle paw against his shoulder. “Rest, my love. You’ve earned it.”

His heart ached with a longing so profound it stole his breath. “Wahu… I am old. My strength is gone. My sons live behind bars. Every cub I sired breathes the air of captivity. What legacy is this?”

She nuzzled his mane, the familiar gesture sending a wave of warmth through him. “Do you remember the waterfalls, Daudi?”

The memory surged, vivid and clear. The roar of the cascading water, the icy spray against his fur, the foolish pride that had led him into the treacherous current. “You pulled me out,” he whispered, his voice thick with emotion. “You saved me from drowning.”

A soft chuckle rumbled in her chest. “You were always a reckless cub, spoiled by your mother’s adoration.”

A ghost of a smile touched his lips. “And what of Taji, the challenger who dared to covet you?”

The canyon, stark and unforgiving under the watchful eyes of the pride. Taji, bigger, stronger, his roar a challenge to Daudi’s claim. The scar on his shoulder throbbed, a reminder of the brutal fight, the desperate courage fueled by love. “You tended my wounds,” he murmured, his voice rough. “You always mended what was broken.”

Wahu’s gaze softened. “And Baraka… do you remember the night he was born?”

The joy, incandescent and pure, flickered in his heart, quickly followed by a searing pain. “Wahu… don’t.”

“You must, Daudi. Speak it.”

The memory crashed down on him, a tidal wave of grief. The gunshot, sharp and brutal, shattering the serenity of the afternoon. Baraka, his firstborn, his pride, his future, lying still, his tiny body a grotesque parody of life. Wahu, her eyes wide with terror, then the crimson bloom spreading across her flank. The second shot, the agony in his leg, and then the blind rage that had driven him to attack the hunter, a primal scream against the injustice of it all.

He had stayed with her for four days, his roars of grief echoing across the empty savannah, a lament for a love stolen, a future destroyed.

“You never left my side,” Wahu whispered, her voice laced with sorrow.

“I didn’t understand grief then,” Daudi confessed, the words heavy with the weight of years. “I only knew pain, a pain so deep it threatened to consume me.”

He remembered the humans who came—the curious onlookers, the somber rangers. He had yearned for

oblivion, for the sweet release of death, but it had eluded him. Instead, he had been captured, caged, his world reduced to the sterile confines of a zoo enclosure.

“Grief is the love we never got to give,” Wahu said softly. “Daudi, you loved fiercely. You loved us with every fiber of your being. But you must let go. For your own peace, for the memory of our love, you must let go.”

He pressed against her, seeking the warmth that had always been his solace. “But what if I forget you? What if the memories fade?”

She smiled, a radiant, heartbreaking smile. “Your heart will remember, Daudi. Even when your mind falters, your heart will hold onto the echo of our love. It’s woven into the fabric of your being.”

The first rays of dawn painted the sky with hues of gold and rose. The acacia’s shadow stretched across them, a silent benediction. As the light touched Wahu, she began to shimmer, to fade, to become one with the dawn.

“Rest, my love,” she whispered, her voice a sigh on the wind.

And then, she was gone.

Daudi lay beneath the acacia, the warmth of the rising sun bathing his old bones. The world had taken everything from him. But here, in this place of whispered memories, in this sanctuary of love, he had known something profound, something that transcended grief.

He had known love. And in the end, perhaps, that was enough. He closed his eyes, the image of Wahu, radiant and eternal, etched into his heart. A single tear traced a path through the dust on his cheek. Then, Daudi, the old lion, the broken king, let out one last, mighty roar. It was not a roar of defiance or anger, but a roar of acceptance, a roar of love, a final, heartbreaking farewell. And then, silence.

Echoes linger, soft and low, A love from long ago. Now silence reigns where laughter flew, I’m here, alone, without you.

chapters.title: When I Am Back
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

How could this be anything, anything else?

Our men went to fight… a war that has nothing to do with us. A war that means nothing to us. A war we don’t understand. They have gone to fight German imperialism, yet those who conscripted them are imperialists themselves. The irony stings like a persistent wound. We resisted, pleaded, even attempted outright refusal. But our cries were swallowed by the wind, our struggles mere ripples against the tide of colonial power. They still snatch our men, forcing them to fight on foreign soil. Those deemed unfit to shoot become cooks, and those too weak to cook become beasts of burden, carrying the white man’s supplies. Women are spared the front lines, confined to the hearth, where we cook, mend, and pray— pray with a desperation that claws at our throats—that our loved ones will return.

Adebowale, my ife mi, my crown, left to fight this war, this charade of defending Western democracy against German imperialism. He promised me, that moonlit night before he was shipped away, that he would return. He swore he would marry me, that we would grow old together, our skin creased with laughter lines, our hair silvered by time. This war, this insatiable beast, has stolen my love, my future.

Every day, the same torturous ritual. I walk to the town center, to the post office, the epicenter of both hope and despair. The white postman sits behind his desk, a gatekeeper of news from the front, methodically calling out names—sons, fathers, brothers—men who have gone to defend the pale man’s ideology. Each name echoes in the dusty air, a hammer blow to the heart. Each name is not Adebowale.

For me, it’s always the same. No letter. But each day, hope, fragile yet persistent, flickers anew. There was a time, not long ago, when the letters stopped altogether. A disruption, they said, a consequence of the growing resistance to conscription. Whispers of sabotage, of delayed shipments, swirled through the town. Many families were left in the dark, their anxieties festering. I received nothing. Not a single word from Adebowale since he left. The silence was a torment, a constant gnawing worry. What if the worst had happened? My grandfather, a veteran of the Great War—the war they called “the war

to end all wars”—had fought for the British, believing, like so many others, that service would somehow translate to freedom. It didn’t. His sacrifices earned him nothing but a faded uniform and a lifetime of quiet disillusionment.

“Chinua!” My name, finally. My heart leaped in my chest, a trapped bird desperate for release. Adebowale had written! I pushed through the throng, a surge of adrenaline coursing through me. The air crackled with anticipation. Oh, how I had longed for this moment! To see his handwriting on the envelope, to know he was alive, to feel the tangible connection to my love across the vast ocean. I practically snatched the letter from the postman’s hand, my fingers trembling. I retreated to the shade of a nearby acacia tree, my breath catching in my throat. I turned the envelope over in my hands, tracing the familiar scrawl of his name and address. Then, with trembling fingers, I broke the seal.

I hurried home, desperate for a sliver of privacy to devour his words. I found a quiet corner in our small hut, the scent of woodsmoke and dried herbs filling the air. As I unfolded the letter, I noticed the faint creases and smudges, a telltale sign that it had been read, perhaps even tampered with. Damn the colonizers and their insatiable curiosity, their disregard for our privacy! But my anger was a slow burn; my need to hear from Adebowale was a raging fire.

“My dearest Ifemi,” I read, his words echoing in my mind, “It has been three long years since I was conscripted into this war. I have seen lands beyond the horizon, lands where our ancestors were stolen, ripped from their homes and sold into bondage. I have seen the white men and women, up close, stripped of the mystique that distance and power afford them. They are human, Ifemi, just like us. They bleed, they weep, they love, they fear.

I know the sweet promises I made before I left. I painted pictures of our future—the earth yielding bountiful harvests under your touch, our children playing in the sun, their laughter echoing through our village. I spoke of the envy our love would inspire, the joy our family would bring. But Ifemi, the war has opened my eyes. I see now that the white men who came with guns and bibles, with their claims of superiority, are not gods. They are men, driven by the same desires, the same greed, the same hunger for power that fuels every human heart. They live freely in their own lands, fiercely protecting what they consider theirs.

Ifemi, our land has been stolen from us. We are strangers in our own home, forced to bow to their laws, to work their fields, to fight their wars. How have we allowed this? How can we be so blind, so foolish, as to fight for their cause, to spill our blood for their benefit?

This war, Ifemi, this war is a mirror. It reflects our own weakness, our own complicity in our oppression. It will not end here, on these foreign battlefields. It will continue, it

must continue, until our people are free in their own lands. This fight will not stop until our children can grow without the shadow of the white man’s boot on their necks. When I return, Ifemi, and I will return, I will dedicate my life to uniting our people, to forging a common front against the true enemy—imperialism. When I return, we will have those beautiful children, and they will grow in a land that is truly theirs. They will laugh freely under the African sun, without fear of discrimination, without the constant reminder of their subjugation. We will raise a generation that knows its own strength, its own worth, a generation free from the white man’s lies.“

I sat stunned, the letter trembling in my hands. His words resonated deep within me, igniting a fire I hadn’t known was smoldering there. He was right. We shared a deep- seated resentment, a visceral loathing for the white man and his insatiable greed. We both understood the bitter taste of oppression, the suffocating weight of colonial rule. Yet, we were here, caught in their web, fighting their battles, while our own land lay bleeding. The irony was a cruel joke. They babbled about freedom and democracy while denying us both.

I looked towards the west, where the sun was setting, painting the sky in hues of blood orange and deep purple.

Beyond that horizon lay the lands where our ancestors had been dragged in chains, where their cries echoed across the ocean. And I knew, with a certainty that settled deep in my bones, that Adebowale was right. This war was not just about distant lands and foreign ideologies. It was about us. It was about our future. It was about reclaiming what was rightfully ours. It was time to fight. But not for them. For ourselves.

I sat there, the letter clutched in my hand, the words burning themselves into my soul. The setting sun cast long shadows across the hut, mirroring the darkness that had settled in my heart. Adebowale’s words had ignited a fire within me, a fierce determination to fight for our freedom, for our future. But even as that fire burned, a cold dread crept in, chilling me to the bone.

My father, a man of influence in the village, had always been… practical. He believed in accommodation, in working within the system, in making the best of a bad situation. He was a pragmatist, some would say, a collaborator, others whispered. He had prospered under colonial rule, gaining land, status, and a measure of power. And now, I knew, with a sickening certainty, that

my newfound resolve would clash violently with his carefully constructed world.

The whispers had been growing louder in recent weeks. My father, it was said, had been entertaining a proposal. Chief Obafemi, a wealthy and powerful man, a staunch loyalist, a man who dined with the colonizers and spoke their language, had asked for my hand in marriage. The thought turned my stomach. Obafemi was old, his face etched with the lines of privilege and complacency. He was a man who profited from our oppression, a man who would gladly sell our birthright for a few trinkets and a pat on the back from the white man.

I knew what my father would say. It was a good match, he would argue. It would secure our family’s future, bring us even greater standing in the community. He would talk of duty, of respect, of the need to be practical. He would not understand the fire that now raged within me, the yearning for freedom that had taken root in my soul. He would see only the opportunity for advancement, the chance to solidify his position in the colonial hierarchy.

The image of Adebowale’s words, his passionate call to arms, clashed starkly with the image of Chief Obafemi’s smug, self-satisfied face. I felt trapped, caught between two worlds, two destinies.

The setting sun bled across the sky, painting the clouds in hues of defiance—crimson and gold against a bruised purple. It felt like a bad omen. I clutched Adebowale’s letter, its words a burning brand against my skin. My father’s intentions were clear, a suffocating weight pressing down on me. Chief Obafemi, the collaborator, the man whose wealth was built on the backs of our suffering, was coming. He was coming for me.

The compound buzzed with a nervous energy. Servants scurried, preparing for the unwelcome guest. My mother’s face was a mask of forced composure, her eyes filled with a quiet sadness that mirrored my own. My father, dressed in his finest robes, paced back and forth, a self-important air about him. He saw this as a triumph, a strategic alliance. He couldn’t see the chains he was forging for me.

I retreated to my hut, the familiar scent of herbs and woodsmoke offering little comfort. I reread Adebowale’s letter, his words a lifeline in the encroaching darkness. “When I return, Ifemi, and I will return…” His promise echoed in my heart, a beacon of hope against the despair that threatened to engulf me.

Suddenly, a commotion erupted outside. The sound of drums, the boisterous voices of Obafemi’s entourage, announced his arrival. My heart pounded in my chest, a

trapped bird desperate for escape. I knew what I had to do. I couldn’t let this happen.

I emerged from my hut, my head held high, my gaze fixed on the approaching procession. Obafemi, resplendent in his richly embroidered robes, strutted like a peacock, his face beaming with self-satisfaction. Behind him, his followers chanted his praises, their voices grating on my ears. My father stood beside him, a proud smile plastered on his face. He reached out to take my hand, but I pulled away, my eyes blazing with anger.

“Chinua,” he said, his voice laced with warning. “Be respectful.”

“Respectful?” I spat, my voice trembling with barely suppressed rage. “Respectful to the man who would sell our people for his own gain? Respectful to the man who would chain me to a life of misery?”

My father’s face flushed crimson. “You dare speak to me like that?”

Before he could respond, a voice cut through the air, sharp and commanding. “Chinua!”

chapters.title: This Is Coincidence
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

I do not believe in coincidences, but I will take a chance with you.

His alarm blared, an unwelcome disruption in the stillness of his room. He groggily reached out and hit snooze. Thirteen times. Then, suddenly, it hit him—he snoozed too much. His body jolted upright in a panic.

“Shit!”

Jumping out of bed, he scrambled toward the water heater. Empty. Alekie had left. That meant he’d have to risk the shower. The lukewarm water played a cruel game, fluctuating between scalding hot and ice-cold before finally settling at a bearable temperature—only to betray him moments later, turning frigid mid-rinse. He gritted his teeth and finished quickly, shivering as he stepped out.

Mental note: ask for a new water heater.

Breakfast was out of the question. He’d have to grab coffee outside. Throwing on his hoodie, he grabbed his bag and darted out of the hostel, the pavement still wet from last night’s rain. As he neared the gate, he nearly crashed into Cici.

“Hey!” she greeted, a bright smile lighting her face.

“Can’t talk now! I’ll call you!” he shot over his shoulder as he ran past her.

She blinked, her smile faltering. She had only meant to say good morning.

He tore through the street, his backpack clutched tightly against his chest. His laptop was inside—fragile, barely functioning, hanging on for dear life. One bad drop, and it would be worse than it already was.

His head throbbed with regret. Why had he gotten high last night? Now he was dealing with the consequences.

A car horn blared. He jumped back just in time, the driver shouting obscenities as he sprinted across the road. But he didn’t stop. He couldn’t afford to be late.

Bursting into the coffee shop, he panted, “Am I late?”

“Nope, your Tammy lemon tea is still on offer.”

Relief washed over him. Just in time—by a minute. He grabbed the steaming cup, took a quick sip, and checked his phone.

Twenty missed calls from his dad. Twenty from the chancellor.

Later. He’d deal with it later. Right now, he had to get to class.

The climb up the stairs felt endless, but he finally reached the computer lab. Tyron was waiting, tapping impatiently on his phone.

“Ninety-four messages, dude! Ninety-four! Where the hell were you?”

“How do you even wake up so early after a night like that?” he muttered, tossing his bag onto a desk and pulling out his laptop.

“Dude! The reviewers are here!”

He barely blinked. “Yeah, yeah. They won’t mind waiting.”

Last semester, he had built a digital database for an insurance company. Now, the opportunity had come to take it further—an internship, maybe even a job abroad. But leaving the country? That wasn’t in his plans. So today, he had one mission: convince them why he should stay.

Megan stirred, shifting in bed. She turned, then—

Thud.

A sharp jolt of pain shot through her elbow as she hit the floor. Disoriented, she blinked at the ceiling before realization struck her.

“Oh, crap!”

She was late.

Scrambling up, she ran to the shower. The icy water hit her skin like tiny knives. Where was the hot water? She groaned but endured it, her mind racing. She dressed quickly, grabbed her things, and made a beeline for the hostel café.

The tea was a disappointment. Too watery, barely any milk. She took a hesitant sip and winced. Nope. Undrinkable.

As she stepped outside, she saw someone nearly get run over.

She gasped, but the guy barely seemed fazed. He just kept running like his life depended on it.

Damn. Some people were dedicated. She smirked, shaking her head. Nerds.

Still, he was kind of cute.

She wondered what school he was in before quickly shoving the thought away. She had a class to get to. She climbed the

stairs, her stomach grumbling in protest. The hunger gnawed at her, but she ignored it.

Ahead, someone rushed past her, agitated, mumbling under his breath.

“Where is this guy?” he grumbled, running a frustrated hand through his messy baby locks.

Megan watched as he disappeared into a meeting hall.

At the reception, she picked up her timetable. Basic computer packages and programming. She sighed. At least it wasn’t a terrible schedule.

From the hallway, a voice echoed.

“Dude! You need to get serious with this!”

She peeked around the corner.

The dreadlocked guy. And the one who almost got run over.

She narrowed her eyes. Faculty members? Maybe. But something about them seemed… different.

She watched as they vanished behind the meeting hall doors, her curiosity piqued.

Byron walked in, Tyron by his side.

The air changed.

Lecturer Kimani’s eyes locked onto him with a deathly cold glare. The chancellor sat at the front, his expression unreadable, while the Swiss reviewers sat stiffly, waiting. Byron could feel the weight of their collective gazes pressing down on him.

“Why are you late?” Chancellor Upungu’s voice was measured, but there was no mistaking the displeasure underneath.

Byron exhaled, shifting his weight. He looked at Tyron, then at the room.

“Would you believe me if I told you I overslept?” He forced a grin, hoping to lighten the mood.

Silence.

The chancellor’s stare was ice-cold.

Byron dropped the act and walked to his designated seat. Tyron slid in beside him, the tension so thick it might as well have been visible.

One of the Swiss reviewers leaned forward, his hands clasped together. “Byron, do you understand what this opportunity means for you?”

Byron nodded, reclining slightly. He knew. Too well.

“Then why would you prefer to work remotely instead of joining the program abroad?” another reviewer asked.

Byron stood, opening his laptop but not bothering to play the presentation he had prepared. That didn’t matter now. He had already made up his mind.

“I’d rather showcase my skills right here.” His voice was steady, unwavering.

“Instead of leaving to understand global markets, I want to first navigate the African one. Running a small team here would allow me to develop my leadership skills. I’m not an export. You’re looking at me like a product to send away, but I have more to do here. And besides…” He smirked. “Keeping me local will be cheaper for you.”

A quiet ripple of surprise flickered across the room. His words hung in the air, undeniable.

The truth? He didn’t want this just because his father was pushing for it. His mother had made it clear—he had a choice. Take it or leave it. Either way, he knew his worth. And frankly, what they were offering? It wasn’t enough.

The reviewers exchanged glances. One finally nodded. “We’ll take this into consideration.”

Standing, they shook his hand before leaving.

Byron slumped back into his chair. “I didn’t even show my presentation!” he groaned once the room was empty, his frustration bubbling over.

Tyron watched him, feeling a mix of pride and anxiety. Byron had worked for this. He had fought his way up, built his skills from scratch, and earned every opportunity thrown his way.

But still…

Tyron sighed. Had he just ruined his shot?

He didn’t have time to dwell on it.

“Get out, I wanna watch porn!”

Byron’s ridiculous grin shattered the serious moment.

Tyron snorted before yanking Byron by the collar of his t- shirt. “You’re impossible.”

They made their way to the computer lab, where Maria was already deep into a lesson on basic computer packages.

“Where’s June?” Byron asked.

“She’s been having issues with the school,” Maria muttered.

Byron barely reacted. That was the thing about him—his focus was like a faulty radio, switching frequencies at random.

Meanwhile…

Megan had been sitting quietly, watching.

Byron walked past her, barely noticing her, but something about him felt strangely familiar. She adjusted her glasses, following his movements as he settled into a workstation.

Tyron and Omar—who looked like he had just walked all the way from the coast—were talking about hostel conditions.

“Dude! How are the hostels down there?” Tyron asked.

“Mid,” Omar shrugged, plugging in his laptop to charge.

Byron, absorbed in his own world, popped in his earphones and disappeared into whatever universe he escaped to when he worked.

Megan kept watching.

Mr. Kimani strode in, his eyes scanning the room before landing on Byron.

“Byron.”

No response.

Kimani’s eyes narrowed. Damn earphones.

A pause.

Then—a light tap on Byron’s shoulder.

His reaction was instant, sharp. He turned as if she had burned him. His eyes locked onto hers—deep, intense, studying her.

Megan blinked.

There was something about him. Something... different.

Kimani didn’t wait.

“I need you to count the computers and give me the number before submitting it to the chancellor. Also—where are you on Project KATIA?”

Byron barely reacted. He leaned back, stretched, and answered in two words:

“Almost done.”

Megan tilted her head.

A project.

A game.

He was faculty?

She wasn’t sure, but she hoped he’d be the one teaching basic programming.

He went back to work, earphones in, completely absorbed.

She looked at his messy hair, his strange mix of energy and distraction.

Byron was a different case.

And she was curious.

chapters.title: The Best Night of Her Life
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

The city hummed a low thrum beneath the laughter. Streetlights painted the wet pavement in shimmering strokes of gold, reflecting the joy bubbling up from the party spilling onto the sidewalks. Her hand, surprisingly warm and firm in yours, felt like a spark in the cool night air. You weren’t even properly introduced, just two souls drawn together by the gravitational pull of the music and the shared thrill of anonymity. She smelled of cinnamon and something faintly floral, a scent that clung to the edges of your memory, teasing you with a forgotten sweetness. Each laugh that escaped her lips was a tiny bell, chiming in the quiet corners of your heart.

You should have just enjoyed it, let the moment wash over you like the warm glow of the streetlights. But beneath the surface, a current of unease tugged at you. It felt like you were borrowing happiness, a stolen joy you didn’t deserve.

You held her hand, walked through the streets, and laughed together. She was a stranger, yet you chose to trust her— someone you randomly met at a party. You laughed through the dark night like children, oblivious to its dangers, as if the world had paused just for you.

The feeling of her hand in yours was different. You should have just enjoyed the moment, but instead, you felt conflicted. You wished you felt something, didn’t you? The stars admired you, the moon watched over you. The beauty of the night painted your story in silver and shadow. She smiled, and you smiled back. She was happy. You were empty.

She talked—about herself, her life, her young siblings, her parents. But you were afraid, too scared to lean in and have that conversation, to reveal yourself, to be vulnerable. You listened, nodding in all the right places, but the words you should have said stayed locked inside.

She wanted to dance away the night. You—rooted in your own silence—felt guilt creeping in, like you were stealing something from her.

Your presence brought her joy. Her presence awakened something deep within you—a yearning you couldn’t name.

“I like peaceful places,” she said. “The stillness of a river calms me down. The silence of the forest calls to me. You probably think I’m strange.”

You didn’t. She was beautiful, wasn’t she? The way she cared, the way she saw the world—it was all mesmerizing.

“I like when people take time to know others. Not rush into things. To truly see someone.”

She talked the night away. You thought you were boring, unworthy of her company. But then—

“This is the best night of my life!” she said, beaming. And suddenly, your self-doubt faltered. Was it because of you?

“I’d really love a coffee right now,” you said, testing the waters. She lit up at the idea. But you were unlucky—she was like Cinderella.

Her clock struck twelve.

She had to leave with her friends. “Raincheck?” she asked, but it wasn’t really a question. “Call me!” she yelled before disappearing into the night like a dream slipping through your fingers.

And you were left wondering: was that goodbye, or was it the beginning of something new?

She didn’t say goodbye, but you felt it anyway. Another story for the vault—one you haven’t told yet, won’t tell, and can’t tell.

Remember her? No, not her. The one who leaned on your shoulder under the fireworks, her eyes shimmering like a reflection of the night’s beauty. “Tonight was beautiful,” she whispered in your ear before hugging you goodbye.

A night so beautiful she wanted to relive it. A night she never wanted to end.

But they all disappeared. No—you shut them out.

This wasn’t one of those nights where you left before dawn. This wasn’t a fleeting moment. You made them happy, yet you—ever untrusting—always left.

Remember that moonlit night under the street lamps? Walking along the sidewalk, she balanced on the curb, arms stretched out like a tightrope walker. You watched, admiring her—the way the night embraced her, the way she seemed to belong in its glow. How were you so lucky?

She loved you. Genuinely. And you loved her madly.

Then she slipped. Her laughter turned into a gasp, her body tilting toward the pavement. But you caught her in time.

Eyes locked, breaths mingling, your face leaned closer to hers. The world faded into stillness.

Then she kissed you.

That night still lingers in your memory, doesn’t it? The ghosts of that moment still whisper in your ear. That’s why you’re afraid to move on, right?

The man came out of nowhere, his voice sharp, demanding everything you had. If she hadn’t stepped between you and him—

You wouldn’t be here. Talking to me. Stuck in this cycle. Making every girl happy but never letting yourself love again.

You miss her, don’t you?

That’s perfectly fine. You’re a good man, kind in ways you refuse to acknowledge. But how long will you let the past haunt you?

Does her pain still echo in your heart? Does the memory still bind you?

Because all you’ve done is hold on.

And that’s where our first session ends.

chapters.title: Against the World
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

He wanted it comfortable. I wanted that pain. He wanted a bride.

“I’ll marry you!” The words echoed, not with the sweetness of promise, but with the chilling resonance of a closing door. A wave of fear washed over me, a fear as primal and deep-seated as the tragedies I devoured in books. Romeo and Juliet? Too sentimental. Give me the sharp political daggers of Julius Caesar, the cunning legal battles of the Merchant of Venice. Love stories were never my forte. You knew that, didn’t you? You saw the pragmatism in my eyes, the way I dissected arguments, the way I prioritized logic over longing.

I was no damsel in distress, waiting for a prince to rescue me. I was a warrior in my own right, battling against the societal expectations that sought to confine me. Marriage, as it was presented to me, felt like a cage, a gilded one

perhaps, but a cage nonetheless. The timeline you envisioned, where I’d happily settle into the role of your wife, felt like a betrayal of everything I stood for. It was the easy path, the comfortable option, and that’s precisely what terrified me. I craved more than comfort. I craved purpose.

You loved me, I knew that. You saw the strength in me, the fire that burned beneath the surface. You chipped away at the walls I’d built around my heart, but you couldn’t control the storms raging within me. The rain outside mirrored the uncertainty inside. My life was meant for something greater than domestic bliss. It was destined for a battlefield, not a hearth.

Then came the hammer blow. “You are getting married to that man!” My father’s words, cold and final, sealed my fate. The member of parliament, a man old enough to be my father, a man whose touch made my skin crawl. The familiar, sickening scenario played out before me. Another girl, another sacrifice on the altar of societal expectations. It wasn’t just my story; it was the story of countless girls around the world, forced into marriages for money, status, or to settle debts. We were pawns in a game we never chose to play.

And in this global tragedy, there was you. My rescuer, my champion, ready to whisk me away from the impending doom. You offered love, a future, an escape. And a part of me, a small, frightened part, yearned for it. But the other part, the fierce, independent part, recoiled. I loved you, yes, but love wasn’t enough. Not for me. What I craved was the freedom to define my own destiny, the space to become the woman I was meant to be. My fear wasn’t just of the arranged marriage; it was the fear of losing myself in the comfort of your love, of settling for a life half-lived. I was afraid you’d grow tired of waiting, of my constant push and pull. I was afraid you wouldn’t understand the fire that drove me, the burning desire to fight for justice, to amplify the voices of the silenced.

I wanted to stand shoulder to shoulder with the women who inspired me: Rosa Parks, refusing to give up her seat; Wangari Maathai, planting seeds of hope and environmental change; Winnie Mandela, a symbol of resilience and resistance. Their names echoed in my soul, a call to action. I wanted my name to resonate with theirs, not as a wife, but as a force, a voice, a champion for the rights of girls and women everywhere. I needed to be more than just your wife. I needed to be me.

The rain hammered against the windowpane, a relentless percussion against the silence that had settled between us. It wasn’t just rain; it was a deluge, a furious torrent mirroring the storm brewing inside me. I sat by our window, the one we’d shared countless conversations by, the one that now felt like a portal to a life I couldn’t have.

“I’ve always wanted to be a bird,” I murmured, more to myself than you. You were engrossed in your laptop, but you heard me.

“Why?” you asked, without looking up.

“They go anywhere. They withstand anything. A bird is free. They perch on power lines without a flicker of fear. I want that kind of freedom.”

“Well, prepare for a lot of predators,” you replied, your voice casual, but your words hitting a nerve. You always had a way of grounding me, of gently reminding me of the realities that lurked beneath my idealistic musings. I knew you were the one, the constant in my chaotic world, the one who would always catch me if I fell. But what if falling was part of the journey?

The rain intensified, a curtain of grey blurring the world outside. “What if there wasn’t a tomorrow?” I asked, the question hanging in the air like a fragile leaf.

“I wouldn’t know. It’s life, so you accept it,” you said, still focused on your screen. Your pragmatism was a comfort

and a frustration all at once. You accepted things as they were, while I yearned to reshape them.

“Would you accept even if tomorrow meant I wasn’t there?” The question was a test, a probe into the depths of your love, but also a shield, a way to prepare myself for the inevitable. You were silent.

Somewhere far away, a girl was being subjected to an ancient ritual, a brutal act of mutilation. Another girl was being bartered, sold into marriage to a man she’d never chosen. These were the realities of the world, the world I was desperate to change.

“Standing against the world,” I said, a bitter chuckle escaping my lips.

“Define the world,” you challenged.

“The people around you. The people who love you. The people you trust.”

“I guess that is the world,” you conceded.

Why couldn’t I just tell you? Didn’t I trust you? The rain continued its relentless assault, washing away the facade of normalcy. Maybe I should become a bird, brave the storm, or soar above it, leaving the tempest behind.

“Something on your mind?” you asked, finally turning your attention to me.

“I don’t feel alright,” I confessed, the words tumbling out in a rush. Doubt gnawed at me. Was I wasting your time? Was I being selfish?

You came to me, your arms wrapping around me in a tight embrace. You kissed my temples, a silent reassurance. “Heard of the words, ‘Nothing lasts long, but at least we have these memories’?”

I wished I could give you more than memories. The rain kept pouring.

“I made a wish...”

“To be a bird?” you guessed.

Yes. To be a bird, but this bird wasn’t ready to build a nest in the heart of the storm. I needed to leave, to protect you, even if it meant hurting you. I needed to defy the world, even if it meant breaking my own heart.

The rain was a deluge now, transforming the streets into rivers. The window, though, remained pristine, the raindrops sliding effortlessly down its surface, a symbol of the ease I craved but couldn’t find.

“Come on, tell me! I will listen, and I will understand,” you urged.

Would you wait for me? Would you understand? Would you let me go?

“I have an arranged marriage,” I whispered, the words trembling.

“We elope then?” Your suggestion was a lifeline, but also a trap. I couldn’t drag you into this maelstrom.

“You don’t have to put yourself in this! Let me go. This is not goodbye. I promise you.” I looked into your eyes, searching for understanding, for acceptance. You were too good for this. Pitting you against my father would be a sacrilege, a betrayal of everything I believed in.

The rain raged on. I was caught in the crosscurrents of duty, love, and ambition. The storm threatened to engulf me.

“Let’s be birds then,” you said, your voice filled with a desperate hope.

“No. Too many predators. Let me face this alone.” I knew you’d fight me on this, but I couldn’t risk you.

The girl, forced to choose between the love of her life and the man chosen for her, left a trail of broken hearts in her wake. She chose a world, but at what cost? My story was different. I stood between two worlds, three choices, forging my own path.

I was a bird, but I didn’t yet know what kind. I only knew that I had a choice. I could rise above the clouds, fight through the storm, or find a way to navigate the tempest. I didn’t know which path I would take, but one thing was certain: I was standing against the world, and I was ready to fly.

chapters.title: Lost in Translation
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

We are a whisper in the chaos, a secret the world will never decipher.

Where did you meet your first love? Some will say Sunday school, school, high school, university, or maybe at a bar. For me, it was in a camp not a summer camp or any good camp.

Picture this you are a Japanese American in the USA, your country of origin chose the wrong side or whatever side you’ll call it. Pearl Harbor happened and what do you know, Roosevelt did the craziest thing and issued Executive Order 9066 that resulted in the internment of Japanese Americans. Xenophobia 101 you know. You know Germans were also put in camps, Italians had it worse business confiscated and then your country surrendered. We lasted longer despite it all, and I’m not proud. Being a large minority and easy to identify, cause let’s be honest

you could point out the Asian guy in a room as quickly as a black guy, we were put in the camps easily.

So there I am with my parents, we came to live the American dream. Yeah, they were also lucky it was before 1924 because see Japanese people were banned from going to America and that was seventeen years after the great The Gentlemen’s Agreement that really wanted us to chill on the whole moving to America thing. So a nineteen- year-old mom met my twenty-six-year-old dad, then someone gave them the bright idea that they should run to New York. Your great-grandmother was married to a white guy who also hated my pops. A laborer and a trust- fund baby moved to the great city. They lived happily ever after till I came around the end!

“I thought this was about you, granddad?” Eva asked as they sat cross-legged in front of him.

“Yeah, how you met grandma!” Alan complained.

“Was it now? Your grandfather is getting old so things are fuzzy!” He said adding more wood to the fire, “do not expect this to be a sweet story.”

So we offered to fight the enemies in the war my father served in the 442nd Regimental Combat Team. I think we

know how this ended, he was decorated but he died later. I am not sure if it was because of your grandmother or my decision not to pursue medicine. So your grandmother was working in this assembly factory in Britain see we were a few days from D-day to liberated France. I wasn’t in the 442nd RCT and I couldn’t live up to my father’s legacy. When I first saw your grandma she was in the engineering a few weeks later she was in mailing. Well I was what you kids would call chicken, I couldn’t walk up to her and ask her out. Then it happened, I was back home to see my mother, the war was not over so we couldn’t leave. The craziest thing happened. Your grandmother was with your great grandma.

“So wait, the love of your life was with you mom? Well talk about arranged marriages,” Eva told him.

“Why do you say that?”

“Well mom is trying to match me with this boy from class and I hate his guts! Though yours seemed to arrange itself.”

Alan teased her making kiss sounds. Eva shoved him away.

“Why can’t Asian parents simply stop butting in the lives of their kids?”

Moving on, she was checking on my mother, she was also a nurse apparently that was what I thought at least till her father walked out with her. Now I was vividly confused when he came out with the stethoscope.

“Hello Mr. Saito,” he greeted me and we all shook hands. I swear my body left my soul when we touched with her, “I am Dr. Smith and this is my daughter Ellie. You mother had a small case of high blood pressure, she’ll be fine.”

“Will you be back Dr. Smith?” My mother asked him of course she was excited to have someone around. The doctor laughed and held her hand.

“Yes your son is supposed to pay me!”

“Stay for some tea!” I said to the doctor. The duo didn’t seem to mind. She walked with me to the kitchen. Now there is something you should know, I was never exactly the type to hold a gun or run through a battlefield. I was more intellectually inclined.

“So they took you out of the infantry?” She asked as we stood there. Ellie had this strange stoic aura to her. I was also surprised that she knew that. She was leaning on the counter as I clumsily moved things around to make tea. With a smile she held my hand, her British accent still had me in a daze. Her dark skin looked supple as the sun touched it, her shade of lipstick seemed to blend right in with her skin.

“Yeah, say that I am more of a brainy guy....” Honestly I was a dork, glasses, messy hair and a thin frame. I was twenty three and she was twenty, as we talked and laughed. We

forgot that my country was dragging this war. We bonded over the troubling times.

“Well at least they put you in camps, we get the worst neighborhoods and worst education, it’s called segregation but you won’t notice it because they say they are doing us a favor!”

We were silent for a moment, we looked at each other. She couldn’t become an engineer because she was a woman and a woman of colour.

“Do you ever feel lost, like you just don’t belong?”

Ellie’s question hung between us, heavy yet familiar.

“Well, Saito-san,” she continued, “what do you prefer—being an answer to someone or finding an answer for yourself?”

I smiled, surprised by the turn of conversation. “Actually, I’m more of a Shion-chan.” Then, curiosity got the better of me. “By the way, where did you learn your Japanese?”

Ellie laughed, a warm, genuine sound that sent a pleasant shiver down my spine.

“I’m just a learner. I like picking up a language or two,” she said with a playful shrug. Then, her expression shifted, a shadow passing over her eyes. “Isn’t it ironic? They talk about fighting Nazism and fascism, yet they put us in cages of reality.”

“Irony seems to be the theme of our lives,” I mused, stirring my tea. “My parents—banned from this country—end up here anyway. And me? Destined to be a doctor, yet somehow… here.” I gestured vaguely around the small kitchen.

Ellie held my gaze, her eyes searching mine. Then, with a teasing smile, she said, “You do realize our parents are still waiting for their tea, right?”

We returned to the living room, where my mother and Dr. Smith were deep in conversation. My mother’s face lit up when she saw Ellie. “Ah, Ellie-chan! You’re back! Dr. Smith was just telling me about his latest research.”

Dr. Smith chuckled. “Just some lighthearted banter, Mrs. Saito. Your son here was keeping me entertained with stories of his… less than heroic war efforts.”

I groaned inwardly. “Dad was the hero, not me,” I corrected him.

“Nonsense,” Dr. Smith said kindly. “It takes all kinds to win a war, Saito-san. Not everyone can be on the front lines. Some fight with their minds, their skills, their… charm.” He winked at Ellie, who blushed slightly.

The afternoon passed quickly. We talked, we laughed, we shared stories. I learned more about Ellie – her dreams of becoming an engineer, her frustration with the limitations placed upon her because of her race and gender, her love of

books and languages. I found myself drawn to her intelligence, her wit, and her quiet strength. She was unlike anyone I had ever met.

As the sun began to set, Dr. Smith announced that it was time to leave. “Thank you for the tea, Mrs. Saito,” he said. “And for the company. It was a pleasure meeting you all.”

“The pleasure was all ours, Dr. Smith,” my mother replied. She turned to Ellie and took her hand. “Please come visit us again, Ellie-chan. You’re always welcome here.”

“Thank you, Mrs. Saito,” Ellie said, smiling warmly. “I will.”

“This is where your mom came in with some crazy idea of children and a marriage proposal?” The youngest, Alan, said. He leaned back into his recliner.

“Will you let me tell the story?” He smirked knowing he had them. He felt satisfied and proud of himself.

Kids believe me when I say nothing was great as hearing that Japan gave up. The air crackled with a strange mix of relief and dread. The news of Japan’s surrender, the end of the war, should have been a cause for celebration. But in the desolate confines of the internment camp, it felt muted, overshadowed by the uncertainty of what came next. The weight of years in

the camps seemed to lift in an instant, but freedom wasn’t immediate. We lingered in uncertainty, bound by more than just fences. My mother wasn’t ready to leave.

“Shion, we lost everything. What do we go back to?” she asked one night, her voice weary, her hands gripping the thin blanket wrapped around her shoulders.

“Hope?” I murmured, though even to my own ears, it sounded fragile.

New York was a whirlwind of noise and motion when we arrived. It was nothing like the stillness of the camp, nor the home we once knew. And then, as if fate had arranged it, I saw her again.

The first time, it was at a march. A crowd moved like a tide, their voices rising in unison, and there she was—a streak of determination in the shifting sea of protestors. My breath caught. I ducked instinctively, unsure why.

“Real smooth grandpa it is a miracle we even exist!” Eva shot.

I had always found reasons to visit her fathers clinic just for a glimpse of her. But when I stopped by her father’s office one day, he shook his head.

“She’s marching with the civil rights groups,” he said. His voice held pride and concern in equal measure.

Then he studied me. “So, what exactly is going on between you and my daughter?”

I hesitated. How could I explain what we were—two people standing at the crossroads of history, trying to carve out space where none had been given? Two souls caught between worlds, yet drawn together in ways even we didn’t fully understand.

“I think… we’re trying to figure it out,” I said finally.

Dr. Smith nodded, his gaze turning thoughtful. He leaned back in his chair, rubbing his chin. “You know, with my profession, I believe I can do something meaningful for the projects, for our people.”

“My mother would love to have you for a son,” I said, half- joking, half-serious.

He chuckled, then grew serious. “Say, what if I made you my apprentice? Taught you what I know?”

Harlem needed doctors—healers who understood its heartbeat, its struggles. An Asian doctor, a Black doctor— two men standing together against the barriers that tried to keep us apart.

“To an internship,” Dr. Smith said, pouring two glasses.

Just as I reached for mine, the door burst open. Ellie stood there, breathless, her skin damp from the night air, her face stricken.

“They shot Dr. King!” she gasped, her voice trembling.

The room turned to stone. The glass in my hand suddenly felt too heavy. Outside, the city roared, grief and anger spilling into the streets. Inside, we stood frozen, knowing the world had just changed forever. The weight of it settled in the silence, a suffocating blanket of despair.

Later, I went to her room to comfort her. The city lights painted long shadows across the walls. “You want to watch the sunset?” I asked gently.

“Why? Is it burning white supremacists?” she replied, a flicker of dark humor in her eyes despite the pain. I managed a weak laugh. We climbed onto the fire escape, the metal cold against our skin, and watched the huge ball of fire descend behind the buildings, painting the sky in hues of orange and purple. She looked beautiful, bathed in the

dying light, a silhouette of strength against the vibrant backdrop……..

“Get to the point gramps!” It was his daughter and her mother. They stood at the door her white Afro seemed to hold more stories than the old man before them.

“Girl! When he was just about to compliment me! You know I get those once every ten thousand years.”

“Your grandfather told me the most inspiring words ever,” Ellie said, sitting on the floor with them, a hint of a smile playing on her lips. “I am too old for this,” she added with a chuckle.

“Well, what did he say?” Alan asked, his young face full of curiosity.

“With each sunset comes the promise of a new beginning, and with each sunrise the opportunity to make tomorrow better,” she said, hugging Alan tightly. “And soon it did. Reagan gave reparations to Asians.” A ripple of murmurs went through the room.

“What about the Black community?” Eva asked innocently, her brow furrowed.

A hush fell over the room. The adults exchanged glances, a mixture of amusement and weariness in their eyes. “Honey, you can read, right?” Ellie’s mother said gently, a wry smile touching her lips. The adults laughed, a bittersweet sound

that hung in the air. The laughter wasn’t unkind, but it carried the weight of generations of broken promises, of a struggle that continued even as the sun rose and set. The “new beginning” promised by each sunrise felt, at times, like a distant dream. More like a recurring nightmare, really. You know, the kind where you’re running in place, convinced you’re making progress, but you’re not actually getting anywhere? Yeah, that kind of dream.

But for Shion and Ellie, that dream began to take shape. Their shared experiences, the prejudice they faced, the love that blossomed between them – these became the foundation of their future. They continued to fight for equality, side by side, their voices joining the chorus demanding change. Shion, inspired by Dr. Smith, became a doctor, serving the community in Harlem. Ellie, with her fiery spirit, became a lawyer, championing civil rights cases.

Years passed. The world changed. Not all the changes were good, but some were. And as the sun set each day, and rose again the next, Shion and Ellie’s love grew stronger, a testament to the power of connection in a world that often tried to tear them apart. They built a life together, a life filled with love, laughter, and the unwavering belief that even amidst the struggles, even after the pain, hope could bloom, and new beginnings were always possible. They proved that love, like the sunset, could be both beautiful and a promise of a brighter tomorrow.

Tell me time will fly by and you will be there for it all. Let the ages carry our story.

chapters.title: The Ocean Between Us
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

When we are apart, my world is shaded in grey.

They stood there at departures, the weight of the moment pressing on her chest. Was she really ready to say goodbye? She’d miss him for sure, but more than anything, she didn’t want him to go. She wasn’t sure if she could stomach the uncertainty, the fear of what might happen once he stepped onto that plane.

“Hey, we’ll be okay.” His voice was gentle, his palm warm as it cradled her left cheek. “I’ll be fine.”

She wanted to believe him, to let his reassurance seep into her bones, but the reality gnawed at her. He wasn’t going on vacation. He was heading straight into the hands of a government that didn’t want him there. The man in power had made his stance clear—immigrants were a problem to be solved, a nuisance to be removed. One wrong move, and he could find himself shackled, awaiting a hearing that

might never go in his favor. And worst of all, he’d be with his mother—the woman who never liked her, who had her own opinions about who he should love.

“You know what I’ll leave with once I’m on that plane?” His voice cut through her thoughts.

She shook her head, her throat tight. Slowly, she lifted her gaze to meet his.

“I’ll leave with your love.”

Her eyes dropped to the floor, overwhelmed. The lump in her throat was impossible to swallow.

“You’ll call every day?” she asked, though she already knew the answer.

“Of course.”

“Just... be careful, okay?”

“I love you.”

“I love you more,” she whispered against his ear, savoring the warmth of him one last time.

Then he was gone.

Back at the apartment, the silence was suffocating. She curled up on the couch, staring at a bowl of instant noodles. She didn’t have the energy to cook. The air felt thick, weighted with absence.

Her phone buzzed.

Just landed.

Relief washed over her. Then another buzz—a video call.

“Did you eat?” she asked as soon as she saw his face.

This was the new normal—an empty apartment, long- distance calls to hold them together. They’d talk until she grew drowsy, and she’d wake up to messages that read, Good night, I love you and Good morning.

Days passed in a blur, and then one morning, the news shattered her fragile sense of security.

“Mass deportations to take effect as most immigrants complain of being shackled to each other!”

Her gut clenched. Her hands trembled as she turned up the volume. The footage showed rows of people in chains, heads bowed, shoulders hunched under the weight of fear. It was appalling. It was real.

She felt sick.

At work, she sat uneasy in her chair, unable to focus. Her mind kept replaying the images. She whispered a

mantra under her breath, over and over: He’s okay. He’s okay.

But was he?

That evening, she paced the apartment, phone in hand, waiting for his call. Minutes turned into hours. Her messages sat unread. She stared at the screen, her stomach twisting in knots. Had something happened? Had he been caught in the sweep? The thought alone made her breath hitch. She tried calling, but it went straight to voicemail.

The silence was unbearable.

She checked the news again, scanning the reports, searching for any hint of what was happening. More raids. More arrests. More families torn apart. Each headline made her pulse quicken, her dread intensify.

She had heard what happened—a sudden arrest, then a grueling court case. It would be months before a verdict would be reached, months of waiting in uncertainty. What if he forgot to renew his documentation? What if they arrested him anyway? The thoughts swarmed her mind like relentless waves crashing against the shore, each one dragging her further into the undertow of anxiety.

That night, he took longer than usual to call.

Her stomach knotted itself into a pit of worry. Should she call him? But what if he wasn’t home? What if he had already been taken? She could see it playing out in her mind—the notorious ICE officers swarming his apartment, their badges flashing, their hands gripping his arms like shackles. They would throw him into the back of an unmarked van, drive him to some small, dimly lit room where they would question him for hours. His voice would go hoarse, his body exhausted, and still, they wouldn’t care. Then, after an agonizing process, they would toss him into a cell to wait for a hearing that might never come.

Her laptop’s ringing jolted her back to reality.

It was him. She picked up the call, her breath catching in her throat.

“Hey, babe, what’s up?” His voice was light, almost amused.

“Finally!” She let out a breath she hadn’t realized she was holding.

“What? I was at the door with some ICE officers! I told you in the text.”

Her stomach dropped. She hadn’t even checked her messages; she had been too lost in her own fears. Then his words registered—ICE officers?

Her heartbeat pounded in her ears. “What did they want?”

“Relax, they were just checking my status.”

But she couldn’t relax. Her mind spun with all the possibilities. What if they weren’t satisfied with his answers? What if they decided to take him anyway? Suddenly, in her mind’s eye, the scene unfolded—officers barging into his apartment, pushing him against the wall, cuffing him as he struggled. She could hear herself pleading with them, begging them to stop, but her voice was drowned out by their cold orders. One of them sneered, calling him a cockroach, a parasite. Then the call would cut out, and she would be left in the silence of his absence.

“Earth to my gorgeous girlfriend!” His voice brought her back.

“Powell, please tell me you’re okay.” Her breath was shallow, as if she had been running.

“Emily, calm down,” he said softly. “Think of the ocean, the blue skies, frolicking in the green, and lightning striking in the distance.”

She closed her eyes, inhaling deeply. The images soothed her—the rhythmic waves, the endless sky, the fresh air of an

open field. She could almost hear the distant rumble of thunder, steady and far away.

“You good?” he asked, his face etched with concern. She could see the longing in his eyes, the wish that he could reach through the screen and hold her, pull her into his arms and make it all disappear.

“Come back,” she whispered, her voice barely above a breath. Her eyes shone with unshed tears, raw with fear and anguish.

“It’s all fine,” he assured her, but she could hear the weight in his voice, the unspoken truth lingering in the space between them. They both knew it wasn’t truly fine. It was never truly fine when the possibility of losing him loomed over them like a storm cloud, dark and unrelenting.

She clutched her necklace—a small pendant he had given her on their first anniversary. A token, a reminder. She squeezed it, grounding herself in the sensation. He was still here. He was still with her.

But for how long?

Days turned into weeks, and each night she dreaded another visit from ICE. Then, one evening, Powell didn’t call.

She checked her phone. No messages.

She called. No answer.

“Hey,”

A text came in. She was in panic mode till she heard a knock on her door.

The stars still hum our quiet song. The wind recalls the words we knew, Soft echoes wrapped in morning dew. Come home, love.

They stood there at departures, the weight of the moment pressing on her chest. Was she really ready to say goodbye? She’d miss him for sure, but more than anything, she didn’t want him to go. She wasn’t sure if she could stomach the uncertainty, the fear of what…

chapters.title: Untitled Part 15
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

“You think this is one of your stories?”

“Yes. I always did.”

Your smile is the kind that lingers in the air, golden and soft, flooding the room with warmth. It strips away the shadows like dawn spilling through an open window. I feel your arms snake around my waist, your presence familiar, safe. A gentle kiss lands on my cheek, and without thinking, my lips part into a smile—slow, unguarded.

I turn in your embrace, searching your face, memorizing the way the light catches the curve of your lips, the slight mischievous glint in your eyes.

“You’re here to bother me, aren’t you?” I say.

You smirk. “Is that what you think of me? A bother?”

You’re not the only one who’s cheeky.

But even as we tease, even as your touch is still warm against my skin, I know the truth.

It’s the memories you left that haunt me now. They drift through my mind like ghosts, slipping in uninvited, whispering in the quiet. They come, and they go. And when they leave, they take something from me—a piece of my breath, the illusion that you’re still here.

And in the stillness, I am left with the reality.

You are gone.

“Yes, I do.”

Life is a story—each moment a sentence, every fleeting glance a paragraph. It’s in the way the wind carries secrets, in the way the rain taps against the glass like an old friend. It’s in the spaces between words, the things left unsaid.

You hop onto my table, legs swinging slightly.

“What do you want?” I ask, leaning back.

Your brows furrow, feigning offense. “What’s with the harshness? Can’t I just say hi?” Your voice is laced with that same playful arrogance that once made me fall for you.

You want to leave. I can see it in the way your fingers fidget against the wood, the way your eyes dart toward the door.

Maybe I should stop you. Maybe I shouldn’t.

Instead, I reach for your hand, pulling you closer.

“You know what I want,” I whisper.

Your breath fans against my lips, but before anything can happen, I break the moment, tickling your sides. You yelp, twisting away, laughter spilling into the air.

I want to give you safety again. I want to bring you back to the version of yourself that still believed in happiness. I kiss the places he bruised, the ones you try to hide, as if pressing my lips against them could erase the pain. I whisper to your heart, “It’s okay. You are safe.”

We run through the rain, an umbrella barely shielding us from the storm.

“Did you know every raindrop is a kiss from heaven?” you ask, tilting your head toward the sky.

“Until you catch a cold,” I counter.

You stop walking, turning to me with a smirk—the kind that holds entire conversations without a word. Then, without warning, you toss the umbrella aside.

I am drenched in kisses from heaven.

And you—you’re glowing. You spin, arms wide open, as if inviting the universe to claim you.

“Did he ever let you out?” The words leave me unspoken, swallowed by the rain.

You pause, glancing at me. “I’m sorry.”

Why are you apologizing?

You step closer, resting your head against my chest. “Someone once told me there’s always a story in the rain. Want to write one?”

Grey—that’s the color of our warm wear as we sit by the window, counting raindrops.

This is how we see the world. Not in black or white, not in absolutes. But in shades of in-between.

The heat of our drinks curls into the air, carrying the scent of nostalgia, wrapping us in its quiet comfort. Our thoughts drift, separate but intertwined.

“I never had moments like this with him,” you murmur, staring out at the streetlights blurred by the storm. “Talking. Just sitting. Thinking.”

“These moments are ours,” I say. “We create them. We make them into memories.”

A rooftop, a cup of coffee, constellations stretched above us like a cosmic map of everything we are.

We trace the stars, our fingers connecting invisible lines, trying to make sense of the universe.

I know you don’t see as much as I do, but I know you see the beauty.

And yet, there’s something distant about you tonight.

“What if I hurt you? Would you ever forgive me?” you ask suddenly, your voice small, uncertain.

“What’s your biggest fear?” I ask in return.

“That I’m addicted,” you say. “That I may not be able to think for myself.”

“Addiction is both pain and joy,” I reply. “You say he hurt you, but then… why did you go back?”

Silence.

Smoke. Alcohol. Painkillers. Slow killers.

I know them well—I was a victim, too. Not because someone broke me, but because I was searching for something. Trying to escape the weight of my own thoughts.

I was just another fool, another knight trying to rescue you from your own demons.

“I want to protect my heart,” you once told me. “I need to.”

“I found you, and I found purpose,” I had told you. “Helping you meant something to me.”

“You complete me,” I say now.

“Hey! That’s my line!” you laugh, nudging me playfully. That smile—God, that smile. It should be bottled, prescribed as a cure for sadness.

You colored my world. You made me feel like I belonged.

But even fairytales have villains.

And the past has a way of creeping in through the cracks.

“I can’t,” you whisper.

“Why?”

“This isn’t going to work. I don’t want to hurt you.”

“That’s not an answer!”

You exhale, shoulders trembling. “My ghosts caught up with me. He came to see me.”

The room stills.

So that’s it.

One visit, and everything we built crumbles.

“So none of this mattered?” My voice is eerily calm.

I watch as guilt flickers across your face. “It did… it does. But—”

“But he still owns a part of you.”

You say nothing.

I feel my heart splinter. Anger threatens to rise, but I push it down. I won’t be like him. I won’t force you to stay.

“It’s fine.”

It isn’t.

“I can’t leave you a mess because I couldn’t draw boundaries with him,” you say. “You deserve better. And I… I’m not better. I never will be.”

The words hit me like a slow-moving train, inevitable but still devastating.

I think back to the first time I confessed my love for you. You rejected me then, too. But back then, it was playful. We laughed about it.

This time, there is no laughter.

I don’t like emotional breakups.

My friends hate you. Your friends think you’re an idiot.

And me?

I am split down the middle.

Part of me wants to hate you. Part of me understands.

I put you on a pedestal, and you let me down. I shouldn’t look at you the same way.

And yet, part of me hopes you’ll come back.

Part of me won’t be there to catch you.

But part of me always will.

“Don’t act like you’re not enjoying this,” you once teased as we walked under the streetlamps, our hands clasped.

I remember how you kissed me then.

And I wonder—will you ever kiss me again?

A whispered trust, a bond so deep, Shattered now, secrets to keep. A smile that hid a venomous dart, A broken vow, a fractured heart. Yet still, a foolish hope remains, To mend the cracks, erase the stains. To feel your hand, your gentle touch, Forgive the wound, I miss so much.

chapters.title: Convenience
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

It is never really about where you are. It is about being there.

Along the highway sat a convenience store—not exactly the setting I’d pictured for a date. It was a cinderblock box lit by humming fluorescents, smelling of floor wax and old coffee, the kind of place people walked in with a purpose and left within minutes. No polished aisles, no music, nothing that could be mistaken for atmosphere. We’d looked for something better first. This was what we landed on instead.

The bell over the door chimed as we walked in, and some of the disappointment I’d been quietly nursing eased, just slightly, without my permission.

“Which coffee blend do you like?” she asked, already at the shelf.

I looked at her, confused.

“I mean”—she didn’t look up from the labels—“if you’re going to crash at my place, I might as well get your favorite.”

Something about how casually she said my place made my heart stumble in a way I didn’t examine too closely.

“Uh. Just pick pure black.”

“Got it.” She dropped it in the basket. “Now go pick the ice cream.”

“Which one would you like?”

She shrugged, already walking. “I’ll go with whatever you pick.”

That answer stayed with me longer than it should have.

We drifted to the cosmetics aisle, where she stopped in front of a shelf of perfume like she was greeting an old friend. “I’d really like to get this Dark Noir scent,” she said, testing it against her wrist.

“Then get it. I’m paying.”

“Don’t be a dummy, I’ve already got a bottle at home.” She laughed—a quiet laugh that always sounded like it had escaped before she meant to let it out.

“When you said you’d take me somewhere,” I said, “I pictured something a little more interesting than this, if I’m honest.”

She was already drifting toward a chaotic display of party supplies, unbothered as ever by my complaining. “If you said that a little louder, I don’t think they quite heard you at the counter.” Then, brighter: “Oh—it’s my niece’s birthday soon. I want to throw her a little party.”

“When?”

“First of April. That kid makes me feel ancient.”

I leaned against the cart, watching her sort through crepe paper.

“What?” she asked, catching me staring.

“Nothing. I just think you’re aging pretty gracefully for a woman in her fifties.” The words came out before I’d fully decided to say them. “What’s the secret?”

She held the crepe paper in one hand, and for just a second a blush crept up her neck, warm as the sunset waiting for us outside. She rolled her eyes to cover it.

“If I told you,” she said, stepping closer, “it wouldn’t be a secret anymore, would it.”

We carried everything to the counter—coffee, ice cream, more party decorations than she probably needed. My disappointment about the venue was still there, a small knot I hadn’t figured out how to untie.

“How’s your baby brother?” she asked while the cashier scanned our things.

“Learned a new trick. He can spit his medicine clear across the room now, like it personally offended him.”

“Cute. He’ll be puking on you within the week.” Her voice softened. “Your stepmom’s lucky to have you, you know that?”

“Just doing what my dad would’ve wanted.” I said it easy, the way you say things you’ve had a long time to get used to saying. She didn’t push it—just laced her fingers through mine for a second at the register, no comment, before letting go to grab the bags.

Outside, the air had cooled, carrying the smell of dry grass and something blooming nearby. I leaned back against the hood, the metal still warm from the day.

“So,” I said, “what was so romantic about a convenience store, exactly?”

She walked over and stopped inches from me, her fingers finding the lapel of my jacket. “Who said I was going for romantic?” Her voice dropped, gentle. “Maybe I just wanted to spend time with you. It’s never really about where you are. Dinner somewhere fancy, house hunting

for a place you know you’re not going to buy, sitting at home doom-scrolling without saying a word—it’s all the same thing, if the right person’s there for it.”

“It’s never really been about fancy restaurants,” I said.

“Or expensive dates.” She smiled. “It’s just about being there. Walking. Listening. Sitting close enough to feel someone.”

I didn’t answer. I couldn’t. For the first time all day, the knot in my chest finally came loose, because I understood —she hadn’t brought me to a store. She’d let me into the quiet, unglamorous part of her life. The part she didn’t hand to just anyone.

The sky had started bleeding out above the highway, crimson melting into orange and gold, like someone had set the horizon on fire and wasn’t in any hurry to put it out. She tipped her head back against my chest, settling into the spot like she’d done it a hundred times, because she had.

“I’ve got a chessboard at my place,” she said. “Want to learn how to play tonight?”

I smiled, reaching for her hand. “I’d love that.”

Somehow, the most ordinary day I’d had in years turned into one I already knew I wasn’t going to forget.
