chapters.title: Between Dreams and Darkness
chapters.text:
A L O V E S T O R Y Between Dreams and Darkness

That’s love. It doesn’t ask permission. It finds the cracks and moves in before you notice you’ve let it.

The med-bay smelled the way it always did—antiseptic and cold, a shroud he’d learned to live inside. Andrew sat where he always sat, in the chair worn to the shape of his own grief, watching the blue hibernation light wash over his daughter’s face. The doctors kept promising soon. Soon the swelling would go down. Soon her body would finish doing whatever quiet, private work it was doing to put itself back together after a fight that had never been hers to fight.

He set the data chip on the table beside her, next to the small collection of things he’d started leaving there—a photograph, a pressed flower, a toy she’d outgrown before

any of this started. A record, this time. A confession, if he was honest about what it actually was.

“Eva.” Her name was the only prayer he still trusted himself with. “I did something tonight. I need you to hear it from me, before the world tells you its version.”

He looked at her a long moment—barely more than a child, and already carrying Valor like a coat two sizes too big—and started at the beginning, because that was the only way he knew how to survive telling it at all.

It began, as these things always did, with the Nebula gang.

Their theft of high-tech weaponry from a downtown lab had put the whole city on alert, and it took less than a day for Moon’s contacts in the underbelly to trace the shipment to a derelict warehouse on the industrial waterfront. Tonight it was the four of them—Andrew, Starknight, Moon, and BlueBolt—a formation that had worked a hundred times before.

Starknight checked the strap on her gauntlet one more time, the stylized star on her chest catching the streetlight. Beside her, Moon adjusted nothing; he never did, his grey costume already perfect, the crescent moon at his chest glowing faint and steady like something that had never once

doubted itself. Their hands found each other for half a second before the comms went live—the kind of touch that isn’t for anyone else to see, and wasn’t.

“Be careful out there, you two,” Andrew said, and meant it more than the words could carry.

They nodded. He stepped off the ledge into the dark, the city humming beneath him, and told himself—the way he told himself most nights—that a man who’d once run from the law had no business being anyone’s symbol of it. He’d built the symbol anyway. Some nights he almost believed in it.

He wasn’t alone on the rooftop for long.

“Well, hello there, Andrew.” BlueBolt’s voice, dry as ash, British consonants sharpened to a point. “How’s the girl today? This hibernation business is really dragging on, isn’t it.”

“What do you want, Morgan?”

“Intel. Bad intel, I’m afraid.” Morgan stepped out of the dark, hands loose at his sides—never a good sign. “Someone’s been helping the Nebula gang move their

stolen tech. I’d like to propose a collaboration. We find the problem. We end it. Together.”

Andrew felt the old lecture rise in his throat—the one about boundaries, about rules, about the difference between justice and appetite—and then he thought of the daughter Morgan had buried, and the man who’d walked free for it, and the lecture died before it reached his mouth.

“You’re a death squad, Morgan,” he said instead. “We don’t work that way. You play by our rules tonight, or you turn around and go home.”

Morgan was quiet long enough that Andrew almost thought he’d left. When he spoke again, the sarcasm had burned off entirely. “I was you, once. A believer.” He came to stand at the ledge, staring out at a city that had never once protected the thing he loved most. “Then Helios killed my daughter and walked free on a technicality, and I watched him do it again to other people’s daughters, and I decided the system could believe in itself without me.”

“Moon, proceed with caution,” Andrew said into the comm, because there was nothing left to say to Morgan that either of them hadn’t already said a hundred times. “New intel. They’re working with someone else.”

“Who?” Starknight, sharp, already suspicious.

The silence on the line went on a beat too long.

“Helios,” Morgan said.

Starknight’s scoff cut through the static. “Do you ever stop trying to kill this man?”

“You don’t know what he took from me.”

“We’ve all lost people, Morgan. We don’t all become—” She caught herself, but not soon enough.

Andrew glanced sideways at Morgan, at the civilian jacket where the tactical vest should have been. “Where’s your costume?”

Another silence, worse than the last.

“Helios took my daughter,” Morgan said, and his voice had gone somewhere flat and far away. “And then he took my wife too. Her brother was dying—needed a host, they told her, or he wouldn’t survive the week. She said yes before she understood what host meant.” He breathed out, slow, like he was setting something down he’d carried a long way. “Whatever came through her didn’t leave when the ritual ended. It just put her clothes on. Wore her voice. I kept telling myself she was still in there somewhere. That’s the only reason he’s still breathing.”

“Oh, please,” Starknight said, quieter now, but no gentler. “Save the platitudes for someone who hasn’t watched you use that excuse for six years.”

“Indeed,” a new voice purred, close enough that Starknight startled—right behind her, though nothing had crossed the rooftop. “Morgan, love, you always did leave out the best parts. Ask him what I did to your girl before I introduce myself properly.”

Helios.

Andrew was already moving, already airborne, closing the distance in the time it took the word to finish echoing through the comm. He wasn’t fast enough. The firestorm hit before he cleared the block, a white- orange bloom that lit the warehouse district like dawn arriving forty years early, and by the time the smoke thinned enough to see, Starknight was a broken shape on the concrete and Moon was on his knees beside her, his costume smoking, his hands shaking too hard to be useful.

They were optimistic, the doctors, in the particular hollow way doctors are optimistic when they mean it could have been worse. Burns, mostly. A few inches closer and there would have been nothing left to be optimistic about.

Andrew brought them both back to the same med-bay where Eva already slept—three beds now instead of one, and he hated, with a shame he’d examine later, how much smaller the room felt with all of them in it.

Moon wouldn’t stay in his. He was up before the sedative finished working its way out of his blood, pulling his costume back on with fingers that wouldn’t quite stop trembling.

“He has to be stopped,” he said, when Andrew tried to put a hand on his shoulder and got shrugged off for his trouble.

“Moon—”

“Helios will face my wrath.” There was nothing boyish left in the way he said it. He walked out like a door closing.

BlueBolt watched him go, something unreadable moving behind his eyes. “You know,” he said, quiet, almost to himself, “I always thought he was her butler.”

Andrew nodded slowly. He was.

He let himself remember it, sitting there—the whole shape of it, because Eva deserved the truth in order, even the parts that weren’t his to tell.

Agatha Meyers had come into their lives as collateral damage, years before any of this—caught in the blast radius of a fight between Andrew and a man called Polaris, back when Andrew still hadn’t learned the difference between power and control. He’d leveled half of State City that night. The world hadn’t been ready for what a god’s mistake looked like from street level, and neither had he. Her butler, a quiet, precise man named Gerald, had looked at Andrew afterward with a contempt so total it took Andrew years to stop deserving it.

Their second meeting had been as enemies. Gerald— Moon, by then—had spent months cataloguing Andrew’s every weakness: the gravity, the solar deficit, the gas that could drop him out of the sky like a shot bird. He’d come close to using all of it. Closer than Andrew liked to admit, even now. It was Agatha’s hand on his wrist that stopped the blade. He knows now, she’d said, and something in the way she said it made Moon lower the knife.

After that, the hostility had nowhere left to live. They traded names, then stories, then—slower, quieter, the way these things actually happen—trust.

One night, the two of them alone on a rooftop with the sun bleeding out over the skyline, Moon had said, almost embarrassed by it: “I never understood why she chose me.”

“As a lover,” Andrew had asked, “or as a partner in this?”

“Both. We started out for revenge—her parents, mine, it didn’t matter whose grief it was anymore. And then somewhere in the middle of all that, we just... didn’t stop choosing each other.”

“That’s love,” Andrew told him, watching the light go copper and gold. “It doesn’t ask permission. It finds the cracks and moves in before you notice you’ve let it.”

Moon had laughed—short, sharp, a sound Andrew still wasn’t sure was aimed at him or at how thoroughly love had ambushed a man who’d spent his whole life planning for everything.

Andrew hoped, sitting there beside Eva now, that his daughter would someday get to laugh like that. That kind of laugh, undefended, was the whole point of any of this.

He went after Moon because Agatha would have wanted someone to.

The fortress was exactly as he remembered it—a hundred files on a hundred weaknesses, because Moon had never once let himself believe any of them were as safe as they looked. Andrew found the folder marked Helios already open, arcane texts stacked beside blueprints, months—maybe years—of quiet preparation for a night neither of them had wanted to arrive.

“Moon. What are you going to do.”

“Stay out of my way.”

“Agatha wouldn’t want this.” Her name, not a title, because titles were easier to ignore.

Silence answered him. Then the floor became a fist.

The gravity contingency—his own weakness, catalogued and weaponized by the man he’d once called friend— closed around him like a hand. He watched, pinned, as Moon climbed into the modified transport idling in the corner.

“If you follow me,” Moon said, without turning, “I will send you to join him in hell.”

The engines drowned out anything Andrew might have said back. The field pressed harder as the distance grew, until breathing itself became a negotiation.

Why do you want to stop him?

The voice that asked wasn’t Moon’s. It wasn’t real at all— he knew that, even as his chest seized around it—just grief wearing the one shape it always chose when it wanted his full attention.

It’s not our way, he told her, the way he’d told her a thousand times in the years since the nightmare realm took her and gave nothing back.

She looked the way she always looked in these visitations—the same ferocity Eva had inherited whole, the same eyes that used to find the good in him even on nights he couldn’t find it himself. “One day,” she said, sorrow riding under every word like an undertow, “you’ll embrace the darkness in you too. History repeats. Prophecy doesn’t get a second telling.”

Then she was gone, and a moment later, so was the weight on his chest.

BlueBolt stood in the doorway when Andrew finally looked up, his expression stripped of every joke he owned. “Mate,” he said. “You’ve got demons of your own to put down. Let’s go put mine down first.”

They found Moon in the lower districts, already kneeling inside a pentagram he’d carved into the concrete himself—the last piece of magic Agatha had ever taught him, put to a use she never would have condoned.

“Thought you’d never come,” Helios said, stepping out of the dark with a grin that belonged nowhere near a human face, a ring of broadcast drones spinning to life around him. “I’m doing a little live event tonight. Show the world what its heroes really are, underneath the branding. A public execution, perhaps? For the ratings.”

“All this to frame us,” Moon said. “Why.”

“There’s a plan in motion. Bigger than one dead demon.” Helios spread his hands, delighted with himself, and didn’t notice—vanity rarely does—the binding sigil beneath his own feet until the fire he reached for came out as a cough and a curl of harmless smoke.

“Man to man, then,” Moon said, and closed the distance.

He didn’t hold back. Didn’t spare a thought for the cameras. Every blow was six years of files and grief and a body on the concrete that used to hold Agatha’s laugh, and by the time Helios’s powers surged back—sudden, volatile, the way fire always finds new air—Moon had already broken his leg twice over. The fight spilled out of the warehouse and onto the street in a brutal, ugly rhythm, until Moon triggered the hydrant he’d rigged weeks ago and holy water laced with retardant put the last of Helios’s flame out for good.

Helios went down gasping. Moon drew his blade.

“Moon, no!” Andrew hit the pavement at a run, BlueBolt a step behind him. “You don’t have to do this.”

“I told you you’d join him.” Moon’s voice had nothing human left in it. “This isn’t yours to stop.”

“Star stopped you once,” Andrew said, and watched something flicker behind Moon’s eyes at the name. “You think she’d let you become this? After everything she already stopped you from becoming?”

Helios laughed, wet and delighted, blood in his teeth. “Embrace it, Andrew,” he rasped—and it was Andrew’s name he used, not Moon’s, because he’d been waiting, Andrew understood then, for exactly this moment, exactly this audience. “You’re the only one strong enough to finish what he started. Why let him die,” he said, softer, almost tender, “when you could make him suffer instead? Isn’t that so much more your speed?”

It should not have worked. Andrew had spent a lifetime building the exact armor meant to stop a sentence like that from finding its mark.

It found it anyway—not as rage, the way it would have with Moon, but as something colder and far more deliberate: a door he’d known for years was standing open somewhere inside him, and had simply never had a reason good enough to walk through.

This is mine to carry. Not his.

He moved before he let himself think about it any further. He took Moon’s wrist in one hand, gentle, almost apologetic, and turned the blade harmlessly aside. Then he closed the other hand around what was left of Helios and broke his spine with a sound like a door slamming somewhere very far away.

Helios didn’t die. Andrew made sure of that, even mid- motion—some final, surgical part of him choosing paralysis over murder even as everything else in him screamed for the opposite. It didn’t matter to the cameras. It didn’t matter to the world watching the feed. What they saw was Astroman, the boy scout, the symbol, breaking a defeated man in half with his bare hands, and no amount of explaining was ever going to unbroadcast that image.

BlueBolt took custody of what remained of Helios—alive, paralyzed, held in a cell built for a thing that had never really needed to breathe in the first place. Andrew didn’t ask what Morgan planned to do with all that time and all that anger. He didn’t think he wanted the answer, and he suspected Morgan wouldn’t have given him a merciful one.

Moon stood over the wreckage of the fight for a long time, saying nothing. When he finally spoke, his voice

had gone hollow in a way Andrew had never heard from him before.

“You did it so I wouldn’t have to.”

“I did it so it would be done,” Andrew said. It wasn’t quite a lie.

Moon let his blade fall to the pavement and didn’t pick it back up.

I wasn’t there for what came next. Andrew was out facing the first wave of a world that had just watched its hope turn its hands into a weapon—statements, cameras, the particular chaos of being hated by people who’d trusted him an hour earlier. But Moon left a log behind before his ship broke atmosphere, timestamped, addressed to no one and everyone. Andrew played it once, alone, before he ever sat down next to Eva tonight. This is what was on it.

He’d gone to the med-bay first. Stood a long moment between two beds that held the two people he’d have burned the world down for, and had, in his own way, very nearly done.

He sat beside Agatha. Her burns had already started their slow, stubborn healing, but she looked impossibly small

under the blue light, and for a long moment he simply held her hand and let himself remember every version of her he’d loved—the girl who’d looked at her butler like he was a person for the first time, the woman who’d stopped his blade with two words, the partner who’d taught him a binding spell she never imagined he’d use to end a man’s fire for good.

“I don’t know how to be near you and be like this,” he told her, quiet, honest in the specific way you can only be honest with someone who can’t yet hear you. “So I’m going to go be like this somewhere you don’t have to watch. I know that’s a coward’s math. I did it anyway.” He pressed his mouth, once, to her knuckles. “If some part of you wakes up angry at me for that—good. Be angry. It’ll mean you’re still you.”

Then he crossed to the second bed, to the small, fierce shape of a girl who barely knew him beyond the sound of his voice through her father’s comm.

“Your dad’s going to tell you I ran,” he said. “He’s not wrong, exactly. But if you wake up and things have gone sideways and you need someone who isn’t him—my name’s Gerald. Not Moon. Gerald. He’ll know how to find me, if it ever comes to that. I hope it never does.”

The ship broke atmosphere a little before dawn, carrying him toward a sun already dying somewhere far kinder than the one he was leaving behind. So you’ll just run, the

old, familiar voice in his chest said—not Agatha’s this time, just his own, refusing to let him off easy even now.

He didn’t correct it. He wasn’t sure anymore there was a version of the truth where he got to.

He thought of her the whole way out past the orbital line —not the girl in the med-bay, but the version of her that only existed in memory now, laughing at something he’d said on a rooftop years ago, utterly unimpressed that he could bend gravity with the right piece of hardware, and completely undone, every time, by the fact that he loved her.

The log cuts out there. Andrew has watched it enough times now to know exactly where. He sets it down, the way he always does, and looks at his daughter’s face— unbothered, unbroken, blessedly unaware of what her father let himself become to keep one more person from having to become it first.

“I don’t know if what I did was right,” he told her. “I don’t know if there’s a version of tonight where I get to be your example and also be the man who did that. Maybe those two things were never going to fit inside the same person. Maybe that’s what growing up in a cape actually costs, in the end.”

He set his hand, briefly, over hers.

“When you wake up, the world’s going to have a story about me already. I’m asking you not to believe it until you’ve heard mine first.” He stood, the weight of the night finally settling into his shoulders like something he’d be carrying from now on. “Rest, Valor. I’ll be right here when you’re ready.”

He left the data chip on the table, beside the photograph and the pressed flower and the toy she’d outgrown, and left the lamp burning low beside her bed on his way out.

Love was never meant to be soft, not for hands that learned to carve before they learned to hold, not for hearts that beat like war drums long before they beat for anyone. We did not whisper. We collided— a tempest of shattered vows, bruises blooming like roses where devotion took root and never once asked permission. You tasted of ruin, of secrets buried in moonlight, of a mercy that trembled every time it almost won.

I drank you in anyway. Your love was a blade I let cut me open— let the proof stain my hands, let it carve your name into whatever is left of my soul when I finally find my way home. They will call it poison. I called it the only prayer I ever learned to finish.

chapters.title: All the Colours
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

Some things are worth more than staying safe and grey forever.

In the Republic of Even Ground, the worst thing a person could be caught doing was thinking. Not lying, not stealing—thinking, on your own, without a form to fill out first. The Ministry of Clarity called it “waywardness,” and waywardness, they said, spread like damp through plaster: quietly, until the whole wall came down. So they kept everything grey. Grey uniforms. Grey classrooms. Grey Mondays that looked exactly like grey Thursdays. Color, we were taught every morning during the Pledge, agitated the mind and unsettled the community. A red scarf was a threat to public order. A yellow smile could start a riot, apparently, though nobody could quite explain how.

I’d known my best friend since we were seven, back when we still had crayons and hadn’t yet learned to be afraid of them. He didn’t talk much anymore. His mother had “gone quiet”—the polite phrase for what happened to people who kept books the Ministry hadn’t approved— when he was twelve, and after that he learned to keep his face as flat as the walls. But he kept her books. A whole shoebox of them, hidden under a floorboard, and every so often he’d bring one to school folded into the lining of his bag, like it was something alive that needed feeding.

Everyone at school called him “the dark one.” Not for anything about him you could point to—for the quiet that hung around him like weather. He sat alone at lunch, alone at assembly, alone in the back corner of the library where the light gave up before it reached the last shelf. I was the only person he let sit that close.

Then there was her—a girl two rows over in Structured Thought class who’d apparently never gotten the memo about grey. She colored in the margins of her workbook with the stub of a pencil she kept sharpened to a dangerous point, shading little suns and impossible flowers in whatever pigment she could scrape off a smuggled paint set. She got caught once and spent a week in Reorientation. She came back and did it again the next day—smaller, sneakier, tucked

into corners a proctor’s eye would skip right over—but she did it again. I liked her instantly, the way you like anyone still fighting a war everyone else has quietly surrendered.

The week before, I’d overheard her by the lockers, telling a friend about a book her grandmother used to describe before she, too, went quiet—a picture book showing every color that had ever existed, back when they were all allowed to exist at once. All the Colours. Banned so thoroughly it wasn’t even on the official Index anymore. They hadn’t just forbidden it. They’d erased it, the way you erase a stain you don’t want anyone to know was ever there.

I knew exactly who had a copy.

I didn’t tell my friend the whole plan. I just mentioned, casually, over stale cafeteria bread, that it might be a good day to bring his mother’s book to school. He gave me a look —he always knew when I was up to something—but he packed it anyway. Some friendships run on trust you don’t have to explain out loud.

That afternoon I made sure I was in the library too, three shelves over, pretending to study a Ministry pamphlet on Correct Emotional Range, watching the whole thing unfold like it was the only good thing on television in the entire country.

The library did what libraries in Even Ground always did in the afternoon—it held its breath. Dry coughs echoed off the

high shelves and dissolved into a silence so complete you could hear the dust settle between them. She came in fast, scanning the aisles like she was running out of time, which, in a way, she was—Clarity sweeps happened without warning, and a girl caught digging through unindexed shelves wasn’t easy to explain. She pulled books out, shoved them back, pulled out more. Her eyebrows had drawn into a hard, furious little line, and she was muttering to herself, quick and low.

“Where is it,” she hissed at a shelf that had personally done nothing wrong.

The librarian, an older man who moved like he’d spent decades practicing not being noticed, appeared at the end of the row. “I’m sorry. Can I help you?”

She startled, then let out a laugh—short, nervous, too loud— and tried to swallow it back down. “Oh—great. You’re a librarian here? Never mind, dumb question.” A breath. “I’m looking for All the Colours.”

I watched something complicated move across his face. Fear, first, quick as a blink. Then something softer underneath it. He’d been at this school long enough, I think, to recognize a particular kind of desperate hope when he heard it—the kind that made a person worth a risk.

“Oh, no,” he said, low. “That one was banned. Properly banned.” He glanced left, then right, the way everyone in

Even Ground learned to glance before saying anything true. “But I could point you toward someone who might still have it.”

“Please,” she said, and I heard exactly how much she meant it. “Please do.”

He tipped his head toward the back corner, where the light gave up. “See the one sitting there?”

She looked. I watched her spine straighten, the way a person’s does right before they do something brave and slightly reckless. “The dark one,” she said, mostly to herself, and went.

I set my pamphlet down. This was the part I’d been waiting for.

She crossed the room slower than she’d come in, like the last ten feet cost more than the first hundred. He looked up before she reached the table—he noticed everything, that was half his problem—and something flickered across his face I’d genuinely never seen there before. Not fear. Something closer to recognition.

“Hi,” she said, and it came out smaller than she’d probably meant. “Sorry—the librarian said you might have—I know it’s a strange thing to ask a stranger, but—”

“All the Colours,” he said. Not a question.

Her mouth fell open a little. “How did you—”

“You’ve been in here every day this week, pulling books off the same three shelves.” A small, careful smile—the kind he handed out maybe twice a year. “You’re not exactly subtle.”

She laughed for real that time, pressing a hand over her eyes as if she could hide the color climbing up her neck. “That’s humiliating.”

“It’s not,” he said, quieter. “It’s the least grey thing I’ve seen in a while.”

I nearly knocked over the whole pamphlet display.

He reached into his bag—slow, careful, checking over his shoulder the way we’d all learned to do before we could properly walk—and drew out a book so worn the color had mostly faded off its cover, which felt, given everything, like the saddest joke the world had ever told. He held it like it weighed more than it did.

“It was my mother’s,” he said. “She used to read it to me before—” He didn’t finish. He didn’t have to. Everyone in Even Ground knew how that sentence ended.

Her whole face changed. Whatever nervous excitement had been carrying her all week softened into something gentler. “I’m sorry,” she said, and meant it, and didn’t try to fill the quiet after with anything else—which I think was exactly

right, because he nodded like she’d passed some test he’d never told anyone he was giving.

“You can borrow it,” he said. “If you’re careful. If you bring it back.”

“I’ll be so careful,” she said. “I promise. My grandmother used to describe it to me—all these colors I’ve never actually seen—and I wanted to know if she was just making it up to make me feel better, or if the world really used to look like that.”

“It did,” he said. “They just made everyone forget on purpose.”

She sat down across from him without being invited, which either of them could have made a whole thing of, and neither did. He opened the book flat on the table between them, and for a while they just looked at it together—two grey kids bent over a page of colors neither of them had proper words for, whispering when they remembered to, forgetting when they didn’t.

A Clarity Warden walked the far aisle twenty minutes later, unhurried, scanning faces the way they always did. My friend slid the book under a Ministry-approved textbook without breaking eye contact with her,

smooth as anything—like he’d practiced it, which, knowing about the floorboard, he probably had. She held perfectly still, the way you learn to by age twelve, and once the boots faded past the next row, she let out a breath that turned into a grin she couldn’t quite stop.

“That was terrifying,” she whispered.

“You get used to it,” he said, which wasn’t exactly comforting, but she smiled at him like it was anyway.

I left before either of them noticed I’d been there the whole time, because a good wingman knows exactly when his job is finished.

It’s been three weeks now. She still has the book—she carries it back and forth in a false-bottomed pencil case she built herself, which might honestly be the most romantic piece of engineering I’ve ever heard of. At lunch, sometimes, she sits with us now, and he talks more. Not a lot more. But more. He tells her which pages his mother used to linger on. She tells him what she thinks the colors would smell like, if colors had a smell, and he doesn’t laugh at her for it, and that alone told me everything I needed to know.

The margins of her workbook have started filling in again, braver every week, like she’s testing exactly how much the

world will let her get away with. Once, a proctor stopped by her desk and stared a beat too long at a smear of blue along the page edge. My stomach dropped through the floor. But he only said, “Keep your work within the lines,” and moved on, and I understood then that the world hadn’t gotten any less grey—she’d just gotten better at hiding in plain sight, the way we all eventually learn to.

Nobody’s caught them yet. I like to think it’s because they’re careful. I like to think it’s a little bit because I taught him everything he knows about not getting caught, though he’d never admit that out loud, and she’d probably just laugh and say he taught himself.

The Ministry can keep the walls as grey as it wants. It can ban every pigment, erase every book, scan every thought that dares to wander somewhere unauthorized. But it never figured out how to legislate the way two people look at each other over a picture book of colors nobody’s supposed to remember anymore. That part, it turns out, they never found a way to make grey.

I was the best wingman ever. I’m not saying it to brag. I’m saying it because someone has to write it down, and in a country where you’re not allowed to keep records of anything that matters, this felt like the one thing worth risking the ink for.

I should have known it wouldn’t stay that easy.

Three weeks after the library, a notice went up in every homeroom, printed in the flat official grey-on-grey the Ministry used for anything it wanted you to be afraid of without admitting it wanted that. Founding Day Inspection—All Personal Property Subject to Review. Every bag, every locker, every workbook margin would be gone through by hand. It happened every few years, always without warning until it wasn’t—a reminder, the announcement said, that Clarity was “a shared responsibility, not a private one.”

My friend didn’t say anything when he read it. He just went very still, the particular stillness he got when something mattered too much to let his face know about it. I understood. Under his floorboard was a shoebox that could get him “gone quiet” the same way his mother had. And in her false-bottomed pencil case, two rows over in Structured Thought, was a book with his mother’s name written in the front in handwriting he probably had memorized.

“We have four days,” I told him at lunch, because somebody had to say the number out loud.

“I know how to count,” he said, which was as close as he ever got to panicking.

She found out that afternoon—I don’t know how, maybe she’d heard the same notice with the same cold drop in her stomach that we had—and she was waiting by his locker before the last bell, which she had never once done before. It should have looked suspicious. It looked, to anyone glancing over, like two grey kids arguing about a homework assignment, which is exactly what a girl who’d survived a week of Reorientation had learned to make it look like.

“Give it back to me,” she said, low and fast. “Tonight. I have an idea.”

“It’s not safe with either of us right now,” he said. “Maybe it’s not safe anywhere.”

“It’s safer with someone who’s already been searched and come up clean.” She almost smiled, the grim kind. “They don’t expect the same person to be stupid twice. That’s the whole trick to it.”

He looked at her for a long moment—the look of someone recalculating exactly how much he’d underestimated a person—and handed it over.

I won’t pretend I know everything that happened in her house that night, because a good wingman also knows when to stop following. But I know what showed up in Structured Thought the next morning: her workbook, cover replaced with a fresh Ministry-issue one she’d

steamed off some other unlucky book, the pages inside re-bound so All the Colours sat disguised as Unit Four: Correct Civic Reasoning, right down to a set of fake worksheet questions she’d handwritten on the first page in case anyone actually opened it looking. She’d stayed up half the night stitching a lie good enough to survive a Warden’s hands. I decided right then that whatever this was between the two of them, she deserved at least as much credit for it as he did.

Founding Day arrived grey and ordinary, which was somehow worse than if it had arrived looking like anything special. They lined us up by homeroom in the gymnasium while two Wardens and a Ministry auditor went row by row, methodical, unhurried, the kind of unhurried that made your own heartbeat feel like evidence of something.

I watched from four rows back as they reached her. One Warden lifted her bag, went through it item by item— approved pencils, approved workbook, an apple with a bite out of it that got set aside and stared at for one truly unnecessary length of time—and then picked up Unit Four: Correct Civic Reasoning and flipped it open to the fake worksheet page.

My stomach did something I don’t have a Ministry- approved word for.

The Warden’s eyes skimmed the handwriting—her handwriting, careful and boring on purpose, all the right phrases in all the right order about shared responsibility and the peace of sameness—and then he closed it, set it back in her bag, and moved on to the next row without so much as a second glance.

She didn’t look at either of us. Not once. That was the part that told me she’d really thought this through—she knew exactly how much a glance could cost.

He got searched two rows later. I watched his face do absolutely nothing while a Warden went through his bag, and I understood, with a strange rush of relief, that the shoebox under his floorboard hadn’t come to school that day at all. He’d left his mother behind, hidden at home, to keep her safe, and brought nothing but empty hands and an ordinary bag to the one day it actually mattered. It must have cost him something, walking in with nothing to protect and everything still to lose.

When it was over—when the Wardens had packed up their clipboards and the auditor had signed whatever form made the whole gymnasium officially, temporarily Clear—the noise in the room came back all at once, everyone exhaling at slightly different speeds. I found her in the crush by the doors. She found him a second later, like they’d been aiming for the same spot without agreeing on it out loud.

Neither of them said anything for a second. Then she reached into her bag, pulled out Unit Four: Correct Civic Reasoning, and held it out to him with both hands, like something ceremonial.

“I think,” she said, a little unsteady, “that might be the bravest thing I’ve ever done.”

“It’s the bravest thing I’ve ever seen anyone do,” he said, and didn’t take the book back right away. For a second they just stood there, both of them holding it, which is a very small thing to notice and I noticed it anyway, because I’d spent three weeks watching two people who flinched from touching anything that mattered finally not flinch.

“Keep it a while longer,” he said finally. “It survived one inspection under your name. Might as well see how far you can take it.”

“That sounds like you trust me.”

“That sounds like I do,” he said, and it might have been the most words he’d used on purpose, out loud, about a feeling, in the entire two years I’d known him.

She walked out of the gymnasium that day still holding his mother’s book against her chest, and he walked half a step closer to her than the hallway strictly required, and I trailed

behind both of them thinking that somewhere, in a country that had outlawed color on purpose, two teenagers had just spent four sleepless days proving they’d rather risk everything than let each other’s proof of the world disappear.

It’s not a resistance. I want to be honest about that—it’s not some grand uprising, no flags, no marches, nothing the Ministry would ever bother writing a bulletin about. It’s just two kids and a book and a very tired wingman, quietly deciding that some things are worth more than staying safe and grey forever.

But I’ve started to think that’s exactly how it’s supposed to start.

chapters.title: Untitled Part 22
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

Maybe, just maybe, this unlikely friendship could work, even with the atheist and the Catholic.

“Ash Wednesday is today and I still have no idea where to get a good Catholic church!” she exclaimed, pacing her tiny apartment. She glanced at her watch. Her mother’s call was imminent, and the inquisition about her attendance at Ash Wednesday mass would be swift and merciless.

“I know my mom will call and ask if I went for mass,” she continued, more to herself than anyone. “Someone can’t take me ‘cause, obviously, it’s in the name. Someone else won’t because they’re in the Salvation Army or something...” She trailed off, a picture of mild panic.

Across the room, he, hunched over his laptop, scrolled through lines of code, seemingly oblivious to her distress. He went through his code one more time, almost as though he hadn’t heard her.

“I’ll take you.”

He suggested so nonchalantly that it caught her by surprise. She stopped pacing and stared at him.

“Really?”

“Yeah,” he said, finally lifting his gaze from the screen. “I mean, I don’t really get the significance of having a tiny cross drawn with ash over your forehead, but yeah, it seems important to you.” He shrugged, a slight smile playing on his lips.

She was taken aback. He, the self-proclaimed coding hermit, the guy who only seemed to emerge from his apartment for coffee and the occasional hackathon, was offering to go to church with her? She wasn’t sure what to say, but the prospect of not facing her mother’s wrath alone was undeniably appealing. And, if she was honest with herself, the idea of spending an hour or so with him outside of their usual coding-fueled interactions was…intriguing.

“Okay,” she said, a smile spreading across her face. “That would be…great.”

They found a small, unassuming Catholic church a few blocks away. The service was quiet and reverent. She, despite her initial anxiety, found herself surprisingly moved by the ritual. He, on the other hand, looked a little lost, his eyes darting around the church, taking in the stained glass windows and the solemn atmosphere. He fidgeted slightly

during the sermon, but he sat quietly, respectfully, beside her.

As they strolled out of church, the afternoon sun casting long shadows, he turned to her, a thoughtful expression on his face.

“How do you feel now that you took me to church?” he asked, the emphasis on the “me” making her wonder what he was implying.

She blinked, confused. “Good? I mean, it was nice. Thank you for coming with me.”

He made a face, a slight grimace that suggested she had missed something obvious. “Why are you atheist or pagan?” she blurted out, the question escaping before she could stop it.

He chuckled. “One, it was a pop song reference,” he said, rolling his eyes playfully. “Two, paganism is an official religion, you know. Three,” he paused, his expression turning serious for a moment, “yes, I am an atheist.”

Her jaw dropped. She felt a wave of confusion wash over her. She had assumed…well, she wasn’t sure what she had assumed. But it certainly wasn’t that he, the guy who had

just accompanied her to Ash Wednesday mass, was a confirmed atheist.

“But…why?” she asked, the question hanging in the air.

He shrugged again. “It’s a long story. Basically, I just… don’t believe. I respect that you do, and I was happy to come with you. It was…interesting. But it doesn’t change anything for me.”

She nodded slowly, trying to process this new information. She had taken his willingness to accompany her to church as some sort of…acknowledgement, perhaps even a shared connection. Now, she realized she had completely misread the situation.

“So, the pop song reference…” she started, trying to lighten the mood.

“Yeah,” he grinned. “It’s from a song called ‘Losing My Religion.’ Pretty ironic, huh?”

She laughed, the tension easing slightly. “Very ironic,” she agreed.

They walked in silence for a few moments, the weight of their differing beliefs hanging between them. Then, she spoke.

“You know,” she said, “it doesn’t matter that you’re an atheist. I still appreciate you coming with me. It meant a lot.”

He looked at her, a genuine smile gracing his features. “Thanks, Maria. It meant something to me too.”

As they reached her apartment building, she paused. “Maybe…maybe we could grab coffee sometime? Talk about…well, anything. Coding, music, the meaning of life…or the lack thereof.”

He grinned. “I’d like that. Though I warn you, I can talk about coding for hours.”

She laughed. “That’s okay. I’m a good listener.”

As she watched him walk away, she realized that their trip to church, despite the unexpected revelation, had actually brought them closer. They were still worlds apart in their beliefs, but somehow, that didn’t seem to matter as much anymore. Maybe, just maybe, this unlikely friendship could work, even with the atheist and the Catholic. It would certainly be interesting to find out.

chapters.title: Is God Black?
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

Is God black? Is God like me, and like my ancestors?

Humanity has come far. Technology, civilization — you’re probably reading this because of an online platform, or because it was brought to you through something called school.

Humanity found ways to comfort itself about its origin. Who is in charge of its destiny. How it came to be, and why it is here.

Humanity found God, or gods, or a teacher who was connected to God.

Humanity also found ways of splitting itself. Reasons to hate, and reasons to fight. Humanity found differences within itself, and used those differences as an excuse to fight each other.

Not all of humanity found God, you should remember. Those who did came and taught others of him.

Do you recall the story in the Bible where a group of people build what history calls the Tower of Babel? Do you ever wonder what would have happened if the tower had been finished?

Some say God saved them from their own failure and foolishness. I say he stopped a great deal of manipulation. If they had finished that tower and it had touched the heavens, those who reached the heavens would have spoken of having God, and regarded themselves as above the rest of us. God saved them from their own stupidity, but he knew it would have resulted in more chaos regardless.

I almost forgot why I am writing this. Oh yes — I did not write to ask where God is, or why he hates a particular people when the devil never declared hatred for us. No. I wrote to ask: if God made us in his image, is he really black?

Is God black? Is God like me, and like my ancestors?

Yes, he is God. He understands the struggles and the difficulty of being a black man. Anyone can understand it — that is why we have empathy.

If God walked down the street and was threatened with arrest just because he looked suspicious, would he give in

and admit to something despite his innocence, or would he resist?

Would God have resisted imperialism over his people and his country?

Would he have taken another man’s life to live as a free man, or would he say that freedom was an illusion he did not need?

Is God black?

Would he have let himself die before reaching a foreign land to be a slave, or would he have happily served his masters? Would he worship a race, or would he die hating them?

I will not forget when this thought first hit me. I remember it as clearly as day. I remember exactly why I asked that question.

I was walking down the street, a local preacher in my suit and tie. The sermon of the week had been delivered, and I was glad by how the congregation received it — a rebuke to those who had disrupted the peace of the protests demanding an end to the killing of black people in the streets. I spared no one. I took no sides.

“Praise God, pastor! Today’s sermon was nothing but the truth! God does not need us fighting each other!” Miriam, one of my congregants, ran up to me.

“Please tell your sons that we need them to maintain the peace,” I told her with a smile, remembering that her three sons were military police. I often wondered how they felt, lobbing tear gas at their own people.

“Pray for their safety,” she told me, and I smiled reassuringly and told her I would.

I walked into the convenience store and picked up a basket.

“Hello, pastor!” That was Ndembu — an African, or to be more precise, a South Sudanese immigrant who had come to this country because of the violence back home. He had surprisingly built a life here: a business as a Walmart manager, and a family with Angie, a white woman from the suburban part of the city.

“Hello! How are you today?” I greeted him warmly.

“I am very good, pastor. My cousin from South Sudan is finally settling in. He says the high school bullies are finally off him. Being a child soldier did a number on him. It’s a good thing you were there to stand up for him.”

Yes. How could I forget? The young man, nineteen now, had been recruited as a child soldier at eleven. He had attacked

a few students who were bullying him, beating them ruthlessly.

“How are the therapy sessions going?” I asked.

“He’s attending them regularly...” I wasn’t really listening. The students who had bullied this young man were like him — black. Only he was African.

“That’s nice to hear! Now let me get some shopping done,” I told him, if only to escape the conversation.

“Ah — I just hope he can survive this new environment. Anyway, fifteen percent off those diapers for the man of God!”

He always did this — slashing prices for me. I had a newborn, not any older than two months. You know children. Always doing everything in their diapers.

I laughed and moved toward the diaper aisle. That’s when the feeling hit me. Fear.

Ndembu’s cousin rushed in — no, more like he barged in.

“Help me!” He yelled, and began speaking rapidly in Dinka.

“What do you mean you’re running from the police?” I asked.

“They pointed a gun at me. You forbade me from attacking, so I ran!” You could hear him struggling to find the English words.

“What did you do?” I asked.

“Nothing!” he said, looking distressed. An officer ran in a moment later, panting and wheezing — you could tell chasing down someone tall and fast wasn’t usually part of his job.

“You are under arrest for resisting arrest,” he managed, somehow saying the whole sentence without pausing for breath.

“Look. I’m sure there’s a misunderstanding here. What happened?” I asked, stepping between him and Ndembu’s cousin.

“He ran when I told him to stop.” That didn’t really explain anything, but I chose to understand it from his perspective anyway.

“Why did you run?” I turned to the young man.

He looked back at me. His eyes said more than words could, and the worry on his face spoke for him.

“Because I was afraid.”

In an instant, my mind ran through every scenario, every probability, of how this could have ended. What if he had been shot? What if his fate had been worse than a knee to the neck? What if — what if —

I suddenly saw my own son in him. An older version of him, living in this unsafe world. My son being stopped by the police, patted down. The scenarios kept running — of him possibly getting shot.

“Are you okay?” I asked him. He seemed rattled, but fine.

“Look, officer. This young man is a foreigner. He’s undergoing psychiatric care for his PTSD. We’re sorry about what happened.” I explained.

“You oughta be, reverend! Now I’ma go ahead and let him off with a warning.”

He walked out of the store as his partner pulled up outside.

I turned back to the young man. The scenes in my head only got worse — children taught how to act when confronted by police, how to respond, before they’ve even had the chance to be children. I couldn’t help it.

“I prayed to him, man of God,” he said. “I prayed, and the answer I got was you, walking toward me. Does God care about us? Aren’t we made in his image? Does God know my suffering? Is God black?”

What could I tell him? He was looking to me for hope.

Did God’s colour even matter? His own son was hated by his own people for his views. His own messengers were hated in their hometowns. We despised God first, then despised our own existence, and that of others. To feel superior, we began to hate each other — despising the fact that we differed in tongue, colour, ethnicity, and creed. Even in religion — even when religion was born of people who went looking for a God, or gods, to believe in.

Back to the question: is God black?

Would God be on a slave ship right now? Would he march up and down the streets, yelling that black lives matter? Would he run from an officer meaning to search him, just because he looked suspicious? Would he beat up the children who harassed him at school, just because he was not only black, but African? Would God yell in anger, telling the imperialists to leave his continent?

Is God black?

Yes. He’s black. He’s white. He’s beyond us. He sent us redemption; we pray to his son for the forgiveness of our

sins. God doesn’t need to pick a side. Gods do not need to pick a side. Humanity should be like God, or gods — whichever you choose.

I never chose a side in my sermon. God doesn’t need to be black to understand us. He doesn’t need to align himself with our thoughts. Humanity doesn’t need to have sides either.

“Yes,” the young man said quietly. “But does he need to be black to have empathy for you?”

chapters.title: They Have Had Enough
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

No child should be forced to hold a gun or kill another man. No child should watch a man die by their own hand.

In all my life, I have seen wars and fights, heard of struggles on the continent of Africa. Fighting for power, struggles for equality, struggles for control. You name it.

The nineties were a time of a wind of change — apartheid coming to an end, civil wars, military coups, child soldiers, and a lot of madness. I, however, have seen much more. The Biafra War. The Nigerian Civil War, which saw the starvation of children. They still ask the question: was this a genocide? I have witnessed much more. I have served as a peacekeeper. Ironic, isn’t it — we maintain peace with guns, keep people safe with the very things that started the chaos. As I served across the continent, in the name of maintaining peace and security, freedom and

democracy, rights and dignity, I have seen atrocities against a people. Death, starvation, disease.

None of it affected anyone more than it did the children.

What is a child? There are a lot of definitions, different understandings. A child is innocence personified, the living embodiment of naivety. Yet somehow you can take that and turn it into whatever you want — a living weapon, a scene of pity, a call to action.

Stories have come before me, all different. War always has casualties — collateral damage, we call them. They say “collateral damage” to avoid saying “innocent people killed.” I have seen children reduced to collateral damage. The truth is, no child should be forced to hold a gun or kill another man. No child should watch a man die by their own hand. We say we are protecting them, to ensure they build the future. Extremists turned children into war machines to serve their own interests. Uganda, Mauritania, the DRC, Nigeria, Sierra Leone — name it. The radicalization of children — they have all done it.

Remember Beasts of No Nation? A story of a child soldier traumatized by the acts he and his comrades committed. Heinous. I felt the storyline speak to his pain, and the pain of every last neglected child soldier out there. We’ve never understood what a soldier feels. We take lives, yes, but what do you feel when it comes down to killing a

child? When a child is no longer innocent, brainwashed by someone who was supposed to guide them.

We walked through the dense jungle of the Congo, every step carefully taken, knowing it could very well be our last. The crickets chirped away to pass the time. We would set up camp after a few more metres. We braved the cold that bit our skin indiscriminately. My friend from Uganda shivered behind me, still wet from falling into a river. The peaceful quiet of the jungle made it impossible to believe that danger lurked here at all — that this ground had once held one of the most vicious wars fought between the Rwandans, Ugandans, and Congolese. Death was a story these grounds had already seen.

“Haya, we’ll take a break now!” our commanding officer said. A fire was started, and we sat around it as we ate our canned food. The fire shone on our faces as we sat in silence; the crackle of the flames was the only thing that tried to break the dead quiet.

“To grow up as a child in Congo, according to God’s will, is to grow up in paradise,” a Congolese soldier said. “Perhaps because of the will of man, growing up in Congo instead means growing up in misery, because of these endless, unjust wars imposed on its people. Congo’s bravest soldier said it once: a child, growing up anywhere, should grow up in peace.”

“Not on this continent. Colonel Mamadou was a wise and brave man — fought hard to see the African child get what he deserved: freedom and peace,” I said, pouring myself another cup of coffee.

“We have been selfish as humans, taken the future from every generation without thinking or blinking,” our commanding officer told us. He was right. Individualism began the death of society and the end of our humane nature. The belief that our needs supersede all other needs is why we end up destroying the future. “Maybe it’s just me,” the commander sighed, “but we are driven by our wants.”

“No lie, that’s why the Rwandans are not here,” someone said.

“Wewe, we are here to maintain peace, not point fingers!” the commander snapped. True — by morning we were to raid the rebel camp a short distance away. I still had a crippling fear in me that this wasn’t going to go well. Why would I want to jinx the whole operation just because of my own superstition?

One person in our ranks had remained silent the whole time. He sat on a log, looking into his wallet. No one knew what he was looking at. We didn’t want to ask, either.

“What do you think? About this whole situation?” someone asked.

“It’s hate. Hate is what drives us to be selfish — to hate is to become selfish. We look at the children and see everything they’ll have, and we grow selfish because we know we’ll never have it ourselves. We manipulate them because we know they know no better than to follow. Haven’t they had enough?”

I am not sure who the question was posed to, or who was supposed to answer it, but I knew the answer myself. The enemy camp probably had child soldiers — rebels tended to recruit from the neighbouring villages. Groups like M7 had approximately two hundred children in their ranks. They had surrendered, but other groups still held the jungle in their claws of terror, waiting to pounce and strike.

“When I was a child... I saw my friends murdered. I was spared because I was Hutu. I asked a soldier, ‘Haven’t you had enough?’ I lived, but the trauma stayed. I vowed to protect children.”

That story came out of the blue, leaving us confused, and thinking. Our train of thought was interrupted by gunfire. No one was hit by the first bullet, but it was followed by a barrage of more fire.

“Positions! Fire back! Fire back!” our commanding officer yelled, and we scrambled to return fire. Some of our own were already hit. I struggled to find the enemy position as shots zipped past me.

“We have to call in an airstrike!” the commanding officer yelled at me. Suddenly I had a flashback — my days in Mogadishu. The East African troops had had to call in an airstrike after we were overwhelmed. There had been collateral damage. Children, women, and men protecting their families — all died in the chaos. Yes, I had noticed something — there would be human casualties, but they were hostages, probably people from the neighbouring villages.

In the depths of the bushes and thickets, I noticed children taking cover, afraid a bullet would find them.

“Sir! Civilian hostages! Calling for backup instead!”

I had the radio, so I made the call. I turned the knobs. Static. I turned them some more — nothing.

“Tango Bravo, this is Charaza Squad! We are under fire! Send backup!”

A moment of silence as we fought back, the sound of a machine gun answering as our rifles spat fire in return.

“Negative, Squadron Charaza — clear the area, we are sending in missile strikes!”

They couldn’t! Why would they?

“Negative, sir! There are civilian hostages within the enemy camp!”

Static.

“There’s nothing we can do! Clear the area! Our forces will be overwhelmed if we attempt to take the area!”

I hissed under my breath and threw the radio away from myself. My commanding officer looked at me, worried.

Why was I even here? A man who should have retired years ago. It was the same question I always asked myself.

I helped a man to his feet as the first barrage of shells began dropping. We were out of harm’s way. The strikes hit the ground, exploding. The agonizing screams haunted me the following morning as I stood near the site. I heard someone say, “The man in charge of this operation is Ugandan — you know they don’t much like the Congolese, right?”

Banter. That was all it was to me. I stood there looking at all the bodies that lay before me, terror still frozen on their faces. I’d had enough. I was finally going to retire. I

was finally going to hang up these boots and let my days of war stay behind me.

A year later, we were brought before a court martial to answer for the incident in the forest.

“We could do nothing — they were in the way?”

Collateral damage. That is what people were reduced to.

“Lieutenant Kabogo! What happened that night?” The lady’s voice snapped me back to reality.

“We hadn’t noticed the civilians, due to the heavy fire we were under,” I lied. The Congolese had seen worse — UN peacekeepers failing to act while villages were under attack from rebels.

I had been awarded my medal of bravery, and soon I would go back to Nairobi to retire. My story — of being a hero, or a cowardly man who hadn’t acted to protect children — would never be told.

“No!” I said, out of the blue.

“No, what, Kabogo?” one of the men asked me.

“We knew about the children and the women. We had to choose — that was the difference — and we chose ourselves, like cowards. We chose the easier way out!”

I had to tell them. The grisly images of that night still raced through my mind, even a year later. We hadn’t attacked an enemy camp. This was a village held under siege. What we attacked were innocent victims.

I saw the children — terrified, hiding away. The less fortunate ones, burned beyond recognition. Charred bodies of more children. If they weren’t already dead, they were holding on to their dear lives, but dying anyway. They had had enough of a world that didn’t care about them.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

No children of mine will become cattle lords. This is no life for you to keep living.

I woke up that morning. She slept quietly beside me. I had to travel, so I didn’t want to bother her. I got up and looked at the clock — it was five thirty in the morning. I would be late if I didn’t move quickly. I stealthily got out of bed and headed to the outdoor bathroom. A cold breeze hit me. I quivered.

The sun slowly rose into the sky, transitioning peacefully, the colours shifting from deep midnight blues and purples to a lighter shade of blue, even pink and orange near the horizon. There was life in the air as the birds chirped in excitement. I’d eventually have to go and let the cows out, herd them as they grazed on the green, rocky hills of the

land. The land is blessed by the sun, as it shows off its beauty.

I am done with my cold shower. He is standing out there, looking at me. He does not greet me. He stares blankly. He’s probably hungry. I walk past him. Not a word exchanged. She has woken up. She is already warming up my breakfast before she goes to bathe. She is silent, very little to say.

He ran up to her and wrapped his arms around her waist as he asked for his breakfast — porridge with yams.

Then there was the bullet.

I took my porridge. She had forgotten the sugar, but I couldn’t blame her.

I walked into the outer houses to wake my sons. The daughters had already woken; they had their duties to the homestead. The boys, however, had been out drinking till late night, so I expected them to still be hungover.

Two shared an outer house. The third had one all to himself, though he wasn’t in it — he was in the city, studying. Even then, we struggled to reach him.

I barked orders as they struggled to wake up. Even after all the groaning and moaning, they woke up and began leading the cattle out.

He stands to the side, looking back at me. Was it my fault, though? They keep leading the cattle out, and his look turns to something close to anger. He stares as resentment begins to grow in his eyes.

A cow crosses in front of us, its bell clanging away. He is suddenly among the cattle. This was the age I stopped him from herding them out.

To prove that you were a man in this community, you had to begin herding and protecting the cattle before you took over the responsibilities of raiding. It had been a custom since we could remember.

I wasn’t ready for him to leave. His brothers would tease him because he was still young and rushing to become a warrior. I had to leave for town. I assured them I’d be back before midday.

Once, I went to town with hope and excitement, looking forward to giving my son another path — the one his brother had taken.

This day would see a different expression on my face.

As I waited in the Huduma office, I sat there thinking, maybe he’d have become something.

“We are sorry to hear the news about your son. We extend our condolences.”

Yes — a scholarship was all I needed him to find, a route out of this life.

“Sir, as much as it’s easier for us to cancel this scholarship, we’d like to take a different approach. We’d love to offer your other sons this scholarship.”

The question was — would they take it?

I go back to the fields, to the hills. The sound of cattle greets me as I ascend.

“We need to end this barbaric culture! This uncouth behaviour of stealing another clan’s cattle to prove your manhood. Real men define their own manhood however

they choose. It is not through acts of aggression that you become a man!”

An activist yelled, her voice begging for the lives of our young to be protected and spared.

I can say I felt her emotions. I knew what she was talking about. I understood her — but did she understand me?

With pain comes the feeling of empathy — the ability to be there, to understand, and to provide nothing. I had empathy, but I didn’t just want to be there. I wanted to do something.

“Our leaders don’t care about us! They sit with the enemy and hold peace talks. They just call for peace! Today we march! We march to find peace! We march to make them see enough is enough! We are tired of having the army deployed to silence the guns! We are tired of having to live our whole lives in fear! We are tired of fear! Say it with me! I am tired of living in fear!”

Our leaders — well, at least they pretended to do something. At least they sent the army.

I never understood who my enemy was.

Cattle rustling, they say, is interchangeable with cattle raiding. I am no expert, but it’s one and the same to me.

Definition: a common practice amongst pastoralists in Kenya, involving the forceful acquisition of cattle from one community by another, using guns and other weapons, and often leading to loss of life and destruction of property.

That’s what you’ll get if you search for it.

Let me tell you all about it.

Cattle lords recruit and arm rural warriors to steal cattle for sale to abattoirs in town, or to smuggle across the border into neighbouring countries, where they sell them. Stolen cattle are easy to traffic, as they can be disguised as a legal commodity. Responses to the problem by East African countries have so far been ineffective.

It is common among pastoralists — the activist didn’t know everything. It’s not just a clan activity anymore. It’s a growing problem.

I am on top of the hill. I see the cattle moving lazily as my sons lie on the grassy terrain. Only one of them got to go to the city to study. How could the others, when I had raised the rest to be killing machines?

I sigh heavily and begin my descent. I see him — he’s laughing his brothers‘ teasing and mockery away. Yet I cannot shake this version of him that keeps giving me a melancholic look as I descend, as if to say: you could have done more.

“I hear it’s the politicians who fund cattle lords, like father!” one said, a chewing stick in his mouth.

“Then that would explain the guns we’re carrying,” one remarked. Guns? Didn’t we surrender those?

“Soon I’ll take Father’s place!”

No. That’s not what I want. That’s not how this should go. I have managed to secure you positions in school. All three of you.

He stands next to me, his abdomen bleeding. He looks at me, tears in his eyes.

“Help me!” he whimpered, tears in his eyes. Why won’t he rest? Why must he come to me? I tried my best.

“Father! What is wrong? Why are you kneeling there, crying?” I raise my eyes to them. All three of them surround me, and they all have looks of sympathy on their faces.

“You are all leaving this godforsaken hellhole! Every one of you! You will finish your education, fund your sisters‘,

and you will all leave! Do you hear me? Even if I have to sell the last head of cattle on this land. Do you hear me? No children of mine will become cattle lords! This is no life for you to keep living! Forgive me — can you ever find it in you to forgive me?”

I wept bitterly, resentment in every word — resenting the life I had chosen, and forced my children into.

“Can you ever find it in you to forgive me?” I asked him, looking into his eyes as he kept crying from the pain.

He looked back at me coldly, his eyes emotionless. He was silent, and his abdomen kept bleeding as I looked at him. Could I do anything to change this? Could I save him? Was this how they would all end up?

I will never find the answer to who shot my son, unarmed in the fields. Bandits? The army? He never had a gun with him, or any sort of weapon. He was simply walking when the raid began.

Who is my enemy?

chapters.title: My People
chapters.text:
A D I A R Y

You will hear stories of the First World War from both sides — but rarely from the men who actually laboured for it.

History is written by the victors. What if a neutral people also wrote history?

I remember the first time I found this diary. It was a version of the story written by a person who had nothing to gain in this battle. You will hear stories of the First World War from both sides, but rarely from the men who actually laboured for it — the Africans. My great- grandfather’s diary told the story from his perspective, and I was glad I found it. He had taken part in a forgotten piece of history called the East African Campaign: four years of guerrilla warfare in which a small German force, led by a colonel named Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, ran rings around an Allied army many times its size. I did not

know any of that yet. I only knew his handwriting, and that he had never once told us any of this himself.

I began to read.

Tsavo, 1914

Dear Margret,

I am writing this because many men here write letters like it, with the crippling fear that they may not see another day — my commander included. Many of us have been taken from our land to labour for a war fought overseas, or so my commanding officer tells me. I hope that with each day that passes, your hunger to learn only grows. Speak their language, gain their skills, so that every day you earn a little more of their respect.

I fight this war because our masters have told us it is important — that it will keep us free, and unoppressed. They turned our peaceful home into a theatre of war and violence to do it. I have not yet wielded a weapon against anyone. I am nothing but a porter. But every day my life finds a new kind of danger anyway.

There is a people called the Germans, and we are told they are our enemies, a threat to our peace. The white man never ceases to amaze me — he fights another people who look just like him, only because they speak a different tongue. Their home, too, has become a battlefield. They came telling us they had brought stability, peace, civilisation. I doubt their words now, and I doubt their intentions more.

We hunt a man they call Lieutenant Colonel Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, who leads what is left of the small German army. He knows, they say, that he cannot win against a force that outnumbers his ten to one. And yet he runs rings around us all the same — inflicting casualty after casualty, refusing to be caught, refusing to be beaten, resorting to tactics no honourable war was ever supposed to need.

Many have been lost. Many more have suffered wounds that will never fully close. Still he does not stop. We have fought through the savannah of Tsavo, battling not only the enemy but every danger that country holds. They have torn up the rail line behind us. We push on into Tanzania now. I have watched my compatriots fall and die. I have watched men who look like me die for a war none of us started. I pray, Margret, that it never costs my people what it has already cost others.

Yours,

Your soldier

FROM HIS OWN HAND

Long after the war, Lettow-Vorbeck wrote his own account of that campaign. I found this line in it, and it has stayed with me since:

“With the means available, protection of the Colony could not be ensured even by purely defensive tactics… it followed that it was necessary, not to split up our small available forces in local defence, but… to keep them together, to grip the enemy by the throat and force him to employ his forces for self-defence.”

— General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, My Reminiscences of East Africa, 1920

Tanga, November 1914

Dear Margret,

I saw a mass of Indian soldiers die today, sent to defend a freedom none of us had been asked whether we wanted. I saw a mass of my own people die today too. I promise you, though — I will not die on this foreign soil. I will come home, and our children will be christened, and they will carry their names into a world I hope looks nothing like this one.

I worry this will go on forever. I hope that one day we will stand as equals with these people who came to give us their religion and their law — the ones who once told us that someone loved us all equally, that before His eyes we were all the same. I have seen the white man die today. I have seen him cry. I have seen him worry that he will not live to kiss his own children goodnight. I feared the very same thing, and in that fear, I understood him completely.

I saw an Indian soldier pray to a god that was not the white man’s god, and I saw that god keep him alive. I saw another die anyway, even after he begged for his life at the end. I saw all of them pray, in their own tongues, to their own heavens. I was not certain who I

was praying to myself, but I prayed all the same, to whoever was out there listening.

Margret, I lived today. I was determined to see you again, just once more, and today that was enough to carry me through. Men fell to my left and to my right, and still I lived. I will come home to you.

Today, for the first time, I saw the white man fail. I had only ever heard stories of how his kind resisted to the last and still somehow won. Today he did not win. Today he lost, and I watched it happen with my own eyes.

Yours,

Your soldier

WHAT THE RECORDS SAY

Years later I learned what my great-grandfather had actually witnessed that week. In August 1914, Lettow- Vorbeck had raided British positions near Mount Kilimanjaro and Lake Victoria. In response, a British- Indian force under Major-General Arthur Aitken landed

near the German port of Tanga on the 3rd of November. Aitken made no effort to hide his plans, and Lettow- Vorbeck used the time he was given to reinforce his defences.

When the fighting began, Aitken’s poorly trained Indian troops broke and ran. Though outnumbered, the Germans counter-attacked and drove them back to their boats; what remained of the force re-embarked on the 5th of November. At a cost of some 150 casualties, Lettow- Vorbeck had inflicted 850, and captured hundreds of rifles, several machine guns, and 600,000 rounds of ammunition — supplies that would keep his army equipped for the year that followed. History would come to call it the Defeat at Tanga.

My great-grandfather had simply called it the day he saw the white man fail.

somewhere near the rail line, 1917

Dear Margret,

There is a new general leading the Allied forces now, a South African named Jan Smuts, brought here with

soldiers of his own and a great column of us to carry what his army cannot carry itself. We march where there are no roads and no railways, only the paths we make ourselves, into country that swallows men whole. Smuts, they say, learned this kind of fighting from the British themselves, years ago, in a war they fought against his own people. Now he uses it against us in a different uniform.

We have taken the rail line as far as Morogoro and Dodoma, and still Lettow-Vorbeck slips away from us every time we think we have him cornered, leaving only skirmishes and ambushes behind him like breadcrumbs. It is the sickness that is truly winning this war, Margret, more than either army. I have seen whole units of the white man’s soldiers reduced to a tenth of their number by fever and disease alone, having barely fired a shot. We askaris and porters seem to weather this land better than they do — perhaps because we have always known how unforgiving it can be, and they are only now learning it.

I met a man this month who speaks a tongue called Yoruba, from far to the west of here. His people have come to fight alongside us too, sent by another kind of white man, the Belgians this time, and he tells me his own home has suffered atrocities I do not have room to write here. It seems there is no corner of this land that this war has not reached, and no people who have not paid some price for wars declared by other men in other countries.

Yours,

Your soldier

A LETTER THAT WAS NEVER SENT TO US

Among the papers pressed into the back of the diary was a photocopy — I never found out where he got it — of a letter from a British officer named Captain Alexander Wallace, written the same year, to the woman he hoped to marry:

“I got 41 wounded off yesterday, but still have 20 serious cases, mostly askaris. Their wounds are all very septic and it takes a long time to dress them. I hope to get the others off in a few days. There is difficulty in getting carriers for them… This is rather a filthy camp [and] the flies are simply swarming. There are also a lot of mosquitoes.”

— Captain Alexander Wallace, in a letter to his fiancée, 7 September 1917

Further on, from a letter the same officer wrote three months later:

“There will be a lot of starvation… The Belgians told us that last year in the Rwanda country — between Lakes Tanganyika and Nyasa — 20,000 natives died of starvation. War is a sad thing for the native population. The troops occupy the country for a bit, take what food there is, leaving nothing for the natives.”

— Captain Alexander Wallace, 10 December 1917

I do not know if my great-grandfather ever read these words himself, or only kept them because someone once told him they belonged with his own. Either way, they sat in the same box as his letters to Margret for over a hundred years, two very different men writing the very same war.

25 November 1918

Dear Margret,

Today. Today we have ended the war to end all wars, as our masters like to call it. We have finally captured the man we spent four years chasing. Lettow-Vorbeck has surrendered. We have brought him to what they are calling justice.

This war is over, but the devastation it leaves behind may be worse than the war itself. My people have suffered enough, and they have suffered plenty. I have heard stories of starvation, of something close to a massacre of children in South West Africa, done by people who still insist they are the civilised ones. A new man took command of our forces partway through all this, a General Jan Smuts — I can barely pronounce his name, and yet he once told me mine was the difficult one. He claims to be South African, and yet he is not Black. Shaka the Zulu was not white, and no one ever called him anything but South African either.

We have taken over now, in our turn. I have held a gun to men who look just like me. We all have. On a kinder note, we received help along the way from another kind of white man, the Belgians, and from more of my own people too, come from the west of this land they call Africa to help us finish this. They spoke of atrocities of

their own, done to their own people. I met men whose tongues I had never heard before. A friend of mine speaks one called Yoruba.

To be honest with you, Margret, this war has worn our masters down as much as it has worn down the rest of us. They say the casualties were worse than anyone expected — Indian, British, and ours alike. My people have fallen for a cause most of us never fully understood. The question that stays with me now is whether my people have learned anything from it at all. Will we go looking for our own freedom now? Our own place as equals? Or will we simply go home, and wait for the next war to ask the same of us again?

Yours, always,

Your soldier

With the war finally over, my great-grandfather came home — only to find a new kind of war waiting for him there instead. His adventures did not end with the peace of 1918. Years later, a second world war would come looking for men like him all over again.

I closed the diary there, only for that day, already eager to keep reading.
