chapters.title: Who Heals the Healer?
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

Maybe healing didn’t mean becoming whole. Maybe it meant learning to carry the pieces without cutting yourself on their edges.

It was the end of the day. Most people leave, go home to their families. But I was sitting face-to-face with my worst nightmare. Most of my clients—no, all of my clients —came with familiar wounds. In a country drowning in trauma and starved for mental health practitioners, I was one of the few stretched thin; the work felt endless. Then the country itself caught fire in a way I hadn’t imagined.

The people had risen against each other. The division was so tangible you could step in it, feel the hate and the anger thick as blood in the air. Violence followed like an answering bell, fed by voices that thought destruction was

a solution. The violence, bloody, fueled by none other than people just like him.

“What brings the government to my doorstep, sir?” I asked, my voice deliberately flat.

“We need to talk,” he said, his tone even.

“Surely you must have formed a commission for my field. Why approach me directly?”

A pause. “This is more personal than it is official.”

In the ensuing violence, I had been a voice of reason.

I remembered the interviews: the late-night appeals for calm, the awkward PR spots billed as reassurance, giving my analysis, begging the people to calm down. Transitioning governments are messy in young nations. When politics is shorthand for origin and belonging, a spark becomes an inferno. “They’re stealing this country!” a frustrated citizen—or a bloodthirsty maniac—would scream. “End those Northerners,” another had shouted. The rhetoric had teeth.

The man who lost the contested election sat by and watched his spark create hell. An inferno that would eventually touch me.

The man across from me—well-dressed, composed—had the face of someone who’d watched the country burn

while sitting on the wrong side of the fire. “So even the rich and mighty need help once in a while?” I said, aiming for a bite.

“Yes,” he said, a sudden weight in his voice. “And, once in a while, to confess to another soul.”

“You mistake me for a priest. There are plenty, and your regime seems to think the church is where hope resides.” I couldn’t hide the snarl.

He didn’t take the bait. “Do you believe they are not working for the people?”

I sighed and opened a notebook. I can boldly say I alienated the government—or did I choose to separate myself from them? I don’t know. My views on religion were not important to anyone; I knew that.

Another file. Another rich brat unable to process the trauma of feeling alone. I am not to ignore his feelings, but out there, somewhere, sat someone who had lost it all because a neighbor turned on them. Displaced because armed men were sent to kick them off land that was as ancestral as it gets—just because they were from some other cardinal point of the compass. A child with the scar of orphanhood because the uncle they called turned on their mother when their father wasn’t around. Then the church would simply pray for healing.

Healing? That the image of the country will be healed? That the people will forget and forego revenge? That what is lost will be restored? Some gave testimonies after being shown in documentaries; the government “repatriated” them, at least some of them. Stories of lost millions and billions gone with the wind. God is sure picky, if you ask me.

“So,” I said, pen poised, “tell me about your confession, Mr....” I realized I didn’t even know his name.

“I am a witness in the case against the Four,” he said. “I’m supposed to testify in their defense.”

The Four: the radio host who whipped the crowd, the billionaire who bankrolled mayhem, the politician who stoked the killings, the general who turned guns on anyone calling for peace. Evidence stacked up like a dossier; witnesses carried scars and stories. Yet the case stalled. Two early members had been acquitted— procedural errors, witness tampering, the familiar grind of delay.

“So, you grew a conscience and can’t testify?”

I wanted to throw the question — what is your name? — at him, but it already felt like I was attacking the man.

He was the one who was supposed to be vulnerable here.

“Tell me,” he countered, his eyes sharp. “What did you lose in the violence?”

That question stung. It was a violation of the sacred space. He was interviewing me.

“Am I the client here, or are you?” I managed.

“Touché.” A ghost of a smile. “Whoever asked you that before?”

I ignored it. “What about the trial makes it so hard for you to testify?”

“Remember the organization of it all? How the bloodshed happened?”

He looked at me as if measuring my anger. I did. The screams of the nation still echoed in my nightmares. Footage of burning churches and homes. Fields full of bodies. Rivers polluted with human flesh. The stench of an amoral people, thick in the air.

There were the ringleaders, majority elected into government. Then the agitators, probably still grappling with the high cost of living.

“So, where did you stand in the great hierarchy?” I asked, not even hiding my disgust and hate.

“Nowhere! Again, I ask: what did you lose in that violence?”

I let out a sigh. He was a smart man. I bet he could see it in my eyes, the apathy and hate I held.

I still remember it all. An interview, and I would receive a police escort home. I had been paid for it—a PR stunt by a government that wanted to look like it had answers. I would talk to the nation, assure them. I didn’t know I was putting a target on my back. Sometimes I question my role in everything. I gaslit a whole nation so they’d think everything was alright when nothing was.

I remember coming home to nothing but smoke and ashes. The air was still hot with hate and anger. The silence was absolute.

My husband and daughter were part of those ashes. I remember the pain, a physical tearing, as if I’d never be whole again. No closure. Nothing. Just memories. A box of tissues appeared in my peripheral vision. He was offering me my own tissues. I never shed a tear in session. I’d heard so many sad stories, but I had never told my own.

He looked at me. Patient. Knowing. What had just happened?

“I... I don’t know what that was. I’m sorry...” I stammered, horrified at my own unraveling. I laughed, not a sound I liked.

“You asked where I sat in the hierarchy,” he circled back.

Then there are those who sat by and did nothing. Said nothing. Or even protected a neighbor.

He paused, the silence between us thick with years of unspoken horror. Guilt arrives in a dozen sharp forms.

“I should have stopped my sons and forbade them from doing what they did,” he whispered, his voice cracking for the first time. “I should have hidden your family when they came. I should have opened that door when they begged, suffocating on the other side.”

I waited for the rage to come. For the scream, the tears, the violence. I waited to feel something other than this hollow, deafening numbness.

Why? Where was my anger? It had been there a moment ago, a roaring fire. It hadn’t disappeared. It had just met something heavier. Now, all I felt was the echo of my own

screams in a burning house, and the crushing weight of a silence I had mistaken for peace. I had sat across from dozens of people and held their grief like it was fragile glass; I had never let mine break in front of anyone. I had been the expert on wounds I would not show my own child. The irony pressed down on my chest.

When Jesus said, “Let he who is without sin cast the first stone,” He saw a world where we would always perceive the sins of others as heavier than our own.

There was a silence as we stared at each other. The air in the room had changed. It was no longer therapist and client, or victim and perpetrator. Just two sinners.

He looked down, guilty and small beside me. I looked at him—at us—at what we had failed to do and what we had done.

“Why after all these years?” I asked, my voice breaking.

He didn’t look up. “I couldn’t live like that. Knowing I made a mother live her worst nightmare.” A pause. “You lost everything that day. I lost my humanity.”

The country was still trying to stitch itself back together— reparations announced on paper, apologies read on camera, a public insistence on hope. Grief lingered like a scent you couldn’t scrub out, a reminder that we had been each other’s enemies.

“Do you forgive yourself?” he asked softly. “For all those interviews? For what you said?”

I shook my head. No. If I had made them aware, if I hadn’t blinded them with false assurances, maybe they would still be alive. The guilt was a mirror I refused to look into, yet there it was every morning. The thought lodged in my throat like a stone.

“I never do,” I whispered. “I look in the mirror and ask myself: What did I become? Was I a healer, or just part of the machinery that broke them?”

Silence settled between us. Where does anyone go after this?

He leaned forward, the distance between therapist and patient dissolving completely, and for the first time, I saw something other than guilt in his eyes. Purpose.

“This isn’t about me,” he insisted, his voice trembling with urgency. “I came here because I wanted you to heal. Who ever asks you how you are? Who checks on the one holding everyone else together?”

“No one,” I admitted, the tears finally spilling over. “I am the therapist.”

“And who heals the healer?” he asked.

We sat with that truth. The healer who never healed. The voice of reason who had never spoken a single kind word to herself. The woman who guided others through grief while drowning in her own.

And for the first time since the smoke cleared, I let someone see me. Not the professional. Not the voice on television. Just a woman who had lost everything and never stopped running from the hole it left behind.

“I was paid to be the voice of calm,” I said. “A PR face for a government that needed the public to breathe. I helped them forget their fear for a while—until the fear turned to flame.”

His eyes were level, not accusing so much as honest. “And what did that do to you?”

“It put a target on my back,” I said. “And later, ash on my hands.”

We sat in the small quiet that follows confession, not because anything was solved, but because something had been named.

“What will you do now?” he asked.

I thought of doors I hadn’t opened, of the little acts that could have shifted a life. I thought of the many times I had chosen a tidy narrative over a messy truth.

“I don’t know,” I admitted. “Maybe living is the work. Maybe silence is its own kind of wound.”

He reached for the tissue box again and offered me a square. I took it like a treaty—small, fragile, necessary.

Maybe healing didn’t mean becoming whole. Maybe it meant learning to carry the pieces without cutting yourself on their edges.

Maybe, just maybe, it started with someone finally asking: How are you? After the stir of the storm. I watched him walk away, then closed the door and leaned against it. We faced only one small thing: the cost of being human in a time of catastrophe. It was not consolation. It was work— unfinished, enormous, and ours. But for now, in the silence, I let myself feel it.

chapters.title: The Shade of Kindness
chapters.text:
A LOVE STORY

No one was going to appear by a window and undo this for her.

She powdered her face, pressing gently under the eye where the skin was still tender. Tonight was going to be special — she had decided that this morning, the way you decide something so you don’t have to feel the alternative. She wore his favourite dress, the deep green one he’d told her once made her “worth showing off.” She had chosen to forget what happened the previous night. The red-shot eye would get the story that it itched, that she’d rubbed it too hard in her sleep.

She sighed and looked into the mirror. The woman looking back was tired in a way powder couldn’t fix.

Then he walked in, holding a dirty shirt.

“Why didn’t you wash this?”

“I thought you’d prefer the other one. This one has lipstick stains and coffee stains,” she explained meekly.

“Are you questioning me?” His voice dropped into that low register she’d learned to fear more than shouting. “When I tell you to wash a shirt, you wash it. Heard me?”

He crossed the room and punched her in the eye.

She caught the edge of the dresser before she fell. For a moment the pain folded itself into last night’s pain, indistinguishable, one long ache with no seams — the same hand, the same silence afterward, the same excuse waiting on her tongue before she’d even chosen it. It itched. I rubbed it too hard. She straightened, touched up the concealer with a hand that had gone very steady, the way it always did once the worst part was over.

They still went to the gala. He insisted. People needed to see them together, needed to see the version of him that shook hands and laughed at the right moments. She wore his dress and his bruise and his smile, and stood near the window while he worked the room.

He’d been gone twenty minutes when she felt someone beside her.

“You look like you’re somewhere else,” a voice said.

She turned. He wasn’t extraordinary to look at — dark suit, no tie, an easy stillness to him, like he wasn’t in a hurry to be anywhere else. He held out a glass of water, not champagne.

“I am, usually,” she said, surprised into honesty.

“Where do you go?”

She almost gave him the itchy-eye answer out of habit. “Nowhere good.”

He didn’t wince or reach for her hand or ask what happened to her eye. He just nodded, like she’d told him the weather, and said, “Tell me something that has nothing to do with there. Anything. The most useless fact you know.”

She laughed — surprised out of her, a real one, the kind she used to have before she learned to keep her face small. “Octopuses have three hearts. Two of them stop when they swim. So swimming exhausts them. They’d rather crawl.”

“Sounds like most people I know,” he said, and she laughed again.

They talked for a long time. He asked questions and then actually waited for the answers. He noticed when her glass

was empty and never made her ask twice. When she said something clumsy, he let it stay clumsy instead of filing it away. Her shoulders, which she realised she’d been holding near her ears for longer than she could remember, came down.

“What if no one ever loves me like this?” she asked, before she could stop herself.

He looked at her for a moment. “Maybe that’s the wrong question.”

“What’s the right one?”

“Maybe it’s who has to love you like this first.”

She didn’t have an answer. He didn’t seem to need one. He reached over and tucked a strand of hair behind her ear — light, unhurried, the gentlest touch she could remember receiving — and for once her whole body didn’t brace for what usually came after a hand near her face. Nothing came after. Just his smile, a little sad now, like he already knew something she didn’t.

“I should go find my husband,” she said eventually, though she didn’t move.

“I’ll be here,” he said.

She stepped away to find a waiter, to ask for another water, and when she turned back to the window to point him out,

to finally say this is who I’ve been talking to, there was no one there.

“Excuse me,” she said to the waiter passing with a tray. “The man I was just standing with — did you see where he went?”

The waiter glanced at the empty space by the window, then back at her, polite and faintly confused. “I haven’t seen anyone standing with you all night, ma’am. You’ve been by that window alone since you arrived.”

She didn’t argue with him. She walked to the restroom, locked the door, and looked at herself for a long time.

He had never existed. He was every kind word she had gone without, assembled into a shape she could stand next to for twenty minutes. She had built him so precisely because she knew exactly, down to the smallest gesture, what she wasn’t getting.

She let herself grieve him. It only took a minute — he had never been real, and missing him anyway felt almost embarrassing, except that nothing about being that hungry for kindness should ever have to feel embarrassing.

Then came the harder thought, the one that didn’t dress itself up as heartbreak: she had spent years believing

that being wanted — by anyone, even by something she’d invented — was the same thing as being safe. It wasn’t. No one was going to appear by a window and undo this for her. She was going to have to want herself enough to leave, because wanting someone had never once been the problem. Needing someone, any someone, to feel whole — that had been the leash the whole time, longer than any bruise.

He was quiet in the car home, which had always frightened her more than the shouting. In the house, he set his keys down and said, without turning around, “You embarrassed me tonight. Standing over there talking to yourself like that.”

“I wasn’t talking to myself,” she said. Then, because it no longer mattered whether that was true: “I’m leaving.”

He turned. “You’re what?”

“I’m leaving. Not tonight, maybe not this week. But I’m leaving.”

He laughed, short and ugly. “You’ve got nothing. No money I don’t know about, no one who’d take you in, nowhere to go. You’ll be back inside a month.”

“Maybe,” she said. “But I’ll find out as myself. Not as whoever you’ve been shaping me into.”

He crossed the room fast and closed a hand around her wrist, and the old fear rose up whole, the way it always had. But underneath it now was something that hadn’t been there earlier that night — something load-bearing. She didn’t wait to see which one would win. She pulled free, and it cost her something, a small tear at the skin, one more bruise for the mirror to catalogue. She kept walking.

“You’ll be back,” he called after her, his voice cracking on the last word.

She didn’t answer. She didn’t need him to be wrong immediately. She only needed to keep walking, out the door, down the driveway, until his voice became one more thing behind her instead of the only thing in the room.

The night air was ordinary — no window light, no soft piano, nothing built to order for her. Just cold, and streetlight, and her own two feet on the pavement, moving.

For the first time in three years, ordinary was enough. It was enough because it was real, and because, finally, so was she.

Enough is not an ending. It is the door she finally opened from the inside.

chapters.title: What Is Not Written
chapters.text:
A T E S T I M O N Y

Is it also written that a people’s gods should be called devils before they’re even named?

By the time Hewitt reached the fig tree, the red dust had already climbed past his boots, dyeing the hem of his cassock the color of old rust — a resemblance he had learned, mercifully, to stop noticing.

He set his Bible on the flat stone the elders used for oath- taking, a use he had never once asked about, and looked out at the crowd gathered in the shade of the mugumo. They were Kikuyu, mostly, though a handful of Akamba traders had drifted in from the lower slopes, drawn by rumor of the white man’s stories — the one who walked on water, who fed thousands from a boy’s lunch, who forgave the men who killed him. Hewitt had baptized eleven of them in the river the week before, cupping the brown water over bowed heads, telling each of them they

were new creatures now. He believed it every time he said it. He had learned not to ask why the belief never seemed to travel with him past the riverbank.

“It is written,” he said, thumb pressed into the page though he no longer needed to read it, “that man shall not live by bread alone.” His Swahili still carried the flat vowels of the Yorkshire dales, and the crowd listened the way people listen to weather being described to them by someone who has never stood in the rain.

Then, from the back, a voice — unhurried, exact.

“Is it also written that your people should conquer lands in the name of your God?”

The crowd parted before she’d taken three steps, the way water parts for something that has always had the right of way through it. She had come without her rifle. That, more than anything, was what made the district officers say she was growing careless, and what made the old women say she was growing wise.

They called her Wanjiru in the villages, though the government gazettes preferred other words — bandit, agitator, the Night that Walks. She had burned three slaving stockades along the Athi in two years and freed everyone she found chained inside them. She had also, the previous dry season, hanged a caravan master from his own yoke-pole, and nobody who told that story ever

seemed sure whether they were repeating a warning or a psalm. She was not sure herself, most nights. That uncertainty was the real reason she’d come — not to accuse the missionary, though the accusations came easily, but to see if his book held an answer she hadn’t been able to find in her own.

“Is it also written,” she went on, “that a child should be taught to be ashamed of her mother’s tongue?”

“Is it also written that a people’s gods should be called devils before they’re even named?”

“Is it also written that you should empty a man’s granary and call the emptying mercy?”

She stopped an arm’s length from him.

“White man in a clergy cloak. Has your God written all of this? Or only you?”

Hewitt did not call for the two constables waiting at the mission fence, though he felt them watching him for the signal. He closed the Bible instead, keeping his thumb between the pages the way a man keeps his place in an argument he isn’t finished having with himself.

“I cannot answer for every man who has worn this collar,” he said. “Only that the ones who did what you

describe were not reading the book I read. They were reading their own reflection and calling it scripture.”

“Convenient,” she said, “that the reflection always tells you to rule.”

He had no answer for that. It sat between them, undefended, and something in her loosened slightly at the sight of a man who did not rush to fill a silence he’d earned.

That evening he found her outside the mission fence, sitting on an overturned water drum, drawing a whetstone along the curve of a panga she was not, that night, planning to use for anything but the drawing of it. He asked if he could sit. She didn’t answer, which he had learned by now to take as permission.

“You asked me something today I didn’t finish answering,” he said. “Ask it again. Just the two of us.”

She considered him a while before she spoke, the stone still moving.

“Why do you think your God is only a conquering God?”

“Because your book tells us we’re made in his image,” she said. “All of us — mine and yours both. So I look at

what your people have built with that inheritance. Roads laid on the backs of men who were told the roads would save them. Chains blessed as commerce. A boy sold twice before he’s old enough to be afraid of it properly. If that is the shape of the maker, printed onto the made, then either your God is a tyrant, or your people have spent so long worshipping their own reflection that they’ve forgotten which one they started with.”

Hewitt was quiet long enough that the fire had time to settle before he answered.

“I have wondered the same thing,” he admitted, “more nights than I have told anyone. I did not cross an ocean to build an empire. But I have eaten from its table since the day I arrived, and I have never once refused a meal on principle. That makes me a poor witness for the God I claim to represent. Perhaps the only honest thing I can tell you is that the God I believe in was crucified by an empire, not the one running it. Men have spent two thousand years getting those two confused — sometimes by accident, sometimes very much on purpose.”

She turned the panga over once, watching the last light run along its edge.

“And you,” he said. “You hang men from their own yoke- poles and call it justice. Why do you think it falls to you to dish out the penance?”

The stone stopped.

“Because no one else was there to dish it out to me.”

She said it the way a person names a fact they stopped arguing with a long time ago.

“I was twelve when the caravan came through my village. My father tried to stand in the gate, and they left him in it. My mother they took north with me, until she was too slow for the coast road, and they left her somewhere I was never permitted to look back long enough to see. I waited three years for someone to come — a district officer, a magistrate, one of your soldiers, whose whole purpose, they always told us, was ending exactly this trade. No one came. The flag that promised to end the chains was busy that season requisitioning my uncles to carry stone for a road that made the traders’ journey faster, not slower.” She set the panga across her knees. “So I stopped waiting for the penance to arrive from anywhere but my own hand. I am not telling you this so you’ll forgive me for what I’ve done since. I am telling you because you asked,

and because — for reasons I don’t yet understand — you are the first person who has asked me plainly instead of asking the rumor.”

Hewitt did not offer absolution. He understood, watching her, that it was not his to give, and that offering it anyway would have been its own small act of conquest.

“I can’t tell you you’re wrong,” he said instead. “I can only tell you what I’ve noticed, which is that the God I read about did not spend his time correcting the world’s ledger. He spent it noticing the people the ledger had already written off. I don’t know if that’s of any use to you. But I don’t think it’s nothing.”

She stood, sliding the panga back into the sling at her hip, and for a moment the firelight caught something in her face that hadn’t been there beneath the fig tree that morning — not ease, exactly, but the particular stillness of a person who has finally stopped bracing for an answer that will never come, because she has decided to stop waiting for it.

“I am not going to stop,” she said.

“I did not ask you to.”

“No,” she agreed. “You asked me why.”

She walked back into the dark toward the hills, where a caravan was said to be moving through the lower pass

before moonrise, and where children who did not yet know her name were about to learn it. Hewitt sat a long while after she’d gone, the fire burning low, the Bible closed and untouched on his knee.

He did not feel he had converted her.

He felt, for the first time since crossing the ocean, that he had been the one asked to answer for something — and that whatever came next in this country would not wait politely for either of their gods to finish deciding whose it was.

chapters.title: The Balance of It All
chapters.text:
A L E G E N D

Finished things are easy to kill.

The orb pulsed on its pedestal like something breathing — a sphere of white so total it seemed to erase the room around it. Vessa did not blink. Seven years of grammar- work, of prying apart the old hatreds between man and orc syllable by syllable, had narrowed to this single act: the last elements sliding into the light, dissolving like salt into water.

“One problem at a time,” she said, more to steady her own hands than the world.

The orb answered — brighter, then wrong. A vein of black split its surface, spreading with the deliberate patience of ink finding the grain of paper. Then, as quickly as it had come, the light swallowed it whole and burned on, serene again.

She didn’t have to turn around to know.

“It had to be you.”

Rekar stepped from the doorway’s shadow the way he always did — not sneaking, just refusing to announce himself. The North Realm’s wicked wizard, they called him, though wicked had always struck her as lazy shorthand for unwilling to lie.

“You built a cage,” he said, “and called it a covenant.”

“I built a bridge.” She rounded on him. “A single resonance, tuned so precisely that no human mind and no orc mind could hold it and still hate. That’s not a cage. That’s the end of eight centuries of war.”

“That’s a leash with excellent craftsmanship.” He nodded at the orb, unbothered by her glare. “You didn’t ask them to stop hating each other. You asked them to stop being able to. There’s a difference, Vessa, and it’s the only difference that matters.”

She wanted to argue. The trouble was that some small, treacherous part of her had already started building his argument for him, brick by brick, from the moment the

darkness had touched the light and the orb had not shattered — it had deepened.

“It lacked a balance,” she said, and hated how much the admission cost her.

“Yes.”

“That doesn’t mean you were right to force it.”

“No,” he agreed, infuriatingly calm. “It means the flaw was already there before I arrived. I only made it visible.”

She looked back at the sphere. It no longer read as a solution — solutions don’t pulse like something deciding whether to trust you. It read as a threat dressed in mercy: feel what I tell you to feel, and call it peace. She thought of every treaty she’d watched curdle in her lifetime, and they’d all failed the same way — not because the symbol was too weak, but because it was too complete. Nothing left to do but defend it, or break it.

“Say it,” Rekar said quietly. “You already know.”

“It would have worked.” Her voice was flat. “That’s what frightens me. It would have worked, and it would have been a lie that held for a generation, maybe two — right up until some orc child or some human king worked out how to resist the hum, or steal it, or smash it out of spite. And then they’d hate each other worse than

before, because now they’d remember what it felt like to have their own minds taken from them and called unity.”

“A shortcut,” he said. “Dressed as a miracle.”

“A tool,” she said, “that was never going to hold the peace for long. It does the forgiving for them. It doesn’t ask anything of them at all.”

Something in his face shifted — not triumph, which she’d braced for, but something closer to relief, as though he’d been waiting years for her to arrive here on her own feet rather than be dragged.

“So,” she said. “If not a closed sphere that finishes the argument for them — what? You’re so certain order needs chaos. Tell me what that actually builds.”

He was quiet longer than she expected. When he spoke, it wasn’t in the register of a man delivering a clever rebuttal — it was slower, more careful, like he was setting something down rather than throwing it.

“Not a symbol that resolves the argument,” he said. “A symbol that requires them to keep having it. Something that can’t be worshipped from a distance — has to be touched, tended, argued over, or it dies. You wanted to show the world they can be one thing. They can’t. They

never will be. But they can be two things that choose, over and over, to stay in the same room.”

She turned back to the orb — still glowing, still perfect, still hollow in a way she could finally name. “Not a monument,” she said slowly. “A discipline.”

“A garden needs both of you to keep it alive,” he said. “A monument only needs you to leave it alone. Guess which one they’ll actually believe in.”

She reached out — not toward the orb this time, but toward him, closing the distance that had always been half argument and half invitation. “You didn’t ruin seven years of work,” she said. “You just made it honest enough to be useless. Now I have to start over building something that can’t be finished in an afternoon.”

“Good,” he said. “Finished things are easy to kill.”

She kissed him then — not as surrender to his chaos, and not as some soft closing of the debate, but as its continuation: two forces agreeing to remain unresolved on purpose, because a peace that could be completed was never peace at all, only a countdown with better lighting.

Behind them, the orb dimmed on its own, as if it understood it had already lost the argument. Not destroyed — just

demoted. A failed first draft, cooling on its pedestal while the real work, unglamorous and unglowing, waited to be planted somewhere between the two kingdoms and watered by both sets of hands, for as long as either side cared enough to keep it alive.

That, they both understood now, was the only kind of symbol mankind and orckind could actually trust: not one that told them the war was over, but one that made the peace their problem, every single day, on purpose.

The orb pulsed on its pedestal like something breathing — a sphere of white so total it seemed to erase the room around it. Vessa did not blink. Seven years of grammar- work, of prying apart the old hatreds between man and orc syllable by syllable, had narrowed to this single…

chapters.title: Liora Amari
chapters.text:
A L E T T E R

Our light, our strength.

Hey there, future troublemaker. I’m writing this from a time before we’ve met, which feels strange to say. It’s like waiting for a main character to show up in a story you already know is going to be your favorite. I’m writing this to a stranger, which feels a little strange, but I know the moment I meet you, that won’t be the case. I know I’ll love you instantly. Completely wrapped around your tiny, probably sticky, finger.

I’ve been thinking a lot about your mom lately. When she arrived, I was only two years old myself. I was barely taller than a knee, but I remember the shift in the world when she came into it. She was small once, just like you, and I’ve had a front-row seat to her life ever since. My first memory of her was thinking, “Huh. So this is the competition.” Now, all these years later, she’s sending me a new tiny human? The

audacity. So, in a way, I’ve been waiting for you my whole life. I have watched her grow from that tiny baby into the woman she is today. Now, watching her prepare for you, I see the same magic all over again. You are the next chapter in a story I love dearly. I’ve had years of practice watching tiny humans grow into amazing people. I’m basically an expert at this point.

When I heard you were coming, I’ll be honest: my first reaction was pure skepticism. I thought it was an elaborate prank your mom was pulling.

But now, knowing you are en route, my skepticism has turned into a promise. I intend to be a constant in your life. I’m not just going to be an uncle. I’m going to be the best uncle.

Here is my official job description:

To pick you up when you fall (and maybe teach you how to fall cooler next time).

To celebrate your wins like they’re Olympic gold medals.

To jump out from behind doors and scare your mom when she walks in from work. It’s for her own good — keeps her reflexes sharp.

You are a gift we didn’t know we needed but now can’t imagine living without. I hope you will never feel alone. Not for a single second. Even when I’m not right beside you, I

will live in your imagination. I’ll be the voice in your head telling you to be brave, to laugh loud, and to take the extra cookie. Because when you inevitably do something you think is the end of the world, just know you’ve got a whole crew of us who have already done way dumber things. We’ll be there to pick you up, dust you off, and then tell you the story about the time your mom tried to give herself a haircut at age four, just to make you feel better.

I pray you always know that no matter how far you go or how old you get, you will always have a safe place in my corner.

Welcome to the family, little one. We’re ready for you.

Love, Your Uncle Bob

chapters.title: The Land
chapters.text:
Shakahola, Kilifi County · Recovered from an abandoned plot file

I never should have bought the land. The land was cheap. That should have been my first warning. I bought the land because nobody else would. That should have been enough. But there is a different kind of fear reserved for land no one will touch. Land that sits too quietly.

In Kenya, people fear many things. Debt. Witchcraft. But there is a different kind of fear reserved for land no one will touch. Land that sits too quietly. I was a man with a dream then: a retreat, quiet cottages tucked into the acacia trees, a place where Nairobi’s noise would feel like another planet. When I drove down the dusty road into Shakahola for the first time, the soil under my tyres was the colour of rusted iron, and the heat shimmered like a living thing. The air smelled of wild sage and something else, something sweet and rotten underneath, as if the ground itself was exhaling a secret.

I signed the papers in the tiny town of Malindi, in a backroom office where the walls sweated and a plastic fan chopped at the muggy air. The seller never showed—just a lawyer with yellowed eyes who slid the deed across the table with a pen that felt greasy in my hand. I asked about the history. He smiled, a tight, lipless thing. “You’re getting paradise for a thief’s price. Don’t ask too many questions, eh?” Laughter bubbled from somewhere inside him, dry as seed pods. The lawyer handed me the deed without making eye contact.

I drove the dirt road to the property alone, in the late afternoon when the light goes gold and syrupy. Red soil. Cashew trees. Baobabs standing like sentinels with their arms thrown up in alarm. The

property was vast, quiet, and beautiful in the way that some beautiful things are — distantly, almost reluctantly. Like it did not want to be looked at.

I got out of the car and stood at the edge of the tree line. The forest ahead was thick and dark even in that golden hour. No birds. I noticed this later — there had been no birds at all. Just the low, hot hum of insects and, very faintly, something else. I wrote it off as wind.

It was not wind.

The nearest village was a twenty-minute drive down a rutted track. I went the next morning to introduce myself. Good business sense — I’d need local labour, local goodwill. I found a duka run by an elderly man named Karisa, who was sitting on a wooden stool sorting dried maize when I pushed the curtained doorway aside. He looked at me the way a man looks at someone he has been expecting.

“You have bought that land,” he said. Not a question.

“I have,” I said. “I’m building a—”

“Sit down,” he said.

I sat on an overturned crate. He poured me weak tea from a thermos and set it in front of me without ceremony. He did not pour any for himself.

“That man,” Karisa began, meaning the preacher, never giving him a name,“told them they would meet Jesus if they fasted long enough.” He said it flatly. Like a man who had said it so many times the horror had worn down to a smooth, terrible fact. “They came from all over. Families. Children. They believed every word.”

I had read the news reports. I said so.

“The news,” he said, “did not capture the sounds.”

I asked what sounds. He looked at me over the rim of his thermos for a long moment. “At night,” he said slowly, “especially in the dry months — you can hear them. Praying. Deep in the forest, around two in the morning. A group of voices. Earnest. Like they are crying out.” He paused. “And sometimes — sometimes — a child. Crying for food. Calling out.” He touched his chest. “Here. It hits here.”

The tea went cold in my hand. I asked if he thought it was people still living out there.

“There is no one living out there,”he said. And that was the end of the conversation.

The former owner had not even bothered taking his belongings.

A broken lantern still sat on a table.

A Bible lay open beside it.

Its pages fluttered though there was no wind.

I remember standing there and laughing nervously.

“You’re being dramatic,” I muttered to myself.

The forest answered with silence.

I had a tent. A good one — the kind that costs too much and promises to handle everything nature can throw at it. I set it up in the clearing closest to where I planned the main lodge. I had a battery lantern, a satellite phone, a box of ugali and chicken from a hotel in Malindi. I was not afraid. I am the kind of person who tells himself he is not afraid.

The forest went dark in layers — first the canopy, then the undergrowth, then the air itself seemed to darken, as though night were a liquid being poured slowly from above. By nine o’clock I could see nothing beyond the ring of my lantern. I read on my phone for a while. Around eleven I turned the lantern off and listened to the dark.

Silence. Not normal silence either. No birds. No insects. Nothing.

I noticed this distantly, the way you notice something that should disturb you but hasn’t yet. I heard movement outside. Crunch. Crunch. Slow footsteps circling the tent. I froze. The footsteps continued. Measured. Patient. Not animal footsteps. Human.

I called out, my voice cracking. “Hello? Who’s there?”

I told myself it was probably villagers cutting through the property. Maybe thieves who had noticed someone new had arrived.

Then came the whisper.

“Brother…”

I stopped breathing.

The voice was soft. Male. Close enough to feel against my ear.

I grabbed the torch and tore the tent zip open in one motion. The beam swung out into the clearing.

Nothing. Red dirt. Baobab shadows. The blank, dark face of the forest.

I stood there in the doorway of my tent for a long time, torch shaking, the light doing nothing useful. No footprints in the dirt around the tent. No flattened grass. No evidence of anything.

“The thing about a mass grave,” the government pathologist had told the reporters, “is not the bodies. It is the personal effects. A child’s sandal. A woman’s Bible, bookmarked at Revelation.”

Morning revealed nothing. No footprints, no flattened grass where people might have stood. Just the same red dirt, the same indifferent sky. I told myself it was fatigue, the wind in the thorn bushes, my own imagination primed by the night. Yet when I paced out the area, I found a small chain half-buried in the soil—a few links of iron, rusted orange, thin enough to fit a wrist. I kicked dirt over it and pretended I hadn’t seen.

Margaret was the woman who operated a small food stall near the highway turnoff. She had lived in the area her entire life and had, she told me matter-of-factly, lost a cousin to the forest. The cousin had gone in willingly. Margaret had not known until the body was exhumed eight months after disappearance. She told me this while frying mandazi, her back half-turned to me, her voice completely level in the manner of people who have grieved so long the grief has become architectural — load-bearing, invisible.

“They chained them together so no one could crawl away for food. Mothers. Children. Husbands. When one died, the others stayed chained to the corpse until it rotted enough to slip the manacles. The preacher said it was good practice for eternity.”

I told her what I had heard the night before. She did not look surprised.

“The police officers — the ones who came to dig up the bodies — they heard it too,” she said. “Some of them refused to go in before sunrise. There was one who said he heard a man preaching. A strong voice. They searched for hours.” She flipped the mandazi. “Nothing.”

“And the journalist?” I had read something about this in an old article.

Her expression shifted, a slight tightening around the eyes. “His camera flashed by accident in the dark. The picture showed two eyes in the bush. Watching.” She set the mandazi on a plate.“He never published the photograph. He drove to Mombasa that same night and did not come back.”

I asked her what she thought it was. She gave me a long look — the kind of look that decides whether a person can handle the truth.

“I am Christian,” she said finally. “I believe in God and in rest for the dead. But those people—” She stopped. Started again. “Those people did not die peacefully. They died starving. Screaming. Chained to each other.” Her voice dropped. “There are things that happen in the

world that are so wrong, so against what God intended — I think the wrongness itself remains. Like a stain. Like a smell.” She looked into the oil. “That forest has a smell now that was not there before.”

I drove back to the property and sat in my car for a long time before I could get out. I had already bought the land. I kept telling myself ghost stories could not scare me away from an investment. People exaggerated tragedies all the time. The human mind loved turning horror into myth.

I had surveyors come. Construction engineers. I was committed; I told myself I was committed. The surveyors walked the property in a grid pattern marking drainage and elevation. One of them — a serious young man from Nairobi named Felix — came to me at lunch and said, very quietly, that he’d found something in the northeast corner. He would not tell me what. He was gone before the afternoon was out, and he did not answer my calls that evening, or the next morning, or ever.

That night I set up a camera on a tripod — flash enabled, motion trigger — pointed toward the northeast thicket. I had told myself this was rational. Evidence-gathering. The thing a sensible person does when their property is apparently being used by trespassers. I sat in my tent with the flap open and my torch in my hand and waited.

The camera triggered at 2:14 in the morning.

The flash lit the clearing white for one fraction of a second — I saw it bloom through the tent fabric and felt my heart seize before my brain could form a thought. Then darkness again. I did not go outside. I sat with the torch in my hand until dawn turned the sky from black to grey to a reluctant coral, and then I walked to the camera on legs that felt assembled wrong.

Nothing outside. The temperature dropped.

Only the trees.

The second click came a minute later.

Then the third.

Then a fourth.

Each one made with the deliberate patience of a person taking photographs.

My mouth went dry.

I stood and stepped out of the tent, torch in one hand, phone in the other. The camera was still pointed at the treeline.

The insects died. Total silence.

Then the preaching started.

Not distant. Inches behind my head.

“STARVE THE FLESH!” The roar rattled my teeth. “Deny the body until the spirit tears free!”

I spun so fast I tore muscle in my neck. Empty tent.

“You came here for purity, didn’t you? Modern Christianity is fat and comfortable. I can show you the real thing. Empty yourself. Just a little longer.” I scrambled backward, tangled in my cot, upending the lantern. The camera toppled.

The photograph on the screen stopped me cold.

The thicket was lit white and sharp in the flash. In the foreground, leaves and brush. In the midground — and this is the thing I have tried, many times, to explain away — in the midground, arranged in a loose row, a dozen figures. Kneeling. Heads bowed. The flash had caught them between blinks: pale, too still for people, their outlines blurred at the edges in a way that could have been motion, could have been the camera, could have been the way certain things resist being photographed clearly. Some were adult-sized. Some were

much smaller. And in the far left corner, where the brush was thickest — half a face. The side of a jaw. One eye, open, aimed directly at the lens.

Watching. I stared at the photograph for a long time. The rationalising engine of my brain tried, with genuine effort, to produce explanations. Pareidolia. Flash artefacts. Branches resolving into shapes because the human brain is a pattern-finding machine that cannot stop finding patterns even in nothing.

But the kneeling figures were not random. They were arranged. They were facing the same direction. And the eye in the corner was not a branch.

I deleted the photograph.

I should have left that night. I had enough. Any reasonable accounting of events would have ended there — with me on the ground outside the forest, shaking, and then with my bags in the car and the dust road unwinding behind me. But the mind that I had built over thirty-eight years was not built for retreat. It was built for acquisition, for problem-solving, for the narrative in which obstacles are temporary and persistence is virtue.

Father Omondi came at my request — a local Catholic priest, recommended by Margaret, who arrived with two younger men in black and a small case of sacramentals. He walked the property slowly, praying in a murmur, pausing at the northeast corner without being told. He stood at its edge for a long time without entering.

“The evil here is not supernatural in origin,” he said quietly, walking back toward me through the red dirt. “Or not only. It is the evil of a man — one man — who understood that faith is the most powerful and the most vulnerable thing in a human heart. He took ordinary people. Good people. People who loved God and trusted in something greater than themselves. And he told them God required

their deaths. Their children’s deaths.” He stopped. “The wickedness of that — the precise, deliberate, surgical wickedness of it — I don’t believe it simply... leaves. When a place holds that much suffering, that much misplaced devotion—” He looked at the trees. “It takes a very long time.”

One of the younger priests told me, walking back to their car, that he had felt watched from the moment he stepped onto the property. That the hair on his arms had not lain flat the entire time. That twice he had heard his name spoken in the middle of a tree line where no one stood.

Father Omondi stopped at his car door and looked back at me.“What will you do with it?”

I told him I was going to build a wellness retreat. Healing, I said. I used the word automatically, the way I had been using it for months. It sounded hollow in that air, in that light, over that ground.

He looked at me for a long moment.“You cannot build healing on a place that has not yet finished its grieving,” he said.“The ground is not ready. And I think, perhaps, neither are you.”

I drove to Mombasa, and called my lawyer from a hotel bar, and told him to donate the land to the government. To whatever memorial purpose they chose. He tried to argue figures. I told him the number did not matter.

He asked:“Did something happen out there?”

I thought about what to say. “People happened there,” I said.“A long time ago. And they haven’t finished.”

The land is still there. A chain-link fence rusts at the boundary. Flowers appear at the gate sometimes — left by people with private reasons, people who need to grieve in the right direction. The government has built nothing. I do not think they will. I stood there looking at them dusk was coming in quick.

Then a flash went off. It wasn’t my camera!

The white burst tore through the dark.

For a fraction of a second the forest was exposed.

And I saw them.

Not standing.

Kneeling.

A line of figures in the dirt facing away from me, heads bowed, backs thin as reeds, as if in prayer. Some had their arms wrapped around themselves. Some rocked slowly in place. One small body leaned against another that did not move at all.

Then the image vanished and the darkness rushed back.

I staggered, blinking hard, waiting for my eyes to adjust.

I turned. No one.

Then a whisper again, this time from inside the tent.

“Brother…”

I backed away, every nerve in me screaming. Something shifted in the tent flap. A silhouette, just for a moment. Too tall. Too thin.

Then the sound of fabric scraping as if someone had sat down on the canvas bed inside.

I ran. Not bravely. Not dramatically. I ran like a child running from a room he knows he has no business being in. The forest tore at me. Branches whipped my face. Roots caught my feet. Behind me, the dark began to fill with sound.

Voices. The praying. The hymn. The children’s voices woven through the adult ones. Closer than they had ever been. I had only run around in circles. I was back where I was.

And standing in the clearing — not kneeling this time, standing — a figure I had not seen before among the others. Taller. Facing away from me, facing the forest. Wearing what might have been a dark robe or simply a very dark shadow shaped like one.

I looked at the figure for a long time. It was the only one not praying. It was the only one not looking toward heaven. That was the thing the others had been afraid of too. I woke up breathless.

chapters.title: Nandi bear
chapters.text:
CONFIDENTIAL

No. 891 · EYES ONLY: Major-General Sir Evelyn Wood

FROM: Capt. Arthur Vance, King's African Rifles TO: Maj-Gen Sir Evelyn Wood, War Office, Whitehall DATE: 14 November 1925 LOCATION: Uasin Gishu Plateau, B.E.A. SUBJECT: Termination of Patrol Delta-7 — Archival Sealing Requested

Sir,

I need you to get me out. Not as a soldier requests reinforcement. As a man requests exorcism.

By the time this reaches your desk, Patrol Delta-7 will have officially ceased to exist. Twelve men marched into the Nandi highlands in September. I am the only one who walked out, if you can call what I did walking. I am writing this from the field hospital at Kisumu under sedation they do not know I have defeated, my hands shaking not from the cold but from the memory of what moves through those hills. You will read this as the ramblings of a man broken by fever or jungle rot. I pray you do not. I had fever, yes. I still do. But it is not the jungle sickness. It is the sickness of having seen what has no place in God’s creation.

I am not, by temperament, a superstitious man. I have crossed hostile country, buried men under artillery fire, and watched capable officers lie to themselves with admirable discipline. I write now with none of that old confidence intact. I write because London must know what we have awakened, what the locals warned us about, and what I now carry in my skull like a splinter of ice.

This is my formal request for immediate medical evacuation to a secure psychiatric facility in England. This is also my demand—and I use the word deliberately—that all records, maps, witness statements, and field notes pertaining to the Nandi Survey of 1925 be sealed under the Archival Sealing Act and removed from general circulation. Do not commission another survey. Do not send another patrol. The thing we encountered is not a zoological specimen awaiting classification. It is a judgement.

We arrived in the high country in early September with twelve men: myself, Lieutenant Devon, Engineer- Inspector Haverhill, Sergeant Aldous Briggs, Corporal Mugambi, six King’s African Rifles askaris, and our Maasai tracker, ole Lekakeny. The brief was simple— secure the old railway survey routes near Kipkabus for renewed administrative patrols. The Uganda Railway, that great iron artery, had been plagued by labour desertions and whispers of something worse than the man-eaters of Tsavo. You remember how the lions of ’98 tore apart nearly thirty souls before Patterson shot them. “Careful,” Haverhill joked when we first heard the distant mutter of Nandi war-drums,

“it could be a case like Tsavo.” He was a heavy, bluff man who collected tusks and native curios. He laughed.

I watched ole Lekakeny spit into the red dust and make a sign with his left hand—the one the Maasai use to ward off ol-kuoni, the evil that has no name.

The Nandi people, as you know, have never welcomed white men past their ridges. The Orkoiyot, their great prophet Koitalel Arap Samoei, had been shot down by our column the year before, lured to a parley and murdered. The tribe simmered. Yet it was not spears the porters feared. It was something the Nandi called Chemosit, or sometimes Chimiset. An old headman came to our fire that first week with three interpreters and no softness in his face. He did not tell us a story as men tell stories to amuse children. He spoke like a man delivering a sentence.

“You build your iron road. You cut the hills. You kill the Orkoiyot. The land remembers. It sends its teeth.”

I asked him what he meant. He looked past me into the dark.

“Do not hunt it. Do not call it. Do not mock what takes the shape of a beast and is not always a beast.”

When pressed, he muttered that the spirit of Koitalel had walked into the forest after his killing and called something from the deep hills. Something older than the Nandi, older than man. A thing that had been sleeping. It woke, he said, with the taste of a dead prophet’s curse on its tongue.

“It is an ape,” Devon said that evening, cleaning his Webley. “A giant ape, like the gorilla of the Congo. That’s all.” Mission station reports had spoken of a “Nandi Bear”—a large, fierce animal, night-ranging, with a long snout and heavy claws, sometimes walking upright like a man. Haverhill snorted. “A bear in Africa? Next you’ll tell me there are elephants in Kent.” We laughed. But I caught ole Lekakeny staring at the tree-line, his knuckles white on his spear. Maasai are not fearful men. That was the first crack in my reason.

The dread began as a sound. It came at midnight. Always at midnight. Not the cough of a leopard, nor the wet roar of a lion. It was lower—a grinding, rhythmic exhalation that seemed to vibrate through the earth itself, ascending into something between a roar and a scream, but with a quality I can only describe as purposeful. As though whatever made it was not expressing fear or hunger, but intention. As though it was announcing itself to us specifically. Our camp dogs, trained German shepherds, would whimper, tuck their tails, and press their bellies into the dirt. One morning we found two of them gone. Not dragged away—unspooled. Their spines cracked open, ribs peeled back like flower petals, skulls hollowed. The ground bore impressions in the mud: five-toed, wider than a man’s spread hand, claws gouging furrows like ploughshares. And between them, faint but undeniable, the narrow, bipedal stride of something that walked upright yet dropped to all fours when it needed speed.

On the third night, the first man died. Private Bell was on the outer watch. He was young, red-haired, fond of whistling when he was nervous. Near midnight, the whistling stopped. We thought he had gone quiet out of discipline until we heard the dog scream. Not bark—scream. The sound tore through the camp like cloth ripped over bone.

We found Bell beyond the firelight. Or rather, what remained of him. His skull was cracked clean open, the top missing as if a mason had taken a chisel to it. The brain was gone. Nothing else had been eaten. His rifle lay unfired.

Briggs vomited. Briggs, who had seen Jubaland. He walked to the edge of the treeline, vomited quietly into the ferns, then straightened and came back, and his face never quite returned to what it had been before.

I must tell you about Briggs. Sergeant Aldous Briggs of Sheffield, eleven years in the African Rifles, decorated at Jubaland, a man who could field-strip a Lee–Enfield blindfolded and held his rum ration each evening with the precise ceremony of someone who had earned it. Briggs did not rattle. Nothing rattled Briggs.

On the seventh night, Briggs rattled.

I was awakened at half past two by one of the askari who said only, “Sergeant. Come.” I found Briggs standing at the perimeter, rifle at his shoulder, pointing at absolute darkness. He was making no sound. A frightened man shouts, curses, calls out. Briggs stood in perfect, rigid silence, his whole body locked toward whatever he saw in the dark. When

I touched his shoulder, he did not look at me for a full ten seconds. When he finally turned, his face in the lamplight was the colour of old ash.

“It was watching us, Sir,” he said. “Standing at the tree-line. Just—watching.”

“What was?” I asked.

He opened his mouth. He closed it. “It was upright,” he said at last. “It stood upright. And it was big, Sir. It was very, very big.”

Haverhill insisted on hunting it. He wanted its head for his study. He took two askaris and walked into the dripping green at four o’clock, saying he’d bag whatever rascal was scaring the coolies. He never came back.

We went searching. The forest was silent—not the silence of an English wood, but a held-breath stillness that hurt the ears. We found the first askari twenty yards in, curled beneath a podocarpus. His skull was opened, the brain removed. His rifle lay unfired. We found Haverhill deeper in, beside a stream. He had been dismembered—torn apart systematically, joint by joint, as though something had worked through its rage long after the life had left him. The limbs were scattered among the ferns. His head we found wedged in a crotch of a tree, staring down at us. The scalp had been peeled forward over his face like a macerated hood.

The Maasai porters melted away that night. Every last one. Ole Lekakeny stayed. I asked him why. “Because if I run, it will hunt me,” he said. “If I stay with you, it will take you first.” A warrior’s logic. I could not fault him.

Men began to fracture. Private Ellis stopped sleeping —he’d sit by the fire, rifle across his knees, whispering to the dark. Corporal Mugambi claimed he saw eyes reflecting the lantern light: two pools of tarnished brass, set too high, too far apart. I ordered extra watches. I rationed quinine and laudanum. I told them it was wind, hyenas, Nandi raiders testing our perimeter. But the Nandi do not dismember. They do not scalp. They do not hunt for sport or for brains.

On the eighth night, it breached the camp. It did not charge. It did not roar. It simply appeared beyond the thorns, as if the darkness had folded itself into flesh. We heard a child crying—a thin, grizzling wail, unmistakably human, coming from the forest fringe. Devon insisted we investigate. “Some native brat’s got lost,” he said, pulling on his boots.

Ole Lekakeny grabbed his arm. “There is no child here,” he hissed. “Only what has learned to sound like one.”

Devon shook him off. He took two askaris and a lantern and walked out of the light. We heard him call, “Hello there! Come on, lad, show yourself.” Then the screaming began. Not the child’s. Devon’s. It rose and rose and cut off with a wet, ripping sound I will not describe. We found his torso in the morning, propped against a termite mound, the head

tilted back to show where the skull had been opened from above, the cavity scooped clean. The two askaris were never found. Only drag-marks and the same vast, clawed prints leading away toward the hill the locals call Tinderet—the place of dark spirits.

That night I heard the howl.

It split the darkness like the shriek of a damned soul forced through a throat not made for screaming. Not a lion’s roar, not a leopard’s rasping saw. It began low, a guttural grinding, and then soared up into a register that vibrated in my molars. The sheer demoniac horror of it froze me. I have heard men die in bad ways. I have heard the death-rattle of gut- shot horses. Nothing compared. The howl held words or what my reeling mind perceived as words—an echoing, mocking cadence that sounded, God forgive me, like the Nandi tongue twisted into a curse. Ole Lekakeny fell to his knees and began a prayer I did not recognise. The remaining askaris broke and bolted into the bush. I did not see them again.

It took Ellis next.

There was no struggle. A single swipe, and his torso opened like a ledger. He did not scream—he made a sound like a punctured bellows. The creature did not maul. It operated. It pinned him with one forelimb, used the other to peel back his sternum with surgical precision, and leaned in. I heard the wet crack of the skull. The sucking sound. It was feeding on the brain. Not out of starvation. Out of ritual. Out of knowledge.

Miller fired. The Martini-Henry round struck its shoulder. The thing turned its head slowly. It did not flinch. It exhaled, and the air grew thick with the stench of copper, rot, and wet pine. Then it moved. Not a charge, a glide. It cleared the fire pit in two strides. Miller’s rifle was torn from his hands. His arms came off at the elbows. He bled out staring at his own hands as if they belonged to someone else.

On the eleventh night, Briggs left the camp.

We do not know why. No one saw him depart. No scream, no shot, no sound. He was simply gone from his tent when Mugambi checked the watch change at three in the morning. We found his rifle propped against the camp table, loaded and cocked, as though he had set it down to attend to something trivial and never returned. His boots were still beside his bedroll. He walked into the Nandi forest in his bare feet and the dark, and we never found him. I ordered the camp struck at dawn without further search. I marched the five remaining men out of the hills as fast as the terrain allowed. I told myself it was a strategic withdrawal.

The truth is worse. I knew that whatever had taken Briggs wanted us to follow. The creature did not simply kill. It thought. It planned. It understood our fear and fed on it. It had begun visiting us each night, not to attack, but to remind us we were already dead. It paced the perimeter just beyond the firelight, that heavy, deliberate tread of two legs— crunch… crunch… crunch—on the dry leaves. It allowed us to glimpse the tips of those branch-like claws dragging through the dirt. At times it would stop and

stand, a dark obelisk against the stars, and simply breathe—a hot, wet panting that carried a stench like opened graves. I sat with my revolver, and I knew it was smiling. Not that I could see its face. I just knew. It was savouring my despair.

And now, Sir, I must tell you what I saw on the final night.

A violent equatorial downpour turned the forest into a churning mass of water and mud. The fire guttered and died. I was blind, soaked, fumbling for my weapons. I heard ole Lekakeny shout in Maa, then a wet, percussive impact—the sound of a man’s body being broken on something solid. His scream lasted three seconds. Then silence.

The rain stopped abruptly, as if a tap had been turned. A moonbeam split the clouds.

I saw it, not ten paces off.

It stood fully upright, water streaming from its pelt, which was patched with grey and black like a leper’s coat. Eight feet at the shoulder, shoulders slabbed with shaggy, mottled fur the colour of old rust and grave-mould. The arms hung past its knees, ending in hands—if you could call them hands, that bore claws long as my forearm, yellowed and cracked, glinting wetly, caked with matter I refuse to identify. The snout, longer than any bear’s, jutted forward like a hyena’s muzzle grafted onto a gorilla’s skull. The forehead sloped low. And from within the matted hair, two eyes found me. They did not shine green or yellow like a cat’s. They were

pits, absolute black, the kind of darkness that swallows light and gives back nothing but the suggestion of old, patient malice.

The snout swung toward me, and I saw the nostrils working, drinking my scent. The mouth beneath it was a wet gash that never fully closed. From it came a clicking—a sound like bones being counted.

Its eyes held an intelligence, a hatred so old and so personal it made me weep. This was not a beast protecting territory. This was punishment. The Orkoiyot Koitalel’s curse given flesh. Kimnyole’s vengeance. Whatever the Nandi had summoned when they killed their own prophet for cursing the land, and then watched the white man shoot his son in cold blood. I understood in that instant that the Nandi Bear was not a zoological curiosity. It was an indictment. It was the Empire’s sins made talon and fang. It took a step forward. I fired point-blank into its chest. The shot hit with a dull, sucking thud, like a stone sinking into a bog. It did not roar. It chuckled a wet, rattling sound from deep in its throat and swiped. The claws sang past my face, close enough that I smelled the copper of old blood on them. I flung myself backward and fled.

I ran. God forgive me, I ran. I crashed through the night while the bushes tore my clothes and that hideous breathing sounded at my back. I heard the others die behind me—not quickly, not cleanly. The creature herded them. It toyed with them. It let them run until their lungs burned, then dropped from the canopy or rose from the ferns, always just behind, always breathing that grinding, wet exhalation. It broke them psychologically before it broke them

physically. I heard Mugambi’s voice, still alive, begging in the dark. Then silence. Then the wet tear of flesh.

I ran until I could not run, and when I looked behind, there was nothing. Only the dripping leaves.

Here is the final cruelty, Sir. The part you must seal away and never let another man read.

As I stumbled through the grey hour before dawn, I crested a ridge and looked back. The rain had cleared. The moon was still high. On the escarpment above the tree-line, two figures stood silhouetted against the dying stars.

One was the beast—hunched, vast, its shaggy outline unmistakable. The other was a tall African man in the full regalia of a Nandi Orkoiyot: the sacred kutwet headdress, the fly-whisk of office in his hand. He stood with the calm authority of a man who had once commanded thousands. His other hand rested on the beast’s shoulder, as a master rests his hand on a favoured hound.

I know what I saw. I know what the locals mean when they whisper that Koitalel Arap Samoei walks with it. The dead prophet did not curse the land. He sent something to shepherd the curse. They watched me stumble away. They allowed me to leave. I am the lone survivor not by skill or luck, but because I was chosen to carry the story.

I reached the mission at Kaimosi three days later, starving, half-mad. They tell me I babbled about a “ghost bear” and “the prophet walking with it.” The fathers gave me water and a bed.

At 2:47 that same night, I woke to the clicking sound outside the window.

The shutters were closed, but I could smell it— copper, turned earth, a sweetness like rotted jackfruit, and the wet, septic breath I had learned to recognise in the dark of the Nandi hills. In the morning, a mission dog was found dead, its skull opened, brain removed. A calling card.

It has followed me. Sir, it has followed me. I hear it still. The clicking. The breathing. The distant, patient growl that the Medical Officer here dismisses as “auditory hallucination” because he has no other word for it. At night, always at 2:47, I hear Devon screaming. I hear ole Lekakeny’s Maa prayers cut short. I hear Briggs walking into the dark in his bare feet, his breath steady, his terror so complete it had become acceptance.

I am not mad. A madman does not bring evidence. Enclosed with this dispatch is a fragment of claw- sheath recovered from my torn tent canvas— unclassifiable keratin, fourteen inches in length, exhibiting crystalline structure unknown to any African fauna. Enclosed also is a field sketch of the footprint compared to a standard lion’s paw. Enclosed is a piece of bark found outside my tent on the sixth night, scratched with an image I did not make: a tall figure in a kutwet, hand on the shoulder of a shambling, clawed horror.

Burn them after you have looked. Do not catalogue them. Do not let them fall into the hands of cryptozoologists or adventurers. The Nandi Bear is not a discovery waiting to be made. It is a calamity waiting to be forgotten.

I request immediate medical evacuation to a secure psychiatric institution in England. I require a locked cabin aboard the next steamer to Southampton, under chemical restraint if necessary, with transfer directly to Broadmoor or any facility with no windows facing the grounds. I require that any officer who has read my previous dispatches be interviewed for sleep disturbances and, if symptomatic, isolated immediately.

I am not being histrionic. I am being precise. The beast moves through consciousness as much as through geography. It found Devon because Devon dreamed of it. It found Briggs because Briggs could no longer look away. I am now its vessel. I carry its attention like a disease.

I further request that all records pertaining to Patrol Delta-7 be sealed under the Archival Sealing Act and removed from general circulation. Do not send another expedition. Do not let another young man with a map and a rifle walk into those hills. The loss of twelve men is a tragedy. The loss of another twelve would be a crime for which I would share culpability. The Nandi hills hold their horror in silence now. Let them keep it.

I am the lone survivor. Let me be the last. I remain, by duty and by doom,

CAPTAIN ARTHUR VANCE — —

— KING’S AFRICAN RIFLES (ATTACHED COLONIAL SURVEY SECURITY) —

PENDING MEDICAL DISCHARGE — —

MEDICAL OFFICER’S ADDENDUM — —

— ATTACHED TO DISPATCH NO. 891, 15 NOVEMBER 1925 —

I, Dr. James Fraser, RAMC, hereby endorse Captain Vance’s request for emergency psychiatric evacuation. The patient was admitted to Kisumu Field Hospital in a state of extreme emaciation, acute hyperacusis, and persistent psychomotor agitation. He has not slept unassisted since arrival. He speaks in a low, level monotone, except when the hour approaches 2:47 a.m., at which point he begins to tremble uncontrollably and recites the names of his deceased companions in sequence, as if taking roll.

I am a medical man, Sir. I do not traffic in native superstition. However, I must record for the sealed file that upon examining the claw-sheath specimen, I found it to be composed of unclassifiable keratin exhibiting a crystalline structure I have never observed in any known animal. Furthermore, on the night of the 14th, while the patient was under heavy sedation in a locked ward, the orderlies and I distinctly heard from the courtyard immediately outside the patient’s window a vocalisation that

matched no known predator. It began as a low, grinding bass, ascended to a frequency that caused visible vibration in a glass of water, and terminated in a series of wet, percussive clicks. The dogs in the compound fell silent and did not bark again until dawn. At first light, we discovered a set of prints in the damp earth beside the window. They measured fourteen inches in length and displayed an opposable digit. The patient has not been told.

I am requesting, alongside the patient, my own immediate transfer from this posting. I am not a superstitious man. I am leaving because I wish to remain one.

DR. JAMES FRASER, RAMC — —
