chapters.title: Madam Koikoi
chapters.text:
Anonymous account, passed hand to hand

They told us about the baptism of fire before the term even began. A girl at the market—her sister had attended Queen’s—leaned close over a basket of bitter leaf and whispered, “When they come for you in the dark, do not make a sound. The ones who scream are the ones who get chosen.” I did not know what chosen meant then. Now I think about that word every night before sleep. It sits on my tongue like a stone.

There is a thing in Nigeria they call a ghost, but the word is too small. We have no word for what walked those halls. A ghost remembers it is dead. This did not remember, or did not care.

The seniors came on a Thursday. They always come on a Thursday, because the British matron, Sister Holford, takes her whisky on Thursday evenings and does not leave her quarters until morning. Everyone knows this. The seniors know this. Perhaps the other thing knew this too.

They lined us up in the corridor between dormitory rows, made us kneel on the cold concrete. My knees went numb. Some girls wept quietly into their palms. I pressed my lips shut and thought of my mother’s compound, the sound rain makes on zinc. The senior girls had torches. When they shone them in your face and asked you questions you could not answer correctly—who was your father, what was your totem animal, could you recite the school song backwards—they would hit your open palms with a ruler. Not cruelly. Almost boredly, which was worse.

Then we heard it. Koikoi. Koikoi.

Like a lady’s heel striking the cement floor. Slow. Deliberate. During the day it meant Madam Cole—the new English mistress—was coming to inspect our uniforms. But at night, when the generators had been silenced and only the hurricane lamps in the prefects’ corridor burned, that sound meant something else. It meant the one the seniors called Madam Koikoi.

It was not loud. That is the thing about the sound. It came from far down the corridor, from the direction of the locked east wing—the wing they told us was closed for repairs, had been closed since 1939, would be closed until funds were available from the colonial ofÏce, which we all understood to mean forever. The sound came from there. Heel on stone. Patient. Even.

You don’t hear her first. You feel her. The floorboards vibrate like a plucked wire. The air thickens. The senior girls stopped talking. I had never seen a senior girl stop talking, not for anything. One of them—Form Five Ego, who had struck my palms three times with apparent enjoyment—reached out and grabbed the arm of the girl beside her. In the torchlight her face was simply blank. The kind of blank that comes when a person’s mind steps away from what their eyes are seeing.

The sound stopped.

Then a door at the far end of the corridor—the east wing door, the one with the rusted padlock that had not been opened in eight years—clicked.

The senior girls ran. They simply turned and fled back toward the upper dormitory, torches swinging wildly. One dropped hers. It lay on the floor at the far end, still on, pointing its beam toward the east wing door, which remained closed, still padlocked from our side.

We knelt there for a very long time.

When the teacher they called Madam Koikoi came—the real one, the living one, in her knee-high boots and wool coat—I nearly wept with relief. She drove us all to bed with her cane raised. I had never been so glad to be threatened by a teacher.

I did not sleep. I lay in the dark and listened. Around two in the morning, I heard it again. Fainter this time, the way a sound gets when it moves away from you. Koi. Koi. Koi. But it was not moving away. I realized that slowly. It was the same distance. It had been the same distance. It was walking in a circle. Around the building. Around us. Patient as something that is not concerned with time.

I counted the steps. Ten, then silence. Then the sound of water dripping. Not a small drip like a leaky tap. It was a heavy splashing, the noise a body makes when it rises from a bath. I pressed myself flat under my blanket. The air grew cold and smelled of carbolic soap and something underneath—a sweetness, like overripe mangoes mixed with kerosene. The cubicle curtain, stiff with starch, began to darken at the bottom. Water was seeping in. It pooled on the cement, black in the darkness, but when it touched my mattress leg the liquid ran upwards, defying sense, climbing the iron frame in rivulets.

I could not move. My throat had locked.

The curtain pulled itself aside, one brass ring screaming on the rail. And I saw her.

She was beautiful. That was the worst part. Her face was composed, the lips painted that bleeding red, her cheeks rubbed with camwood. She wore a dark blue blouse and a pencil skirt, and over it a teacher’s coat, dripping. Her hair was braided into a high crown, threaded with white cowries that glowed like tiny moons. But her eyes—her eyes were not eyes. They were holes. In the dark of the sockets, water churned, deep and grey, with things moving inside. She had no cane. Instead, her right hand ended in a long, swollen stick of flesh, ridged like bamboo, and she pointed it at my face. Her left foot was naked. The toes were smashed, the nails peeling back, and around the ankle was a wound that would not close, pouring a clear, endless liquid.

She leaned close. Her mouth opened, and water, cold and rank, dribbled onto my cheeks. She spoke, but the voice did not come from her throat. It came from the bucket, from the drains, from the wet slap in the laundry shed a hundred yards away.

“Where is my heel? You have it, yes? Every junior has a piece of it. Give it back or I will take your feet.”

I could not speak. She kept pointing. The stick tapped my ankle, and my foot immediately went dead, a cold like deep well-water spreading up my calf. I heard the prefects’ bell ring for morning inspection and she dissolved—not like a person leaving, but like a reflection swallowed when the water is disturbed. I was left with a wet bed and a left foot I could not feel until midday. The matron called it hysterical paralysis. But she did not see the mark: on my sole, a faint circle of red, the exact diameter of a woman’s heel.

I want to say first that I did not put her there. I want that recorded. I want Father Okeke to write that down in his good handwriting so that it is there for whoever reads this later. I did not put her there and I did not know she was there and I do not know how long she had been there.

She was under my bed.

I found her on a Friday morning in the third week of term. I had dropped my pencil box and it rolled under the bed and when I crouched to get it I found myself looking at a face. A woman’s face, turned toward me, eyes open. For a moment—perhaps three full seconds—I thought she was simply resting. The way the face was arranged. Peaceful. Red lipstick perfectly applied. Hair pinned and correct. One arm outstretched along the floor as if she had reached for something in her sleep.

She was wearing a red dress. It was pressed and clean and the hem had no dust on it. She had red heels on her feet. One heel was cracked clean across— not broken off, but cracked, a neat fracture through the heel block—and she was wearing them still, wearing a broken heel, and both her feet were together and straight as a soldier’s, and she did not breathe.

She smelled of roses. Not death. Roses.

A body that has been dead even twelve hours in this heat—you would know it. This smelled of roses. We kept checking that it was real. Touching the cold hand and then smelling roses and then looking at each other.

I screamed. My dormitory-mates came. We looked at her together. Someone went to fetch Sister Holford. The British matron came down in her dressing gown—it was only seven in the morning—and looked under the bed and looked at us and said, “Well, you must have done something to deserve a punishment like this,” which is a sentence I have rolled around in my mind for many years since and still cannot fully explain. Then she sent a house girl to the village for the constables.

The two constables came at half past eight. By that time all of Block A was gathered in the corridor outside my cubicle. The constables went in. I heard them talking to each other quietly. I heard one say “ah ah.” Then one came out and told us to go to assembly immediately. His face was doing something that faces are not really designed to do.

At noon, they came to tell me that there was nothing under my bed. No woman. No red dress. No broken heel. No roses. The floor was dusty as if nothing had touched it. One constable suggested I had an overwrought imagination. Sister Holford agreed. Fourteen girls had seen the body. Not one of them contradicted the constables in front of authority.

That night I could not sleep in my cubicle. I slept on the floor of the dining room wrapped in my uniform coat. The following morning my bed was made. I had not made it. No one admitted to making it. The sheets were folded with the hospital corners the teachers required—sharply, precisely—and on the pillow there was a single red petal.

This happened every morning for eleven days. I would refuse to touch the bed. In the morning, made. Hospital corners. One petal. One morning the petal was still wet, as if it had been placed there moments before I came in. I was the first person in the room. I had been watching the door from the corridor. The door was the only entrance to the cubicle. No windows. I watched that door and then I went in and the bed was made and the petal was wet.

On the twelfth morning there was no petal. Only a smell of roses that lingered until midday, when it simply was not there anymore, and the bed was not made, and there were two long marks in the dust at the side of the bed as if something had lain there and risen and walked to the window and through it, though the window was twenty feet above the ground and latched from the inside and was still latched when I checked it, which I did immediately, with both hands, twice.

I stopped trying to run. I stopped trying to scream. I understood then what the market girl meant. The chosen are not the loud ones. The chosen are the quiet ones who learn to carry the weight without buckling. The baptism of fire was never about fire. It was about drowning. It was about learning to hold your breath while the water rises past your nose, past your lips, past your mind.

Last night, the sound returned. Koikoi. Koikoi. It did not circle the building this time. It stopped outside my cubicle. The curtain did not pull aside. Instead, a single red heel slid beneath the door. It was cracked. Cleanly. Across the middle. It sat on the cement like an offering. Like a key.

I picked it up. It was cold. It fit perfectly in my palm. And when I closed my fingers around it, I felt the water rise again, but this time it did not drown me. It filled me. It settled in my lungs. It cooled my blood. I looked at my left foot. The red circle was no longer a mark. It was a footprint. Mine.

This morning, I woke before the bell. I did not wait for the matron. I stood at the end of the corridor, alone. I wore my dark blue blouse. I wore my pencil skirt. I threaded white cowries into my hair. I painted my lips the colour of a fresh wound. And when the juniors lined up for inspection, trembling on the cold concrete, I raised my cane. I did not strike them. I only tapped it once against my thigh.

Koikoi.

The sound echoed down the hall. From the east wing. From the drains. From inside my own ribs. I did not feel the cold anymore. I do not remember the water. I only know the rhythm. And I know what to do when they come for me in the dark.

I will not make a sound.

The ones who scream are the ones who get chosen.

I am already chosen.

I am already walking.

Koikoi. Koikoi. Koikoi.

chapters.title: Tulimū
chapters.text:
As told at the edge of the fire, where the dark can hear but not see

The Kamba have stories they do not tell loudly. They are the kind of stories meant for the edge of a fire, where the darkness can hear but not quite see. They speak of the tulimu—small demons, not witches. Not spirits. Not quite men, not quite anything that should be seen by the living.

The house had always breathed differently at night. I never noticed it during the day — not when the workers moved through the rows of maize, not when Musembi dragged the feed buckets across the yard, not when my mother’s voice carried from room to room ordering the world into her preferred arrangement. But at night, alone, I could feel it. The inhale of wind through the gaps in the window frames. The slow exhale of the old timber walls settling. The house breathing like something that had been waiting for everyone else to leave.

I was twenty-three. I thought I was too old for fear. I was alone in it, charged with guarding my mother’s estate—a sprawling colonial-era farmhouse that sat like a broken tooth in the jaw of an overgrown shamba. The workers had all gone home to their families. The storm came not as a blessing but as a punishment, cracking the sky open with sheets of lightning so frequent that the world outside strobed between black and bleached bone.

My mother had called me on a Thursday.

“Mwanake. I need you to go to the estate.” Not a request. With her it never was.

She was travelling to Mombasa for a church retreat — something about spiritual warfare and the laying of hands — and the estate needed watching. Three days. Just me and the house and forty acres

of Kambaland stretching into acacia forest. Musembi had locked up the chickens. The dogs knew the property. There was a backup generator in the kitchen if the lights went. Simple. The clouds were already building in the west, bruised and heavy, dragging their bellies low over the hills. By the time I turned off the murram road and through the gate, the first lightning had already begun — silent at that distance, just a pale flickering behind the treeline, like something enormous turning a light on and off in an empty room.

I remember thinking: the acacias look like people standing very still.

The house smelled of my mother. Red earth and camphor and the particular mustiness of old Kikamba Bibles left on shelves too long. I moved through each room the way she’d asked — checking windows, checking doors, making sure the world was in its proper place. Her bedroom. The store with its sacks of maize. The sitting room with its doilies and framed scriptures and the one bookshelf where she kept everything she considered worth reading.

I picked one at random. Something in Kikamba — a collection of old narratives, the kind she used to read aloud when I was small, back when evenings meant sitting at her feet and learning which neighbours were to be pitied and which were to be feared.

I remember she had a particular voice for the Tulimū stories.

Not frightened. Careful.

“They are small,” she would say. “Not like a child — nothing innocent about them. Small the way a very old thing becomes small. They come and sit. They stitch. They rock.” She would demonstrate the rocking, forward and back, forward and back, a rhythm like a heartbeat slightly off. “You must not call out to them. You must not let them know that you have seen them.”

I had asked her once what they did, beyond the sitting and stitching.

She had looked at me with that particular expression — the one that meant the answer existed but was not for me to have yet.

“Nothing good,” she said.

By nightfall the clouds had swallowed the moon. Lightning kept opening the sky in white cracks, and each flash made the house seem to change shape. One moment it was familiar. The next it looked too tall, too narrow, its windows like blind eyes staring into the black field.

Musembi and the hands had gone home before the first thunderhead bruised the sky. By dusk, the wind had turned feral, tearing through the acacias like claws on corrugated tin. I walked the halls, checking locks, windows, the generator switch in the kitchen. The house felt hollow, but not empty. It breathed. Floorboards sighed under my weight.

With no television and no company, I sat in the sitting room with one of my mother’s books on my lap, pretending to read. The language was easy enough when spoken, but on the page it became a puzzle of old words and formal phrases. My eyes moved across the lines without holding on to them. I listened instead.

The silence in a rural house is never truly silent.

The lights died at half past ten.

Not a flicker. Not a warning. Just: darkness. The complete and total kind that only exists in the countryside, where there are no streetlights, no distant glow of a town on the horizon, nothing between you and the full weight of an overcast night.

The solar security lights outside snapped on — thin and pale, throwing more shadow than light — and I sat for a moment letting my eyes adjust.

Outside, the dogs began to bark.

I went to the window. The two of them — old Simba and the younger one my mother called Wathina — were moving strangely within the radius of the security light. Not barking at the fence, not barking at the treeline. Barking at the air in front of them. Snapping at nothing. Pivoting sharply as though tracking something fast and low to the ground, something that kept changing direction. Wathina lunged sideways and her teeth clapped shut on empty darkness.

I told myself it was the lightning. Animals go strange in storms. Everyone knows this.

I remembered my mother’s voice.

Dogs see what you do not see.

She had said it once when I was younger and had asked why the dog kept staring at the hallway.

I had answered, It sees a rat.

My mother had looked at me for a long moment and said, Or it sees something wearing the shadow of a rat.

I went to find the generator switch.

I should have brought my torch. I knew where it was — bedside table, second drawer — but I’d been certain I wouldn’t need it, the way you are always certain of the things that will later undo you. The hallway from the sitting room to the kitchen was perhaps fifteen metres. Fifteen metres of darkness that felt, in the walking of it, considerably longer.

The chickens had begun.

The coop was on the far side of the house and I could still hear them through the walls — that frantic, layered clucking that means something is very close and they are very aware of it. Not the drowsy shifting of birds disturbed by noise. This was alarm. Every bird in

that coop crying out at once, the sound rising and tightening until it became almost like screaming, if screaming were a thing with feathers.

I stopped walking.

The kitchen was ahead. I could see the faint oblong of the back door — open, which it should not have been, which Musembi should have secured, which I should have checked — and through it the weak grey light of a sky full of lightning not yet arrived.

There was someone sitting in the doorway.

Low to the ground. Hunched. The shape of it was wrong in a way I could not immediately name — not wrong like an intruder, not wrong like a person where a person shouldn’t be, but wrong in some more fundamental sense, like a word you’ve read so many times it stops looking like a word. The proportions were off. The thing was small in a way that had nothing to do with being young.

It was moving. A slow, rhythmic rocking. Forward. Back. Forward. Back.

And its hands — I could hear it before I could see it properly — its hands were doing something. A soft, regular sound. Like thread being pulled taut. Like teeth on a needle. The lightning came then. One long, world-splitting flash that threw the kitchen into total white relief for perhaps half a second.

Half a second was enough.

I will not describe what I saw in detail. I have tried to find language for it and the language doesn’t hold — it slides off the memory the way water slides off a stone, and I think perhaps that is a mercy. What I will say is this: its face was turned away from me, and even so, even in that white half-second, I had the absolute certainty that it

knew I was there. That it had known since I entered the hallway. That the rocking had not changed rhythm when I stopped walking because it did not need to react to me. It was not afraid of me.

It was waiting to see what I would do.

I spoke.

I don’t know why I spoke. Every story my mother ever told me, every careful word of her warnings, and still I opened my mouth.

“I thought I told you to go home.”

The rocking stopped.

For a moment nothing in the world moved. Not the air. Not the shadows. Even the chickens went silent, all at once, like something had pressed a hand over every beak.

Then it turned.

I did not see its face. I want to be precise about this — I did not see it because the lightning had already gone and the darkness was back and my eyes were not adjusted. What I saw was the turning, the movement, the wrongness of the proportions shifting. The figure gave a thin sound, almost a laugh, almost a cough, and then it moved.

Not standing.

Not rising.

It simply slid backward across the floor, too quickly and too smoothly for a human body, and vanished through the open back door as if the darkness outside had opened to let it in.

The last night was the worst, though it didn’t feel like horror in the moment. That came later. That came in the replaying.

I saw it at the front door just past midnight. I was sitting in the sitting room with every light I could find burning — candles, a kerosene lamp I’d dug out of the store — and I heard something on the veranda. A soft, repetitive sound. The sound of thread being pulled taut.

I did not go to the door. My mother’s voice in my head: do not let them know that you have seen them.

But I looked through the window.

It was sitting against the front step. Its leg — one leg, just the one — extended forward into a small fire that burned without any wood beneath it, and above the fire a small pot was going, and steam rose from it in the lightning-light. And it was stitching. Rocking forward and back. Pulling thread through something dark in its lap, something I could not and did not want to name. The rhythm of it was so regular it became, over time, almost soothing. Forward. Back. Forward. Back.

It did not look at the house.

It did not look at me.

It just stitched, and rocked, and let the leg burn, and the pot boiled, and I sat on the inside of the glass and watched it work and could not look away and could not move and did not call my mother because I knew — I knew — that if I made a sound, if I gave any sign that I was there, it would turn around.

And this time the lightning might not save me from seeing what was in its face.

Then another lightning flash came.

The thing in the doorway was stitching my mother’s name into the mat.

Slowly. Neatly. Carefully.

When it felt me standing there, it paused.

Its head turned a fraction.

Not enough to look at me fully.

Enough to let me know it had known I was there all along.

Then, as my mother had said in every story, it ran.

Not away from the house.

Into it.

It disappeared through the front door as if the wood were only smoke. The house went quiet. I listened for something, anything. I left that morning and I have never spent a night there since.

The dogs never came back. I asked Musembi about them a week later, and he said they had found Simba near the fence the following Monday — not dead, just sitting there, staring at the treeline with an expression he could not describe and did not want to. He said the dog refused to eat after that. He said the dog had stopped barking entirely.

“Stopped barking at what?” I asked.

Musembi looked at me for a moment.

“At everything,” he said. “At anything. It doesn’t bark anymore. It just watches.”

I have not asked about Wathina.

My mother called me the week after. She’d heard something from Musembi, I think, or perhaps she simply knew the way she always knew things about that land and what moved through it at night.

“Did anything happen?” she asked.

I thought about the back door. I thought about the sound of thread being pulled taut. I thought about the leg in the fire and the pot and the boiling and the rhythmic, patient rocking — forward and back, forward and back — and the way it had not looked at the house.

The way it had not needed to.

“Nothing happened,” I said.

chapters.title: Kanungu
chapters.text:
S P E C I A L E D I T I O N · C O N T I N U E D I N S I D E

Kanungu District, Uganda

The first thing anyone tells you about Kanungu, before they tell you about the fire, before they tell you about the church or the bodies or the smell, is that the hills here are beautiful. They rise in smooth green waves above the valley, eucalyptus forests trembling in the highland wind, and on a clear morning you can look east and feel, briefly, that the world is made of nothing but grass and light and birdsong.

That was the first lie the place told me.

I arrived on March 16, a full day before the anniversary, because I wanted to see it fresh: the compound’s scorched footprint, the chapel’s concrete ribs still clawing at the sky, the pit latrines where they found the ones who didn’t burn. A local stringer named Asiimwe meets me by the rusted gate. He doesn’t shake hands. He just nods toward the valley and says, “Tomorrow at six, you’ll understand.”

One old man at the roadside did not greet me. He only touched two fingers to his throat and looked away, as if warning me not to ask the wrong questions too loudly.

An old woman named Esther, said to me within twenty minutes of my arrival, before I had even unpacked my recording equipment.

“You should go back. You should go back tonight. Because at six o’clock, when that smell begins, you will understand something about this place that cannot be ununderstood. And you will carry it home with you. And it will never fully leave.”

I had come as a reporter to gather facts. Names. Dates. Numbers. The kind of things newspapers print when the rest of the world wants a tragedy turned into a square, manageable box.

I’ve covered war, famine, the kind of grief that calcifies into ritual. But Kanungu is a wound that refuses to scab.

Every horrific nightmare needs an architect. The Movement for the Restoration of the Ten Commandments of God had two.

JOSEPH KIBWETERE — —

“The Father” — Born: Rukungiri District, Uganda, approx. 1932

Before the visions, he was the kind of man who appears in church newsletters. Respectable. A former headmaster and local government ofÏcial. Catholic. A husband, a father of several children. Neighbors from his earlier life describe a man who wore his faith like a well-ironed shirt — presentable, deliberate, something you admired from a distance. The kind of man who always knew the correct answer and always wanted you to know that he knew it.

The visions came in 1984. Or so he claimed. The Virgin Mary, he said, appeared to him and delivered a message: the world was corrupt beyond redemption. The Ten Commandments had been abandoned. The end was coming, and God was angry. He began speaking of it in whispers at first, then louder. His diocese grew concerned. His bishop distanced the Church from him. His wife and children, in the years that followed, became increasingly estranged. He was, by the early 1990s, a man who had walked away from everything real in pursuit of something he could not prove. What those who knew him before cannot reconcile is how ordinary his dissolution was. He did not arrive at Kanungu as a monster. He arrived as a disappointed man who had mistaken his disappointment for divine revelation.

But Kibwetere was not the engine of the Movement. He was its face. Its flag. Its collateral dignity — the respectable former headmaster whose name lent the organization gravity. The engine was someone else entirely.

CREDONIA MWERINDE — —

“The Programmer”— Born: Kanungu District, Uganda, approx. 1952

She had been a bartender. She had sold waragi — the local gin — from a roadside establishment, and had, according to multiple sources, also sold herself. This is not a judgment; it is the texture of the life that made her. She was a woman who had lived close to the floor of things, who had learned, through necessity and through watching men, exactly how power worked, exactly how want could be shaped and exploited. She was, by all accounts, uncommonly intelligent. Charismatic in a way that was not warm but magnetic — the charisma of someone who knows exactly what you need before you have named it. Her own visions, she claimed, also began in the 1980s. The Virgin Mary again. The same message. When she met Kibwetere and recognized in him something she could use — the legitimacy, the Catholic credentials, the name — the partnership was, in retrospect, inevitable.

She became “The Programmer.” It was the title the Movement gave her. She controlled information. She controlled access. Members who had questions — about doctrine, about the End, about their duties — wrote them on slips of paper that were passed to Mwerinde. She wrote back. No one questioned her answers. By the mid-1990s, she was not merely controlling the Movement. She was the Movement, operating behind the wooden face of Kibwetere’s authority the way a puppeteer crouches behind a screen.

What happened to her — what turned a woman who had merely survived a hard life into something capable of what occurred on March 17, 2000 — remains, to me, the most frightening unanswerable question in this entire story. She was seen leaving Kanungu on the morning of the fire. She has never been found.

Around Mwerinde and Kibwetere, they gathered others. Priests who had been dismissed from the Church. Nuns whose vows had been revoked. People already estranged from institutional faith, already angry at the ofÏcial Church that had cast them out, who found in the Movement both a cause and a revenge.

FATHER DOMINIC KATARIBABO — —

Defrocked priest. PhD graduate. Believed to have been the Movement’s theological architect.

He is the one who disturbs me most, perhaps because he is the one I understand least. A man with a doctoral degree who chose this. Who took the scaffolding of genuine Catholic theology and used it to build something that locked five hundred people inside a burning room. His charred body was found at the entrance of the church, his dog collar fused into the skin of his neck by the heat. He either died with them, or he was disposed of — another question no one has answered. What I keep returning to is the collar. What does it mean that even in death, even burned, he wore the collar? Was it faith? Was it theater? By the end, had he ceased to distinguish between the two?

SISTER URSULA KOMUHANGI — —

Former nun. Role: Discipline and member compliance.

Survivors describe her as the one who enforced silence. Who walked the dormitories at night. Who assigned penances. One woman I interviewed — who had left the Movement in 1998 and requested her name be withheld — described being made to recite the rosary one thousand times as punishment for whispering to another member without permission. “Sister Ursula would stand over you while you counted,” she said. “She never blinked. I used to think she did not need to sleep. I still believe that.” Her fate remains unknown.

To understand what happened on March 17, 2000, you must first understand the years that preceded it. The slow architecture of control. The way a life can be dismantled so gradually that the person living it never feels the walls going up.

The compound at Kanungu was not a prison, in the conventional sense. People arrived voluntarily. They brought their families, their savings, their faith. They surrendered their possessions upon arrival — this was framed as spiritual discipline, as liberation from material attachment. They were assigned dormitories, separated by sex. They were given identification numbers. They were issued identity cards.

They were told not to speak.

The silence was not incidental. It was the first and most important instrument of control. In silence, the mind turns inward. In silence, the voices of leadership — delivered through Mwerinde’s written pronouncements, through sermons, through the endless repetition of prayer — become the only voices. One former member, a man named Francis who now farms on the edge of the district, described it to me this way:

“You stop hearing your own thoughts after a while. Or you start to think that your thoughts are sin. Because you have been told — every day, in the morning prayer, in the evening prayer — that your natural mind is corrupt. That anything you want is the devil speaking. So you stop trusting yourself. You trust the leaders. You think you are becoming holy. You do not understand that you are becoming nothing.”— Francis Murungi, former member (left Movement 1997)

When members needed to communicate with each other, they used signs. A hand gesture for water. A particular look for hunger. Permission to speak had to be requested in writing and was rarely granted. Children who grew up in the compound, sources tell me, sometimes arrived at adulthood with speech difÏculties. Their mouths had simply not been used.

Field Note — Ochieng, April 3, 2001I have been having trouble sleeping. I keep thinking about the children. There were children in that church. The police reports list no specific count of how many were minors. I have asked three times. I have not received an answer. I am beginning to suspect there is no answer anyone is willing to give me.

The pilgrimage was the other cornerstone. A steep, treacherous hike through the eucalyptus forest to a rocky hill nearby, where a formation of stone had been designated as the face of the Virgin Mary. Members made this climb regularly, some in bare feet as acts of penance. The terrain was unforgiving — sharp rock, loose soil, the kind of path that punishes the body, that makes you bleed. This, too, was intentional. Pain administered in the name of God becomes devotion. The body’s suffering becomes proof of the soul’s sincerity.

Those who sinned — and sin was defined broadly, encompassing any unauthorized interaction, any display of individual will — were required to recite the rosary one thousand times. Not alone. They had to recruit friends and

family within the compound to help them count. This was genius in its cruelty: it made the community complicit in each other’s punishment. It made surveillance collective. Everyone watched everyone. Not out of malice, but because they had been made to believe that watching was love, that reporting was mercy, that the salvation of your brother depended on your willingness to hold him accountable.

It was, a psychiatrist I spoke with described it, a system designed to produce a very specific kind of madness: one that looked, from the inside, exactly like enlightenment.

January 1, 2000 came and went. The world did not end.

Mwerinde’s solution was genius in its monstrosity. She announced a new date: 17 March 2000. But this time, the Virgin would not descend like a thief. She would enter the chapel physically, veiled in flame, and take only the pure. To prepare, the faithful must settle all earthly accounts. Debts must be paid. Feuds must be forgiven. A great feast must be held, a final communion of roasted meat and Fanta, because in heaven, the body would no longer need to eat. The boarded-up doors and windows, she explained, were not to trap them but to protect them. Sinners would try to storm the sanctuary when they saw the Virgin’s glory, and their unworthy eyes would turn the miracle to ash.

I find the testimony of a man named Musinguzi, a farmer from the neighboring village, who sold three bulls to the Movement on March 16. He delivered them himself, and the cult leaders insisted he stay for the feast. “They were laughing,” he recalls. “Not the way people laugh before a journey. The way people laugh when a secret has swallowed them whole.” He remembers the Programmer standing apart, watching the congregation eat with a face as still as a knife blade. He remembers Father Kataribabo blessing the meat in Latin, but the words sounded wrong, conjugated into a grammar that hurt to hear. He left before dusk. That night, from his hut across the valley, he saw the chapel windows glow orange, then yellow, then a white so bright it seemed to silence the insects. Then the screaming started. It didn’t last long. The boards held.

The ofÏcial investigation concluded that the doors and windows had been nailed shut from the outside. The fire was not an act of collective ecstasy but a massacre dressed in sacramental robes. Inside, forensic teams found bodies contorted into the postures of terror—arms cradling faces, spines arched backward, a mother curled around a child so tightly their bones had fused in the heat. Some had tried to dig through the concrete floor with their fingernails. At the entrance lay Kataribabo, his priestly collar melted into the skin of his throat like a brand. Mwerinde and Kibwetere were never found. Witnesses saw them walking calmly down the road toward the Tanzanian border an hour before the smoke rose. They carried no luggage, only a small wooden box, the kind used to store sacramentals.

But the horror was only beginning. In the weeks that followed, police excavated the compound’s latrines and gardens. They found bodies that hadn’t burned— members who’d been garrotted, beaten, doused in battery acid weeks or months before the fire. One pit contained six corpses arranged in a circle around a seventh, whose skull had been opened and filled with a hardened black resin the lab couldn’t identify. Another grave held the remains of children who’d been starved to death, their growth plates showing evidence of prolonged, systematic deprivation. It was as if the cult had been murdering its own members long before the final conflagration, culling those whose faith wavered or whose questions grew too loud. The Programmer’s box of written queries had become a death warrant, each folded paper a potential sentence. Her answers, investigators later realized, often consisted of a single word: “Purify.”

The annual stench, the villagers tell me, began exactly one year later. At first they thought it was a fire—someone burning trash or a bush clearing gone wrong. But the smell was unmistakable, the same wave of charred pork and hair and something else, something like incense made from ground bone. It started at the chapel ruins at 6 p.m. and crept outward, meter by meter, until the whole valley was marinating in it. Dogs howled. Children vomited. An old woman who’d lost her daughter in the fire ran toward the chapel screaming a name, and they found her in the morning, alive but catatonic, her lips moving ceaselessly in the Movement’s sign language. The phenomenon has repeated every March 17 since, like a wound exhaling.

I’m skeptical, of course. My editor expects a piece that debunks this as mass psychogenic illness, a collective olfactory hallucination triggered by trauma and the power of suggestion. I set up recording equipment on the evening of the 17th: a digital thermometer, an air quality monitor, a notebook, a strong stomach. At 5:45 p.m., the air is clean, carrying only the green scent of wet earth and the distant smoke of cooking fires. I’m standing by the chapel’s threshold, where the door once was. The concrete is blackened, bubbled like old skin. I breathe deeply, ready to document nothing.

At 6:00, the temperature drops four degrees in twelve seconds. My eardrums pop. And then I smell it.

Not a memory. Not a suggestion. A thick, hot, viscous reek that curls into my nostrils and coats the soft tissue with an oiliness I can taste. It’s sweet and savory at once, like pork belly cooked in a sugar glaze, but under it runs a chemical tang—gasoline, certainly, and the metallic prickle of roasted blood. But there’s a third note, impossible and unmistakable: roses. The same cloying, funereal sweetness Mwerinde’s letters allegedly carried. The smell does not drift. It pours, a dense current flowing uphill against the breeze, as if something is exhaling it from the earth itself.

I double over, gagging. My instruments go haywire—volatile organic compounds spiking, particulate matter reading “error.” The air shimmers, and for a moment, I see them. Not ghosts, not exactly. A superimposition, like a double-exposed photograph. A woman in a white kanzu, her back to me, leading a line of figures into the roofless chapel. Their mouths are open in silent song. Their eyes are seared shut. At the front, a thin shape in a priest’s collar, his face a smear of charred meat, beckons. And behind them all, watching from the tree line with a smile that contains no joy, a woman in a gomesi the color of dried blood. Her lips move, and though I hear nothing, I feel a word scrape across the inside of my skull like a nail:Still here.

I run. I’m not ashamed to admit it. I run down the hill, through the eucalyptus, past the rock where the Virgin’s silhouette now seems to slump, exhausted and malevolent. I don’t stop until I reach Asiimwe’s truck. He’s already there, engine running, his face slick with sweat. “You saw her,” he says. Not a question.

I don’t write a debunking piece. I can’t. The horror of Kanungu isn’t that a group of deluded followers burned themselves alive for a lie. It’s that the lie was a door, and what came through it never left. The Programmer’s genius was not in fabricating visions but in recognizing that the boundary between this world and something hungrier is thinner than we think, and that faith, weaponized, can tear it open. The followers in the compound weren’t just waiting for the Virgin Mary. They were incubating her—a version of her, at least, shaped by Mwerinde’s will into a thing that required suffering as tribute. Every recited rosary, every hidden sin, every moment of enforced silence fed it. When the fire came, it wasn’t an end. It was a birth. And what was born is still there, in the smoke that crawls uphill every year, in the stench that will not fade, in the hunger that watches from the rock.

I leave Kanungu on March 18. Before I go, I visit the mass grave where the unidentified dead were reburied. Someone has planted red flowers over the mound, amaranth maybe, that droop in the heat. A small girl stands nearby, holding a plastic rosary. She watches me with the unblinking stare of a child who has seen too much. “They are not resting,” she tells me in Runyankole. “The Mother still writes their names. Every night, she writes them down, and they have to obey.”

On the bus back to Kampala, I open my notebook to transcribe my interviews. Tucked between the pages, I find a folded piece of paper I don’t recognize. It’s cheap, lined, the kind sold in village shops. The handwriting is ornate, sloping, and it smells faintly of roses and something burnt. There is only one word on it, in blue ink that glistens wetly even now:Remember. I close the book. The smell in the bus is very strong, and it will not wash out of my clothes for weeks. When I sleep, I dream of a church with no doors and a voice that knows everything I’ve ever done wrong, reciting it slowly, lovingly, in a language that sounds like static. I wake with a start, my tongue blistered, and I understand, finally, why Kiconco tried to dig the demon out of her wrists. Because once you know you’re being read, you can never unfeel the eyes on the page.

chapters.title: The Man
chapters.text:
Witness present Statement voluntary Follow-up required Form One Dormitory Block

The year the KCPE results came out, I was posted to St. Augustine’s—a boarding school deep in the Rift Valley, where the mornings tasted of woodsmoke and the nights carried the damp breath of the Mau Forest. I arrived as a Form One, fourteen years old, clutching my metallic box like a cofÏn for a previous life. My mother had warned me about “monolization,” that made-up word the seniors used to brand the ritual humiliation of new students. She’d chosen St. Augustine’s precisely because the administration had a reputation for stamping out physical bullying. What she didn’t know— what none of the parents knew—was that the school had refined a crueler art: psychological monolization. They didn’t need to touch you. They just needed you to believe.

The first night, after prep, the seniors swarmed into our dormitory like a discharge of static. The corridor stretched long, a gullet of cubicles without doors, just arched entryways yawning into a central passage lit by a single bulb that swung on a frayed cord. Our beds were iron-framed, arranged head-to- head, one metallic box per boy, our entire lives compressed into blue-painted tin. The seniors banged open their own boxes, pretending casualness, pulling out clean vests, and then one of them, a tall boy with a premature mustache, paused as if struck by divine revelation.

“Did y’all pray?” he asked, his voice suddenly grave.

We shook our heads, a dozen small animals quivering.

“If you didn’t —” he shook his head slowly, the way adults do when they’re describing consequences they can’t prevent, ”prepare for him to haunt your sleep."

Him.

Another senior leaned into the doorframe, voice lowered now, which was somehow worse than the loudness.

“Every night he moves. Cubicle to cubicle. Looking for those who didn’t pray.” A pause, architectural, placed there deliberately. “Some have disappeared. Mysteriously. You won’t see his face. But his eyes —”

He stopped.

“His eyes glow.”

The story spilled out like black water. Every night, they said, a figure moved from cubicle to cubicle, searching for the prayerless. You never saw his face, only his eyes—two pinpricks of phosphorescent rot, the color of jackal eyes caught in torchlight. Some boys who saw him never woke up. They simply vanished from their beds, leaving behind only the warm depression in the mattress. The figure didn’t walk like a man; he glided. He didn’t speak; he inhaled your name. And if you were unlucky enough to be awake, to meet that twin glow in the darkness, he would take something from you—not your body, not yet, but something softer, a thread pulled from the fabric of your mind.

Then they went back to their section, laughing about something entirely unrelated, leaving the word disappeared hanging in the dark above fifty-four beds like smoke.

This is important to understand about imagination: it is not passive.

People describe imagination as though it is a cinema screen — something onto which images are projected while you sit still and watch. This is wrong. Imagination is a living thing. It is hungry. Feed it one detail and it will build an entire architecture around that detail, complete with weight, texture, temperature, and smell. It will construct rooms you never described. It will people those rooms with figures whose faces you never imagined but which feel — inexplicably, horrifyingly — familiar.

I stared at the entrance to my cubicle. Our cubicles had no doors. Just an opening, three feet wide, a rectangle of slightly-less-dark in a corridor of darkness.

My mind began its work.

That night, I lay rigid, my blanket a useless membrane. The dormitory had one main door at the far end of the corridor, and each cubicle opened into the same hollow throat. I watched the archway of my cubicle, that dark rectangle that contained all the world’s possibilities. At some ungodly hour, a scream tore through the dormitory—a raw, guttural noise from three cubicles down—and then silence, absolute and swallowing. I prayed, a frantic jumble of half- remembered verses, pressing my palms together so hard the knuckles cracked. Sleep came like a head injury. And in that sleep, I saw him. He stood at the foot of my bed, a silhouette carved from absence, a shape that devoured the dim light. He turned, and I saw his face. It was not a face. It was a suggestion of features, a smudge of something almost human, but the eyes—God, the eyes —glowed with a faint, sickly luminescence, like pus catching the moon.

In the morning, the rumor burned through the corridors: Otieno from 1B was gone. His bed was empty, his metallic box unlocked, a single sock lying on the floor like a shed skin. The seniors’ story suddenly had flesh. We huddled, whispering, and I felt the horror not as a sudden stab but as a slow, creeping seep, a stain spreading through the white cotton of my sanity.

It took a week for a sharp-eyed Form One named Kiprop to dismantle the myth. “Otieno wasn’t taken,” he announced, smug with his revelation. “He was sick. His cousin is a senior in 4B. They carried him to the sanatorium before dawn. The whole thing’s a mindfuck.”

We believed him. Of course we did. Logic is a warm blanket. We wrapped ourselves in it and forgot the draft.

The relief should have been total. And for a few hours, it was. That night, the seniors had an exam the next morning, so the prefects ordered lights-out at nine. The dormitory settled into the familiar geography of nightÝme— breathing, rustling, the occasional clank of a box latch. I was awake. I was always awake now, my brain rewired by fear to dread unconsciousness. I stared at the archway, telling myself the story was over, chanting it like a mantra.

Then I saw the shape.

Someone was sitÝng on my bedmate Wanjala’s metallic blue box. The box was at the foot of Wanjala’s bed, a hard rectangle of painted tin. Wanjala slept with his right arm dangling out of the bed, a habit he’d had since childhood, so he said, and the hand was still there, pale and inert, so I knew he hadn’t moved. But the figure—the figure was solid, a darkness denser than the room’s natural shadow, a crouched thing that seemed to be waiting. I could not make out legs or arms, only a hunched mass with the suggestion of a head. It shifted, slowly, creaking the box as if it had weight, and then it turned toward me. The eyes were not a rumor. They were real, two embers that seemed to burn backward, away from light, consuming it. They fixed on me with a knowing intelligence, a terrible, patient hunger.

His face was not a face. It was the suggestion of a face — a void shaped approximately like something human, with two points of pale light where eyes would be. Not bright. Not theatrical. Just faintly, biologically wrong.

He looked at me.

I woke to the sound of someone screaming from a cubicle four doors down. Then silence. Then the particular quality of quiet that arrives after a scream — charged, held-breath silence, everyone awake and no one willing to confirm it.

I shut my eyes. I counted to ten. I opened them.

Sunlight. Morning. Birds. Normalcy.

And another empty bed.

Mwangi, a small, devout kid who prayed the rosary every night before bed, was simply gone. His bed was neatly made, his box closed, his shoes aligned. The seniors, summoned by our panic, arrived with no scripts, no smirks. I saw their faces. One of them, the mustached storyteller, looked genuinely nauseated. “We didn’t do this,” he said, and the admission was more terrifying than any ghost story.

By breakfast the story had metastasized.

Someone was missing from Cubicle Seven. The name moved through the dining hall in whispers, multiplying the way stories do when there is no authority to stop them and plenty of imaginations to accelerate them. By the time I heard it, the details had already evolved: he had been dragged. He had vanished. His bed had been found empty and cold. Someone claimed the sheets were disturbed in a specific, directional way.

We ate our uji and believed every word.

This time the seniors were not laughing. I watched their faces during the investigation — the deputy principal asking questions in the corridor, the Form Fours conferring in clusters — and what I saw was not the private satisfaction of people whose prank had worked. It was something adjacent to what I had felt at two in the morning.

They were doing math they didn’t like the answer to.

Over the following days, the mythology underwent its second evolution.

The first evolution had been debunking — the rational contraction of a ghost story into a prank. This was supposed to be the terminal state. Ghost story collapses into prank; prank is laughed at; story ends.

But a second disappearance had occurred and no sick cousin was offered as explanation, and into that vacuum the stories rushed and expanded in new, stranger directions.

The dormitory split into factions of belief. Some boys said the myth had drawn the real thing, that our collective terror had called something across a threshold.

Once fear enters a place, it leaves residue.

After that, the stories multiplied.

People claimed they heard footsteps at night.

Someone swore the figure floated.

Another boy said it stood beside his bed whispering in a language he didn’t understand.

One junior claimed the thing had no face.

“They say he walks through walls. Literally through the concrete.” “I heard he was a student here. A long time ago. Before the school was the school.” “Someone said you can only see him if he wants you to see him, which means if you’ve seen him —” a meaningful pause “— he made a choice.”

“I heard he sodomizes people.” (This one from a Form Two with boundary issues who was simply trying to participate.)

“My cousin’s former classmate said if the moon is full and you’re outside after lights-out, you can see him floating. Just above the trees.”

The seniors laughed less and less each time these stories spread.

That was when the fear changed. Because a lie is safe only while the liars remain in control of it. The seniors started their own rumors, perhaps to reassert control, perhaps because they were just as scared.

I listened to all of it. I catalogued it. This is what I did with fear — I transformed it into information, into a map of what other people were afraid of, as though understanding the topology of the terror would place me outside it.

It didn’t work. But the habit was already formed.

I could not stop thinking about the figure on the box.

There are different qualities of darkness.

The darkness of cities is polluted — orange-grey, shot through with ambient light from a thousand sources, never truly dark. The darkness of a Kenyan highland boarding school, in a dormitory without electricity after nine, bordered on three sides by indigenous forest and one by a concrete wall —

that darkness is complete. It has a presence. It presses against your eyes with the same weight as something physical. After enough hours inside it, your eyes begin inventing light simply to have something to process.

This is documented. This is science. Humans deprived of visual input for extended periods begin generating their own visual experiences. Hallucinations, clinically. But here is what the clinical literature doesn’t quite capture: the hallucinations are not random noise. They are shaped by what you’ve been thinking about. I knew this.

I stopped sleeping. When the dormitory lights died each night, I became a sentinel of my own terror, counting the breaths around me, mapping the small noises, the creaks and sighs of the building. I began to notice the forest. Our dormitory backed onto the edge of the Mau, a dense wall of cypress and wild olive that seemed to breathe its own slow, vegetal respiration. The windows at the corridor’s end looked directly into that black tangle, and on moonless nights, you could not tell where the building ended and the woods began. It was in that borderland that the figure seemed to exist, a thing of thresholds.

A week after Mwangi vanished, I found myself awake again, this time counting sheep—a childish tactic that only sharpened the silence. The particular absurdity of counting sheep, which I had read about in a book and had never actually worked for me, the sheep always becoming something else after the fourth or fifth one, morphing in the dark theater of the eyelid into less pastoral shapes.

Someone walked past my cubicle.

I turned. Male, walking with purpose, dressed in something dark. Not unusual — boys went to the bathroom after lights-out. But the bathroom was in the other direction.

He was walking away from the bathroom.

Young man! — the deputy principal’s voice from somewhere in the building, sharp and administrative, chasing someone down. I heard a door slam. The adult world, intruding, pursuing something it could apparently see. I exhaled. A student, then. Just a student trying to flee his own fears.

But then he came again. The same unhurried stride, the same silent passage. And this time, he stopped directly in the archway of my cubicle. The glowing eyes found me immediately, as if they had always known exactly where I was. They did not blink. I felt the gaze like a physical probe, something sliding behind my eyes and testing the weight of my brain. Then he walked on, toward the back of the dormitory, where a small exit door led to the lavatories and, beyond them, the forest.

A switch flipped in my chest. Rage, or the closest cousin of rage that terror allows. I would unmask this clown. I would prove to myself that it was a senior in a mask, a fabric phantom stitched from my own gullibility. I grabbed my torch from under my pillow, a cheap plastic thing with a weak beam, and I slipped out of bed. The concrete was ice on my bare soles. He was moving into cubicles and out of them. Not searching exactly. More like — checking. The way you check rooms in a house you own, not looking for anything specific, simply ensuring each space is as you left it. I followed, pressing myself into the darkness of each cubicle entrance as he emerged from the one ahead.

I moved with a predator’s stealth, hugging the walls between cubicles, ducking into the archways whenever I lost sight of him. He was ahead of me, a moving stain, and I tracked him by the faint, sick glow of his eyes that reflected off the whitewashed walls like candleflame through a fingernail.

He entered the last cubicle, the one closest to the back door. I pressed myself into the adjacent cubicle, barely breathing. The boy who slept there—Oduor, a heavy snorer—was a reassuring bulk of human warmth. I couldn’t see the figure, but I heard the soft creak of the back door opening, a sound I knew well, the slight grind of rusted hinges. I counted to ten, then peered around the archway. The door stood open, a rectangle of deeper darkness exhaling the forest’s cold. I counted to ten. I stepped out.

The full moon was enormous and specific and white, the kind of moon that makes Kenya’s highland nights feel like something between a place and an idea. It laid a clean, hard light across the dormitory’s exterior wall and the

narrow strip of packed earth beside it, and the first twenty or thirty feet of the forest’s edge — enough to see the individual textures of bark, the particular way the leaves held the light.

He was standing at the edge of the trees.

Not moving. Just standing, his back to me, looking into the forest the way you look into the sea — not at anything specific, just at it. At the whole of it. At the fact of it.

I could not make myself call out. I could not make myself run. I stood with my flashlight pointed at the ground, switched off, entirely useless, and I watched.

He rose.

Not jumping. Not climbing. The physics of it were simply wrong in the specific, stomach-dropping way that wrong physics announce themselves to the body before the brain catches up. He rose, gradually, with a composure that was somehow more horrible than any dramatic ascent would have been, the way a man stands up from a chair — casual, unhurried, as though this were simply the next thing he intended to do.

He rose until he was above the tree line. The moon was at its apex. He rose into the plane of it.

And the moon swallowed him.

Not dramatically. Not with any sound or light or theatrical effect. He entered the circle of white light and he was not there anymore. Present one moment. Absent the next. The moon continued to be the moon. The trees continued to be trees. The forest made its night sounds undisturbed.

I stood on the packed earth for what was probably four minutes and felt like a geological epoch.

I never told anyone. The school closed within the week — unrest, the kind of institutional chaos that descends on Kenyan boarding schools periodically like weather, all accusations and investigations and panicked parents collecting their children. I gathered my metallic blue box. I sat in a matatu back to Nairobi and watched the highlands flatten into suburbs.

A riot over food, they said. Rocks through the administration block windows. A teacher beaten. The school was closed indefinitely, and we were all sent home in a flurry of anxious phone calls and hired matatus. I never went back.

Here is what I can tell you with certainty: I was thirteen years old, I was sleep- deprived, I was in the grip of an imagination that had been deliberately inflamed by older boys who understood exactly what they were doing. The human brain under those conditions is capable of extraordinary productions. Visual hallucinations. False memories. The confabulation of detail so convincing it becomes indistinguishable from perception.

This is the rational explanation. It fits everything. I would give it to you with full confidence in any other context.

But I want to tell you something about imagination, since this whole thing began with imagination.

Imagination builds. That’s its nature. You give it one dark room and it will construct an entire building. You give it one pair of glowing eyes and it will grow a whole figure around them, complete and breathing and there.

But imagination — even at its most vivid, even at its most terrifying — doesn’t subtract.

It doesn’t take things away.

If your imagination puts a figure on a box, you will see a figure on a box. You will not, in the same moment, fail to hear the door that the figure should have come through. Your imagination fills in. It adds detail. It does not erase the creak of a hinge that existed every single other time that door was opened.

And imagination, when it constructs a figure rising into the night sky, constructs it rising. Sweepingly. With emphasis, with drama, with the cinematography of fear.

It does not construct the casual, utterly indifferent physics of a man standing up from a chair.

I saw a man vanish in the face of the moon.

I am no longer thirteen. I no longer sleep with one eye on the entrance to a doorless cubicle. I have not been haunted, have not been visited, have not seen anything since that night that could not be explained by the ordinary machinery of a tired brain in a dark room.

But I check, still.

Every night before I sleep, I check the corners. The doorframes. The specific quality of the dark behind the door. The arrangement of objects in the room, whether anything has moved or been added or been removed.

I check.

And most nights there is nothing.

Most nights.

chapters.title: She is.....
chapters.text:
folded twice, passed under three desks before it reached you

This story has been passed between bunks in every girls’ boarding school in Nigeria. Nobody knows where it started. Everyone knows how it ends.

Every boarding school in Nigeria has a girl like her.

Not the loud one. Not the prefect with the whistle and the long-held grudge. The quiet one. The one whose uniform is always pressed while yours is a crime scene, whose face never quite settles into an expression, who exists at the precise edge of a room — present enough to see, too still to disturb.

At Federal Government Girls’ College, Ikeja, that girl was called Amara.

For two terms she drifted through assembly and prep like something trying to remember how to be a person. What people noticed — what they always noticed — was the hair. Tight, intricate cornrows, geometric patterns so precise the Oromo girls in the northeast dorm said they looked like something old. Like something remembered rather than learned. When Chisom, captain of the social committee and certified authority on everything, finally cornered her and demanded — Who does your hair? Tell me, I’m begging you in Jesus’ name — Amara only smiled the way a door smiles when it has been bolted from the inside.

The myth arrived before anyone knew to call it that.

A trembling JSS2 girl swore she’d woken to find a headless body upright on a mattress, long fingers sectioning hair on a severed head cradled in its lap, humming a church hymn in reverse. We called her a liar. We told her Madam Koi Koi would visit her next for telling stories. That was how these things worked — currency, passed dormitory to dormitory to terrify new girls, to make night trips to the latrine feel like a death sentence.

But the Oromo girls had an older name for her.

Oroma. The one who tends herself. The one whose hands know only one head.

Ifeoma was my friend. Not just any friend — the girl. Popular the way certain people are popular, effortlessly and without effort, luminous in assembly and at dinner and in every ordinary moment that became less ordinary because she was in it. Her hair was a different kind of impossible — shiny cornrows feeding into a perfect bun, never a flyaway strand, always fresh, always done. When girls asked who plaited it, Ifeoma would only smile her slow smile and say, “Someone who really knows my head.”

We thought she was being coy.

I know better now. I know that a head can be known the way a house is known — intimately, from the inside, by something that has walked its hallways for a very long time.

The first time I saw Oroma — the real Oroma — was deep in harmattan.

I woke because the air tasted like dust and through the dormitory window, beyond the rusted fence separating our block from the bush, a figure stood in the dark. A girl. Motionless. Watching. I lay still and counted breaths. Two hours passed and she did not shift, did not sway, did not do anything but stand there while the harmattan wind worried the edge of her gown. When she finally turned and dissolved into the dark I heard something worse: soft footsteps in the corridor. Flip-flop. Flip-flop.

“Ifeoma?” I whispered.

From the cube beside mine, Ifeoma’s voice came thick with sleep. “Stop calling me for nothing, na!”

My blood became ice water. Because whatever was walking was already inside.

The weight that settled on the edge of my bed was wrong in a way that has no vocabulary in any language I was taught. I could smell palm kernel oil and underneath it something wet and mineral — soil turned from below, from somewhere deep and lightless. The body carried its head in the crook of one arm, and the head was making a low, formless sound, not quite a song, the kind of sound hands make when the mind is somewhere else entirely. I lay rigid

as a corpse, cover pulled to my chin, and listened to the soft sectioning of hair, strand by strand, row by row, the patient geometry of fingers that had done this longer than I had been alive.

When the mattress finally lifted, I found them on the floor: coiled braids, dark and glistening with oil, finished and perfect.

I showed Ifeoma in the morning. She laughed until tears came. She told everyone Esther wanted to be a Nollywood horror queen. I wanted to believe her so badly I nearly managed it.

The next night was the last night Ifeoma was herself.

She agreed to walk with me to the latrines because she was still laughing at my fear. “I’m only coming because you’re scared — lest Madam Koi Koi finds you. Or was it Rebecca? Which one again?”

“Neither,” I said, and my voice was a thin wire. “Her name is Oroma.”

Ifeoma laughed the way people laugh when they are certain they are safe.

I squatted over the pit toilet with my eyes on the door. Nothing came. I finished and rushed out into the dark and found the path empty — then saw her, a short distance away near the water tank, back turned, the familiar soft shape of Ifeoma’s nightgown.

“Ifeoma! You just left me, abi?”

She turned.

I wish I could unmake what I saw next, but some things root in the mind like a seed that feeds on light. She turned, and her neck ended in a glistening stump, dark and wet as raw liver, and in her hands — cradled gently, the way you might hold a lantern or a sleeping infant — was her own head. The hair was freshly done. Perfect, intricate cornrows. Impossibly patient work. And the face was smiling. Ifeoma’s smile, but emptied of everything that had ever made her my friend. The mouth moved, and what came out might have been my name if water could learn to speak.

I don’t remember screaming. The night matron found me at 4 a.m. curled around the base of the tank stand, making a sound no human should make.

They searched for Ifeoma for three days. They never found her.

The school closed ranks. She ran away, they decided, with the confidence of people who needed that to be true. Her parents came, wailed, signed forms, left. The counsellor listened to my account, wrote things on a pad, nodded in the careful way of someone who had already decided what they were hearing. Stress, she said. Pre-examination anxiety. Hypnagogia. She prescribed rest and cocoa at bedtime. She did not explain the braids I had kept in a plastic bag, dark and oiled and smelling of something that had no name in the school’s vocabulary.

Nobody could explain what happened to Amara’s hair.

The matted, neglected clumps she had worn for two terms were simply gone. Monday morning she walked into assembly with cornrows — neat, impossibly shiny, identical in pattern to the ones Ifeoma had worn the night she disappeared. When Chisom saw her she dropped her hymn book. The sound of it hitÝng the floor was the only honest thing in that assembly hall.

Amara turned and looked at me across four hundred blue-and-white uniforms.

She smiled. Not Ifeoma’s smile. Her own — the bolted door, the room with no light on inside. But in it I saw something that hadn’t been there before. Something settled. Something satisfied.

I understand now what the Oromo girls understood long before any of us. Oroma is not a ghost. She is not a demon in the evangelical sense, not the kind that retreats from oil and prayer. She is a hunger that moves from one girl to the next, from one head to the next, braiding herself into the follicles, into the scalp, into the bone. She is patient in the way that only things without time can be patient. She finds the quiet girl first — the strange, untethered one with no visitors on Sundays — and she keeps that girl and tends her and marks her for something none of us have a name for. Then she finds the popular one. The luminous one. The one whose head everyone admires.

And she learns it from the inside.

In every boarding school in Nigeria there is a quiet girl whose hair is never explained. There is a popular girl who will one day learn her name. And there is always, eventually, a third girl — someone like me — who sits in the dining hall the morning after, watching hands that have done extraordinary and terrible work move steadily through rice and stew, and feels the myth settle into her lungs like dust.

I put down my spoon.

Into the noise and steam and ordinary living of four hundred girls, I said it — quiet as a story passed between bunks in the dark, a word that was either a warning or an invitation and I have never been certain which.

“Oroma.”

Amara did not look up.

But she smiled.
