chapters.title: The Tokoloshe
chapters.text:
Never sent, never spoken — Grahamstown Care Home, twenty years on

My grandmother screamed at something only she could see.

I’d flown back to South Africa after twenty years — my parents left when Mandela won, convinced we were the bad guys, which we were. I drove to the care home in Grahamstown alone and she’d lit up the moment I walked in. Then mid-sentence something shifted behind her eyes. She stared at me the way you stare at a stranger wearing a dead man’s face. Then she pointed — at me, at my face, at whatever she believed walked beside me — and screamed until three nurses came running.

The nurses said it was the dementia. I told myself they were right.

The cab driver from Jo’burg had ranted for two hours — politicians, monuments, foreigners stealing jobs — before going silent at a crossroads where a half-rotted scarecrow hung from a telephone pole. His knuckles whitened. Then, abruptly, without looking at me:

“You ever heard of the Tokoloshe?”

I hadn’t thought about that word since childhood. My nanny used it the way some women use God — not lightly, not as decoration. She said it with the specific weight of something she’d seen.

The driver didn’t turn. Just kept his eyes fixed on the dark road ahead as if the darkness itself might be listening.

“1977. My cousin’s village near King Williams Town. A police officer — the kind who didn’t just follow orders. Who enjoyed them.” His jaw worked like he was grinding something bitter. “They found him in

the morning. Door locked from inside. Chest opened from sternum to hip. The marks were curved. Human, almost. Except no man’s fingers grow that long, or bend that way.”

I laughed — the nervous, unconvinced kind. “You’re saying a monster did it.”

“I’m saying it was sent.” He glanced at me once, eyes flat and serious as a surgeon’s. “The Tokoloshe doesn’t wander. It is summoned. By a witch. By debt. By ancestors who have not been answered.” He paused. “The ones who owe, they don’t always know they owe.”

The rest of the drive came and went in silence. When we pulled up to The Umzimvubu Rest — a sagging colonial structure at the edge of a low hill, balconies warped, stucco cracked, porch light buzzing like a trapped insect — he set my bag on the gravel with a tenderness that felt like pity.

He did not say goodbye. He drove away and his tail-lights shrank through the thorn trees until there was nothing.

My foot caught a loose brick on the path. I hit the ground hard, palms raking gravel. The driver’s voice came back: They wedge bricks under the bed legs. A Tokoloshe cannot climb over uneven ground. I put the brick back where it lay and went inside.

The foyer smelled of bleach, dust, and something beneath both — old meat, or fabric left sealed too long in a hot room. The night clerk, a lean man with exhausted eyes and a ledger thick with dust, slid a heavy iron key across without looking up.

“Room six. Top of the stairs.” He went back to his register. “Wedge something under the bed if you sleep light. Drafts.”

The word drafts sat wrong in the air, like a translation of something he didn’t want to say directly. I almost asked him to explain. I didn’t.

Room six was at the corridor’s far end, number stencilled in paint the color of dried blood. Peeling wallpaper. A sagging iron bed with no base — just a mattress over bare wooden slats. A wardrobe with a cracked mirror that reflected the room in slightly the wrong proportions. A clay ashtray on the nightstand and a Bible with a broken spine. On the floor, shoved half beneath the bed and catching the hall light: a single brick.

I stared at it for a long time. Then I did what people do when they are frightened but still consider themselves rational. I smiled at it, dropped my bag, and decided superstition was just poverty dressed in old language.

The scratching started at half past midnight.

Not from the walls. From beneath the bed — a wet, deliberate drag, like a damp cloth pulled slow across pine. Too rhythmic for rats. Too patient for pipes. I lay rigid, sheets knotted in both fists, and counted my own heartbeats. Then came the breathing. Shallow, ragged, suspended between animal and something that had learned to study animals. It paused. Listened. As if it knew exactly where my ear was relative to the floor.

The air turned cold. Not the cold of a window left open. A cold with intent to it, rising from below, carrying the smell of turned earth and copper and something floral and wrong — crushed marigolds, my brain offered, though I had no idea why.

The brick under the bed shifted. Not much. Just enough that I saw the shadow of it move.

I was out of the bed before I decided to move, back against the wardrobe, staring at the mattress. The corner shadows thickened into a shape that refused to hold — swelling, contracting, like something breathing inside the dark itself.

From Room five, through the thin plaster wall: a sound like canvas tearing slowly. A gasp, choked to a gurgle. Then a thud. Then the rhythmic, wet pounding of something I made myself not name.

I lunged for my phone. No signal. The landline gave a dead, hollow tone. I crossed to the window — painted shut, rusted through. Beyond the glass, thorn trees clawed at a moonless sky and the Eastern Cape dark pressed close and total.

The tearing stopped.

Footsteps in the corridor. Not heavy. Delicate. Bare skin on old wood — padding, pausing. Right outside my door. Something pressed against the wood from the other side. A slow, wet exhalation seeped under the door, smelling of river mud and marigolds and old graves. Then a voice, mimicking the night clerk’s exactly:

“Wedge something under the bed.”

I stumbled back over my own suitcase. By the time I recovered, it had moved on. I heard Room seven’s handle rattle. A sharp intake of breath. A wet crack. Silence.

I grabbed the clay ashtray from the nightstand and shoved it under one of the bed legs. It wasn’t enough. I knew it wasn’t enough. But my hands needed something to do while my mind refused to process what was happening in the rooms around me.

Through the ceiling: a dull impact, then another, like something leaping beam to beam. A scream from the floor above, severed mid- frequency. Then the clerk’s voice from downstairs, swallowed mid- sentence into a single wet sound. Then nothing.

Then footsteps returning. Slowing. Stopping outside my door.

The deadbolt turned from the inside.

I hadn’t touched it. I was across the room. But I watched it turn — slow, deliberate — and heard the lock seat itself with a sound like finality. Then the scratching began again, directly beneath me. The ashtray against the bed leg was gone. In its place sat a single smooth river stone, placed with care against the iron frame. Placed by something that didn’t need to climb. Something that could simply wait until it was ready.

I clawed at the door. The frame had swollen, sealed itself. I threw my shoulder against it — solid oak, immovable. The window bars held. I was the only locked room in the building.

The newspaper clippings were on the wall behind the wardrobe, plastered under decades of whitewash that had bubbled and split in the damp. I tore the loose plaster away with my hands. A 1952 headline: BUSINESSMAN FOUND DEAD — DOOR LATCHED FROM WITHIN. Beneath it, 1977: POLICE OFFICER GUTTED IN SEALED ROOM — WILD ANIMAL SUSPECTED. Then 1994. 2001. 2015. Each one the same building, the same room, the same curved marks, the same locked doors, the same absence of evidence. And in the margin beside each clipping, in different handwriting over seven decades, the same line:

Room six. Always room six. Do not put them in room six.

The Tokoloshe hadn’t haunted this hotel. It was bound to it — fed here, returned here, perhaps made from this place in some way I didn’t have the language or lineage to understand.

My grandmother’s scream surfaced from wherever I’d buried it. She hadn’t been afraid of me. She’d been afraid of what stood beside me — what had traveled with my bloodline, patient as a stone in a river, waiting for me to come back and open the door.

Something pressed flat against the other side of my door.

Not the knob. The whole surface of the wood, as though something wanted to feel the shape of what was inside. Then a voice — perfectly mimicking my own, using a cadence I recognized as mine — came through the grain, quiet and deliberate:

“We don’t care if you believe in us.”

A shape rose at the foot of the bed.

Small — barely three feet at its tallest — but the space around it warped, stretching its shadow into something that touched all four walls at once. Scalp smooth and gleaming like wet river stone. Eyes the color of banked coals. Its mouth unhinged slowly, revealing teeth like filed needles, too many for any jaw that size, glistening and clicking against each other with the sound of settling bones. It did not look at me with hunger. It looked at me with the patient, considered interest of something completing an old appointment.

It stepped past me. Dragged one claw along the door’s edge — a long, slow groove — then looked back over its shoulder with that mouth still stretched, that gaze still burning. I understood what it was telling me. I was not the kill. Not yet. I was the room it returned to. The anchor. The open door through which it entered the world of this building, again and again, each time a new guest arrived who carried the right kind of debt, the right kind of blood, the right kind of hollow where belief used to be.

It melted through the door without opening it. The lock held. The wood never moved. But the sounds that followed were immediate — padding footsteps, a crash, a scream splitting open and going silent, another door, another scream, the systematic, unhurried rhythm of a thing that had done this many times before in this exact place.

I sat on the bed and pulled my knees to my chest. The river stone sat against the leg beneath me, smooth and deliberate as a signature. Somewhere above, a child began to laugh. Then, through the walls, another voice joined it. Then another.

And I understood — not with my mind, but with something older, something my grandmother had tried to warn me about across the distance of dementia and twenty years of ocean — that this hotel had never been a guesthouse.

It was a feeding ground.

And I had walked in carrying the invitation.

The official record lists seven unexplained deaths at The Umzimvubu Rest between 1952 and the present. Investigators note the consistent details: locked doors, curved lacerations inconsistent with any known animal, no forensic evidence of entry or exit. One witness — identity withheld by court order — was found unharmed and unresponsive in Room Six. He was clutching a smooth river stone and a crumbling piece of old brick. He has not spoken since. He responds only to sounds that come from beneath the bed.

chapters.title: Djin of Garbatula
chapters.text:
OFFICIAL

OB/No. 2241 · Two-Vehicle Patrol, Garbatula Dry Riverbed

The dust of Garbatula does not settle after violence. It hangs in the air like ground bone, tasting of salt and old blood, and the wind that moves through it does not clean — it rearranges. By the time the two pickup trucks reached the dry riverbed, the desert had already begun erasing their tracks, smoothing the land behind them as though it refused to keep records of what they had done.

They had hit the village of Kachuru before dawn. Five men. One rifle. And the understanding, well-worn as a blade handle, that the world belonged to whoever was willing to be the most frightening thing in it. They broke doors. They took grain, cooking oil, jerrycans, a bright blue radio someone’s child would never see again. Khalif had fired once into the air, and the men of Kachuru had scattered like birds. That was the part none of them spoke about now. How easy it had been. How the ease of it sat in the stomach like a stone swallowed whole.

Khalif rode in the front truck with his rifle across his knees. Beside him, Hassan drove with two hands tight on the wheel. In the second truck came Wario, Abdi, and the one everyone called Musa — not his real name, but names in this work were mutable things. The stolen goats rode tied in the back, and their bleating came and went with the wind.

The laugh reached them before the fire was even built.

It rose from somewhere past the ridge — low, rolling, wet at the edges, the way a hyena laughs but stretched too long and bent at an angle that no animal throat should manage. Every goat surged against its ropes at once. The men looked at each other over the flatbed and said nothing, which was its own kind of answer.

“Hyena,” Abdi said.

Nobody agreed with him. Nobody disagreed. Khalif began building the fire, and the silence filled back in around them like water.

Abdi was the youngest and the loudest, and he had laughed during the raid when an old woman fell trying to protect a sack of maize flour. He was the first to need the dark.

He went twenty paces past the firelight, enough to feel the desert close behind him, and was standing there when the temperature changed. Not dropped — changed, the way temperature changes in a room when someone else enters it. He turned.

The figure stood between two acacia trees. Black robe hanging completely still while the night wind moved through every other thing. And above the robe, where a face should have been, a skull. Not the bleached, sun-dried bone of animals. A living skull, the colour of old ivory, its hollow sockets burning with two points of coal-red light that did not flicker and did not blink.

Abdi opened his mouth.

The laugh came out of it. Not his laugh. The laugh from beyond the ridge, now here, now inside his chest, and Abdi’s hands went to his eyes — not in horror, but with the deliberate calm of something reaching for something it owns. He dug in. His fingers found the rim of his own socket and pressed.

The scream that came after was the kind that makes men run toward it before they’ve decided to.

Khalif reached him first. Abdi was kneeling in the sand, a ruined thing, both hands webbed with dark fluid. The marks in the earth around him were not footprints. They were grooves, circular, as if something had orbited him in a frenzy without touching the ground.

Then Abdi stood.

Every man there took a step back.

His hands dropped. In the pits of his face, two things glowed — coal-red, patient, belonging to something much older than the boy whose body wore them. His mouth opened and the laugh came out clean and perfect, the hyena note filling the desert, and then his spine yanked him backward and he hit the sand and lay still.

Khalif knelt beside him. Where there should have been blood, there was only ash.

No one slept. They sat with their backs to the fire and their rifles on their knees and their eyes on the dark, and the dark gave nothing back.

Hassan began to hum around two in the morning.

“Stop that,” Khalif said.

Hassan looked at him with the expression of a man being accused of something he genuinely does not know he is doing. “I am not humming.”

But the melody continued — soft, childlike, tuneless in the way of songs sung to feverish children in the middle of the night. It came from Hassan’s throat without his consent. His face had gone waxy, his eyes fixed on something past the fire.

Then the voice changed.

It was a woman’s voice. Dry. Patient. It used Hassan’s mouth like a borrowed instrument.

You took bread from hungry mouths.

Hassan clamped both hands over his lips. His whole body shook on the single wire of his own terror.

You kicked an old man in the chest for the satisfaction of it.

The fire collapsed inward. Every coal went black at the same moment, as if something had reached across the camp and pinched them out. In the darkness, Hassan rose. Khalif could hear him moving — the shuffle of boots, then the sound of something striking stone. Once. Twice.

Khalif grabbed for him in the dark, and something hit him across the chest and sent him into the dust.

When his eyes adjusted he saw Hassan at the edge of the camp, kneeling at a flat rock, and he was hitting his own face against it with the measured obedience of a man following instructions. Not in panic. Not in madness. With the steady rhythm of a task being completed.

The skull-face was there beside him. Present in the way water is present — not arriving, simply there, as if it had always been in that exact spot. It leaned close to Hassan in the dark. Its coal eyes pulsed. Its hollow mouth made no sound, but the laugh lived in the air around them both, almost gentle.

On the fourth strike, Hassan’s skull gave.

They buried him with their bare hands because none of them were willing to leave him for the desert. And around the shallow grave, when the sun came up, Khalif found the tracks. Bare feet. Too long. Pressed too deep, as if whatever made them carried a weight that had nothing to do with a body.

Musa tried to reason his way out. He said aloud, several times, with increasing certainty, that the desert played tricks on guilty minds. He said the thing with the skull face was a hallucination of collective fear. He said the laugh was a hyena, a jackal, acoustics, the wind channelling through stone formations. He was still saying these things when they found him.

He lay beneath a dead acacia one mile from camp, arms spread wide, eyes bright with fever. Alive. Trying to speak.

His tongue was gone.

Not torn, not bitten. Cut. The absence was clean, deliberate — a removal performed by something that understood anatomy and had patience for precision. Blood had soaked into his beard and pooled in his collar. His eyes tracked toward the branches above him, and Khalif looked up.

It stood on a branch that should not have held any weight, the black robe hanging in a perfect column, motionless. It studied them the way a person studies something almost interesting. Then it tilted its skull, and Wario raised his rifle and fired and the bullet passed through the figure like a stone through still water — no resistance, no evidence it had ever touched.

The figure was no longer in the tree.

It was behind Wario.

The coal eyes flared at his ear, and the laugh arrived — not from the air but from inside the cartilage of his jaw, vibrating in his teeth and his fillings and the roof of his mouth. Wario grabbed at his throat, at something no one else could see, his boots cutting furrows in the earth. His neck stretched. The sound it made was wet rope pulled past its tolerance.

His head turned past the point of turning.

Musa died an hour later, choking quietly in the dust. Khalif said his name once. Then left him.

There were only two of them now, and the desert had become the kind of quiet that is not quiet at all but the absence of everything that should be there.

Khalif and Nadir drove with the headlights off, the road a pale ribbon beneath a moon that gave just enough light to confirm the world was still there. Neither of them spoke. The engine noise felt like the only tether.

Khalif watched the side mirror.

Something was pacing the truck. Tall, unhurried, black-robed, keeping perfect speed forty metres to the right of the road. Not running. Not walking in any way that required feet. Simply matching them, as if speed were a courtesy it had decided to extend.

“Nadir.” Khalif’s voice had nothing in it. “Don’t look at it.”

Nadir was already looking.

His face had changed. The waxy stillness, the fixed expression, the same vacancy Khalif had seen pass through Hassan and Abdi — it moved across Nadir’s face like weather crossing a plain, slow and total.

“It’s sitting beside me,” Nadir said.

The passenger seat was empty.

Nadir’s hands left the wheel.

They went to his own chest, fingers curling into hooks, clawing at the fabric of his shirt as if something beneath the skin needed to be let out. His mouth opened too wide. The woman’s voice came through it again — the dry, patient one, the voice that knew everything that had been taken from Kachuru and could name all of it in sequence.

Khalif grabbed the wheel. Too late.

The truck lurched into a ditch. The windshield became white spiderwebs. Metal screamed against the earth and everything tilted and then stopped.

In the silence, Nadir was still clawing.

Khalif watched the skin of his companion’s throat split — not gore, but thin black lines, branching like riverbeds drawn by a hand working from memory. Something moved beneath the surface. Something small and purposeful and ancient, finding its way out.

Khalif did not stay to see where it went.

He ran. The truck caught fire behind him, a thin orange stain in the enormous dark. The laugh came from the flames, from the sky, from inside the hollow of his own chest — and Khalif ran until the sand became tarmac and the tarmac became the headlights of a lorry coming out of Isiolo, and he grabbed the driver by the shirt and could not let go for forty minutes.

At the police post, he confessed everything. The raid. The broken doors. The women pulled aside. The boy whose phone Rage had taken, the kick to his chest for the pleasure of it. He spoke in one continuous stream, as if the words were something his body needed to evacuate before it could rest.

He was still speaking when he stopped.

Mid-sentence. The officers would argue afterward about what he had been saying in those last moments. One said it sounded like a name. Another said it sounded like a laugh — not Khalif’s laugh, but something older using him.

The truck was found at dawn. Four bodies in the desert. Each one distinct in its ruin. One with no eyes. One whose face had met stone on its own terms. One whose tongue was a clean, deliberate absence. One twisted past the tolerance of the human neck.

And in the sand beside the wreck, not yet covered by the morning wind, a single set of footprints walking away from the wreckage.

Bare feet. Long. Deep.

Beside them, at intervals, the faint impression of something else entirely. Not feet. Not hooves. Something the officer who found them could not name and chose not to write down, because some things, once committed to paper, have a way of following you home.

In Garbatula, the old women say the Jinn does not hate.

They say that is the terrifying part.

Hatred has a shape. Hatred can be reasoned with, bargained with, survived. The Jinn that moves through the Isiolo wastes is not in the business of hatred. It is simply old. Patient. It watches through windows and stands on rooftops at dawn and waits in the silence between a man’s heartbeats.

It was there before the first bandit. It will be there after the last.

The cattle of Kachuru were found three days later, calm, not a single head missing, grazing at the edge of the escarpment in the early morning light.

Not one of them had a mark on them.

chapters.title: Popobawa
chapters.text:
✦✦

M.V. Kilindi Star · 14 November 1974 · Dar es Salaam Harbour

VESSEL: M.V. Kilindi Star MASTER: Capt. O. Baraka POSITION: Dar es Salaam Harbour, 6°49'S 39°17'E WEATHER: Overcast, light swell LOG PAGES: 61–79

We dropped anchor at first light, the hull groaning against salt-crusted bollards while a bruised sky pressed down on the Tanzanian coast. Docking should have been routine. We had survived monsoon swells, engine failures, pirate rumors. What we faced in the waters off Pemba and Zanzibar was none of those things. It was older than weather and older than men. The crew gathered in the mess hall not for rations but for confessions. We needed to set it down before the sea swallowed our words. I opened the logbook myself. Every man spoke. Every account matched. We called it Popobawa.

The locals had warned us before we ever charted the Pemba channel. Men sat in compounds with bonfires blazing at midnight, faces drawn amber in the firelight, repeating the same phrase in the way a man repeats a prayer when he has run out of all other options: “Yule shetani. Popobawa.” That devil. Popobawa. They said it had crossed the Indian Ocean long before our ships drew maps. Ujunga knew it. Mombasa feared it. Pemba was where the stories were born, where the myth drew its first breath. A shape-

shifter. A winged horror that fed on violation. They accused it of sodomising men in their sleep, of taking women near the shore, of lifting children from their beds and carrying them out over black water until their cries dissolved into the wind. We dismissed it as coastal folklore. Sailors always do. That is how it begins.

Our First Mate Elias had walked near Pembe za Ndovu in Mombasa years before this voyage, drawn by talk of a tree thick with roosting bats. He said the air grew cold as dusk fell without any wind to explain it. The sky darkened not with clouds but with wings — thousands of them — and among them a larger silhouette. Four feet tall, he reckoned, with a wingspan wide enough to swallow a man’s view entirely, and a single eye that caught the lamplight the way a cat’s eye catches it, only yellower and larger. He said it turned that eye toward him and he ran. He locked himself in a storeroom until morning, listening to claws work across the wood outside and something like breath hissing through the cracks. When he finally stepped out it was gone — circling the canopy with the bats, silent, watching from height.

Our Chief Engineer Kariuki recalled Fort Jesus on a shore leave three years prior. He was standing near the old cannons when a scream tore the evening open. Tourists assumed a trapped bat; the locals knew otherwise and scattered into alleys shouting its name. A night guard told him afterward that he had seen it near the rusted artillery, talons gripping a man who kicked and thrashed against its chest while itdragged him toward the ocean, wings beating the

humid air, until both vanished over the waterline. No body was recovered. Only blood on the stone steps. We had charted our course assuming the coast and its stories were behind us. We were mistaken on both counts.

Two nights past Pemba, the creature boarded us. We heard it first as a wet tearing sound near the cargo hold, then a screeching — high, metallic, bouncing off steel bulkheads in a way that made the sound seem to come from everywhere at once. Deckhand Juma dropped his lantern and ran. He said he saw a black mass detach from the rigging: one eye, movement like a man but folding like a bat, landing on the starboard rail with wings dripping seaweed and something darker. It looked at him. Then it smiled. I use that word carefully. It was a human expression on a face that had no right to make one. Juma froze. It lunged — not to kill, but to take. It dragged him toward the rail. We fired flares. The light made it hiss but it did not release him. It dropped into the dark water pulling him under. We never found him. Only his cap, torn in half, floating near the wake. The ocean did not return him.

Captain’s Mate Omondi organised the first strike. We rigged harpoons with barbed tips, soaked in kerosene and salt, on the theory that fire and corrosion could hold it. We waited on deck with shotguns, floodlights, and netting. It came at midnight — not from the sky but from below. It crawled up the hull like an insect, joints articulating backward, claws scoring rust and paint as it climbed. We fired. The buckshot passed through it as if through smoke given the shape of a living thing. It dissolved and

reformed behind Omondi, wrapped its wings around him, and whispered. In Swahili. It called him by his mother’s name. Then it squeezed until his ribs cracked. We shot again. It laughed — a sound that echoed in our skulls long after the deck was empty. We learned that night that violence only feeds it.

The engineer’s team laced the deck with gelignite wired to remote detonators. We lured it with raw fish and bloodied rags. It stepped into the trap with the unhurried confidence of something that has seen traps before and found them amusing. We triggered the charge. The blast tore a hole through the steel plating and sent a column of smoke forty feet into the air. When it cleared, the creature stood in the crater unharmed — wings scorched at the tips, one eye reflecting the emergency lighting — and it picked up a shard of torn metal and pressed it slowly against its own chest. Then it flew straight upward and vanished into the low cloud. We had nothing left in the armory worth trying. It was not flesh. It was fear given a body, and our arsenals were built for flesh.

We made port at Stone Town hoping the creature had stayed with Pemba. It had not. A boy at the gangway asked whether we had bats in the rigging. When our boatswain laughed, the boy did not. He only said the name. By evening every tea stall along the harbor was speaking it. Old men sat in courtyards with charcoal fires between their knees and told us what to do after dark with the weary precision of men reporting weather, not ghost stories. They said the same things the Pemba men had said. Same creature, same eye, same word.

Our carpenter Ellis and the cook Nuru went ashore with lanterns to prove, as Ellis said, that nonsense feeds on empty heads. They returned before the moon was high, both pale. Ellis had a cut across his cheek. Nuru sat with his back to the galley wall and rocked. At last they told it: at the edge of Stone Town they had heard a scream that was neither human nor animal but something between a bull’s bellow and a woman’s cry. A figure dropped from the darkness — broad as a man, wings too large, the membrane of them pulsing in the moonlight, one eye white and glistening. Ellis threw a stone. The creature turned its head toward him with the slow deliberate motion of something that has never needed to hurry. It opened its mouth. What came out, Nuru said, was a sound that should not exist in any throat. Then it moved inland, and behind it they heard a door torn apart, and shouting, and then silence.

Every dog on the lower road barked at once and then went silent so suddenly the silence itself felt struck. The lamps along the pier blew out one by one with no wind to explain it. The first alarm came from a fish warehouse where two stevedores were loading crates. We went in force. Inside we found claw marks on the rafters, a smell of wet earth and old meat, a crate crushed inward as if by a great falling weight. And on the wall beside the door, smeared in something dark: a handprint. Too large for any man. Too long in the fingers.

It came to the ship at two bells past midnight. The watchman shouted once. By the time we reached the deck it was on the rail, hunched against the moon, wings folding and unfolding, the single eye moving

from face to face with an intelligence that was the worst part of it. Not simply monstrous. Malicious. Knowing. The mate fired and the shot spun it sideways; it screeched and dropped to the deck with the weight of wet hide on planks. Ellis rushed it with an iron bar. One wing struck him and sent him sliding ten feet. The cook swung a cleaver and caught nothing. Then it vaulted into the rigging and a hundred bats rose with it as though summoned. When they cleared, the thing was gone. Ellis’s shoulder was broken. No one spoke for a long time.

Our Bosun Saidi gathered elders from the dockside village. They drew protective circles on the deck in crushed coral and ash and said the old words. We stood inside the markings breathing smoke, waiting. It came at three in the morning and stepped over the chalk as though it were air. It touched Saidi’s forehead and he collapsed weeping, speaking of things he could not make us understand. It left without taking him. It did not need to. Breaking a man’s mind is a kind of taking all the same.

A sheikh came aboard and recited verses. A priest blessed the hatches. A fisherman brought herbs. No one mocked any of it. A local healer — an old woman with milky eyes — came aboard unbidden and told us the creature was a spirit of betrayal, a punisher of those who dismiss old agreements. She said it had been bound once in a brass vessel and sunk off Fort Jesus, and that a fisherman had dredged it up. Our only safety was to leave, and even then it might follow. We tried one last trap — a goat at the fort’s old cistern, paraffin soaked into the ground, blasting caps from our stores. It came at sunset. It

fed on the goat. We triggered the charge. The explosion sent fire two hundred feet into the air. When the smoke cleared, it was sitting on the edge of the crater licking blood from its claws, its single eye finding me on the ridge. It laughed — a wet clicking — and rose into the air. We ran.

We weighed anchor before dawn. The engines coughed to life. No one looked over the rail. We had recorded everything in those last days: every sighting, every attack, every failure. The men we lost. The wounds that did not respond to bullets or blades or fire or prayer. We wrote until the ink ran low and the pages curled from humidity. Documentation became our only armor. We could not stop it. We could only witness it and leave the testimony for whoever came after.

The harbor watchman came down to see us off. He touched the rail and said: “It has shown you enough to follow in your dreams. Do not answer if it calls your name.” The captain asked whether it would return to these waters. The old man shrugged. “Perhaps to Pemba. Perhaps to Mombasa. Perhaps wherever men boast too loudly of killing what they do not understand.”

Tanzania receded into the haze. The Indian Ocean opened before us, vast and without opinion. We did not look back. We knew it was still there. Some demons cannot be killed. They can only be outrun. And even then — they fly faster.

— Captain Odongo Baraka, M. V. Kilindi Star, Reg. No. DS-1967-318 Sealed and witnessed, Dar es Salaam Harbour Authority, 14.xi.1974

chapters.title: Mbwiri
chapters.text:
✝

Central African Republic · Account of Resident Aid Workers

The humidity in the Central African Republic does not merely cling to the skin. It seeped into the marrow, a breathing, living weight that made every step feel like wading through warm ash. We were missionaries, though the paperwork called us humanitarian workers — a distinction that matters until the moment it stops mattering entirely. Our mandate was clinical and sterile: vaccinate children, treat adults, educate the locals on the invisible enemies of polio, autism, cerebral malaria. The village, however, answered to older gods. They preferred the drumbeat of the shaman to our syringes, the smoke of burning herbs to our antiseptic wipes.

I should tell you about Kilumë first, because most people know that name. An East African spirit among the Kamba people — you summon it with dance, with communal rhythm, with bodies that surrender to exhaustion until something else steps inside. It is a consensual occupation, almost beautiful in its own terrible way. The Mbwiri is different. I know that because of my first encounter with it. It does not wait for an invitation. It does not ask.

Jake was my opposite in every meaningful way. He had the kind of faith that buzzed under his skin like electricity looking for a ground. The kind that made him touch things he should not have touched. We had been in the village of Mbaïki for three days when he suggested the walk, wiping sweat from his brow, restless in the way of a man whose body has not yet understood where it is.

Neither of us spoke French, and the afternoon heat had driven the usefulness from us both, so we wandered the periphery of the village where the structures grew older and the trees pressed closer. There were objects tied to posts and strung between branches — carved

figures with hollowed eyes, bundles of feathers and dried grass bound with red thread, clay pots sealed with wax and something darker. Jake moved through it all like a tourist at a carnival.

He lifted a mask from where it hung — a face of twisted, exaggerated anguish, the wood distorted as though in the process of becoming something other than wood. He pressed it to his own face and looked at me through hollow eyes.

“Reminds me of tales we were told,” he said, his voice muffled and suddenly thin. “Kill me.”

He laughed. I did not.

He was reaching for something else — a carved figure, dark and smooth from years of handling — when the man appeared. He came without sound from behind the largest hut, bare-chested, wearing cloth of deep indigo at the waist, his skin dusted with ash and clay, his eyes carrying the particular stillness of a man who has spent long years in communion with things that do not speak in any human language. He was a shaman, and he spoke immediately — syllables that ran beneath French, beneath anything our translator had taught us, sounds that seemed to land in the chest rather than the ear.

Then I heard it from inside the hut. Not a groan exactly. Something rhythmic, something that began in the throat and descended into the body’s lower registers, a sound that raised every hair on my arms and kept them raised.

“Who’s in there?” I asked.

The shaman’s arm shot out, palm flat. His eyes were wet and red- rimmed and absolutely afraid — not of me, I understood later, but of what he saw standing just behind my shoulder, or perhaps inside my companion’s eyes.

“Go away,” he said. The only English he offered us. His gaze moved to Jake, and something shifted in his face. A door closing. A light going out.

We reported it. Of course we reported it. I had seen things in my own country — healers who exploited suffering, tradition used as cover for neglect. By dusk the boy had been pulled from the hut: emaciated, eyes rolled back, his small body drumming the packed earth. The UN medevac chopper carried him to the nearest regional hospital. The shaman was handcuffed and put in a Land Rover, his face carved from cold stone.

But just before the vehicle pulled out, he looked at us. At me first — a long, measuring stare that felt like a needle finding a vein. Then at Jake.

His composure cracked.

The fear that flooded his face was not the fear of a man facing arrest. It was the fear of a man who has just seen the fire inside someone else’s house and understands with absolute certainty that no one inside knows it is burning.

Jake didn’t notice. He was rubbing his temples, complaining of a heaviness that had settled into his bones without warning.

We found the boy’s parents afterward. The father said, in halting French, that the Mbwiri would not be pleased to be driven from its house. That a guest sent away without proper rites must find another home. I asked him what the Mbwiri was, exactly, and he looked at me the way adults look at children who have asked an obvious question at the wrong moment.

“The spirit that seizes the body,” he said. “The one that dances.”

The word stayed with me through supper. It followed me to the dormitory — a concrete schoolhouse smelling of chalk dust and old rain — and into my bunk, where I lay and listened to the ceiling fan click its metronome rhythm, counting toward something I could not name.

Jake didn’t eat. He climbed into the lower bunk fully dressed and was silent.

I don’t know what woke me.

Not a sound — an absence. The specific absence of Jake’s snoring, that reliable, maddening machinery I had fallen asleep to every night for three weeks. I lay in the dark and listened and heard nothing where something should have been.

I leaned over the edge of the bunk. The lower bed was empty. The door at the far end of the dormitory stood open, a dark rectangle that seemed, in my half-woken state, to breathe.

I found him in the courtyard, on all fours in the red dirt.

He was moving. Not convulsing — moving, deliberately, his spine undulating in a rhythm that bore no relationship to any motion his body had a right to make. His back rose and fell in long, fluid waves. He was chanting.

“Eh, Mbwiri—”

Then other words. A language I did not recognize and have not since identified. The sounds rose from his throat in registers that belonged to no single human voice — there were harmonics in it, undertones, as though the syllables were being spoken through him rather than by him, his larynx rewired by invisible hands.

He rose.

He stood with his arms spread wide, palms upturned, head thrown back. And then he danced. His shoulders first — that violent, isolated tremor — then his chest, his whole upper body shaking at a frequency that should have been exhausting and was instead utterly sustained, perfectly rhythmic, ancient beyond any choreography I had witnessed. He bowed toward something in front of him. Something I could not see. Something that, for one terrible moment, I felt was present — vast and patient and deeply, deeply attentive.

His eyes were closed. His face was slack and peaceful. The body was a vessel, and whatever filled it danced with the grotesque precision of something that has been performing these movements since long before there were words for them.

I called his name. I crossed the distance between us and grabbed his shoulder.

He turned on me with a speed that belonged to no man I had ever touched — his hand finding my throat before I’d processed the movement — and then I had his wrists and he was straining against me, his eyes still sealed as though sutured shut. I held him. I spoke his name again. I told him we needed to go inside.

The tension left him all at once, like a rope cut. He swayed.

His eyes opened.

“Wetin be happening here?” He blinked at the dark, at his own hands still held in mine, with the expression of someone who has surfaced too quickly from deep water and cannot yet account for the shore.

Jake remembered nothing. Not the words, not the language, not the invisible master he had been prostrating himself before. I walked him back to the dormitory and put him to bed and climbed to my own bunk and lay in the dark telling myself the rational things: somnambulism, dissociation, stress acting on an exhausted mind.

Then the bed began to shake.

Not the building. Not a tremor. My body — the fit beginning in my legs and moving upward with the terrible, purposeful efficiency of a thing that knows exactly what it is doing. My jaw locked. My back arched off the mattress. And in the last splinter of clarity before the darkness closed entirely, I felt it: something cold and precise entering through the base of my skull, spreading through my sinuses, filling the hollows behind my eyes. It tasted of ash, old copper, dried river mud. It did not speak. It did not need to. It simply settled into me the way a tenant settles into a long-familiar room — moving the furniture, learning the dimensions, making itself comfortable in the space where I used to live.

I understood then why the shaman had built the hut. Why he stayed with the afflicted through the curing. It was not medicine. It was not even ritual, not exactly. It was negotiation — a long, patient conversation with something that did not experience time the way we do, conducted in a language made entirely of the body.

The dance does not ask permission. It is not a violence and it is not a seduction. It is simply a recognition. The Mbwiri notices you, and in being noticed you become a door, and the door swings open in directions you did not know your architecture contained.

My mouth opened. From my own throat, in a voice I did not recognize, came the syllables:

Eh, Mbwiri.

They tasted familiar. They had always been familiar.

In the morning Jake was already outside when I woke on the floor, my fingernails split, my spine aching as though I had been bent backward over something for hours. I found him standing at the edge of the treeline, perfectly still, his back to the compound, facing the forest.

He was not moving. He was not chanting. He was simply standing there the way a man stands when he is listening to something very far away with the whole of himself.

I called his name. He turned and smiled, and the smile was his, mostly his, almost entirely his.

“Good morning,” he said. “I slept like the dead.”

I looked past him into the tree line. One of the masks hung there that I had not noticed before — dark wood, hollow eyes, a mouth open in an expression that was not quite anguish and not quite hunger but occupied the precise space between them.

I did not remember seeing it yesterday.

I did not ask about it.

Some doors, once you understand their dimensions, you choose not to look at directly. You learn to navigate by peripheral vision, to speak in careful, measured sentences, to sleep in small pieces and monitor the space beneath you before allowing your eyes to close.

The Mbwiri is patient. It has always been patient. It does not require your belief or your fear or even your awareness. It only requires your body — the architecture of bone and nerve and breath that you have been walking around in your entire life without ever once questioning who else might find it habitable.

I still feel it sometimes. In the pause between heartbeats. In the moment before sleep, when the body relaxes its grip on its own musculature and something else tests the slack. In the way my feet sometimes move, very slightly, to a rhythm no one else can hear.

I have learned not to follow the rhythm. I have learned to wait it out.

But on certain nights, in the hours when the ceiling fan clicks its slow metronome and the dark presses close and warm, I hear the syllables forming in the back of my throat like a stone rolling uphill:

Eh, Mbwiri.

And my shoulders begin, very gently, to shake.

Central African Republic · Account of Resident Aid Workers

The humidity in the Central African Republic does not merely cling to the skin. It seeped into the marrow, a breathing, living weight that made every step feel like wading through warm ash. We were missionaries, though the paperwork called us humanitarian workers —…

chapters.title: Bendu Sudan
chapters.text:
UNSOLVED

Case file extract · Monrovia, Liberia

CASE NO.: LR-1994-0732 STATION: Monrovia Central COMPLAINANT: Withheld at family's request STATUS: Closed — Insufficient Evidence

The legend of Bendu Sudan was the kind of story told in low voices when the light was failing and the room had begun to feel like it was listening.

My mother told it to me in pieces, never all at once— as if speaking the whole thing in one sitting might call something toward the door. A young woman of eighteen. A powerful man. A pregnancy hidden in shame. A crude abortion that left her in a coma while the man counted his relief and called it solved. She woke up in a funeral home and was killed a second time by the man paid to bury what the first man had broken. But her grandmother had warned her long before that death would not be the end of her story.

So Bendu came back wrong.

Not alive. Not quite dead. Something wearing the shape of a woman, walking the streets of Monrovia with the patience of a thing that no longer had anywhere else to be. They said she seduced men. They

said she took from them what they had taken from her. They said those who truly saw her never survived long enough to describe what they had seen.

I had filed all of that under childhood noise by the time I was twenty-four, out in the world and behaving like nothing in it had teeth.

It was a Friday in Monrovia—the kind of Friday Monrovia does well, hot and thick and charged with the feeling that the night belongs to you. There were four of us: Alex Kollie, who was the loudest person in any room and wore it like a crown; Emeka, our Nigerian, who had come for a construction contract and stayed because he discovered he liked who he was here; Ronald, who grew up in a house where you didn’t whistle after dark and who we never took seriously; and me.

We ended up at Club Mirage, tucked off Broad Street like it was hiding from something. Alex had already mapped which table had sightlines to the whole floor before we sat down. Emeka had already identified three women worth speaking to. Ronald was already warning us about something that none of us were listening to.

“Bendu Sudan,” he said, over the bass, “is said not only to haunt roads but inns and bars. Places where men go hunting.”

“Perfect,” Alex said. “I hope she has good taste.”

I laughed. Emeka laughed. Ronald watched us the way a man watches children play near a hole in the ice.

The trouble came an hour later, wearing the shape of an old man.

He occupied a stool at the far end of the bar where the light barely reached—a small, dry person in a shirt that was wrong for the heat, with eyes that caught white at the edges in a way that had nothing to do with age. He was not drinking. He was watching the room with the settled ownership of something that does not need to announce itself. On the bar before him sat a small iron object, rusted, shaped like a closed eye, which he rolled slowly between two fingers without ever looking at it.

Emeka walked into him. A graze, a shoulder. “Sorry, papa.” He was already moving. The old man did not react. He simply turned his head and looked at our table. At Alex specifically, with the flat, considered attention of a man consulting a list he had carried for a long time.

Alex caught the look and returned it with a grin and a raised glass—a joke, a greeting, the particular confidence of a man who has never once been made to feel small. The old man regarded him the way you regard a signature on a contract that has already been signed. Then he set the iron piece on the bar, rose without sound, and disappeared toward the back corridor.

He was never seen again.

Alex had not noticed the iron piece. He was watching a woman.

She sat alone at a table near the wall, dressed differently from everyone around her—no glitter, no performance. Dark clothes and hair arranged with an almost old-fashioned care. She held her stillness like a stone holds heat, and the music seemed to bend

away from her. She was beautiful the way old grief is beautiful—completely, and without any interest in being observed.

Alex sent her a drink through a waitress and came back grinning.

Ronald was staring at the empty barstool. “Where did he go?” he said, almost to himself.

Nobody answered. Nobody had paid the old man enough attention to miss him.

Forty minutes later, the drink had not moved. Alex went to the counter to ask. He came back and stood at our table without sitting down, and something in the architecture of his face had changed.

“The waitress I sent,” he said slowly. “Management says there’s no waitress by that name working tonight.”

“Maybe you got the name wrong,” Emeka said.

Alex shook his head once. “And the table I sent the drink to.” He paused. The pause was too long. “They say no one has been sitting there all evening.”

The bass kept pressing through the floor. Someone somewhere laughed loudly and too long.

“I looked at her,” Alex said. “She looked back at me. Her eyes were not right. They were like two holes and something behind them was watching through.” He stopped. Reached for his drink and set it back down without touching it to his lips. “I’m going home.”

He said it pleasantly, the way you say things when the alternative is falling apart in public. He picked up his jacket, straightened it with both hands, and walked out of the club looking like a man keeping himself together through sheer force of pride.

That was Thursday.

By Saturday morning he was calling from a number I did not recognise. His voice arrived through the phone wet and distant, like he was speaking from the bottom of a stairwell. He said to come and get him. He told me where he was.

A cemetery.

He did not know which one. He had woken up there among the stones. The last memory he had was lying in his apartment, flat on his back in the dark, listening to something drag itself slowly across his bedroom floor.

Ronald and I found him sitting on a broken headstone near the gate, elbows on his knees, staring at the red earth between his bare feet. His shirt was torn at the shoulder. Dirt was packed under his fingernails. When he finally opened his right hand to show us, there were three marks across his palm—not cuts, not scratches. Punctures, curved and deliberate, arranged like fingernail crescents pressed upward through the skin from below.

He closed his hand before we could look too long.

“She was in my room,” he said. “Beside the bed. She said my name. She said it exactly right.” He looked at the graves around him as though they were

familiar. “She smelled like old flowers. The kind left in a room after everyone who remembers them is gone.”

Ronald made a sound in his throat that was almost a word.

“She said I owe her.” Alex’s voice fractured slightly at the edges. “I don’t know what I took. I don’t understand what that means.” He looked at me then, and I saw it—Alex Kollie, who had never respected anything he couldn’t see, who laughed at darkness like it was performed for his entertainment, was genuinely and completely afraid. “The old man at the bar,” he said. “He put something down. Something small. Metal.”

Ronald stood very still. His lips moved without sound, like he was counting something terrible.

We brought Alex home. By nightfall his phone went to voicemail on the first ring. The following morning we broke the door in. Every window in the flat was latched shut. The curtains moved anyway, steady and slow, as though the room were breathing. Alex stood in the center, barefoot, soaked through with sweat, staring down the hallway with his arms hanging at his sides like he had forgotten they were attached.

Above the bedroom door, written in something dark and thick that had not yet fully dried, were four words:

SHE ALREADY KNOWS YOU. Below the words was a handprint. Not pressed against the surface of the wall. Through it—as if a palm had pushed in from the other side and the plaster had simply accepted it.

Emeka called the police.

We sat in Monrovia Central Station for two hours beneath a ceiling fan that rotated with the dull resignation of something that had stopped believing in its own purpose. Then an officer led us to Chief Kortu, a thick-necked, slow-moving man who had the face of someone who had not been surprised since before the war and had no intention of starting now. He read Emeka’s statement. Read it again. Set it flat with two fingers.

“Gentlemen,” he said. “You are telling me a spirit followed your friend home, inscribed your friend’s wall, and is now—what? Collecting him? This is the case you are filing.”

“We are telling you what we found,” I said.

“What I am hearing,” Chief Kortu replied, “is three young men constructing a story to cover something they would rather not explain. Debt. Violence. A transaction that went badly. These are real. Spirits are not.” He reached for his pen. “Start from the beginning. Every time the word ghost appears in this account, I will ask you to leave.”

I looked at Emeka. Emeka looked at me.

Alex sat between us without speaking, staring at the floor between his bare feet. His wounded hand rested open on his knee, palm upward, the three curved marks dark and deliberate against his skin.

I opened my mouth.

The chief of police stopped writing.

Not suddenly—slowly, the way a person stops when something in the room changes without making a sound. His pen hovered above the page. He was looking at the window behind us. Not through it. At it. At the glass, and what the glass was showing him.

His face changed. Just enough.

“What—” he began.

Every light in Monrovia Central Police Station went out simultaneously, and in the half-second before the darkness became total, I turned toward the window.

In the glass, reflected perfectly, stood a woman in a dark dress with her head tilted at an angle that no living neck would allow. She was not looking at the chief.

She was looking at Alex.

And she was smiling with the slow, unhurried patience of something that has never once been wrong about how a story ends.

Alex made a sound I will not try to put into words.

It was the sound of a man who had just been recognised.

chapters.title: Kony
chapters.text:
CLASSIFIED

Do not speak the name aloud — Northern Uganda / South Sudan Border Region

Do not say his name near running water.

Do not say it near a fire, because fire carries sound across distances that physics cannot explain, and there are things in the dark between the trees that have been listening for decades, that have learned to love the frequency of that name the way a dog loves the whistle only it can hear.

I will tell you this story once. If you hear it again, it will mean you were not supposed to hear it the first time.

The day Joseph Kony was born, the rain in Odek fell upward.

No one speaks of this. But the old women remember. They remember how the water beaded upward from the red soil and climbed into a sky that was the color of a bruise, and how the midwife who delivered him emerged from the hut thirty minutes later with her hair entirely white, though she had been twenty-two years old when she walked in.

She died the following Thursday. She did not get sick. She simply stopped. Sat down in the shade of an acacia and folded into herself like a letter being sealed.

The thing that was born that day was called Joseph. But Joseph was only a coat. A coat of flesh and name and Acholi blood, worn over something that had been waiting in the red soil for a very long time.

He left school, they say. They make it sound like a decision. Like a boy yawning, stretching, walking out of a classroom into the afternoon sun.

It was not like that.

He went into the bush for three weeks and no one saw him. When he came back, his shadow was wrong. Not much — just enough that dogs noticed. Dogs would not approach him. Goats would scatter. Children, who have not yet been taught not to see things, would stop mid-play and watch him with the stillness of small animals near a predator. Ask them what they saw and they would say, very quietly, that there were too many people walking inside him. Too many shapes behind his eyes.

He became a healer. Of course he did. The thing wearing Joseph’s skin understood that access is everything. You want to touch a community at its roots — tend to its sick. Lay your hands on the feverish. Breathe your oil onto the suffering. Let them feel that something immense is flowing through your palms.

It was not love flowing through his palms.

But it was power. And from a distance, the two look identical.

Alice Lakwena came and went like a fever that breaks without curing anything.

She was magnificent. She was aflame. She told the Acholi people — ground down by Obote’s fall, suffocating under Museveni’s boot — that God had put a rifle in her hand and pointed it south. Her warriors anointed themselves with shea oil. They marched into gunfire. Some of them survived in ways that could not be explained. Most of them did not.

When she fled, broken, into exile, the thing inside Joseph leaned forward.

It had been watching her. Studying her. Not admiringly — the way a scientist studies a specimen. It understood something Alice had not understood, which is that faith is most useful when it is also terror. Alice had given people something to believe in. The thing inside Joseph would give them something they could not stop believing in, even when they wanted to. Even after they had tried to run.

This is the part of the story where the human beings become something else.

The children came first. Not all at once. One by one, sliding out of the villages at night like teeth worked loose from a jaw. They would wake the next morning and a child would be missing, and everyone would know, and no one would say it, because saying it invited the attention of whatever had taken the child.

They were brought to him in clearings that felt wrong — clearings where the grass grew in the wrong direction, where the air tasted of iron and old hymns. He looked at each child with those flat-water eyes, and the children felt themselves being emptied. Whatever was theirs — the mother’s face, the smell of

the cooking fire, the particular weight of being themselves — it drained out through the soles of their feet into the soil.

What filled the empty space was the ritual.

The cross drawn in oil on the forehead. On the chest. On each shoulder. On the barrel of the rifle. Precise, always precise, because precision is the difference between a sacrament and a gesture.

“The oil is the power of the Holy Spirit,” the demon told them. And then it gave them evidence.

Because the children who forgot the ritual did die in the next firefight. Every time. The demon arranged this. It is easy to prove a theology when you control the battlefield. It is easy to make faith unshakeable when failure to believe is punishable by death.

The children stopped thinking. The oil replaced thinking. The cross replaced longing. The ritual replaced the self.

And the demon moved among them like a cold front, invisible, organizing, never quite there.

From the 1990s onward, the villages learned a new grammar.

The sentence it spoke was written in flesh.

Ears first. Sliced at the root with blades that had been blessed — if you can call what the demon did a blessing — in ceremonies conducted at the lip of the jungle at three in the morning. Ears taken because the demon had a theology of faces, a belief that God’s true image was buried beneath the human features, and each removal brought it closer to the

divine. The nose next. The wet, quiet pop of cartilage. Lips peeled back until the skull grinned through. Hands sometimes left intact, deliberately, so the survivor could touch their own new face in the dark and understand what they had been turned into.

A message. Every mutilated body was a sentence. And the sentence always said the same thing: I am not a man. I am a grammar. I am something older than law, older than mercy, older than the God you were taught to pray to.

The demon told its soldiers it was theology. The soldiers believed it. They had to.

The oil was still on their skin.

He did not command. He announced.

Generals have strategy rooms, radios, chains of command. The demon had none of these. Orders arrived in the dreams of captains, spoken in a voice that woke them sweating, certain, never doubting. Some commanders swore they received instructions through the shaking of a lieutenant who went rigid and spoke in a voice not his own and then collapsed and remembered nothing.

Captain Sunday — a man who had killed more human beings than he could count past thirty — told a BBC camera crew with the absolute serenity of total belief that the demon could not die. That he had seen bullets pass through it. That it could call a swarm of ten thousand bees out of a hollow tree and direct them with the precision of a conductor’s baton.

The captain was not lying. He was describing what he had seen. And what he had seen was real, because the demon made it real. It had spent decades mastering the art of making the impossible appear on schedule.

The rains came when it needed to disappear.

Not the polite, seasonal rains. Sudden rains. Violent rains that turned roads into the bottom of rivers and drowned the signal from every radio on the continent. Government soldiers would have him surrounded — helicopters overhead, coordinates confirmed, fingers on triggers — and the sky would split, and the sky would pour, and when it stopped, the camp would be empty.

Only footprints. Always footprints leading inward.

None leading out.

Once, in a clearing deep in what the maps called the Central African Republic, a Ugandan tracker found something carved in the wet soil in the center of a space that should have been unreachable. The carving was still fresh, the edges not yet blurred by rain. He would not tell anyone what shape it was. He quit the army the following week. He moved to a city and never went near the jungle again and never slept without a light on.

But one person heard him describe it once, late, when drink had loosened the lock on his mouth. He said it was a cross. And around the cross, spreading outward in every direction, was something that looked like writing in a language he had never seen. And beneath the cross, barely visible, two depressions in the soil.

Footprints.

Going down.

In 2006, the demon gave its interview.

It sat before the microphone and spoke in the voice of a reasonable man. It said: I cannot cut the ear of my brother. I cannot kill the eye of my brother. It blamed the state. It blamed Museveni. It said the mutilations were a government operation, performed by soldiers who then pointed north and said: the LRA.

And here is the thing that will keep you up at night — the thing that makes this worse than any simple monster story:

It was calm. It was articulate. And for exactly four and a half seconds, in a studio in Kampala where journalists sat with their recordings, every single person present felt, before the rational mind could intervene, that it might be telling the truth.

That is the demon’s true power. Not the bees. Not the rain. Not the oil.

The ability to make you doubt the horror you already know.

They say he is down to fewer than a hundred men now.

They say the US government has declared him no longer a threat.

They say the jungle has reduced him, the years have reduced him, the world has moved on.

They say this in offices with electric lights and armed guards and systems of accountability designed by people who believe that monsters follow declining trajectories.

They do not say it near running water.

They do not say it near a fire at night.

And none of them — not one — has been into the jungle to confirm.

I will tell you what I believe.

I believe the demon is still there. Not because it needs an army. Not because it requires territory or logistics or the infrastructure of violence. But because the demon is a story now, and stories do not diminish, they condense. They become more concentrated as they age. Every year of absence makes the next appearance more impossible to explain.

A man who survives thirty years in the teeth of the modern world, who evades satellites and drones and the combined military apparatus of three nations, who leaves no trail, who appears in no photograph taken in the last decade — that man has either died, or he has become something that does not need to be seen to exist.

The demon does not need a body anymore.

It lives in the place between the last moment the birds go quiet and the first moment the machete sounds.

It lives in the oil still on children’s fingers.

It lives in the cross drawn in soil that no boot left behind.

It lives in the question no one has ever been able to answer — not the generals, not the journalists, not the governments with their satellites and their warrants:

Where is he?

Because the question keeps him alive. The question is him. He is not a man in a jungle anymore. He is the sound of leaves parting when there is no wind. He is the shadow on the wall of a hut that no candle throws. He is the name spoken in whispers by people who have never met him, in villages he has never visited, in languages he does not speak.

He is the thing that happens to a monster when the monster becomes a word.

And words, as every demon knows, are immortal.

Do not say his name near running water.

Do not say it near a fire.

And if the birds go quiet while you are reading this —

do not look up.
