chapters.title: The Mat and the Lantern
chapters.text:
A homecoming tale, Lagos · as the elders still tell it

Nobody tells you that coming home can feel like trespassing.

We had been away long enough that Nigeria had started to exist only in the small rituals my mother kept — the way she pounded yam with a particular fury, the Yoruba she slipped into when she was angry, the smell of ẹ̀ fọ́ riro on Sunday mornings in a London flat where the neighbours definitely complained. When Baba finally said we were going back to visit the village — not Lagos, not Abuja, the village — my sister Jovial and I looked at each other the way children do when they understand something enormous is about to happen and there is nothing to be done about it.

Jovial was six. Small for her age, with eyes that always looked like they were solving something. She had been born in England, which meant she had never felt red dust under her feet, never slapped a mosquito at dusk, never known a darkness so complete it had texture.

I was fourteen. Old enough to be embarrassed by my own foreignness, young enough to still be frightened by stories. We were the Tokunbo children — returned goods, shiny but second-hand — and the village would know it the moment we opened our mouths.

The journey from Lagos took hours. Each mile made the world thinner, stranger. Roads dissolved from tarmac to cracked laterite to red dust that coated our teeth and settled in our hair. Streetlights disappeared. Buildings gave way to huts. Then even the road seemed to lose confidence, narrowing to a rough path of broken stone that the car swallowed with a series of jolts so violent my mother made a sound I had never heard her make before.

By the time we arrived, the city had become theoretical.

The compound was my uncle’s — Uncle Sayo’s — a sprawling, slightly tired collection of buildings arranged around a central courtyard that had once been grand and now wore their age the way old men do, with dignity and without complaint. Cousins everywhere. My older cousin Feni, seventeen and untouchable, who looked at me the way people look at things they find faintly ridiculous. Tuma, who was twenty, studying medicine in Ibadan, and who moved through the world with a quiet authority I found both admirable and frightening. And the small children — names I was still learning — who ran between adults’ legs and disappeared and reappeared like they had their own private geography.

The generator died at ten and took the lights with it. I had not prepared for what the dark looked like here. Not the city dark of London, which is never truly dark, which is always threaded through with orange streetlight and the blue suggestion of screens. This dark was complete. It pressed against the windows. It settled into the room like something that lived there and was merely tolerating your presence.

I had not prepared for the bush, either.

It was right there. A dark, breathing wall of trees and undergrowth that began exactly where the compound ended, close enough that on a still night you could hear it thinking.

It was Uncle Sayo who told us about the Egbére.

We were sitting outside on the third evening — the adults on chairs, we children on mats on the ground, the air thick with woodsmoke and the smell of something sweet I never managed to identify. The generator hummed. Someone had made zobo, and the children’s mouths were stained red from it. One of the younger cousins had been asking about the lantern — not ours, the one that seemed to

appear each evening at the edge of the path, its light a shade of green that belonged to no natural flame — and Uncle Sayo looked at it for a long moment before he smiled.

It was not an entirely reassuring smile.

“That,” he said, “is not ours.”

He waited until we were all very still.

“You children born abroad,” he said, “you think bush baby is a cute animal. Big eyes, soft fur. Like that cartoon — Mort, from Madagascar. Very sweet.” He shook his head slowly. “That is not what lives in this bush.”

Jovial had climbed into my mother’s lap without anyone noticing. My mother’s hand went to her back automatically, the way hands do when they know before the mind does that something needs protecting.

“The Egbére,” Uncle Sayo said, lowering his voice until we had to lean forward to catch it, “is a gnome. A dwarf. It wanders the forest day and night and it is always weeping — tears on its face, snot running from its nose, mouth open in a misery so old it has become its only weather. It carries a mat. A tattered, filthy mat it drags through the undergrowth. And a green lantern.” He nodded toward the edge of the compound.

Nobody looked. We were all looking at him.

“Why is it crying?” my cousin Bola asked. He was nine. He still believed that things had reasons.

“Nobody knows,” Uncle Sayo said. “That is the terrible part. It is not sad the way you or I are sad. It is angry. There is a foul mood in it that has lasted its entire existence and shows no sign of lifting. And its anger is not like our anger, which comes and passes. The Egbére’s anger has no object. It does not hate you specifically. It hates that you exist. And it does not forgive that.”

He paused.

“It walks up to people’s doors at night. It stands in the dark and screams like an infant — like a newborn — right there on your threshold. And when you go outside to investigate, when you walk into the bush following that sound...” He let the sentence end where it ended.

“You don’t come back,” I said.

“You don’t come back,” he agreed.

Feni laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that is performing its own confidence. “Uncle, it is like the leprechaun,” she said. “You told us this before. A little man with a pot of gold.”

Uncle Sayo looked at her the way you look at someone who has said something they will one day regret. “A leprechaun is sometimes kind,” he said. “A leprechaun can be bargained with, tricked, appeased. The Egbére has never been kind. It has no gold. The only thing it offers is this: if you can steal its mat — that ruined mat it carries — you will either become immensely rich or you will die. Those are the only options. Many have chosen to believe in the first one.” A pause. “They are not here to report back.”

“Has anyone ever seen it?” I asked. My voice came out smaller than I intended.

Uncle Sayo considered this for a moment, looking into his cup. “Those who have seen its face,” he said, “they have not seen another day.”

The silence that followed was not the comfortable silence of an evening winding down. It was the kind of silence that has weight.

“And it doesn’t leave anything behind,” Uncle Sayo added, almost to himself. “The Egbére doesn’t devour slowly. It swallows you whole. There is no body. No remains. One moment you are there. The next you are simply inside something that has been hungry since long before your grandfather’s grandfather drew breath.”

"Bed time!" Aunt Remi called from inside.

We scattered.

I found Feni walking with theatrical calm along the footpath between the main house and the sleeping quarters, her torch cutting a pale stripe through the dark.

“Don’t be scared,” she said, which is the thing people say when they want you to be scared. “It’s just a story.”

“Your uncle doesn’t tell it like a story.”

She bumped my shoulder. “Uncle Sayo likes to watch your face.” But she didn’t look back toward the tree line, I noticed. She kept her eyes very deliberately forward.

Then we heard it.

Not loud. Not even clear. Less a sound than the memory of one — the way a sound sometimes arrives before you’re certain you’ve heard it. From somewhere beyond the fence, from somewhere inside the dark mass of the bush: a cry. Thin. Rhythmic. An infant working its way up to something worse.

I stopped walking.

Feni kept going. “Probably a bird,” she said, without turning around.

The sound came again. Not louder. Just more present. More certain of itself, like something that had decided to stop being subtle.

I went to find Tuma.

She was sitting on the edge of a cot, plaiting her hair with practiced hands, the kerosene lamp making shadows lean against the walls. She looked up when I came in. She saw my face. She did not laugh. That was the first thing I registered — she did not laugh.

“You heard something in the bush,” she said. Not a question.

“Like a baby crying. Very quiet.”

Tuma’s hands slowed in her hair. She looked toward the window, which was shuttered but not latched. Then she pointed — not at the window but past it, in the direction of the trees, at a specific place in the tree line as if she had looked at it before, as if she knew it the way you know a wound you keep returning to.

“There was a baby abandoned in that bush,” she said. “Years ago. Left to die in the rains. The child was never found. Never given burial rites. The earth does not take what is not offered to it. So he has never been at rest.” She looked back at me. “That cry is his. He is still looking for what he never had. A name. A grave. Someone to hear him.”

The room felt much smaller than it had a moment ago.

“Tuma,” I said. “How am I supposed to sleep?”

She went back to her hair. “You’ll learn,” she said. “Everyone who stays long enough does.”

The lamp guttered. Neither of us moved to fix it.

I did not sleep.

I lay on my back and listened to the compound breathe — the insects, the distant dogs, the wind moving through the trees outside in a way that sounded almost conversational, as if the bush were discussing something among itself and had not yet reached a conclusion. Jovial’s cot was across the room. I could hear her breathing, soft and even, the unconcerned breathing of someone who did not yet understand what lived at the edge of things.

Around midnight, something shifted.

Not a sound. An absence. The room had a different texture to it — the way a room feels when you are suddenly alone in it, even before you’ve confirmed that you’re alone. I lay still for a moment, feeling this, trying to identify what had changed.

Then I looked at Jovial’s cot.

It was empty.

The mosquito net hung undisturbed. The small pillow still held the indentation of her head. The blanket had been pushed to one side with the casual ease of a child who has gotten up to use the bathroom, which is what I told myself. She had gone to my mother. She had gone to Aunt Remi. Children wandered at night, this was known, this was normal, there was nothing wrong.

I told myself this for approximately thirty seconds.

Then, from outside — not from the bush line but from the compound itself, from the space between the buildings, from close — a sound came that I cannot describe to you accurately. I can tell you it was not a bird. I can tell you it was not a child. It existed somewhere between those two things, in a register that the human ear was never meant to receive, and it lasted only a moment before it stopped as completely as if it had been cut.

I pulled the blanket over my head.

I lay there listening to my own heartbeat count off the minutes until morning.

I did not move until the roosters started and the first gray light came under the shutters to prove the world had continued without me.

Jovial was not in her cot. Jovial was not in the compound. Jovial was not anywhere.

Her slippers were still by the bed. Her small wrapper was folded at the foot of the cot with a neatness that a six-year-old did not possess, the kind of neat that something else makes.

The search was immediate and total. Men went into the bush with machetes and torches, calling her name until the trees absorbed it. Women prayed in the compound with a particular urgency that had no room in it for comfort. The village moved with a grim efficiency that told me this was not the first time it had organized itself around a loss. The elders came from further along the road. The pastor came. My father’s face had aged between the previous night and that morning in a way that I had not previously believed faces could do.

There were no footprints. No torn fabric caught on a branch. No toy dropped on a path. Nothing that a child leaves behind when she wanders. The bush had simply taken her without leaving a receipt.

I sat outside and said nothing about the empty cot I had found before the sound. Said nothing about what I had heard. Said nothing about the half-formed shape I thought I’d glimpsed through the crack in the shutter before I pulled the blanket over my face — something small and bent and wet-faced, with a faint greenish light held low in one hand and something tattered and dark draped around its narrow shoulders, standing in the compound where the compound had no business being entered.

I told myself I had not seen it clearly. That the dark invents things. That stories, if you hold them long enough, begin to cast shadows of their own.

I said nothing because I could not bear what saying it would mean.

Jovial has never been found.

This is the part where I would tell you there was an explanation, a resolution, some version of events that arranged itself into sense. There isn’t. The searches ended. The village absorbed her absence

the way it absorbed everything — slowly, without ceremony, with the practiced resignation of a place that has learned not to expect the bush to return what it takes.

Three weeks later, when the searches had grown too thin to continue, Uncle Sayo sat me down.

He said: “Jovial was adopted. We did not tell you because it was not ours to tell. Her birth mother left her in the bush as an infant — right there, not far from where you heard the crying. She was found wrapped in a tattered mat. A green lantern was burning beside her. My wife brought her home. We thought we were saving her.” He looked at me steadily. “But you cannot take what belongs to Egbére. It does not make a gift of what it has claimed. It may wait. It waits a very long time. But it comes back to collect.”

I looked at him for a long time.

I thought about the lantern that was not ours. About the mat. About the crying that had come on the first night, which Tuma had told me was a ghost infant, and which I now understood was something else — something that had been circling the compound each night, patient and weeping, measuring the distance between itself and what it considered its property.

I thought about the sound I had heard after I found the empty cot. The way it had lasted precisely as long as it needed to.

“What was wrapped around her?” I asked.

Uncle Sayo did not answer.

He did not need to.

My parents took us back to London the following week. The official story is the story of a child who wandered off, the tragic dangers of the rural bush, the inadequacy of fencing. Nobody says the other thing out loud, not in any room I have been present in. The police

were involved briefly and then were not. There were no leads because there was nothing to lead anywhere — no trail, no evidence, no beginning of a thread to pull.

I still hear it sometimes.

Not often. Not on ordinary nights. But on certain nights, when the wind is particular and the dark outside the window has that specific quality of weight — the kind that presses back when you press against it — I hear what sounds like an infant crying somewhere in the distance. Thin. Patient. Circling.

And I think about what Uncle Sayo said: you cannot take what belongs to Egbére.

And I think about the mat found beside her on the day she was born, tattered and dark and left with her like a signature.

And I think about what I saw through the shutter crack — what I told myself I did not see clearly enough to name — and I understand now that I saw it clearly. I have always seen it clearly. I simply needed several years of distance before I could admit that what I saw was real, was present, was standing in the compound with its ruined mat reclaimed and its green lantern extinguished and its face wet with the tears of something that had gotten exactly what it came for.

It did not look triumphant. That was the thing that stays with me most.

It looked the same as it always looks. Still weeping. Still wretched. Still carrying its grief like a mat on its back through the dark.

It wanders, they say. It has no destination. It takes, and it wanders, and it takes again, and the taking does not satisfy it, and the wandering does not end, and the crying does not stop.

And somewhere out there, in whatever the Egbére calls home, my sister is inside it.

I have been waiting for morning ever since.

The mat is still out there. Nobody has taken it. The lantern at the edge of the path still burns green. If you hear a baby crying in the bush, do not go looking. You already know this. You have always known this. But you will go looking anyway. They always do.

chapters.text:
DID YOU KNOW? DID YOU KNOW? Local Maasai call the crater the burial ground of a defeated king.

Menengai Crater · 'Hell's Gate of the Rift'

The crater of Menengai was supposed to be beautiful.

That was the lie people told in brochures and travel videos, in the clipped voices of guides who smiled too widely and pointed at the horizon as if the word breathtaking had not once meant something very close to dying. The photographs online all looked the same: green ridgelines, pale sky, steam rising from the crater floor like incense, like something held up to a god whose name you weren’t meant to know.

Mary had come to Kenya for the open spaces. She’d wanted Mount Kenya first — the altitude, the glaciers, the ridgeline at dawn that people described in their blogs with that desperate reverence that means they are searching for a word bigger than beautiful and cannot find one. But the weather had turned violent and the local ofÏce had cancelled the climb, and so she accepted Menengai instead. Safe. Popular. Perfect for tourists.

She believed all of it.

At first.

“The name Menengai,” the guide said as the group started uphill, “is said to be a Kikuyu word meaning a place for many gods. Some locals call it Kirima kia Ngoma.” He paused the way people pause before they’ve decided whether to enjoy what comes next. “The place of devils.”

A few people laughed nervously.

Mary smiled because everyone else did. She was the only white person in the group, and she could feel the attention resting on her skin like heat — not hostility exactly, but that particular attention reserved for someone who has walked into the wrong story. People kept glancing at her. She kept looking at the ground.

Only one person did not stare.

He was tall, young, loose-limbed, and somehow separate from the rest of the group, as if he had joined the excursion by accident and had not yet decided whether to stay. He carried no heavy bag. No camera case. No jacket tied around his waist. Just himself, a smile, and the kind of calm that felt almost practised — too level, too patient. He caught her looking and lifted two fingers in greeting.

“Hi. I am Mark.”

No handshake. No reach for her hand.

“I’m Mary,” she said.

The guide kept talking over them, his voice threading through the dry air.

“According to legend, Ilaikipiak Maasai warriors were killed by being thrown over the edge of the crater during the great battle of the 19th century. Sixty thousand, some say. Some say more. Stories grow when people are afraid.” He gestured toward the valley below. “The fumaroles rising from the crater bed — the locals believe these are the souls of the vanquished. Seeking to find their way to heaven.”

Mary looked out over the slope. The crater spread below them like an enormous wound in the earth, the walls green and brown and almost peaceful from this distance. Steam rose in pale threads from somewhere below, curling into the sky like unfinished prayers.

Mark fell into step beside her.

He was easy to talk to in the way that people rarely are — the kind of easy that feels effortless from both sides, that makes you forget you are talking to a stranger. He knew the plants, the birds, the old names of things. He knew

which stones were loose underfoot, which patches of grass hid sharp roots, which way the wind shifted when the fumaroles were active. He knew a ridiculous number of ghost stories and told them with such dry humor that they sounded like jokes.

“During Josh Gates’ Destination Truth—” he began once, and Mary laughed before he could finish because of the way he said it, like he was announcing a scandal.

He grinned. “You know the show.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You did with your face.”

He told her about the apparitions people claimed to see in the grass, there for a second and then gone. About the singing heard from a cave where no one stood. About tourists who wandered off the path and were found hours later in the valley below, staring at nothing, with no memory of how they got there and only the sensation that something had been walking a few steps behind them the whole time.

Mary rolled her eyes, but she was listening now.

“The volcano is dormant,” he said, kicking a stone off the path. “Or extinct. No one can agree. That’s how you know it’s dangerous. Things that are truly dead never need to be discussed this much.”

She laughed again, and he liked that. She could tell.

The group paused at the crater’s edge to take photographs. The wind was stronger there — it lifted hair and dust and the corners of shirts, and carried with it something mineral and old, like the smell of a room that has been closed for a very long time. The ground beneath Mary’s shoes felt softer than it should have, almost responsive, as if the rock itself were registering her weight.

She stepped closer to the edge than was wise.

Below, the crater floor looked like a second world. Green and still and waiting. The fumaroles swirled in their slow, deliberate patterns, and for a moment she thought she saw shapes moving inside the steam — not animals, not anything she had a word for — but the wind shifted and they were gone.

“Careful,” the guide called. “No one crosses the line.”

Mary raised her phone. Took the photo. Her own face in the screen, the crater behind her, the tourists to her left.

And behind her right shoulder, where no one had been a moment ago, a tall figure.

Standing too still.

Smiling.

She turned around.

Nothing.

Just wind over the rim.

When she looked back at the screen, the figure was gone.

She blinked at the empty space behind herself in the photo. Then she lowered the phone.

“Wanna go see the Mau Mau caves?” Mark asked, as if he had not heard her breath catch at all.

He was already looking toward the trees below, where the route dropped away through tangled roots and dark stone. His smile had changed. It was still friendly — it was always friendly — but there was something impatient underneath it now, like a door held open for too long.

Mary hesitated.

She should have said no. She should have stayed with the group. She should have listened to the thing in her spine that had begun, quietly, to whisper that the crater was not a place you simply visited. It was a place that noticed you back.

But Mark was already moving, and she followed. She would wonder about this later — every time she was allowed to wonder — why she followed. She never found a satisfying answer. The best she could manage was that his back, moving ahead of her through the dry grass, looked like a direction. And she had not had a direction in some time.

The trail to the Mau Mau caves wound down through a small oasis of trees surrounded by black volcanic rock. The roots of an enormous fig tree hung from the earth like ropes, like a ladder grown rather than built. The guide had called it a natural ladder earlier, and Mary had noted the phrase without examining it.

Standing before it now she understood why some things should never be described too casually.

It looked less like a ladder than a throat.

The air changed as they descended. The light thinned first, as if the trees above were drinking it. Then the temperature dropped — not gradually but in a single step, like crossing a threshold you couldn’t see. The sounds of the group above became mufÒed and distorted, their voices arriving flattened and wrong, like recordings of voices rather than the voices themselves. Mark moved ahead with the ease of someone who had been here before, many times, and was bored of it.

“You know a lot of spooky stories,” Mary said, trying to keep her voice light.

“I am Kenyan,” he said, and flashed the grin back over his shoulder.

Then, almost as an afterthought: “Besides, the caves like to be spoken to.”

Mary stopped walking.

Mark did not.

“Mark?”

He turned halfway down the stone steps and tilted his head. In the dimness of the cave, with the light coming only from above, his face had changed. Not dramatically. Not enough to name. But the light had gone wrong around him

the way it does before a storm, when your eyes cannot agree on distance, and his shadow on the wall behind him was too tall and its head was not shaped like his.

“What?” he said.

His voice echoed from all four walls at once.

She followed.

Slogans and prayers were scrawled on the cave walls in faded paint and charcoal. GOD IS HERE. LEAVE THIS PLACE. WE ARE WATCHING. Beneath them were newer marks — deep gouges in the stone as if fingers had tried to write directly into the rock, and the words they had made were in no alphabet she recognised.

Mary touched one of the walls and jerked her hand back.

It was warm.

Not cave-warm. Not stone-warm.

Human-warm.

Mark noticed. He said nothing.

They came to a chamber where broken stones lay scattered in the dirt. Pale shapes gleamed in the half-light. She crouched slowly, her breath shortening.

Bones.

Human bones.

The jaw. The long thin curve of a finger. Cracked teeth set in a skull that had been lying here long enough for the stone to grow into it.

“Mau Mau fighters,” Mark said. “Some of them. Bombed in 1959. The ones who didn’t make it out. The ones who were buried where they fell.” He looked at them with an expression she could not name. “The cave kept them.”

“Why are they still here?” she asked.

Mark looked at her with the patience of someone explaining something to a child.

“Where else would they go?”

Her phone buzzed.

Signal. Impossibly, there was signal.

She pulled up the browser with fingers that barely worked and searched Menengai missing tourists because she needed to feel the world outside the cave, needed something to anchor her to the ordinary fact of being a person on a trip who would go home in five days to a flat and a cat and a kettle that needed descaling.

The first result loaded.

A news article from 2019. Two adults who had disappeared after Easter prayers. A couple who went for a walk and were never found again. A two- week search that found nothing notable. A photograph of the two of them, taken before.

The man in the photograph had an easy smile.

Mary read the article aloud without meaning to, the words falling out of her as if she had no say in them. She read about the trance-like state other visitors had described, the people who entered the crater and emerged days later having lost hours they couldn’t account for, the ones who never emerged at all. She read until her voice ran out.

Then she looked up.

The chamber was empty.

“Mark?”

Nothing. The bones. The rock. The scratched prayers on the wall that she understood now were not prayers at all but warnings, written by people who had tried to leave a message for the ones who came after.

She turned in a slow circle. The cave had rearranged itself while she wasn’t paying attention. The exit tunnel behind her was narrower. The prayers on the wall had shifted — she was almost certain of it — into words that had not been there before, and though she could not quite read them, she understood they were meant specifically for her.

Then the singing began.

A woman’s voice.

Wordless and high and ancient, coming from the deep rock behind the far wall, from beneath the cave’s floor, from inside the bones themselves. It came from everywhere and nowhere, and when Mary pressed her hands over her ears the singing continued inside her skull, warm and insistent, resonating in her back teeth.

She ran.

The tunnel stretched.

She ran for what felt like several minutes and never reached the opening she had seen from below. The rock walls pressed inward. The ground rose and fell beneath her feet. She ran until she burst out into daylight—

And froze.

She was standing at the crater’s edge.

The same group. The same guide. The same wind pressing against the same backs of the same tourists. A woman in a red hat laughed at something. A man in a blue jacket adjusted his camera strap. The dry grass flattened and rose and flattened again in the same rhythm.

The same mark of dust across her wrist.

She had been in the cave. She was certain of it — the warmth of the walls was still on her palm. The singing was still fading from her molars. But she was back at the rim, at the moment before they descended, and no one in the group had moved.

“We were just in the caves,” she said to the guide. Her voice sounded very far away.

The guide looked at her with professional patience. “Madam. We have not descended yet.”

The group stared back. Someone whispered.

Mary looked down at her shoes.

Clean.

Not a grain of cave dust on them.

She opened her phone with shaking hands. The last photo she had taken was still there. The selfie at the crater edge. Her own face, smiling. And behind her right shoulder—

Mark.

Eyes open too wide. Mouth stretched past the point where smiles end.

She dropped the phone. The screen cracked against the stone. The sound was very small against the wind.

On the seventeenth day, search teams found her backpack near the Mau Mau cave entrance. Her phone lay face-down in the dirt inside. The screen was cracked. Battery dead. The last photograph on the camera roll showed the crater edge: a woman smiling, and behind her, just visible over her shoulder, something that investigators logged as a photographic artifact. A reflection, perhaps, or a smear on the lens. The figure appeared to be smiling back.

The loop began to compress.

Later — many loops later, in the part of her that was still cataloguing things — she would understand that this was how it worked. Not a circle. A spiral. Each iteration a little tighter than the last. A little less room to move. A little less of herself to bring with her.

On the second loop she recognised the guide’s speech in her body before it reached her ears.

On the third she started to move her lips with his words and didn’t notice she was doing it until Mark glanced sideways at her, amused. You’ve been here before? he asked. Ha, she said. And felt sick.

On the fourth loop she wrote on the inside of her wrist with the pen from her pack. DO NOT GO WITH MARK. DO NOT GO INTO THE CAVES. The ink was dark and certain. By the time she was halfway up the mountain it had changed. The letters remained but the words had rearranged themselves into something in a language she did not know, something that felt like a set of instructions.

On the fifth loop she tried to stay with the group. She held back from Mark, stood in the middle of the crowd, kept her eyes on the guide’s jacket collar. But the group grew strange around her — a woman in red who had been on her left was now on her right, and a man who had been photographing the fumaroles was simply not there when she looked again. The guide’s speech developed additions no human tour guide would ever include: Some visitors report that the crater speaks to them. It says the same thing to each one. No visitor will say what it is. The group around her thinned. By the crater edge there were five people. Then three. Then just the guide, alone, finishing a sentence that no longer had a beginning.

Then just the crater. Just the wind. Just the steam below.

And Mark’s voice, somewhere ahead of her on the path that had reformed in front of her feet.

She could hear him pointing out animals she could not see.

The caves on the sixth loop held something new.

Fresh gouges in the wall, white against the dark stone. Not warnings this time. Not prayers. Just one line, carved in fingernails from the other side of the rock:

SHE CAME BACK. Mary looked at those three words for a very long time.

Then she looked at the bones. They had shifted since the first loop — she was almost sure of it. The jaw had moved. The finger bones were differently arranged. She had a photograph from the first loop and she held it up against the current configuration and the positions were similar enough that she might be imagining the difference.

She was not imagining the difference.

On the ninth loop, one set of remains was wearing clothes.

On the twelfth, she knew the clothes.

She kept walking. She had learned not to look too long at things that wanted to be looked at.

The photo was the worst of it.

The two missing adults from the 2019 article. Every loop she opened the website and every loop they were a little different. On the first loop the man’s smile was merely familiar. On the third loop it was Mark’s smile. On the seventh the caption said a name that was not Mark but she had stopped reading captions.

On the ninth loop she finally looked at the woman.

Tired eyes. A pale oval face. A backpack — green, with a small black strap across the front that she had bought in a camping shop in Edinburgh eighteen months ago.

Her own face.

Her own backpack.

And the date on the article was 2019. Six years ago. Six years before she had ever come to Kenya.

She put the phone in her pocket. She did not look at it again for many loops. When she finally did, the photo showed three people. The man with Mark’s smile. The woman with her face. And between them, barely visible in the background, a third figure.

Tall. Empty-handed. Smiling at something off-frame.

Two months after the disappearance, the case was quietly closed. The presumption of death was filed under the category used for missing persons who entered the crater and were never recovered — a small but consistent file. Her family held a memorial service with an empty casket. Her mother placed her favourite book inside it. Friends posted photographs: her laugh, her off-key singing, a video of her mispronouncing something and doubling over. The world moved forward. The world is very practised at this. The Menengai crater remained a top tourist destination. The trail was beautiful. The guide was good. The fumaroles rose every morning from the crater floor, pale and patient, and the locals called them what they had always called them. The souls of the vanquished, seeking to find their way to heaven.

She tried jumping on the four-hundred-and-thirty-seventh loop.

She walked to the crater’s rim in the dark, when the fumaroles glowed faint blue and the sky held no stars, and she stepped over the edge. The fall lasted seconds. It lasted decades. She saw the crater floor rushing up, and the steam opened to receive her, and the sixty thousand were there below the surface — not as bodies but as an awareness, as a weight of attention, as the accumulated consciousness of everything the crater had ever kept — and she hit the bottom, and felt the impact, and lay still.

And opened her eyes at the trailhead.

The guide was mid-sentence.

—demons and ghosts, and therefore is referred to as Kirima kia Ngoma.

The crater floor has no bottom. She had confirmed that now.

The fumaroles began to show her things.

Shapes in the steam. Not quite bodies. Not quite shadows. Things that had once been people and were now something more like impressions — the outline of a person stamped into smoke, faint but persistent. On some loops they moved. On some they faced upward with their mouths open and their eyes gone pale. On some they raised a hand toward the rim.

She tried to count them.

The number never stayed the same.

On one loop she stood at the rim for what might have been six hours, watching them. By the end she could distinguish individual shapes. A woman whose hair still moved in a wind that wasn’t there. A man whose hands were still carrying something heavy. Two figures standing so close together they overlapped.

One of them was wearing her jacket.

The other looked, from this height, like Mark.

She lost count of the loops somewhere past the five-hundreds.

By then the machinery of the thing had become almost familiar. She knew where the guide’s speech would pause and where it would quicken. She knew which turn in the path would feel wrong and which feeling to ignore. She knew the singing in the cave by heart — its key, its rhythm, the way it would shift when she stopped trying to block it out and simply listened. She knew the warmth of the cave walls. She knew the bones.

She knew Mark’s smile, the way a person knows a face that has always been at the edge of a dream without ever entering it. She knew the exact quality of his patience — ancient and mild, like water that has been wearing away the same stone for ten thousand years and is in no hurry to finish.

She tried, for many loops, to resist.

She took different paths. She walked backward. She plugged her ears before the singing could begin. She tried to speak directly to the cave, to the crater, to whatever had built this trap and was running it — she shouted at the walls and the steam and the bones and the warm pulsing rock, and occasionally something in the dark whispered back, but never anything she could use.

She tried staying awake through what should have been the reset. She pressed herself against the cold wall of a cave deep inside the caldera and kept her eyes open and her mind focused and told herself she would not go back, she would not let it begin again, she would simply remain in this moment for as long as it took.

She woke at the trailhead.

The guide mid-sentence.

—demons and ghosts.

The forgetÝng came the way most terrible things come: gradually and then all at once.

First it was the smaller loops she lost — the experiments, the attempts to break free, the variations. She could remember that she had tried things but not what they were. The memories stacked on top of each other and merged into a feeling more than a recollection, a dull weight like a bruise she could press but not see.

Then she lost the loops themselves. Not all of them — not at once — but their specificity blurred. She knew she had been here before. She knew Mark was not what he appeared to be. She knew the cave was waiting. She knew the singing was hers. But the knowing sat in her like a stone in deep water, heavy and submerged, not touching anything.

Then she lost that too.

She stood at the trailhead on a morning that felt entirely new and smelled of dry grass and ozone and something that might have been rain on its way, and the guide was explaining the name in Kikuyu, and someone in the group was laughing nervously, and she was the only white person here and people kept glancing at her, and only one person was not glancing.

He lifted two fingers.

“Hi. I am Mark.”

Mary looked at him. Something moved in the deep water of her mind, something trying to surface. A word. A name. A number so large it had lost its shape.

She smiled.

“I’m Mary,” she said.

He was easy to talk to.

The steam rose from the crater floor as it always had. It rose in the mornings and in the evenings and in the hours between, in thin pale threads that curled upward and joined the sky and dissipated into nothing the tourists could name. From the rim they looked like prayers. From below, inside, they were something else — each one a consciousness turning in a slow and patient spiral, seeking an exit that did not exist. The locals called them what they had always called them. The guide repeated the phrase to every new group, every new face at the edge of the rim, and the tourists nodded and took their photographs and stepped back from the drop. Mary Evans, 28, was listed in one such photograph from a local news archive — visible just over the shoulder of a tourist who had come in late 2031, a small pale figure at the far edge of the frame, very still, looking upward from somewhere inside the steam. The photograph circulated briefly. Investigators examined it. They could not account for the figure. The depth of the crater made the image difÏcult to explain. It was logged as a photographic artifact. No formal conclusion was reached. The crater remained open to visitors. The guide remained good. The fumaroles rose.

Mark was already moving, and somehow she followed.

She was laughing at a joke she would not remember.

And below them, in the long throat of the earth, sixty thousand mouths opened in a chorus with no beginning and no end, and one more voice joined them — high and sweet and entirely American — and the crater, which had always been patient, simply kept breathing.

It had been waiting for a very long time.

It could wait longer.

chapters.text:
SEALED

Cpl. Lin Bao, 4th Signals Corps · recorded March 1938 · re-opened: never officially

There are things in war that do not belong to war.

Bullets belong to war. Hunger belongs to war. Men split open in frozen fields belong to war, and eventually even madness belongs to war, because if you stare long enough into slaughter, something inside you begins to rot like wet paper. You accept all of it. You file it somewhere behind your eyes and you keep walking.

But what happened in the hills above Nanjing did not belong to war.

I know this because I was there. Or near enough to hear the silence it left behind, which is a thing I have been unable to stop hearing for forty years.

My name is Lin Bao. In the autumn of 1937 I was a signals corporal attached to the 4th Bridge Division, stationed at the Yangtze crossing one kilometer downstream from the defensive ridge. My job was radio — transmissions, confirmations, relay. I maintained the line between Colonel Li Fu-Sien’s command tent and the 2,988 men he had stationed across 3.2 kilometers of rolling, mist-choked hillside to guard our position against a Japanese advance.

I knew those men only by their voices. That is perhaps why I still hear them.

The night before the disappearance, I stood post outside the command tent while the generals argued within.

It was cold enough that the breath froze mid-air and fell as crystals. Lantern light moved across the canvas walls in nervous, shapeless shadows. Cigarette smoke drifted from the tent flap like the structure itself was burning slowly from inside. I could hear chairs scraping, boots pacing, voices rising and falling with the particular cadence of men who know they are gambling other men’s lives.

Then Colonel Li spoke. His voice carried clearly even through canvas.

“I have two thousand nine hundred and eighty-eight men stationed in the hills overlooking Nanjing.”

Silence absorbed the words.

He continued without pausing.

“They are spread across a 3.2-kilometer defensive line with clear sight of the Yangtze bridge. If the Japanese attempt crossing, we hold them at the ridge. If our forces attack from behind at dawn — here, and here — we trap them between the high ground and the river.”

I imagined his finger tracing the map. I had seen him do it before. He was a man who trusted maps, terrain gradients, ammunition counts. He did not believe in spirits or omens. He believed in numbers because numbers did not dream.

One of the generals asked: “Your men are prepared?”

“They have two days of ammunition. Heavy weapons are positioned across the slope. They were ordered not to abandon the ridge under any circumstances.”

A pause. Then:

“And if they fail?”

Li answered without hesitation.

“They will not.”

I remember the certainty in his voice precisely because of what came later. Confidence becomes a terrible thing once it dies. It lingers in a room like the smell left behind by something that has been hanged there.

The meeting ended near midnight. Officers emerged grey-faced and smoking. Colonel Li was last out. He stood at the tent entrance for a long while, staring north toward the invisible hills, and I approached him once — briefly — because I needed to confirm the transmission schedule for the dawn assault.

“Sir,” I said. “Do you anticipate Japanese movement before first light?”

His eyes didn’t move from the dark.

“No,” he said softly.

Not certainty. Something older than certainty.

Recognition.

As though he had been listening for something else entirely and was beginning to understand what it was not going to be.

I went back to my radio station.

That night the camp did not sleep. Horses shifted and strained at their lines. Dogs whined without cause, pressing low to the ground with their ears flat. Somewhere around two in the morning, a sentry fired three shots into the darkness after swearing he had seen figures standing motionless between the trees at the camp’s edge. The investigation found nothing — no tracks, no blood, no bodies.

Only the snow around the sentry himself was disturbed, churned into circles, as if he had been slowly turning and turning in place while something watched him from every direction simultaneously.

I noted the time in my log.

I do not know why. Habit, perhaps. Or the sense that time was becoming important in a way I didn’t yet understand.

At 23:54 I sent the coded transmission to the ridge.

STAND FAST. DAWN ASSAULT. SUPPORT EN ROUTE. ACKNOWLEDGE.

The reply came back clean and immediate, the Morse key steady and sure.

ACKNOWLEDGED. READY.

I logged it. Signed off. Wound my watch.

At 05:30, the line went dead.

Not static. Not a severed wire. Not the gradual degradation of a failing battery. There was no hiss, no interruption, no trailing off.

One moment the frequency was live.

The next, silence.

A silence that felt heavier than the artillery we had grown accustomed to. A silence with mass and texture, like a hand placed over a mouth.

I sent the call sign three times. Nothing. Switched to the secondary frequency. Nothing. Fired the flare sequence over the ridge line. No answering flare came back from the hills. The dawn came up grey and still, and the ridge sat in the mist exactly as it always did, and nothing moved on it.

I reported to the lieutenant. The lieutenant reported to Colonel Li.

Li’s assistant came to headquarters so pale that his lips had turned almost blue.

“The ridge is not responding,” he said.

Li looked up sharply. “What do you mean not responding?"

“No signal fire. No radio. No horn reply. The messenger unit sent before dawn has not returned.”

One of the generals said the word desertion under his breath. Li heard him.

“No,” he said instantly.

“You cannot know—”

“My men were ordered to hold position.”

The general laughed, short and bitter. “As if orders stop fear.”

Colonel Li did not answer. He turned and looked out the tent opening toward the northern hills, and for the first time since I had served under him, I saw something in his face that was not anger or calculation or discipline.

It was fear.

Not the fear of failure.

Something older than that, from a place in the mind that precedes reason.

The investigation team departed within the hour. I was among those selected — I knew the northern terrain, and Li wanted his signals man close in case communications resumed. There were eight of us total. Lieutenant Chen. Two junior officers. Four infantry. Me.

We marched through a morning so bitter that breath froze on the lips before it finished forming. The mist between the pines was thick as burial cloth, pressing in from every side, muffling sound in a way that felt less like weather and more like intention. Private Liao joked that the hills were too quiet. No birds. No distant clatter of a camp stirring to life. No smoke rising from cook fires.

At the first outpost, we stopped.

The machine gun sat on its tripod, belt loaded, locked and aimed at the valley approach. Beside it on the sandbag, a half-smoked cigarette lay with its ash long and completely undisturbed. A pot of tea had been poured — the cups full, the surfaces filmed with ice. The fire beneath the pot had burned down to cold charcoal.

No bodies.

No blood.

No spent cartridges.

We stood there for a while without speaking. Then we moved into the main encampment, and I remember the smell hitting me first — rice and gun oil, the homely smell of last night’s meal still hanging in the cold air, impossibly persistent, as if the men had simply stepped away to relieve themselves and would return any moment to finish their bowls.

I walked through that silent bivouac like a man moving through the wrong layer of a dream.

Everywhere I turned, the same scene. Rifles leaned neatly against tent poles. Personal effects lay where they had been set down: a jade pendant on a cot, a stack of letters tied with string, a half-carved wooden bird with the carving knife still resting against it, mid-stroke, as if the hand that held it had simply ceased to be. Heavy weapons — mortars, anti-tank rifles — were positioned exactly as they should be for the planned ambush, loaded, ready,

aimed. Tents stood open. Bedrolls spread out. In one tent, a Go board held a game at mid-play, black stones poised for a finishing move.

Nobody had won.

I stopped beside a cooking fire and knelt. A bowl of rice sat frozen where it had been abandoned, chopsticks thrust upright into the hardened food.

Like markers above a grave.

Steam stains still darkened the inside of the cooking pot.

Lieutenant Chen shouted into the trenches, demanding a response. His voice bounced strangely through the fog. The echo came back once. Then the second shout produced no echo at all, as if the sound had been absorbed by something.

He did not shout a third time.

I found one tent near the command post that stopped me longer than the others. Inside, on a folded cloth: a matchbox. I recognized it. In October, when Li’s men had passed through the bridge position, there had been a boy — too young for war, sixteen at most — who carried a cricket in a matchbox. For luck, he’d explained, showing it to anyone who’d look, grinning with the particular pride of a child who believes in talismans.

I opened the box.

The cricket was still inside.

Still alive.

I set it back down exactly as I had found it. I have tried many times since to explain why that detail undoes me more than anything else. It is an irrational fixation. But whatever had taken the boy — whatever had taken all of them — had not touched the cricket. Had not disturbed it. Had not wanted it.

It had taken only the souls.

It had left everything else.

We found the footprints on the eastern slope, and that is when the true shape of the horror became clear.

Not one set of tracks. Not a scattering of individual paths. Not the chaotic imprints of men fleeing in panic.

Rows.

Hundreds upon hundreds of bootprints, pressed deep and deliberate into the frost, arranged in perfect military order facing outward toward the tree line. As if the entire regiment had assembled in the night, silently, without order given, and stood there at attention staring into the forest.

They did not look like the tracks of men who had run.

They looked like the tracks of men who had watched.

Private Huang started crying when he saw them. Another soldier vomited against the trench wall. I stood at the edge of the rows and tried to count — tried to find some rational interruption, some break in the pattern that would suggest panic or accident —

and found none. The rows went on for nearly two hundred meters. Steady. Even. The footprint depth consistent, like men standing easy, weight distributed, comfortable.

And then they stopped.

Not faded. Not disrupted. Not continued around a corner or down a slope.

Stopped.

The snow beyond the final row was completely undisturbed. No continuation. No return path. No divergence. The men had stood there — nearly three thousand men — and then the snow kept record of nothing further.

As if the earth had simply inhaled them.

Colonel Li himself found me standing at the edge of those final footprints. He walked the length of the rows slowly, hands behind his back, the way he walked when he was calculating something that resisted calculation. He stopped beside me and stared at the untouched snow beyond.

Then he walked to the tree line.

I followed.

The forest beyond the ridge was silent in a way that forests should not be. No birds. No wind through branches. Even the snow seemed to fall more quietly there, as though afraid to make noise. The trees stood dark and very close together and between them was only shadow.

Li stared into it for a long time.

“What is it, sir?” I asked.

He didn’t answer immediately. When he spoke, his voice had changed in a way I cannot precisely describe — reduced somehow, as if something large had been removed from it.

“They were looking at something,” he said.

My stomach contracted.

“What something?”

He kept his eyes on the trees.

“I don’t know.”

Then, after a silence that lasted perhaps thirty seconds and felt longer than the war:

“But whatever it was—” His voice nearly failed him. He recovered it. “—they did not run.”

He was right. I could see it in the footprints. No scattering. No forward surge. The rows had held even at the moment — whatever the moment was. They had stood and looked.

And then they had gone somewhere the snow would not follow.

We canvassed the bridge garrison that afternoon. Each man was interviewed separately. Each told the same story.

Nothing had crossed in the night. Not a single soldier slipping through in darkness, not a column moving along the river road, not a boat, not a sound of flight. The river had been still. The bridge clear.

What they had heard — and here several of the men hesitated, exchanging glances before speaking — was music.

A flute, carried across the water from the direction of the ridge. Faint, they said. High and slow. It had drifted from the hills sometime after the moon set, perhaps two in the morning. It had lasted perhaps thirty minutes.

Then it had stopped.

And they had thought nothing of it, because men play music in camp, and the fires had still been glowing softly on the ridge, and why would they imagine that an entire regiment could dissolve like salt in water?

One of the bridge guards — an older man, face like carved leather — pulled me aside when the others had gone.

“After the music stopped,” he said quietly, “the fires went out. All of them. All at once. I noticed because there were many fires and they should not all die at the same moment. It is not how fires work.”

I wrote it down.

He looked at my notebook and then at me.

“What does it mean?”

I had no answer for him.

We searched those hills for four months. Through winter and into a cold, ruined spring. Through the fall of Nanjing and the aftermath of things I will not describe here because some records should carry only one wound at a time.

Nothing.

Not a scrap of uniform. Not a button. Not a bone. Not a dog tag. Not a name spoken by anyone who had seen those men alive after the night of November 26th.

An old woman in the village below the ridge, when we came through in the early weeks, looked at our faces and seemed to understand without being told. She spoke in a dialect I only half-followed, and Lieutenant Chen translated for me quietly, as if he didn’t want the words to be heard too clearly.

She said: “The ground here is old. It has been fed before. What you’re looking for isn’t somewhere. It went somewhere there isn’t a name for.”

Chen looked at me after he translated it.

Neither of us wrote it in our official report.

Official reports, in the end, said nothing at all. The disappearance was classified, buried, re- classified, and buried deeper. Historians would not touch it. Peer-reviewed journals treated it like a campfire rumor, which perhaps is what it was, and perhaps campfire rumors know things that journals do not. Even the most thorough military archives of that period make no mention of 2,988 men who were there at midnight and gone before dawn. Their names appear on

no memorial wall I have ever found. Their families received no notification, no pension, no death certificates.

In the barracks, it became a story told after curfew with the lanterns low. New recruits called it the Nanjing Vanishing. Some placed it in December 1937, the night before the siege broke. Others swore it was 1939, months after the fighting shifted south. The dates began to bleed into each other. But the silence at the center of the story never changed. Silence is not something that erodes with retelling.

And every winter, in the years that followed, soldiers posted near Nanjing reported the same thing.

On nights when the frost became thick enough to mute the world, shapes appeared along the ridge line. Standing. Shoulder to shoulder. Facing outward toward the forest, the way the footprints had faced. Not moving. Not speaking. Almost three thousand silhouettes in complete stillness.

Waiting for something that had already come, or perhaps for something that had not yet arrived.

The army buried those reports as quickly as they surfaced.

Fear, however, is not something that files well.

I returned to the ridge once, alone, in 1978.

I do not know why. Perhaps guilt ages into curiosity if you wait long enough. Perhaps I simply needed to confirm that the place was real, that I had not invented it in the particular way that the mind invents things it cannot hold in their true shape.

The trenches had collapsed. Trees had reclaimed most of the cleared ground. Ammunition boxes lay buried under frost and moss. The mountain itself looked somehow wrong — not ruined, but heavy, as if it had been carrying something for forty years and had grown stooped with the weight.

I found the eastern slope an hour before sunset.

The footprints were still there.

Not all of them. But enough.

The rows. Pressing down into the earth beneath a skin of fresh ice. I stood at the edge of them and felt my breathing change against my will, the body knowing before the mind what it was seeing.

The snow around the prints was fresh and undisturbed.

But the impressions beneath it had not filled in.

As if the earth refused to release them. As if something beneath the surface was keeping the shape of those men open, holding the void where they had stood against the pressure of every season that had tried to close it.

I stood there until the light failed.

I should have left. I knew I should have left. But I have never been good at leaving places that have not finished with me.

When I finally looked up from the footprints, I noticed two things.

The first: somewhere far down the ridge, almost beyond hearing, the wind moved through the pines in a pattern that was almost — almost — rhythmic. Almost

intentional. The way a Morse key sounds when someone is sending. I stood still and listened. The pattern came and went with the gusts, and I cannot tell you with certainty that it was signal and not weather, because that is the honest answer, and I have tried my whole life to give honest answers even when they cost something.

But I listened for a long time.

The second thing I noticed was worse.

In the last grey light before full dark, I looked back at the rows of footprints I had been standing beside.

They were no longer facing the forest.

They were facing me.

All of them.

Every impression in the frost, for two hundred meters in every direction, turned inward.

Facing the spot where I stood.

I left then. Quickly. I did not look back.

I am an old man now. Japan was defeated. China endured. The world’s larger war came and went and became history and then became something people argue about the edges of.

But 2,988 soldiers never came home.

And I cannot explain the morning rice that was still warm. I cannot explain the cricket still living in its matchbox. I cannot explain the footprints that

stopped in untouched snow, or the guns that moved when nobody moved them, or the flute that played across the water until the fires died all at once.

I cannot explain the footprints that waited forty years and still held the shape of men.

I cannot explain what they were facing when I went back to look.

What I can tell you — what I have told myself every winter since, on mornings when the frost comes in and the world goes briefly, terribly quiet — is this:

Whatever came for them in those hills above Nanjing, the 2,988 men of Colonel Li Fu-Sien’s ridge detachment did not run.

They stood in their rows.

They faced it directly.

And they were taken anyway.

I find, after everything, that I cannot decide whether that is a comfort or the worst thing of all.

— Cpl. Lin Bao, 4th Signals Corps Dictated: February 1978. Transcribed by request. Original recording: unknown whereabouts. The official military record of the Nanjing hill detachment contains no mention of a disappearance. The families of Colonel Li’s men received no correspondence after November 1937. No death certificates exist. The Wikipedia entry on the Battle of Nanking does not reference the incident. Colonel Li Fu-Sien died in 1962. His personal journals were seized at time of death and have not been recovered.

The ridge above Nanjing is unremarkable on any map. It has no name.

chapters.title: Zhongyin
chapters.text:
LIN JIAN HOLDINGS · INTERNAL USE ONLY · DO NOT FORWARD

14th Floor, Glass Tower District · Lin Jian Holdings

He had built his company from one laptop, two chairs, and a stubbornness so fierce it passed for courage. Lin Jian rented the glass-walled box on the fourteenth floor for a pittance, watching the twin towers rise beside his desk like wax candles left too long in a shrine — their pointed crowns scraping Shenzhen’s perpetual construction haze, their facades plastered in rose-tinted windows that bled the afternoon sun into something apricot and wrong. The building’s other tenants were few: a shadowy import-export firm that never seemed to import or export anything, a defunct travel agency still displaying sun-bleached posters of 2019 package deals, a palm reader who kept a ceramic toad by the door. When his employees joked that the tower was haunted, Lin Jian rolled his eyes and told them every empty building invents stories to keep itself occupied. He would say it again, later, to the kind of silence that tells you something is listening.

He worked late because the silence suited him. A failing fintech app, a divorce, a studio apartment in Longgang that smelled of his neighbor’s fermented bean curd — the ofÏce was an escape. Until the night he heard the singing.

It began as a thread of sound winding through the air-conditioning vent. So faint he mistook it for tinnitus. He paused, fingers hovering over the keyboard. A child’s voice, reedy and tuneless, chanting something in Cantonese so archaic he could not parse the words — a nursery rhyme, perhaps, or a game, its melody a descending spiral, each repetition lower, slower, sadder. He told himself it was a recording from a neighboring ofÏce, some forgotten video left playing. But when he pressed his palm to the vent grille, the metal felt cold in a way that had nothing to do with air conditioning, and the sound vibrated up through the bones of his hand as if it came from somewhere far beneath the floor.

✦

PART TWO — FOOTSTEPS THAT PASSED THROUGH — —

He left at midnight, locking the glass door with trembling hands. The corridor stretched empty, lit by motion-sensor panels that flickered as he passed. He had almost reached the elevator bank when the laughter came — not from the vent but from behind him, a bright, breathless giggle, the kind a toddler makes when caught at hide-and-seek. He spun. The corridor was a narrow tube of grey, terminated by a fire door with a push bar. Nothing moved. The glass doors reflected only pale light and the rectangle of his own doorway.

Then the footsteps: bare soles slapping polished concrete, running directly at him. The sound grew, a pummeling rhythm that vibrated in his sternum. He braced for impact. It passed through him. He felt no touch — only a wave of cold that left his teeth aching and a sudden, inexplicable smell: wet earth, old iron, and something sweet and rotten beneath it, like flowers left on a grave too long.

When he opened his eyes, a man stood at the far end of the corridor, facing the wall outside the defunct travel agency. He was dressed in a suit at least a decade out of fashion, the shoulders of his jacket dusted with something pale. His posture was locked — not in thought, but in a terror that had calcified into stillness.

Lin Jian called out, his voice cracking. “Did you hear that? The child?”

The man turned with a slow, creaking reluctance, as if his neck hadn’t moved in years. His face was the color of old newsprint. His eyes were sunken and ringed with shadows so deep they seemed carved. He held something in his hand: a long, rusted iron nail dangling from a string, and a small metal rod. Without a word, he raised the rod and tapped the nail three times.Ting. Ting. Ting. The sound was unnaturally loud, a clean resonant note that sliced through the corridor’s mufÒed silence. An old folk method, Lin Jian would later read on a

paranormal forum buried in the tenth page of search results — a way to test whether the person before you was still human, the iron’s ring revealing a ghost’s resonance.

“You’ve heard them, too, then,” the man whispered. His Cantonese was old- fashioned, laced with a rural accent. “The hungry ones.”

He seized Lin Jian’s wrist — his grip shockingly cold and dry, like a bundle of sticks — and pulled him toward the emergency stairwell.

What the Ground Remembers — Gangxia Village, before the towers

The Zhongyin Building sits on the edge of what was once Gangxia Village, an urban settlement absorbed and erased by Shenzhen’s relentless expansion. Before the glass and steel, before the pink monstrosity pierced the skyline, the old villagers called this parcel the field that nobody planted. Not because the soil was poor — the soil was fine. They didn’t plant it because they knew what had been left in it.

Families too poor for a burial plot used the field for the children: infants lost to fever, children whose names had not yet been decided, given to the earth without ceremony or marker. The clay received them and the understanding settled — this was where the unmourned went. Then the Cultural Revolution came, and the field received others, brought at night by men with armbands and quick, whip-sharp voices. Adults this time, no laughter in them at all. No records. No prayers. Only the relentless rhythm of falling, and the earth drinking what was offered. When the skyscrapers rose in 1990, the foundations were poured directly over those pits. The dead had never been exhumed. They were simply concreted into the new China.

✦

PART THREE — THE SHAPE OF A GAME — —

As they ran, the laughter erupted again — not from one voice now but many, a chorus with a frantic, hysterical edge. The lights failed completely. In the dark, the children began to sing the same descending rhyme, accompanied by a rhythmic clapping:clap-clap-slap, clap-clap-slap. The sound slid through the hall with bare, running feet, ahead of them, then behind them, then inside the walls. “Don’t stop,” the man hissed, hauling Lin Jian upright when he stumbled. “Never stop when they play.”

The emergency lights stuttered on, painting the stairwell in jaundice yellow. And on a landing below, a woman stood. Her hair hung across her face. Her skin had the gray translucence of paper left in rain. She looked neither old nor young — only unfinished. She whispered, with a child’s eagerness and an adult’s exhaustion at once:“We are still here.”

The man raised his nail as if it were a charm. But when Lin Jian grabbed for his arm, the man tilted his face upward and smiled with the wrong mouth. The laughter that spilled from his lips was not his own. It was the children’s — high, piping, unguarded, wholly wrong. Whatever had taken him had not announced its arrival. It had simply settled in while they were running.

Lin Jian ran harder. He burst through a fire door into another corridor that should have been familiar but was not. The ofÏces on this floor were open and empty. Desks stood beneath humming ceiling lights. Cups of cold tea sat beside computer monitors covered in a film of gray dust. A reception bell rested on a counter, polished by use that had no recent owner. All through the corridor, as if the building itself had exhaled, phones began to ring. One by one. Then all at once.

✦

PART FOUR — THE CHILDREN’S DRAWINGS — —

In one room he saw children’s drawings taped to the wall, crude smiling faces in red and black crayon. Below each face, a name. Some names had been scratched out. Some had been written over. Some were only smudges where a hand had dragged across wet ink. He stopped, staring, and that was when someone behind him said his name.

Not the man’s voice. Not a child’s. Something older. Dry. Familiar in the way a wound is familiar.

He turned. A little boy stood in the doorway, head bowed, hands behind his back. His school uniform was too neat. His shoes were too clean. His face was almost invisible in the dimness — and as Lin Jian watched, the features did not settle into one face. They shifted, overlapping, like reflections in water touched by rain. Eyes opened where eyes should not be. A mouth stretched wider than the bones beneath it allowed. The boy’s skin was the color of mushroom flesh. When he smiled, his teeth were black with soil.

“Why did you leave us here?”

Lin Jian could not breathe. The corridor seemed to lengthen. At its far end, pale figures appeared one after another, standing shoulder to shoulder — some in ofÏce clothes, some in old civilian jackets from another decade, some barefoot. One woman wore a blood-red scarf. One man held his hands as if he were still carrying something heavy. They did not rush. They did not threaten. Their patience was worse than either.

The boy took one step forward. “We were waiting.”

Flashback — The Field, Cultural Revolution

The air in the ofÏce turned heavy and tasted of iron and wet soil. The rose- tinted windows dissolved into a gray, open field. Rain fell, cold and relentless. Figures knelt in rows, hands bound behind their backs, their faces stripped of identity by fear and exhaustion. Men in faded armbands moved like specters, their voices sharp as whips. The ground was already scarred with trenches. A boy, no older than ten, shivered in a torn jacket. He did not cry. He stared at

the horizon as if hoping to see something beautiful before it was taken from him. A shot cracked. The sound was swallowed by the rain. Another fell. Another. The mud drank them. There were no markers. No prayers. Only the quiet dignity of the discarded, and the earth absorbing what the living had thrown away.

When the ofÏce snapped back into focus, Lin Jian was on his knees. Blood trickled from his nose. The journal on his desk lay open, its pages warped by moisture that had not been there before. Under his fingernails — mud. Wet earth exactly like the smell that had permeated the corridor. And one tiny fragment of bone, white as chalk, resting in the crease of his palm.

✦

PART FIVE — WHAT THE BUILDING WANTED — —

He stumbled backward, then turned and ran. He found the stairwell and descended — the walls narrowing around him, the smell of wet earth following, the laughter following, the tapping following: dozens of tiny knocks striking the exterior glass from the outside, many floors above the street, as if small hands were counting against the panes.Don’t look down, he heard the man’s voice say, though the man was gone. He looked. The glass reflected the corridor behind him, but not quite correctly. His own reflection lagged a second behind his movements. In one pane, a little girl stood in the hallway where no one stood. In another, a line of pale shapes watched from the far end with the calm of people who had already endured the worst thing and were now waiting to see what it looked like when it came again.

At last he reached the lobby. The marble floor shone. The rose windows overhead glowed with a faint, sickly warmth, as if the setÝng sun were burning behind them despite the hour. In the center of the lobby stood a dozen pairs of tiny shoes arranged in a neat semicircle, their toes pointing outward like a chorus turned to greet an audience.

The boy was there. The lobby had filled with people — not all at once. First one in the corner. Then another by the stairs. Then two more near the lifts. Pale and still and attentive, their faces washed thin by time. They did not rush him. They did not threaten him. And he understood, with a nausea that made him bend at the waist, that this building was not hungry in the simple sense of wanting blood. It was hungry for remembrance. For witness. For someone to hear what had been buried beneath the concrete and painted over with prosperity. The laughter, the tapping, the old game-song, the pale workers in the hallways — all of it was a rehearsal of loss. The dead here had not been allowed to finish leaving.

The front doors opened on their own. Cold night air rolled into the lobby, and Jian fled into the street. The city swallowed him back into its trafÏc, its neon, its ordinary noise. He turned once, expecting to see the tower blazing with faces, but the building stood as it always had — pink and polished, its two spires pointed calmly at the sky.

From outside it looked almost harmless.

✦

CODA — WHAT WAS LEFT BEHIND — —

Friends said his hair had gone white at the temples. Former colleagues said he went silent whenever the building was mentioned. He never returned to his ofÏce. He left Shenzhen a week later, though he could not remember packing his bags. A reporter tried to interview him once, and he refused and locked the door. Another man, years later, claimed Lin Jian had told him, in a voice too flat to be called calm:“The ghosts were not haunting the building. They were trapped inside the years we built over them. They are still trying to get out.”

A month after his disappearance from the fourteenth floor, a new tenant took the space. A young woman running an online craft store. She commented to the building management that the ofÏce had a strange, sweet smell — like

burnt sugar and damp earth — and that late at night she could almost swear she heard children singing. But Shenzhen is a noisy city, and the mind plays tricks. She bought an air freshener and went on with her work.

She never noticed the small, pale handprint that appeared on the inside of the window every evening, just as the rose-tinted light began to fade. Too small for an adult. Too high for any living thing to have reached. It was gone each morning, replaced only by a line of ants marching across her desk, carrying crumbs of something grey and crystalline.

The Zhongyin Building still stands. Its businesses still fail with a regularity that defies ordinary explanation. The twin candle-spires still catch the sunset and hold it longer than they should. Skeptics call it an ugly old ofÏce tower with bad maintenance and worse tenant turnover. Believers say it stands on a graveyard of the forgotten, where the dead learned to wait until the living invited them in. Tourists still point at the towers and laugh at their pink windows.

Yet when dusk settles and the glass begins to burn rose-red in the last light, some of them hear it: a child laughing from somewhere deep inside the floors, followed by the faint, unmistakable tap of a nail against metal, as if something inside the tower is counting the years.

And waiting for the next person to look back.

The soil is patient. The soil remembers everything.
