chapters.title: Shadows of the city
chapters.text:
CASE 04

Personal case notes, recovered notebook — teahouse district

The widow wore black gloves despite the heat. She ordered tea and did not drink it, only held the cup through the gloves as though warmth were something she was trying to remember how to receive. The tea shop had paper walls. Every whisper sounded like a confession being made to the wrong person, and the city outside moved with the clean efficiency of a place that has decided, collectively and without discussion, never to look directly at what it remembers.

Her husband had been a restoration surveyor. Freelance. Careful. She described him in past tense with the flatness of someone who has already done their crying in private and now needs only a professional. He had been contracted to assess structural decay around preserved sites in the Peace Memorial Park. He went on a Tuesday. He filed no written report. At 2:13 in the morning he sent a voice note, and the voice note was only breathing — and beneath the breathing, something like a room full of people trying very hard not to be heard.

Three weeks later the hospital called it cardiac arrest. She did not believe them. She did not say what she believed instead. She slid a photograph across the table and let it do the work.

The Atomic Bomb Dome at dusk. Its iron ribs against the sky like the inside of something that had forgotten it was dead. At the base of the pavement, silhouettes stood where no bodies stood — the colour of old ink, but with depth, which was the thing wrong with them. Shadows are flat. These were not flat. These had been pressed into the world by a hand that understood geometry but had no interest in mercy.

I took the case. I have since asked myself why. The honest answer is that I have always been more afraid of not knowing than of knowing. Hiroshima cured me of that particular courage permanently.

I arrived three days before the anniversary. The city was clean. The trams ran on time. Tourists raised phones toward the cenotaph with the mild reverence of people who are moved but not changed, and the Ōta River moved alongside the park with the patience of water that has absorbed more than water should be asked to absorb. I spread the widow’s photograph and a park map across the hotel bed and read everything I could find about what a nuclear detonation actually does to a human body at the hypocenter. The answer was clinical and annihilating: at six thousand degrees Celsius the body does not burn. It sublimates. Skin separates before the nerves can register the instruction. Organs reach boiling point while the skeleton is still deciding. There is no body to recover because the body has become the air, and the air moved on within the first second, and what remained was only the negative — the silhouette burned into stone by the sudden violent subtraction of a person from the world. The famous imprints on the Sumitomo Bank steps. The shadow of a man waiting

for the bank to open. The shadow of a woman with her arms at her sides. The Kage no hito. Not ghosts. Not echoes of personality. The precise record of a moment that was interrupted before it could conclude.

The museum stopped me at a single line of text: the heat was so instantaneous that consciousness had no time to depart. I stood at that display case for longer than I meant to. Behind me, at the back of my neck, something applied a careful pressure — the quality of a hand checking whether I was still made of matter. When I turned, a child stood at the far end of the hall in a school uniform from another decade, the fabric faded to the colour of old tea. His face was turned away. Around him the glass cases reflected empty air. He drifted between the exhibits without moving his legs and then he was not there.

I noted the time. I noted my pulse. I wrote possible visual disturbance, stress-related in my case file and closed the notebook on the lie without ceremony.

The Dome after midnight. A guard let me in on a fabrication about university research. The park was empty, the river black, the floodlights making the Dome look dignified in a way that struck me as a profound institutional error. I had not reached the steps when the recorder in my coat pocket began transmitting a waveform on its screen — the device switched off, the battery cold, and yet the waveform moved in slow even cycles, the breathing rhythm of a person keeping very still in the dark.

They were already there when I looked up.

Not appearing. Becoming visible — the way things that were always present become visible when the eye stops refusing them. Dozens of silhouettes on the pavement and against the walls, each one darker than the surrounding dark, which should violate the physics of light and did. They carried the specificity of interruption: one arm half-raised, one figure turning at a sound it would never finish hearing, one child- height shape holding the outline of a school bag. None had faces. Not blank faces. The geometric absence of faces — as though whatever flash had fixed them to the stone had taken the face first as a matter of priority.

My thermal camera showed nothing. Not cold spots. Not heat signatures. Absolute nothing — the screen black in the way that a screen goes black when it is being shown something it was not built to measure. I raised my regular camera. Seven frames. Every frame came back black on the preview. Not underexposed. Not corrupted. The lens had made an agreement with the subject and I had not been consulted.

Then I heard it. Not with my ears. In the back teeth, in the fillings, a frequency that built slowly from tinnitus into something that had structure — a pitch that resolved, the way a radio finds a station through static, into words. Names. Tadashi. Emiko. Okāsan. A child’s voice cycling through one word in a register between statement and accusation: atatakai, atatakai, atatakai. Warm. It’s warm. Still warm. The word that a twelve-year-old girl walking to school on an August morning would have felt in the microsecond

before the second sun opened above the city and the warmth became the last sensation available to any nerve that had not yet been cancelled.

The child-shaped figure turned toward me. It extended an arm. The air around my sternum went cold, then hot, then cold in a cycle that made my heart stutter and my shirt, I noticed afterward, show a faint scorch at the chest. And in that touch — briefer than a breath — I understood what Hasegawa had meant when he said the consciousness had no time to leave. I was a girl named Yuki, age twelve, mid-laugh, mid- sentence, the sky impossibly blue, and then the light arrived without warning and without mercy and the sentence simply stopped, unfinished, the mouth still shaped around the next word, the word still waiting somewhere in the suspended architecture of a moment that physics had frozen rather than ended. Then I was a father. A grandmother. A soldier with one boot unlaced. The hive of a single morning’s dying, sharing itself in fractions of a second, not for revenge and not for recognition but for the simple unbearable reason that pain of that magnitude cannot be held by any one shape alone.

I came back to myself on my knees, the recorder melted against my thigh, my cigarette burned to the filter between my fingers without my having felt it.

Hasegawa found me the following night, or I found the basement below the shuttered cafe by following the smell of developing chemicals through a city that had begun to feel less like a place and more like a position. He had nicotine fingers and the eyes of a man who had made a practical decision to stop

sleeping. Along his walls hung prints of the Dome in every season. In every print, shapes stood where no one had posed.

He said, before I spoke: “You’ve seen them.”

“They are not the Kage-onna,” he said. “Kage-onna is longing. This is older in the wound.” He turned a print to face me. “The flash did not only take the body. At that temperature, at that speed, the self was mid-sentence. What remains on the stone is not the shape. It is the shape still trying to finish what it was saying.”

He handed me a contact sheet. Among the images of the Dome and the river was a frame from the afternoon I had spent in the museum. It showed my back, my coat, my height — and behind my shoulder, a second figure in my coat and my height, facing the camera directly. Its face, where a face should have been, was darkened from the eyes inward. Overexposed into nothing. The quality of a photograph taken too close to a light source that had no intention of being recorded.

“They do not follow,” Hasegawa said, watching me set the sheet down. “They wait. They wait for a person to stand in the correct position, at the correct hour, on the correct anniversary, and to stay long enough to be recognised. Once they recognise you —” He stopped. He looked at his hands. “The imprints are not records. They are thresholds. The blast made a door of every absence. Once a year the door opens and what comes through is not the dead. It is the dying, still in progress, wearing the shape of whoever was there. And sometimes,” he said quietly, “the shape fits someone new better than it fit the original.”

I asked about the couple whose disappearance had been logged in the police files. The tourists. The Japanese man who had tried to stop them. The shorter man with the camera who had run.

Hasegawa looked at me for a long time.

“The shadows were not following them,” he said. “They were offering.”

On the anniversary I went back. I told myself it was professional obligation. The crowd moved from the river to the Dome in silence — men, women, children, nurse’s caps, school uniforms, a soldier still working at a boot he will never finish tying. Among them, wearing a hotel jacket, one arm half-raised, the gesture of a man waving through thick glass at someone he is not certain can see him, was what remained of the widow’s husband. His outline nested — shadow within shadow within shadow, Russian dolls of absence going inward without terminus, each shell the shape of a different person who had stood in the wrong place on the wrong August morning and been filed away by a city that does not know how to stop remembering.

His mouth opened. My voice came out.

Who is standing inside my outline.

I walked to the river. I looked at my reflection in the black water. My reflection looked back. Then, after a moment that lasted several seconds longer than any moment has the right to last, it smiled.

Slowly. Deliberately. The smile of something that has just confirmed a measurement it had been taking for several days.

I had not smiled.

I left before sunrise. I drove out of Hiroshima the long way, past the city limits, past the point where the road stops feeling like a wound and starts feeling like a road again. I submitted this report to the widow’s contact address. There has been no reply.

The granite sample I removed from the Dome’s perimeter sits on my desk. A fragment with a partial handprint pressed dark into its face — smaller than mine, thinner, the hand of someone who was twelve years old and walking to school and laughing at something that no longer exists. It is warm to the touch. Not room temperature. The warmth of a thing sustained from inside across eighty years, without diminishment, without the concession of even a single degree.

My reflection has been careful lately. Punctual. Arriving when it should, leaving when I do, performing synchrony with the diligence of something that has recently been reminded to be less conspicuous.

Last night the lights dimmed twice.

This morning my shadow on the wall was raising its arms before I raised mine.

I know that warmth. I know what it is waiting for.

The case is open.

It has always been open.

chapters.title: Coleman's Head
chapters.text:
NAMIB · 19—

Namib Desert, Namibia — Wish You Weren't Here

The bus driver would not look at you when he dropped you at the edge of Kolmanskop. He stared at the cracked windshield instead, jaw set, eyes tracking something that wasn’t the road. When you asked him what time he returned, he said only:“Before dark. You must be at the gate before dark.” Then he left. The dust he raised hung in the air long after the sound of the engine died — a red-brown curtain between you and the rest of the living world.

The sign greeted you in Fraktur script, the old Germanic lettering that looked like it had been carved by something that hated straight lines. KOLMANNSKUPPE. Coleman’s Head. The name had always struck historians as oddly anatomical, as though the desert had swallowed a man whole and left only the topmost part of him visible above the sand. The sun at midday was a white, surgical thing. It illuminated everything and explained nothing.

You had come, as most journalists did, for the photographs. Ghost town. Abandoned diamond rush. Sand eating the ballroom floor. These were the postcards people wanted. You had not come for the ostrich enclosure. You had not even known there was one until Marta, the local guide, mentioned it in passing three weeks ago during your pre-trip call, her voice dropping a half-register as she said it. “The cage,” she said. “We do not open the cage.” You had laughed. You were not laughing now, standing in the yellow heat with the gate behind you locked and the town spread out ahead like the skeleton of something that had died mid-sentence.

The buildings breathed. That was the only word for it. The wind moved through the broken window frames and the sand shifted and the walls seemed to expand and contract with a slow, patient rhythm — like lungs that had forgotten they were supposed to have stopped.

The first house you entered had been swallowed to the waist by a dune. Sand curved through the doorway in a smooth, muscular wave, pressing against a rusted bedframe, climbing the wallpaper — pale blue flowers, hydrangeas perhaps, now the color of old teeth. Someone had left a teacup on the windowsill. Inside the cup was sand, perfectly level, as though poured with care. As though set there to welcome you.

You noticed the footprints in the second house. Not tourist prints — those were the scuffed, overlapping chaos of shuffling feet. These were deliberate. Narrow. Two-toed, pressed deep, as if whatever made them was very heavy, or moving very slowly, or both. They crossed the room from the far wall to the door and stopped. Stopped cleanly, without a drag or a stumble, in the center of the threshold. As though the thing that made them had simply ceased — had been switched off, mid-stride, between one room and the world outside.

Zacharias Lewala had been a Shaman. This was the part the tourist pamphlets left out between the sentences about diamonds and German architecture and the X-ray machine that was, for a time, the only one in the southern hemisphere. Lewala’s people had been massacred. Sixty thousand Herero, driven into the desert by Kaiser Wilhelm’s soldiers, shot and hanged and starved in the sand. Lewala had survived and found work on the railroad and one day, in 1908, had picked up a stone that caught the light wrong. He had brought it to his German employer, August Stauch, and Stauch had confirmed what Lewala already knew from the feeling in his chest when he held it — that it was a diamond, and that it was extraordinary. Stauch had told the world. Lewala had told no one, and received nothing, and

then had disappeared. “Under mysterious circumstances,” the old documents said. This is how history buries its crimes — under circumstances. Under mystery. Under sand.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ostrich enclosure was behind the theatre. You found it late in the afternoon when the sun had begun its long collapse toward the dunes and the shadows had grown long and deliberate. The enclosure was larger than you expected — a wide iron cage, the bars thick as a man’s wrist, sunk into a concrete pad that the desert had not yet managed to consume. The lock was still on the door. Old, German-made, heavy as a fist. The sleigh was inside. A wooden sleigh, the kind you pulled through snow at Christmas, painted red once, now the color of dried rust or dried blood, you couldn’t quite decide which in the failing light. It sat in the center of the enclosure on its runners as if the sand beneath it had recently been ice.

There had been an ostrich. This was documented. A family in the Kolmanskop of the 1920s had kept one — the same family, whispered Marta on the phone, that had terrorized their neighbors, that had forced other residents to pull the sleigh through the snow at Christmas while they watched from the balcony of their grand house and laughed. The bird had been their pet, their familiar, their proof that wealth could make even a monster domestic. When the family left — when everyone left — the ostrich had not. The records showed no removal, no slaughter, no death of any kind. The lock on the cage remained locked. The sleigh remained inside. And the ostrich simply remained too, for a while, and then did not, and the space it left behind was never explained.

You pressed your face between the bars the way children do at a zoo. The sand inside the cage was undisturbed. Perfectly flat. The sleigh cast a shadow that was slightly wrong — slightly longer than it should

have been given the angle of the sun, pointing in a direction that did not correspond to any light source you could identify. You did not go inside. The lock was old, but not as rusted as it should have been.

Night in the Namib does not fall. It arrives — suddenly, completely, with a confidence that suggests it was there all along, merely waiting behind the daylight. You were still three hundred meters from the gate when the dark came down like a curtain being drawn by a very large, very certain hand. Your torch cut a white corridor through the black. The sand glittered at the edges of the beam. Diamonds did that, you remembered. Even after the mines were depleted, the sand itself held trace elements, ghost-fragments of the stones that had made men rich and kept other men enslaved and been pried from the earth and shipped to Berlin and cut into shapes that caught the light and were called beautiful. The desert floor still sparkled. It had never stopped.

You heard it before you saw it. A sound like the tearing of heavy fabric, rhythmic and patient, coming from the direction of the enclosure you had left behind. You turned. Your torch swept the dark. Nothing. The sound stopped.

Then started again, closer.

An ostrich in full stride covers five meters per step. They can reach seventy kilometers per hour. Their eyes are larger than their brains, which is the detail the biology textbooks always include as though it explains something. It does not explain anything. What it explains is that an ostrich sees everything. Every tremor of grass, every shift of sand, every pale human face floating in the beam of a failing torch. It sees everything and it processes very little and it acts with a simplicity that is almost theological. It is beak and claw and speed and that vast, unblinking eye.

Coleman’s oxen vanished in a sandstorm. This was the historical record. John Coleman, the transport driver, had been stranded on a hill, and his oxen had gone, and the place had taken his name as though the land itself had found him significant. Some versions of the story said the oxen were found wandering two days later, miles north, their eyes rolled back in their skulls, frothing, refusing to eat until they died. Some versions said the oxen were never found. Some versions said Coleman himself was found on the hill three weeks later, sitting in his wagon with the reins loose in his hands and his eyes open and his mouth forming a word that no one who found him could quite read, even up close, even when they turned his face toward the light.

The word, one account suggested, was a name. Not a German name. Not an Afrikaans name. Something older, worn smooth by the desert’s long patience, the way water wears stone — except there is no water in the Namib. There is only sand, and time, and whatever has lived in both of them since before the first human being made the catastrophic decision to call this place a home.

The torch died. You knew, even as your thumb found the switch and stabbed it again and again in the sudden absolute dark, that it would not come back. There was no mechanical reason for this. The batteries had been new. The torch had been good. The dark simply did not want it.

What you heard next was the sound of a lock opening. Not breaking — opening, with a clean, deliberate click, the sound a mechanism makes when the correct key is turned in it. From the direction of the enclosure. From behind you, and then somehow ahead of you. From inside the dark that now pressed against your skin like a warm, patient hand.

The footprints. Two-toed. Pressed deep. Ending in the center of the threshold as though the thing that made them had been switched off.

Or as though it had learned, over a hundred years of waiting in its locked enclosure with the sleigh and the sand and the ghost-light of diamonds in the desert floor, that it did not need to cross thresholds anymore. That it did not need to step through doorways. That it could simply arrive, the way night arrives, the way the desert arrives inside an abandoned house — not by entering, but by having always been there, behind the wallpaper and beneath the dune and inside the chest of every person who ever stood in Kolmanskop and felt, without being able to say why, that something was looking back.

The gate was locked when you reached it. You know that it was unlocked when you went in — the guide had opened it with a key and told you it would remain open until five. It was four-forty by your watch. The gate was locked. You stood at it for a long time with your hands on the iron and the dark behind you making no sound at all, which was worse than any sound, worse than the tearing-fabric rhythm, worse than the click of the lock, because at least sound is a thing with location, a thing you can turn your back to or run from. Silence has no edges. Silence fills every space equally, the way sand does, the way the Namib has filled Kolmanskop — slowly, completely, without malice, without mercy.

You were at the gate before dark. You kept telling yourself this. You were at the gate before dark, so whatever the bus driver meant, you had obeyed it. You had done everything right. You heard the bus before you saw its headlights. You heard it and you held the bars and you did not turn around, not even when the warmth came — that specific, animal warmth of something very large standing directly behind you, close enough that you could feel it breathing on the back of your neck in slow, deliberate pulses.

The bus driver did not ask how it went. He looked at you once in the rearview mirror, looked away, and drove. Later, cleaning your camera at the hotel in Lüderitz, you found the photographs. You had taken forty-three. The ballroom. The dunes inside the houses. The teacup with sand level to its brim. The footprints. The enclosure. The sleigh and its too-long shadow.

In forty-two of them, you were alone.

In the forty-third — the last one on the card, the one you did not remember taking, timestamped four-fifty-one in the dark — something stood behind you at the gate. Enormous. Black as the night, blacker, a darkness with mass and intention and that one detail which would not let you sleep: a single eye, pale as a diamond and about the size of your fist, catching the light from no discernible source, open completely, looking not at the camera but slightly past it.

Looking, with terrible patience, at whoever would eventually look back.

chapters.title: DHEGDHEER
chapters.text:
Postmarked Mogadishu · March 2017 · sender unknown

The package arrived on a Tuesday in March 2017. No return address. The postmark read Mogadishu, though the ink had run, and Amina Odhiambo could not say how long it had wandered before it found her. Inside were two sets of documents. The first she recognized — her brother’s field notebook, green cover, the corner stained a dark reddish-brown she did not let herself think about. The second was a sheaf of loose papers, handwritten first in Arabic and then translated, haltingly, in English beneath each paragraph, as though the author had done it himself over several nights, alone, with a dictionary he didn’t fully trust. She didn’t know who had assembled them together. She didn’t know who had sent them. She read them the way you read a letter from the dead: slowly, all at once, and only once.

DOCUMENT ONE — —

Field Notebook of Cpl. David Odhiambo, KDF 9th Battalion Recovered. Entries begin November 2015.

12 November 2015 Rained last night. The flat kind that makes no sound — just falls straight down and disappears into the sand like it was never water at all. Baraka says Somalia drinks rain like a man who doesn’t believe it will come again.

We are three weeks on rotation. The work is manageable. Patrols. Checkpoints. Radio checks at 0200. The land is strange. I have been north before, to Turkana, and I thought I understood desert. I didn’t. This place is different. There is something old sitting in it, the way there is something old in very thick walls. Something that has been waiting so long it no longer minds waiting.

Mama asked me to write. She says writing keeps a man honest. I don’t know about honest. I think writing keeps a man from going too quiet inside himself.

19 November 2015 Sergeant Mutua told us something after supper tonight. He has been on two tours and does not scare easily — I have confirmed this. He said: when you are on night patrol, you do not look behind you more than once. Once is a soldier being careful. Twice is a soldier who already knows something is there.

I asked what he meant.

He said: The elders in Kismayo warned us. There is a woman who follows at night. Not al-Shabaab. Older than al-Shabaab. You hear her before you see her. She sings.

Baraka laughed. I did not laugh. I have learned that the most dangerous men in any unit are not the ones who frighten easily. They are the ones who have stopped laughing at things.

3 December 2015 Something happened on patrol that I did not radio in. I’m writing it here so it exists somewhere.

We were on the eastern perimeter — myself, Kiptoo, and a Somali soldier named Farah who’s been attached to our unit for six weeks. The night was completely still. No wind. This is unusual here; there is always wind, even a small one. The stillness was the first warning.

Then I heard singing.

I cannot describe the melody accurately. A woman’s voice, low, but the tune did not move the way a melody should move. It rose where it should have fallen. It turned back on itself. It was as though she was singing around something, circling it the way water circles a stone, and I could not make out the centre of it, could not find the words, could not find the end.

I turned.

Nothing behind me.

Farah had stopped walking. He stood completely still and I said his name twice before he responded. When he turned his face was — I don’t have the right word. Not afraid. Past afraid. On the other side of fear, where a man arrives when fear has stopped being a useful tool and simply become weather.

He said one word. In Somali.

I didn’t know it then. I know it now.

Dhegdheer.

14 December 2015

I have been asking. Quietly, the way you ask about a thing you don’t want to name too loud. The Somali soldiers know it. They know it the way a man knows about an old injury — not a story, just a fact carried in the body.

What I understand: she is old. She has been here longer than any measurement. She was a woman once who ate her own kind — her children, her neighbors, travelers, strangers — and the elders cursed her. The curse did not kill her. It only fixed her here, tied her to the land, married her to her hunger. She cannot leave. She cannot stop.

She has long ears. They say this first, every time. Long ears that hear everything — heartbeat, prayer, the specific quality of a man’s guilt.

I asked Farah what she wants with us, with Kenyan soldiers, with men from a country entirely different from this one.

He was quiet a long time. Then: She does not care who you are. She cares what you are made of.

I did not sleep well after he said that.

27 December 2015 Merry Christmas, Amina. I hope the boys are eating enough and that Mama is resting.

I am fine. Do not worry.

8 January 2016 Orders came. El Adde, Gedo Region. We move on the 14th. We are taking over from another unit at a forward operating base near the town.

Farah requested a transfer when he heard the location. He was refused. That night I watched him pray for longer than usual. Much longer. I didn’t ask. I already knew.

El Adde is south. Deeper in. Closer to the unmapped parts.

I have not been sleeping well.

14 January 2016 We arrive tomorrow.

Last night I dreamed of Ngong Road in the morning — matatus and the smell of mandazi from the woman near the stage. All the ordinary things. The kind of ordinary you don’t know is precious until you are somewhere that has no ordinary left in it at all.

I heard her singing again last night. Outside the tent. I did not go out.

Amina, if you read this: I am not afraid in the way you might fear. I am something else. Paying attention. I think this is the most important thing a person can do in a place like this.

The land here has been telling me something for weeks.

I have not been listening hard enough.

DOCUMENT TWO — —

Papers of unknown origin. Written in Arabic; translated below each passage by the author. The English is imperfect. It has been kept exactly as found.

No author name. The translation breaks in several places where the author has written only: “I do not have the English word for this.”

I write this because a man who does not record what he has seen becomes a man who is no longer sure of what is true.

I have been with the movement for seven years. I am not young. I have fought in Kismayo, Baidoa, in the spaces between. I have killed men. I have made peace with what I am. I believe in God and in judgment.

I say this so that what follows is understood. I am not a man who frightens easily.

What I know of her: The name is Dhegdheer. Long-ears. Names given in truth always hold.

She was a woman. She became something else. I have heard scholars debate what she is now — a jinn, something shaped from old hunger, something the land itself produced from its own suffering. I do not settle the debate. I only describe what she does.

She eats. This is her nature, what remains of her after everything else was burned away. The elders say she ate her own family first, then travelers, then anyone who crossed her valley. She was cursed and confined, but confinement is not the same as weakness. She is not a caged thing. She is more like a tree. Rooted. Growing. The roots spread with every season of violence, and the men who bring their wars here have been feeding her roots for years.

I did not think of her as a child thinks of her — a story to frighten the disobedient. I thought of her as men think of God: yes, probably real, but not here, not now, not watching this specific patch of ground.

Then the Kenyan soldiers came. Then she became interesting again.

Why soldiers? I have thought about this for a long time. I believe it is because soldiers bring so much dying with them. Not just the deaths but the atmosphere of death — the intent, the readiness, the way men in a war zone carry their own mortality like a smell. She is drawn to that smell. She has been growing on it.

The war has been very good for her.

What I saw before El Adde: Two nights before the attack, I was moving along the southern approach to the Kenyan base when I first heard her. I have heard her before — in the Jubba Valley, once near Afmadow — and I recognized the melody immediately. The tune that rises when it should fall. The vowels dragged too long, like wet cloth pulled across stone.

I told the men near me: keep moving, do not look, do not stop.

Some listened.

The ones who did not—

I do not have the English word for this.

On the night of the attack: I will not record the operation. That is not the purpose of this.

I was moving through the camp in the hour before dawn when I found the Kenyan soldier hiding in a collapsed hut at the southern perimeter. He was alive, which surprised me. He had no weapon — dropped or lost, I didn’t know. He was in no condition to run. He sat very still when I came in, and he looked at me the way a man looks at something he doesn’t have the energy to be afraid of.

In other circumstances this would have been a simple encounter. But I had heard her still moving through the camp behind me, and I am a practical man. Two men are harder to take than one.

I sat across from him. We looked at each other.

I said: You heard the singing.

He said: Yes.

I said: You know what it is.

He was quiet for a time. Then: Tell me.

So I told him. What I have written above — the elders, the curse, the long ears that hear everything. I watched his face while I spoke. He was young. Twenty-five or six. The kind of young that still has the shape of a boy in it, but not anymore, not quite, not after tonight.

When I finished he said: Why is she here? Why tonight?

I said: She goes where the dying is.

He thought about this. Then: There are so many of my men—

I said: Don’t count them. Don’t count them now. We have to move.

Moving through the camp: I will write this carefully.

We went south, away from the engagement. I kept my rifle and walked ahead. He followed. I told him: stay directly behind me, do not stop for any reason, do not look to the left where the sound is coming from.

He asked why not to the left.

I said: Because she is there. And looking is an invitation.

This is what the elders teach. Dhegdheer can smell virtue and sin alike — she can smell the character of a man the way a hound smells meat. But she must be invited by the eyes. To look directly is to say: I see you. I am present. And to her, presence is hunger, and hunger is invitation.

She doesn’t need to be called. She needs only not to be refused.

He asked how I knew all this.

I told him: the same way he knew whatever stories his own mother told him in the dark, to keep him from wandering, from disobeying, from going where small children should not go. She was that story. Every culture has that story — the darkness that waits for the unvirtuous, the thing that knows when you have done wrong. I had thought it was only a story.

I no longer think that.

What I saw: There is one thing I have not written yet, because I have been deciding.

At the edge of camp, near the perimeter wire, I turned briefly — one turn, no more — and I saw her.

She was crouched over a body. Her back was to us. She was feeding. I use that word because there is no gentler one and gentler words are a form of lying.

She was taller than a woman should be, though crouching made it hard to measure. Her dress, if it had ever been a dress, was the color of the ground — the color of things that have been in a place so long they have taken on its color, become part of it, been absorbed into the texture of it. Her ears were long. Long enough that I could see them even from behind, sweeping out from the sides of her head, twitching — and this is the detail that I cannot explain any other way — twitching with something that seemed very much like joy. The specific joy of a hunger finally answered.

She was not moving quickly. She was thorough.

The Kenyan soldier made a sound. Small, involuntary. The kind of sound that happens in a man’s throat when something reaches through his ribs and takes hold.

I grabbed his arm and we moved. Not running. Fast, but not running. Running is also an invitation.

She did not follow.

I think she had enough. I think that is the only reason.

What I believe: I am a man of faith. I believe in God, in mercy, in judgment. I ask forgiveness every day for the things I have done in this war, and I believe the asking is heard.

But I believe what I witnessed that night sits outside the usual accounting. She is not a test. She is not a punishment. She is something the land has been carrying for a very long time, something that predates the borders and the flags and the reasons men give for killing each other here. She was here before the war. She will be here after.

The war has only made her larger.

When I was young, the elders said she was trapped — confined to her valley by her own sin, unable to leave, unable to stop. I believed this meant she was diminished.

I do not believe that anymore.

The trapped thing and the growing thing are not different things. They are the same thing.

She is getting bigger.

I do not know how large she will become.

The translation ends here. The remaining pages are in Arabic only. The handwriting is larger and pressed hard into the paper, as though written in the dark by a hand that was shaking. The final line, in English, is written separately at the bottom of the last page:

“He was a good man. I hope he found his way home.”

DOCUMENT THREE — —

Continuation of Field Notebook, Cpl. David Odhiambo Final pages. Undated.

I don’t know what day it is. I have been moving south for what I think is two nights. There is a man with me.

I will not say what he is. It no longer seems to matter much out here what anyone is. He knows this land. He is keeping me alive and I am letting him because the alternative is not being alive.

He is afraid of what I might know about him. I am suspicious of his reasons for helping me. We do not trust each other. We walk.

He explained more tonight. We stopped at a dry riverbed and he told me about the valley, about the first time he heard her as a young man, about what the elders say she smells and hears and wants. He told me about the widow and her son who once escaped through that valley — a story he knew from childhood, a woman who had nothing left but her virtue, and how even Dhegdheer could not reach through that to her. She passed through untouched. The son too.

He told me some of his commanders knew about her. Left prisoners in places she hunted. Called it strategy. Called it using the land. He said this with the face of a man who has carried something a long time and is not sure he has the right to put it down.

I asked: Is she following us now?

He didn’t answer immediately.

Then: Don’t look behind you more than once.

I keep starting to count the men and then stopping, because he told me not to and I think he is right about this — that counting them makes it impossible to keep walking. The numbers become weight. The weight becomes the ground. You stop moving.

I keep hearing the singing in my head. I cannot tell anymore whether it is memory or whether it is actual, out there in the dark, coming from somewhere in the bush on our left. The melody that goes the wrong way.

She sang about the valley. Oh Hargega holes, they can stop a flying man.

What is a flying man? A man who escaped? Or a man who only thinks he has?

I am very tired.

Something happened last night.

We had stopped to rest. My companion was awake, watching — I could see his outline. I had been drifting in and out of something that wasn’t fully sleep.

Then I heard the singing. Close. The closest it has ever been.

And inside the singing — underneath it, the way a root is underneath soil — I heard something else. Older. A child’s voice, or what had once been one. I do not know what it was doing there inside her song. I do not know if it was part of the lure or a remnant of something she carried from before she became what she became.

My companion heard it too. I know because I saw his hands tighten on his rifle and then, very slowly and deliberately, he lowered it. He set it on the ground.

I whispered: What are you doing?

He said: She hears metal. She hears the hunger inside a weapon. Put yours down.

I said: That is insane.

He said: Do it anyway.

I put my rifle down.

The singing came closer. The bush to our left went absolutely still. And then — it stopped. Not faded, not moved away. Stopped, the way a question stops when it receives an answer.

We sat in the silence for a long time.

He said, very quietly: She found what she came for.

I asked what he meant.

He said: She smells what a man has done. What he carries. She circles the ones who carry the most and she waits for them to invite her. He paused. We put our weapons down. A man with a weapon is a man who is still planning to kill. We are, right now, two men who are not planning to kill anyone. Not even each other.

I thought about this.

I said: Is that really why?

He was quiet. Then: I don’t know. Maybe she was simply full.

I can see a road from here. Real road, with vehicle tracks pressed into the earth. We have been walking toward it since dawn.

My companion stopped this morning, two kilometres back. He said he couldn’t go further. That the road was mine to reach alone. I understood. I didn’t argue.

Before I left he said:

She is not going anywhere. She is growing and she is not going anywhere. Everyone who comes here — soldier, fighter, anyone — she is here for them. She was here before the war and she will be here after it. The land is hers now.

I held out my hand. He looked at it for a moment as though he had not shaken another man’s hand in a long time.

Then he shook it.

Then he walked back into the bush.

I walked toward the road.

I can hear trucks. I don’t know whose yet. I don’t care much.

Amina, if you read this —

And you will read this. You always read everything. You were always the one who paid attention, even when I made you promise not to worry.

I want you to know I am writing this in actual daylight. There are birds somewhere to the north. Ordinary birds, not doing anything, just existing in a tree.

I want to tell you what I know now that I didn’t know in November.

The sergeant was right. You don’t look behind you more than once.

But here is the part he didn’t say. The part I had to learn myself, in a country that is not mine, in a darkness that belongs to something older than all of us:

Sometimes the thing behind you is not hunting you.

Sometimes it is only watching.

Waiting to see what kind of man you are.

I think I know now what kind of man I—

The entry ends there. Mid-sentence. The remaining pages are blank. Amina Odhiambo stacked the documents and set them on the table. She sat for a while. Outside on Ngong Road the morning was moving — matatus and dust and the smell of cooking from the woman near the stage. All the sounds of a world that had kept going. She thought about the sealed government files. The arrested blogger. The official numbers that didn’t match any honest count. She thought about what is buried and what is kept, and whether keeping something is a mercy or a cruelty. She placed the documents back in the envelope. She put the envelope behind the books her mother had kept on the high shelf.

She went and made tea. Some things, if you report them, make you sound like a man whose mind has broken. And some things survive without being reported. They survive in the whisper before sleep. In the pause on a night patrol when a soldier’s boots stop moving and he is not sure why. In a melody that rises when it should fall, heard once, remembered always — circling and circling, looking for the center, finding it in the dark. Somewhere in Somalia, a woman with long ears is still walking. She has been walking a long time. She is not tired yet.

Postmarked Mogadishu · March 2017 · sender unknown

The package arrived on a Tuesday in March 2017. No return address. The postmark read Mogadishu, though the ink had run, and Amina Odhiambo could not say how long it had wandered before it found her. Inside were two sets of documents. The first she recognized — her brother’s…

chapters.text:
Ghost Signal · 1.4M subscribers · Chernobyl Exclusion Zone

“All this activity starts at 1:23:45 a.m. No man from the Chernobyl fact-finding mission lived.”

THE CHANNEL — —

They had 1.4 million subscribers and nothing left to fear. That was what Marcus kept telling himself as the van rattled along the crumbling asphalt outside Kyiv, the dashboard camera blinking its red eye at the dark fields rolling past. Marcus drove. Dasha sat in the passenger seat editing thumbnails on a laptop, her face lit blue. In the back, Tomás slept across the equipment bags with the practiced ease of a man who had spent the last three years sleeping in abandoned buildings for content.

Their channel was called Ghost Signal. The banner read:WE GO WHERE CAMERAS AREN’T SUPPOSED TO GO. Chernobyl was not, technically, where cameras weren’t supposed to go. You could book a licensed tour. You could pay a guide, walk approved paths, leave by sunset. But Marcus had built 1.4 million subscribers by going where the tours didn’t. Through the fence. Past the dosimeter checkpoints. Into Reactor 4′s sarcophagus itself, if they could manage it. Two days, two nights inside the Zone of Alienation. No guides. No permissions. Just three cameras, a thermal

scope, a rack of radiation badges, and the certainty that this would be the video that finally broke three million.

The dosimeters were already clicking before they crossed the checkpoint wire.

I — THE FOREST — —

They entered at dusk, under a sky the color of a bruise. The Red Forest was the first thing that hit them — not the radiation readings, not even the silence, but the color. Everyone said the pines had died red and stayed red, burned from the inside by the fallout of April 1986. What the photographs didn’t prepare you for was the texture. The dead trees didn’t look burnt. They looked preserved— a forest vacuum-sealed at the moment of its dying, bark the color of oxidized copper, needles still clinging to branches that had not moved in thirty-eight years. Nothing rotted in the Red Forest. The bacteria themselves had been irradiated into stillness. The wood simply stood and waited.

“Rolling,” said Dasha, swinging the camera to Marcus’s face. He gave his intro, the one they’d scripted on the drive: the history, the explosion, the 350,000 displaced, the 31 official deaths that most researchers quietly multiplied by orders of magnitude. He was good on camera. His voice had the practiced steadiness of a man performing calm.

Tomás was fifteen feet into the tree line, sweeping the thermal scope in slow arcs, when he stopped.

“Marcus.”

The tone stopped Marcus mid-sentence. Tomás never said his name like that. Tomás narrated everything with the flat affect of a nature documentary —and here we can see the mold pattern consistent with Soviet-era construction— the voice that had earned him the nickname Professor in the comments. He did not say names in that voice. That was a different voice entirely.

“What do you have?”

“Come look at the scope.”

[ RECOVERED FOOTAGE — GHOST SIGNAL ARCHIVE — FILE GS_CHERNOBYL_RAW_01 ]The thermal camera file shows a heat signature at grid reference N51.389 E30.098. Duration of visibility: 4 seconds. Shape: bipedal. Height estimate: approximately 2.1 meters. The signature does not match any known fauna native to the exclusion zone. When enhanced, the outline appears to show extended lateral appendages inconsistent with human anatomy.

In the viewfinder, something moved between the copper trees. It walked upright. It walked slowly. The thermal image rendered heat as white against black, and this thing was barely warm — not the bright flare of a body generating heat, but a dim, smudged luminescence, like something that had absorbed just enough ambient temperature to register. Like something that had been cold for a very long time and had only recently, reluctantly, begun to remember what warmth was.

It turned its head toward them.

Tomás lowered the scope. In the bare optical dark of the forest, there was nothing. No shape. No movement. Only the copper trees standing in the windless air, and beyond them, nothing.

Nothing except the two points of red light, at height, perfectly still, watching.

1 : 2 3 : 4 5

II — PRIPYAT — —

The city of Pripyat was built to be beautiful. Soviet modernism at its most optimistic: wide boulevards, the ferris wheel that had never once turned for an actual visitor, the mosaic murals still vivid on the walls of the Palace of Culture. In the photographs it looked like decay. In person it looked like something else. It looked like a city that had been paused. The trees had grown up through the asphalt, yes, but the trees were themselves wrong — too tall, too dark, the bark discolored in patterns that suggested something cellular and wrong. The buildings had been emptied in forty-eight hours, 49,000 people told to take only what they could carry, told they’d be back in three days. They were never back. What they left behind had marinated in radiation for four decades.

Dasha filmed the apartment blocks. Marcus narrated. Tomás swept the thermal scope in slow arcs, not finding anything, and then finding something on the fourth floor of Block 9 — a window, curtains still hanging in the shreds of what had once been printed cotton flowers — and in the window, a shape. Sitting. The shape of a person sitting very still in a chair

that should not have still been there, in a room that should have held nothing but fallen plaster and irradiated dust.

“Fifth floor,” said Tomás, and his voice was the wrong voice again. “Fourth window from the left.”

Marcus looked. The window was dark. The shape was there.

“Can it see us?” Dasha asked.

Nobody answered that.

They moved deeper into the city. The dosimeter badges had turned a darker shade — they checked them against the color chart and agreed not to discuss what the chart said for that shade. The street they were walking turned, and they turned with it, and then Dasha grabbed Marcus’s arm because at the far end of the street, where the boulevard opened into the main square, something was standing in the open. Standing still. Enormous. The thermal scope rendered it in that same wrong, barely-warm luminescence — a wingspan that Tomás later estimated at nine feet, folded now, a hunched silhouette against the sodium black of the sky, its head — if it was a head — turned away from them.

Then it screamed.

Not a bird sound. Not anything from a throat shaped for the natural world. It was a sound that belonged to the place the way radiation belonged to the place — invisible, penetrating, wrong at the cellular level. Dasha’s footage shows her hand moving involuntarily to cover her own mouth. Marcus stepped backward into a pothole and went down hard on one

knee. Even Tomás, who had documented the documented the documented — who had been in the Catacombs and Waverly Hills and the basement levels of Eastern State — even Tomás put the scope down and stood very still, breathing through his nose, until the thing spread those wings and rose without a sound into the dark above the ferris wheel and was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

The phones stopped working at 11 p.m. Not signal loss — the bars were still there, the connection icons still displayed, but calls would not complete and messages would not send. Tomás opened his satellite communicator. It showed a green light. When he tried to transmit, the device emitted a sound that none of them had ever heard a satellite communicator make. A sound that was almost like breathing.

They made camp in the ground floor of a kindergarten. The murals on the walls were intact: cartoon animals on a cheerful green hillside, a smiling sun in the corner. Their sleeping bags went down between small overturned chairs and scattered primer books and the particular specific horror of children’s gas masks, still in their boxes, arranged along one wall by a teacher who must have believed, in those final hours of April 1986, that order was still possible. That preparation was still possible. That whatever was coming could be survived if you only followed the correct procedures.

III — THE SARCOPHAGUS — —

It was Dasha who heard it first. She woke the others at 1:15 a.m. Her face in the torchlight was very white and very still.

“Someone is screaming,” she said. “Inside the plant.”

They lay in the dark and they listened and the screaming was there — faint, and frantic, and unmistakably human, and unmistakably coming from the direction of Reactor 4. A voice begging, in Russian, for help with a fire. A voice that knew it was dying and had not yet finished dying. A voice repeating the same twelve words in a loop that suggested it had been saying those twelve words for a very long time.

Marcus pulled up the research on his downloaded files. Andrei Kharsukhov. University of Buffalo. 1997. A nuclear physicist who had entered the sarcophagus for readings and come running back up the stairs, ashen, telling the guards he could hear someone screaming for help in putting out a fire.You are the first person to enter in three years, they told him. The building required a password, a handprint, an alarm system. There was no one inside. There could be no one inside.

The screaming continued until 1:23 a.m. Then it stopped.

In the forty-five seconds of silence that followed, none of them moved.

Then the second second came, and the third, and they understood they were counting, all three of them counting without meaning to, counting the seconds as they added up and adding them to the minutes and the hour, and at precisely 1:23:45 the dosimeter badges

turned a color that wasn’t on the chart. And every camera they carried turned on by itself. And pointed at the wall.

REACTOR 4 SARCOPHAGUS — INTERNAL TEMPERATURE LOG — 26.04.1986 — 01:23:45 ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒ TEMPERATURE: [DATA CORRUPTED] PERSONNEL ON SITE: 2 PERSONNEL ACCOUNTED FOR: 0 ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒ END RECORD — NO FURTHER ENTRIES

The thing the cameras were pointing at was a shape on the wall. Not painted. Not scratched. The shape of a man, standing, arms slightly extended, rendered in a darker stain against the plaster — the way bodies near the hypocenter at Hiroshima had left their shadows burned into walls and pavement. A permanent record of a body’s final moment. A negative space where a person had been.

The shape’s head was turned. Turned toward the door. Turned — it seemed to them, in the torchlight, in the 1:23:45 silence of the Zone of Alienation — turned toward them.

IV — THE HOUR BEFORE DAWN — —

They did not sleep again. They sat with their backs to the mural of the smiling animals and they watched the wall and the wall watched them back, and when Tomás quietly pointed his thermal scope at the shape on the plaster it registered the same dim not-quite- warm luminescence as the thing in the forest, as the shape in the apartment window, and he set the scope face-down on the floor and did not use it again.

Dasha was the one who began to understand. She had been going through the research files they’d downloaded before the phones died, reading the entries on Valery Legasov — the lead Soviet investigator, the man who had gone to the site months after the explosion, who had been exposed, who had returned changed. Not ill, exactly. Changed. As though the place had written something into him that his mind could not stop reading. He had hanged himself on April 26, 1988 — the exact second anniversary of the explosion. They found him in the stairwell of his Moscow apartment. His investigation report, due the following day, was never submitted. The cause of the disaster, in the most complete and honest account anyone had ever attempted, was buried with him.

“He came back,” Dasha said. “After the investigation, he kept coming back here. In the early morning. This time.” She turned her phone so Marcus could see the screen, the downloaded archive page, the timestamp entries. “Every record of every fact-finder who came here. All of them.” She scrolled. “None of them lived longer than two years after the last visit.”

Marcus said: “That’s a coincidence.”

Dasha looked at him. She had very dark eyes, and in the torchlight they were darker still. “Is it,” she said. It was not a question.

Somewhere above them — above the kindergarten, above Pripyat, above the entire Zone of Alienation with its copper forest and its frozen ferris wheel and its shape on a wall — the winged thing screamed again. And this time, listening to it, Marcus felt something

he had not felt in three years of ghost-hunting and urbex and trespass into every dark building that the internet said was haunted. He felt the specific fear of someone who has just understood that the camera is not protecting him. That being the person holding the camera does not make him the observer. That in this place, at this hour, with these shapes moving through the irradiated dark, he is not documenting something.

He is something being documented.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left at first light, moving fast through the Red Forest. The copper trees stood in the windless morning, preserving their dead. The dosimeter badges were a color none of them mentioned. The cameras were still running — they ran the whole walk out, eight kilometers of footage that none of them have reviewed since returning.

The footage has been reviewed by others.

The footage shows, in the background of almost every frame, something following them through the trees. Walking upright. Moving at the exact pace they moved. Stopping when they stopped. Dim in the thermal readings, like something that has been cold for thirty-eight years and will never quite be warm again.

Ghost Signal posted no video. The channel has been inactive since April. The last post on their community tab reads:taking a break, back soon. It received 47,000 likes. The comments are full of people asking when the Chernobyl video drops.

Nobody has answered them.

1 : 2 3 : 4 5

The No. 4 reactor at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant experienced a catastrophic explosion at 1:23:45 a.m. on April 26, 1986. The sarcophagus built to contain it is the largest movable structure ever built by human hands. Inside it, in a room that has been sealed for decades, sits an object researchers call the Elephant’s Foot — a mass of melted reactor core and structural material that solidified into a grotesque shape in the hours after the explosion, in a room no living person reached for months afterward. The Elephant’s Foot is still intensely radioactive. The men who first photographed it used cameras on long poles because to enter the room was to die. Some of them died anyway.

Inside the sarcophagus, in certain rooms, at certain hours, the radiation detectors occasionally register anomalous readings. Patterns in the noise. Not random. Not explicable. The technicians who monitor the plant have learned not to log these readings. They have learned not to be there when they occur.

They have learned, above all, not to be there at 1:23 a.m. when the second hand reaches its forty-fifth position, and the Red Forest stands in its copper silence, and the figures rise with the moonlight over the city that has been waiting, patiently, since 1986, to be seen.

chapters.title: ABAGORE BABIRI
chapters.text:
overheard at a guesthouse bar, Kigali — three Primus beers in

His name was Pieter van der Berg, and he had the kind of laugh that made you feel safe.

I was three Primus beers into a Tuesday night at a guesthouse bar in Kigali when he sat down next to me — uninvited, in the easy way of men who have spent too long in the bush to remember that social contracts exist. He was broad-shouldered and sun-leathered, with a beard that had surrendered to grey somewhere in the middle of a forest and never found its way back. He smelled faintly of woodsmoke and something medicinal underneath, bitter like crushed fern.

He ordered two beers without asking me. Slid one across the counter like we’d been friends since boyhood. Did not touch his own.

I noticed that. I filed it somewhere I could not retrieve in time.

“You’re the one asking about the old stories,” he said. Not a question.

I was. I’m a folklore blogger — the kind of person who ends up in rural Rwanda because a thread pulled me here, slow and insistent, beginning with a dead- end archive in Nairobi and ending with an elderly woman on a hillside who told me a story like a bedtime tale and then stopped, abruptly, and fixed her eyes on the valley below with the flat, patient stillness of someone watching for something they fully expected to arrive.

Pieter already knew the story. He knew it better than I did.

"Umwicanyi wa babiri," he said, and his Kinyarwanda was flawless. That was the first warning I did not heed. “I have been tracking it for eight months.”

He said it the way a man talks about tracking a leopard. With patience. With a respect that had something underneath it I read, then, as obsession.

He told me he was from the Northern Cape. That he’d followed the creature’s trail from the DRC, where four rebel soldiers had filed reports of something in the canopy outside Goma. Two of those soldiers were found at dawn, alive but unable to give coherent testimony. The other two were found distributed across thirty square metres. The distribution was not random. It was considered.

“It never takes more than two,” he said, folding his hands around the beer he had not touched. “That’s what makes it extraordinary. Most predators are opportunistic. This thing is disciplined."

I told him what I knew. About the elderly woman and the story she’d carried like a wound. About two women, long before the colonial era, who had married brothers and outlasted them — who had been stripped of land and cattle by greedy in-laws and built a life from the leftover pieces of a life, held together by the refusal to be separated. About how they were found one morning torn apart. Not killed. Torn. Limbs wrenched from the body at the joints. A corner of their home preserved their final position: pressed together, hands clasped, the posture of two people who understood that what was coming would not be stopped by screaming.

“Why two?” I had asked the old woman.

She had not paused. “Because one can run.”

I told Pieter that. I watched his eyes as I said it.

He nodded slowly, like a man confirming something he already knew.

I told him about ABAGORE BABIRI — the women’s group, Two Women, whose secondary doctrine, buried beneath the language of sisterhood and mutual aid, was protection from something called Umwicanyi wa babiri. The killer of two. I told him about the old woman chanting at dusk — uturinde umwicanyi wa babiri — protect us from the killer of two — with her forehead pressed to the earth and her voice scraped raw. I told him about the thing that moved in the bushes behind my cottage after dark, and about the two friends who had appeared at my bedside and whispered a word I’d had to translate in the morning.

Bariri. Two.

Pieter listened to every word. When I finished he was quiet for a moment.

Then he smiled. Wide. Warm.

“There’s a cottage,” he said carefully, “on the hill where those women died. I’ve been trying to get close to it for three weeks.”

He thanked me for joining him. Genuinely, warmly. As if I had offered something he hadn’t known how to ask for.

I should tell you — I want to be honest with you about this — that there was nothing about Pieter van der Berg that felt wrong. He was funny. He knew the food. He translated my broken Kinyarwanda with a patience that made me feel understood rather than corrected. He had the comfortable warmth of a man who is very good at making people feel comfortable, which is a different thing entirely, though I did not know that yet.

I agreed to go with him in the morning.

Only later would I understand that the story itself had been the trap. That by listening, by leaning in, by letÝng his fear become my fear across a bar table in Kigali — I had formed the bond. I had become the second. The creature did not need us to be lovers or sisters or lifelong friends. It only needed us to be two people who had chosen each other, even for a single night, even over a single shared story. The warmth of that choosing was a scent it could follow across hills.

He had known that. He had ordered two beers.

The cottage was exactly as I remembered it. Facing the slope. The smell of red earth and something underneath that I could not name — something older, something that soil accumulates over generations of specific tragedy. The quiet there was not peaceful. It was held.

Pieter moved through the space with the efÏciency of someone who had been there before — or someone who had prepared. He set up a gas burner, cut dried meat, filled the room with warmth and conversation and the smell of something cooking. We ate as the sun dragged itself below the ridge and the valley below went the colour of a bruise.

He did not mention the creature again.

I noticed things in the way you notice things when the rational part of your mind is still arguing with the part that already knows. He checked the door twice. He placed his sleeping bag closest to the window — nearest the exit. He positioned me against the far wall, in the corner. The corner.

I told myself I was tired. I told myself I was projecting. I slept.

The flashbacks came for me like something physical, with edges and weight and the smell of copper.

I am standing in the corner of a room that is this room. The walls are older — mud-daubed, rougher — but the ceiling slopes the same way. Two women are pressed against the wall where my sleeping bag is. One faces outward, praying in Kinyarwanda so fast the words have lost their seams. The other has buried her face in the first woman’s shoulder and is making no sound at all, because she has already understood that sound will not save them. Something is in the room. The door has not opened. Nothing has been disturbed. It is simply inside, the way a thought is inside — present before you know you’ve had it. I cannot look at it fully. The mind will not permit the complete image, the way the eye cannot hold the centre of the sun. I register structure: dense, low, the musculature of something that has never needed to be afraid of anything. Fur matted flat against the body like wet cloth. Forelimbs too long, hanging too low, the knuckles almost grazing the floor. It moves without sound — not quietly, but without. As if the air itself has agreed not to carry it.

It takes the first woman slowly. That is the detail I cannot un-know: the slowness of it, the absence of any rush. The sound is green wood splitÝng, but wetter. Her left arm leaves her body. She is still alive. Still looking at it. The sound she makes is outside any register I can find words for — it is the sound a person makes when they have abandoned any idea of being heard. The second woman runs. Two steps. The crack of her ankle seizing in a grip that stops her mid-stride is so complete it seems to fill the room. The thing does not rush. It does not snarl. It makes a sound — low, grinding, percussive — that is the closest thing I have ever heard to satisfaction expressed as noise. It takes four minutes. It does not hurry. When it is finished, the corner is changed permanently, the walls altered at a level deeper than stain. Then it looks at me. No eyes I can name — no whites, no iris, just depth, like looking into standing water at night. But it is looking. It tilts what might be a head. It makes the grinding sound again and I understand, in the lucid logic of the not-dream, that it is not going to touch me. I am alone in this corner. And it only kills two. As it turns to leave, I see something I could not see before: a strip of cloth hanging from its chest, caught there like a trophy or a marking. Old cloth. Faded. Khaki.

I woke with the sound still vibrating in the bones of my face.

Pieter’s sleeping bag was empty. Folded neatly at the foot of where he had lain. Not abandoned. Folded. His pack was gone. His boots. The gas burner, the satellite phone, the rifle, the knife — all of it removed with the quiet efÏciency of someone executing a plan they had considered for a long time.

My hands were already shaking before my mind finished the thought.

I’ve been trying to get close to it for three weeks.

Not we. Not a camp. I.

I sat in the dark and I thought about scent. About proximity. About the fact that if a creature has tracked you across a hillside for three weeks it knows exactly where you breathe at night and which paths you favour in rain. I thought about what it would take to break that trail. What you would need to put in its place. Something new. Something whose fear was fresh and whose bond with you was real enough — warm enough, specific enough — to redirect attention.

You would need someone who had chosen you. Even briefly. Even over a bar table over a shared story.

You would need to be the kind of man whose laugh made people feel safe.

The silence outside shifted. That is the only way to say it — the quality of the silence changed, the way a room changes when something large enters it. No footstep. No branch. No breath. Only the silence becoming, suddenly, occupied.

I pressed myself into the corner. The corner.

My phone lit the room when I grabbed it. The translation app was still open from three nights ago — my clumsy Kinyarwanda phonetics, and underneath them, the English I had laughed at when I first read it. Back when all of this was still a good story I’d been handed by a warm stranger.

Protect us from the killer of two.

A shadow crossed the gap at the bottom of the door. Dense. Low. Patient.

And then, from the direction of the valley below — from a distance that meant safety, that meant escape — I heard another sound begin. Deeper than the first. Slower. The sound of something that had been waiting its turn.

Not one.

Two.

I thought of the old woman on the hillside, fixing her eyes on the valley with that flat, still expression. How she had not answered when I asked the creature’s name. How she had watched me walk back toward the cottage.

How she had thanked me for listening.

It is never the same when you are alone, she had said.

I had not understood her then.

I understood her now.

The door handle turned. The second sound from the valley rose to meet it.

Because Pieter had not been keeping the creature out.

He had been keeping me in.
