chapters.title: The Stones dream
chapters.text:
DRAFT

Unfinished ethnographic survey · Kitui County, Kenya

PAPER NO.: KU-EA-114 FIELD SITE: Kitui County, Kenya AUTHOR STATUS: Field researcher, unwell — entry written under fever, day four STATUS: Unpublished — withdrawn from review

The fever came for me on the third night in Kitui, the night the dreams began.

My colleagues at the university called it an ethnographic survey. I called it an exhumation. I have been unwell for four days now and I need to get this down before the logic of it dissolves back into that red haze where nothing coheres the way daylight insists things must. The truth about these stones does not lie in geology textbooks. It pulses beneath the surface like a swallowed heartbeat — slow, vast, utterly patient, belonging to a chest cavity the size of a cathedral.

The rocks are not rocks. They never were.

Let me speak plainly before the fever consumes the last of my coherence. What I have assembled from cracked mission archives, from the elliptical silences of Kamba elders, from the unspeakable geometry of fly-clusters in the ancient fissures — is this: these sacred formations are not shrines. They are not monuments. They are not the geological accidents the textbooks describe with such cheerful confidence.

They are prisons. And what they hold has never once slept.

I. WHAT WALKED BEFORE US — —

Long before the Kamba settled the red-earthed hills of Kitui. Long before the Luhya planted their fig trees in the rich soil of Vihiga. Long before any human foot pressed its print into the soft mud of what we now call Kenya — there were other things here.

I use the word things deliberately. The Swahili word viumbe contains everything — God, worm, cloud, grief. These were viumbe. But they existed in the space between hunger and intent, between animal and geometry, in a category that our language has no precise slot for because every culture that knew them made a collective decision to stop naming them. Names are invitations. The old people understood this.

They did not roam in packs. Pack is too sociable a word, too mammalian, too warm. They moved the way cosmological events move — with distributed, terrible purpose, no single intelligence directing them, only a shared need that preceded consciousness itself. And they were immense. The oldest account I found — a water-damaged missionary transcription from 1891, itself a copy of something older, rendered in handwriting that grew increasingly irregular toward the final page — described them as walking at the height of the mtama tree line, their torsos disappearing into cloud cover during the long rains. Shoulders like collapsed hillsides. Necks too long. Heads that did not resolve into any familiar animal configuration, that seemed to shift their geometry depending on the angle of observation, as though the skull itself refused stable form. Their footprints — some of which I have seen, preserved in the petrified mud of a dry riverbed near Mwingi — are four metres across and pressed so deep that the earth around them is still, after three thousand years, slightly compressed, as if the land itself remembered the weight and chose not to forget it.

They came down from the ridges in silence. No tremor of footfall that would, by rights of physics, have shaken every hut in a village radius to powder. Only the dry whisper of mtama grass parting around legs the height of ancient trees. Villages woke to find the sky was wrong. Too much of it blocked. A darkness moving against the stars with deliberate patience.

They hunted with ceremony. This is the part that should be metaphor and is not. They could have killed quickly — could have simply stepped. They chose not to. Something in their nature required the prolonged specific act of being witnessed in their choosing. They circled. They waited. They wanted the last face a person ever raised skyward to meet theirs — whatever arrangement of organs and geometry constituted a face — before descending. They struck with the measured satisfaction of something that has been looking forward to this for longer than civilisation has existed.

The Kamba had a name for them. Two elders I interviewed separately, in villages forty kilometres apart, both went pale when I said the word I had found in the 1923 mission archive. One of them placed her hand physically over my mouth and shook her head, her eyes saying what her voice would not: do not call them. Do not remind them you have a throat.

I had already said the word.

That night the fever came, and with it the first dream, and in the dream the horizon was moving and the horizon had teeth.

II. THE RATIONING — —

Before the mage came, there was a system. This is the part no one includes in the brochures, the part the colonial ethnographers recorded in detached horror and then buried in mission archives in Machakos where I found them a century later, pressed between the pages of a hymnbook as though proximity to sacred text might neutralise them.

The sacrifices at these rocks were not goats. The goats came later, after the binding — maintenance payments to keep the seal intact. Before the binding, the payment was human, and it was not coerced tribute. It was managed rationing. You give the creatures enough that they stay distant, that the enormous patient dark shapes on the ridge remain there and do not descend. You give them the ones you can afford to lose. You call it holy. You do not look at the faces of those you give. You tell your children it is prayer, because prayer is easier to

carry than the truth, which is that your ancestors purchased their safety with the blood of people they decided mattered less, offered up to mouths the size of grain stores.

The Kilume — the Kamba possession ritual, the sacred drum-rhythm said to induce spiritual trance — was not originally a ceremony of worship. It was a selection ceremony. The possessed were the chosen. The trance was not divine visitation. It was the creature’s attention, lowering itself from some unimaginable height to taste what it was being offered, to confirm the offering was acceptable. A colossus, stooping to examine whether what was being held out in open hands was worth the bend.

We have been calling this religion. It was never religion. It was an invoice, written in bodies, settled in blood, administered by elders who looked away during payment.

III. UKASI ROCK — THE FLY THAT REMEMBERS — —

Ukasi Rock rises twenty-five metres from the scrubland of eastern Kitui like a fist frozen mid-punch. The travel guides will tell you about Mormotomyia hirsuta, the Frightful Hairy Fly — wingless, bristly, endemic only to this specific boulder, first described by entomologist E. E. Austen in 1936. They call it a biological curiosity, a remarkable example of island endemism, and move on with their lives.

They will not tell you what Mwende told me. Mwende is seventy-three years old and has lived within sight of Ukasi her entire life and has never agreed to live any closer. She told me, in a whisper I had to lean into like a penitent, that the flies do not feed on bat guano as the scientists maintain. She said: They feed on memory. They bore into skin not to eat but to taste the bloodline. They remember what the rock remembers.

Consider what it means for a fly to lose its wings. Wings are not vestigial appendages one sheds casually across geological time. The metabolic cost of losing flight is enormous unless something in the immediate environment made

flight actively dangerous. What would make flight dangerous in the vicinity of a single rock? What exhalation, what emanation, what invisible pressure radiating from those crevices punished any creature that lifted itself into the air above them?

The creature sealed at Ukasi was not fully outside its prey when the mage arrived. It was mid-consumption — one of the vast cyclopean entities, kneeling, its monstrous head lowered to the earth, feeding through fissures in the rock bed with an apparatus I will not describe because the elder who described it to me has not spoken since. The stone rose around it during that act. The consumption never technically stopped. It is still feeding, in arrested geological time, from whatever it had hold of at the moment of sealing. The fly is its exhalation. The pores of the rock are its nostrils. What emerges in the rainy season, fat and obscene, is looking for something warm to continue what the stone began.

I sat at the base of Ukasi for seven hours. At dusk the insect chorus of the bush — continuous since morning — stopped. Not tapered. Stopped. In the absolute silence that followed I heard breathing that was not mine. Deep and enormously patient, the pause between inhale and exhale belonging to lungs of unimaginable volume somewhere below the rock. Below the ground itself. The rock pulsed once, barely perceptibly, like a body the size of a hill remembering it once had a heartbeat.

I left before it could pulse twice.

— IV. KOMA ROCK — THE MOUTH THAT WAS NEVER CLOSED —

Any Kenyan Christian knows Koma Rock. Shrine, pilgrimage destination, peaceful meditation site on the Nairobi–Kangundo road. The Catholics built a seventy-foot Pietà at the summit — the dead Christ in his mother’s arms, serene in finished suffering. They built it directly over the seam.

The 1923 mission archive account describes what the hill was before the Pietà, in the testimony of a dying elder whose voice the catechist wrote down with the shaking hand of a man recording something he wished he had not heard. The

elder said the rock would grow warm at dusk. A seam would open like a mouth — and something would emerge from it, slowly, with geological patience: a single limb, and then another, and another, the rock unfolding like a doorway, and from the door came a thing of such disproportionate scale that the elder could not complete its description without stopping and pressing his face into his hands.

What was sealed at Koma was the largest of them. The mage used the sound of a stolen infant’s crying to draw it back — because these giants, for all their enormity, were oriented toward the intimate; they found the sound of suffering irresistible not from cruelty but from something like a connoisseur’s compulsion, the need to be proximate to the distilled essence of human anguish. The cry is still performing its function, looping in the darkness below the shrine. And the creature — still believing it is being asked a question by something it has not yet consumed — has been answering from inside the stone for over a century.

When the construction company Mowlem arrived in 1970 to blast through the hill, the machinery worked perfectly on every other formation along the route and failed specifically at Koma. Then the Israeli site supervisor began hearing a child crying in the dark, and a vast low voice answering it from somewhere beneath the earth — a voice so deep it was felt more than heard, vibrating in the fillings of his teeth and the marrow of his sternum. The workers left their tools where they stood. You can still see some of them rusting in the grass if you know where to look.

I pressed my ear to the base of the Pietà, where Italian marble meets raw Kenyan rock, and heard it: the child, still wailing in the dark below. And below that — vast, subsonic, patient as tectonic movement — the answering voice. We will never leave. This will always be our home.

That is not a ghost. That is a colossus the size of a cathedral basement, still awake, still listening, still believing the bait is real. Every Catholic procession that crosses that seam is walking over a conversation between a lure and a leviathan that does not know it has been sealed.

— V. MATSIGULU ROCK — THE LOCK AND WHAT IT HOLDS —

On a five-acre farm in Gavere, south Maragoli, there is a rock whose surface is covered in writing no one can read. Not petroglyphs. Not symbolic registers of ancient hunters. These are characters in an alphabet that exists nowhere else in the world’s catalogue of human inscription, and every linguist brought to examine them has eventually stopped talking and started looking at their feet.

Beside the writing: handprints. Human in shape but proportionally wrong — fingers too long by half, palm too narrow, the impression of a hand that spent a very long time pressing against a surface from the other side. Beside the handprints: an engraving of a lock and a key, rendered with technical precision belonging to no period of regional history. The teeth of the key are individually cut. The keyhole has depth. I am locked in here. I know about locks. I know what a key is for.

The creature entombed at Matsigulu was the smallest of them — barely the height of a two-storey building at its most compact — and in some ways the worst, because it was the shapeshifter, the intimate one. It could compress its enormous body into beloved forms: a missing child, a returning spouse, close enough to pass at distance, enough to lead its victim into the bush on the strength of longing alone. Up close the proportions were always wrong. The eyes too high. The neck slightly too long. The hands, when they reached — the handprints on the rock are the truest thing about it. The mage tricked it into its smallest configuration and cast the cofÏn-stone around it while it slept.

In 2009 a stonemason was warned in a dream not to break the cofÏn rock. He broke it anyway with a pneumatic drill. He was bedridden for six months with a grotesquely swollen abdomen. The swelling was not metaphorical. It was the creature’s last exhale — a reservoir of necrotic gas compressed for centuries — recognising the vibration of the drill and attempting to migrate into the nearest available living tissue. He recovered only after a mghanga who still remembered the old words performed a ceremony the stonemason later refused to describe, speaking the unbinding phrases that told the gas: not free. Not yet. Not like this.

The mghanga who knows those words is ninety-one years old. She will not live forever. And the gas is still in the stone, pressing.

VI. NZAMBANI ROCK — THE STONE WOMB — —

The gender-change story is a corruption. What was lost across generations of retelling is the direction of the warning. The original instruction was not walk around it seven times to change yourself. It was do not walk around it seven times or it will change you. The transformation promised is not the charming magical sex-swap of tourist legend. What happens on the seventh circuit is that you offer your own body as a key, and the thing inside the stone — one of the vast ones, sealed in a foetal compression that the rock only barely contains — stirs in its mineral sleep and feels for the first time in millennia the warmth of a living human outline pressed against its prison wall.

The founding story: a girl collecting firewood found a stone, perfect for grinding tobacco, and tucked it inside her breast cloth. It attached to her flesh and grew. By the time the medicine man arrived it was the size of a fist and warm. By the time he gave up it had calcified through her completely. She did not become a rock. She was used as an aperture. The creature used her as a door into this world, and when it had fully contracted through that opening it sealed the door with her body. The screaming at night is not wind. It is her — still inside, still pressing against a wall made partly of her own calcified remains.

The cave at Nzambani’s base is the birth canal. People simply arrive at the cave mouth and find they cannot continue. Their bodies decline before the mind understands why. The prohibition is older than language. The bone knows before the brain does.

I walked around Nzambani seven times. I will not pretend I did not know what I was doing. By that point in my research I had crossed too many thresholds not to test the last one. On the seventh circuit the world tilted. The cave entrance widened. The air smelled of wet iron and deep earth, of something that had been enclosed for longer than iron has been smelted. I felt a pressure against my palm — something pressing from inside the stone with the flat, sustained force of a body of enormous size shifting its weight against a door. And then a voice, not a

scream. A lullaby. Low and vast, emanating not through air but directly through the bones of my skull, bypassing hearing entirely, resonating in the jaw, in the back teeth, in the place at the base of the skull where the spine begins.

It called me Mwithi.

We are not researchers. We are the maintenance. I understood this on the seventh circuit, when the rock pressed back against my palm and I felt the heat of something that has not slept once in three thousand years.

CODA: WRITTEN AT DAYBREAK — —

The fever broke before dawn. For the first time in five days the dreams did not come, which means either the writing is complete and something is satisfied — or the writing is complete and something no longer needs to reach through me to communicate.

The mage’s binding required not just physical sealing but continuous witnessing — an unbroken chain of people who know what the stones hold, passing the knowledge forward through whatever medium their culture provided. For centuries this was oral tradition, encoded in the Kilume rhythms and the warnings about the cave. Then the colonial period disrupted the chain. The knowledge began to leak out of cultural memory. The seals began to weaken in direct proportion to how thoroughly the witness-chain thinned.

The rocks escalated their communication strategy. The child’s voice at Koma. The construction machinery failing. The dreams of researchers who stay too long near the wrong boulders. The fever that sits in the marrow of anyone who presses their ear to stone and listens. They are not haunting. They are recruiting. Because a prison without a warden who knows it is a prison is simply a rock. The knowledge is the final layer of the lock. Without someone who understands what is sealed and why, the seal is just geology.

I have pages in this notebook written in a hand I do not fully recognise as my own. On three occasions the pages smelled of deep earth and copper when I opened the book in the morning, the smell of a space that has been closed since before the pyramids.

The Crying Stone at Ilesi, in Kakamega — forty metres tall, water flowing from a central groove in a motion indistinguishable from grief — has stopped crying. Eucalyptus trees sucked the water table dry. The groove went silent. And now, at night, in the canopy around the stone, something laughs. I have stood in that grove at eleven at night. The laughter comes from inside the rock. It has the quality of a sound that has been waiting a very long time to be made — the laughter of something of enormous volume and patience that has just been given reason, for the first time in centuries, to believe that the conditions for its release are changing.

Not joy. Not cruelty. Just the recognition, vast and subsonic, that the door is getting tired.

Visit the rocks if you want. The Pietà at Koma is genuinely moving. The mystery inscriptions at Matsigulu are genuinely strange. The view from Nzambani at sunset is, by all accounts, spectacular.

But do not walk around Nzambani seven times.

And if you are on the Ilesi road at night and hear laughter in the eucalyptus canopy — laughter with deep geological patience in it, laughter emerging from something that once strode across this land at the height of tree lines, that has been compressed into stone for three thousand years and has only recently remembered that it is still hungry — do not stop. Do not look up into the branches.

Drive.

The rocks have been containing something since before the first human being walked this land. Every prayer, every Kilume drum, every pilgrim’s candle, every goat brought to a boulder at dusk, every researcher’s fever notebook filled at three in the morning — all of it is weight against the door.

The door is very old.

And what presses against it from the other side has not once, in all that time, stopped pressing.

chapters.title: Ruiru mansion
chapters.text:
FOR SALE

Ruiru, Kiambu County · Eleven Bedrooms · Gated Compound

The first thing the house taught us was that silence has a weight.

Not the silence of empty rooms or dead batteries or a city asleep. The silence of something holding its breath. Waiting to see whether you were worth the effort.

We arrived at eleven, five of us — Zara, Biko, Tej, Amina, Makena — armed with thermal cameras, EMF readers, condenser mics, ring lights, and the specific arrogance of people who have confused having followers with being protected. The driveway was a broken spine of cracked tarmac disappearing into overgrowth. The gate stood open. Not forced, not rusted free. Open. As though someone had unlocked it that afternoon and simply not come back.

The Kariuki Mansion occupied its plot the way old grief occupies a family — structurally, silently, reshaping everything around it. Three floors of colonial stone, window frames still intact, walls holding the memory of paint in grey flakes. The bougainvillea had grown through the fence in deliberate coils. The front door was unlocked. Tej pushed it open and the hinges moved without a sound, smooth and patient, and that — not any ghost, not any sound — was the first thing that made the back of my throat close.

Inside: a living room that should not have existed. Deep mahogany furniture still arranged, cracked leather couches still facing each other in civilized conversation, a chandelier overhead fouled with grime. On the shelves, books. Their spines faded but readable — Weep Not Child, A Grain of Wheat. Someone had loved something here. The smell was dust and old cloth and something beneath it I kept refusing to name, something metallic and sweet and ancient, like soil from a grave turned over after a long rain.

We set up our equipment. Biko placed the EMF reader on the coffee table. Its needle sat at zero, which was normal. Tej unpacked mandazi and a thermos and narrated into his camera about keeping energy up, and for twenty minutes the house allowed us this normalcy. Allowed us our lights and our bravado and our comment sections.

At midnight, nothing had happened.

Kefa — I mean Tej — I mean all of us — we all started to breathe again. Our bodies began translating fear back into content. Zara was already composing a caption in her head. The live stream sat at sixty thousand viewers, restless, bored, telling us to go upstairs.

Then Biko looked at the EMF reader.

The needle had moved to the far left of the dial. Below zero. Into the register the manual described as theoretically impossible, the reading that indicated not the presence of electromagnetic energy but its consumption. Something in this house was eating the air.

He opened his mouth to speak.

That was when we heard it.

From upstairs. A tapping, soft and patient as a secretary waiting to be acknowledged. One tap. Then another. Not random — measured, deliberate, the intervals identical. Like someone counting.

The camera was handed to me. The moment my fingers closed around the rig the cold came — not from the air but from inside my wrist, from the metal itself, as though the camera had been sitÝng in a freezer for three days. I tightened my grip. Amina took the light. We looked at each other and climbed.

The staircase amplified. Every footfall landed with a resonance that had no right to exist in a carpeted space — a deep, structural sound, as though the house were receiving us in its bones. The cold intensified with each step. Not the cold of a room. The cold of something directed at us, washing downward in slow deliberate waves. Finding the backs of our necks. Finding the spaces between our fingers.

“Do you feel cold?” Amina said.

I felt it in my teeth.

The corridor was long and narrow. Four doors, all closed. Our phone lights carved weak tunnels through the darkness and left everything outside those tunnels deeper than black — not an absence of light but a presence of something that light would not touch. I moved the camera along the walls. The walls showed brown stains in uneven patches, old water damage or old something-else. At the far end, a window.

Gravel hit it. Three small stones, deliberate intervals, not trying to break the glass. Trying to get our attention. Come look. Here. Come.

I shone the light through the pane. Outside: the yard, the overgrown garden, the fence leaning inward, and beyond it darkness so complete it looked structural. No person. No animal. Nothing that would throw a stone.

Another pebble struck the glass.

Then the house inhaled.

I have no better description for it. A change in pressure so total and abrupt that my eardrums registered it — a drawing-in of the air itself, as though the building had been holding its breath for fifteen years and had just decided to breathe.

One voice began. Low. Female. A single sustained note that was not quite a note but a shape — modal, old, the kind of melodic form that predates notation, that lives in the body before it lives in the mind. Then a second voice found the fifth above it. Then a third. They wove together with the terrible ease of people who have sung this together for a very long time, the harmonies locking into place the way old joints lock — irreversibly, completely.

Cha kutamaini sina, cha kutegemea wewe.

I have nothing else to hope in. I have nothing else to lean on but You.

My grandmother had sung this hymn. I had heard it at two funerals. I knew it as a sound of surrender, of a person who has come to the absolute edge of what they can hold and set it down. Here, in this darkness, in this corridor, sung by voices with no body, no origin — here it was the most frightening sound I had ever heard. Not because it was hostile. Because it was sorrowful. Because the grief in it was so enormous and so old that it had become indistinguishable from devotion, and both of those things pressed against the walls with a weight that was physical, that I felt in my sternum.

Amina was weeping. She didn’t know it until her own salt reached her lips.

Then the woman passed us.

She did not walk from one room toward another. She simply was not there and then she was — a woman in a long dark skirt that swept the floor, a high- collared blouse yellowed with age, hair pinned back with the severe tidiness of another century. Her face was visible and I wish it had not been. Not because it was monstrous. Because it was tired — exhausted with a depth that suggested not years but decades of waiting, of standing in corridors, of watching people like us arrive with our cameras and our arrogance and our failure to understand what we had walked into.

She did not look at us.

She moved to the end of the corridor and passed through a door that had been closed and opened it without touching it and was gone.

Amina grabbed my arm with both hands.

Neither of us screamed. That was the thing none of the commenters ever understood when they watched the footage later — that we did not scream because we were too frightened to make a sound, and that not screaming is so much worse, that the silence we made was a mirror of the silence the house was making, and that in that moment we understood without language that we had entered something that did not require our participation.

The singing swelled.

More voices now, filling in from below, from the walls, from the ceiling, from the specific nowhere that large coordinated sound comes from in buildings that should be empty. Tenors folded under the sopranos. A low male voice held the drone beneath everything. And under the choir, beginning soft and clear as a struck bell:

A piano.

One note. Then another. The melody of Cha Kutamaini Sina picking itself out with a slowness that was deliberate — not hesitant but patient, note by note as though giving us time to recognize it. To feel what it was. To understand that we were not observing a haunting but standing inside one that had been running since before we were born.

Then the sound changed.

Not a transition. A rupture. The singing dragged itself downward out of melody into something animal, a growling that was not one voice but many, a sound like wet stone scraping stone, like something large turning over in mud. The piano stopped. The silence that followed had a texture — dense and close, a silence with things moving through it. Then from every wall simultaneously: wailing. Not spectral, not atmospheric. Specific. Close. Human grief in its rawest register, the sound a person makes when they have run out of strength to hold the grief in shape and it simply spills. It was coming from inside the walls. From the other side of the plaster. From somewhere that should have been stone and insulation and nothing else.

The cold hand found my shoulder.

Fingers. A full palm. The precise, unmistakable weight of a hand — cold as metal left in a river, pressing against me with a gentleness that was more terrifying than violence, the gentleness of something claiming rather than attacking. I screamed and spun and grabbed at nothing. The warmth where the hand had been vanished instantly, replaced by an absence so complete my skin registered it as a burn.

Then the scream from inside the wall answered mine.

Long. Ragged. MufÒed by plaster and years. The scream of someone who had been in there a long time and was not screaming from panic but from habit — the sound of someone who had learned to keep trying even after hoping was finished.

We were all facing the wall. We had forgotten the staircase entirely.

The gravel struck the windows again, frantic now — not three stones but a rain of them, urgent, furious, as though whatever was throwing them had shifted from invitation to warning — get out get out get out — and it was Tej who turned first because Tej always laughed at the wrong moment and looked toward the wrong thing and this time he made no sound at all, just went completely still, and that stillness was the loudest thing in the room.

She was on the stairs.

Coming down slowly. Her bare feet made no sound on the wood despite the weight of her skirt. The knife hung from her right hand the way a tool hangs from someone who knows their work — not raised, not menacing, simply present. A kitchen knife, old, heavy-handled, its blade catching the thin light from our cameras in one thin stripe. But the blade was wrong. In the footage we would watch later, frame by frame, at four in the morning with our hands shaking — the blade had been wrapped at the handle in something dark, dried rafÏa or cloth or both, and the metal itself was a colour that steel should not be, darker than iron, the colour of something that had been used for purposes beyond cooking.

Her face.

I spent six months trying to reconstruct what I saw on that staircase and failing. Not because it was inhuman. Because it was so precisely human and so fully known — the face of someone who has been waiting for a specific visitor and has recognized them. Not anger. Not hunger. Recognition. She looked at us the way people look at debts that have finally arrived to be settled.

Her mouth was moving.

I believe now that she was counting.

We ran. The body, when truly frightened, does not consult the brain. We ran through the living room and through the kitchen and Ray — Tej — someone shoulder-charged a back door and we went over the wall and I tore my palm open on the iron sheet and felt nothing until we were two kilometers away under a streetlight, all five of us standing in the rain that had started without our noticing, breathing like animals, alive and not remotely okay.

The live chat had been screaming at us for eleven minutes.

Who is behind you. Look at the mirror. She’s been in the frame since the corridor. Why is she closer in every shot. At 1:22, why is she smiling.

We didn’t see any of it until Zara’s phone died and came back on and the notifications loaded in a cascade, hundreds of the same message arriving in different fonts from different strangers who had watched from their comfortable beds and had seen what we, standing inside it, had failed to see.

She was in the footage. Beginning to end. Not in the house only — she appeared in the reflection of the car window as we drove away. A shape too tall, too still, framed in the glass. No one had been walking on that road.

The comments never stopped. The video went to two million views in eight hours and in the comment section of every clip, every reaction, every frame- by-frame breakdown uploaded by strangers in countries that had never heard of Ruiru — the same question, in English and Swahili and languages we did not recognize:

Who is standing behind them.

Zara heard the piano first. Three in the morning, her Kilimani apartment, the living room empty and dark. Cha Kutamaini Sina, note by note, with the same patient slowness as on the stairs. She sat up. Went to the living room. Silence. Lay back down. The piano resumed — fainter now, as though drifting from a room one wall beyond the furthest wall of her flat.

Makena woke at three every morning for eighteen consecutive days. She described it in a video she posted without makeup, without lighting, without any of the apparatus of her usual content — just her face in the blue light of an early morning, eyes that had not slept: “It’s not a sound. It’s more like a pressure. A cold that comes from inside the room even when the windows are closed. And I know — I know — it’s not what died. It’s what never was human. And it came home with us.”

Four million views. In the comments: pause at 2:34. Look at the window behind her.

Biko drove to the hospital himself. He sat in the waiting room for two hours before he spoke, and when he spoke he chose his words with the precision of a man who has thought about nothing else for a week: “I went somewhere I was not supposed to go and I left a door open behind me and I need help learning how to close it.” The admitÝng psychiatrist noted his affect as calm. She did not note it as the specific calm of someone who has moved past the point where panic is useful.

Tej stopped being funny. Those who knew him said this before anything else — not that he had become frightened or erratic or lost sleep, but that the humor simply ceased, like a signal cutÝng out. He went live one final time from his apartment, nine days after Ruiru, the camera showing his face and the room behind him. He talked normally for six minutes. In the comment section: look at the corner above the door. She’s been there since you turned the camera on. Tej she’s been there the whole time. The stream ended mid-sentence. He did not post again.

They admitted all five of us within six weeks. Not coordinated — we had barely spoken since that night, the shared experience creating not closeness but a mutual distance, the instinct of people who know that looking at each other is too close to looking at the house. The psychiatrists called it shared psychogenic illness with acute delusional features. They said sleep deprivation and viral stress and the feedback loop of comment sections. They said mass hysteria. They said these things in the tone of people who needed these things to be true.

None of them watched the footage.

The night nurses did. In whispers, in groups of two, in the break room with the volume low. Because the footage kept changing. Not the original file — that had been archived, frozen. The copies. The screenshots. The reaction videos. In each generation of re-upload, the woman was closer. In the earliest clips she stood at the far edge of the living room, barely visible. By the seventeenth generation of re-posts, she was directly behind us. By the twenty-third, she occupied the foreground and we were the background.

Room 14. The five of us, at some point gathered in one ward or adjacent ones by coincidence that our families were asked to believe was administrative. The fluorescent lights hummed at fifty hertz. The vinyl floors reflected us back faint and distorted. And at three in the morning — every morning, never varying, never late — the old wall radio in the corridor crackled and went not to static but to a clear, unhurried piano.

The doctors said it was a frequency bleed from a transmitter nearby. We said nothing, because by then we understood that she did not need us to say anything. She only needed us to hear.

The last time I was coherent enough to look at a screen, the video had 40 million views. I read the comments until I couldn’t anymore. Different names, different countries, different languages, but always the same question, over and over, the question no one in the footage could hear because we were inside it, the question that strangers watching from safety kept typing into the box beneath a video of five people running through a dark house in Ruiru:

Who is that standing behind them.

The TV screen across the ward was off. Dark glass, perfectly reflective.

In it I could see the room, the beds, the white walls, the door.

And behind me — patient, still, the long skirt falling to the floor, the knife held loosely at her side, her mouth moving around words I had finally learned to read:

Cha kutamaini sina. I have nothing left to hope in. Neither do you.

She was smiling. Not at me. At the screen. At the camera that was always, somewhere, always still rolling, always still broadcasting, always still feeding whatever she was to whatever was watching.

I turned the TV off.

The piano began to play.

The Kariuki Mansion still stands. The gate is still open. The door is still unlocked. In the comment sections of forty-seven countries, people are still pausing at the same timestamps and typing the same question. No one has gone back to answer it. The woman in the long skirt does not need them to.

GPS: SIGNAL LOST · LAST FIX 22:14 · SPEED 0 km/h

Thar Desert Crossing · GPS signal intermittent

They had been driving for miles, for hours, perhaps for longer than time permitted—and the road had the peculiar quality of a dream that refuses to end. The Thar Desert stretched in every direction beyond the van’s windows, vast and lightless, as though the universe had simply forgotten to finish building the world out here. Lakshmi sat rigid in the passenger seat, her jaw set in that particular angle that preceded something worse than shouting. Sandheer pressed his face against the back window. Priya had stopped speaking an hour ago, which frightened Singh more than anything else because Priya never stopped speaking. And Singh drove, because that was what Singh did when everything else was falling apart — he drove, and he said nothing, and he hoped the road would save him from having to be honest.

“If only you had asked for directions. Maybe we wouldn’t be in this situation.”

Lakshmi did not look at him when she said it. She said it to the windshield, to the dark, to whatever listening thing the dark contained. The van was full of that particular exhaustion that settles into the bones after too many hours on a road that loops back

on itself without announcing that it’s doing so. They had passed the same crooked acacia tree three times. Singh had not mentioned this.

The desert at night near Jaisalmer is not merely dark. It is the absolute dark — the dark before the first fire, the dark inside a closed eye, the dark that preceded the Vedic gods themselves. No stars were visible. There had been stars an hour ago. Singh was trying not to think about where the stars had gone.

— then Sandheer saw the lights —

“Look! Lights!”

They all leaned forward at once, six bodies suddenly reunited by hope. Forty kilometers, perhaps, by the eye’s reckoning. Distant amber points floating in the black like a constellation that had descended to earth. A settlement. Other people. The impossible promise of ordinary things — a glass of water, a working phone, a road that went somewhere other than back to itself.

But here was the first wrong thing, the thing that Singh would later understand was the village introducing itself: the lights did not behave as lights should. When they drove toward them, the lights receded. Not drastically, not obviously — just enough. Just enough that the forty kilometers remained forty kilometers for twenty minutes of driving. As if the settlement were breathing, drawing back on the inhale, releasing on the exhale, deciding whether to let them in.

Then all at once — as if the decision had been made — the lights were close.

The Mohini of Hindu mythology is the only female avatar of Vishnu, but her darker twin haunts the roadways of Rajasthan — a beautiful illusion that appears at crossroads to travelers who are lost, exhausted, or dying. She does not lead them to safety. She leads them to the place from which no direction leads out. In village lore, she is the light at the end of a road that should not exist. She is the settlement on the map that the map does not show. The old texts say:Do not follow a light that approaches you. You did not choose it. It chose you.

II · THE SETTLEMENT — —

Grass-thatched. Mud-walled. Waiting.

The settlement was wrong in the way that a smile on a corpse is wrong — structurally correct, functionally impossible. Grass-thatched roofs. Mud walls the color of old skin. Torches burning in the absolute absence of anyone to have lit them. The architecture was old in a way that modern poverty is not old — this was not abandonment, not decay, but something more deliberate. This was preservation. As if the village had been kept exactly as it was, exactly as it had been, on the night it ended.

The temple squatted at the village’s edge like a patient animal. Its bell swung without wind, slow and rhythmic, and the sound it made was not quite a bell’s sound — too low, too deliberate, as though the

bell were being rung by something that had practiced ringing it but had never heard what bells were for.Gong. Gong. Gong. Three beats and a silence. Three beats and a silence. Like a breath with a pause in it.

“Maybe there’s a festival,” Lakshmi said.

No one asked her why a festival would be held in a place with no people.

The eerie silence that hung around the village was not the silence of emptiness. Singh understood this before he understood anything else. Emptiness has a flat quality, a two-dimensional stillness. This silence had weight. It pressed against the van’s windows. It filled the space between words. It was the silence of a room full of people who have all simultaneously decided not to move, not to breathe, not to announce themselves — the silence of watching.

They stepped out anyway. They were tired, and tired people make bargains with themselves that rested people would never countenance.

The torches burned. The bell rang. The village waited.

The streets between the mud walls were narrow and labyrinthine, each turn revealing another identical arrangement of abandoned doorways and dark thresholds. Priya walked close behind Singh. She had not yet understood what her body already knew — that she was walking faster than the group, that she was pushing into Singh’s back because some animal part of

her had decided that the front was marginally safer than the gap between bodies. Sandheer had stopped exclaiming. He walked with his phone raised, its flashlight cutting a white cone through torchlight that should have been sufficient and somehow was not. Lakshmi held Priya’s daughter, Meera, who was five years old and who had not cried despite the darkness, which was wrong. Five-year-olds cry in the dark. Meera was looking at the doorways.

“What are you looking at, baby?” Lakshmi whispered. “The people,” Meera said.

They searched every doorway. There were no people.

The Preta — the restless dead of Hindu cosmology — are souls trapped between lives. They died with unfinished desire or unconfessed sin, and so they remain, thin as shadows, hungry as fire, attached to the places where their bodies last knew comfort. They cannot be seen by those whose third eye is closed. But children — children younger than seven, before the mind learns to disbelieve — children see them as clearly as they see the living. They crowd doorways. They fill thresholds. They press against the membrane between the worlds and they watch the living the way the dying watch the healthy — with terrible, unassuageable longing.

III · WHAT THE HISTORY BOOKS DARE NOT NAME — —

— ONCE UPON A TIME, NEAR JAISALMER, A VILLAGE SIMPLY CEASED —

The village of Kuldhara had eighty-four villages under its name, and within a single night, without sound, without spectacle, without a single witness to their departure, every last soul within them was gone.

No bodies. No carts left mid-packing. No dogs running loose with no masters to answer to. No fires left burning. They were there at dusk; by dawn, the houses stood empty as cracked eggs. The how and why and where remained forever unanswered, and it was precisely the unanswered quality of it that made the place permeable — that tore a hole in the membrane between what is and what will not stop being.

History offers the tidy version: a minister, cruel and powerful, desired the village chief’s daughter. He sent his ultimatum on a night that smelled of woodsmoke and bad stars. Give me the girl by morning or face consequence. The villagers, rather than surrender her, chose the impossible — they gathered every soul, every child, every animal, and walked off the edge of the known world in a single night.

But before they went, the elders stood at the borders of all eighty-four villages and spoke a curse in a language older than Sanskrit, in a voice that carried not as sound but as intention, as a change in the quality of the air, as something that settled into the soil like slow water:

Let no life take root here. Let no joy last here. Let no traveler who enters unwelcome leave unchanged. We do not curse the land — we return it to what it was before men named it. We give it back to what was here before us.

What was here before them had been patient. It had been waiting for exactly this.

The Brahmarakshasa is among the most feared entities in Hindu demonology — the ghost of a Brahmin who misused sacred knowledge, condemned to haunt the place of his transgression for an age. But Kuldhara’s curse did not summon a single entity. It opened a door. And what comes through an open door is not always what you expected to find on the other side. The Vetalas — spirits that inhabit corpses, that speak in riddles and feed on confusion — are drawn to places where the boundary has been deliberately weakened. They do not chase. They arrange. They rearrange the landscape of the mind until escape becomes impossible not because the road is blocked, but because the mind has forgotten what escape means. The Pishacha — flesh-eaters, shape-changers, the entities that wear familiar faces over their own inhuman ones — are drawn to grief. To the grief of people realizing they are trapped. To the grief of recognition.

IV · THE ARCHITECTURE OF ENTRAPMENT — —

The van was where they left it. Except it wasn’t.

They returned to the van by the route they had come, which took forty minutes instead of the five minutes it should have taken, and the route was not the same route. The temple was on the wrong side. The crooked doorway that had been on their left was on their right. Singh stopped walking and looked at his shoes and said nothing because there was nothing to say that would make the geography un-wrong itself.

The van started.

This was the cruelest thing the village did to them — it let them think, for twenty seconds, that the van starting meant something. The engine turned, the headlights blazed, the GPS screen lit up and showed them a map and a road and a glowing blue line leading out. Singh drove. The road was there. The road was clearly there beneath the wheels and the headlights. They drove for six minutes and arrived back at the temple.

The bell was still ringing.

“That’s not possible,” Sandheer said, and his voice was the voice of a man whose understanding of the world had just been surgically removed. “Drive again,” Lakshmi said. “Different direction.”

They drove in every direction. North. South. East. West. Diagonally. At speed. Slowly. With the windows up. With the windows down. Singh drove until the fuel gauge needle kissed empty and every road, without variation, without mercy, without the slightest

acknowledgment of their distress, deposited them back in front of the temple and its bell that rang without wind.

It was Meera who said it, from the back seat, in the quiet and certain tone of a child stating a fact:

“We’re inside it now.”

The first face appeared in the third hour.

Priya saw it in the rearview mirror — not Singh’s face, not Sandheer’s face, not any face she could name, but a face assembled from the wrong materials, from something that had studied faces without ever possessing one. It was in the seat behind her. When she turned around, the seat was empty. When she looked back at the mirror, the face was still there, and now it was smiling, and the smile went in the wrong direction, turned up at the edges in the way that smiles turn up, but the muscles beneath it were arranged wrong, as though something had remembered the shape of a smile from a description rather than an experience.

She did not scream. She understood, with the clarity that extreme fear sometimes provides, that screaming would make it solid. That giving it her terror would feed it into a form. She looked at the road. She breathed. She did not look in the mirror again for the rest of the night.

ThePishachadoes not announce itself. It slides into the peripheral vision, into the space behind a shoulder, into the face seen in glass. It feeds on

the moment between seeing and believing — the half- second when the mind knows what the eyes have found but has not yet processed the impossible weight of it. In that half-second, it is most itself. Most powerful. Most hungry. The correct response, according to texts as old as the Atharva Veda, is to refuse to complete the recognition. To look away before the mind closes the circuit. But this requires a discipline that the seeing almost never allows.

V · WHAT THE VILLAGE DOES TO MINDS — —

— BY MIDNIGHT, THEY HAD STOPPED TRUSTING WHAT THEY SAW —

The village was demonstrating its capabilities methodically, the way a predator demonstrates patience — not rushing, not overwhelming, just arranging things. It arranged the streets so that Sandheer, who had walked ahead to scout, appeared suddenly behind them. It arranged the shadows so that shadows moved when nothing casting them moved. It arranged the torchlight so that, for one moment, every torch threw the same shadow, the shadow of a tall thin figure with too many joints in its arms, and then that shadow was gone and the torches burned normally and no one mentioned it because mentioning it would make it real.

Lakshmi began to see her mother.

Her mother had been dead for three years. She appeared at the end of streets, at doorways, at the margins of torchlight — not as a ghost in the

conventional sense, not translucent and trailing light. She appeared as herself. As she had been the last time Lakshmi had seen her well and whole and herself, in a yellow sari at a festival, laughing at something that Lakshmi’s father had said. She appeared and she beckoned, and every time she beckoned she was deeper into the village, further from the van, further from any plausible route outward.

Lakshmi walked toward her mother twice before Priya caught her arm the second time and said her name sharply enough to break it.

“It’s not her,” Priya said. “I know,” said Lakshmi. “I know it’s not her. But it has her face.” “It has her face on purpose.”

The thing wearing Lakshmi’s mother’s face had paused at the doorway into which it had been leading her. It stood very still for a moment — the way animals go still when they realize they’ve been seen for what they are — and then it smiled with Lakshmi’s mother’s mouth and the smile was wrong in the same way the other face had been wrong, the muscles underneath moving in the wrong directions, and then it was gone, and the doorway was dark, and the bell rang its three notes in the silence it left behind.

The Vetala that inhabits a beloved dead will wear that person’s face with the accuracy of a craftsman who has studied every line. It will know names. It will know private gestures. It will know the

particular way the lost person tilted their head when they were listening. What it will not know, cannot know, is the warmth behind the eyes — the quality of attention that is love rather than mimicry. The living know this warmth without being able to name it. They know its absence as wrongness. Follow it anyway, and the Vetala leads you into the space between. Not death. Not life. The terrible in- between where the village keeps the ones it swallows.

Sandheer broke at approximately 2 AM — not dramatically, not loudly, but in the quiet devastating way that rational men break when reality becomes structurally unsound. He sat down in the street and he said, with great calm:

“We’re dead. We died on the road. The van crashed somewhere and we’ve been dead and this is whatever comes after.” “We’re not dead,” Singh said. “Then explain the road.”

Singh could not explain the road. He sat down next to Sandheer in the dirt of a village that should not exist and he put his head in his hands and he tried to think through the architecture of what had happened to them. There was a logical explanation. There had to be a logical explanation. The GPS had malfunctioned. They were driving in circles unconsciously, some spatial confusion produced by darkness and exhaustion and a featureless landscape.

The faces they had seen were tricks of torchlight on shuttered windows. Lakshmi’s grief had produced a hallucination. These were all possible things.

He looked up. Across the dark street, in the mouth of an alley, something was squatting. It was the size of a grown man but arranged differently — too many bends in it, an excess of angles, as though it had been folded into the shape of crouching rather than having grown into it. It was watching them. It was not hiding. It had no interest in hiding. It was simply watching with the patience of something that has all the time that remains.

This is what the Brahmarakshasa does. It does not move. It lets you know it’s there. It waits for you to run, because it prefers the chase to the finding.

Singh looked at it for three seconds and then he looked away and he stood up and he pulled Sandheer up by the arm and he said, very quietly:

“We are not dead. We are trapped. There is a difference. And the difference is that one of those has a way out.”

VI · THE HEADLIGHTS — —

THEY HEARD THE ENGINE BEFORE THEY SAW THE LIGHTS — —

It was Meera who heard it first, because Meera had remained the most intact, the most present, the least eroded by a night that had been specifically designed

to erode them. She tugged at Lakshmi’s hand and said nothing, only pointed — and there, at the edge of the village, where the desert met the first row of mud walls, a pair of headlights came slowly through the dark.

A white SUV. Moving slowly. Cautiously. The way people drove through unknown terrain, alert and unsure and full of the ordinary hope of people who have not yet understood that they are no longer in ordinary territory.

They ran.

They ran with everything left in them, all six of them, Meera on Lakshmi’s hip, Sandheer ahead because fear had unlocked something in his legs, all of them running toward the headlights with their arms out and their voices open and their names torn out of them by the running.Stop! Here! Please! Here we are!

The SUV stopped. Its headlights held them in white light. Through the windshield Singh could see a woman in the passenger seat leaning forward, squinting out at them. A man driving. Children in the back seat pressed against the window glass, looking out at the wild people running toward them from the dark.

And then —

And then it hit them all at once, with the force of something the mind had been refusing to fully assemble: the dread. The specific dread of recognition. They had seen this before. This exact configuration of headlights and hope and people in a car peering out at the unknown. They had been in it.

They had been the people in the car.

Hours ago — an eternity ago — they had pulled into this village tired and lost and full of the ordinary hope of people who have found lights in the dark. They had looked out through their windshield at the torches and the temple and the deserted streets and they had thought:maybe people, maybe a festival, maybe help.

They had not seen anyone watching them.

But there had been someone watching. There had been eyes on them from the first second the van crossed the village’s border. There had been something observing their arrival with the patient interest of a trap that knows it is about to be sprung. They had felt it — all of them, they now understood, had felt it — as a prickling at the back of the neck, as a reluctance in the chest, as the small animal voice beneath language saying wrong, wrong, go back, this is wrong. They had ignored that voice. They had walked into the dark to find the festival that was not there.

And now they were the ones in the dark. And the people in the SUV were the ones still on the outside, still in the ordinary world, still crossing the threshold they hadn’t understood was a threshold.

Singh screamed. He screamed with everything in his lungs, every molecule of air his body contained, screamed GO BACK, screamed DON’T STOP, screamed TURN AROUND, screamed the word in Hindi and in English and in the pure vowel-sound of terror that needs no language —

The SUV did not go back.

The SUV eased forward slowly, carefully, into the village. The man driving was leaning toward his window now, looking at them, his face creased with something between concern and wariness — the face of a person watching wild strangers shout on a roadside, calculating the calculus of help versus danger. He was still in his world. He could still see only a group of distressed travelers. He had not yet understood that the distress was a symptom of a geography that would shortly become his as well.

The woman in the passenger seat pointed. She was pointing at something behind Singh’s group.

Behind them, the temple bell rang. Three notes, and a silence, and three notes.

Singh turned.

The thing that had been squatting in the alley was no longer in the alley. The alleys were empty. The doorways were empty. The streets stretched away in their labyrinthine arrangement, torches burning in their impossibly windless way, and for one moment — for one stretched, crystalline, horrible moment — the village was just a village. Silent. Old. Empty. A place where people had been and then were not.

And then the doors of the mud houses began to open.

All at once. Every door on every visible street, opening outward on hinges that should have been seized with rust, opening quietly, purposefully, as if in welcome, as if something inside each one had been waiting the entire night and now understood that the time had come, that the census was complete, that the village had everything it needed.

The Asuras of the Puranas are not simply demons in the Western sense — they are beings of immense power who chose the material over the eternal, who hoarded what was meant to flow, who built their dominions in the places between the divine and the human and extracted tribute from every soul unfortunate enough to pass through. The greatest of them cannot be slain by ordinary means. They are bound to their territories. They cannot leave. But within their territories, they are everything. Kuldhara’s curse did not create what lived here. It removed the last protections against what had always lived here. It withdrew the dharmic boundary that kept the settlement safe and gave whatever waited in the dark what it had been waiting for since the first human laid the first stone in this cursed earth. The settlement was never a village. It was a mouth. The eighty-four villages of Kuldhara were teeth. And the night the people fled, the mouth learned to smile.

VII · WHAT CANNOT BE UNSEEN — —

THE WORST PART WAS THE REMEMBERING — —

Lakshmi remembered it first, and then Priya, and then one by one the memory arrived in each of them like cold water rising — the memory of driving in. The memory of the lights in the distance that they had found and followed. The memory of the sensation, gone unexamined in the excitement of having found

something, of being watched. Of not being the ones who found this place. Of being the ones the place had found.

They had discussed it briefly, a throwaway remark absorbed by the noise of the van.Strange that it’s deserted. Strange feeling here. Strange that the torches are lit with no one to light them. They had catalogued the wrongnesses and filed each one under explainable, probably. They had been so tired. Tired people talk themselves into things.

“We knew,” Priya said. She said it to no one. She said it to the understanding itself. “We knew when we drove in. We all felt it.” “We didn’t know what we were feeling,” Singh said. “We knew. We talked about it for thirty seconds and then we drove in anyway.”

The new family was out of their SUV now. They were walking toward Singh’s group with the careful approach of people who are concerned but uncertain. The man had his hands slightly raised in the universal gesture of we mean no harm. The woman was looking around at the village — at the torches, at the mud walls, at the temple with its rhythmically ringing bell — and her face held the expression that Lakshmi recognized as the one her own face had worn several hours ago: uneasy but manageable, curious but contained, the expression of someone whose unease hasn’t yet outrun their reason.

It was the expression of someone still on the outside of it.

Singh grabbed the man by both arms before the man reached him and he said, with great care, with all the authority of a night’s worth of education in what authority means here:

“Get in your car. Get in your car right now and turn around and drive and do not stop driving until you see a city. Do not look at anything that looks familiar. Do not follow anything that leads you inward. Get in your car.”

The man looked at him for a long moment. Then he looked past him at the village — at the open doors, at the torches, at the bell. At Lakshmi, who was holding Meera against her chest with the grip of a person holding the only solid thing in a dissolving world. At Sandheer, who had gone very still and very pale with the stillness and pallor of a person looking at something over Singh’s shoulder that they have decided not to react to.

Singh did not turn around.

He had learned, in the course of this night, that turning around was a mistake. That looking directly at a thing gave the thing purchase. He kept his eyes on the man’s face and he waited.

The man turned to his wife. His wife turned to him. Something passed between them in the silence that was not words — the private semaphore of people who have shared enough of their lives to communicate in the unspoken.

Then the woman said, softly, with great regret, the thing that sealed it:

“We’re almost out of fuel. The GPS stopped working. We haven’t had signal in two hours. We can’t go anywhere.”

The doors stood open. The torches burned. The bell rang its three notes in the dark.

Inside each open door, in the darkness that the torchlight didn’t reach, something waited with the patience of things that have been waiting for centuries, with the absolute certainty of things that have never yet been disappointed, with the quiet contentment of things that have just received what they were owed.

Meera turned her face away from the doorways and pressed it into Lakshmi’s neck and said, in a small voice, with her eyes squeezed shut:

“Don’t let them touch me.” “I won’t,” said Lakshmi. “They’re everywhere.” “I know.” “They’re happy we’re all here.”

The village of Kuldhara had eighty-four villages. Twelve families to a village, the historians had estimated. Roughly a thousand people who walked off the edge of the known world in a single night and left their houses and their curse and the darkness behind them. The darkness had been patient for two hundred years. Had been fed occasionally — the tired

traveler, the lost pilgrim, the low-battery, exhausted soul who followed lights they shouldn’t have followed — and been patient about it. Not greedy. Methodical.

The bell rang. Three notes, silence, three notes.

The settlement was not looking for visitors. It was looking for residents.

Singh stood in the torchlit street of a village that should not exist and looked at the new family and looked at his own family and understood, with the specific clarity that accompanies acceptance of the unacceptable, that the question was no longer how to leave. The question was how long. How long could they remain themselves. How long before the Vetala found the right face and Lakshmi followed it into a door. How long before the Pishacha found Priya’s particular weakness, her particular love, and used it as a key. How long before the thing in the alley stopped merely watching.

How long before they became the lights in the dark.

How long before they were the ones who brought the next family in.
