chapters.title: The Monstrous Mongolian Death Worm
chapters.text:
✦✦

Gobi Desert Crossing · Olgoi-Khorkhoi Survey

You hear the word worm and you think of soft things. Mud. Rain. A child pinching something harmless between two fingers. You think of a creature that bows to the earth. That is not the thing the old men in the Gobi meant.

I — THE MONK’S TEA — ORIGIN — —

The first account came from a monk whose name the desert kept. Only his account survived, passed through centuries of telling until it was worn smooth as river rock: that he had felt something following him across the Gobi, and that it had no feet.

He was on pilgrimage. The desert was known to him — its indifference was part of the discipline. One walks through a place that does not care whether you live and finds, perhaps, a useful clarity about one’s smallness. But two days into the crossing he became aware of a presence he could not name. Not a sound. Not a sight. The sensation of being tracked by something that moved without moving, that had been waiting since before he arrived.

He checked behind him. The Gobi was empty in all directions, honest in its emptiness. He continued. He tried to pray. The prayers scattered each time he gathered them — something was disrupting the frequency on which devotion travels.

He stopped and made tea. Pilgrims learn this early: when the mind will not settle, give the body something deliberate to do. He built his small fire with methodical patience, set the copper kettle on the flame, and sat back on his heels to look at the vast and empty desert.

His journal — found wedged beneath a slab of wind-scoured basalt, its pages stiff with alkali dust — recorded what happened next in a single sentence:“It does not walk. It waits beneath the breath of the earth. I felt it before I saw it. A pressure in the teeth. A hum in the marrow. When the sky wept, the ground opened like a mouth.”

The sand near his fire rippled — just once — and was still. The monk did not run. He was a man of considerable discipline. He watched the place where the sand had moved and drank his tea and waited.

They found his bones a year later, stripped clean and arranged in a spiral, no tracks leading to or from the site. Only his staff remained upright in the sand. And the black mark where he had been standing — a perfect scorch, as though the earth itself had decided to keep him.

The herdsmen still whisper about it:the worm knows when you seek it. It just needed to attack at a moment you couldn’t expect.

✦ ✦ ✦

II — THE SURVEY TEAM — DAY THREE — —

Dr. Nara Ochirbat did not believe in monsters. She believed in strata, mineral composition, the cold arithmetic of a ground-penetrating radar screen. She had led surveys in the Gobi basin a dozen times and knew its indifference the way you know a difficult colleague — intimately, without affection.

Behind her came Ruslan, the field tech from Almaty who could repair any equipment blindfolded. Then Sofi, the German postdoc who had published on Gobi sediment layering and spoke with the specific precision of someone who had trained herself out of uncertainty. And finally Davan, the Mongolian grad student who had grown up two hundred kilometers from this survey site and who had, on their first morning, quietly asked Nara whether they could leave before the rains came.

Nara had smiled and said there was no rain forecast for ten days.

“The forecast was wrong,” Davan said. It was not a prediction. It was a statement of something he already knew.

On their second afternoon, the ground-penetrating radar began returning anomalous data. Deep in the substrate — eight meters, nine, the return unclear — something disrupted the signal in long, irregular curves. Not a fault. Not a void. The line moved. It branched. Along one section of the readout it carried a regular, rhythmic texture, like the cross-section of something peristaltic. Like something digesting.

“Equipment error,” Ruslan said, not sounding convinced.

“I recalibrated twice,” Sofi replied. She had the screen tilted so they could all see. None of them spoke.

The third morning the sky was purple by nine. By ten the first drops fell — not a Gobi drizzle but real rain, purposeful, the desert turning dark and slick beneath it. The seismograph, which Sofi had left running overnight, began screaming before any of them were fully dressed.

Not a spike. A cascade. Low-frequency tremors rippling through the soil in sync with the falling rain. Something ascending. Slow and unhurried, the way a man climbs stairs when he is not in a hurry because the thing he is coming for cannot leave.

The legend said it hibernates underground. The legend said it wakes when it rains.

“We leave,” Nara said. She said it with the particular calm of a person spending all available resources on calm and having none left for anything else. “Now. Not at first light.”

They broke camp in silence. They were loading the last of the radar array into the vehicle packs when Davan stopped walking.

“The ground,” he said.

It was vibrating. Not earthquake-random but organized. Rhythmic. A pulse coming up through the soles of their boots, through the bones of their feet, in that awful middle register between sound and feeling that the body recognizes as warning before the mind has words for it.

The sand nine meters to their left erupted.

✦ ✦ ✦

III — THE CREATURE — WHAT THE LEGENDS OMITTED — —

They had expected a worm. Something like the cave-adapted pale things found in deep soil. Long and red and dangerous, yes — but a worm. A thing of the category of small, soft, ground-dwelling invertebrates. The word “worm” is a diminutive. The word implies a limit to the imagination.

What came out of the Gobi sand was red. That much the legends had right — a deep arterial red, not the red of fresh blood but of blood dried on stone, old and concentrated. Its skin was too smooth in places and too ridged in others, as though different creatures had been pressed into one design. It was thick as a man’s torso, not his arm, which meant the accounts they had read — even the ones that seemed exaggerated — had been conservative. It rose from the earth

like something returning from a long absence and its body kept coming: two meters above the surface, three, and clearly much more remaining below, anchored in the dark.

It had no face that any of them could identify. No eyes. And yet each of them — separately, without discussing it — felt the absolute certainty that it was looking at them. That it had been aware of them for three days. That the survey and the anomalous readings and the radar array positioned directly above its hibernation chamber had not gone unnoticed. That it had felt every footfall, every vibration, and had decided — in whatever way such a creature decides — to wait for the rain.

The air around it crackled. A static charge that lifted the fine hairs on their arms and made the metal frame of the radar equipment hum a high, thin note. Sofi’s headlamp flickered. Ruslan grabbed the battery pack from the antenna stand and it shocked him hard enough to drop it. Not lethal. Not yet. A demonstration:I can do that to all of you.

The hum in the earth intensified. Nara understood, then — understood in the animal part of her mind that predates language — what the seismograph had been recording for three days. Not geological noise.The creature’s awareness of them, rendered as frequency. It had been reading their weight on the ground above it the way a person reads a face.

“Back,” Nara said. “Walk. Slowly. To the packs. Do not run.”

They moved. It watched. It swayed — a slow, testing motion, like something reacquainting itself with open air after a very long absence.

Davan caught his boot on a buried stake and stumbled, one knee striking the wet sand. The creature’s upper body swung toward him with a speed that was absolutely wrong for its mass, and the crackle spiked so hard all four of them felt it in the metal of their zippers, the fillings of their teeth, the steel tips of their boots.

Don’t fall. Nara did not say it aloud. She was past speech. She thought it with the concentrated force of someone spending the last of something.

The legend had said: it does not attack a group.

It was waiting for them to fracture.

✦ ✦ ✦

IV — THE RUN — WHAT PANIC COSTS — —

Ruslan ran first. Not a decision — an animal event, the body taking over before the mind could weigh consequences. He broke from the group and sprinted toward the ravine at the basin’s far edge, and the moment he separated, the ground between him and the others erupted.

The worm did not slither. It tunneled and erupted, tunneled and erupted, moving beneath the surface at terrible speed and then breaching with explosive force — a wet crimson arc against the grey sky, landing between the fleeing Ruslan and the others with a sound like a wet towel struck hard against tile. The air went blue-white and Ruslan convulsed once, every limb locking, and he dropped sideways into the rain-slicked sand with his eyes wide and terrified and fully present, completely unable to move.

He was not dead. That was the worse thing. His chest still rose and fell in slow, shallow rhythm. His eyes tracked them as they passed. He was fully inside himself, frozen into stillness by the current, his final expression one of complete and terrible understanding.

Nara grabbed Davan’s sleeve. Sofi needed no grabbing — she had understood before any of them that the worst thing you could give this creature was a single body moving fast and alone. They ran together, three people compressed into a single footfall pattern, trying to become one organism, one seismic signature.

It wasn’t working.

The basin offered nothing: no cover, no elevation, only rain-darkened sand and slabs of fractured rock. The creature was circling. Not chasing —circling, the way an animal circles when it has already decided the outcome and is arranging the geometry. It felt their panic as vibration. Their every stumble was a signal. Their ragged breathing, transmitted through the soles of their boots into the wet ground beneath, was a language it spoke natively.

“We’re making it worse,” Sofi gasped. “Every step. Every shake.”

“Don’t stop,” Nara said. “If you stop you become part of the collection.”

Along a dry wash they passed rows of bleached ribs — not scattered, but arranged. Fused by thin red calcified threads. Not livestock only. Others.

The worm didn’t consume. It archived. It turned living vibration into stillness and kept the stillness. The herdsmen who had disappeared, their animals wandering riderless across the deep Gobi — this was where they had ended up. Propped and preserved, their final expressions locked in that same glassy recognition Ruslan wore now.

A ravine opened ahead — narrow, stone-walled, the creature too thick to follow inside. They scrambled in as the ground behind them exploded for the fourth time. The worm battered the ravine walls. The whole passage shook. Dust poured into their mouths. Nara hauled Davan upright when he fell and did not look back to see what she was pulling him away from, because she had understood by then that looking back was itself a kind of vibration — that grief and attention and terror were all frequencies the creature could read.

They emerged into a narrow basin of black boulders. At its center stood a ruined stone shrine, half-buried in sand, its walls carved with images Nara recognized from the monk’s account: a figure with a walking staff, a shape beneath him, small people with their hands raised.

And beneath all of it, in script she could not read but Davan could, one line:he who seeks it teaches it his fear.

✦ ✦ ✦

V — WHAT WAS NOT FILED — AFTERMATH — —

The survey was officially incomplete. Equipment failure, the university report stated. Adverse weather conditions. Unrecoverable data. The grant committee received this without question because geological surveys in the Gobi fail all the time and the paperwork for abandonment is straightforward.

Ruslan was recovered by a search team four days later, alive and physically unharmed, seated in the sand where he had fallen. He could walk. He could eat. He answered questions in a flat, cooperative tone. He returned to field work the following season and was considered by his colleagues to be exactly as he had always been, except that he no longer spoke unless spoken to, and he never again walked on wet ground.

Sofi has the sensor data. The university called it corrupted. She has not corrected them. The readout showing the anomaly ascending through the substrate as the rain began — the smooth, rhythmic, peristaltic signature of something enormous waking up — lives in an encrypted folder she has not opened since the night she made it. She has written three papers since returning. None of them are about the Gobi.

Davan went back. Once, three months later, alone, in dry weather. He would not say what he was looking for. He came back the same day and said only that the shrine was gone, collapsed, and that the basin had been scoured clean — no bones in the dry wash, no calcified threads, no circular holes in the sand. As if the desert had tidied up.

Nara still works the basin. She knows every stratum, every formation, every ancient drainage pattern. She is not superstitious. She will tell you this herself, clearly and without defensiveness, as a person who has given the matter serious thought.

She no longer surveys when it rains.

She has also noticed — she has tried not to notice but she has — that in certain areas of the deep Gobi, the seismograph returns a particular class of anomaly that her colleagues classify as thermal artifact and she classifies as nothing, writes nothing in the log, moves the survey grid away from. Long, branching, rhythmic disruptions in the substrate. Eight meters down. Nine. The signature of something large and patient, breathing slowly in the dark below the bone-dry clay.

Waiting, as it has always waited, for the rare gift of rain.

For the precise vibration of a team of scientists who have come to prove it does not exist.

For the moment — and there is always a moment, in every group, when terror has been building long enough — when one person breaks from the others and runs.

It does not need to see you to know where you are. It needs only to feel the earth remember you. And in the dark, under all that stone and silence, patient as the oldest geology, it is still listening.

chapters.title: KGOMO
chapters.text:
| | | | | | | | | | |

MARK HEAD STATUS Brand 14 Bull, 4 yrs Returned Brand 09 Cow, in-calf Missing Brand 22 Calf Unmarked

Barolong cattle country · kept by oral count and tally-stick

The first thing you learn about cattle is that they do not lie. Their eyes are flat, their breath is honest, their weight tells you the truth of the earth beneath them. The herdsmen of the Barolong people understood this in their marrow. Cattle were not mysteries. They were stubborn, living things with hooves and temper and need. Every herdsman who later told his story about Kgomo began the same way — with this certainty, this professional confidence in the simplicity of beasts. They all said it. And then they described what broke it.

His name was Rra-Molefe, and he owned the most beautiful animal in the territory. An Ankole-Watusi, blood-red as laterite earth after rain, with horns that spread wider than a man’s full reach and curved like twin scimitars wrapped in copper. Men traveled for three days simply to stand near it. To watch the muscles slide beneath that shining hide. To see how the other cattle parted around it like water splitting at a stone. We called it Lefika. The rock. It walked as though it owned the earth, and in the hearts of those who saw it, it did. That was 1889. That was the last year any of us were simple.

No one knows what broke first inside it. A disease, said the British later, writing in their ledgers with the confidence of men who believe that naming a thing is the same as containing it. Mad cow disease. The words folded the horror into something manageably small. But the Indian family who had settled near the trading post — good people, a cloth merchant and his wife — watched from their veranda for three weeks and told anyone who would listen: no disease makes

an animal murder with purpose. No fever gives a beast the patience of a man who has already decided. They did not know this land. But they knew the difference between sickness and intent. The British did not listen. They rarely did.

It began with two herdsmen before breakfast. Not a stampede, not a charge driven by territorial rage. Lefika simply turned its head, lowed once — a sound witnesses described as low and wet and drawn-out, like something dragging itself through bone — and put both men through the ribs with those magnificent horns. The village called it bull-rage. Such things happen in the moraka. The world held its shape for another week. Then Lefika walked into the market at noon with the steady tread of something that knows no fear, and the world’s shape cracked open like an egg.

It did not stampede. It did not run. It moved between the stalls with a terrible calm, lowering those horns and swinging, selecting, and the selection was the worst part — not the blood, not the screaming, but the evidence of choice. Women, children, old men: it took them apart with the methodical patience of someone settling a debt. And when it was done, when the soldiers finally came and the rifles were raised and the smoke had cleared, what remained of the red bull was only a skull. Great white bone, stripped clean. Horns curving outward like the ribs of some sky beast. The district commissioner, a man called Hartley, had it boiled and hung above the porch of the government office. A trophy of order restored, he told his subordinates. A proof that the territory could be managed.

The skull grinned at the sun for three days. On the fourth night, the lowing began.

◆ ◆ ◆

I was seventeen the first time I heard Kgomo breathe in the dark. My father had gone to the trading post with two oxen. I was left with my younger brother, Tau, and the herd. We slept in the cattle enclosure,

wrapped in blankets that smelled of ash and hide. The moon that night was bright enough to make the thorn branches cast shadows like spear points across the ground. Near midnight the dogs began to whine. Not bark. Not growl.Whine, as if their bones had been pulled loose from inside them.

The sound came from beyond the thorn fence. A cow’s call, yes, but wrong in a way I felt in my back teeth. Deep and wet and drawn out past the point where any living throat could sustain it, until it seemed less like an animal and more like a voice that had forgotten the shape of language and was trying to reconstruct it from memory. Another followed. Then another. The herd stirred as one, every head lifting simultaneously, as though invisible strings had been pulled taut from the sky. One of the calves began to scream. Calves do not scream like men. But when terror enters them completely, they do. That sound woke every dog in the village. It woke the women. It woke my father’s empty bed inside my chest, though he was far away.

I went to the fence. The night outside the kraal was open, silver, and still. At first I saw nothing. Then the cattle in the outer field pressed backward, parting in unison as if giving way to a chief. And there, standing among them, was the largest cow I had ever seen. Red as fresh clay after rain. Horns arching long and white in the moonlight. Its body was lean in the way of a beast that has not eaten for many days, yet its eyes gleamed too bright — wet and glassy, polished stones lit from inside. It was not one of ours. I knew that immediately. I knew something else, too, a knowledge that arrived not through thought but through the skin: it was not entirely here. Its edges were slightly wrong. Not blurred, not soft. Wrong, the way a reflection in water is wrong when the water is beginning to move.

It lowered its head.

The cattle nearest to it moved aside with a panic I had never seen in beasts — not the sharp, surging panic of a predator’s approach, but something slower and more broken, like the panic of creatures who

understand that fleeing will not help and are doing it anyway out of the last shreds of animal instinct. An old cow stumbled. The red shape struck once. Fast as lightning. The sound was not a bellow, but a wet crack. The old cow folded her legs and lay down without a cry, the way cattle lie down when commanded, and in the silence that followed I heard something I have spent forty years trying to unhear: the sound of the thing eating. Not tearing. Not gulping. A sound like a careful man excising a single perfect piece from something larger. The sound of selection.

When it raised its head, something dark and glistening was in its mouth. It chewed. It looked directly at me.

Not at the fence. Not at the kraal. At me. And I had the sudden, absolute certainty that it knew my name. My lineage. The names of every man who had walked these grasslands before me. That it was not looking at a boy of seventeen but at something much longer: a line of witnesses stretching backward into the dark.

I write this in haste as the candle is already low. The creature circled the office building for the better part of an hour. We fired sixteen rounds into it. I watched the bullets enter and pass through as through smoke — no impact, no flinching, nothing. It descended on Corporal Phiri near the east steps. We found him in the morning with a hole in his chest. Round as a shilling. Clean through the sternum. Inside the hole: nothing. The heart was gone. Not torn out — simply absent, as though it had never existed. The flesh around the edges was smooth and dry. His face wore a smile. God forgive me, I cannot stop thinking about the smile. I saw a huge creature in the sky with wings and long horns. It was almost as though I had seen Lucifer. I will not sleep again.

By the time I was a grown man with a wife and cattle of my own, three hunters had gone out into the grasslands to find Kgomo. The first returned alone and never spoke another word for the rest of his life — not when his wife died, not when his children cried, not when

they held his hand in his final fever. He sat in his chair and breathed and looked at the middle distance, and whatever he had seen out there behind his eyes was the only thing that still mattered to him. The second hunter was found at the edge of the dry pan. His body intact. His cattle — he had brought his own cattle as bait — gone. All of them, every animal, vanished without tracks, without blood, without even the compressed earth that a herd leaves behind when it moves. As though they had been lifted. The third hunter did not come back at all.

That was when the village learned the silence. Not ignorance — respect. The respect you give a sleeping thing you do not want to wake. We stopped saying Lefika. We said only Kgomo. The cow. As though stripping it of particularity might confuse it. As though it hunted by name.

◆ ◆ ◆

I am old now. My knees are the age of the grasslands themselves. Decades have passed since I stood at that fence as a boy of seventeen and watched something eat the essential part out of a cow while leaving the flesh behind. I have had time to think. Time to understand what the excised wounds mean — those perfect round voids, dry-edged, bloodless, never in the muscle, never in the fat, always deeper. Always in the place where, if you reached your hand inside a living creature and felt around, you would find whatever makes it itself. Not the heart. Not the organ. The interiority. The witness. The part that knows it is alive.

This is what Kgomo eats. This is what it came back for. We fed its body to dogs. We boiled its skull and nailed it to a porch. We wrote its madness into ledgers and called it disease and turned away. And the land, which forgets nothing, which holds every debt in its red dust and its dry grass and its bitter water — the land did not accept our accounting. When grief has no grave, it grows horns. When

memory has no mouth, it grows wings. Not feathered wings. Not the wings of birds. Leathery sheets of folded dark, ribbed and veined, stretched between frames of bone, and when they open above you, the air thins, and the temperature drops, and you feel in your chest the particular cold of a thing that was killed by men who thought killing was an ending.

My cattle know when it is near before I do. They do not stampede. That is what I need you to understand: they do not run. A predator causes flight. Kgomo causes stillness. The whole herd simply stops breathing. Every beast stands frozen with steam wisping from its nostrils and its eyes rolled white in the starlight, and the silence that comes over them is not the silence of prey animals freezing against a lion’s approach. It is the silence of creatures in the presence of something that has authority over them at a level deeper than fear. Older than fear. The silence of things that know, in whatever wordless way animals know anything, that the thing above them is a version of themselves — flesh that died and came back wrong, cattle- shaped but not cattle, wearing the old form the way a ghost wears the face of the person it used to be.

Last dry season it came to my ridge. I had been watching the eastern fence for seventeen nights running, sleeping in fragments, waking to check the herd, walking the perimeter with a lantern that did not push the dark back but only showed me how deep it ran. That night the grass bent without wind. The temperature dropped ten degrees in the space of a breath. My lantern guttered and went cold — not out,cold, the flame still burning but giving no heat, as though something had taken the warmth out of the fire and left only the light. I looked up.

It did not descend. It unfolded. There is no other word for it. One moment the sky above the ridge was empty, and then something was in it that had always been in it, that had been there the entire time waiting to be noticed, and the shape of it against the moon was this: a body the size of a bull, red hide visible in patches where the rot had

not yet taken it, the face half-bone-half-skin with the teeth exposed in a permanent lipless grin, and between the curving horns a pair of eyes that were not red so much as they were the idea of fire — burning without fuel, giving no light, only recognition. And the wings. God, the wings. Not attached to shoulders. Emerging from behind the ribcage like thoughts emerging from behind a mind. Layered dark that drank starlight and gave nothing back.

It hovered. It looked through me. Not at me.Through me, into the years, into the lineage, into every man who had ever stood on this ridge and looked up and felt the sky lean. I understood then what the Indian merchant’s wife had tried to explain before they packed their things and fled. It did not eat to survive. It ate to remember. Every clean round hole in every dead heifer, every missing piece inside every smiling corpse, every hunter who went mute or went missing — these were not attacks. They were an archive. Kgomo was building something out of stolen interiorities. Collecting the essential pieces of the living to reconstruct the essential piece of itself that the British rifle and the British dogs and the British skull-on-the-porch had taken away. Building toward something I did not want to understand. Building toward completion.

I opened my mouth and I bellowed back.

I do not know why. I am an old man and I have no explanation for it. Some animal reflex, some inheritance from forty years of walking among cattle, from a life spent learning their language from the inside. The sound that came out of my chest was not a human sound. It was low and resonant and it vibrated the air in a frequency I had never used before and will never use again, and for one moment, one terrible clear moment, Kgomo stopped its circling. Hung motionless above the ridge. And in the silence between us I heard — or felt, the line between hearing and feeling had dissolved — something that might have been, in a living creature, hesitation.

Then it was gone. Not flying away. Dissolving. The sky reassembled itself around the place it had been the way water closes over a stone. Below me on the ridge, a young heifer stood alive and breathing. On her right shoulder: a perfect circle of flesh missing. Dry edges. No blood. Just the mark.

◆ ◆ ◆

I still herd. I still walk the fence. My hands shake now when I hold the staff. The bellowing never truly stops — it lives inside my skull as a constant low thrum, the drone of something patient, something that has all the time that the dead have, which is all of it. My grandchildren ask what I am listening for when I stand outside at dusk with my face tilted up. I tell them: nothing. Go inside. Lock the gate.

I tell them this because I love them. Because some sounds, once truly heard, do not leave. They become part of the architecture of your interior life, nested in there alongside everything you love and everything you fear, indistinguishable after a while from your own heartbeat. I will carry Kgomo to my grave. And perhaps — this is the thought I do not share with my grandchildren, the thought that comes in the hour before dawn when the grasslands are very still and the stars are very close — perhaps that is precisely the point. Perhaps that is what it wants. Not the flesh. Not even the essential piece excised from the flank. Perhaps it wants the witness. The one who cannot unhear it. The one who bellowed back. The one who, in the moment of dying, will carry in his chest the clearest image in existence of the red bull walking in the morning sun — alive, magnificent, not yet broken, horns sweeping the sky like the scimitars of a god.

That is the piece it has always wanted. The memory of its first life. The last person who saw it as it was before the bullet, before the dogs, before the skull on the porch.

That person is me.

The ground trembles tonight. My cattle are silent. The dogs have fled into the bush with their tails gone rigid. I have barred my door, but I know — I have always known — that wood cannot stop a thing that does not need to open doors. It does not need to open doors because it does not enter through doors. It enters through the chest. Through the same round void it leaves in all the others. It comes in through the space between the ribs, through the place where the essential self lives, and it takes what it came for, and it leaves behind a corpse with a smile on its face that no one around it can explain.

I am ready. I have been ready since the night I was seventeen and stood at the fence and it looked through me and I felt myself become a page in something’s ledger. All of it since then — the years, the cattle, the children, the dead, the long walks in the dark with a lantern that showed me only how deep the dark went — all of it was simply the filling of that page. The accumulation of witness. The fattening of the memory it came to collect.

I do not resent it. The land collects its debts. A bullet was fired. Dogs were fed. A skull was nailed to wood and made to grin at the sun. These things happened, and the earth held them in its red dust, and the sky held them in its darkness, and eventually — this is the truth no ledger will record, no commissioner will write, no expert will name — eventually the debt comes to stand above you with its wings spread and its burning empty eyes and its lipless permanent smile, and it waits, with the patience of everything that has already died, for you to smile back.

If you find this testimony, do not search for me. Do not search for Kgomo. Burn this. And if you are ever outside at night and the wind stops and the cattle go still and you hear a moan from the sky that is shaped like the memory of something that used to be alive —

Do not look up.

That is the only mercy I have left to give you.

chapters.title: Cell 46
chapters.text:
D-WING

D-Wing · Restricted Access · Institutional History, 1645–Present

I have worked in prisons long enough to learn that every building has a memory. Some remember the sound of boots on stone. Some remember keys. Some remember prayers. But old European prisons — the ones whose foundations go down farther than any planning record — remember something else entirely. They remember fear so deep it sank into the mortar, soaked through the walls, and settled in the dark like damp rot that never dries.

Cell 46 was the worst of them. It had a reputation before I was ever assigned to D-Wing, before I first touched the iron ring on its door, before I stood outside it with my flashlight and my breath clouding in a cold that should not have existed in summer. The older wardens spoke of it in half-voices, the way men speak of a grave they have seen open. They said the cell had been a punishment chamber long before it was a cell. It had held heretics, witches, blasphemers, lunatics, thieves, and men whose crimes were so ugly even the prison records seemed to flinch around them.

The building was old enough to have tasted the smoke of the witch trials. This is not a metaphor. The yard outside still carries the black ring where the pyres stood. When it rains hard enough, something rises from that soil. Something that has no name in any language spoken by the living.

II — THE SEVENTEENTH CENTURY — —

WHAT THEY DID TO THE WOMEN — —

They laid this wing in the 1600s to cage the inconvenient. Women who spoke to crows or brewed teas that worked too well. Herbalists, widows, a girl of fourteen accused of congress with a black hound who confessed only after they had broken three of her fingers. In the ledgers of the Bury St Edmunds trials of 1645, their names appear thin and incomplete — Sarah Goode, Anne Whittler, Mary Spenser, and a dozen more crossed out as if the recording clerk had second thoughts about history finding them.

Most were kept here before being taken to the yard. They were hung by their wrists from iron rings set into the ceiling — toes scraping stone, arms wrenched to angles no shoulder was built to sustain. Blood pooled in their boots through the long Suffolk nights. Their minds went black before morning. Some died in that position, which meant they were found at dawn still standing, still suspended, still wearing the last expression their faces had ever managed. History called it justice. The stones called it something else. They called it dinner.

The cell drank that agony the way an altar drinks wine — not passively, not coincidentally, but with the patient appetite of something that had learned what it was for.

Innocence, as ever, was beside the point.

III — THREE CENTURIES OF FEEDING — —

THE COMPLAINTS BEGIN — —

When the witch trials ended, the cell became solitary confinement for the worst the prison system produced — murderers, defilers, men who had clawed out God’s image in other men’s faces. It did not become quieter. It became more particular.

At first there were only complaints. The prisoners assigned there said the room was colder than the rest of the prison, even in August. They said someone breathed beside them when they were alone. They said they heard weeping through the wall — then laughing — then a wet, choking sound like a person trying to scream underwater. The temperature dropped so suddenly at three in the morning that their lungs burned with it, not the cold of winter but a cold that was deliberate, that had intention.

— PRISONER TESTIMONY — CIRCA 1890, IDENTITY UNKNOWN —

It got cold and I could see mist as I breathed. The chilly air made it hard to sleep and with the thin blanket it became practically impossible. The wailings started at 3 a.m. in the morning — they wept, and the weeping turned into screaming, and what was a voice soon multiplied and gave birth to more screaming. I put my hands over my ears. It made no difference. The sound was not in the room. The sound was in the walls.

— Inmate, records destroyed in administrative fire,

The prisoner who wrote that was dismissed as hysterical by the duty surgeon. Two nights later he bit off his own tongue and bled out on the stone floor before the duty officer reached him. The report listed cause of death as self-inflicted injury under severe psychological distress. The usual language. The usual lie.

One inmate — a poisoner with hollowed cheeks and dead eyes like pressed coin — told me he had heard a woman crying in the corner all night.

“She sounded hurt,” he said. Then, after a pause long enough to have its own weather: “Then she sounded hungry.”

I should not have laughed. By morning he had torn his nails bloody against the wall, repeating the same phrase until they sedated him:she was in the wall, she was in the wall, she was in the wall. He was found three days later hanging from the sink pipe. The CCTV showed him standing upright at 3:07 a.m., swaying gently, lips moving as if listening to someone speak. There was no sound on the recording. Only his mouth opening in answer.

IV — SEPTEMBER, 1943 — —

THE NIGHT THAT SEALED IT — —

The riot of September 1943 was put down in three hours. The prison was overcrowded, understaffed, and nobody was keeping proper order. The governor — a man with more efficiency than sense — ordered the overflow of solitary cases consolidated into Cell 46

as an administrative expedient. No intake screening. No documentation. Seventeen men thrown in together like cordwood.

One of them was a cannibal. A butcher from the London slums, a man who had eaten his way through a famine and kept doing it after because hunger had rewired something behind his eyes that could not be rewired back. His prior conviction had not followed him from his previous institution. Nobody knew. Nobody checked.

The corridor smelled of copper and opened bowels by the time the night ended. When they unlocked the door at dawn, sixteen men were strewn across the floor in pieces — limbs separated, ribcages cracked open, soft organs missing. The official report described what was found inside in language so dry it made the horror worse:organic matter distributed radially across the cell floor. The only survivor — a scrawny creature named Albert Mosely — was squatting at the centre of the room, chewing something that still wore a wedding ring. He was howling. Not with madness. With a kind of ecstasy. They dragged him out still laughing. He never spoke again.

They renovated the cell after that. Scrubbed the stones. Whitewashed the walls. Sealed the iron rings. Poured new plaster. As if paint could smother what had soaked seventeen men into the mortar. As if renovation could close a wound that was still, in every measurable sense,breathing.

⌇⌇⌇⌇⌇ ⌇⌇⌇⌇⌇ ⌇⌇⌇⌇⌇ ⌇⌇

That was when the temperature drops became permanent. That was when the number seventeen began to repeat itself — in testimonies, in the CCTV timestamps, in the ring of footprints found beneath hanged men, in the precise number of faces the camera captured pressed against the ceiling like fossils in shale. Seventeen was not a coincidence. It was a pattern. It was a count. The cell was keeping inventory.

V — THE CAMERA DOES NOT LIE — —

— WHAT THE NIGHT SUPERVISOR WATCHES AND DOES NOT REPORT —

The CCTV footage from C-Wing is reviewed weekly. Everyone who has worked here long enough knows about the figure. It appears between 3:04 and 3:17 a.m. — always in that window, never varying by more than forty seconds — moving along the corridor toward Cell 46 with a gait that is not quite walking. Not the dragging gait of the exhausted, not the deliberate gait of the purposeful. The gait of something that has no relationship with effort. It passes through the door. The footage from inside skips. The digital record jumps seventeen minutes without explanation.

I showed the footage to the governor once. He paled, called it a malfunction, and ordered the tape wiped. I kept a copy. I have watched it fifty-three times. It never changes. The figure stops at the centre of the cell and raises its head, as if it knows it is being observed, as if it has always known, as if it has been waiting since the seventeenth century for someone to finally look directly at it.

The night supervisors watch it on the monitor. Nod. Turn the page. They all know. There is an unspoken agreement among the longer-serving staff: you do not say what you see in that corridor. You do not file a report. You initial the overnight log and you go home and if you dream, you do not say what of. We are all, in our way, complicit in what the cell is allowed to continue doing.

— SENIOR OFFICER MARCUS VENN — NOTEBOOK, RECOVERED POSTHUMOUSLY —

I will never forget when I heard the howls of a mad man screaming as the night agonisingly flew by. It all starts in the dead of the night. I am not alone. I am never alone. The cell doesn’t just show you its dead. It shows you your own.

— Officer M. Venn, deceased. Found hanging in Cell 46, cause listed as self-inflicted.

VI — WHAT I SAW — —

The Night of the Rapist. My Own Account.

The cell was occupied by a man convicted of rape and torture. He had been in three nights. On the fourth morning, when I came for the six o’clock check, I could feel the cold through my gloves before I reached the door — not the cold of the corridor but the other cold, the one with intention behind it, the one that pushes rather than merely persists. I looked

through the observation slot first. That is procedure. I am glad I looked before I opened the door.

He had hanged himself from the original Victorian pipework near the ceiling. He had used his bedsheet, twisted tight. He was still. But he was not alone.

At his feet, gathered in a loose circle, were seventeen figures. They were not transparent, not spectral in the way stories promise. They were too solid for that — the solidity of things that have been pressed by centuries into a concentrated form. Some wore the rough cloth of earlier ages. Some wore nothing at all. Several were women. One was a boy, no older than twenty, clutching his throat as if he could still stop the moment of his death. Several had their arms raised at that particular angle — wrists up, the posture of suspension — even though nothing held them. They had simply kept the shape that had been forced upon them.

They were not looking at the body. They were looking at me.

One of them — a young man with a cavity where his throat should have been — opened his lips. I heard a sound like a damp cloth tearing. I closed the observation slot. I stood in the corridor for a period of time I cannot estimate, my hand flat against the iron door, feeling the cold pulse through it like a slow heartbeat. When I finally opened it again, the cell contained only the hanged man. I called it in as a Code Red. I did not mention what I had seen. I did not mention it in my report, at my debrief, or to the duty psychologist.

I am mentioning it now because I believe the cell wants me to. I believe it has been slowly reorganising me toward this confession the way it reorganises everything placed inside it — toward disclosure, toward complicity, toward the particular surrender that lets it in permanently.

VII — THE FINAL NIGHT — —

WHAT THE CELL IS AND WHAT IT WANTS — —

I turned the key on Cell 46 at 2:58 a.m. The door did not creak. It sighed. Like a lung releasing. The air inside was thick, heavy, dense with the smell of wet ash and burnt hair and old blood gone brown and mineral. My breath plumed in slow spirals. Frost spiderwebbed the iron rings. I pressed my back against the door and it did not help.

The weeping started at exactly three o’clock. Soft at first. Then it fractured. Multiplied. A dozen throats in a space that could not hold four. I felt the sound not in my ears but in my jaw, my ribs, the hollow behind my sternum. It sank into the floor and rose back through the soles of my boots. Then silence — heavy, complete, the silence of something that has finished gathering itself.

I opened my eyes.

The room was full. Not with ghosts exactly. Not with bodies exactly. With presence— layered, compressed, the accumulated memory of every person who had been placed there to rot. Women with burned faces stood against the wall. Men with torn mouths paced the

floor. Figures hung from the ceiling by their wrists, rotating slowly, dozens of them now, shoulders stretched to their historical angles. And in the centre of them all stood the woman I had seen once before, through the observation slot, on the night the poisoner died.

Closer now, I could see that her wrists were raw from iron. Her dress was singed black at the hem. Her face was not monstrous. That was the worst part. She looked tired. Ancient. Furious in the way the earth is furious when it splits open. She raised one hand and placed it against my chest. The cold that entered me was not cold like winter. It was cold like a grave opening. Cold like a body left too long in stone. Cold like water under ice at the moment the ice gives way.

I felt every memory in the room pour through me at once — chains tightening, flames rising, hands bound overhead, prayers swallowed before they reached God, screams pressed into the mortar, names erased, bodies stacked, blood on straw, the stink of fear condensed by centuries into something that had learned to be a single, breathing, feeding thing.

I saw the riot. I saw Mosely in 1943. I saw seventeen men dying while one howled in the corner. I saw the women burned in the yard. I saw the heretics dragged through the gate. I saw men standing all night with their arms suspended until their shoulders tore free. And I saw, more horribly than all of it, that the cell had not merely witnessed these things. It had kept them. It had digested them. It had become a throat — a place where suffering went in and did not come back out the same.

The paranormal community calls it a haunting. It is not a haunting. A haunting is residue. What Cell 46 contains is something that has rotted past its component parts — the witches’ pain, the heretics’ despair, Mosely’s feast, the suicides that followed — all of it layered and compressed by three centuries of weight into a single sentient presence. Something that counts the living. Something that has been counting since 1645 and has not once lost track.

The woman leaned close enough for me to smell ash on her breath. In a voice like broken glass sliding through water she said:Now you know us.

I do not remember falling. I woke in the infirmary with my hands wrapped in bandages. The usual lies were administered: stress, overwork, hallucination. The usual lies men tell when truth would force them to do something. I resigned three days later.

But the haunting did not stay behind the door. It followed me home. It lives in the corners of rooms. It breathes from the dark end of hallways. It wakes me at 3:00 a.m. with the sound of weeping in the walls. Sometimes I find footprints on my floor, wet and bare, leading from my bedroom door to my bed. A woman’s.

Sometimes, when the house is silent enough, I hear scratching. Always on the same side of the wall. Always as if something is trying to get out. Or as if something is making itself comfortable, rearranging the dark around it, settling in for however long it takes.

VIII — EPILOGUE — —

What Are You Supposed to Do with Multiple Ghosts?

You don’t exorcise them. The Church burned the women. The state broke the men. There is no institution with the moral authority to clean this particular floor. You don’t photograph them — the investigators come with their equipment and their gooseflesh and leave to write their books, having understood nothing about what they were standing inside. You don’t pray them away, because what inhabits Cell 46 has heard ten thousand prayers and consumed the faith of everyone who uttered them.

What you do — what Officer Venn did, what the poisoner did, what the rapist who understood something in his final moment did — is feed it. With your breath. With your fear. With your sleep. With the slow, particular surrender of a person who has been counted too many times to pretend he hasn’t been noticed.

Cell 46 is occupied tonight. I checked the roster before I sat down to write this. Some man is lying on that cot right now, listening to a cold that has no meteorological explanation, watching his breath come out in visible shreds, waiting for 3:00 a.m. to tell him what this building remembers.

A prison can hold a body. A cell can hold a scream. But some places learn how to remember the suffering so completely that memory becomes a living thing. And once a place like that knows your name, it does not forget you. It does not stop counting. It does not stop feeding.

Not ever.

Not even when you leave.

What are you supposed to do with multiple ghosts? You don’t. You become one more for the next poor bastard to find.

chapters.title: Liwan plaza
chapters.text:
尸

Liwan Plaza Shopping Centre · Guangzhou, night shift

Stare at the sign long enough — let your eyes go soft while the Guangzhou smog blurs the neon — and it happens. The strokes shift. The top horizontal tilts. The left stroke shortens. The sweeping right leg bends inward.广, vast and auspicious, collapses into something older. Into 尸. Corpse. The building announces itself honestly, if you know how to read it.

Wei Songlin noticed it on his sixth night working the security desk. He laughed. Sleep deprivation. He should have walked away.

He didn’t. The pay was good. No one else wanted the night shift.

The cold hit him first — not the mechanical exhale of air conditioning but something dry and subterranean, a chill that bypassed skin entirely and settled in the marrow like a memory of a winter he’d never lived through. He’d checked the vents. He’d checked the thermostats. He’d filed three maintenance reports. The cold had no source, no explanation, and did not respond to documentation.

The building breathed with vents and metal and money. Roll- down gates rattled in the dark. The PA system gave small, intermittent chirps — nervous birds in a closed space. Somewhere overhead, pipes clicked as if something heavy shifted inside the walls. The mall had been built over a Qing Dynasty sacrificial chamber; eight empty cofÏns had been unearthed during construction and relocated without ceremony, despite a Taoist priest’s warning that they were not to be disturbed for a thousand years. Their purpose had not

been burial. They had been sealed in the earth to thwart what was already down there — a lid on an old, patient thing. The developers had lifted that lid in 2003 and poured a jewelry market over the hole.

The building’s architects had made it octagonal, like the bagua. An apology in concrete and steel. It did not help.

II — —

THE FIGURES BEFORE ANYONE ELSE ARRIVES — —

Every morning, before the first shopkeepers arrived to raise their shutters, they were already there.

A woman in a faded floral blouse at the fifth-floor railing, one hand on the balustrade, head bowed as if listening to someone below. A thin old man in a white undershirt sitting cross-legged beside an escalator, feet floating just above the step. A boy with a schoolbag pressed to his chest staring into the reflective surface of a closed watch store. A pair of workers in dust- streaked uniforms arguing in silence near the food court, mouths opening and closing without sound.

They looked alive from a distance. That was the cruelest part.

Up close, they were all wrong. Their faces held the pallor of paper left in rain. Their eyes had no moisture — only the glassy sheen of things that had once been human and no longer knew what to do with being seen. Their outlines trembled, blurred at the edges, as if being badly remembered. When they moved, they didn’t walk so much as drift, pulled by a current Wei couldn’t feel. And they vanished every morning before anyone else arrived to see them.

The cold intensified whenever one was near. The PA system — switched off every night at eleven — would occasionally crack with static that resolved into a whisper in Cantonese:It wasn’t my fault. I changed my mind. Please. I changed my mind.

He told himself: stress. PTSD. The mind cannot process certain quantities of witnessed death. He told himself the stories the old vendors whispered — the cursed land, the sacrificial chamber, the cofÏns that should have remained sealed — were superstition kept alive because fear is easier to name than grief.

But every morning there were the figures.

III — —

THE PUSH — —

FIFTH FLOOR — 22:26 — NOVEMBER — —

The woman in the floral blouse arrived at 9:45 PM. Wei watched her on the monitor: slim, a gray coat, riding the escalator to the fifth floor with the unhurried pace of someone who had already decided something. She walked to the railing. She looked down. She stepped back. She paced. She approached again. Her body was performing the universal, terrible arithmetic of someone choosing between two unbearable things.

This went on for forty minutes.

Then her body language changed entirely. She stopped pacing. Her head snapped to the right — sharp, involuntary — as if someone had called her name from just off-camera. She went rigid. And behind her, detaching itself from the shadow of the corridor wall, a second figure stepped forward.

It wore the shape of a person badly, the way a child draws one from memory. Limbs too long. Shoulders hunched under invisible weight. Where the face should have been: a dark smear, a compression artifact of flesh. But it moved with terrible intimacy — leaning in close, pressing something like a palm flat between her shoulder blades. Not a shove. A settling. The way you press a book into a shelf.

She didn’t scream. She simply tipped forward. The wind swallowed her descent. Below, a sound: wet, structural, final — a crack-squelch against polished granite that Wei would hear in his sleep for the rest of the time he had left.

He ran. Four floors. Three minutes. The fifth-floor corridor was empty. The thing behind her was gone. He reached the railing and looked down at what the building had made of her, and then he looked up because he couldn’t look down any longer, and he saw his own reflection in the brass elevator doors at the end of the corridor.

In the reflection — standing directly behind his reflection — was a second figure. His own height. His own build. His own gray security jacket.

He spun around. Nothing.

When he looked back, his reflection was alone. And smiling. In a way that his face was not.

— Security Log, Liwan Plaza, Nov. 2011 —Woman, approx. 30s, fell from fifth-floor atrium railing, 22:26. No witnesses to direct contact. Footage reviewed: victim appears alone at railing.

Manner of fall: unassisted. Reporting ofÏcer: Wei Songlin. Addendum — footage review produced anomaly in elevator- door reflection, timestamp 22:29. Anomaly attributed to lens compression. No further action.

IV — —

THE GAP IN THE RECORD — —

The blackouts started three weeks later.

He would be sitting at the security desk, watching monitors, and then he would be somewhere else — standing by the eastern railing on the fifth floor with no memory of climbing the stairs, his palms cold from gripping the metal, the atrium below arranging itself around another small crowd and their hands pressed over their mouths. He would come back to himself the way someone surfaces from deep water: disoriented, lungs wrong, the world slightly too loud.

His hands always ached afterward. Deep in the joints. Muscle memory of weight and release.

He found the previous guard’s logbook in the desk drawer. The man had circled one date and written:Dreamt I was the boy with the glasses. Pushed myself. Woke up on the atrium floor. No injuries. Quitting tomorrow. He’d circled another date after that. The entries stopped before the second circled date.

Dissociation, he told himself, isn’t a break. It’s a slow leak. The mind fractures to survive guilt. He told himself this even as he couldn’t account for three hours on a Thursday in December, during which two people fell from the fifth floor within forty minutes of each other, and the security booth smelled when he returned to it of dry earth, old lacquer, and the particular cold of something long buried.

— — —

The new high-definition cameras were installed after the seventh death. Management wanted pattern recognition. They wanted to see the faces of the victims more clearly. What the cameras gave them instead was this:

A middle-aged man stood at the railing on the night of December 14th, crying. His lips moved — prayers, or apologies, or the names of people he was leaving behind. He kept looking over his shoulder at nothing. His hands shook so badly he could barely grip the metal.

Then the nothing behind him resolved.

A figure stepped from the right side of frame — same height, same build, same gray security jacket with the small tear near the left cuff that Wei had been meaning to repair for two months. Same receding hairline. Same slight hitch in the left knee from an injury sustained playing football at seventeen.

The figure’s face was the victim’s face. Exactly. Every wrinkle, every mole, the scar above the left eyebrow.

The victim looked at his double for three seconds with an expression not of terror but of recognition — the recognition of someone understanding, too late, a thing they have been refusing to understand for a very long time.

The double placed its hands flat against the man’s spine. He screamed without making any sound the microphone could capture. Then he was gone.

The double remained at the railing for a full minute. Then it turned and looked directly into the camera. It adjusted its collar with a gesture Wei had made ten thousand times without

thinking. And it walked out of frame — toward the service corridor, toward the stairwell, toward the basement security booth.

Wei showed the footage to two junior guards. He made them watch it four times. Each time, the doppelgänger was there — crisp, 4K, undeniable. Each time, the guards frowned and said:“There’s no one. He’s alone. Just climbs over.”

The monitoring room dropped ten degrees in one second.

He felt breathing on the back of his neck and turned to an empty room. On the darkened screen of the monitor nearest him, his reflection looked back. His reflection was not turning around. It was still staring at the footage. Still smiling with a patience that had nothing to do with him.

V — —

WHAT THE MEMORY RETURNED — —

It didn’t come back all at once. Memory never does. It seeped — the way damp moves through old concrete, finding the cracks before you know the cracks are there.

A man on the fifth floor, leaning on the railing, saying he didn’t know how to go on. A hand on a shoulder — his hand. A voice, his own voice, calm and low:“There’s a way down. You only have to let go.” The art of standing where cameras couldn’t catch his face. Learning which people were already half-gone and needed only a small, intimate push — less a murder than a suggestion given precise physical form.

He had told himself they came because they were already leaving. He had told himself he only nudged. Only gave their despair a shape to fall into.

In his own mind the thought tasted like rot.

But the horror wasn’t that he had done it. The horror was that he did not know, could not determine, where his will ended and something older began. The cofÏns were empty. The Taoist priest had tried to explain this: the emptiness was the point. Void to swallow void. Silence to swallow suffering. They were sealed to contain something beneath the chamber that predated the dynasty, predated the city, predated every human attempt to name it. When the developers opened them in 2003, the containment broke. And the thing below — patient, cold, immeasurably practiced — had been looking for a vessel ever since.

The building didn’t create monsters. It mirrored them. It took what was already in a person — the part that stood a little too close to railings, that felt a little too intimate with the despair of strangers — and it amplified that into something with hands.

The plaza was a resonance chamber for buried conscience.

And Wei Songlin had been feeding it his own.

VI — —

The Receipt. The Gathering. The Railing.

He found the paper on his desk at 3 AM on a January night. Old at the corners, yellowed, no numbers. Only his name. And below his name, in handwriting too neat to be hurried:

YOU ALREADY KNOW WHAT YOU DID.

He went to the fifth floor at midnight and stood at the railing as if drawn by a cord attached to something inside his sternum. Below, the mall lights glimmered like drowned eyes. Around him, the dead assembled without ceremony.

Not four. Not seven. Dozens. They arrived as if summoned by a bell only Wei could hear — and perhaps only the part of him that was no longer entirely Wei. The man in the yellow jacket. The ofÏce worker. The boy with the schoolbag. A woman with a broken wrist, a security guard with dried blood in his left ear, a young mother carrying something too small for the light to show clearly. Some wore clothes decades out of fashion. Some wore silk robes from before electricity, before the market, before any of it. They gathered shoulder to shoulder by the railing, and they looked — not at the floor below — but at him.

They arranged themselves in a perfect octagon.

The bagua complete. The apology finally answered.

They were not here to punish him. They were here to anchor him. To make him part of the structure. The cofÏns were sealed empty to hold silence. They would hold him the same way.

One figure stepped forward from the circle. A woman in a gray blouse, dark hair knotted at the base of her skull. One side of her face had collapsed inward — not grotesquely, but with the softness of an old photograph left too long in sun, the features blurred by damage that time had made almost gentle. She had no feet. Her cuffs were damp, as though she had been dragged through water.

He knew her. Not by name. By consequence.

She had been the first. She had been trembling. Not asking to die — asking not to be alone. He had stood behind her and spoken with the intimacy of someone offering mercy, and she had gone over the railing with a look of stunned, final betrayal.

She raised her hand.

Not in accusation. In invitation. The gesture of a creditor who has found, after a long search, exactly where the debtor has been living.

He turned to run. The corridor behind him was already full. New arrivals, expressions still holding the shape of last thoughts — a young man with blood on his collar, a woman whose glasses were cracked, a mother with one shoe missing. All of them with the same absolute certainty, the certainty of people who died knowing exactly what face they last saw.

He backed against the railing. The cold crystallized at his ankles. He felt hands — small and large, dozens — pressing flat against his spine. Not a shove. A settling.

The way you press a book into a shelf.

He looked down at his own hands, gripping the railing. They were clean. No mark, no blood, no proof except the dead surrounding him. That was the worst part. That had always been the worst part.

— — —

The woman in gray smiled for the first time. The expression was not revenge. It was not anger or justice or any of the things terror tells you to expect from those you have wronged.

It was relief.

Because at last — at last — the one who had opened the door was standing on the other side of it. Because the jumper always hesitates. Because the jumper always changes their mind. Because it never, in the end, matters.

Below, somewhere deep in the building’s foundation, a sound rose through the concrete: many feet, or what had once been feet, moving at once. The old sealed things, remembering the names of everyone who had disturbed them.

The PA system crackled.

All the voices spoke together, in the woman’s voice, in his own voice, in a voice that predated both:

“Careful.”

The railing pressed against his hips. The hands pressed against his back. The atrium opened below him like a mouth that had been waiting — patiently, quietly, for years — to receive exactly this.

广 尸

Two hours later, the goldsmiths arrived. The jade merchants. The tourists from Shenzhen. They walked past the sign outside without looking up. They felt the cold and blamed the air conditioning. They rode the escalators and did not look down. The fifth floor, they said, had always been a few degrees colder than it should be. No one could explain why. No one asked too long. The silent still run amok. The merchants count their cash. The plaza breathes.

chapters.title: The old station
chapters.text:
TIME NOTE SIGN 22:00 Incoming shift — 02:00 Round, Sector B — 06:00 Relief arrives —

Assignment: 'Routine Security Posting' (see remarks)

The assignment sheet said routine security posting. It said nothing about the fact that every officer who had held the post before me had either resigned, been found dead, or stopped being able to speak properly about what they had seen.

I learned this later. By then it was too late to matter.

My name is Constable Dube. I arrived at Muzvare Station on a Wednesday evening, as the last light was draining from the sky in long red streaks, the colour of something torn open. The building sat at the end of a dirt road that the bush had been slowly reclaiming for years — red brick gone brown with age, a corrugated roof buckled in the middle like a broken spine, arched windows that had swallowed all their glass long ago and now simply gaped. The platform ran the length of the building, its concrete cracked so deeply that grass had grown up through it, and in places the growth was so dense it looked less like a station than a field that had simply decided to impersonate one.

The rails were still there. That was the part nobody mentioned when they described the place. I had expected them to be gone, salvaged, hauled away like everything else of value. But they remained — two lines of rust stretching away through the tall savannah grass in both directions until the darkness absorbed them completely. They looked less like infrastructure than like scars.

I set my lamp on the old ticketing counter and told myself to be professional. I had heard the stories, of course. You could not work in the rail district without hearing them. The siege of 1966. Six armed men, rebels or patriots depending on which version of history you were permitted to know, who had walked into this station with rifles and held it for seven days while the Rhodesian government debated whether the place was worth the logistics of a response. The conductor. The ticket seller. The passengers who had been preparing to board and instead boarded something else entirely, something with no scheduled arrival and no destination worth naming.

Then the silence. Then the shots. Then the man who walked out alone, stood in the sunlight in front of the assembled police, and put the rifle in his mouth as though it were the most reasonable conclusion to seven days of impossible arithmetic.

And beneath that story, the other one. The commissioner’s visit to the witchdoctor. The ritual done in darkness, the price of which was not disclosed until it had already been paid. The witchdoctor’s body, found two weeks later in the bush without a mark, without a wound, without any explanation that did not require you to accept the

existence of things that operated outside the boundaries of what the government was currently willing to call real.

I told myself stories were stories. I checked the lock on the gate, arranged my flask and radio, and settled in to wait for morning.

The first thing I noticed was the ledger.

It lay open on the ticketing counter, which I should have found strange because the counter was filmed with dust that had not been disturbed in years — except around the ledger, where the surface was clean. Recently cleaned, or recently placed. The pages were yellowed but the ink was not. The last entry read: June 12, 1966. Six boarding. Destination: unknown. The handwriting was neat and administrative, the penmanship of a man who took his work seriously. Below it, a line had been drawn across the page as if to indicate the day was closed.

Below the line, in different ink, in a hand I did not recognise: They have not left.

I told myself the ink was old. I told myself the discolouration was irregular and I was misreading its age in the low lamplight. I told myself a great many things that Wednesday evening, and some of them I almost believed.

Then the lamp began to pulse.

Not flicker — not the random brown-out of failing electricity. Pulse. Steady, rhythmic, like a heart deciding something. I checked the battery. Full. I set it down, and it pulsed again, and in the half

second of dimness between one beat and the next I saw, in the cracked glass of the ticket booth window, a face that was not mine.

Wide-eyed. Hollow-cheeked. A beret at an angle that had once been jaunty and was now simply eternal. The face of a man who had been twenty-something in 1966 and had not aged a day since, because the dead have no use for years. He was not looking at me. He was looking past me, at the platform, with an expression of such absolute and patient expectancy that my stomach turned.

I spun around. The platform was empty. The grass moved. There was no wind.

By midnight, the quality of the air had changed.

There is no more precise way to describe it. The air became dense with something that was not humidity, not cold, not any atmospheric phenomenon I had words for. It had the quality of held breath. Of a crowd going still. I moved my lamp to the platform archway and stood in it and looked out at the rails, and that was when I saw them.

Four figures on the platform. Standing at intervals along it, facing the rails, motionless. A woman in clothing that belonged to a different decade, a small case at her feet. An elderly man with a newspaper folded under his arm, the headlines long since faded to grey. A child, perhaps eight years old, standing with its hands clasped before it in the posture of a child that has been told very firmly to behave. And at the far end, near the old signal post, a man in a

conductor’s uniform with his back to me and his hands behind him, as though he were waiting for something that was late.

I knew, with a certainty that preceded and overrode rational thought, that these were the passengers. The ones from 1966. The ones who had come to catch a train and instead became something the station kept.

I did not move toward them. I did not call out. I had the instinct, very clear and very loud, that acknowledging them directly would be a kind of invitation I could not afford to extend. So I watched, and they stood, and the rails stretched away into darkness, and nothing arrived.

Then the child turned its head.

Not toward me. Toward the booking office, where the ledger lay open on the counter. And slowly, in a movement that had the terrible deliberateness of something that understood it was being watched and did not care, it raised one arm and pointed at the ledger.

I went back inside. I turned the ledger pages.

Every page was filled. Names, dates, times of arrival, destinations. Hundreds of entries spanning decades, the oldest ink brown and crumbling, the newest sharp and dark. Near the back, the entries stopped being travel records and became something else. Fragments. A ticket seller’s handwriting: I saw them again last night. Standing. Just standing. A different hand: Something in the grass has learned my walking route. Another: I found my name in here. I did not write it. Then a series of entries in

deteriorating penmanship, the letters growing larger and less controlled as the pages progressed, until the last one was almost illegible — a single word, repeated across an entire page in characters that had torn through the paper in places: WATCHING WATCHING WATCHING.

At the very back of the ledger, on the last page, in handwriting I recognised as my own, were two lines:

Constable Dube. Arrived Wednesday. He has not left.

The growling began at half past two.

Not from inside the station. From the grass. It was low and resonant and it had, as the worst sounds do, an almost-linguistic quality — as though meaning were being expressed in a register below the frequency of words. I had read in the file, in a footnote someone had failed to redact, about the witchdoctor. About the ritual the commissioner had requested and the thing the ritual had summoned and the price the witchdoctor had not lived to negotiate. I understood now that the growling was not an animal. It was the ritual, still running. A process without an endpoint, circling the station the way water circles a drain, patient and structural and entirely indifferent to whether anyone remained inside.

I tried my radio. Dead air. Not static — dead. The silence of a channel that had never been opened.

At three o’clock, with the precision of something that observed schedules the way the living observe gravity, the wailing started.

It came from everywhere. From the grass, from the platform, from the walls of the building itself, from somewhere directly beneath my feet. Old voices, cracked and ruined, layered over one another until they were indistinguishable as individuals and became instead a single enormous sound that was less like crying than like the earth attempting speech. I heard Shona. I heard English. I heard at least one language I could not identify, something older, something that the continent remembered in its bones.

And within the wailing, repeated over and over, the same phrase in a dozen different voices, a dozen different registers, some pleading, some resigned, some that had gone so far past terror they had arrived at a kind of hideous peace: We only wanted to cleanse this place. We only wanted to send them home.

The elders.

Shot on their knees by men with newer rifles and older certainties, their prayers dismissed as sedition, their rituals dismantled by a government that understood power as the exclusive right to determine what was and was not permitted to exist. They had been trying to do the thing that the commissioner’s witchdoctor had botched — to properly release the dead, to give the hungry spirits leave to rest, to close the wound this place had become. Instead they had been added to it, their own

unresolved deaths folded into the accumulation, their voices joining the chorus, their terror becoming part of the architecture.

The station had not been haunted by accident. It had been deliberately filled.

I saw him at ten past three.

He came from the grass in the way that things from the grass always come — at the edge of vision, peripheral, so that by the time your eyes moved to find him directly he had already shifted, was already somewhere else, was always in the place you had just stopped looking. He wore skins and carried the remnants of things I could not identify in the lamplight. His eyes were opaque, milky, the eyes of a man who had seen across boundaries that vision was not designed to cross and had paid the standard price for the crossing.

The witchdoctor. Dead since 1966, still performing the function he had been hired for, unable to stop because the ritual had never been properly closed, because you cannot simply cancel an arrangement made with the things that live below the surface of the world without someone completing the terms.

He looked at me with those ruined eyes and his mouth moved and I heard, inside my own skull rather than through my ears, a single word in a voice like soil being turned: Witness.

And then I understood what the station actually was.

Not a haunting. Not a curse, not in the superstitious sense, not in the way the word is used to describe something arbitrary and malicious. It was a record.

An archive of every unacknowledged death, every silenced voice, every body found with terror on its face and no wound to explain it, every prayer interrupted by a rifle. The passengers who had never been permitted to leave. The rebels whose siege had ended in something so terrible that the sole survivor had preferred the barrel of his own rifle to another minute of remaining in that building. The ticket seller. The ticket master. The elders. All of them, held here not by malice but by incompletion, the way a sentence without its final word holds your breath.

The station needed a witness. Someone who would not look away. Someone who would carry the weight of what had happened here outward into the living world, because the dead have no way to do it themselves.

I understood this at ten past three on a Wednesday night, standing on a platform with a failing lamp and a useless radio, with the wailing pouring through the walls and the growling circling the grass and the passengers watching the tracks for a train that would not come.

I also understood that understanding it was not the same as surviving it.

They found me at dawn, sitting on the platform bench.

I am told my face required significant effort to look at directly. I am told the expression it held was not one that faces are designed to hold, that it had the quality of something printed rather than worn — a final frame, a terminus. I am told I was breathing, which is the reason they knew I was alive, because nothing else about me suggested it.

I cannot tell you what I saw in the last hours before dawn. The part of the mind that processes such things does not use language as its filing system. I can tell you that I remember the train. That I remember its windows lit from within by a light that was not electricity. That I remember the doors opening. That I remember faces at the glass, arranged in the particular stillness of people who have been waiting for a very long time and have made a kind of peace with waiting that the living find unbearable to look at.

I can tell you that I did not board it. Whether that was will or something else, I cannot say.

What I can say is that the ledger, when they found it, had a new entry in my handwriting. I did not write it. I have not been able to write legibly since that night. The entry read:

Six boarding. Plus the ticket seller. Plus the ticket master. Plus thirty-one elders. Plus the witchdoctor. Plus the passengers. Plus the officer who finally understood. The destination remains unknown. The train is never late.

They closed the station again. They always close it again.

And every night, at three o’clock exactly, if you stop your car on that dirt road and roll the windows down, you will hear the wailing begin. You will hear the names of people whose graves were never dug in the right places, or dug at all. You will hear the

low structural growling of a ritual that has been running since 1966 and has never been given permission to stop.

And if you stay long enough — long enough for the grass to notice you, long enough for the silence to acquire weight, long enough for the lamp you did not bring to start pulsing at the edge of your vision — you will hear, very faintly, the sound of a train whistle.

Do not try to find where it is coming from.

The station does not want your body. It does not want your fear.

It only wants someone to carry what happened here back out into the light.

The problem is the carrying tends to break the carrier.

And the station has never once been short of patience.
