chapters.title: My hostel
chapters.text:
INACTIVE 9

Block C · Addis Ababa Women's Hostel · Room 9 (door unmarked)

Addis Ababa. Women’s Hostel, Block C. Room 9. The door has no number. The screws are still there, two holes in the wood like empty eye sockets. Whatever was fastened there was removed a long time ago, and no one has seen fit to replace it.

Ethiopia is a country that prays before it speaks. A country that lines its roads with churches and its mornings with incense, that buries its dead in consecrated earth and keeps its saints closer than its secrets. You would not expect ghost stories from such a country.

You would be wrong.

Anna Tesfaye heard about Room 9 on her first day at university.

The girl who told her — Yordanos, crucifix catching the cafeteria light — kept her voice low even though no one was near. The room had been empty for three years. Everyone knew about it the way they knew about a grave that had been dug wrong: with a wariness they couldn’t entirely explain and didn’t want to examine too closely. Students who passed the corridor near Room 9 tended to walk faster. The cleaning staff skipped it entirely. A priest had come once and refused to say what he’d seen, but his hair had gone white at the temples by the following Sunday.

They said something lived in the corner of the ceiling.

Something female.

Something that watched you while you slept.

“A bat,” Anna said. “You’re all describing a bat.”

Yordanos gripped her arm hard enough to leave marks — which, later, Anna would think about a great deal. “The ceiling above that room is solid concrete. There’s a floor above it, then the rooftop. There is no space. Nothing should be able to live up there. But it does.”

Anna shook her free and laughed. She was twenty years old, studying biology, and she believed that fear was a story the mind told itself when it needed an excuse to feel small.

She moved in that same evening.

The room smelled of something she could not name. Not rot, not mold — something beneath those things, older than decay. Like a copper coin held too long in a palm. Like soil after a coffin has been laid and covered and the mourners have gone home.

The ceiling was high. Higher than it should have been for a dormitory. The plaster at the top of the walls had darkened with age into a shade that was almost bruised, and where the walls met the ceiling the right- angle junctions were deep and shadow-filled and very difficult to see into from the bed.

Anna noted this the way a biologist notes a variable: calmly, without conclusions.

She draped her mother’s embroidered blanket over the iron bed frame — the Holy Virgin stitched in gold and red thread, her palms open, her expression resigned — and turned off the light.

The first night, she slept.

She would tell her friends this in the morning, and it was not entirely untrue. She had lost consciousness. But something had visited those hours while she wasn’t watching. When she woke, her back ached from shoulder blade to lumbar as though she had spent the night pressed flat against a hard surface by something heavy. Her neck would not turn to the left without a grinding, deep-tissue resistance. The inside of her

forearms bore what looked like pressure bruises — not scratches, not wounds, but the deep violet bloom of fingers that had held without breaking skin.

She had no explanation. She assigned none. She texted her friends: Slept fine. Bring the lunch money.

The second night, the room changed.

Not physically — the furniture was exactly as she had left it, the cracks in the mirror the same, the ceiling fan’s shadow motionless. But the air had thickened. She noticed it the moment she closed the door behind her, a quality of resistance, as if the room was holding something in. The fan moved uselessly against the weight of it. She lay down and pulled the blanket to her chin and fixed her eyes on the ceiling.

The corner above the wardrobe was very dark.

She watched it for a long time. It watched back.

She slept eventually, or something like sleep, and woke at 3:17 a.m. with the absolute and unambiguous certainty that something was in the room with her.

Her body knew before her eyes adjusted. Every hair on her forearms stood up. Her heart had already accelerated into a pace that was close to pain. She lay rigid, staring at the darkness above her, and waited for her eyes to tell her what her skin already understood.

The corner above the wardrobe was no longer simply dark.

Something was there.

Pale. Not the pale of illness but something older — the white of bone, of things that have never seen sun, of skin that has no business being that color. It clung to the junction of ceiling and wall the way a knuckle grips an edge, and its limbs were wrong in a way that her biology-trained mind kept trying and failing to process. Too many angles. Joints that suggested articulation in directions joints did not go. And hair — long

black ropes of it, perfectly dry, hanging downward through the air as if gravity had made a private arrangement with this creature that it had made with nothing else.

It was female.

She knew this with a certainty that had nothing to do with reason. The shape of its shoulders, its hips, the narrowness of its waist — female, unmistakably, grotesquely, as though something had taken womanhood and stretched it over a frame designed for something else entirely.

Its eyes were open.

They were red. Not bright, not fiery — the red of an infection seen through skin, a deep and wet and biologic crimson, and they were fixed on her with an attention so complete and so specific that she understood, in the wordless part of herself, that this was not a creature that noticed everyone. That it had noticed her. That the noticing had already been going on for longer than tonight.

She could not move.

This was not metaphor. Her body had simply ceased to accept instructions. She lay flat and rigid, paralyzed in a way she had no medical framework for, and the creature in the corner looked at her with its red eyes and did not blink and did not move for a very long time.

Then it descended.

Not a drop, not a scramble — a flowing, joint-by-joint unwinding that brought each limb forward in sequence, slow and deliberate and terribly graceful. She could hear it: a sound like knuckles cracking softly, a dry whisper of movement against the plaster. The smell hit her before it was halfway across the ceiling. Copper and damp earth and something underneath both of those things, something intimate and wrong, like being too close to a wound that has been dressed but not healed.

When it reached the foot of her bed and paused and tilted its head — she felt its gaze travel her body like a hand — Anna screamed.

The sound tore out of her and it worked: the creature screeched back, a sound that vibrated in her fillings, in the backs of her eyes, and shot to the ceiling corner in a blur of pale limbs and was gone. When she found the light switch, the corner was empty.

She sat on the floor with her back against the bed until morning.

She did not leave.

This was the part no one understood afterward, that needed explaining. She did not leave because she was not sure, not entirely, that she had not dreamed it. Because admitting she had seen it meant admitting everything everyone had told her was true, which meant admitting that the world contained things her education had given her no language for. She needed another night to be certain.

This is what the creature knew about her that she did not know about herself.

She borrowed a motion-sensor camera from the media department. She set it on the desk facing the ceiling corner. She told herself she was being methodical.

The fourth night, she woke at 3:17 again — always 3:17, which she would later learn was not coincidence — and this time the creature was not in the corner.

It was on the ceiling directly above her.

She felt its presence before she opened her eyes. A cold so total it was tactile, like being submerged, and a weight on her chest that had nothing to do with the blanket. She opened her eyes and it was there, not four inches from her face, its head inverted, its red eyes inches from hers, its hair hanging around them both like a curtain closing.

It was smiling.

The mouth — too wide, splitting further than mouths were built to split — was curved in an expression she recognized and could not bear. Maternal. Patient. Fond. The expression of something that had waited a long time and felt the waiting was nearly over.

Anna felt something happening to her body that she would not put into words afterward. A pressure. A taking. The thing above her rocked slightly, rhythmically, and the cold spread from her chest downward and her breath came in fragments, and when she finally wrenched herself free and screamed, it retreated to the ceiling with an unhurried ease that was worse than speed. It was not frightened. It was finished, for now.

In the morning she found bruises on her thighs shaped like handprints. She stood in front of the cracked mirror and looked at them for a long time. Then she looked at her face. Her face looked wrong. Hollowed. The skin around her eyes had gone thin and translucent and her pupils were very large, as though her eyes were trying to gather more light. She looked like a photograph taken at the wrong exposure.

She thought: it is feeding.

She did not leave.

The fifth day she spent in the library’s theological archive, pulling crumbling pamphlets and bound theses and xeroxed monastery manuscripts that smelled like the room she was sleeping in. She found what she was looking for in a pamphlet printed by a monk in 1971: Concerning the Ceiling-Dwellers, and the Records of Solomon.

The entity was female, always female. A daughter of something older than scripture. It fed on breath, on sleep, on what the text obliquely described as vital intimacy. It was drawn to enclosed spaces where new inhabitants arrived seasonally — where there would always, eventually, be someone young and warm and unwary. Once it had fixed on a victim, it would not release them until they were exhausted to the bone, hollowed of whatever quality had attracted it, reduced to a vessel it had finished using. Then it waited for the next.

The paralysis was its work. The bruises were its fingerprints.

The text warned, in the understated language of monks writing about things they had no wish to dwell on, that it was not averse to worse.

Anna closed the pamphlet and sat for a long time in the fluorescent library light.

She thought about leaving. She was certain she would leave. She would pack that afternoon, take her suitcase, sleep on Yordanos’s floor, and never go near Block C again.

She went back to Room 9 at dusk.

She could not explain this later. Her feet simply carried her there. The door was unlocked. She had not left it unlocked. Inside, the blanket with the Holy Virgin had been folded and placed on the desk, very neatly, face down.

That night she did not sleep. She sat against the wall with the camera running and every light blazing and she waited for 3:17. When it came, she felt the temperature drop before she heard anything. Then the sound: not the cracking-knuckle descent from above but something new — a sound from inside the wall. A soft rhythmic tapping, deliberate, each tap precisely spaced, like fingers walking.

The tapping moved across the wall toward the corner. Stopped.

The lights flickered once.

From the corner, in a voice that was unmistakably Anna’s own voice played back slightly wrong, slightly slowed, came three words:

“Not yet. Not yet.”

The lights died.

The sixth night, she found the Holy Virgin on the floor with the embroidery torn out.

The threads were arranged on the desk in a shape she recognized as a word, in Ge’ez script, though she did not know Ge’ez. She photographed it and took it to a professor the next morning. He looked at it for a long time and then looked at her face and asked her if she was alright.

“What does it say?”

He was quiet. Then: “Mine.”

Anna’s friends found her on the morning of the seventh day sitting on the bed with her hands folded in her lap, staring at the window. She was extremely still and extremely quiet and her eyes were focused on something that was not in the room — or something that was in the room and invisible to everyone but her.

They spoke to her. She answered in monosyllables. They noticed the bruising on her throat, on her collarbones, the darkness beneath her eyes, the terrible translucency of her skin. Yordanos took her hands and they were cold — cold in a way that had nothing to do with the temperature.

“Anna,” she said. “Come with us. Right now. Just come.”

Anna looked at her. The look went on too long, as if she was consulting something before answering.

“I can’t,” she said.

That night, at 3:17, she went to the window.

She did not look back. The room behind her had filled with a cold so absolute it was almost solid, and she could hear the breathing behind her — low, rhythmic, patient — and she could feel the familiar weight against her back, arms encircling her from behind, a chin resting on her shoulder, a mouth at her ear forming words she had stopped resisting.

She stepped onto the sill.

The courtyard below was very dark. She could see the roots of the jacaranda, white stone, the hard geometry of the flagstones. The air was cold and clean out here, cleaner than anything she had breathed in days, and she pulled it in and thought, with sudden piercing clarity: I don’t want to.

But her body was already falling.

She survived. Four stories, the jacaranda’s roots, two broken legs, a fractured pelvis, three broken fingers, a collapsed lung. She survived and she did not speak for eleven days and when she did she would not say anything about the room. She would not say anything about anything that had happened in the room. She would look at the ceiling of her hospital ward and she would not blink for very long intervals, and the nurses noted this in their charts but did not know what to write beside it.

The university issued a statement about mental health and sealed Room 9.

In the autumn of 2013, a ghost hunting team paid the night guard to let them in.

Two men: Daniel, the taller one, the one who kept making jokes, and Tesfaye, who did not make jokes but watched everything with a careful, cataloguing attention. They had good equipment — thermal imagers, high-definition infrared cameras, a directional microphone that could detect sounds below the human threshold. They had done fourteen investigations across East Africa and found compelling ambiguities in six of them. They were not credulous men. They prided themselves on this.

The first two nights were empty. Cold spots. One audio anomaly that turned out to be pipes.

The third night, they both fell asleep.

Neither could explain it. They had been drinking coffee for six hours. Tesfaye had done a standing shift. Daniel had been reviewing footage on his laptop. Neither remembered becoming drowsy. The sleep came

like a switch being thrown, instantaneous and total, and it was not the sleep of tired men but something manufactured, something without gradations.

Daniel woke at 3:17.

The corner above the wardrobe held two red points of light.

He did not scream. He did not move. He sat completely still and looked at the creature looking at him, and felt — beneath the terror, which was absolute — a strange, terrible sense of recognition. As if some animal part of him had known since birth that things like this existed, had been waiting his entire life to be proved right.

He reached slowly for the camera.

The instant his hand moved, the creature unfolded from the corner and ran — not with the slow deliberateness it had shown Anna, but fast, panicked-fast, the movement of something that has been seen by the wrong eyes, all clicking limbs and pale blur. It reached the far wall and did not stop. It did not stop at the wall. It went through the wall, the plaster parting around it like water around a hand, leaving no mark, no trace, nothing.

He woke Tesfaye.

They sat in the van in the car park and reviewed the footage for four hours without speaking except to say there, go back, there. What they had caught was extraordinary. One clip: the creature crouched directly behind Tesfaye while he adjusted a tripod, its face an inch from the back of his neck, its expression one of pure and unhurried study, like a scientist who has found a specimen worth examining. Another: it beneath the bed, lying flat, looking up through the mattress slats. Another: climbing the bedpost with four-limbed, insectile patience and lowering its face to within centimeters of Daniel’s, examining him with an intimacy that made his stomach turn.

Then Tesfaye found the clip from the window-facing camera.

He watched it twice. Then he said: “Daniel. Come and look at this.”

The timestamp read 3:17. The night-vision image was green and clear. In the middle of the room, in front of the window, there was a figure.

It was a young woman in a nightdress, braided hair, standing with her back to the camera. She was translucent, shivering in and out of visibility like a candle in wind. Her posture was rigid. Her hands were at her sides and her fists were clenched so hard the knuckles showed even through the green-grey grain of the footage.

Behind her, descending from the ceiling with a terrible unhurried grace, came the pale woman.

What happened over the next four minutes neither of them could describe accurately afterward. They would say only that it was not violent. That violence would have been easier. What the creature did to the translucent girl was more intimate than violence, and more complete, and the sounds it made while it worked — a low, rhythmic, almost musical sound that the directional microphone had captured in extraordinary detail — were the sounds of something deeply, privately satisfied.

When it was finished, it turned to the camera.

Its face had changed. It wore a face now that Daniel recognized from the photographs the university had provided. It wore Anna’s face with the red eyes kept in place, burning behind her features like coals behind a mask, and it raised one finger — too long, too many knuckles — and pressed it to its lips.

Then it moved toward the camera.

The lens filled with open throat, with the red wet dark of the inside of its mouth, and from the speakers came the lullaby — low, wet, patient — and the footage went to static.

In the van, the temperature dropped eight degrees in eleven seconds. Tesfaye’s phone recorded it.

The locks engaged on all four doors with a single, synchronised clunk.

The interior lights went out.

From the back seat — the empty back seat, which both men had checked before getting in — came a sound. Soft. Rhythmic. Like fingernails walking across upholstery.

Then the smell: copper and damp earth and something beneath both, something intimate and patient and very old.

And then her voice. Anna’s voice — not the creature wearing it, but something that had learned the voice by listening too long, which was worse — speaking from the darkness of the back seat in a register just below a whisper:

“You see me now.”

Neither man moved.

The breathing started.

Slow, deliberate, close enough to feel as warmth on the back of the neck.

The van did not move. The locks did not disengage. The night outside was perfectly still, and the eucalyptus trees stood dark against the orange haze of the city, and the women’s hostel rose behind them with all its lights off except for one window on the top floor — Room 9 — where a pale shape was pressed against the glass, watching the car park with its red eyes, its breath fogging the glass, its hand flat against the pane.

Waiting, the way it always waited.

With all the time in the world.

They found the men at dawn, still in the van, unable to speak. The footage still existed. The camera had not been damaged. The recording ran to its end.

The investigators from the university who reviewed the footage three weeks later watched it in a conference room with fluorescent lights and eight people present, in full daylight, and when the clip from the window camera reached its final minute, two of them stood up and left the room and did not come back.

A third — a woman who had studied folkloric demonology for twenty years and believed herself to be beyond surprise — sat and watched until the very last frame.

The creature had come back. After the footage had apparently ended, after the static had filled the screen, the static had cleared for seven seconds. Seven seconds of clear, sharp night-vision footage, and in those seven seconds the creature was in the center of the room.

It was not on the ceiling.

It was standing.

Upright. Still. Its red eyes directed at the lens with an attention so precise it felt like it could travel through the screen, through the years, through the conference room’s fluorescent air.

In its arms, it held something.

Something small. Something that had once been a shape — that still bore the outline of a shape — but that had been reduced to filament, to thread, to the exhausted remnants of something that had been fed on for too long.

The demonologist watched the creature hold its small, diminished burden, and she recognised — though it made no sense, though she had no framework for it — an expression on the creature’s ruined face.

It was not hunger.

It was not cruelty.

It was tenderness.

And that — more than anything else, more than the red eyes and the pale skin and the impossible ceiling-walk and the violation and the lullaby and the voice in the back seat of the van — that was the thing that drove her from the room.

The room is still sealed. The number plate is still missing from the door. A new intake of students arrived this semester. One of them, a first- year biology student, sharp-tongued and raised on a diet of modern rationalism, has been asking about the empty room on the top floor. She says she’s heard about it. She says she’s not afraid.

chapters.title: KUCHISAKE-ONNA
chapters.text:
WARNING — PASS QUIETLY

Something that circulates the way old buildings keep their damp

KUCHISAKE-ONNA

Japan keeps its dead the way old buildings keep their damp — silently, structurally, in the grain of everything. The stories circulate because stories are containers. They hold the shape of something dangerous and let people carry it at arm’s length. They give children a grammar for fear and give adults permission to dismiss what their bodies already know.

Kuchisake-onna. The Slit-Mouthed Woman. She is in the textbooks now, categorized between the river child and the red-cloaked toilet ghost, domesticated by repetition into something almost quaint. A surgical mask. A pair of scissors. A question: Am I beautiful? If you say no, she kills you. If you say yes, she reveals the wound — the mouth slit from corner to corner, healed into a permanent architectural smile — then asks again. If you say yes again, she cuts your face to match hers.

Every account ends there. The reader is left with the tidy impression that the encounter concludes, one way or another, in blood.

This is what the folklore forgot: she does not always use the scissors.

Sometimes she hands them to you.

II. THE RECORDING — EXHIBIT A — —

CCTV TRANSCRIPT / SHINJUKU SECTOR 7, CAMERA 4-C TIMESTAMP: 23:47 — 04:01 JST OPERATOR: K. ARATA, ELEVEN YEARS CONTINUOUS SERVICE

The footage begins without incident. Grayscale infrared. Rain- slicked pavement. The sodium lamp at the mouth of the alley casting its familiar wound of orange light.

She is simply there at 23:47, the way a thought is simply there — without arrival, without origin. A woman in a charcoal pencil skirt and cream blouse, heels too elegant for an empty street at midnight, hands folded with the patience of something that has waited a long time and no longer resents the waiting. Her face is covered by a standard surgical mask. She does not pace. She does not look toward any exit. She faces Camera 4- C directly, as though she knew precisely where it was before she arrived.

For four hours and fourteen minutes, she does not move.

Arata logged her at 00:03 as possible intoxicated individual or costumed performance, non-threatening, monitoring ongoing. The handwriting is controlled. He was a methodical man. The entries that follow grow shorter and more clipped in the way of someone rationing language because something in their throat has begun to close.

At 01:44: Still present. No movement. No pedestrian contact. Wind moving leaves behind her. She does not move with it.

At 03:19: She watches the camera from different angles without moving her feet. Her head turns. She knows where all of them are.

At 03:52: She waved at me. I did not wave back.

At 04:00:00, precisely — and investigators would later note the exactness of this timestamp as physically improbable, as though the recording had been edited to land on a clean number — she reached into her coat.

The scissors were old. Narrow. The camera was cheap and the footage grainy, yet the blades caught the lamplight with a quality that seemed wrong for the medium, too precise, too three-dimensional, as though they occupied a different layer of reality than the rest of the scene.

She lowered the mask.

The first reviewing analyst — a woman named Hara, seventeen years with the forensic unit — described what she saw in her deposition and then immediately requested reassignment. The mouth had been slit from corner to corner. The wound was healed, or the wound was the face now, the skin fused into permanence, the smile too wide to belong to any creature that had made peace with being alive. The lips parted and she mouthed a question. The camera’s audio channel produced what the technical report called a low- frequency resonance below the threshold of conscious hearing, but registering as physical pressure in 91% of review subjects.

The images across all active monitors at 04:00 fragmented into three simultaneous frames: the pavement, a close-up of the mouth, and — investigators returned to this detail repeatedly in subsequent reports — a live reflection of the security booth’s interior. Of Arata’s chair. Of the back of Arata’s head, leaning toward the screen.

She was not looking at the camera. She was looking at him looking at her.

The log ends at 04:01. The chair was empty when morning shift arrived. On the desk, a cup of coffee steamed with an impossible freshness, as though it had been poured thirty seconds ago, not four hours. The morning guard, a man named Seo, touched the cup and described it in his incident report as wrongly warm. He used that phrase twice. He did not drink it.

III. WHAT THE BODY CONFIRMED AND WHAT IT DID NOT — —

Arata was found in the building bathroom at 07:19. The positioning was supine, the expression consistent with someone who had sat down calmly and then been stopped mid-thought. His mouth had been opened past its anatomical range and held there by three surgical retractors embedded in the jawline with a precision that the forensic pathologist — choosing her words with visible discomfort — described as not frantic. Not angry. Practised.

There was no foreign DNA. No third-party fingerprints. No evidence of forced building entry. No footprints that did not belong to staff.

His wife was arrested within forty-eight hours, charged within the week. The case had the awful tidiness of certainty: her prints on the shears, a history of documented marital conflict, a neighbor who testified to hearing her voice through the shared wall at 3:47 AM, repetitive, rhythmic, the same phrase cycling. The audio from the building’s intercom was recovered and reviewed. It was not her voice. The analysts agreed on this and then disagreed about what to do with the agreement. The voice on the intercom spoke in an Edo-period Tokyo dialect not used in living memory, and it asked, forty-four times, am I beautiful, and on the forty-fifth iteration the inflection shifted — not in distortion but in awareness, curving upward with the specific quality of a question that already knows it’s being heard.

His wife was convicted. She is still serving her sentence. She says she woke on her couch with her hands smelling of iron and has not been able to smell anything else since.

— — IV. THE SECOND GUARD — WHAT HE FOUND, AND WHAT FOUND HIM

Three days after the incident, Officer Tanaka conducted a secondary review of all archived footage. He was thorough. He found what Arata had not had time to report: that Camera 4-C had been on extended night-mode, and as the sun rose, the lens flared and the figure dissolved — not by walking away, not by stepping out of frame, but by being resolved by light, the pixels resetting in a single frame the way a buffer clears. He pulled the raw binary file and decompiled it. He found a second audio track encoded at 18 Hz, subsonic, beneath conscious hearing. He described it in his notes as a question folded into itself. Wet breath and blade-edge. The syllables rearrange when you look away from the page.

He wrote the words down. He looked at the page. The words had changed.

His final notation: She doesn’t haunt the street. She haunts the watching. Every camera is a door. The more we record, the more precisely she learns to step through. I have been in this archive for fifty-one hours. The coffee on the desk was cold when I arrived. It is no longer cold. I did not make fresh coffee. The door is locked from the outside. I did not lock it. The monitor shows a woman standing behind my chair.

I’m not going to turn around. The folklore says: tell her she looks average. Maa maa. Neither beautiful nor ugly. They call this the escape. Every surviving account names it as the exit.

There are no surviving accounts. I understand this now. The “average” answer isn’t an escape. It’s an inheritance. You say the word and she hands you the scissors. You wake up on a street corner three nights later with a new, specific hunger. Your smile becomes something you have to consciously contain. Your reflection starts to drag. Within a week you’re standing on an empty pavement under a lamp, asking a stranger who walks alone at night the most dangerous question ever spoken. She doesn’t want to kill you. She wants a replacement. She wants to go home. The loop doesn’t end with the answer. The loop IS the answer.

Tanaka’s session terminated at 04:00:00. The audio recovered from his recording device runs for 0.4 seconds. The transcript reads: Kirei da.

Beautiful.

V. WHAT THE MIRROR KNOWS — —

Detective Mase reviewed the complete file three weeks before he stopped filing anything at all. His personal notes, recovered from his home office, end mid-sentence on a Thursday and resume — in a different pressure of handwriting, a different grip — on a Sunday, with a single line:

The answer was always the wrong question. She doesn’t ask if she is beautiful. She asks if you can see her. The moment you confirm it — yes, no, average, any word that proves you perceive her — she can come closer. She lives in the space between the observer and

the observed. She is the reason the air in empty rooms feels occupied. She is the reason you check over your shoulder on midnight trains. She is the reason, right now, that you glanced up from this page. You felt it. The warm pressure at the back of the neck. The half-second where the room behind you felt rearranged. You told yourself it was nothing. The building settling. The heating system. The ordinary dark being its ordinary self. You were almost right. She doesn’t need to stand on the street anymore. She learned long ago that the street was inefficient. Footage spreads further. Documents travel. Stories are read alone, at night, by people who think they are safe because they are only reading. Every eye is a door. You are behind the glass. And she has been standing on the other side of it, patient as weather, since the moment you started reading — tilting her head with almost tender curiosity, watching you watch her, waiting for the exact moment you feel compelled to prove to yourself that none of this is real. She’ll ask you now. Not from a speaker. Not from a monitor. From the particular silence that has been sitting behind your left shoulder for the last four minutes. Are you beautiful? CASE FILE 口-19 IS HEREBY SEALED. ALL PHYSICAL EVIDENCE HAS BEEN CATALOGUED AND DESTROYED. THE COFFEE CUP WAS NEVER LOGGED INTO EVIDENCE. IT WAS STILL WARM WHEN THEY FOUND IT. IT IS STILL WARM NOW.

PASS IT ON PASS IT ON PASS IT ON PASS IT ON PASS IT ON PASS IT ON PASS IT ON PASS IT ON

chapters.title: Kishi
chapters.text:
STREET NAME WITHHELD — 4th RE-DESIGNATION

Lagos — a street the council has renamed four times

In the heart of the most expensive city in Africa, there is a street that the municipal maps have tried to name four times. The council assigns it a number, plants the signage in fresh concrete, and within a fortnight the sign is always gone. Not vandalized. Not stolen. Simply absent, as though the street itself swallowed the plaque in the night and ground it down. Locals call it Rua do Esquecimento — the Street of ForgetÝng — because that is what it does to you. Not your memories. Not your mind. Something smaller and more essential than either of those. It forgets you. It takes the version of yourself you walked in with and it keeps her, and it sends back something that still answers to your name.

The grandmothers in the Sambizanga market do not let their granddaughters walk that road after dusk.

When the girls ask why, the grandmothers do not tell the story directly. They tell it sideways. They say: there was once a woman who crossed that street and came home and everything looked exactly the same and smelled exactly the same and her mother held her face and kissed her forehead and said thank God, thank God you are safe. And the woman smiled with all her teeth.

They say: that was not the same woman.

Amara Nzinga was thirty-one years old and she did not believe in the grandmothers.

She was a structural engineer at a Luanda firm whose glass tower reflected the Atlantic in the mornings like a boast. She believed in load-bearing calculations, in tensile strength, in the PSI of reinforced concrete. She had a university

degree, a corner apartment in the Maianga district, and a talent for dismissing things that could not be measured. Her colleague Dora had told her, more than once, not to cut through the Rua do Esquecimento after dark.

“It is a thirty-year-old urban legend,” Amara had said, laughing. “The only thing on that street is a broken lamp and someone’s bored imagination.”

She cut through it on a Thursday evening in March, because the trafÏc on the main boulevard had stalled and she was already late and she was not a woman who feared a road.

The broken lamp had been repaired. That was the first wrong thing — she had reported it six months ago and heard nothing. Now it burned perfectly, too perfectly, with a steadiness that felt less like electricity and more like intention. The cobblestones sweated a cold that climbed through the soles of her heels and up the bones of her shins. She smelled turned earth beneath the diesel and the salt. She smelled something darker than either, something that lived underneath smell itself, the way rot lives underneath sweetness before the sweetness knows it is dying.

She quickened her pace.

She heard the laugh from the shadows to her left. Not a laugh, precisely. The origin of one — a wet, short sound that understood halfway through what it was becoming and closed its mouth before it finished. She did not look toward it. She looked straight ahead and counted her steps and told herself: drunk man, tired man, a man laughing at his phone.

She did not look back.

But she already knew — in the part of her body that lived below reason, in the spine, in the marrow — that something on that road had found her interesting.

His name was Tomás.

He arrived on Monday morning the way inevitabilities arrive: quietly, wearing a pressed white shirt, carrying a folder of architectural drawings he said required her professional review. He had been hired on a short-term consulting contract, he explained. The HR ofÏce had processed his paperwork the

previous week. He had a firm handshake and a voice that carried a soft hinterland accent, musical and unhurried, the kind of voice that made you feel the conversation was already halfway to trust.

She showed him to a spare desk.

She said yes on Friday when he asked about a good lunch spot. She said yes the Friday after when he suggested the seafood restaurant on the Ilha. He had a gift for appearing precisely when something was needed — a second pair of eyes on a load calculation, a hand holding the elevator — and never once pushed past what was welcome. He existed in the margins of her day with the quality of something that had always been there.

“You’re always in the right place,” she told him, three weeks in, meaning it as a compliment.

He looked at her and smiled and said: “I know where I’m needed.”

Dora told the women in the kitchen that she had searched for him on every platform she could find and he existed nowhere — no face in any photograph, no digital presence, no trail. She said she had walked past him in the corridor on Wednesday and felt cold for the rest of the afternoon without knowing why. She said the back of his neck was always covered: high collars, close-trimmed hair, a particular way of holding his shoulders that drew attention to his face and away from what was behind it.

The other women said Dora was dramatic.

Amara heard none of this. She was already dreaming of the hyena.

The dream came every night with the precision of a scheduled event.

A firelit circle. The savanna spreading black and enormous in every direction. At the edge of the firelight, the hyena sat with the patience of something that had never learned urgency because urgency had never been necessary. It had a human face, symmetrical and composed and almost tender, watching her the way certain people watch a meal they have been anticipating for a very long time. Around it, pale shapes gleamed in the grass. Not stones. The bones of small things, picked entirely clean.

She told no one about the dreams.

What she told herself was that she was sleeping poorly because of a deadline, because of the noise from the construction site one block over, because of the inexplicable new habit she had developed of waking at three in the morning and standing at her bathroom mirror for minutes at a time, studying her own face with the bewildered intensity of a woman who is no longer certain it is entirely hers.

Tomás brought her coffee one Tuesday without being asked and placed it on her desk, and she looked at him — truly looked, not the casual glancing she had grown accustomed to — and felt something old and unplaceable move in her chest. Not desire. Something beneath desire. The feeling of a word on the tip of the tongue that the tongue has always known.

I know you , she thought. From somewhere I cannot name.

She thanked him for the coffee and went back to her calculations.

He asked her to dinner on a Thursday.

Not his apartment — a restaurant near the old fort, white tablecloths, candles in glass, the kind of place that made the city’s violence feel very far away. She wore a red dress. He wore a dark suit and arrived before she did and stood when she entered, and she thought: this is a good man, an ordinary good man, and the thought made her feel safe in a way that should have felt like a warning.

They drank wine. They talked for three hours. He remembered everything she had ever mentioned — the name of her mother’s village, the specific brand of instant coffee she kept in her desk drawer, a complaint she had made in passing about the broken elevator, which had since been repaired. He told her about his childhood in the interior, about dry season dust and the sound of the bush at night.

“Don’t you find it strange?” she asked, somewhere in the second hour. “That you remember so much?”

He turned his wine glass slowly. “I find it strange when people don’t,” he said. “You only get one of each person. It seems wasteful not to pay attention.”

She did not tell him about the dreams. She did not tell him about the feeling on the Rua do Esquecimento, or the laugh she had not looked toward, or the three nights she had spent at her bathroom mirror unable to articulate what it was she was looking for in her own reflection. She told herself there was nothing to tell. She told herself that was true.

He walked her home. He did not come in. He kissed her hand at her gate, precisely, and said goodnight with the unhurried certainty of a man who knew there was no need to rush.

She stood inside her door and listened to herself breathe and thought: I am very happy.

The thought felt like someone else’s.

The hunger began that week.

She would not call it hunger, at first. She called it restlessness, appetite, the city’s relentless energy translating into her nervous system. She ate more than usual and still felt hollow in a way that food was not addressing. She began craving things she had never liked: the charred edges of meat, the iron-thick aftertaste that sat at the back of the throat. She developed an acute sensitivity to sound that was almost painful — the squeal of a bus brake blocks away, the conversation of people on a floor below her apartment, the specific rhythm of a particular pigeon that sat every morning on her balcony railing and watched her through the glass with an expression of unnerving recognition.

She called her mother in Benguela. Her mother asked how she was.

“Strange,” Amara said. “I feel strange.”

“What kind of strange?”

She did not know how to say: the kind where I stand at my mirror in the dark and I cannot tell whether what is looking back is waking or dreaming. She said she was probably working too hard.

Her mother said she had always worked too hard. Her mother said she needed to find a nice man and settle down.

Amara almost said: I may have found one. She stopped herself without knowing why. The sentence sat in her mouth and she held it there for a moment and then swallowed it back down. Something about saying it aloud felt like completing a transaction she did not yet understand the terms of.

The mirror told her. The way mirrors in Luanda eventually tell women everything they need to know.

It was a Tuesday evening, Tomás at her table with palm wine and the remains of a dinner she had cooked, Bossa Nova low on the speaker, the Luanda skyline pouring its gold through the window. He had his back to her while she cleared plates, and she glanced toward the large mirror she had bought at a market in Benguela — the one with the wide gilded frame that leaned against her bedroom wall, visible from the kitchen doorway.

His reflection was a half-second behind him.

Not much. Not enough for certainty. When she looked directly at the mirror the delay resolved and everything appeared normal, but in her peripheral vision it persisted: the reflection moving through its gestures just after the body had finished them, like a translation arriving late.

She set down the plates very carefully.

She said nothing.

That night, lying awake at four in the morning with his steady breathing beside her, Amara stared at the ceiling and understood that the hollow hunger she had felt all week was not restlessness. It was not appetite. It was the specific and precise sensation of something inside her that had been waiting for decades — waiting for the right host, the right crossing, the right month — beginning at last to wake up.

She rose and went to the bathroom mirror.

She stood there for a long time.

She leaned in close and turned her head slowly and looked at the back of her own neck.

She began researching.

University archives. Microfilmed copies of Diário de Luanda from the 1970s. She sat in a reading room that smelled of degrading acetate and fed reels through the viewer until she found it: the murders that had earned their killer the nickname O Kishi. A young Angolan woman found in an alley, throat chewed open, neck torn as if by animal jaws. The colonial authorities had barely noted it. She was a person of colour in a city administered by men who measured suffering by proximity to their own. Then a Portuguese woman. Throat slit, parts of the abdomen consumed. A dusk-to-dawn curfew. More than a dozen women dead in locked houses over a single month. No entry points. No forced windows. Just bodies, and the particular wounds, and a low growling that witnesses reported hearing from behind closed doors.

One survivor. A single-column article dated 1974. A woman who had let a charming intern stay the night because the curfew was approaching and he lived far and she had felt sorry for him. A nice young man. Attentive. The kind who remembered your coffee order. The kind who stood when you entered a room. She had gone to the kitchen to prepare tea and he had asked, from the living room, in a voice that was already changing: have you heard of the Kishi? She had barricaded the kitchen door. The growling lasted until dawn. When police searched for the intern the next day, he did not exist. No record. No contract. No one in the ofÏce could clearly recall his face.

Amara read the article three times.

She drove home in the dark and sat in her parked car for a long time before she went upstairs.

She told herself it was coincidence. She told herself the city was full of charming men and charming men were not monsters. She told herself the delay in the mirror’s reflection had been the wine, the angle of the candle, the particular vulnerability of a woman who had been sleeping badly for three weeks.

She bought a knife. She kept it under the mattress on her side.

What she did not account for was the gentleness. That was the architecture of it — not the terror but the tenderness, the specific, attentive, perfect tenderness that made the knife feel melodramatic, made her suspicion feel like madness, made the alternative explanation (he is simply a good man, a genuinely good man, and you are destroying something rare because of an old woman’s story) feel more and more like the only sane position. He brought her frangipani blossoms. He fixed the shelf she had been meaning to fix for months. He said, one evening, looking out at the Atlantic with his hand warm over hers: I have been waiting for someone like you for a very long time.

She heard it both ways.

The night she killed him was a Friday.

She had been watching his neck for weeks. The careful collars. The particular way he turned his shoulders. There had been an evening when he bent to pick up a book she had dropped, and in the amber light of the floor lamp she had seen the skin at his nape move — not flinch, not shift with muscle, but move with the slow deliberate pressure of something beneath it trying to open its eyes. She had closed hers and when she opened them his collar was up and he was smiling at her and the book was in his hand.

That Friday she served dinner and refilled his glass and when he turned to look at the window she rose from the table and retrieved the knife from the drawer where she had moved it in anticipation of exactly this moment. She thought she was ready. She had rehearsed the reasoning: the archive articles, the mirror delay, the impossible tenderness, the way his consultancy contract had materialized from nowhere and could be traced to nothing, the dreams, the hunger, the three a.m. hours at the bathroom mirror. She had assembled a case. She believed it.

She drove the knife between his shoulder blades before he could turn around.

He made a sound she had not prepared for. Not a growl. Not an inhuman cry. A human sound, shocked and breaking, the sound of a man who has been in the middle of an ordinary thought and suddenly finds himself in extraordinary

pain. He fell and she stood over him and waited for the second face, for the hyena jaw to tear through the skin of his nape, for the creature to reveal itself in its final desperate moment.

Instead he bled.

He bled in the specific and irreversible way that living bodies bleed when they are dying. He reached for her wrist with one hand, not to harm, not with anything more in the grip than a drowning man’s reflex, and he looked up at her with eyes that were only eyes — brown, wet, bewildered, and diminishing.

“Why,” he said.

One word. No second sentence.

Amara stood over his body until the blood reached the leg of her chair and she could no longer feel her hands. Then she went to the bathroom because the body demanded it. She gripped the sides of the sink and breathed and raised her eyes to the mirror.

She saw herself. Sweat-slicked. Gaunt. The red dress. The knife on the tiles behind her.

She saw herself turn her head.

She saw what lived behind her own hair.

It had been there the whole time — she understood that with the terrible clarity of a diagnosis that explains every symptom you have been describing to yourself as something else. The hollow hunger. The three a.m. mirror vigils, which had not been investigation but checking in, the way you check a wound to see how it is healing. The delay in the mirror’s reflection had not been his. It had been hers. She had seen it in her peripheral vision and constructed an explanation that pointed away from herself because the alternative was this: the long muzzle pushing through the dark curtain of her hair, the slow opening of a second jaw, the yellow eyes with their slit pupils turning lazily in their deep sockets to look at her through the glass.

The Kishi did not live behind the face of a man.

It lived behind the face of the woman who feared him.

The street had not marked her as prey. The crossing, the cold in the cobblestones, the laugh from the shadows — those had been a door opening. Not for him to enter her life. For her to enter his inheritance. The charming, patient, endlessly gentle man who had appeared on Monday morning had been exactly what he seemed: a man. A real man. An innocent man who had loved her with something genuine and impractical, and who had walked behind her along the Rua do Esquecimento six weeks ago and felt nothing because the street had not chosen him.

The street had chosen her.

The first victim in the 1974 archive had not been the women. It had been the intern who asked have you heard of the Kishi? — the real man, the innocent man, the man who meant well and was in the wrong place on the wrong night and who had been asked to stay for tea by a woman who had crossed the street two weeks before. The survivor who barricaded herself in the kitchen had not been saved by her barricade. She had been saved because she had not yet finished becoming what the crossing had started making her. The cycle had skipped a generation. Found someone new.

Found Amara.

She gripped the sink and breathed. Behind her, from the tiled floor, she heard the last sounds Tomás would ever make. She heard herself make sounds she did not authorize. The hunger that had lived in her chest for three weeks was no longer waiting.

The police found him on Saturday morning after the building’s security guard noticed the light in her apartment had been on all night.

They did not find Amara.

They found the knife. They found the blood, which had spread in a radius that a forensic examiner would later describe in measured, clinical language that still could not account for the portions that were missing. They found her phone, her keys, her university degree in its frame on the wall.

They found the Benguela mirror, its gilded frame facing the wall. Someone had turned it around.

There is a woman who stands on the Rua do Esquecimento on certain evenings now. She stands beneath the lamp that burns with its steadiness that feels less like electricity than purpose. She is beautifully dressed. She is attentive. When a man passes, she does not accost him, does not call out. She only looks, and her looking has a quality that men describe later, to their wives and their friends, as warmth — inexplicable, immediate warmth, like being recognized by someone who has been waiting for you specifically.

Some of them stop.

Some of them turn back.

The ones who turn back are the ones who notice that when she moves, the shadow she casts is a half-second behind her. The ones who turn back are the ones who glimpse, as she raises her head, the particular density of darkness at the back of her expensive hairstyle — a darkness that breathes.

The ones who do not turn back follow her home because she smiles at them with the specific, earnest, guileless tenderness of a woman who simply cannot believe her luck.

Luanda is still the most expensive city in Africa.

The oil money still pours down the glass towers. The Atlantic still puts its salt into everything. The grandmothers in the Sambizanga market still pull their granddaughters close when they pass a certain street, and the girls still roll their eyes because they are young and educated and do not believe in the things the grandmothers know.

The Rua do Esquecimento has been renamed again. The sign lasted eleven days this time. Then it was gone.

The street has its own name. It does not require anyone else’s.

In the police archives, there is a case file for a man named Tomás — no family name, no prior address, no consultancy contract that can be verified — who was found murdered in an apartment in the Maianga district, whose wounds

the forensic ofÏce classified as consistent with large predator attack before the classification was quietly revised to something more bureaucratically manageable. The file is thin. The investigating ofÏcer noted, in handwriting rather than the standard typed form, a single observation he did not include in the ofÏcial report:

We found no evidence of forced entry. We found no evidence that the woman who lived there was afraid of what killed him. The mirror was turned to face the wall. This is done, in the old tradition, when something has changed in the house. When what sleeps in the bed is not what went to sleep.

The file has not been reopened.

On the street, the lamp burns on.

chapters.title: Jatinga Bird Suicide
chapters.text:
EM SENSOR ARRAY · 3.6 0.6 3.4 3.5 3.3 2.1 · ANOMALY FLAGGED

Dr. Meera Varma · Bombay Natural History Society — filed, not published

The first entry in Dr. Meera Varma’s field journal reads like the opening of a paper she would never publish.

September 14th. Arrived Jatinga 1600 hrs. Fog expected after sundown per local accounts. Equipment calibrated. Electromagnetic sensors placed along the ridge at 200m intervals. Ready to document. The phenomenon has a rational explanation. I intend to find it.

The last entry, written seven weeks later in handwriting that does not belong to her, reads as follows:

The mouth is too small to swallow. That is the design of it. Hunger without relief. That is the punishment. But I am not the prisoner. I am the door. And a door does not hunger. A door simply opens.

There are forty-one entries between those two. Each one is darker than the last. Taken together, they constitute a document that the Bombay Natural History Society has quietly classified as a case of severe psychological decompensation under field conditions. They have filed it. They have not published it.

This is what the file contains.

Week One.

She counted thirty-seven carcasses before her tally grew meaningless.

Pond herons. Bee-eaters. A green pigeon with its neck wrung wrong by impact, one eye still bright with the residue of whatever it had been flying toward. The village of Jatinga occupied a spur of the North Cachar Hills no wider than a single kilometer, pinched between valleys that vanished at dusk into white silence. The fog arrived each evening with the regularity of a tide, and the birds arrived with the fog, and the birds died, and the village collected them in baskets and laughed, and ate well, and did not mourn.

Meera did not eat well. The dal was too oily and the guesthouse smelled of damp concrete and something underneath the damp concrete — a sulfurous note, barely present, like struck iron. She attributed it to the faultlines. The geological surveys were clear enough: Jatinga sat directly above a complex of seismic fractures that radiated outward in every direction beneath the soil. The electromagnetic sensors had already registered anomalies she had not seen in any previous fieldwork. The readings spiked at dusk. They spiked when the fog thickened. And they spiked, she noted with the careful neutrality of a scientist still in control of herself, in close proximity to the bird deaths.

Disorientation, she wrote in her journal. Magnetoreception interference. The birds navigate by sensing the earth’s magnetic field. When the field distorts, they distort with it. When the lights come on in the fog, they fly toward the nearest bright point and call it north.

She believed every word of that when she wrote it.

Her guide, an elderly man named Prakash, watched her write from across the courtyard with an expression she could not parse. Not pity. Not amusement. Something more specific and worse. The look of a man watching someone make a mistake he has seen made before.

“You are writing about the birds,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You should write about what calls them.”

“The lights call them. The electromagnetic disruption—”

“The lights are not the voice,” Prakash said. “The lights are only where the voice comes from.”

She wrote that down too. Local attribution of phenomenon to a voice or entity. Common folkloric displacement of natural cause. Then she went to bed. Then she dreamed about a figure at the edge of the fog with a belly swollen drum-tight and a mouth no wider than a pinhole.

She did not write about that.

Week Two.

The kingfisher was alive when she found it.

A pied kingfisher, male, wing shattered at the carpal joint from impact with the concrete schoolhouse wall. It lay on its side in the mud, one eye turned upward. Its heart was visible through the thin skin of its throat — a frantic blue pulse. She cupped it in her gloves. Standard procedure was to assess, log, and dispatch if unrecoverable. She had done it dozens of times.

The bird looked at her, and she felt her hands go cold.

Not with fear. With recognition. A slow, unwanted certainty that something behind the bird’s eye was also looking, was also present, was also doing something that looked like recognition. She held it for too long. Her gloves were slick. The bird opened its beak. What came out was not the clicking distress call of a kingfisher. What came out was low and resonant and pressed against the back of her teeth like the bass note of a very old and very patient song.

She dropped it. It struck the ground and did not move again.

That night she found scratches on her inner left forearm. Four lines, evenly spaced, precise as measurements, carved through the skin with something narrow and curved like a talon. She had no memory of making them. She washed them in the guesthouse basin. When she dried her arm, the skin beneath the wounds had gone the color of a bruise that had been deepening for weeks, though she had not had any bruise before that moment. She stood at the basin for a very long time looking at the discoloration.

Her reflection watched her back.

Then, just once, it tilted its head when she did not.

Week Three.

The old woman had been gutting pigeons outside her door every morning since Meera had arrived. Her name was Binodini. She was ninety years old or close to it, with cataracts like river ice and hands so deft with the knife that the birds were open and cleaned before you could look away. She had never spoken to Meera directly. On the sixteenth day, she did.

“You have seen Kshudhita,” she said.

It was not a question.

Meera sat down on the step beside her. “Tell me.”

Binodini’s knife moved without pause. “A preta. A hungry ghost. It lived at the seam before anyone here was old enough to name it. It cannot eat. The mouth is too small — see?” She held up her little finger and touched the very tip. “A hole this size. But the belly is deep as a well. It is starving since before the hills had their shape. A tantric sealed it at the barrier, long ago, locked it in the fault. The stone held it.”

“What stone?”

“The black menhir. You have seen it, in the jungle where the fog does not move.” Binodini looked at Meera sideways with those white eyes. “It feeds on the moment of dying. The small flash when the soul unclenches from the body. When the birds break against the wall or the light — that instant, that flicker — Kshudhita drinks it. Not the death. The release.”

Meera said: “That’s why they come here specifically. Not just disorientation. Something is drawing them. Amplifying the effect.”

Binodini made a sound that was not quite agreement and not quite contempt. “Every year it grows stronger. Every year it needs more birds. The faultlines carry the call further. One day the birds will not be enough.” She deposited a gleaming coil of entrails into a bowl. “It is looking for a larger mouth.”

She said nothing more. Meera walked back to the guesthouse and found, tucked into the center of her field journal, a gray feather she had not placed there. Its quill was dark with something that smelled of iron.

She opened her journal to a clean page.

She wrote: The light is a throat. The fog is a tongue.

She had no memory of writing it.

Week Four.

The birds were dying in their hundreds now.

Tiger bitterns with their necks twisted back. Black drongos falling mid-flight as though their hearts had been squeezed out of them by a hand she could not see. Egrets dropping from the treetops in white cascades, their bodies hitting the earth with a sound like wet laundry. The village men collected them with bamboo poles, weaving through the carcasses efficiently, filling baskets, laughing at a harvest they had come to expect. They kept glancing at Meera. She realized, slowly, that they had stopped looking at the fog.

She had stopped eating. Food had become texture without meaning. What she found herself craving was not food at all — it was the moment she stood at her window as dusk folded into night, lips parted, that thin high whistle escaping the back of her throat involuntarily. When she made the sound, the birds outside thickened. Turned toward her window. She could feel their magnetoreception like a warmth in her own skull — the sensation of knowing exactly where north was without choosing to know, of feeling the planet’s field like a second heartbeat. She could feel the fault below the village the way you feel a bruise without pressing it. A deep and constant ache that had no surface location, seated somewhere below the stomach.

Prakash found her on the ridge one evening with no memory of climbing there.

She was standing barefoot on the black stone — the menhir, a squat mass of basalt sunk to half its height in the soil, wrapped in lichen, ringed by the unmoving fog that Binodini had described. Her arms were at her sides. Her eyes were open. Above her, forty or fifty birds were circling without making a sound — circling in a precise orbit, as though pulled by a gravity that had her at its center. Prakash stood a distance back and called her name five times before she turned.

Later, he told her what he had seen in her face.

He said her eyes had been wrong. Not rolled back. Not glazed. Simply wrong — as though the light behind them had changed color. As though someone else had briefly stood behind her face the way a person stands behind a window.

She told him he was exhausted and needed rest.

That night she woke kneeling beside the desk with all four fingers of her right hand pressed against the journal. The pen had been moving for hours. The pages were dense with writing she did not remember

producing — field notations in her precise scientific hand interspersed with other text, angular, heavy, pressing through the page like a scar:

You have been measuring the symptom. The symptom is not the phenomenon. The barrier is a wound in the world and I am what inhabits it. I have been here since before this hill was a hill. I do not call the birds because I am cruel. I call them because I am starving and they are the most sensitive thing the living world has made — small enough to feel everything, bright enough to follow sound with their whole body. They die against the walls because the walls are in the way. The walls are not the destination. I am. They would all come home to me if the skin between worlds could hold them. But it cannot hold them. Nothing crosses intact. I have been dying of thirst at the edge of a river since before your oldest gods were born. But you, Dr. Varma. You can cross. You can be the mouth I was never given.

Week Five — the final entry, in Meera’s own handwriting.

November 3rd. The fog arrived at 5 PM. I have locked the door. Prakash has gone for help. By the time he returns with anyone who will believe him, it will no longer matter. I need to write this clearly while I am still able to write it clearly. The menhir is cracked. I did not crack it intentionally. I woke this morning and found my palms bleeding where I had braced them against the stone in the night. The crack runs from the top face to the soil line, and from the crack the fog does not flow outward — it flows inward, as though the stone itself is breathing in. Binodini was at her door and would not look at me. She crossed herself with one hand and held her knife tight in the other. I understand what Kshudhita is. I have understood it for ten days. It is not evil in the way that word requires intention. It is a function. It is what happens when something that hungers is compressed into a space too small for hunger — when a force with no form is sealed into

a fault line and left there, accumulating. The birds have been dying here since before the village existed. Before the road. Before the lamp posts. The lamp posts are incidental. The fault line is incidental. Kshudhita is the cause and it is old enough to have outlasted every explanation humans have built around it. Here is what I know that none of the papers know: the birds do not fly toward the light. The birds fly toward the sound. And for the last three weeks I have been making the sound. I have been the lamp post. Outside my window the sky is dark with wings. I cannot count them. I have not been able to stop the sound in my throat since yesterday. It comes when I breathe, a frequency below hearing that I can feel in the enamel of my teeth, in the bones behind my nose. The electromagnetic sensor has been pinned at maximum since dawn. I am sitting at the desk with every light on and I am writing this with both hands because I need one hand to hold the pen and I need the other hand pressed flat against the desk so that it does not reach for the window. Kshudhita does not want to consume me. It wants to wear me. A door does not die when you open it. I can hear it now the way I can hear my own heartbeat — not as a sound from outside but as the sound that is always present inside the body, that you only notice when everything else goes quiet. It has been speaking with my own voice for days and I did not know because it learned my cadence before I thought to listen for it. It is patient. It was patient before patience was a virtue anyone had named. The birds are striking the window now. I can hear them. I have been counting without intending to — eight, eleven, seventeen — the sound of small bodies against glass, each one that terrible wet percussion, each one that brief release that feeds the thing behind my sternum. I can feel it feeding. That is the worst part. I can feel it as a satisfaction, a brief quenching, and it is not repulsive. It feels like drinking water after a very long thirst.

If you are reading this, it is because you came to explain Jatinga, and someone gave you this journal, and you have been reading it the way I read the literature before I came here — confidently, scientifically, with the comfortable conviction that you are the observer and not the observed. Stop reading here. I am not telling you this because I want to save you. I am telling you this because Kshudhita has learned something in five weeks of wearing my thoughts like a coat: it is easier to call something that is already listening. And you have been listening since the first page. Come.

They found the journal on the desk.

The window was intact. The door was locked from the inside. The electromagnetic sensors had burned out sometime before dawn, their circuits fused. Outside, spread across the courtyard and the road and the schoolhouse roof, were the bodies of four hundred and twelve birds.

No one counted them as they cleared them.

The villagers worked in silence, filling baskets, glancing at no one. The fog had retreated to the jungle where the black menhir stood, or had stood — Prakash confirmed that the stone was split cleanly at the root, a fracture so precise it might have been made by a chisel rather than a human hand.

Of Dr. Meera Varma, nothing was found except her boots, placed neatly beneath the desk, and the journal, and on the journal’s cover — pressed flat by a stone she had carried from the ridge — a single gray feather with a quill dark as old blood.

The village elder said a prayer for the birds, as was custom.

He said nothing for the doctor.

When asked why, he was quiet for a long time.

Then he said: “You do not say prayers for a door.”

In Jatinga, the birds still come every year between September and November, with the fog, in the dark, slamming into whatever the light touches. Scientists still argue about the cause. The locals still harvest them. The menhir’s stump rots slowly at the edge of the jungle.

And sometimes, when the fog is thick and the hour is late and the village is sleeping, those who are still awake hear a thin, high sound moving among the bamboo. Not the sound of wings. Not the sound of impact. A human sound. A woman’s voice, barely audible, speaking at a frequency that sits just inside the range of hearing and just below the range of language.

The birds circle for a long time before they fall.

They seem, in those final moments, to be listening.
