chapters.title: The vanishing path
chapters.text:
SEALED

being the story of a name that was stolen

Being the true record of a name that was stolen, a path that remembered, and what the jungle did with the debt of a man who would not pay it.

I · THE PRICE OF THE PATH — —

I commit this to paper not as a chronicle of discovery but as a warning dressed in confession. I write it because the dead have begun to dictate our history. I write it because maps are not drawn in ink — they are drawn in debt — and the ledger of this particular debt remains open, its columns still filling, its final sum not yet calculated, though I believe I am near enough to guess at it.

You must understand what brought us to that tangled green country. King Ramathibodi II received Duarte Fernandes at Ayutthaya with silk and elephants and the patient hospitality of a man who has learned to take the long view of visiting Europeans. Over roasted river fish, the king described a village of the long-neck women — Huai Sua Tao, high in the mountains of the north, where women wore their beauty like a burden in brass and the forest seemed to bow to their quiet strangeness. Duarte laughed when he heard of it. He loved curiosities. He loved anything that made him feel chosen by history.

The king offered guides. Duarte refused. He would find his own way. He was that kind of man.

He sent Ruy de Sousa ahead with three others to locate and clear the route. Ruy was a hard-handed scout from the Algarve — a man who mistrusted anything that could not be weighed or stabbed, a man whose laugh always came half a second too late, as though he had learned it by imitation rather than instinct. He returned two days later, alone, waving a square of bark paper, the other men not mentioned and never subsequently found.

What Ruy told us about the path he had found: that it was steep but passable, that it wound along a ridge above the treeline, that they would reach the long-necked women in a single day’s march. What he did not tell us: that the jungle had boxed him in, that the limestone ridges had refused him passage, that he had stumbled in desperation upon a leaf-thatched hut where a shaman sat grinding paste with a stone as if he had been waiting — as if he had expected precisely one frightened Portuguese scout to come stumbling out of the undergrowth at that hour.

The old man wore a coat of bird feathers. He had eyes, Ruy told me later in his mutterings, old and empty as a grave that had not yet received its body.

The shaman demanded a price that was not gold, not trade cloth, not the things Europeans understand. He asked for recognition. “When the great traveller comes,” he said in the Shan tongue Ruy half- understood, “you will speak my name before him. Tell him I am the one who unrolled the mountain for you. That is all I ask. A name before a name.”

He had asked this humbly. He pressed his palms together and bowed his head. It was a small price. An absurdly small price for a route through unmapped mountains.

They walked together along the ridgeline, the shaman pointing out marks invisible to European eyes — a bent fern, a fallen hornbill feather, a split bamboo that bled water in the correct direction. A true path emerged where before there had been only cliff and green. When Ruy had memorised it, when the shaman crouched to tie a grass knot as a final guide, Ruy drew his dagger and slid it under the old man’s ribs. He told me later the shaman did not scream. He only looked at Ruy with an expression not of horror but of profound, bottomless disappointment.

Ruy dragged the body into the thicket. He sketched a map by the light of a resin torch. He came back to us a hero in his own mind, and his hand, by his own account, did not shake once.

✦

II · WHAT THE JUNGLE KEEPS — —

We marched the next morning: sixty men, porters, soldiers, Duarte at the head in a breastplate already dark with sweat. By midafternoon we reached the narrow defile between the karst towers where Ruy’s map promised a passage. What we found was a wall of thorny acacia so dense it appeared to breathe, its vines interlaced like brass coils around elongated throats. The path was simply not there.

Ruy’s face went the colour of candle wax. He hacked at the thicket with his sword, screaming that it had been open, that he had walked it with his own feet. Duarte stared at the thorns, then at Ruy, and I watched his patience move through several stages — confusion, then a particular quality of stillness that those who knew him understood to be the most dangerous thing about him.

I walked to the edge of the undergrowth and pressed my hand flat against the leaves. They were cold. Not cool as shade makes leaves cool — cold as stone pulled from a river in January. In the mountains of Siam, in the dry season’s heat, the jungle wore the temperature of burial.

We lost a day circling the long way. Men grumbled. Duarte did not speak to Ruy that evening. But that night Ruy slipped out of camp alone. At dawn he staggered back with a wild light in his eyes: the path was open under moonlight. He had followed it all the way to the village and seen the long-necked women drawing water. He had proved it. He swore it.

Duarte ordered us to pack. We followed Ruy to the defile. The acacia stood exactly as before — thicker, if anything, glossy with dark sap. Duarte called Ruy a liar. Ruy fell to his knees, tore at the thorns until his arms ran red, pleading. The path was there, he insisted, clear under moonlight, the shaman had shown him — and at the word shaman, Duarte’s expression changed from fury to something colder. He had Ruy hung from the largest thorn tree at the mouth of the dead-end pass.

A short drop. A long strangulation. The scout’s boots kicked the air while the forest watched in silence. I counted four minutes. I was young enough to still count such things, still young enough to believe that numbers made the unbearable comprehensible.

The map was lost in the commotion. No one cared to retrieve it. We turned back toward the coast, the village unseen.

That, I thought, was the end of it. I was not yet old enough to understand: murder is never an end. It is a door left ajar. And something always shuffles through.

✦

III · THE HAUNTING OF DUARTE FERNANDES — —

The first thing Duarte lost was sleep. He would lie in his tent and whisper to someone I could not see. I shared his quarters as his scribe, and I heard him ask, night after night:what do you want? No voice answered that I could detect. But Duarte would flinch at the pauses, as if a cold finger were being pressed to the back of his neck, as if the silence itself were leaning down to speak.

He began to scratch at his own throat. He complained of pressure, of constriction, as though an invisible coil were tightening there — slowly, patiently, in the manner of something that has infinite time and no particular urgency. He stopped eating river fish. He stopped consulting maps. He walked the perimeter of camp at dusk and stared into the treeline with the expression of a man waiting for an appointment he had forgotten to make.

Then came the drawings.

He stole paper from my chest — fine Portuguese paper meant for correspondence with the Crown — and covered it with maps. But every map he drew was the same: a winding path that ended not in a village but in a crude figure of a hanged man, the noose drawn like a necklace, the figure’s neck stretched long and impossibly thin, bulging at the vertebrae in the manner of the brass-coiled women we had never reached. He drew it again and again, dozens of times, his fingers black with ink to the second knuckle. When I confronted him, he looked at me with eyes that had retreated far back into their sockets and said:

“He wants his name. The scout promised him a name, and he was given a blade instead. The debt has passed to me. He will not stop until I speak it.”

“Then speak it,” I urged him.

“I don’t know it,” Duarte hissed. “Ruy killed him before he gave it. The only man who heard that name is dead. The name is lost.”

That was the horror that coiled around us like the brass spirals on those distant women’s necks. The shaman had asked for a single, simple currency — recognition. But Ruy, in his murder, had erased the name from the earth. The debt could never be paid. The path could never be appeased. And so it came for Duarte by inches: a psychological maceration that turned a great explorer into a shivering thing that begged the dark for a word it could not pronounce.

He dreamt of a road made of ribs. He told me this one morning with the flat affect of a man reporting the weather. He said the ribs were arranged too neatly to be anything but deliberate. He said the shaman walked ahead of him on this road, carrying his own severed head under one arm like a lantern, and the lantern lit the path but Duarte could never close the distance between them, no matter how fast he walked. In every dream the shaman turned at some point and the severed head opened its eyes and its mouth shaped a word — the same word, always the same word — and Duarte woke before it was spoken, gasping, reaching for a pen to write down what he had not quite heard.

He also dreamt of the long-neck women. They stood in a line at the village edge, their brass coils catching moonlight, their faces carrying the still, impersonal attention of witnesses. In every dream they were not women at all, but judges. Or perhaps the future itself, looking

back at him from a position of complete knowledge, patient in the way that only the future can be patient — which is to say, without any patience at all, because it has already happened, and he was merely catching up.

One night, anchored off the coast while we waited for a fair wind, Duarte rose from his cot and walked into the sea. The water was only knee-deep where he stopped. He stood there under a full moon, staring at the jungle onshore, and I swear the moon-glitter on the waves arranged itself into the shape of a path — a silver road on the water leading straight into the mangroves. Duarte raised one hand as if greeting someone he had long expected. Then he walked forward, and the water swallowed him by degrees, and the splash barely disturbed the men sleeping on deck. By the time I raised the alarm he was gone.

We never found his body. Not then. Not ever. Only, some weeks later, at the mountain’s foot where we had made our first camp, one of the local porters found a piece of fine Portuguese paper pressed flat against a stone. On it was drawn the same map Duarte had drawn a hundred times — the winding path, the hanged figure, the neck stretched impossibly long. But this version had something the others did not: at the head of the path, where a cartographer would mark the point of origin, Duarte had written a single word in his careful scholarly hand. The word was in no language any of us could identify. The porter refused to touch the paper. He said it was a name.

✦

IV · THE GEOLOGIST · FIVE CENTURIES ON — —

They will come again. They always come again.

Men with instruments instead of swords. With satellite images instead of bark paper maps. One of them — a professor, a careful rational man, trained to read the earth’s memory in stone and

stratigraphy — will see a line in the mountain from far above, a thread of different green against the green, a seam in the rock that runs too straight for geology. He will feel in his chest the particular excitement of a man about to find something that does not wish to be found. He will not recognise this feeling for what it is. He will call it intellectual curiosity. He will write a grant proposal.

His name is Dr. Marcus Vaz. He will wait for days at the mountain’s foot and see nothing. The path will not appear. The jungle will offer only mud and mosquito hum and the ordinary beautiful indifference of an old forest. He will grow impatient. He will question the villagers. And an old woman will look at him with the expression the shaman must have worn when Ruy came stumbling through the undergrowth — the expression of someone who has been waiting for a specific person for a very long time — and she will explain the sacrifice.

Not blood. Not the kind of price Europeans imagine when they hear the word sacrifice. The price is recognition. The sacrifice is to speak, before you enter, the name of the one who first found the way. To say aloud:this passage was found by the one who watches the path. I know this. I will not pretend otherwise. That is all. That has always been all.

Dr. Vaz will watch the women of the long-neck lineage remove their brass coils and lay them in a spiral on the pale limestone slab at the mountain’s foot. He will watch the oldest among them — a woman whose neck seems to float above her shoulders as though gravity has agreed to make an exception for her — lean forward and whisper a single word into the brass. The sound will be like a wet finger circling a glass rim. His scientific vocabulary will dissolve on his tongue.

The moonlight will thicken. The air will taste of copper and old rain. And where the limestone had been blank and impassable, a path will open — a smooth ribbon of pale stone winding upward into the dark,

its edges laced with flowering vines that had not existed an instant before. Not a trick of light. A concession of reality. A wound reopening.

He will step onto it. Of course he will step onto it. He is that kind of man.

A few metres in, where the track curves around a karst spire, he will see them.

Two figures. One wears the rags of a sixteenth-century Portuguese seaman, his neck broken and lolling at an angle that rests his chin on his own shoulder blade, a noose of flowering vine still cinched tight. The other is grander, older — a velvet doublet rotted to black lace, a face that is a mask of exhaustion and eternal supplication. Duarte Fernandes, or what the mountain has made of him. His neck has elongated grotesquely, each vertebra bulging against the parchment of his skin, brass-coloured ligaments visible in the moonlight. He has been walking the path for five hundred years. He is one name short of the end of it. He holds out his hand and in his palm is a map, rolled tight, and Dr. Vaz will recognise the map because the shape of the route is the same shape as a noose.

And beside them — calm, and small, and utterly still — stands the shaman. He wears no brass. His neck is ordinary. He simply looks at the professor, and his mouth moves, and though no sound arrives, the question forms fully inside the professor’s skull, in a language he has never learned and yet understands completely:

What is my name?

The professor will not know it. No one will have told him the secret word. He will stumble backward, the path dissolving under his heels, and he will run all the way back to the longhouse and the villagers will find him at dawn with both hands wrapped around his own throat, trying to loosen something that is not there.

He will feel it from that morning forward. A tightness. A promise of elongation. He will write a paper — a celebrated paper, published in three languages — about the geomorphology of disappearing karst routes and the oral preservation of sacred geography among the Kayan people. In the acknowledgements, almost as an afterthought, he will write:and to the unnamed shaman of Huai Sua Tao, whose knowledge made everything possible.

He will not know why he wrote that. He will feel, for weeks afterward, that the words came through his hand from somewhere else. He will re-read the acknowledgements before the paper goes to press and consider removing them, and then he will feel the tightness in his throat tighten further, and he will leave the words where they are.

He will become, like Duarte, a man who looks slightly past everything — a man quietly aware of the second world arranged just behind the first. He will not sleep well. He will tell himself it is the altitude, the excitement of discovery, the change of water. He will lie in hotels and university residences and the homes of colleagues and stare at ceilings with eyes that have retreated far back into their sockets.

He will never fully arrive at any destination after that night. Not in the way he used to arrive. He will always feel, just at the threshold of wherever he has come to, that something is following — not with hostility, not with hunger, but with the patient incurious attention of something that has seen a very large number of men walk through a very particular place and has learned that most of them do not finish what they start.

✦

V · WHAT THE SCRIVENER KNOWS — —

I am what remains of this particular story. An aide who witnessed the geometry of damnation. I have filled seven books with this account. The beginning is always the same. The ending changes slightly each time, as though the story is still looking for a version it finds acceptable.

It has not found one.

Let me tell you what I have come to understand in the years since we left that coast, since the night I stood on the deck of the Santa Catarina and watched my master walk into the sea: the shaman does not punish. This is the essential and most terrible thing. He does not torment or drive men mad or extract revenge in the manner of the stories that will be told about him. He does nothing at all. He sits in the place where he was left, in his coat of bird feathers, on the path between the karst towers, and when men pass — all the men, in all the centuries remaining to this world — he turns to watch them go.

And they feel it. Every one of them, from the moment they are given what they came for. They feel the weight of being watched by something that does not blink, does not tire, does not forgive because it does not need to forgive — because the debt is not a matter of feeling. It is a matter of arithmetic. One name was owed. No name was paid. The balance remains. The ledger stays open. The jungle keeps its accounts with the patience of geography, which is to say: forever.

Ruy stole the credit and lost the map and lost his life. Duarte carried the debt home inside him like a stone in his chest and did not survive the sea voyage. I have carried the witnessing — and perhaps the

witnessing is its own form of debt, perhaps to watch a thing clearly and record it carefully is to become implicated in it, to have the story crawl inside you and put down roots.

Some nights I feel my own throat lengthening in the dark, vertebrae pulling apart like pulled taffy. I know what it means. I have known for years. I press my palms to the floor of my cabin and feel the grain of the wood and I breathe until the feeling passes. It always passes. But each time it takes longer than the time before.

I have dreamt of Duarte. He appears at the end of a long road and I understand without being told that the road is the path, that I am approaching the village, that I am closer than any of us ever came in life. Duarte stands at the point where the road curves. He turns to face me. He is not what the sea made of him, not what five centuries of walking will make of him — he is as he was, my master, the man I served, the man who sat at the head of a table in Ayutthaya and laughed because a king had offered him a wonder. He opens his mouth.

He says:do not follow the road into the future. It is only the past, returning to collect its dead.

I wake before I can ask him what he means. Though I think I already know.

The path to Huai Sua Tao does not disappear. It waits. It remembers. It measures, with a geographer’s precision, the distance between a man’s boots and his conscience. The route was never lost — it was merely waiting for the proper body, the proper debt, the proper time. Every expedition that follows, every eye that studies the satellite image, every foot that steps onto that hidden road, only feeds the same ancient hunger. They will think they have discovered something. They will not understand that it has only decided to be seen.

And somewhere on the path, between the first karst tower and the last, Duarte Fernandes is still walking. He is one name short of the village. He is one name short of rest. He walks in the space between recognition and erasure, between the past that demands a voice and the future that has not yet agreed to listen, and his neck grows longer with each decade, the brass-coloured ligaments catching whatever light the mountain permits, and behind him, at a fixed and uncloseable distance, the shaman walks too.

Carrying his own severed head under one arm like a lantern. Lighting the way for a man who will never arrive. Patient as a path. Patient as a name waiting to be spoken by someone who will never know it. This account was found sealed in a clay jar stoppered with black wax, buried beneath the floor of a ruined spirit house at the edge of Huai Sua Tao. The jar bore no date. The wax had never dried. Beneath this final page, the journal continued for six more leaves — each one blank, save for a single phrase repeated until the ink ran out:
chapters.preview:
SEALED

being the story of a name that was stolen

Being the true record of a name that was stolen, a path that remembered, and what the jungle did with the debt of a man who would not pay it.

I · THE PRICE OF THE PATH — —

I commit this to paper not as a chronicle of discovery but as a warning dressed in confession. I write…

chapters.title: The Cold That Stays
chapters.text:
Found near Morningside Drive · transcribed verbatim

I’m dictating this into a dead man’s recorder I found near the dumpsters on Morningside Drive. If you’re hearing this, Officer, don’t look for the address. It won’t show up on any map. Search engines spin. City records skip over it like a scratched disc. I know how I sound. I know what you think when a man like me walks through that door — unwashed, shaking, talking about things that cannot be explained. But I was inside that place the whole night. And I am not the same man who walked in.

I was looking for light. That is how it starts when you have nowhere to sleep and the city has folded itself shut around you like a fist. You move through the dark with your head down, your hands in your pockets, listening for the small mercies — an open gate, a quiet corridor, a place where the security guard is bored or asleep or pretending not to see you. That night in Morningside, the roads were slick with old rain, and the wind carried the smell of damp dust, cooking oil, and something colder underneath it all. January cold. Dry Joburg cold that comes in fast after the sun goes.

Then I saw the front of the place.

At first it looked like a village — that was the trick of it. A little cluster of restaurants, all stitched together in one sprawling body, with balconies and awnings and a false warmth painted into the architecture. But the facade had a colour that did not belong to any place where people eat.Sickly ochre, or perhaps a faded coral, like the pink of a dead fish’s belly— the colour of old bruises, of water-stained bone, of something left too long in the sun and gone sick with memory. Even in the dark, the paint seemed to hold a dim light of its own, a feverish shade that made my stomach tighten the moment my eyes found it. Like a healing wound that has not healed at all. Like something infected and pretending to be well.

The sign above the entrance was half-unlit:CODFATHER VILLAGE. I remember thinking: village. Maybe some kind of indoor market. I just needed a corner to sleep in. A place the January wind wouldn’t chew through my coat.

The glass door was wedged open an inch by a chunk of brick. I slipped in.

✦ ✦ ✦

[ TRANSCRIPT CONTINUES · 02:24 hrs ]

The first thing I noticed was how clean it was. Not clean in the way rich places are clean, where everything shines and smells of lemon. Clean in the way abandoned places try to look when they are hiding their rot. The walkway swept. The tiles wiped. The glass polished. But the neatness felt staged, as if

someone had arranged it all hours earlier, expecting I would not notice the difference between order and life.

Menus on stands by the doors. Tables set with folded napkins. Chairs tucked so tightly they looked bolted to the floor. Waiter’s stations with pens aligned in perfect rows. A dining hall stretched out in perfect symmetry: booths lined with cracked vinyl, framed menus on walls advertising Italian, Thai, braai, sushi. Back in its day, they said it was the fastest- growing chain in Joburg. The restaurants offered everything. Cuisine for every hunger.

But dust didn’t fall in that place. It hovered. And nothing moved.

The first thing I felt was the silence. Not empty silence.Holding silence. Like the air itself was braced for something. And beneath the floorboards, if you stood very still, you could hear them. Not voices. Fragments. Static-laced, crackling through dead intercoms somewhere in the walls.

[ EVP · Recorded from ambient audio during site investigation · SAPS Technical Unit ]

“…register’s open…”“…table four needs water…”“… please… let us out…”“…cold. God, it’s so cold.”

I had heard the word EVP on late-night radio. I never understood what it meant until it crawled into my teeth that night.

I chose the first corridor that seemed to lead deeper into the complex. It bent left, then right, then opened into another passage lined with framed food photographs and dark windows. Every restaurant had its own face — seafood, grill, sushi, steak, pasta, white tablecloths, candlelight fittings that no longer held candles. But no matter which doorway I looked through, I caught the same feeling each time. Not emptiness.

Presence. The sensation of entering a room where someone had just turned their head away.

✦ ✦ ✦

[ TRANSCRIPT CONTINUES · 02:31 hrs ]

I passed a door with a brass number 4 hanging loose by one screw. Twenty steps later, I passed it again. Same loose 4. Same chip in the doorframe. I stopped, heart kicking, and turned around. The corridor behind me looked longer now, the ceiling lower, the walls sweating that same sick coral. I told myself I was just turned around. Tired. Hungry. I kept walking.

There were mirrors at the edges of some walls. And once I saw my own reflection and nearly cried out, because for a moment I was not alone in it. A pale shape stood just behind me in the glass, close enough that I should have felt breath on my neck. I spun around. Nothing. Only the corridor stretching away behind me. I laughed then — a small cracked sound — and said to the dark:“Alright. Fine. I’m leaving.”

I turned back the way I had come.

The corridor was gone.

Not blocked. Not changed. Gone, as if I had never entered it at all.

Ahead of me was a different hallway, narrower now, with red carpeting running down the middle like cloth laid for a funeral. I pushed through a fire door into a dining room — huge, full of round tables stacked with chairs like antlers, and a long bar at the far end. There was a chandelier that flickered once, twice, and then went steady as a heartbeat. At the corner near the window was a cashier’s desk with an old mechanical register.

And someone was sitting at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

[ TRANSCRIPT CONTINUES · 02:39 hrs ]

A figure in a dark waistcoat and tie. Head bowed. Its fingers were moving on the keys —clack-clack-clack— and the register drawer slid open with a soft ding. It counted nothing. It closed the drawer. Opened it again. I could see frost on the metal keys. A bloom of white spreading across the till like a living thing. The frost moved.

I called out. The figure’s head lifted, slow. Its face was grey-blue, the lips the colour of a sky before rain. Eyes like milky marbles. Skin dusted with ice crystals that caught the weak light from somewhere I could not identify. It looked at me without seeing, and whispered a string of numbers —

an old transaction, a transaction from another year — and then its head dropped again.Clack. Ding. Clack. Ding.

I backed out so fast I nearly fell. I pushed through a door marked Kitchen. Bright, buzzing fluorescent light. Stainless steel gleamed under dead fluorescents. A radio playing static. At the centre island: a chef in full whites, toque and all, bent over a chopping board. The knife rose and fell.Thud. Thud. Thud.

But there was nothing on the board. Just a dark stain that never dried.

The chef’s movements were jerky, wrong, like a puppet with half the strings cut.

I edged past and I swear to you — the chef paused. It turned its head, and its face was a face I half- recognised. A neighbour. A man from years ago. I couldn’t place it, the way a dream gives you a face that is and isn’t someone you know. It smiled, and the smile split its frozen cheek like lake ice cracking after a long thaw. It pointed. Toward the walk-in. Then its body dissolved, quietly, into a cloud of freezer vapor that drifted upward and vanished before it reached the ceiling.

It said, just before it went:“You came back. It’s been so cold.”

I did not know who it thought I was. I ran.

✦ ✦ ✦

[ TRANSCRIPT CONTINUES · 02:47 hrs ]

You need to understand. I tried to leave. I pushed through a swinging door into what should have been a back corridor and found myself standing in the same dining hall. The same overturned chair with the red wine stain and the splintered leg. The cashier — clack-ding, clack-ding. The room had shifted. The doors had rearranged themselves. I tried the fire exit. It opened back onto the lobby. I tried a hallway marked Toilets. It opened onto the kitchen, where the chef was now standing at the walk-in fridge, one gloved hand on the heavy steel handle, head cocked like a man listening for a sound coming from the other side.

That was when I saw the third.

A young woman. Black, like me. Wearing the restaurant’s uniform — rust-coloured apron, crisp collar, hands folded at her waist. She stood in the middle of the dining room between the tables. She was pale in a way that did not belong to the living. Not light-skinned.Unearthly pale, like marble left a long time in the dark. Her skin had the quality of wax stretched over sharp bone. Her eyes were glass.

She walked toward me.

She did not move around the tables. She moved through them. Her body passed through wood and brass table numbers like mist — a shimmer of something impossible — and she stopped right in front of me. Her breath smelled of cold air and old ice. I could see the wall directly through her chest. Her lips did not quite

move with the words. The words came from somewhere else — from the walls, from the floor, from inside my own skull.

“What will you be having tonight?”

Then she sank through the table at her side — wood swallowing her ankles, her knees, her chest — and was gone. Only a smell of frost and old lemon polish remained.

I screamed. The scream came out as radio static.

✦ ✦ ✦

[ TRANSCRIPT CONTINUES · 03:01 hrs ]

I tried writing my name in the dust on a table. The letters rearranged themselves. When I looked down again they read:TABLE FOUR.

My fingers went numb. Not from the cold. From time. Or the lack of it. The windows all showed the same streetlamp, the same puddle, the same rusted delivery truck that had not moved in what felt like hours. I would pass the same water stain. The same cracked tile. The same shadow of a potted fern that never shifted. The chandelier flickering once, twice, then steady. The brass 4, loose on its screw.

I started seeing myself in the glass partitions.

Older. Gaunt. Wearing a server’s apron. Then a chef’s coat. Then a cashier’s uniform. The haunting was not around me anymore. It was inside me. Fitting me to the loop. I was not escaping. I was being cast. Written into the shift that would never end.

Then I heard him.

The gentleman’s voice, behind me. Quiet. Old-world. Courteous. The voice of a man who opens doors for women and says please and thank you.

I turned.

He stood at the far end of the aisle in a clean shirt and pressed trousers. One hand slightly raised, as if offering help. His face was too still. Too patient. As if it had been waiting years to be recognised. He began to walk toward me with the calm dignity of someone who knows he will arrive before I can escape.

I backed away. He kept coming.

“Do not leave,”he said, when he was close enough that I should have felt the warmth of him. There was no warmth.“They forget us when the shift ends.”

I whispered:“What are you?”

His smile widened by a fraction.

“A host. A waiter. A cashier. A cook. A customer. It depends on who asks. We have been waiting to finish our shift.”

✦ ✦ ✦

[ TRANSCRIPT CONTINUES · 03:14 hrs ]

I knew the story by then. I had not known I knew it. But standing in that corridor with the fridge door at my back and that patient face in front of me, the knowledge came up through the floor like cold through tile. January 27, 2010. A robbery. A siege that lasted a full day. Three staff members locked into the walk-in fridge while the robbers took what they came for. And then — whether they forgot, or whether the screaming had stopped and no one thought to check — three people were left inside. The cold did what cold does, over hours, over a day, over however long it took before the silence inside that fridge became the permanent kind.

Found days later. Blue. Rigid. Fingers curled like claws. The Sandton Triple. That is what the papers called it before they pulled the articles. Before the chain shuttered every location. Before the internet forgot the address existed.

But the dead don’t forget.

They rehearse.

The door behind me banged once from the inside. Then again. Then a third time, harder. The handle turned on its own. Cold air spilled into the hall in a wet, icy breath. I saw white light inside — harsh and fluorescent, the kind that does not flicker, the kind that has no mercy. Metal shelves. A hanging thermometer with the red line buried so low I could not read it. Three shapes standing close together in the room, their outlines blurred by frost.

One of them turned its head.

Its face was pale and unearthly, the skin stretched blue-white as if the blood had long since made its final decision and left. Its eyes were open. They fixed on me with a look of terrible, offended hunger — the hunger not of the body but of the unfinished. The hunger of three people who clocked in for a shift that has not yet officially ended.

In the frost on the floor of the fridge, I could see three sets of footprints. Circling. Circling. Circling. The same circle, worn into the frost over fourteen years of the same slow loop.

✦ ✦ ✦

[ TRANSCRIPT CONTINUES · 03:22 hrs ]

I screamed and ran.

Through dining rooms and kitchens and corridors that rearranged themselves the moment I stopped looking directly at them. I passed the cash register where the woman sat with her hands poised over the keys, recording transactions into a ledger that had no customers left to serve. I heard plates being set on tables behind me. I heard cutlery clinking in a room I had just left empty. A waiter asked, in a voice frayed at the edges like old rope:“Will there be dessert?” I heard a freezer door slam from somewhere far above. I heard someone cough — the dry, broken sound of lungs that should not have been trying to work anymore.

I would burst through a doorway and find the same red carpet. Turn left and emerge beside the hostess podium. Throw open a glass door and see only another corridor lined with menus and framed photographs of food that no one would ever eat.

I was moving but not escaping. Circling, always circling, as though the building itself were chewing me slowly and had no intention of swallowing until it was satisfied.

The circular path wasn’t architectural, Officer. I understand that now. It was psychological. Every corridor bent toward the same memory. Every step replayed their final hours. I heard the robbers’ boots on tile. I heard the fridge door slam. I heard the silence that followed. The temperature that dropped. My breath turned to ice. My joints locked. I tried to turn back. My legs moved forward. I was caught in their gravity. Their trauma. Their unfinished shift.

Their dead frequency.

✦ ✦ ✦

[ TRANSCRIPT CONTINUES · 03:31 hrs ]

At last I reached the front entrance.

I know it was the front because I saw that bruised facade through the glass. The empty parking lot. The road shining faintly beyond the gate. I nearly wept. I grabbed a chair and hurled it at the glass wall. The chair struck with a sharp crack and fell sideways. The glass did not break. It rippled — soft,

like the skin of water touched by a finger — and through it I saw another version of the restaurant beyond. Same lamps, same tables, same dark-red carpet. But there were shapes of people there. They sat in booths with their heads bent low. A waiter moved between them carrying plates that might have been empty or might not have been. At the far end a woman stood behind the cash register, one hand on the drawer, her face turned toward me as if she had been waiting for me to notice her for fourteen years.

Then the glass returned to solid darkness and my own reflection stared back.

I looked awful. Hollow-eyed. Starving. A man assembled from leftover pieces of other men.

The gentleman stood behind my reflection. His mouth moved near my ear, though I could not hear the sound — only see the words forming, patient and clear:“Do not leave. They forget us when the shift ends.”

The doors were unlocked. I threw myself through them and hit the cold night air and fell onto the pavement and rolled onto my side, expecting hands to drag me back, expecting that corridor of red carpet to swallow me again.

Nothing.

The gate stood open behind me. The building was dark and still.

I looked up at the front of it — at that sick, feverish colour,that pale ochre bruise— and for one awful moment the windows filled with figures. A woman at a table. A man behind a counter. A cook at his station. A hostess at her podium. All of them

watching from within, with the calm of people who know exactly where I have been and who know, with certainty, that they will be there long after I am gone.

I blinked.

They were gone.

A taxi passed on the road. Headlights swept over the facade. Just a restaurant. Just an abandoned chain. Just a place where business died and rumour grew in its place.

✦ ✦ ✦

[ TRANSCRIPT CONTINUES · 03:39 hrs ]

When I got back to the shelter near dawn, my shoes were wet with freezer water. On the inside lining of my coat, where no one could have written it and where no cold had any reason to reach, there was a line of frost. Clean. Deliberate. Like a signature.

It melted before noon.

I have not been warm since that night. Not once. Blankets, fires, sunlight — none of it reaches all the way in. There is a depth in me that stayed behind in that building. Or that the building put there. I cannot tell the difference anymore.

That is all I can tell you. That is my full statement. I do not have anything more.

I will say only this. Those three people — they are still in there. Still working. Still serving. The waitress at her table. The chef at his counter. The cashier at her register. They do not know the shift has ended. Or perhaps they know, and this is simply all that is left of them — the act of doing the thing they did every day, going through the motions long after the motion has any meaning. Serving no one. Cooking for no one. Counting money in a restaurant that no longer exists for customers who will never come.

The Codfather Village does not appear on any map. It does not exist on the internet. But it is there. That pale bruise of a building in Morningside, its facade the colour of something that should have been dead long before now. You can stand outside it and feel the cold that has no reason to exist. Not in January. Not in Joburg. You can feel it through the wall.

I would ask you, very respectfully, not to go inside.

Because I do not think the door opens from the other side.

And if you’re cold, and lost, and hungry — it will find you. And the door that sighed open when you leaned against it will not sigh open again when you need it to.

Sometimes, when I close my eyes, I still hear the cash register opening. And in the dark behind my eyelids, a young woman asks me again, in the gentlest voice in the world:

“What would you eat?”

Nothing from the fridge.

Please. Nothing from the fridge.

SAPS DOCKET 2024/02/0038 — ADDENDUM — INVESTIGATING OFFICER N. MOKOENA — BADGE

Witness displayed acute hypothermia upon arrival · Core temp 34.1°C Toxicology clear · No signs of intoxication · No history of psychosis on record · Witness accounts internally consistent across three separate recorded sessions

Site confirmed: former Codfather Village complex, Morningside, Sandton · Sealed since 2011 · All entry points padlocked · No evidence of forced entry · Witness was observed exiting front entrance by private security at 05:43 hrs · Security confirms: front door was padlocked when he arrived at post at 05:00 hrs

The door was padlocked when he went in. It was padlocked when he came out.

File remains open. Recommend no further site investigation.

chapters.title: The Knot
chapters.text:
Queenstown Municipal Archive · Page 412 · 17 August 1897

The rope was cut from a living blue gum tree on the morning of 17 August, 1897. Every account omits this. Colonial ledgers list aged hemp, properly dressed, purchased from a Grahamstown merchant. But the warden’s private journal — recovered from an estate sale in 2003, never digitised, never cited — is specific. The original rope had rotted through overnight. Inexplicably. The warden replaced it at dawn with cord cut from the tree in the gaol yard, the one whose roots had been splitting the flagstones for thirty years. The hemp was green. Still wet. Still living.

That is why it took eleven minutes.

A proper rope kills in the first second. The drop, the snap, the sudden cessation. This rope stretched. It absorbed the fall and gave Friedrich Badenhorst back to the air — alive, strangling slowly, his body’s weight collapsing the windpipe in fractions while the hemp fibres whitened under load. The cells of his brain extinguished one by one, the way lamps are turned down in an empty house, room by room, at the end of the night, when the last occupant is finished with each room forever and will not be returning.

He made sounds for eleven minutes.

Three lines of the warden’s journal entry are scratched out. Whatever a man produces when eleven minutes of dying are extracted from him before forty witnesses, the warden had decided that it must not be committed to ink. He was wrong. Nothing committed to the air of that courtyard on the morning of 17 August has ever fully dissipated.

Beside Badenhorst, Mthunzi ka Dlamini died in the first second. His neck broke clean — a wet crack like a green branch snapping in frost, sharp enough that three people in the crowd flinched simultaneously. He had been chanting from the moment they brought him out: a low Zulu invocation the guards could not identify and did not like. The chant stopped mid-syllable when the trap fell, cut off with such total abruptness that the crowd felt the silence as a physical impact, a closed door against the chest.

They were buried in quicklime. The grave was unmarked. The magistrate, Hartley, closed his ledger and moved to his next case, which was a cattle boundary dispute, and was resolved within the week.

The ledger is still in the Queenstown municipal archive. Page 412. Two names. Two verdicts. The ink around both entries has bled — not from moisture, not from age, but from pressure — into a shape so precise that a visiting archivist in 2019 photographed it three times before she understood what she was looking at, and once more after, with hands she could not entirely steady, before she closed the book and did not request it again.

I. WHAT THE ROPE LEFT BEHIND — —

It began as an absence. The blue gum tree in the gaol yard — the one from which the rope had been cut, still standing when the sentence was carried out — was dead by morning. Its bark had split from root to crown in a single vertical line, as though something had exited through it at speed and the wood had never closed over the wound. The sap bleeding from the split was dark and smelled of iron.

Then the livestock refused their pens. Then the dogs stopped crossing the road past the gaol. Then the light in certain rooms began to behave as though it had somewhere else to be, thinning toward the door, pooling in corners, avoiding the centre of a space the way water avoids a drain in reverse.

Then came the first man.

A clerk named Josiah Mthembu, three streets from the market, was found in the slaughteryard behind his cousin’s house eleven days after the execution. The doctor recorded self-inflicted strangulation. Nobody in Queenstown believed it — not after they counted the marks. Four of them. Four rope burns around his neck, spaced unevenly, as though several different hands had each taken a turn. His fingers were still curled in the tight specific arc of a man who has been gripping a rope and has understood, midway through gripping it, what the rope intends.

The mud beneath his body smelled of the gaol yard. Not mud from the slaughteryard. From the gaol. The smell of that specific earth: damp stone and old iron and the urine of terrified men and something beneath all of it, something older, something that had been in the ground there long before the British built the prison on top of it.

II. THE CHILDREN — —

Eight children, across three households, over the span of a single week. Ages seven to twelve. None of them with access to the gaol, none with prior knowledge of the execution, none who had been told the name Badenhorst or the name Mthunzi. All of them drawing the same image without coordination and without being shown each other’s work: a crossbeam, a trapdoor, and below the beam two figures who were not hanging but standing — watching something above their heads. Between them a third shape. Too elongated. Too still. Its face in permanent shadow. Its feet not reaching the ground.

One girl of nine, Elspeth, drew it thirty-seven times in five days. When her teacher pried away the pencil and asked what the faceless figure was, Elspeth answered without looking up from the desk where the pencil had been:

“The one that stayed to make sure.”

The teachers burned the drawings. That night the school bell rang three times, alone in the dark, in a building no one had entered. The bell’s rope, when they checked it the next morning, smelled of green hemp. The kind just cut from a living tree. The kind that is still wet with what it was.

III. THE PASTOR — —

He arrived from the next district with holy water, scripture, and a confidence that would not survive the courtyard. He entered at noon, which he later said he had believed would protect him. Noon protected no one. The sun was overhead and the shadows in the gaol yard were wrong — they fell against the wind, at angles nothing solid was casting them from, as though bodies were standing in the yard that only the light could detect.

He saw the rope. New. Green. The noose knotted so tightly the hemp fibres had begun to whiten, as though under load, as though something of great weight had been recently suspended from it. The beam was not rotten. The beam was fresh-cut. The wood around the joint was still weeping sap.

He backed away from it. Then a voice spoke from directly behind him — not loud, entirely conversational, with the patient tone of something that has been waiting long enough to no longer need urgency:

“Do you know which of us you came to bless?”

He turned. No one was there. The noose had lengthened by a foot.

The pastor was found on the Komani road an hour later, walking away from Queenstown without his coat, his lips moving continuously. He said one thing before he closed his mouth for good on the subject: the rope was fresh. It had been cut that morning. From a living tree. He could smell the sap. He could feel the fibres still pulling toward the wood they had come from, the way a cut will always search for the wound it belongs to.

IV. THE BASEMENT — —

My name is Siyanda Ndaba. I am a crime journalist. Murders, disappearances, the administrative violence of bureaucracies designed to lose people between their departments. I am not a man given to panic or to invention. I am writing this down because Friedrich Badenhorst scratched his name into a cell wall with a bent nail and begged the stone to hold it, and the least I can do is the same.

I went into the basement of the building on Cathcart Road at one in the morning on a Wednesday with a torch, a recorder, and a printed restoration of the warden’s journal entry — the full version, scratched-out lines recovered by infrared imaging at a document lab in Cape Town. I had already read the restored lines before I went down. I will come back to that.

The basement: sixty feet of cracked concrete, walls sweating a damp no plumber has sourced in six attempts, a fire door at the far end that has not been opened since 2003. I stood in the centre of the corridor. I breathed. I waited.

At 1:14 AM the temperature dropped — not gradually, all at once, the specific cold of a space from which something has just been suddenly subtracted. And then the smell arrived. Green hemp, fresh- cut, resinous and alive, the smell of a tree still living and newly

wounded. Not old rope. Not museum rope. The smell of 17 August, 1897, preserved in the dark of that basement like a letter sealed before it was ever sent.

I turned my torch to the far end of the corridor.

They stood at the fire door.

Friedrich Badenhorst: large across the shoulders, collarless shirt, leather braces. His neck leaned a permanent inch to the left — not grotesque, just geometrically wrong, in the way that locates itself in the spine before the eyes understand it. His face held the expression of a man who has made every available argument and been refused and has run out of time within which further refusal is possible.

Mthunzi ka Dlamini: broader, shorter, in full inyanga regalia — beadwork, skins, head-ring, a cracked wooden staff resting on the concrete floor without a sound. His eyes were open and had been open for a hundred and twenty-seven years. They were looking at something above the fire door, above the building, above the night — some long reckoning that had no interest in the present moment and would continue uninterrupted when the present moment was long past.

Between their necks: a rope. Green hemp. Not attached — present. Lying between them with the natural drape of something that has made its peace with gravity. Not a restraint. Evidence. The only remaining physical fact of what had been done, the only thing the quicklime could not reach and the magistrate’s pen could not scratch out.

I opened my mouth to speak. I had words prepared. Journalists always do.

What came out instead was eleven minutes of silence.

Not my silence. Theirs. The silence of eleven minutes on the morning of 17 August, 1897, passed through me like current through copper — and I understood then what the scratched-out lines in the warden’s journal had said. What the warden had tried to unrecord, because some things must not be given the permanence of ink:

He did not stop speaking. Not for eleven minutes. He spoke his own name. Only his name. Over and over, with the last full breath available to him, as though a name repeated with enough force becomes a thing the air cannot simply absorb and disperse. As though it becomes, instead, a knot. Load-bearing. Something the rope itself cannot undo.

Friedrich Badenhorst said his name for eleven minutes.

Then he stopped saying it.

And the name continued without him. In two languages at once. In a basement in Komani, in the dark, with the patience of something that understands that time is not a river moving in one direction but a rope — and a rope, properly knotted, holds whatever weight is placed on it for as long as you refuse to cut it down.

I left the basement at 3:17 AM. The rope smell followed me into the street. It followed me to my car. It has not fully left my clothes.

I am writing this down.

It is the only thing I know how to do that matters. The only reason I went in the first place. Not to prove anything. Not to debunk or to sensationalise. But because two men were killed in that yard for a crime that was not a crime, before a crowd that raised no objection, and their names were entered in a ledger under Guilty and the ledger was filed under Concluded and a hundred and twenty-seven years have passed and the file has not been reopened.

Friedrich Badenhorst said his own name in the dark for eleven minutes because he had nothing left but the fact of himself, and he refused to let even that be taken.

The least the living can do is say it after him.

Friedrich Badenhorst · executed 17 August 1897 · Queenstown Gaol · Eastern Cape · Mthunzi ka Dlamini · executed 17 August 1897 · Queenstown Gaol · Eastern Cape Neither conviction has ever been reviewed.

chapters.title: The Mouth of the Moon
chapters.text:
ALT 4,890m · TEMP −6°C · WIND NW 32km/h

Rwenzori Range

The Rwenzori do not rise. They remember.

Stand at the base long enough and you feel it — not altitude, not weather, but the specific psychic pressure of being recognised by something that has been watching since before the word watching existed. The Greeks called them Mountains of the Moon and built cosmologies around their silhouette. Ptolemy inked them into his maps with the trembling hand of a man recording something he had not personally survived. The colonial surveyors came with theodolites and fever and wrote coordinates in journals that were later found without their authors. Everyone who named these mountains named them wrong. You do not name a thing that has already named you.

We drove four hours from the Congolese side under military escort, rifles angled not outward at the treeline but downward, toward the road itself, as though the threat came from beneath the tarmac. I noticed this and filed it. The driver had not looked away from the windscreen once. Not at the scenery. Not at us. He kept his eyes fixed forward with the specific vacancy of a man performing an act of deliberate forgetting — as if the road could only be navigated by those who refused to fully acknowledge where it led.

No one spoke.

Even Ted was quiet, which I had believed, until that morning, to be a physical impossibility.

My team assembled at the trailhead in the grey wool of early morning. Martha wound her braids into a ponytail with hands that did not quite steady themselves. Ted brandished his ice axe in his best approximation of a bullwhip and managed half a laugh before the forest absorbed it. The laugh did not echo. It simply ended — swallowed by the moss and the mist and the particular silence of a place that has learned, over geological time, to digest human noise.

The guide watched us the way a priest watches children asking the wrong questions beside an open grave.

His face was carved bark and patient dark eyes, and he said the names the way you say the names of things that can hear themselves spoken.

Kalisa. A ruin of a man. One arm, one leg, one eye, one ear, half a nose, half a body — the other half simply absent, as though something cosmic had torn away its portion mid-construction and fled with it to another dimension, leaving the remainder to drag itself forward through eternity on its single grinding hip socket. Not a demon. A description. A medical record of something that existed in two realities simultaneously and was whole in neither.

Nyabarika. Power over life and death. To whom sacrifices were made. The guide did not say were once made. He said are made, in the present continuous tense, and when I looked at him he had already moved on and I could not tell if it was a slip of grammar or a confession.

I told him I was not there for gods.

He looked at me with an expression I would not understand until much later — the particular compassion of someone watching a person walk into a room they cannot warn them about in any language the person will believe.

I was there for the photographs.

I kept them in a waterproof sleeve inside my jacket, against my sternum, where I could feel them. Four images, sourced from different expeditions, different decades, different cameras and film stocks. In each one, caught at the edge of frame, was a shape. Not a ruin. Not a natural formation. Something with walls that were upright, geometry that was not accidental, a structure that appeared in all four photographs at a different distance from the camera and in all four photographs appeared to be closer than the photographer had understood when they pressed the shutter. As though it moved. As though it positioned itself to be found, partially, by each expedition in turn, and in each case the expedition had returned incomplete.

The guide had told the truth. There were no ruins. No city. No treasure.

There was only the hunger of a thing that needed new nerve- endings.

I did not know this yet.

We began to climb.

The forest on the Ugandan slopes is a fever architecture of giant lobelia and groundsel that have grown, over centuries, into shapes that suggest ritual rather than botany. Their crowns nod in synchronized rhythm, slow and deliberate, as if counting something. The moss that drapes the heather branches is the particular grey of old skin, not the clean grey of stone but the exhausted grey of tissue that has been under stress for a very long time. The air smells of cold iron and something beneath it — sweet, organic, familiar in a way that the rational mind refuses to complete, the way you sometimes smell something in a crowded place and almost recognise a memory before the recognition arrives and you understand that what you’re smelling is human and it is not living.

The ground gave slightly under our boots. Not mud. Not peat. Elasticity. A tautness, like drum skin over resonant hollow. I felt it with every step and told myself it was the accumulated sponge of centuries of moss growth, and I almost believed it until I noticed that the compression beneath my left foot felt different to the right. Subtly different. Textured differently. As though the substrate was not uniform. As though it was not one continuous surface but many, pressed together.

The soldier, Francis, moved with the alert silence of someone performing a constant calculation of sightlines. He did not scan the treeline. He scanned the spaces between the trees — the negative space, the gaps, as though that was where the relevant information lived. I asked him what he was looking for.

He took a long moment before answering.

“The invisible cave,” he said. “And the disappearing lake.”

He said it without inflection. The others laughed behind us, and Francis did not react to the laughter in any way, which was itself a specific kind of answer. The guide’s smirk appeared then — not amusement but the fossilised expression of a man who has told a joke so many times he no longer remembers that it stopped being funny, that it was never, in fact, a joke.

The Bwamba, he said. The first people. The guardians. They knew a cave that strangers could not perceive, a lake that vanished when approached, and they had tended both for generations, maintaining something that the guide described as balance in the tone of someone describing the operation of a mechanism they do not fully understand but have been instructed not to touch.

And then one day they were simply not there.

No bodies. No belongings. No fire remains. No indication of migration, conflict, famine, or disease. The space where a people had been was just empty, with the particular quality of emptiness that is

not absence but consumption — the way a room feels when something has been removed from it that was structural, that held the walls apart.

"Did the cave go with them?" Ted asked, still performing lightness, his voice cracked at the corners like old paint.

The guide said nothing.

Francis had gone perfectly still.

Forty meters ahead, the mist was moving in a way that was not wind — not dispersing, not drifting, but circling, slowly, as though something at the centre of it was breathing it in and releasing it again. As though the air itself were being metabolised.

The gunshots came from below, and they were not the irregular, opportunistic sound of poaching.

Three shots. Then a silence with texture in it. Then two more, flat and deliberate, with the specific cadence of someone who knows they are not stopping what they are shooting at but firing anyway because the alternative is to do nothing and the human mind cannot accept the alternative.

Francis worked through radio frequencies with increasing urgency. The static on every channel had a quality to it that I noticed and tried not to name — wet, rhythmic, almost but not quite random, the way breathing sounds from another room at night when you wake and lie still and listen and cannot be certain whether the sound you hear is another person’s respiration or simply the house settling against the dark.

"They do not go beyond Gessi," Francis said, and I watched something change in his face at the same moment as the words came out, as though hearing himself say it completed a calculation he had been avoiding. His professional composure did not collapse. It

restructured. The expression of a man who has just understood that the rules he memorised apply to a different situation than the one he is currently inside.

He told us to make camp.

I told him Baker was important.

He looked at me with an expression I now understand was not a warning. It was an elegy. He was already grieving, with the specific foreknowledge of a man who has escorted enough expeditions up these slopes to know the difference between the ones that come back whole and the ones that come back in instalments, and the ones that do not come back at all, and the ones that come back as something else.

The first sign was a footprint.

Half a footprint, technically.

Pressed into a seam of dark mud beside the trail, large enough to accommodate both my hands. The heel was sunk too deep — not the depth of weight but the depth of wrongness, as though the thing that made it was heavier on one side than physics accounts for. The toes ended not in a clean margin but in a rough, collapsed edge, like a sentence abandoned mid-word. Like something only partially committed to having a foot.

The guide’s face went the colour of ash above his collar.

The soldier crouched and touched the mud with a single finger and stood with white knuckles and said, very quietly: Fresh.

Martha asked, in a voice that had lost its register, what made it.

The answer arrived from above us, not as sound but as feeling — the sensation of a vast weight settling its attention, a shift in the air pressure equivalent to being regarded by an eye the size of a cathedral window. Not looked at. Regarded. The distinction is

important. A gaze has direction and terminus. What we felt had neither. It was environmental. It was the mountain deciding to concentrate.

The guide began to pray.

Not to Nyabarika. Not to any named god.

He prayed in the grammar of a man who no longer believes the named gods are in a position to help.

We ran, in the direction that had been downward, and the trail that had been downward was no longer downward. This is the fact I keep returning to because it is the most quietly annihilating detail of the whole account — not the creature, not what happened to Ted and Martha, not the city in the basin below the ridge, not the moment I saw my own face in Kalisa’s ruined shape. The most horrifying thing is the trail. That the path behind us was simply different than the path we had ascended. The same mud and root and stone, rearranged. Not dramatically. Not surreally. Just enough — the way a familiar face looks wrong in a dream, the wrongness located not in any single feature but in the relationship between features, the architecture of recognition shifted two degrees off true.

We had not taken a wrong turn.

The guide said: ”We were turned."

The forest, in this new configuration, held a silence so total it had texture. Not absence of sound but active suppression of it — the way a held breath suppresses sound, the muscular effort of silence, a silence that was working.

And beneath it, barely distinguishable from the sound of blood in my own ears: a wet clicking. Patient. Rhythmic. Something learning, through practice, to approximate the sound of a jaw.

Ted went first.

I will not dress it as anything other than what it was. He was beside me and then he was not, his fingers raking bright red furrows in the wet stone as something beneath the surface — beneath what should have been solid mountain bedrock — pulled him in by the ankle with the calm, unhurried efficiency of a thing that has done this countless times and has long since ceased to register the screaming as relevant data. The soldier fired into the stone. The shots sounded small. They sounded like someone knocking on a door on the wrong side of a continent.

Martha lasted longer.

Long enough to see the trees.

The faces in the bark were not abstract. Not pareidolia. Not the mind assembling pattern from randomness. They were specific, detailed, anatomically precise, and they were not all faces I recognised. But they were faces — mouths stretched in an expression that was not pain and not sleep but some tertiary state for which there is, as far as I know, no word yet. Eyes not painted or carved but actual, glassy, embedded in the grain of the wood, oriented outward with the fixed regard of something still processing sensory input from a nervous system that has been rerouted.

The Bwamba had not left.

They had been restructured.

The invisible cave was not hidden. It was a wound in the skin of causality, and when the first people entered it to perform whatever final negotiation they believed would restore the balance, they emerged as something else. Their nervous systems flattened and pressed into the stone and soil of the trail. Pain-sensitive. Continuously aware. Feeling every footfall of every expedition that had ascended these paths for centuries, the crush of every boot on what remained of their consciousness, screaming in a frequency that registers as the mountain’s general atmosphere of unease.

This is what the guide’s smirk had been protecting.

This is what the static carried.

The footsteps of Kitasamba and Nyabibuya are not metaphors. They are a people. They are what the mountain does with its guardians when it decides it needs new pavement.

Martha’s braids were nailed to a slab of bark with an iron spike that should not have been there, that had no explanation, the hair fanning into the grain of the wood, the scalp still attached and glistening with fresh tissue. I could smell her coconut oil. From inside the bark came a sound that had once been a voice and was now trying to remember how to be one, working its way back toward language one phoneme at a time, not yet arrived.

I did not stay to hear what it was working toward.

The ridge opened onto the basin and the basin held the city and the city was not ruins.

I need to be precise about this because every account I had read used the word ruins and the word is wrong and the wrongness of it is important. Ruins imply a prior wholeness, a former completion, a structure that was once functional and has since decayed. What occupied the basin was not a city in decay. It was a city in process. The walls were upright but they breathed. The archways pulsed with a slow, organic rhythm, slightly out of phase with each other, like the overlapping contractions of a digestive tract. The stone was not stone. It was calcified biology, the architectural expression of a growth that had developed, over millennia, the structural properties of rock while retaining all the properties of living tissue.

The peaks of the Rwenzori are not peaks.

Baker is not a summit.

The entire massif is a cranium, colossal and buried, the skull of something that died in an ecstatic state and has been dreaming ever since, generating unreality from its decomposing architecture, exhaling mythology the way a corpse exhales gas. The peaks are its dentition. The valleys are the spaces between its thoughts. The disappearing lake is its saliva, pooling and receding with the rhythm of a dreaming jaw. The invisible cave is the soft palate of a god that swallowed an entire civilisation and found the sensation instructive.

What the four photographs showed was not a city at all.

They showed a mouth.

Approaching.

From the direction of the invisible cave, Kalisa finally resolved itself.

Not from the mist. Not from the forest. It resolved itself from the corner of my vision the way a migraine aura resolves — not appearing but becoming available to perception, as though it had always been present and my brain had been, until now, successfully refusing to process it. It filled the horizon. Not in scale, or not only in scale, but in the way it occupied the available space of comprehension — crowding out the capacity for any other thought, filling the cognitive field entirely, the way extreme pain fills the body and leaves no room for anything else.

One eye the size of a cathedral window. A pupil that was not dark but absent, a void within a void, a hole in the visual field through which something on the other side was doing its own looking.

Half a body.

The missing half was not absent. The guide had described it wrong, as had every account, every legend, every iteration of the story across every culture that had approached these mountains and survived long enough to speak afterward. The missing half of Kalisa was not gone. It existed in an adjacent plane, partially inserted into

our reality, the way a hand is partially inserted into a glove — what was visible was the portion that had successfully made the crossing. The rest of it occupied a dimension we had no sensory apparatus to confirm.

The psychic pressure of its attention was not a metaphor.

I felt my left side go numb.

Not anaesthesia. Not cold. The specific absence of sensation that precedes disconnection, the feeling of a limb you have slept on wrong beginning its long slow betrayal of the body it belongs to. My left hand, my left ear, the left hemisphere of my face — all of it going quiet, going offline, going somewhere adjacent that I could not access. I understood then with the total, pre-linguistic certainty of something felt in the hinge of the jaw: this was not happening to me. This had already happened. The version of me that arrived at the summit would not have a left side. Would have one eye, one arm, one ear, half a nose, half a body. Would join the long cartographic record of explorers and guardians and sacrificial porters who had climbed too far and arrived at Baker not as people but as raw material.

My own face smiled at me from within its ruined shape.

It looked relieved.

They found one of us at the base of the mountain eleven days later. The official record names which one but I have chosen not to repeat it here, because the name no longer applies with any accuracy to what they found. The medical examination produced no conclusions that the examining doctors were willing to sign. The written account submitted to the national parks authority described a survivor in good physical health who demonstrated no memory of the expedition, no recognition of their own name, and no reaction whatsoever to pain stimuli applied to the left side of the body.

The survivor kept asking, in a calm and patient voice, to be taken back to the trailhead.

They kept asking, every day, for seven months, until the request simply stopped.

The attending physician noted in the final report that on the last morning, the patient was found facing the window, very still, watching the distant treeline with one eye — the other having closed, sometime during the night, and simply not reopened.

The remaining eye, the physician wrote, looked satisfied.

The mountains look the same from the road.

They always look the same from the road.

That is how they want you.
