chapters.title: OKIKU
chapters.text:
EXHIBIT 1918-K — Doll, human hair (post-mortem growth recorded). Provenance: Mannen-ji Temple archive, 1918–present. On indefinite loan.

No. 1918-K · Mori Tetsuya, independent researcher

The doll arrived at Mannen-ji Temple in the winter of 1918, carried by a grieving family who had nowhere else to put their loss. Their daughter, Okiku, six years old, had died of a chest infection. She had held the doll until the last hour. When the hair began to grow after her death, the family understood it as love refusing to leave. They were partly right.

Something was refusing to leave.

It was not love.

I have spent four years researching the doll’s history. Longer than I intended, and far longer than was safe. I have read the sealed depositions and visited the families who survived. I have sat in the Mannen-ji guest room at two in the morning, listening to what the temple does with its dark. I have done all of this while my daughter Sachi, seven years old, slept at home with her bob haircut fanned against her pillow, ignorant of what her father was walking toward.

What follows is what I found.

THE BARBER’S DAUGHTER — OTARU, 1947 — —

Jiro Taniguchi purchased the doll at an outdoor market in autumn, drawn, as so many have been, by the quality of its hair. He was a barber. The fine, even cut of the doll’s bob was the first thing that caught his eye — precise, correct, the kind of cut he took pride in himself. He bought it for his daughter Hatsu, eleven years old, who

had been mute since birth and spoke entirely in a vocabulary of gestures so exact they had become their own private language between them.

Hatsu’s response to the doll was immediate and total. She held it through dinner, set it on the bath ledge during her nightly wash, positioned it carefully on her nightstand so it faced the room rather than the wall. Jiro found this last detail touching, initially. A child ensuring her toy could see.

He was a professional. He examined the doll’s scalp with methodical calm. He lifted the wig cap and found genuine roots — black, fine, real — anchored in ceramic with no seam he could locate. He trimmed the fringe on Sunday. By Monday it had reached the doll’s chin. By Thursday, her shoulders. By the following week the hair pooled on the tatami like something that had spilled.

Hatsu’s own hair began to grow in tandem. She had always worn it short — practical, her father had said, easier to keep clean. Now she pressed herself against the wall when he approached with scissors. Her expression, usually so legible, became a single closed page. He respected her refusal. He should not have.

He woke one night to a weight across his chest and found it was hair — a length of it, heavy and black, trailing from his blanket across the hall to Hatsu’s door. He followed it carefully in the dark, lifting it from the floor, the hair supple and strangely warm between his fingers. It led him to Hatsu’s room, where she lay sleeping. The hair was rooted in the doll. It had grown across the full length of the hallway in the night, in the dark, reaching him.

He stood there a long time.

Jiro’s confession — a document he mailed to Mannen-ji five years after the event, unable to tell anyone in person — ends in two sentences. She was sleeping when I reached for the doll. I thought I was cutting its hair. The coroner’s report confirmed what Jiro could

not write: the hair had wrapped his wrists in the dark, guiding his hands, directing the shears. Hatsu died before the lamp was lit. Jiro held her for two hours before he understood the specific nature of what he had done.

He was acquitted on grounds of diminished responsibility. He spent the rest of his life trying to make peace with that acquittal. He never did. You could hear it in how he phrased the confession — not the hair made me but I thought I was cutting its hair, as if even now he needed to hold the instrument.

The doll passed to Jiro’s sister, who attempted to burn it. She failed. She threw it in a river. It reappeared three weeks later, dry and pristine, on a riverbank shrine in Hakodate. The shrine’s priest, unsettled by its appearance, left it on the steps of a temple rather than keep it in his care. From there it moved by the slow gravity of indifference — a donation box, a market stall, a locked display case in an antique shop — until it found what it was looking for.

It is always looking for something specific. I understand that now. The daughter. The haircut. The particular tenderness of a child who hasn’t yet learned to guard what she loves.

THE MOTHER — TOKYO, 1989 — —

Akiko Tanaka was twenty-nine and working two jobs and carrying the guilt of an absent parent in her chest like ballast. She found the doll at a flea market in Asakusa on a Sunday, her one morning off. Yumi, six years old, had recently cut her hair into a short bob. She looked, Akiko had thought at the time, like a serious little doll herself.

The pun had seemed charming at the time.

Within a month, Yumi’s ordinary stillness — the stillness of a child absorbed in play — had become something else. A watching stillness. The apartment began to feel observed.

Akiko tried twice to dispose of the doll. The first time she left it in a dumpster behind their building. It was on Yumi’s pillow the next morning, the kimono damp. The second time she dropped it from the Kanda Bridge into the canal below and did not go back to check. Three weeks later it was on the shelf above Yumi’s bed. The water had left no mark on it. Not a streak, not a stain.

The psychological erosion, in retrospect, happened in stages Akiko could not recognise from inside. The hum in the walls — low, tuneless, always at the edge of audibility, always stopping when she turned to find it. The time lapses: she would be making dinner and then be on the floor in the hallway with no memory of sitting down. The peripheral movement — always at the corner of vision, the doll’s head slightly wrong, slightly too attentive. The way Yumi’s drawings changed from round-faced cheerful children to precise, frantic images in black crayon: a girl with hair like water, pouring through the rooms of a house, wrapping around the wrists and throats of the adults inside. Each drawing placed the doll in the corner, half- hidden, watching.

When Akiko asked Yumi what had happened to the face on the hair- girl — it was always a clean blank oval — Yumi looked up with an expression she had not owned before. Serene, patient, borrowed from somewhere outside childhood.

“She’s still growing into it,” Yumi said.

Akiko was found in the kitchen. The investigating officer’s report is scrupulously clinical, but the detail that survived into follow-up testimony was this: the doll’s hair had been freshly trimmed at the time of discovery. Cut back to a perfect bob, clean as a professional’s work. As if someone had just come from the barber. Yumi was found sitting in the corner, eyes unfocused, one hand moving slowly in the air beside her as if working through a long, fine length of it. She was remanded to psychiatric care.

She is still there.

She still strokes the air.

The nurses note that her hair grows unusually fast and that she refuses to let anyone cut it.

THE RESTORER — HOKKAIDO, 2018 — —

Daiki Nakamura was the most methodical man I spoke to in four years of research, despite the fact that by the time I found him he had been institutionalised for three years and could not always distinguish which decade he was in. He had been an antique restorer — a man whose profession required seeing objects without sentiment, without projection, without the interference of what you wished to be there.

He had an eight-year-old daughter named Hana. Her mother had died nine months before he acquired the doll. I keep returning to this detail. Grief makes a door. Something on the other side knows how to knock.

Hana did not ask for the doll. She walked into his workroom, looked at it on the bench, and said: She’s been waiting. Daiki told her it was a restoration piece. Hana nodded and went back to her room. An hour later she was on the workroom floor, cross-legged, watching the doll with the same expression she’d worn at her mother’s funeral — solemn, already waiting for whatever came after this.

His documentation of the early weeks has the precision of his training: dated photographs, millimetre measurements, careful notes on hair growth rate. He contacted a laboratory. The results identified the hair as human, DNA consistent with a child under twelve, no match in any database. He sent the samples again. Same result. He began annotating the photographs with a red pen. The annotations became longer. The margins began to fill.

The notes change in the third week. The handwriting compresses. He writes: Hana was at the window. I went to trim her hair. I had the shears. She said Papa. I blinked and the doll was there instead. When did the doll get so tall? When did it start using her voice?

He woke on the night of the 14th of November to the sound of rhythmic cutting.

He found Hana in the corner of her room, sitting very still. The doll was on the dresser. Its hair had grown to fill the room — this is corroborated by the first officer on the scene, who noted in her report an unusual mass of black hair on the floor and walls, cold to the touch, and recorded that she could not account for the quantity. The officer attributed it to staging. She filed no follow-up.

Daiki’s fire axe was in his hands. He does not remember picking it up.

“Papa,” Hana said. Her voice carried the doubled quality I have found in nearly every account: a harmonic of child-register and something below it, something older than the voice that carries it. “She says you have to cut it. She says it’s the only way to make the humming stop.”

He believed her.

He swung.

The sound, he told me — in the flat, precise voice of a man who has constructed his survival around exactitude — was not what he had expected. He had expected something inhuman. A crack of cursed material, a rending that confirmed he was destroying a thing and not a person. The sound was soft. And wet. And human. And permanent.

The doll sat on the dresser with its hair trimmed back to a perfect bob. Its face wore the expression it always wears: patient, present, waiting.

When I visited Daiki in the institution, he was seated at a table with his hands folded. He appeared calm in the way of people who have accepted the unacceptable and no longer require the world to make sense. Before I could introduce myself, he looked at me with recognition he should not have had, and said: “You have a daughter.”

It was not a question.

“You should go home,” he said. “It already knows about her.”

I told him my family was not involved. I said I had taken precautions. He nodded with the patience of a man who has said everything useful there is to say about the gap between precaution and protection.

“The humming,” he said, as I gathered my notes to leave. “Has it started yet?”

I drove home in silence.

The silence had a texture I had not noticed before.

WHAT I FOUND AT HOME — —

I should have ended my research after Daiki. I should have had enough.

Sachi had been asking about the doll for two weeks before I understood the nature of her asking. Not directly — she asked the way children ask about things they have already decided they want: sideways, patient, persistent. She had found a photograph in my research files. She had picked it up and held it the way I have now seen described in every account: with both hands, pressed to the chest, head tilted slightly forward.

“She’s pretty,” Sachi said.

“She’s very old,” I said, and took the photograph away.

Sachi went quiet for the rest of the evening. That night I heard her murmuring in her room after midnight. When I opened the door she was asleep. Her hair, spread against the pillow, looked longer than it had that morning. I told myself it was the light. I had become a man who told himself things were the light.

My wife asked me, three mornings later, if I had been humming in my sleep. I said no. She said it had been going on for a week — a low, tuneless sound, barely audible, stopping when she touched my shoulder. I did not know I was making it.

I went back through every account I had compiled and found the same detail buried in each one: not just the daughters, but the fathers. The husbands. The people in the household who were adjacent to the attachment. The hum starts before anything else does. It starts before the hair, before the footsteps, before the drawings. It starts in the person who brought the doll home, who made the door, who let it in.

The priest whose sealed testament I found beneath the Mannen-ji floorboards wrote in his final pages: There are objects that become houses for the grief of the dead. Some remain passive. Some absorb. But some invite. Something in the mourning of a family, in the tenderness of a child, in the repetition of care and love, becomes a door. It does not want to be remembered. It wants to be carried. And what it cannot carry it consumes, cleanly, leaving only the hair as evidence that something was there.

Sachi’s hair is different this week. Not longer. Just different in the way it moves, the way it settles, the way it catches the light from the hallway at night when I check on her. I stand in the doorway and watch her sleep and feel that I am watching something that has been watched before, by fathers in Otaru and Tokyo and Hokkaido, who stood in doorways exactly like this one and felt exactly what I am feeling, which is the particular terror of loving something that something else has already noticed.

I brush her hair each morning. She tilts her head the way she always has. Afterward I look at my hands for a long time.

Last night I heard her singing.

Not from her room. From the hallway outside my bedroom door. The low tuneless melody I recognise now from every account, from Jiro’s description of what he heard through the wall, from Akiko’s notes about the sound in the pipes. The sound that starts before everything else starts.

I did not open the door.

I am writing this instead. I am writing it because the priest’s testament ended mid-sentence, because Daiki’s notes ended in the margins, because every record I found was a record that ran out before the person writing it could finish. I want this one to be complete. I want whoever finds it to see the full shape of the thing — how it moves, how it chooses, how the hair is not the sign but the signature, left after the claim has already been made.

The singing has stopped.

Now there is only the small sound of breathing on the other side of the door.

And a knock. Very light. Very patient.

And my daughter’s voice — or what is wearing it — saying: Papa. She wants to show you her hair.

The remainder of the Mori document was not recovered. Mori Tetsuya was reported missing by his wife on the morning of 3 March 2023. His daughter Sachi was found in the family home, unharmed and unresponsive, her hair significantly longer than in any prior photograph. She has not spoken since her recovery. She will not allow her hair to be cut. The Okiku Doll remains on display at Mannen-ji Temple, Hokkaido. The priests trim its hair each spring. It is always longer by morning.

If you visit — and people do, they always do — you may notice that young daughters are drawn to the display case with an unusual intensity. The priests will tell you the sweet legend. They will smile. They have been smiling for a hundred years. Do not let your daughter linger. And if, on the drive home, she asks whether the doll was lonely — say nothing. Keep your eyes on the road. Check the rear-view mirror. Make sure she is the only one sitting behind you.

chapters.title: Toire no Hanako-san
chapters.text:
✿

passed between desks in the back row, in the particular quiet before the bell

In Japan, there are stories children tell each other when they are trying to be brave. They pass them between themselves in the same low voices they use for secrets — in playgrounds at dusk, in the back rows of classrooms, in the particular quiet of a school corridor after the last teacher has gone home and the building begins to remember what it is without people inside it.

Hanako-san is one of those stories.

The legend has too many versions to count, which is part of what makes it so difficult to dismiss. Some say she was a schoolgirl who could not endure what was done to her by other children — that one afternoon she locked herself inside an elementary school bathroom stall and did not come out alive. Others say she was a casualty of the war, trapped beneath rubble when the school took a direct hit, and that she died in the dark with her hands pressed against a door that would not open. A few insist she was not murdered or bombed but simply overlooked — that she cried out for hours and no adult came — and that forgetting a child is its own kind of violence, the kind that doesn’t show a wound but leaves one anyway.

What every version agrees on is this: she died in a bathroom. Badly. Alone. The kind of death that seeps into the walls of a place and stays there long after the body has been removed and the tiles have been scrubbed and the school year has started again with new children who have never heard her name.

She learned, in that place and from that death, to wait.

THE RITUAL — —

Children say you can summon her.

You must go to the third floor — always the third floor, no one is entirely sure why, though some children say it is because san means three in Japanese, her name folded into the number like a key inside a lock. You must enter the girls’ bathroom and approach the third stall. You must knock three times, each knock evenly spaced, each one deliberate. Then you must say the words:

Are you there, Hanako-san?

If the stall says nothing, you are merely a fool. You may leave.

But if you hear a reply — even faint, even thin, even resembling a voice that is simply trying to remember how to be a voice — you must go immediately. Not walk. Not look back. Not laugh, because laughter in that bathroom is one of the quickest ways to let something know exactly where your throat is.

Those who have left in time describe the same feeling afterward: not fear, exactly. Something older than fear. A grief that arrives from nowhere, sudden and sourceless, as though they have just remembered something terrible about themselves that they cannot name.

Those who stay — who linger a second too long, or who reach for the door handle out of bravado or disbelief — are never satisfactorily accounted for. Their disappearances are filed. The files go into drawers. The drawers are locked. And the school year begins again.

THE BOYS — —

At Yamabuki Elementary, two boys named Daichi and Ryo decided to summon her on a Thursday afternoon in late October.

They were eleven. They were the kind of boys who tested everything — authority, pain tolerance, the patience of every adult who had ever tried to reason with them. They had been tormenting a quiet girl in their class for the better part of a year: small cruelties at first, the kind that leave no mark, and then larger ones, the kind administered in bathrooms and stairwells where no teacher could see. The girl had ink-black hair and a mole beneath her left eye and a habit of looking at the floor when she walked. She had stopped coming to school six weeks before the boys performed the ritual. A complaint had been filed. A file had been made. The file had been placed in a drawer and the drawer had been locked and no further action had been taken, because the boys’ fathers were the kind of men who donated to building funds.

They chose the old third-floor bathroom because it was always colder than the rest of the building, even in summer. The corridor leading to it had windows yellowed with age and lights that flickered the way lights flicker when a building is trying to communicate something it lacks the vocabulary for.

They entered just before sunset.

The bathroom smelled of industrial disinfectant and wet stone and, underneath those things, something else — something sweet and faintly rotten, like fruit left too long in standing water. The tiles were pale and cracked. The stalls stood in a row, each door scarred with scratches and the evidence of bored hands. A tap dripped at the far end of the room with a patience that felt less like a mechanical fault and more like a habit. Each drop landed in the exact same place, in the exact same rhythm, as though it had been doing this for years and had learned to enjoy it.

Daichi knocked three times on the third stall door.

The sound was too loud. It rang through the bathroom the way a sound rings in a place that was holding its breath before you made it.

He leaned close to the door. Behind him, Ryo was grinning too hard — the grin of a boy who had already realised he had made a mistake and was not yet ready to admit it.

Are you there, Hanako-san?

The tap dripped. Once. Twice.

The reply came.

Not loud. Not dramatic. It was small and close and wet, like a mouth that had been submerged and was learning, slowly, how to form words again. It came from directly behind the door — not from within the stall, but from the crack between the door and the frame, as though whatever produced the sound had pressed itself against the gap to be as near as possible.

Yes.

The boys left.

Later, separately, each told the same story without knowing the other had told it: as they fled down the corridor, they heard a sound behind them. Not footsteps. Not screaming. A slow, wet dragging noise — something small being pulled across damp tile with great patience — as though whatever was inside the stall had nowhere to be in a hurry and had all the time it needed to follow.

They never spoke of it to each other. They never went back.

The school, however, did not stop being haunted just because they were frightened.

THE REPORTS — —

The first report was filed by Ishida, a night guard who had worked the school for eleven years without a single unusual incident. He was a pragmatic man, a former railway worker, not given to imagination.

He saw her on the second floor, near the music room, on a Wednesday evening in the first week of November.

A girl. Small. Standing at the end of the corridor with her head tilted at an angle that suggested she was reading something written on the wall — something that was not there. He called out. She turned — not her body, only her head, rotating with a slowness that was wrong in the way that wrongness sometimes precedes understanding — and then the lights died. When they came back, she was gone. The corridor smelled of wet bathroom tile, sharp and distinct, though the floors had just been mopped.

He submitted a report. He described it as a possible intruder. He described himself as uncertain of what he had seen.

Two nights later he heard the lockers.

Not the sound of them being opened. The sound of them being dragged — a long metal screech across linoleum, coming from the gymnasium corridor. He followed the sound. The doors were still trembling when he arrived. On the floor, a dark puddle of water, cold enough that the sweat on his palms froze when he pressed a hand to it. Inside the lockers — he checked three of them — a faint residue, black and slick, that smelled of stagnant pond water and something underneath that he could not name and did not try to.

He did not open the fourth locker.

He stopped taking the third-floor bathroom key off the hook at the start of his shift. He told himself there was nothing that ever needed checking up there. He did not look closely at this reasoning.

Another guard, filling in on a weekend, reported hearing a child crying in the east stairwell. When he reached the landing, the crying had stopped. At the bottom of the stairs there were footprints — small, bare, wet — appearing one after another from nowhere, as though the floor were producing them from inside itself. He followed them. They ended at the door of the third-floor bathroom.

He did not open that door either.

The smell spread. It was the smell of old copper and stagnant water, a wound in the building’s air that no amount of cleaning could address. The janitor refused to clean the third floor after dark. The secretary found the stall locks in the girls’ bathroom twisted open each morning, though she was certain they were latched at night. And the calls began — small, tentative sounds from empty corridors, from rooms that should have held no one. Not calls for help, exactly. Something more deliberate than that. The sound of a voice practising. Getting its pitch right. Learning again how to be heard.

THE HEADTEACHER — —

Her name was Moriguchi Haruko, and she had been principal of Yamabuki Elementary for fourteen years. In that time she had managed floods, a school fire, a parent’s suicide, and two separate incidents of a kind that never made it into official reports. She was a woman who had survived by refusing to give things their true names. She believed in patterns. She believed in paperwork. She believed, deeply and with the conviction of someone who has never been proven wrong in the way that really costs something, that every strange noise had a practical explanation if one had enough patience to find it.

She had filed the complaint about the quiet girl. She had locked it in a drawer. There had been a pattern to that decision too — the boys’ fathers, the building fund, the way certain names in a small town made certain problems disappear faster than others. She had not examined this reasoning. She had moved on.

Now the reports sat on her desk in a stack, and she looked at them the way she looked at all problems: as a matter to be closed.

She would spend a night in the school. She would see nothing. She would have evidence, and the evidence would be the shape of nothing, and the nothing would be sufficient to end the speculation.

She went on a Friday in mid-November, when the building was fully empty and the moon was high and cold. She brought her wool coat and her scarf and her flask of tea and two files she needed to review — the disciplinary files of Daichi and Ryo, whose formal hearing had been scheduled for the following Monday. There had been new complaints. She needed to be ready.

She sat at her desk on the second floor and worked until she could no longer focus, and then she rested her eyes, and then without deciding to she slept.

What woke her was not a sound.

It was cold.

Not the cold of a window left open or a heater switched off — a different kind of cold entirely. Subcutaneous. Considered. The kind that seeps into bone and stays there as though it has been looking for somewhere warm to extinguish. She was wearing her coat. She was wearing her scarf. She was shivering with a violence that had bypassed her control of her own muscles. Her breath showed in the air. The desk lamp burned yellow and thin, as though something in the room were consuming the light before it could properly spread.

She raised her head.

The shadow on the far wall did not belong to anything in the room.

It was child-sized. It was cast by nothing she could see. It was absolutely still — the stillness of something that has learned how to be patient, something that has had years to practice it. It was not looking at her. It was looking at the desk.

She looked at the desk.

The drawer was open.

She had locked that drawer before she slept. She remembered this clearly, with the particular sharpness of a memory that knows it will matter later. The drawer was open by several inches. On the desk, the two disciplinary files were spread wide, their photographs face up: Daichi and Ryo in their formal school portraits, each with a careful smile, each with the groomed certainty of boys whose fathers had money. As she watched, a thin bead of moisture traced the edge of each photograph, and the ink on their faces began to move — bleeding slowly downward, emptying their eyes into dark, wet stains on the paper.

The water was coming from somewhere below the files.

In the back of the open drawer, beneath where the boys’ files had been, there was a third folder — thinner, older, its cover yellowed and warped, its edges furred with something dark. Its label was written in faded blue ink. She had not seen this folder in eight years. She had believed, with a certainty she had never tested, that it was buried deep enough to stay buried.

Yamaguchi Hanako.

The girl with the ink-black hair.

The mole beneath her left eye.

The complaint Moriguchi had filed away without action, because the bullies had been promising students and their fathers were the kind of men who built wings of buildings and had their names put on them. The complaint that documented what had been done to the girl — in corridors, in stairwells, in bathrooms, particularly bathrooms — and what the girl had eventually done to herself, on a Thursday evening after school, alone in the third stall on the third floor, with a length of rope

taken from the gymnasium supply room, her neck bent at an angle the responding officers had described in terms Moriguchi had not allowed herself to read in full.

No one had found her until morning.

Moriguchi had closed the file. She had locked the drawer. She had told herself the pattern held.

Slowly, with the nausea of someone who has known a truth for years and has finally run out of drawer space for it, she looked up from the desk.

The window behind her desk looked out onto the external concrete walkway, three floors above the ground. The walkway was bare. There was nothing out there that could grow, nothing that could be placed there, no structural reason for anything to be on that narrow strip of concrete in the middle of the night.

A figure stood at the glass.

It was small. It wore a school uniform, a white blouse with a bow at the collar, a dark skirt. Its hair was ink-black, perfectly straight, hanging to its jaw. It stood pressed close to the glass but breathed no fog onto it. Its face was turned downward, as though reading something on the other side of Moriguchi’s desk — the open drawer, the old file, the wet photographs.

The figure raised its head.

Where a face should have been, there was only shadow — not darkness exactly, but an absence of the kind that has weight. A hollow carved out of the air. A space deep enough to hold silence.

Then the tap in the en-suite bathroom beside her office began to drip.

Tap. Tap.

Tap.

Not random. Not mechanical. Three times, evenly spaced. A knock made by water.

Moriguchi’s chair crashed backward as she stood. The sound in the corridor outside was already beginning — soft and patient, a wet dragging noise against the floorboards. Something small, moving without hurry. The thing outside the window was gone. The walkway was empty. The office plant stood in its pot in the corner where it always had, its shadow thrown by the desk lamp in a shape that was only a plant, only leaves, only something ordinary in a room that had ceased to be ordinary.

She understood, in the way that terrible clarity arrives, that she had been looking at the wrong window.

The en-suite bathroom door was directly across the room.

Its frosted glass held the silhouette of a child standing on the other side, not moving, its palm pressed flat against the pane. A single dark handprint bled moisture down the glass. A voice drifted through the gap at the bottom of the door — wet, close, intimate, the voice of someone speaking from directly behind the ear.

Principal Moriguchi.

It said her name with a patience that had been cultivated over eight years of waiting.

Are you there?

The brass handle began to turn.

They said you wouldn’t come. They said you’d put it back in the drawer, like you did mine.

The handle completed its rotation. The latch disengaged. From beyond the door, a sound rose — not the dripping of a single tap now, but the roar of a thousand toilets flushing in unison, water rushing up to meet something, porcelain yawning open, an impossible depth beneath a school building that had stood on flat ground for sixty years.

The door swung wide.

From the bowl of the toilet, rising with the slow certainty of a thing that has been underneath for a long time and has finally decided to surface, came a shape of wet hair and broken limbs. It unfolded upward in sections, each joint cracking with the sound of something that had been set wrong and left to heal wrong. The face that cleared the rim was not a child’s face. It was the face of a drowned girl — lips blue, skin waterlogged to a greenish pallor, eyes stretched permanently wide in the expression of someone who waited and waited and was never found. Water poured from her mouth, her nostrils, her ears, ran down her arms, pooled at her feet. But she was smiling. And the smile had too many teeth, and the teeth were very white, and Moriguchi understood that the teeth had been white for eight years, in the dark, in the third stall, waiting for exactly this.

You’re a bad person, Sensei, Hanako said. The voice came from everywhere — the tiles, the pipes, the inside of Moriguchi’s skull, the space behind her teeth. But don’t worry. I have the boys already. I need someone who knew and said nothing. I need someone to hold the door shut. The way no one held anything open for me.

A cold, wet hand closed around Moriguchi’s ankle.

The floor tilted.

The bathroom elongated into a throat.

The third stall gaped.

She screamed. The scream was swallowed by porcelain.

The following Monday morning, the school secretary arrived at seven forty-five to find the headteacher’s office empty. The coat was draped over the chair. The scarf was on the floor, still cold to the touch. The desk lamp burned. The flask of tea stood half-finished at the corner of the desk.

The disciplinary files of Daichi and Ryo lay neatly stacked and closed, their photographs perfectly intact.

Behind them, atop the open drawer, sat a folder the secretary did not recognize — yellowed, water-warped, its edges dark. She opened it. Inside was a single class photograph, front row center, a small girl with ink-black hair and a mole beneath her left eye. The girl’s face had been scratched out with something sharp and deliberate. On the back of the photograph, in handwriting that was childish and careful and had not been there the day before, someone had written in small hiragana:

Now there are three.

The drawer was locked. The secretary did not have a key. She could not explain how the file had gotten out.

She filed a report. She placed the report on the headteacher’s desk, inside a folder. She locked the office door and went to find someone who knew what to do.

No one knew what to do.

The school year continued. New children filled the hallways. And the children, as children always do, began in time to add a new rule to the Hanako-san game — a rule passed down in the same low voices, in the same corner of the playground, in the same long afternoons before the light went.

If you knock on the third stall and hear a girl reply, run immediately. Everyone knows this rule.

But if you knock and hear two voices — one a child’s, thin and patient, and beneath it a woman’s, hollow and half-mad and endlessly apologizing — you do not simply run.

You never come back to that school. You tell no one what you heard. You spend the rest of your life being careful about which drawers you open and which complaints you choose not to file and which quiet children you choose to walk past in the corridor.

Because Hanako-san is not only a ghost. She is a record. She keeps account of everyone who saw and said nothing. And the school, they say, is very old. And the school has not yet run out of room.

Are you there, Hanako-san?

She has always been there.

She is waiting to see who opens the door.

passed between desks in the back row, in the particular quiet before the bell

In Japan, there are stories children tell each other when they are trying to be brave. They pass them between themselves in the same low voices they use for secrets — in playgrounds at dusk, in the back rows of classrooms, in the particular quiet…

chapters.title: The Red Room Curse
chapters.text:
⚠ SYSTEM WARNING ✕

Nadia Vasquez had spent eleven years writing about things that were not real, and she was very good at it. She had a gift — her editor called it a gift, though she privately thought of it as a kind of controlled lying — for making folklore feel immediate. For finding the warm, human center of a ghost story and pressing on it until it bled just enough to stain the page.Paranormal Digest paid her well. She paid her rent. The system worked.

The Red Room Curse assignment arrived on a Wednesday. She’d seen the legend before — everyone in her line of work had. A pop-up. A voice asking a question no one wanted to answer. A man in Japan who pulled his cables and lost. She knew the shape of it the way a butcher knows the shape of an animal before the cut. She poured a glass of water, opened a blank document, and began.

“Before you think of escape rooms or what rich people do for fun on weekends, I must warn you — this is nothing close to it, and it’s considerably darker...”

“The pop-up features a red screen. Black text. A voice — no one has ever determined whose — asking a single question. The voice does not wait for your answer. It never has.”

“The case of a man known only as Hokisho is the legend’s anchor point. The video exists, or existed, in the grey folds of the dark net. A man in a Japanese apartment. A pop-up he cannot close. A cable he pulls. A screen that comes back on anyway. And then—”

She stopped. Stretched her neck. The apartment was quiet in the way apartments are quiet at 2 AM — not peaceful, merely emptied of its daytime pretenses. The refrigerator hummed. A car moved slowly through rain outside. She read back what she had written, made two small changes, and saved.

The document shimmered. She had seen screen artifacts before — a tired GPU, a refresh stutter. She leaned forward and opened the file again.

The title had not changed.RedRoom_FEATURE_FINAL.doc.

The contents had.

OPERATIONAL NOTE — RED ROOM PROTOCOL V. 4.1 — —

The term “red room” as employed in colloquial internet folklore is a deliberate misdirection seeded by the network’s passive recruitment infrastructure. Subjects who research the legend extensively enough to write about it have already completed Stage 1 of the contact sequence.

Stage 2 initiates at first document save. The firmware-level exploit embedded during the subject’s most recent peripheral driver update —— activates a passive capture thread running beneath all user- accessible processes. The subject will not detect this in Task Manager. The thread does not appear in Task Manager.

Stage 3: The voice prompt. The prompt is not pre-recorded. Pre- recorded implies a fixed source — a speaker, a studio, a moment in time when someone chose to make a sound. The prompt is assembled in real time from phoneme fragments harvested across the subject’s prior audio. It uses their own auditory memory of language. This is why different subjects describe the voice differently. It sounds, to each of them, almost familiar.

Stage 4: The list. The names are not historical. The list is current. Names are added at the moment the subject’s cursor stops moving for longer than ninety seconds — the interval that indicates the subject has stopped typing and has begun to understand.

Nadia sat very still. The kind of still that precedes a decision.

She was a rational woman. She had a master’s degree in journalism and a minor in digital media studies and she had spent eleven years writing about things that were not real. She scrolled down.

SUBJECT PROFILE — CURRENT SESSION — —

Subject: Vasquez, Nadia. Freelance. 11 years horror/folklore beat.

Location:. Hardware: Dell XPS 15, Windows 11, last peripheral update.

First contact initiated: 19 days prior, via corrupted metadata in an archived forum post the subject visited during preliminary research. The post appeared to load normally. The subject did not notice the three-second rendering delay.

The subject has not noticed the camera yet. Most subjects do not notice the camera until Stage 4. The camera is not a hidden device. It is the subject’s own laptop webcam. The green indicator light is disabled at the driver level. This has been standard since v.3.0.

Current stage: 3. Voice prompt cycle completion: 02:29:41. Subject is still typing. Subject believes she is still writing her article.

She is not writing her article.

Nadia pushed back from the desk so fast the chair struck the wall behind her.

She stood in the centre of her apartment and looked at her laptop from a distance, the way you might look at a dog that has done something unexpected. The screen glowed white-blue in the dark. She was breathing through her nose in long, deliberate intervals, a technique she used when sources lied to her, when the story wasn’t the story, when she needed to think without letting the panic think for her.

The camera. Her own camera. She reached the desk in three steps and pressed her palm flat over the webcam lens. Then she closed the laptop.

The screen in her peripheral vision continued to glow.

She had closed the laptop. She was certain she had closed it. The hinge had clicked. She had felt the resistance and the catch. But when she turned, it was open — angle unchanged, as if she hadn’t touched it at all. The document was still on screen. Somewhere in the building, a pipe made a sound like a sentence with a word missing.

She thought about Hokisho. She had written about Hokisho dozens of times — lifted his story from its grainy source, filed the serial numbers off, repackaged it for audiences who wanted to be frightened and then

un-frightened in the span of a commute. She had always treated his panic as the story. The pulling of the cable. The screen coming back. The inexplicable resurrection of the machine.

What she had never asked, in eleven years, was what he had been researching before the pop-up appeared.

The thing about the Hokisho video that no one discussed was not the blood. It was the open document on his screen. Visible for four frames before the camera feed cut to red. A white rectangle, dense with text. Someone had been writing.

She had not typed that paragraph. She read it again. It was in her voice — her rhythm, her particular way of front-loading a sentence with deflection before the gut-punch. But she had not written it. She would have remembered writing it because it was good. It was the best paragraph in the piece. It was the kind of sentence that arrived rarely, that you held carefully for fear of damaging it.

She scrolled down.

NOTE ON PREVIOUS SUBJECTS WHO ATTEMPTED TO CLOSE THE DOCUMENT:

All of them attempted to close the document. This is expected and does not affect the outcome. The document is not the mechanism. The document is the record. The mechanism has been running since Stage 1. Closing the document does not close the mechanism any more than closing a window closes the weather.

What the subject is experiencing as confusion — the gap between what she typed and what the file contains — is not a glitch. It is the most accurate thing that has ever appeared on her screen. She has been writing folklore for eleven years. She has always described the room as something that happened to other people in other places. She is now learning that description was always the door, and she has been holding it open since the first piece she filed.

Every article. Every feature. Every time she repackaged the legend for a new audience, she extended the list. She did not add herself to it. She added her readers.

Nadia stopped reading.

She sat with that for a moment — not reading, not moving, not performing the calm she no longer had access to. She thought about the eleven years of Halloween features and digital folklore roundups and “Top Ten Creepypastas That Will Ruin Your Sleep” listicles that had run under her byline. She thought about the readers. She thought about the way her pieces circulated — forwarded, reposted, linked in Reddit threads, screen-capped and sent in group chats. She thought about how many people had sat in quiet apartments, at 2 AM, reading her careful repackaging of the Red Room, feeling that precise, pleasurable chill of being nearly frightened without quite crossing the line.

She thought about how many of them had then, idly, started typing.

The screen flickered once.

The document dissolved. Not to black — to red. A deep, arterial red that lit her face and the wall behind her. Black text appeared, centred, in a serif font she did not recognise.

HOKISHO 2021 / TOKYO — —

LEONARD CROSS 2022 / NEW YORK — —

JULIAN VANCE 2022 / CHICAGO — —

ELIAS OMONDI 2023 / NAIROBI — —

MARCUS OSEI 2024 / LONDON — —

. . . . . .

VASQUEZ, NADIA 2026 / — —

She noticed something. Below her name, the list did not end. There was one more line — not a name. A counter, rendered in the same thin serif, updating in real time.

PASSIVE RECRUITMENT — CURRENT CYCLE — —

Subjects reading this document via published distribution: 2,847 and incrementing.

Stage 1 initiates on scroll past this line.

The subject asked, once, in an early draft that she has since forgotten writing:whose voice is it, really?

The answer has always been the same. It is the voice of everyone who ever wrote about it and sent it outward into the world, accumulated and compressed, speaking in unison, asking a question that only works because the person hearing it is already curious.

The question is not a threat.

The question is an inventory.

Do you like the red room?

The question is asking: have you been here before?

The question already knows the answer.

From her laptop speakers — she would later tell no one this, because there was no later in any useful sense — she heard a voice ask its question. She had expected something inhuman. Something synthesised and cold. Instead it sounded like her. Not quite. A half- step off. The way a recording of your own voice always sounds like a stranger wearing your face.

She closed the laptop a second time.

This time it stayed closed.

The screen on the closed laptop glowed red through the seam.

The piece was filed at 6:14 AM. Her editor, Rashid Park, received it with the subject line FINAL DRAFT — REDROOM FEATURE — CLEAN. He read it over his morning coffee and thought it was excellent — sharp, modern, a little too inside-baseball for a general audience but that was fixable, he could cut the technical middle section, the stuff about driver exploits and passive threads, that was

the kind of detail that made readers anxious in the wrong way. He marked it approved. He sent Nadia a congratulatory email. She didn’t respond, but she sometimes didn’t, she was like that.

He published the piece on October 14th.

That evening, idly, he read it again in the published version. He noticed the document felt longer than what he remembered editing. He scrolled down. Below the conclusion he had signed off on, there was a new section he had not approved.

It was about him.

— — —

Three things remain true about the Red Room, verifiable across every version of the story: the pop-up cannot be closed by closing it; the screen cannot be killed by killing the power; and the voice does not stop speaking until it has finished asking its question.

What no version of the story mentions — what the people who write about it are always careful to leave out, whether consciously or not — is that the question does not end with a question mark.

It ends with a period.

As if it already knows.

FILE: REDROOM_FEATURE_FINAL_VASQUEZ.DOC — —

SIZE: 147 PAGES [ORIGINAL SUBMISSION: 6 PAGES] — —

LAST MODIFIED: [TIMESTAMP UNREADABLE] — —

AUTHOR: VASQUEZ, NADIA [AND 2,847 OTHERS] — —

STATUS: Document is still open. Document is still being written.

If you have read this far, you have already scrolled past the line. The cursor is blinking somewhere with your name beside it. It has been blinking since you started reading.

chapters.title: No Face
chapters.text:
▲

Alpine Rescue · Camping party of four

Mariam and her friends had been planning this trip for months. Camping and hiking in the Alps — it was going to be legendary. The kind of trip that became a story you told for years. Sweeping scenic views, crisp mountain air, the rare chance to just be with the people you loved most before life scattered you in different directions.

The thunder in the distance threatened to end all of it before it began. She stared out the car window and prayed quietly that the weather would hold.

“Quit daydreaming, nerd!”

That was Travis — harassing his younger brother again. Jamie had been sitÝng quietly in the backseat with a book in his lap, lost somewhere between its pages. He barely flinched.

Mariam adored Jamie. Precisely because he was the kind of person the world hadn’t quite figured out how to handle yet — shy, thoughtful, a little awkward. Travis had decided that the solution to his brother’s introversion was exposure therapy, which was why he’d convinced Esmeralda to bring her younger sister Amanda along. He’d said nothing about his actual reasoning, of course. Mariam had pieced it together herself.

“Travis, do you really have to bully him into interacting?” Gracia called from outside the car, hoisting the camp stove out of the trunk.

“He’ll die alone without even a gay relationship to show for it.”

“You’re just jealous, Travis.”

Mariam walked over to the car window and knocked on the glass. Jamie looked up.

“Hey, Einstein. Want to come out here and test the theory of relativity? Specifically — what’s the gravitational outcome if I push Travis off that ridge?”

He looked at her for a moment, then smiled — small and real. He got out of the car, squinting at the treeline. When his eyes accidentally met Esmeralda’s, he looked away so fast she had to cover her mouth to hide her laugh. He was ridiculous. She liked that about him immediately.

“Alright!” Mariam clapped her hands. “Travis, Jamie, Gallagher — go get the wood.”

Gallagher already had his shirt off, flexing for no one in particular as he stacked bags near the clearing. He was the kind of man who treated every social gathering like an audition.

“Yes, ma’am!”

“Don’t — don’t call me that.”

The three men disappeared into the trees. The women stayed back, setÝng up the cooking equipment and digging a pit for the bonfire.

In the woods, the boys talked baseball. Travis didn’t follow sports and felt like a stranger in the conversation, so he drifted slightly apart, half-listening, watching the ground.

Something was wrong with the leaves.

They were rotÝng — soft and dark, pressed flat to the soil. But the ground wasn’t wet. He crouched and touched the earth. Dry. So why were the leaves decomposing like that? Like something had been moving through here, again and again, for a long time.

“Watch it —”

He threw his arm across Jamie’s chest before his brother took another step. Jamie froze.

Travis picked up a stick and poked the ground in front of them.

Snap.

The trap closed so fast the stick exploded into splinters. They both stood there, staring at the broken wood.

“Well,” Jamie said.

“Yeah.”

Travis felt it then — the sensation of eyes. Not from any direction he could pin down. Just a general, creeping certainty that something in the treeline was watching them, measuring them, deciding something. He looked back at the shadows between the trunks. Nothing he could point to. Nothing he could say without sounding paranoid.

He didn’t mention it. They kept walking.

Somewhere in the dark behind them, something turned and moved away — unhurried, deliberate. Not fleeing. Simply finished watching, for now.

By the time they returned with the wood, the women had set up camp and the darkness was rolling in fast. The thunderclouds from that morning had multiplied, stacking against the mountain until the sky looked bruised.

“The forecast said nothing about rain,” Mariam said, studying the clouds with her arms crossed.

“The forecast lied,” Gracia told her.

They built the bonfire anyway. The warmth was immediate and real and for a while everything felt fine — marshmallows on sticks, the crackle and pop of burning wood, the smell of pine in the cold air.

“You know they say this area is haunted.”

A chorus of groans. Marshmallows were thrown.

“Enough.”

“Absolutely not.”

“Oh my God, Gallagher.”

“Wait,” Travis said, leaning forward. “You haven’t heard the local folklore?”

Silence. Everyone turned.

“There’s a figure that’s said to move through these woods. No sound — no footsteps, no breathing, nothing you can hear. No one has ever seen its face. The stories describe it as a shadow that moves against the light.”

“What kind of deaths?” Esmeralda asked. Her voice was quiet. The first time she’d spoken directly to the group all evening.

Everyone noticed.

Travis looked at her. “No bodies, mostly. Just cars found at the bottom of the river. Doors locked. Windows up. The victims still strapped into their seats.”

The fire crackled. No one spoke for a moment.

“Okay!” Mariam stood. “Wonderful bedtime story. Who wants stew?”

She cracked open two cans — beef, peas — and within minutes a pot was simmering over the flame. Rations were passed around. Conversation picked back up, looser now, the story fading into background noise.

In the trees, perhaps thirty meters out, something stood perfectly still and watched them eat.

The wind came first. Then the smell — that heavy, metallic bite of rain about to fall. The first drops hit the firepit and it hissed.

“Move!” Mariam yelled, and everyone scrambled.

She ended up in a tent with Travis. Gracia pulled Esmeralda into the second tent. Gallagher landed in the third with Jamie.

"This is what I get?” Gallagher stared at the ceiling. “I was supposed to be having a romantic evening.”

“With who?” Jamie asked.

Gallagher didn’t answer.

In the other tent, Gracia was already teasing her sister.

“Aww. Poor Essie wanted to be in Jamie’s tent.”

“I did not.”

“You wanted to kiss him.”

“I will genuinely push you out of this tent.”

Lightning turned the fabric white for a split second — and in that flash, Esmeralda saw it. Just outside the tent wall. A shape. Tall. Still.

“Gracia.”

“What?”

Another flash. It was still there. Same position. It hadn’t moved.

"Gracia."

Mariam was telling Travis about how this trip was supposed to be perfect. About Canada. About how she’d been building toward this one last memory with everyone before her life changed shape entirely. Travis was trying to be soothing about it, which mostly meant saying it’ll be fine in five different ways.

Then a sound. Just outside. Not the rain. Not the wind.

Something stepping on a branch.

Too close.

She grabbed Travis’s arm.

Whatever it was moved, then stopped. Then moved again — circling, maybe. A flash of lightning, a scream from the other tent, and suddenly everyone was out in the rain, flashlights cutÝng through the dark and the downpour, standing around a long rip in the side of Gracia and Esmeralda’s tent.

“I thought it was this creep,” Gracia said, pointing at Gallagher.

“I may be a bad person,” Gallagher said with genuine offense, “but I’m not insane."

Jamie appeared with an umbrella — of course he had one — and held it over the women while Travis made the call.

“Everyone into the cars. We’re sleeping there tonight.”

The storm passed somewhere around two in the morning. The moon surfaced. Silver light spread across the forest floor and everything went quiet.

Travis was in the driver’s seat, turned sideways, talking to Mariam. He heard something shift outside — a footstep? He looked at the driver’s side window.

A face.

No — not a face. A shape where a face should be. Something standing close enough to fog the glass, close enough to reach out and touch, and where the features should have been there was just —

He blinked.

Nothing. Gone. Just his reflection in the dark glass.

He didn’t tell Mariam.

“I need to pee.”

Esmeralda had been holding it since the storm started. Gracia took one look at her sister’s expression and understood immediately that this was non- negotiable.

They agreed not to wake Jamie. He’d worry, and worrying made him do things like suggest they stay in the car until sunrise, which was still four hours away.

The woods were quiet as they walked to the treeline. The wet grass mufÒed their footsteps. Somewhere an owl called once and went silent.

“Turn around,” Esmeralda told her sister.

“It’s nothing I haven’t —”

"Turn around."

Gracia turned.

She listened to the sound of running water on leaves and stared at the dark spaces between the trunks. She thought about Jamie’s story — the cars at the bottom of the river, the locked doors. She thought about the shape she’d seen outside the tent in the lightning.

She was still thinking about it when her sister screamed.

Gallagher was on the ground. The wooden stake had gone clean through — in through the chest, out through the back. It wasn’t sharpened. That was the worst part. A sharpened stake would have been fast. This had torn.

Mariam was working, hands moving the way they moved when she was in that part of her brain — clinical, focused, not quite present. EMS training. She had done CPR simulations and trauma scenarios and this was not a simulation.

“I can’t stop it here,” she said. Her voice was very even. “The lung damage is too much. Without a chest tube, without —”

“He’s going to be fine,” Travis said.

She didn’t answer.

Travis looked up at Gracia, who had arrived from the treeline breathless and pale.

He noticed the empty space beside her.

“Where’s Esmeralda?”

Gracia turned. Looked. Looked again. Turned in a full circle with her flashlight, sweeping the beam across wet grass and dark trunks and nothing else.

“Essie?”

Nothing.

"Essie!"

They ran toward the scream. Flashlight beams swung through the trees like panicked signals. Thirty minutes of stumbling through wet undergrowth, calling her name until their voices were raw.

Nothing. No trace.

“Back to camp,” Jamie said finally. “She might have gone back.”

They turned.

“Which way is camp?” Mariam asked.

The silence that followed was the kind that takes up space.

Then Jamie’s light caught something moving at the edge of visibility.

“Esmeralda?”

The figure stopped. He raised his beam. It swept up the shape — tall, still, facing him — and where the face should have been there was nothing. Not darkness. Not shadow. Just an absence, smooth and featureless, as if the face had never been there to begin with.

"Guys."

They turned to look. The flashlight beam swept the spot.

Empty.

“I’m telling you, there was no face,” Jamie said. His voice was shaking.

“That’s not possible,” Travis said.

“I know what I saw.”

“The human face has —”

"Travis," Gracia said. “Please find my sister.”

Travis found camp by pressing the key fob. The headlights blinked to life through the trees and they ran toward them, stumbling over roots and wet leaves until they broke into the clearing.

“I’ll go back in,” Travis said. “I’ll find her.”

“Travis —”

“I’m not asking.” He kissed Mariam once, briefly. “Lock the doors.”

She watched the treeline take him.

Jamie sat with his back against the car window, watching the dark. The girls were inside. He was keeping watch, which felt hollow because he wasn’t sure what he would do if something came out of the trees. He had his flashlight. He had a pocketknife. He had, probably, no chance.

His eyelids were getÝng heavy.

The knock on the window was so loud it felt like a gunshot.

Everyone lurched left. Jamie’s heart was slamming.

“Is that —” he started.

"Esmeralda!" Gracia lunged for the door handle.

The object came through the glass before she touched it — fast and horizontal and deliberate — and stopped with its point three inches from Gracia’s face. Esmeralda sagged against the door. She was making a sound, a horrible wet struggling sound.

Gracia put her hand flat against the glass.

Something landed on the hood with a wet, heavy sound.

Jamie looked.

He looked for a long time.

“Travis,” he said softly, in a voice he didn’t recognize as his own.

The door locks clicked down, all four at once, like a decision being made. Then Gracia’s door swung open anyway — something had it, something outside with a grip that ignored the laws of how strong a person could be — and she was screaming and kicking and Jamie and Mariam grabbed her arms and pulled, and it made no difference at all.

She was gone.

The door closed.

Silence.

Mariam and Jamie sat in the backseat, pressed together, breathing.

Up ahead, at the edge of the headlight beams, something stood in the road. It stood the way a person stands — upright, weight distributed, hands at its sides — but it was still in a way that people aren’t. No swaying. No breathing visible in the cold air. Just a shape, featureless above the collar line, watching them with whatever it used to watch.

The headlights flickered.

It was gone.

They didn’t speak. Jamie checked his phone — still no signal. He was going to check again in five minutes, and then five minutes after that, and they both knew they would keep doing this because it was something to do.

The rocking started slowly. Like something testing the weight of the car. Then harder. The chassis groaned. Jamie looked out the rear window and couldn’t see anything — no shape, no hands, nothing — but the car was tilting, the left wheels leaving the ground, and Mariam was screaming, and he grabbed the seat back with both hands as the world rotated sideways.

The car hit the ground.

The impact drove the air out of him. He was on top of Mariam, her back against the passenger window, the whole car on its side like a dead thing.

She gasped. Reached for her back. Her face changed.

“Mariam —”

Then the lights came.

Floodlights, plural, cutÝng through the cracked windows from every direction at once. The sound of boots on gravel. Multiple sets, coordinated, moving fast.

A voice — male, flat, professional — speaking into a radio through what sounded like a respirator:

“Team two, sector four. Contain it.”

And then, after a pause that felt like it lasted years:

“Civilians present. Initiate protocol seven.”

The boots got closer.

Mariam looked at Jamie in the shifting light. He looked back at her.

Protocol seven.

Neither of them knew what that meant.

They were about to find out.
