chapters.title: Drip
chapters.text:
Estate of the late occupant

Oh, Uncle Will. What did you get yourself into?

The will and the title deed had arrived in the same envelope. Jayden Vile stood in the doorway of his uncle’s house — his house now, technically — and stared at the taps.

The death had been sudden. Strange, even. Heart attacks happened, sure, but not usually in bathtubs. Not to men in their late sixties who swam laps three times a week and kept a blood pressure journal. The coroner’s report was still pending, sent off to a city lab for further assessment, and Jay had a feeling he wasn’t going to like what it said.

What bothered him most, though, were the dripping taps.

“Sorry, Jayden. I’ve checked them six times. Nothing I can do right now.” The plumber had shrugged, tools in hand, the kind of man whose apologies meant this is beyond me. Everything tested fine. Every joint sealed, every valve tight. But the moment Jay was alone, it started again. Drip. Drip. Almost taunting.

One morning he woke to find his bathroom flooded. Drops falling into standing water, each one sending out a perfect ring.

“Changed all the pipes. Should be fine now.” The plumber seemed almost offended by the house. Jay stared at the old pipes piled by the curb and told himself: tonight I’ll sleep.

He hadn’t planned to stay this long. His original idea had been simple — sell the house, collect whatever Will had left him, go back to the city. But the repairs stretched on, and somewhere in those two weeks the house had stopped feeling temporary.

He was in the Walmart checkout line, radio humming overhead, when a voice said his name.

“You’re Jayden Vile?”

He turned. Short woman, dark hair, bright eyes, the kind of smile that assumed friendship before it was offered.

“Yes—” He extended his hand. She pulled him into a bear hug before he could finish the gesture.

“Grace Njambi. Welcome to the neighborhood!”

He stood there, arms half-raised, unsure whether to hug back.

Welcome to the neighborhood. Like he was staying. Like he’d moved in with a couch and a houseplant and a five-year lease.

“Technically, I’m not here that long,” he said, when she let go.

“Doesn’t matter. We make everyone feel at home.” She tilted her head toward the exit. “Some friends and I are grabbing drinks. You should come. Nothing else on your list, right?”

He looked down at his basket — canned beans, instant rice, a box of granola bars. She had a point.

Outside, three people were leaning against a truck: two women and a man with crossed arms and a look like he’d already decided something.

“Alex, Hilda, Brandon,” Grace said, moving down the line. “Guys, this is Jayden.”

The women smiled. Brandon looked him up and down. “City boy, huh?”

Hilda slapped his arm.

Jay said nothing. He’d met Brandons before.

They drove into the woods and built a fire. Jay hadn’t expected that either. He sat on a log with a beer going warm in his hand, watching the flames, and thought that this was the first time he’d relaxed since arriving.

“So how’s the house?” Hughie asked — the driver, a big man with an easy laugh. “Heard it’s haunted.”

“That what people say?” Jay asked.

Brandon pointed with his beer. “Your uncle was weird, man. Everyone knew it.”

“Well,” Jay said, “I haven’t seen a poltergeist. Just leaky taps.” He smiled at the fire, feeling the quiet triumph of the replaced pipes. Past tense. “Won’t be missing those.”

They laughed, and the night folded in around the fire, easy and warm, and for a few hours Jay forgot about the house.

He forgot until he got home.

He set his grocery bags on the kitchen table and noticed the silence. Real silence, the kind the house had denied him since he arrived. He heated his beans, ate standing at the counter, thought about Grace’s laugh, Brandon’s scowl, Hughie’s ridiculous driving.

The kitchen tap turned on.

He had not touched it. He was on the other side of the room.

He crossed to the sink and reached for the handle — and then the bathroom tap started. Then the shower. Then the clawfoot tub, all the way down the hall. One after another, a sequence, almost like an introduction.

Jay stood very still.

He woke on the couch. The kitchen tap was dripping. Just dripping — he must have dozed off, left it running. He got up and turned it off.

Had he dreamed the rest?

The house was quiet. Not entirely — there were more drips. More than one. Getting louder. He stood at the base of the stairs and listened, and the sound resolved into rhythm, a pattern, almost like language he couldn’t quite parse.

The floor was wet.

Not flooded, not yet — just a thin sheen, as though the house was beginning to sweat. He took the stairs slowly. The bathroom door was ajar, darkness behind it, and he told himself he just needed to find the light switch and get a look at the pipes.

He reached through the gap. His fingers found the switch.

Something wet found his fingers first.

He hit the light and scrambled back, and what he saw before he hit the floor was a woman standing over the bathtub, her back to him, water pooling at her bare feet, hair hanging dark and heavy down her spine.

The light was still on when he got his eyes open. The bathroom floor was dry. The tub was empty. He sat on the tile for a long time before he went back to bed.

“A naked woman in your bathroom,” Brandon said flatly.

“I know what I saw.”

“Sure you do.” He leaned back in Grace’s kitchen chair, all performance. “You on something, city boy?”

They were having lunch at Grace’s — the whole group, plates of steak and salad, afternoon light coming through the windows. Jay had thought that saying it out loud would make it more real. It was having the opposite effect.

“The floor was dry when I checked it,” Jay admitted. “But there was a — I saw her. Standing over the tub.”

“What did she look like?” Alex asked, fork halfway to her mouth.

“Just her back. The hair. She was—” He stopped.

“Naked,” Hughie finished, amused.

“Yeah.”

“So your house has a ghost,” Grace said, not unkindly, “and she’s naked.”

Jay pushed back from the table. He was done. He stood and walked toward the door, and Grace was there before he reached it, a dish of something in her hands, the smell of grilled meat in the air.

“Hey. Where are you going?”

“I can’t take it in there.” He didn’t mean the ghost. He meant Brandon, the smirk, the city boy before every sentence like it explained everything.

Grace set down the dish. She didn’t say anything. She walked past him to the table, and the way she moved made everyone go quiet.

“Apologize,” she said to Brandon.

“For what? He comes in here with his haunted house story and his—”

She grabbed a fistful of his t-shirt over the table. Not hard, not threatening. Just present. “Apologize and make our guest comfortable.”

A beat. Brandon looked at Jay, then away. “Sorry. I was being an ass.”

The silence that followed was the ordinary kind — cutlery on plates, Hughie’s satisfied grunt, the small sounds of people eating. Alex broke it.

“So. I’ve actually heard things about that house.” She speared a piece of lettuce. “Your uncle was into some strange stuff.”

“What kind of strange stuff?” Jay asked.

“Occultism. Old texts. People said he was obsessed toward the end.” She looked at him carefully. “You knew?”

He’d known some of it. The last few times he’d spoken to Will, there’d been talk of primordial forces, of doorways, of opening something and letting something through. Jay had thought it was what happened when a retired doctor with too much time and too many books found himself alone in a house with no one to talk to.

He wasn’t as sure anymore.

He drove home to a dripping tap.

The sound hit him when he opened the door — one note in the silence, the house’s greeting. The living room floor was dry. He stood in the entryway and swept his phone light around and confirmed what he already somehow knew: the drip wasn’t coming from the kitchen, or the bathroom, or any of the places he’d already fixed.

It was coming from the basement.

He hadn’t been down there since he arrived. He found the door under the stairs, found the light switch that produced nothing, and went down with his phone in front of him, step by step, into the dark.

Water. His feet sank in before he registered it, cold through his socks, a good inch of it covering the floor. He swept the light around and stopped.

His flip-flop was floating toward him. He hadn’t left it down here. He hadn’t been down here.

Something else floated with it — a piece of paper, water-softened at the edges. He crouched and lifted it. The handwriting was his grandfather’s.

In the beginning, a beginning no religion will accept, there existed chaos. The waters were part of it. And someone existed in the waters—

The rest was torn away.

He didn’t hear it coming. Didn’t feel the presence until the hands were already on him, pressing down, and then his face was underwater and the cold was everywhere and he was fighting for his life against something that didn’t move like a person, something that held without strain, that breathed without sound.

He clawed. He punched. He got nowhere.

Then it simply let go.

He ran.

It was past one in the morning when Grace opened her door. She took one look at him — soaked, still shaking — and didn’t ask for an explanation.

“Come in.”

He called the police from her couch. They came, they searched, they found no sign of forced entry, no second person, no flood — just a minor puddle on the basement floor, maybe a slow leak in the foundation. They wrote it up that way.

Later, while Grace went to get him sheets, he made another call.

“This is Jayden Vile,” he said. “I’m following up on the autopsy for William Vile.”

He listened. He asked the woman to repeat herself. She did.

Drowning. Cause of death was drowning. In a bathtub with no water in it, in a house where the taps had been dripping for months before anyone noticed.

They came back to the house the next day — all five of them, because Grace had made the case and no one, not even Brandon, had been willing to let her go alone.

Will’s research filled two crates in the study. Grace worked through it while Hilda and Alex spread across the living room floor with laptops. Jay and Hughie pushed through box after box of notes.

The scope of it was larger than Jay had imagined. Sumerian tablets. Pre-flood mythology. The waters that existed before the world, before light, before form. The Lady of the Lake, traced not as Arthurian legend but as a fragment of something older — a spirit bound by Merlin to a specific purpose, drawn from waters that pre- dated the world, serving as an intermediary between the surface and what moved beneath it.

Will’s own notes were pressed between the pages. The ocean is not empty. The lake is not empty. The rain is not random. The mechanism is sound. The question is the door.

“He thought he could open something,” Grace said, looking up from a page covered in Will’s handwriting. “Let something through.”

“He was a doctor,” Jay said. “He believed in blood pressure readings and cholesterol levels. He was not the kind of man who opened portals.”

“He wasn’t, once,” Grace said quietly.

Hughie said, from across the room: “What changed him?”

No one had an answer.

The house settled into night. They ordered food, pulled chairs into a loose circle, let the silence do what it did. Alex had a documentary going low on her laptop. Hilda had fallen asleep against Brandon’s shoulder, which surprised everyone, including Brandon.

It had been quiet for a long time — genuinely quiet, no drip, no creak, no suggestion of presence — when Brandon said, to no one in particular: “Silent night, unholy night.”

No one knew what he meant. He pushed himself up off the floor. “Bathroom break.”

“Use the one downstairs,” Jay said.

Brandon gave him the look, and went upstairs.

The sound came a moment later.

A wet palm dragged slowly across a window pane — deliberate, like a greeting, like something making sure they could hear.

They looked at each other. No one spoke. The sound stopped.

They were still holding their breath when the toilet flushed and Brandon came out of the upstairs bathroom, wiping his hands on his shirt.

“Jesus,” he said, reading the room. “You all look like you’ve seen a—”

He stopped. He looked down. A thin line of water was threading across the floor from behind him. He turned.

She stood in the hallway. A figure, barefoot, dark hair hanging over her face and chest, skin that wasn’t any color Jay had a name for. She seemed almost still. Then one hand came up, and the drips began — one drop, two, a slow building rhythm that Jay felt somewhere behind his sternum.

Brandon barely made a sound. She grabbed him by the face and took him through the bathroom door, which shut behind them, and the screaming lasted only seconds before it stopped.

No one moved for a long time.

“What just happened,” Hughie said. It wasn’t a question.

The drips resumed, louder now, from everywhere at once. Jay’s feet were wet. He looked down: they were standing in water, somehow, an inch of it, though he couldn’t say when it had appeared. The lights died.

Grace’s phone flashlight swept the floor. It caught Brandon’s face just beneath the surface, eyes open, completely still. Somewhere in the dark, Alex screamed — and then stopped, the way sounds stop when something removes them.

They made for the stairs. Dry ground. Jay swept the upstairs hall with his light, everything still, bathroom flickering on and off. He moved toward it and saw, through the half-open master bedroom door, two figures in the bathroom: one holding the other face-down in the tub, the held one barely struggling. He ran in and threw himself at the attacker and went through it like it was made of cold air.

He turned around. Hilda was on the floor in the bedroom, water coming up from her mouth in small waves, her hands reaching for something she couldn’t reach.

By the time they crossed to her, she was still.

Alex was on the bed. Had been there the whole time, they realized, laid out neatly, soaked through, eyes open.

Hughie stood beside Jay at the foot of the bed, both of them looking at what the room had become. Grace was behind them, very quiet.

“We need to—” Hughie started.

The hand came from under the bed. It found his ankle, and he jumped sideways onto the mattress, and looked down, and said her name — Hilda — before Jay realized what he was seeing. She was there. Beneath the bed, in the water, staring up at nothing.

Hughie sat on the edge of the mattress, the mattress now soaked, and put his head in his hands.

Jay went to the bathtub. He couldn’t have explained what he was doing. He knelt beside it, the water still, and put his ear close to the surface.

“Jay.” Grace touched his shoulder. Hughie looked up.

“I should listen,” Jay said. He wasn’t sure why he said it. It had come to him the way the shape of a word sometimes comes before the meaning — instinctive, preceding sense.

He leaned in.

There was nothing. Then there was something. A sound below hearing, below frequency, a pressure in the inner ear that wasn’t sound at all but that he understood the way you understand a dream while still inside it.

Hughie made a sound that was less than a word.

Jay turned.

Alex was standing in the room. Not the Alex that had been on the bed — this one was upright, facing them, hair streaming, and she moved with the wrong kind of patience. She caught Hughie by the back of the head and broke him the way a storm breaks a branch, and then she was gone, and Hughie was on the floor.

Grace was against the wall, shaking visibly. Jay was between her and the door. They both knew what it meant that they were the last two.

Something stepped through the wall behind Grace.

It was feminine, or had been, or was wearing the shape of it. Pale gray, green-black hair matted to its neck and shoulders. Where a face should have been, there was — absence. Not a blank surface, not damage. Absence. Jay’s mind refused to hold the image. He looked directly at it and it kept escaping the edges of his attention.

He tried to move and found he couldn’t.

It put its hands on Grace’s shoulders, almost gently, and the floor opened beneath her — not in any physical way, just: the floor was there and then it wasn’t, and Grace was in it, and he could hear her but couldn’t see her, her hands grasping for the edge of something he couldn’t perceive, and then that sound too was gone.

Jay stood alone in the room.

The dripping had stopped.

He crossed to the bathtub — still full, still still. He didn’t know why he did it. He was past the point of knowing why. He swung one leg over the edge, then the other, and lowered himself into the water, and the cold of it moved through him like a second skeleton.

He thought about his uncle. He thought about the page from the basement, the torn edge, the words that ended mid-sentence. The waters were part of it. And someone existed in the waters—

He let himself sink until the water closed over his ears. The house sounds muffled, then vanished. In their place: that pressure again, that frequency below sound. He lay there and let it come.

You could drown , he thought. You could just drown.

But he kept listening.

In the morning, sunlight came through the bathroom window at a low angle and turned the water gold. The house was dry. Every floor, every pipe, every tile — dry, and silent, and completely still.

The bathtub was empty.

The wet handprint on the downstairs window was still there. Three of them had seen it. The police, when they were called again, photographed it and said nothing.

Will’s notes remained in their crates. The torn page from the basement had been placed — carefully, it seemed, almost deliberately — on the kitchen table. The torn edge faced up.

The last line, before the tearing: And someone existed in the waters—

Whoever had brought it up from the basement had smoothed it flat.

As if they wanted it read.

chapters.title: Under
chapters.text:
Item recovered — chain of custody incomplete

The bed was six inches from the floor. Marcus had measured it once, for no reason he could explain now — six inches, the width of his hand laid flat. Not enough for a cat. Not enough for anything.

He lay rigid, staring at the ceiling, the sheet bunched at his chin despite the heat.

Something moved.

He told himself: the house settling. Pipes. The particular complaints of old wood in an older building. He had a catalogue of excuses by now. He’d been using them for three weeks.

Then came the growl.

Low, almost polite. Like something that didn’t want to be noticed yet.

His phone was on the nightstand. Mom would answer on the second ring, no matter the hour. She kept a list of scriptures folded in her Bible specifically for nights like this — she’d told him once, laughing, though neither of them had laughed very hard.

He reached for the phone.

The growl came again, directly beneath him. Closer to the surface now, as if something had risen through the mattress springs like smoke.

His fingers found the phone. The bed shifted. Just slightly. Just enough.

Not like something crawling under it.

Like something pressing up.

He dialed. It rang once. The room went very cold. His mother answered on the second ring, the way she always did — but before she could speak, Marcus heard the sound again, right beside his ear now.

Still quiet. Still patient.

Still waiting.

chapters.title: The Casket Walker
chapters.text:
✦

a verse, told the way old forests keep their dead

On a night cold enough to hear bones, Through the dark

wood he trudges and moans, A casket on back, Through

the moonlit-cracked black, And the forest just shudders

and groans.

Skin as dry as the cracked desert clay, Like a reptile

preserved from decay, He mumbles and creeps, As the

whole forest sleeps, His tall shadow stretched long in the

grey.

“A dead man will never tell tales!” He hisses beneath the

night gales, Step after slow step, His grim secret is kept,

As the moonlight grows thin where it pales.

Where he walks, not a living soul knows, Through the

black where no lantern light glows, But woe unto thee

Who dares follow and see — Your grave shall be shallow

as those.

In the dark he will turn, fix your eyes, And you’ll scream

but the scream only dies, For the last thing you’ll feel Is

that cold dark reveal, As your shallow grave quietly lies.

✦ ✦ ✦ ✦
